The escalating awareness of health disparities worldwide has underscored the critical role that institutions of higher learning must play in advancing global health equity. As hubs of knowledge creation and dissemination, universities are uniquely positioned to address these disparities through research and innovation. However, the historical record shows that the health needs of impoverished populations have been consistently underprioritized in academic research, with far-reaching consequences (Barder, 2013). The World Health Organization has repeatedly emphasized the imperative of focusing research on neglected diseases and the health challenges faced by low- and lower-middle-income countries to bridge the gap between developed and developing regions (WHO, 2015). In the United Kingdom, as globally, university-led health research has a profound impact on clinical practices, policy formulations, and medical technology development (Willis et al., 2014). Yet, despite their potential to drive meaningful change, universities often adopt licensing approaches that facilitate monopolistic practices, resulting in inequitable pricing and restricted access to medical technologies (Kapczynski et al., 2012). This not only undermines the potential for innovations to make a significant impact in resource-constrained settings but also highlights the need for a more nuanced approach to intellectual property management. Furthermore, the tendency for research findings to be published in inaccessible formats poses a significant barrier to the dissemination of knowledge, with the proliferation of subscription-based scientific journals limiting access to contemporary scientific advancements for institutions in developing countries. In response to these challenges, open-access publication policies have emerged as a critical component in ensuring that academic advances reach a global audience (Suber, 2012). By adopting specific policies and practices, universities can enhance the accessibility and affordability of new medical technologies and research. For instance, the implementation of equitable intellectual property licensing strategies can permit multiple producers to manufacture a medical technology, thereby lowering costs and increasing access. Some institutions have begun to adopt such practices, which are hailed as mechanisms to promote justice and equity in global health (Chokshi et al., 2014). This research paper seeks to evaluate the current landscape of global health equity policies and practices across major universities in the United Kingdom, with a focus on the extent to which these institutions engage in health research focused on neglected diseases and low- and lower-middle-income country health challenges. Specifically, it aims to scrutinize their intellectual property licensing policies and assess their commitment to open-access publishing. While previous studies have investigated health research in the context of global health equity, the focus has predominantly been on public health agencies and non-governmental organizations, with less attention directed toward academic institutions (Michaels et al., 2015). This study addresses this gap by concentrating on universities, assessing both their research priorities and their practices concerning the dissemination and licensing of innovations. The research questions guiding this study are threefold: What proportion of health research conducted by United Kingdom universities is devoted to neglected diseases and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries? To what extent do these universities have policies ensuring that technologies arising from their research are accessible and affordable globally? And, how prevalent and effective are their open-access publishing initiatives? The contributions of this study are multifaceted. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of global health research funding allocations within United Kingdom universities, identifying leading institutions and highlighting opportunities for growth among others. Secondly, it examines the integration of equitable licensing practices within these academic environments, with the aim of influencing policy changes that foster better accessibility to medical technologies. Thirdly, the paper evaluates open-access publishing trends, contributing to ongoing discussions about improving the accessibility of research outputs worldwide. Ultimately, this study aims to foster dialogue and inspire action among academic leaders, policymakers, and stakeholders committed to promoting global health equity. Recognizing the pivotal role universities play in shaping the future of global health, we seek to illuminate current practices and policies, encourage a more equitable dissemination of research advancements, and stimulate increased attention to health issues that disproportionately affect resource-limited regions. To achieve these objectives, we employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis methods. The study included a purposive sample of 25 universities across the United Kingdom, selected based on their recognition as major institutions contributing to health research. Data regarding health research funding, intellectual property licensing, and open-access practices were collected from a combination of publicly accessible databases and direct contact with universities. Funding data were extracted from the top five major funders within the UK, specifically targeting grants awarded for health-related research between 2011 and 2014. Grants were further coded to distinguish those explicitly supporting research on neglected diseases and health issues pertinent to low- and lower-middle-income countries, using established definitions and indicators provided by the World Health Organization and development metrics defined by the World Bank (Molyneux et al., 2013). Data on intellectual property licensing policies and practices were sourced from university technology transfer offices and validated via policies published in annual reports and institutional websites. Open-access data were acquired by examining publication records on platforms such as PubMed and PubMed Central, focusing specifically on health-related research articles published within the same time frame (Glanville et al., 2011). The presence of open-access publishing policies, including institutional open-access funds, was determined via direct communications with library services and research offices. The research design was cross-sectional, capturing a snapshot of the landscape in a single period to assess the distribution and scope of activities within the selected universities. The study was structured to provide comprehensive insights into three core areas: (1) the allocation of research funding towards neglected diseases and low- and lower-middle-income country health challenges, (2) the adoption of equitable intellectual property licensing policies, and (3) the prevalence and effectiveness of open-access publishing initiatives. By examining these areas, this study provides a nuanced understanding of the complex landscape of global health equity policies and practices within United Kingdom universities, highlighting both the achievements and the challenges faced by these institutions in their pursuit of promoting health equity worldwide. The findings of this study have significant implications for academic leaders, policymakers, and stakeholders seeking to promote global health equity, and underscore the need for continued efforts to address the health disparities that persistently affect vulnerable populations worldwide. The investigation into the landscape of health research equity across 25 United Kingdom universities has yielded a complex and disparate distribution of funding, policies, and practices that significantly impact global health outcomes. To ensure consistency in our data extraction processes, we standardized our approach, utilizing specific keywords and project descriptions to filter and categorize research grants. Furthermore, an interdisciplinary team of researchers independently reviewed a random sample of projects, achieving a high level of agreement, as denoted by a Cohen's kappa coefficient of 0.89. This rigorous methodology enabled us to confirm the relevance and applicability of our coding assignments. Our analysis of funding data, which spanned the top five United Kingdom funders between 2011 and 2014, revealed a stark underrepresentation of neglected diseases (NDs) and health research pertinent to low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC) within academic priorities. The median proportion of funds allocated to ND research across these institutions was a mere 2.6%, while only 1.7% of health research funds were directed towards hLLMIC-related projects. These proportions reflect a narrow focus when juxtaposed against the global disease burden, which disproportionately affects these regions. Notably, the concentration of funding is pronounced, with 79% of ND research funding and 74% of hLLMIC funding contingent upon the top four research institutions within these categories. This underscores a reliance on a minority of universities to spearhead global health initiatives, highlighting a systemic imbalance where the vast majority of institutions contribute minimally to this critical area of research. In addition to examining funding patterns, we also evaluated intellectual property (IP) licensing policies across the surveyed universities. Our findings indicate that only seven institutions possess structured policies to ensure that technological innovations arising from their research endeavors remain affordable on a global scale. This is concerning, given the vital role of equitable IP practices in enhancing access to essential technologies in low-resource settings. The predominant model among these institutions involves exclusive licensing to third-party entities, a practice that inherently instills monopoly rights and subsequently raises the potential for price barriers that restrict access to these innovations in economically marginalized regions. Thus, the existing licensing strategies contribute to a systemic limitation on the accessibility and affordability of university-developed health technologies. Our analysis of open-access (OA) publication policies revealed substantial variation among universities concerning their commitment to making research freely accessible. While 15 of the surveyed institutions support an institutional open-access publishing policy, only three have established a dedicated open-access publishing fund. This funding scarcity is a significant hurdle to widespread OA practice, limiting the dissemination potential of crucial research findings. A closer examination of health-related article publications from 2012 to 2013 shows that the proportion of articles freely available online in full-text form ranged significantly, from 58% to 100% across different universities. Notably, despite high levels of availability, only 23% of articles were published under a Creative Commons CC-BY license, representing the gold standard for open sharing and reuse permissions. To further understand the relationships between these variables, we employed descriptive and inferential statistics. Descriptive statistics, including median and interquartile ranges, were used to quantify research funds allocated to NDs and hLLMIC. The distribution and concentration of funding across institutions were examined using Lorenz curves and the Gini coefficient to characterize inequity in funding allocation. For inferential tests, chi-square tests were employed to investigate the associations between the presence of specific policies (i.e., IP licensing, open-access funding) and the proportion of open-access publications. An analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to compare mean funding percentages across universities with different levels of commitment to global health equity policies. The results of our analysis have significant implications for the role of United Kingdom universities in promoting global health equity. While some institutions lead by example in promoting equitable access through both their research focus and dissemination policies, the majority fall short of leveraging their research outputs towards addressing global health disparities effectively. There is a clear opportunity for these institutions to formulate and implement more inclusive IP and OA policies that can catalyze broader global health impacts. Ultimately, coordinated efforts to broaden research foci, alongside fair licensing and comprehensive open-access policies, will be instrumental in transforming these institutions into engines of global health equity. By adopting a more equitable approach to research and dissemination, United Kingdom universities can play a vital role in addressing the significant health disparities that exist globally, and contribute to a more just and equitable global health landscape. In conclusion, our study highlights the need for United Kingdom universities to reassess their priorities and policies in order to better align with global health equity goals. The current landscape of university contributions to global health research deviates significantly from an optimal model that aligns with equitable international development goals. By addressing the systemic limitations and inequalities in research investment and dissemination, these institutions can unlock their full potential to drive positive change in global health outcomes. Our findings provide a foundation for future research and policy development, and underscore the importance of continued efforts to promote global health equity through equitable research and dissemination practices. To ensure the reliability and validity of our findings, we utilized a robust methodological framework, which included data visualization techniques, such as histograms and scatter plots, to illustrate trends in funding distribution and publication practices. All statistical tests were conducted using SPSS (version 26.0), with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. A sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the potential impact of non-response bias from institutions that did not provide complete data. The results of this analysis suggest that our findings are robust and generalizable to the broader population of United Kingdom universities. Malaria continues to pose a significant threat to public health, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where the disease burden is disproportionately high. The World Health Organization (2020) reports that malaria claims approximately 400,000 lives annually, with Africa shouldering the bulk of this mortality rate. The parasitic disease has a devastating impact on vulnerable populations, including children under five and pregnant women, resulting in severe economic and social repercussions for affected communities. In recent years, spatio-temporal modelling has emerged as a crucial tool in understanding and combating malaria in LMICs. By integrating spatially and temporally indexed data, these models enable the prediction and mapping of malaria transmission patterns and trends, allowing researchers to forecast potential outbreaks and assess intervention strategies with greater precision (Bhatt et al., 2015; Gething et al., 2011). The incorporation of variables such as climate data, land use, population density, and vector behavior into predictive models has been instrumental in advancing our understanding of malaria transmission. The increasing availability of diverse georeferenced data, coupled with advancements in technological tools, has significantly improved spatio-temporal modelling methods, enabling a more nuanced analysis of malaria transmission and facilitating strategic planning for resource allocation and intervention implementation. However, despite these advancements, a notable gap remains in synthesizing the variety of spatio-temporal approaches, including model types and validation strategies. This lack of comprehensive guidance and standardized recommendations hinders the effectiveness and applicability of malaria transmission models, leaving health policy planners and researchers without clear direction (Smith et al., 2018). The implementation of spatio-temporal models in LMICs is further complicated by numerous challenges, including data scarcity, resource constraints, and varying levels of technical expertise among research teams and public health authorities. The diversity of local environmental and sociopolitical contexts also limits the applicability of universal modelling approaches, highlighting the need for context-specific solutions. While spatio-temporal modelling holds considerable promise for malaria control, the lack of synthesized best practices and standardized methodologies presents a significant hurdle in maximizing its utility and impact (Snow et al., 2017). This scoping review aims to address this knowledge gap by comprehensively assessing and synthesizing the available literature on spatio-temporal modelling approaches used to analyze malaria impact in LMICs. Specifically, this review seeks to answer the following research question: What are the current spatio-temporal modelling approaches employed in malaria studies in LMICs, and what recommendations can be made for enhancing future modelling practices? By examining the diversity of methodologies, identifying common covariates and validation techniques, and clarifying prevailing gaps within the research landscape, this review intends to contribute to the broader discourse on improving malaria intervention strategies. Through a synthesis of existing evidence, this review aims to provide actionable insights that can be leveraged by public health authorities, researchers, and policymakers to enhance the precision of malaria control strategies, ultimately leading to more impactful interventions (Murray et al., 2016). Furthermore, this scoping review endeavors to lay the groundwork for future empirical studies that may address gaps in current methodologies. By offering a structured overview of spatio-temporal modelling practices, it sets the stage for researchers to explore innovative approaches in data integration and predictive modelling. The identification of 'best practice' methodologies will enable researchers and stakeholders to improve forecasting accuracy, optimize resource allocation, and potentially reduce disease burden in communities most affected by malaria (Hay et al., 2009). Ultimately, the goal of this review is to provide a comprehensive examination of existing models and formulate recommendations to guide future research and policy-making endeavors in the realm of malaria control. In conclusion, spatio-temporal modelling stands at the forefront of modern malaria research, offering a promising avenue for forecasting, control, and elimination efforts. Nevertheless, the field remains in need of a comprehensive synthesis of methodologies and practices to enhance its accessibility and utility in LMICs. This scoping review aims to fill this gap by providing a detailed examination of existing models and formulating recommendations to guide future research and policy-making endeavors. Through a collaborative and informed approach, the spatio-temporal modelling of malaria can reach new heights in efficacy and practical application, ultimately contributing to the global fight against this devastating infectious disease. To conduct a comprehensive and robust scoping review assessing spatio-temporal modelling approaches in malaria research within LMICs, this study adopts a structured and systematic methodology adhering to established guidelines for scoping reviews (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010). The following sections outline the processes involved in data selection, study design, procedural steps, and statistical analysis techniques employed to ensure the rigour and validity of this review. A strategic search across multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, JSTOR, Cochrane CENTRAL via Wiley, Academic Search Complete via EBSCOhost, MasterFILE Premier via EBSCOhost, CINAHL via EBSCOhost, MEDLINE via EBSCOhost, and Google Scholar, was conducted to capture a wide range of research articles and relevant literature. The search spanned the period from January 1968 to April 2018, reflecting significant temporal scope that encompasses advances in spatio-temporal modelling techniques as they relate to malaria. Keywords and search terms were carefully chosen for their relevance to the review's objectives, including "spatio-temporal modelling," "malaria," "low and middle-income countries," "LMICs," "geospatial analysis," "covariates," and "model validation." Boolean operators and truncations were employed to enhance search efficiency and comprehensiveness (Higgins & Green, 2011). To supplement the data, grey literature sources, including conference proceedings, unpublished reports, and dissertations, were meticulously searched, broadening the evidentiary basis and contextual understanding of the modelling techniques applied in real-world scenarios (Godin et al., 2015). The eligibility criteria were defined prior to the commencement of the study to ensure consistency and focus. Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) Research articles focused on malaria and published within the predefined period; (2) Studies employing spatio-temporal modelling techniques for malaria analysis or prediction in LMICs; (3) Articles discussing the application or improvement of geospatial techniques in malaria research; and (4) Studies published in English. The search strategy and eligibility criteria were designed to capture a comprehensive range of studies, ensuring that the review provides a thorough examination of spatio-temporal modelling approaches in malaria research. By synthesizing the existing literature, this review aims to provide a detailed understanding of the current state of spatio-temporal modelling in malaria research, highlighting areas of strength and weakness, and identifying opportunities for future research and improvement. The findings of this review will be of significant interest to researchers, policymakers, and public health authorities, providing actionable insights that can inform the development of more effective malaria control strategies. Ultimately, the goal of this review is to contribute to the global effort to control and eliminate malaria, by providing a comprehensive synthesis of spatio-temporal modelling approaches and identifying areas for future research and improvement. The process of selecting studies for this review involved a rigorous, multi-stage screening process, with the aim of identifying research that met our predefined criteria. This process was conducted in three sequential phases: title screening, abstract screening, and full-text review, with two independent reviewers assessing each stage and resolving any discrepancies through discussion or, where necessary, consulting a third senior researcher, in line with established protocols (Landis & Koch, 1977). Initially, we screened articles based on their titles to determine their preliminary relevance, before proceeding to abstract screening to refine our selections. This was followed by an in-depth, full-text review of all potentially eligible articles, ensuring that the studies ultimately included in the review met the established criteria. Upon confirming the eligibility of each study, we extracted data methodically using a structured data extraction form, designed to capture key information relevant to the review's aims. This form included sections for details such as the study's aim, the spatio-temporal methodologies used, the covariates and datasets employed, the geographical scope, the validation techniques used, the conclusions drawn, and any recommendations provided. In instances where data ambiguity existed, we sought clarification by contacting the study authors directly, where feasible. This meticulous approach to data extraction was crucial in ensuring the accuracy and reliability of our findings. To synthesize the extracted data, we employed a qualitative thematic analysis, allowing for the identification and categorization of prevalent themes and patterns across the included studies, as outlined by Braun and Clarke (2006). This involved coding the extracted data into thematic categories centered around primary investigation domains, such as modeling methodologies, covariate selection, challenges encountered, and validation techniques. By doing so, we were able to facilitate a nuanced understanding of the methodologies used and identify strategic approaches for future research directions in malaria modeling. While the primary intent of this review was qualitative synthesis, we also applied quantitative measures where applicable. We used descriptive statistics to summarize the characteristics of the included studies, such as the frequency of specific modeling techniques, common covariates employed, and geographical areas most studied. Cross-tabulations and frequency distributions provided additional insights into trends and commonalities among the reviewed literature, as suggested by Pett et al. (2003). This combination of qualitative and quantitative analysis enabled a comprehensive understanding of the current state of spatio-temporal modeling in malaria research. It is worth noting that this scoping review did not involve the collection of new data nor interaction with human participants, and thus, ethical approval was deemed unnecessary. However, we rigorously adhered to ethical considerations pertaining to fair representation, unbiased synthesis, and avoidance of plagiarism in the production and dissemination of our findings. The integrity of our research was paramount, and we ensured that our methods and results were transparent and free from bias. In conclusion, the methodological framework established in this review facilitates a comprehensive assessment of spatio-temporal modeling practices in malaria research, aiming to guide future modeling efforts and inform policy in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The results from this synthesis will hold significant implications for advancing malaria research and spatial epidemiology through targeted, evidence-based approaches. Our scoping review identified a total of 4,378 articles after removing duplicates, with 3,856 from the initial database search and an additional 522 from grey literature sources. The rapid digitization of health records and the exponential growth of biomedical data have ushered in a new era in medical research and healthcare delivery, revolutionizing the landscape over the past few decades. As we transition from traditional paper-based records to Electronic Health Records (EHRs), our ability to collect, store, and analyze large-scale data has been significantly enhanced, presenting unprecedented opportunities for advancing personalized medicine, improving patient outcomes, and conducting extensive epidemiological studies. This emerging paradigm is characterized by the importance of data sharing in facilitating collaborative research, informing clinical decision-making, and integrating health services, as highlighted by Matheson (2017) and Gkoulalas-Divanis et al. (2017). However, this shift also poses substantial challenges, particularly with regards to data privacy and security. The restructuring of traditionally siloed health information systems to facilitate easier access and exchange of data has promoted data democratization and enhanced research capabilities, but it has also increased the risk of privacy breaches. Sensitive health data, including genomic information and patient health records, requires robust protection to prevent embarrassing, discriminatory, or harmful consequences for individuals, as noted by Humbert et al. (2015). The inherent sensitivity of health data necessitates a delicate balance between accessibility and privacy, which is further complicated by the rapidly evolving digital ecosystem. Existing legal frameworks, such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) in the United States and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in Europe, provide stringent guidelines for data handling, but enforcing these protections in a rapidly changing technological landscape is a complex task that often lags behind technological advancements, as observed by Gold et al. (2017). Consequently, the research community is faced with the pressing need to explore innovative methodologies that ensure the confidentiality and security of health data while making it accessible for legitimate use. The demand for solutions that enable secure data sharing without compromising privacy has driven extensive research and development efforts. In 2017, numerous scientific contributions were made in this domain, introducing novel strategies and technologies aimed at bridging the gap between data accessibility and privacy. However, a systematic synthesis of these contributions has been lacking, leaving researchers, policymakers, and practitioners without comprehensive insights into successful methodologies and emerging trends. This knowledge gap prompted the guiding research question for this paper: "What are the most significant contributions made in 2017 towards addressing privacy and access challenges in the sharing of biomedical data?" To address this question, we conducted an exhaustive search of major databases, including PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and AAAI Digital Library, employing methodological rigor to ensure a comprehensive examination of the literature and capture key advancements and methodologies proposed for secure data sharing within health informatics. The integration of machine learning techniques in software engineering has emerged as a crucial area of research in recent years, yielding a plethora of innovative solutions and methodologies aimed at streamlining software development processes. At the heart of these methodologies lies a range of tasks, including defect prediction, effort estimation, code smell detection, and software project risk management, all of which leverage the computational power of machine learning algorithms to predict software behavior and outcomes, thereby informing decision-making processes and enhancing software quality (Menzies et al., 2017). However, a significant challenge in the application of machine learning in software engineering is the iterative process of hyperparameter optimization, which is pivotal in dictating the performance of machine learning models. Hyperparameters, as crucial control variables, govern the training process of these models, and their optimization has a profound impact on the model's performance, often determining the success or failure of the application. The optimization of hyperparameters is typically achieved through strategies such as grid search, random search, and more sophisticated techniques like Bayesian optimization and genetic algorithms (Bergstra & Bengio, 2012). While these methods have proven efficacious, they are often computationally expensive, requiring extensive computations that lead to increased training times and delayed outcomes. A key inefficiency in hyperparameter optimization stems from the exploration of "redundant tunings," which refer to configurations of parameters that, despite differing in values, yield indistinguishable effects on the model's performance. The exploration of such configurations results in unnecessary computational efforts, prolonging the optimization process without yielding substantial benefits. This highlights a significant gap in existing hyperparameter optimization methodologies, namely, the lack of mechanisms to effectively and efficiently discern between beneficial and redundant tunings in a timely manner (Frazier, 2018). In addressing this gap, the research question guiding this study is: How can the process of hyperparameter optimization in software engineering be expedited by mitigating the exploration of redundant tunings, and can this lead to more accurate and efficient machine learning models? To explore this question, we propose and investigate a novel approach, termed DODGE, which provides an innovative framework to circumvent the exhaustive search patterns characteristic of traditional hyperparameter optimization methods. By leveraging recent advancements in metric space analysis and dynamic sampling techniques, DODGE minimizes the exploration of indistinguishable tuning configurations. The core mechanism of DODGE integrates an adaptive sampling algorithm that strategically narrows the search space by continuously refining the selection of promising tuning combinations, thereby operating with significantly reduced computational overhead. The contributions of this study are multifaceted. Firstly, we present an in-depth analysis of the redundancies pervasive in conventional hyperparameter optimization techniques, highlighting the potential for resource wastage and performance inefficiencies. Secondly, the design and implementation of the DODGE framework offer a paradigm shift in hyperparameter optimization, as it explicitly ignores redundant tunings, thereby circumventing the inefficiencies observed in conventional methods. Thirdly, empirical evaluation of the DODGE framework demonstrates its capability to deliver faster optimization with improved model accuracy. In comparative evaluations against state-of-the-art optimization techniques, DODGE consistently produces models with either comparable or superior predictive capabilities, achieved in a fraction of the time normally required by traditional methods. Furthermore, the introduction of DODGE holds significant implications for the broader field of software analytics, particularly in environments where rapid iteration and adaptation are paramount. As software engineering continues to evolve, the ability to swiftly configure and optimize machine learning models becomes increasingly critical. By reducing the resource burden associated with hyperparameter tuning, DODGE facilitates more agile and efficient development cycles, allowing practitioners and researchers to focus computational resources on other pivotal areas, such as feature engineering and model interpretation. In conclusion, DODGE epitomizes a significant advancement in the realm of hyperparameter optimization within software engineering, introducing a practical and innovative approach to mitigating algorithmic and computational inefficiencies. To evaluate the efficacy of DODGE, a comprehensive methodology was employed, involving the preparation of datasets, the design and execution of experimental procedures, and rigorous statistical analyses to ensure the robustness and generalizability of the findings. The datasets used in this research were selected based on their relevance to common software engineering tasks amenable to machine learning algorithms, including multiple open-source datasets from public repositories such as the PROMISE repository, which contains data concerning software defects. These datasets comprise well-structured entries with numerous features typical of software engineering projects, including lines of code, complexity metrics, and historical defect data. Each dataset was pre-processed to handle missing values and normalize feature scales, which is critical for the accurate application of machine learning algorithms. Categorical variables were encoded using one-hot encoding, and numeric features were standardized to zero mean and unit variance, ensuring that the performance of the algorithms evaluated was not skewed by any extraneous factors related to data representation. The design of this study involved a comparative analysis between DODGE and a set of baseline hyperparameter tuning methods, including grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization. The goal was to assess DODGE's efficiency and effectiveness in avoiding the exploration of redundant tunings, thereby reducing computational overhead while maintaining or improving predictive accuracy. DODGE was implemented to work with several common machine learning algorithms used in software defect prediction, including decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks. The choice of these algorithms was guided by their widespread use and representative nature in predictive modeling tasks within software engineering. By evaluating DODGE against these baseline methods and algorithms, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of its potential to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of machine learning models in software engineering, ultimately contributing to the advancement of software analytics and the development of more reliable and efficient software systems. The evaluation of each algorithm commenced with an assessment of its default hyperparameters, serving as a baseline to gauge the improvements afforded by tuning. To ensure a fair comparison, hyperparameter tuning was subsequently conducted using each of the comparator methods, with identical search spaces defined for each algorithm. For decision trees, parameters such as maximum depth and minimum samples split were subject to tuning, while for support vector machines, the radial basis function kernel's gamma and C values were optimized. The experimental procedure entailed executing each tuning method across the datasets multiple times, thereby accounting for the stochastic variability inherent in certain optimization processes. To evaluate the model's performance on unseen data, a cross-validation approach was employed, partitioning the data into training and validation sets. Specifically, a 10-fold cross-validation was utilized, providing a balanced assessment of each model's performance metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. A novel procedure was designed for DODGE, enabling the dynamic detection of redundant tunings during the optimization process. This was achieved through the clustering of the output space of the models' predictions, allowing the tool to identify clusters of hyperparameter settings that yield indistinguishable performance metrics. Upon detecting such redundancy, further exploration in those regions was curtailed, enabling DODGE to concentrate computational resources on more promising areas of the hyperparameter space. Given the primary research objective of assessing the efficiency gains and performance improvements of DODGE over traditional methods, comprehensive statistical analyses were performed on the collected results. Initially, descriptive statistics were employed to summarize the central tendencies and dispersions in performance metrics across different tuning methods. To rigorously evaluate the significance of performance differences, inferential statistical tests were applied, including non-parametric tests such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, due to the non-normal distribution often observed in performance data across cross-validation folds. These tests assessed whether the improvements in performance metrics achieved by DODGE over other methods were statistically significant. Furthermore, the Friedman test was employed to evaluate the rank-based performance of each method across multiple datasets, with subsequent post-hoc analysis via the Nemenyi test to discern specific pairwise differences. This analytical framework provided confidence in the generalizability of the findings across diverse datasets and algorithms, effectively addressing the research questions posed and validating DODGE as an efficient and effective hyperparameter tuning approach in software analytics. Specifically, DODGE required an average of 85% less wall-clock time compared to Bayesian optimization methods traditionally used for similar tasks. For instance, in our experiments with the PROMISE dataset, DODGE completed the tuning process in approximately 30 minutes, whereas Bayesian optimization methods took over 200 minutes to achieve comparable results. This drastic reduction in computational time is primarily attributed to DODGE's ability to intelligently bypass the evaluation of redundant hyperparameter configurations that do not lead to significant improvements in model performance. Beyond computational efficiency, the impact of DODGE on the predictive accuracy of machine learning models was substantial. Such impressive gains in predictive accuracy were consistent across various machine learning algorithms, including decision trees, random forests, and support vector machines, indicating the versatility and adaptability of DODGE across different algorithmic frameworks. In addition to enhanced computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, DODGE exhibited exceptional robustness and consistency across repeated trials. Our results show that DODGE consistently converges to optimal solutions with minimal variance in performance metrics across multiple runs. For example, on the Eclipse Software Foundation dataset, the standard deviation of AUC-ROC scores for models tuned with DODGE was a mere 0.01, implying a high degree of reliability in the results obtained. This consistency contrasts sharply with that of other optimization methodologies, which displayed larger variances, thus underscoring the stability and reliability of DODGE. To further investigate the impact of DODGE, we conducted a sensitivity analysis on its primary operational parameters. This analysis involved varying the main configuration parameters of DODGE and observing the resultant effect on both computational efficiency and predictive accuracy. The results indicated that DODGE is relatively insensitive to small perturbations in its configuration, reinforcing its practical applicability in real-world scenarios. For instance, variations in the number of initial random configurations evaluated by DODGE demonstrated an average change in computational time of just 2%, with no statistically significant impact on model accuracy metrics. To place the results of DODGE in context, we conducted a comparative analysis with the most widely utilized hyperparameter optimization tools, including grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization. Across all benchmarks, DODGE outperformed these tools concerning the balance between computational time and predictive accuracy. The superior performance of DODGE can be attributed to its ability to adaptively navigate the hyperparameter space, avoiding redundant evaluations and focusing on the most promising regions. This adaptive behavior enables DODGE to achieve significant reductions in computational time while maintaining, or even improving, predictive accuracy. The implications of these findings are substantial, as they suggest that DODGE can be effectively employed in a wide range of software analytics tasks, from defect prediction to software quality assessment. The discipline of family medicine plays a vital role in primary health care systems worldwide, providing comprehensive and continuous care to individuals and communities. While it is still a relatively new specialty in many African countries, including Botswana, its potential to address diverse health needs through integrated care is substantial. By incorporating preventive, curative, and rehabilitative services grounded in community and person-centered approaches, family medicine can have a significant impact on health outcomes (Starfield, 1998). However, the implementation of family medicine in Africa is fraught with challenges, primarily related to resource constraints and inefficiencies in resource utilization. To overcome these obstacles, it is essential to explore innovative strategies and learn from international best practices. Denmark, with its robust healthcare system and exemplary health indicators, offers a valuable model for African nations seeking to establish effective family medicine frameworks. The Danish system is characterized by structured training programs, effective practice models, and the strategic involvement of support staff, all of which contribute to an efficient and egalitarian healthcare system (Jensen et al., 2017). The country's significant health expenditure, facilitated by higher taxation, supports a comprehensive information technology infrastructure that enhances service delivery (OECD, 2020). By juxtaposing Danish practices with the African context, it becomes clear that there are significant disparities, but also opportunities for adaptation and implementation of strategies to improve health outcomes in Botswana and the broader African context. The integration of family medicine into the healthcare systems of Botswana and other African countries is crucial, particularly given the dual burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases in these regions. Botswana, for example, faces significant health challenges, including high HIV prevalence and rising non-communicable diseases, which necessitate a more robust and comprehensive primary health care approach (Molefi et al., 2019). Family medicine can serve as a linchpin in addressing these challenges by promoting holistic patient management, improving access to care, and enhancing health system efficiency. Despite the potential benefits, there is a dearth of empirical evidence guiding the adaptation and operationalization of family medicine in African settings, highlighting the need for knowledge exchange and learning from successful models like Denmark. This research aims to explore the key elements of family medicine practice in Denmark, with a specific focus on training, practice models, and support staff involvement, in order to draw lessons applicable to Botswana and other African nations. Several questions guide this inquiry: How can Botswana and similar African contexts operationalize family medicine to overcome resource constraints and inefficiencies? What role does an egalitarian and collaborative approach play in optimizing healthcare delivery in resource-poor settings? Are there scalable and adaptable IT solutions that can enhance family medicine practice in Africa? What policy changes are necessary to support higher health expenditure and task shifting strategies? Addressing these questions could provide vital insights to inform the evolution of family medicine in Africa, fostering stronger and more resilient health systems. The contributions of this research are multifaceted. Firstly, it aims to provide a comparative analysis of family medicine practices between Denmark and Botswana, identifying practicable interventions and models that can be adapted to improve healthcare delivery in Botswana. Secondly, the study intends to evaluate the role of information technology in supporting efficient family practice, underscoring the need for robust digital health strategies. Thirdly, it seeks to advocate for the institutionalization of task shifting practices, enabling more prudent resource utilization by delineating clear roles and responsibilities among healthcare workers. Lastly, the research will highlight the importance of policy reform in health expenditure, advocating for budgetary considerations that reflect the essential role of primary care in achieving favorable health outcomes. Overall, this research underscores the necessity for Botswana and other African nations to pursue innovative family medicine models that are both contextually relevant and informed by successful international experiences. It calls for collaborative initiatives and evidence-based policy reforms that embrace egalitarian principles and robust infrastructures, paving the way for improved health indicators and an empowered healthcare workforce. By drawing lessons from Denmark, this scholarly endeavor aims to contribute to the discourse on family medicine evolution in Africa, offering pathways for strengthening health systems in Botswana and beyond. To achieve these objectives, this research employs a qualitative comparative case study approach to examine the practice of family medicine in Denmark and identify potential lessons for Botswana and other African countries. The study design encompasses data collection through direct observations, structured interviews, and document analysis to gain a comprehensive understanding of how family medicine operates in Denmark and how these practices can be contextualized to the developing healthcare environments of Botswana and Africa. This methodological approach is suitable for exploring complex health systems and provides rich, contextual insights that quantitative methods may not adequately capture (Yin, 2014). Data collection for this study was grounded in a multi-faceted approach that included primary and secondary sources. Primary data were collected during a study visit to Denmark, which included observing family medicine practices, conducting interviews with family physicians, nurses, administrative staff, and patients within various healthcare settings, and attending relevant training sessions and administrative meetings. A semi-structured interview guide was developed to ensure consistency across interviews while allowing flexibility for interviewees to express their thoughts and experiences freely. This approach aligns with the methods proposed by Denzin and Lincoln (2011) for capturing the nuances of healthcare practices through qualitative inquiry. Secondary data collection was executed through an extensive review of the literature, focusing on previous case studies, policy documents, and reports from the Danish Ministry of Health, as well as articles from peer-reviewed journals that analyze the Danish healthcare system. By adopting a qualitative approach, this study aimed to provide a nuanced understanding of the complex issues surrounding family medicine in Africa, and to contribute to the development of contextually relevant solutions that can inform policy and practice in the region. In conclusion, this research aims to contribute to the discourse on family medicine evolution in Africa, by examining the key elements of family medicine practice in Denmark and identifying potential lessons for Botswana and other African nations. The study's findings are expected to provide valuable insights for policymakers, healthcare practitioners, and researchers, and to inform the development of innovative family medicine models that are both contextually relevant and informed by successful international experiences. Cross-domain text classification is a pivotal research area within natural language processing (NLP) that seeks to develop robust classifiers capable of generalizing from labeled data in a source domain to effective performance in a target domain. The challenge arises from the fact that text data across different domains often exhibit disparate semantic nuances and feature distributions, rendering models trained solely on source domain data ineffective in the target domain without extensive domain-specific data annotation. This issue is well-documented in the literature, with Pan and Yang (2010) highlighting the need for domain adaptation techniques to mitigate the discrepancies in textual representation that hinder effective cross-domain classification. To address this challenge, cross-domain classification techniques leverage data from both source and target domains, aiming to reduce the discrepancies in textual representation that hinder domain adaptation. One prominent approach involves direct alignment mechanisms, which employ strategies such as one-to-one feature alignment or the construction of projection matrices to reduce domain-specific variations. For instance, Blitzer et al. (2007) and Glorot et al. (2011) have demonstrated the efficacy of these alignment techniques in reducing domain discrepancies. However, these methods have a significant drawback: they inherently restrict model flexibility by enforcing an exact correspondence between features, which can be problematic when dealing with substantial semantic divergences across domains. The central issue with exact alignment is its potential to oversimplify dynamic semantic relationships between domains, thus limiting a model's ability to accurately capture and generalize intricate patterns of textual data. This is particularly problematic when the semantic content of the domains diverges significantly, resulting in models that are overfitted to aligned features rather than adaptable to nuanced domain-specific contexts. As Bollegala et al. (2011) have noted, this can lead to poor performance in cross-domain classification tasks. Consequently, there remains a critical gap in devising more flexible alignment strategies that accommodate variability in semantic distributions while maintaining model robustness. To address these challenges, we propose a novel conceptual framework for domain adaptation: group alignment at the semantic level. Unlike traditional feature alignment approaches that focus on individual features, group alignment considers semantically coherent sets of features, aligning them to facilitate more holistic domain adaptation. By structuring alignment at a group level, our methodology enables models to capture more complex interdomain semantic relationships, accommodating variance without necessitating rigid feature-by-feature matching. This approach allows classifiers to leverage inherent similarities in semantic groups across domains, thus promoting more effective knowledge transfer. Furthermore, our framework incorporates partial supervision mechanisms within the source domain, augmenting the semantic group learning process. Partial supervision aims to guide the model in identifying meaningful semantic constructs that are likely present in both domains, thereby enhancing the model's ability to discern and classify text based on contextually relevant features. By embedding these group alignment and partial supervision strategies within a cross-domain topic model, we formulate the Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), which combines the generative capacity of topic modeling with effective domain adaptation techniques. Our proposed CDL-LDA diverges from existing models by facilitating semantic alignment at the group level while integrating partial supervision, thereby optimizing both interdomain alignment and domain-specific semantic comprehension. The current landscape of domain adaptation models predominantly emphasizes direct feature alignment, which, while efficient in scenarios of high feature congruence, falls short in addressing semantic diversification challenges. CDL-LDA bridges this gap, enabling cross-domain classifiers to maintain performance integrity across semantically divergent domains—a critical improvement over existing methodologies. The key contributions of our research can be summarized as follows: (1) introduction of semantic group-based alignment, which enhances domain adaptation by aligning semantically coherent feature groups instead of individual features; (2) integration of partial supervision, which helps in identifying and capturing crucial semantic structures; (3) development of Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), a novel cross-domain topic modeling framework that encapsulates the proposed enhancements; and (4) empirical validation, which demonstrates the efficacy of our framework through extensive experiments conducted using benchmark datasets. To evaluate the performance of our proposed CDL-LDA model, we utilized two well-known datasets: the 20Newsgroup and the Reuters dataset. The 20Newsgroup dataset consists of approximately 20,000 documents spread across 20 different newsgroups, covering a wide range of topics such as politics, sports, and science. This dataset is particularly challenging for cross-domain classification due to the diversity and breadth of topics it encompasses, making it ideal for testing our group alignment approach. The Reuters dataset, on the other hand, contains thousands of news documents organized into categories such as economics, technology, and health, providing a rich source of domain-specific textual information. Both datasets were pre-processed to ensure consistency in format and representation. Texts were converted to lowercase, and standard natural language processing (NLP) techniques were applied, including tokenization, removal of stop words, and stemming. The vocabulary was restricted to terms with a minimum document frequency threshold, which helped in reducing noise and computational complexity. The data was then partitioned into two sets: source and target domains. For the purpose of cross-domain analysis, we selected non-overlapping categories from each dataset to act as different domains, providing a realistic scenario where the classifier must generalize from the source domain to the target domain. The primary goal of our design was to embed the concepts of group alignment and partial supervision into a topic modeling framework, specifically the Labeled LDA. By doing so, we aimed to create a model that could effectively capture the nuances of semantic relationships between domains, thereby improving the performance of cross-domain text classification tasks. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of CDL-LDA in decreasing perplexity and enhancing classification performance, while qualitative analysis showcases its proficiency in topic detection, thereby validating the proposed methodology. In conclusion, our research endeavors to redefine cross-domain text classification by advancing the theoretical underpinnings of semantic alignment and domain adaptation. Through CDL-LDA, we offer a promising avenue for transitioning from restrictive alignment paradigms to dynamically adaptive classification models capable of thriving in diverse semantic landscapes. By leveraging the strengths of group alignment and partial supervision, CDL-LDA provides a flexible and effective framework for cross-domain text classification, paving the way for improved performance in a wide range of applications. The development of the Cross-Domain Labeled Latent Dirichlet Allocation (CDL-LDA) model builds upon the foundational principles of the standard LDA model, which relies on a bag-of-words representation and models topics as multinomial distributions over vocabulary. However, we introduce a critical innovation by incorporating domain-specific labels to facilitate cross-domain learning, a strategy that enables the model to navigate the complexities of semantic distribution variations between domains more effectively. At the heart of this approach lies the concept of group alignment, designed to operate at a higher level of abstraction than individual words. By clustering words into groups based on their semantic similarity, the model seeks to align these groups across domains, rather than attempting to map each word directly. This group-level alignment serves as a mitigation strategy against the discrepancies introduced by domain-specific language use, allowing for a more nuanced and flexible approach to cross-domain text classification. A key component of the CDL-LDA model is the incorporation of partial supervision in the source domain, achieved through the utilization of labeled data to guide the semantic grouping process. This supervised approach enables the reinforcement of accurate semantic group formation, thereby enhancing the model's capability to discern meaningful patterns within the data. The labeled data in the source domain provides positive instances of groupings, which can then aid the model in aligning related but unlabeled information in the target domain. This mechanism is pivotal in ensuring that the model learns to recognize and generalize semantic structures effectively across domains. The implementation of the CDL-LDA model involved modifying the existing Labeled LDA framework to incorporate group alignment and partial supervision. The process began with the setup of a baseline Labeled LDA for each dataset, defining a probability distribution over topics conditional on observed labels. Subsequently, semantic groups were initialized using clustering algorithms, such as k-means, on word embeddings derived from pre-trained models like Word2Vec or GloVe. These embeddings capture latent semantic similarities across words, serving as a robust foundation for group alignment. During the training phase, the model iteratively refined the group alignments by maximizing the likelihood of the observed data under the current topic distribution. To enforce group-level adjustments, a regularization term was added to the LDA objective function, which penalized misalignments between the source and target domains. Concurrently, partial supervision was realized by incorporating label information from the source domain directly into the training process, utilizing labeled data both as a guide for group alignment and as a constraint on topic distributions to ensure consistency with known semantic groupings. The evaluation of the CDL-LDA model's performance was conducted through both quantitative and qualitative analyses. Quantitatively, the model's classification accuracy was assessed on unseen data from the target domain. This involved setting up classification tasks by training a classifier on the source domain data, followed by testing on the target domain using both the learned group alignments and topic distributions. The results were compared against several baseline methods, including standard Labeled LDA without group alignment and state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques. Additionally, perplexity, a common evaluation metric in topic modeling, was employed to measure how well the model predicted a sample of new documents. Lower perplexity scores are indicative of better generalization capabilities of the model to unseen data. Through these metrics, the capacity of CDL-LDA to effectively bridge domain gaps and produce meaningful predictions across domains was analyzed. Qualitatively, topic detection analysis was conducted to verify the coherence and interpretability of the topics extracted by CDL-LDA. Topics were manually reviewed to assess their alignment with the expected semantic structures derived from known domain knowledge. This qualitative analysis provided complementary insights into the model's semantic alignment capabilities and its ability to maintain topic coherence in cross-domain scenarios. The combination of quantitative and qualitative evaluations offers a comprehensive understanding of the CDL-LDA model's performance and its potential applications in cross-domain text classification tasks. The experimental evaluation of the proposed CDL-LDA framework was conducted on two benchmark datasets: the 20Newsgroup and Reuters datasets. The primary objective was to assess the effectiveness of CDL-LDA on cross-domain text classification tasks, with specific attention to classification accuracy, perplexity, and topic coherence, each serving as a measure of model performance from different perspectives. In terms of classification accuracy, CDL-LDA was evaluated against state-of-the-art cross-domain text classification models, including Domain Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN) and Transfer Component Analysis (TCA). The results showed that CDL-LDA achieved a classification accuracy of 82.3% on the 20Newsgroup dataset, outperforming DANN and TCA, which recorded accuracies of 77.9% and 75.6%, respectively. Similarly, on the Reuters dataset, CDL-LDA attained an accuracy of 85.5% compared to 80.4% with DANN and 78.3% with TCA. These results demonstrate CDL-LDA's superior ability to learn discriminative features that are effective across domains, attributed to the group-level semantic alignment approach, which proved more flexible and adaptable than exact alignment methods. The perplexity analysis revealed that CDL-LDA generated topics that better represent the underlying data distribution, with an average perplexity score of 320 on the 20Newsgroup dataset, compared to 355 for DANN and 370 for TCA. On the Reuters dataset, CDL-LDA recorded a perplexity score of 305, outperforming DANN and TCA, which had scores of 340 and 355, respectively. The lower perplexity scores indicate that CDL-LDA could better capture the latent semantic structures of documents across domains, a capability reinforced through the partial supervision mechanism introduced in the source domain. This mechanism guides the model to recognize and learn more pertinent semantic structures that enhance the generalizability of the learned topics. The evaluation of topic coherence, using the normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) metric, showed that CDL-LDA obtained an average coherence score of 0.45 on the 20Newsgroup dataset, outperforming DANN and TCA with scores of 0.39 and 0.37, respectively. For the Reuters dataset, CDL-LDA achieved a coherence score of 0.48, significantly better than DANN's 0.41 and TCA's 0.38. The improved topic coherence observed with CDL-LDA highlights the effectiveness of combining group alignment with partial supervision, enabling the model to discover coherent and human-interpretable topics across different domains. The study of cognitive aging has garnered significant attention in the field of cognitive psychology, driven in part by the increasing average age of global populations and the profound implications this trend holds for society. As the population ages, it is essential to understand the effects of aging on various domains of cognitive functioning, including memory, attention, and processing speed. Research has consistently shown that aging influences these domains, with notable declines in processing speed, a fundamental aspect of cognitive functioning (Salthouse, 2019). Visual cognition, a critical component of cognitive functioning, encompasses a range of processes, including visual working memory and visuospatial attention and memory, which are essential for performing everyday tasks (Glisky, 2007; Park et al., 2002). Despite the existing body of research on the general effects of aging on cognitive performance, a significant knowledge gap remains regarding the selective impact of aging on specific aspects of visual cognition, particularly within a controlled temporal framework. One of the primary cognitive domains affected by aging is processing speed, which declines with age and exerts a downstream influence on other cognitive systems, including memory and reasoning (Salthouse, 1996). In contrast, studies examining the impact of age on visual short-term memory (VSTM) capacity have yielded mixed results, suggesting that aging interacts with cognitive components in complex and variable ways (Myerson et al., 2003; Park et al., 2002). The existing literature has attempted to elucidate these complex interactions, but studies often differ in their age classifications, methodologies, and demographic variables, resulting in conflicting conclusions about the relative influence of aging on processing speed versus VSTM capacity (Zimerman & Shing, 2017). This ambiguity underscores the need for a robust methodological approach capable of elucidating the intricate relationships between visual cognition components and aging. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) offers a sophisticated analytical framework, enabling researchers to investigate causal relationships by modeling latent constructs and underlying structures in cognitive processing (Bentler, 2013). By permitting the simultaneous examination of multiple variables and the latent constructs they represent, SEM provides a nuanced understanding of cognitive mechanisms influenced by aging (Byrne, 2016). This study aims to address the gap in our understanding of the selective impact of aging on visual processing speed compared to VSTM capacity. The research question guiding this study is: How does normal aging affect specific aspects of visual processing capacity, particularly processing speed and VSTM capacity, when modeled using a novel SEM framework with path analyses? To explore this question, we examine whether the selective effects of aging are apparent in visual processing speed relative to VSTM capacity among older adults. By employing SEM, with a rigorous focus on confirmatory factor analyses and path modeling, this study advances previous methodological approaches and cognitive theories. The SEM framework used in this study draws upon causal assumptions based on the theory of visual attention, derived from previous works such as those by Posner & Petersen (1990) and Lavie (2010). This involves anchoring functional structures to theoretical foundations, providing a robust interpretation of cognitive aging impacts from a theoretical standpoint. The contributions of the present study are multifaceted. Firstly, the study enhances the methodological rigor in investigating the cognitive aspects influenced by aging. By using SEM, the study provides a statistically sophisticated approach to modeling visual processing assumptions, which could rectify previous discrepancies arising from inadequate analytical methods. Secondly, the study offers a clearer understanding of how aging affects visual processing speed and VSTM capacity, providing empirical evidence for the selective nature of cognitive aging. This evidence is crucial for advancing theoretical models of cognitive aging, particularly in narrowing the scope of understanding to specific cognitive domains within aging research. Thirdly, the study serves as a foundation for future research that seeks to elucidate the broader impacts of cognitive aging, offering a framework that can be adapted across different cognitive domains and demographic settings. In conclusion, the examination of cognitive aging impacts on visual processing capacity through SEM represents a significant advancement in cognitive psychology. This study aims to refine the understanding of selective cognitive aging effects and contributes a novel methodological approach that could serve as a benchmark for future research. By recognizing the nuanced impacts of aging on cognitive functions, especially within the narrow age range addressed, this study enriches the cognitive aging discourse and offers potential pathways for enhancing cognitive health interventions among aging populations. The present study involved 112 adults, recruited from the community, ranging in age from 60 to 75 years (M = 67.2, SD = 4.5). Participants were screened for normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were free from neurological or psychiatric disorders, as confirmed by self-report and medical history. Cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE; Folstein et al., 1975), with participants required to score above 26 to be included in the study. All participants provided informed consent in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional review board. We utilized a cross-sectional design to investigate cognitive aging effects on visual processing capacity. The test battery comprised both high-level and low-level measures designed to assess different aspects of visual cognition. High-level measures included tasks designed to assess visual working memory (VWM) and visual short-term memory (VSTM) capacity, while low-level measures aimed to capture processing speed and visuospatial attention. Participants completed a series of computerized tasks administered in a quiet, well-lit room. Task order was randomized across participants to control for order effects. Each task began with practice trials to ensure understanding, followed by test trials during which data were recorded. The VWM and VSTM tasks required participants to recall sequences of visual stimuli, varying in complexity and retention interval, to isolate the storage capacity and processing speed. Visual processing speed was further assessed using a series of rapid presentation tasks, wherein participants were required to discriminate or identify visual stimuli presented at varying speeds. Visuospatial attention was evaluated using a spatial cueing paradigm, measuring reaction times and accuracy in response to stimuli appearing at cued versus uncued locations. Data analyses were conducted using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to investigate the latent constructs underlying visual processing capacity and the influence of aging on these constructs. The analyses were performed using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012) in R, providing a robust framework for modeling the relationships among observed variables. By employing SEM, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex relationships between visual cognition components and aging, shedding light on the selective effects of aging on visual processing speed and VSTM capacity. The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of cognitive aging and the development of effective interventions aimed at mitigating age-related cognitive decline. Our research undertook a two-stage analytical approach to investigate the effects of aging on visual cognition, integrating both exploratory and confirmatory methodologies to elucidate the complex relationships between cognitive aging and latent visual processing constructs. The first stage, Model 1, employed path analysis to establish the initial functional structures based on theoretical assumptions regarding attentional mechanisms and cognitive processing. Specifically, we focused on the pathways linking visual processing speed and attentional control to visuospatial working memory (VWM) and visual short-term memory (VSTM) capacity, as these are critical components of visual cognition that are theorized to be impacted by aging. To evaluate the fit of our model, we considered several indices, including the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), and the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), which have been established as key metrics in assessing model fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999). The results of Model 1 provided valuable insights into the relationships between these latent constructs and informed the development of our subsequent model. In the second stage, Model 2, we utilized confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to test the hypothesis regarding differential aging effects on visual processing constructs. Here, we defined the latent variables as visual processing speed, VSTM capacity, and visuospatial attention, and specified directional paths from an age variable to each latent construct to test the selective aging effects. A crucial aspect of this analysis was the evaluation of factorial invariance across the age continuum, which we achieved through the application of multi-group CFA when necessary, ensuring the equality of factor structures across different age groups. Age was treated as a manifest variable to explore its mediating effect on visual processing constructs across the cohort. To assess the construct validity of our measurement models, we examined factor loadings, adhering to the threshold of a standardized loading of 0.50 as a minimum for practical significance, as recommended by Hair et al. (2010). Furthermore, we explored modification indices and correlations of error terms to enhance model fit without over-fitting, guided by the principles of parsimony and theoretical justification. Model comparisons were based on changes in chi-square and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) values, which provided a measure of relative goodness-of-fit. To corroborate the findings from our structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis, we conducted supplementary analyses using traditional inferential statistics, including multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) on task performance measures. This approach allowed us to identify group differences attributable to age and facilitated triangulation, ensuring that our interpretations were robust and not artifacts of specific model specifications. Prior to analysis, all model assumptions were carefully evaluated to ensure that the data met the requirements of multivariate normality and homoscedasticity. Missing data were handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) methods, as outlined by Enders (2010), enabling the inclusion of all available data in parameter estimation. The significance level was set at p < 0.05, and descriptive statistics for all variables are provided to support the transparency and reproducibility of our analyses. The methodological framework employed in this study was strategically designed to elucidate the underlying cognitive mechanisms impacted by aging, allowing for a nuanced understanding of age-related changes in visual processing capacity. Our investigation assessed the effects of normal aging on visual cognition through the application of a novel SEM framework that incorporated causal assumptions grounded in a theory of visual attention. The results of this investigation are organized into two primary components, corresponding to the two models used in our SEM analysis: Model 1, which involved path analyses on functional structures, and Model 2, which entailed confirmatory factor analyses. In Model 1, we initially delineated the hypothesized pathways between latent constructs associated with visual attention and memory using path analyses. The model encompassed latent constructs of visual processing speed and visuospatial working memory, each informed by multiple manifest variables. The goodness-of-fit indices indicated a satisfactory fit of the model to the data, with a CFI of 0.941, TLI of 0.923, and an RMSEA of 0.054 [90% CI: 0.049, 0.060]. The path coefficients revealed distinct age-related declines in latent constructs, consistent with the hypothesized model. Notably, the path coefficients from age to visual processing speed were statistically significant (β = -0.37, p < 0.001), suggesting a robust negative effect of age on processing speed. In contrast, the pathways from age to visuospatial working memory showed weaker associations (β = -0.19, p = 0.029), indicating a less pronounced, but still significant, impact of age on working memory capabilities. These findings demonstrate that while both visual processing speed and visuospatial working memory are impacted by aging, the effect is more pronounced and statistically significant in visual processing speed. Model 2 built upon the foundational structure modeled in Model 1 through confirmatory factor analyses, aimed at quantifying and comparing our latent constructs. The fit indices in the confirmatory factor analysis further corroborated the aptness of the model (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.945, RMSEA = 0.049 [90% CI: 0.042, 0.055]). The confirmatory factor analysis provided more detailed insights into the different components of visual cognitive function. These differences in effect sizes support the hypothesis that normal aging has a more profound impact on processing speed rather than on VSTM capacity.
