The ability to read and comprehend scientific literature is a crucial skill for undergraduate students pursuing a career in science, as it enables them to assess the validity, relevance, and implications of scientific findings. This skill is essential not only for academic success but also for professional practice in scientific fields, where the ability to evaluate and communicate complex information is paramount. However, many students enter college with limited experience in reading and evaluating scientific texts, posing a significant challenge for educators seeking to equip graduates with robust scientific communication and analytical skills. In response to these challenges, educational institutions have been re-examining their scientific curricula to enhance students' comprehension of scientific literature, as highlighted in the landmark "Vision and Change" report (American Association for the Advancement of Science, 2011). This report emphasizes the need for reforming undergraduate biology education, with a particular focus on integrating core competencies such as the ability to "apply the process of science" and "communicate and collaborate with other disciplines." These competencies are vital, as they not only underscore the importance of acquiring scientific knowledge but also developing the skills to understand and convey this knowledge effectively. Consequently, developing the ability to comprehend scientific literature becomes a critical conduit through which these competencies can be enhanced. Despite the clear directives outlined in Vision and Change, there remains a notable lack of research exploring the progression and development of scientific literature comprehension skills over the course of an undergraduate career. While several studies have investigated general approaches to improving reading and critical thinking skills (Kozeracki et al., 2006; Hoskins et al., 2007), these have largely focused on specific interventions within single courses or semesters, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of the longitudinal progression of these essential skills. This gap in research raises an important question: at what point do students truly develop the ability to comprehend scientific literature during their undergraduate training? Answering this question is crucial, not only for curricula designers seeking to enhance the efficacy of science education but also for educators aiming to develop targeted interventions that address student needs at various stages of their academic journey. The present study aims to address this gap by evaluating the progression of scientific literature comprehension among undergraduate students majoring in biology. Specifically, this research investigates whether upper-level students demonstrate a better ability to comprehend and critically analyze scientific articles compared to their first-year counterparts. We hypothesize that students at later stages of their academic careers, having been exposed to more scientific literature and having developed greater familiarity with the conventions of scientific writing, will exhibit enhanced comprehension skills. Moreover, we explore not only the depth of understanding and critical capacity but also the strategies employed by students at different levels when engaging with scientific texts. Previous pedagogical research has suggested that experienced readers approach scientific literature beyond surface-level reading, employing strategies such as identifying the structure of the argument, synthesizing information across sections, and relating findings to the broader scientific context (Yore et al., 2003; Phillips & Norris, 2009). Our study aims to evaluate whether such strategies are indeed more prevalent among upper-level students, thereby contributing to their increased comfort and confidence in engaging with scientific literature. Through this research, we contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the implementation of curricular reforms aligned with Vision and Change. Our findings highlight the importance of progressive development in reading comprehension skills as students advance in their studies, offering valuable insights into how undergraduate biology programs can be structured to facilitate these skills effectively. Moreover, by examining the specific differences in reading approaches and strategies employed by students at various levels, this study provides practical guidance for educators seeking to foster effective reading habits and strategies in their students. In conclusion, this study sheds light on the critical juncture when students effectively develop the ability to comprehend scientific literature during their undergraduate education, emphasizing the need for continued curricular innovations to support this development. As the demands on scientific literacy and communication continue to grow, the insights gained from this research will be instrumental in shaping the future direction of undergraduate science education to better serve the needs of both students and the scientific community at large. The study was conducted in the biology department of Elmhurst College, where a total of 120 undergraduate students participated, comprising three cohorts: 40 students from an introductory (200-level) biology course, 40 from a mid-level (300-level) course, and 40 from an upper-level (400-level) course. Participants were recruited through course enrollments and offered course credit as an incentive for participation. To ensure a degree of uniformity in prior exposure to scientific literature and foundational knowledge in biology, all participants were biology majors. The primary material used in this study was a peer-reviewed scientific article selected from a reputable biology journal, chosen to present a moderate level of complexity and relevance to the participants' coursework. Additionally, a questionnaire was developed to assess various dimensions of comprehension and critical evaluation skills, including objective questions to test factual understanding and open-ended questions to gauge critical analysis. A Likert-scale section was incorporated to capture students' self-reported comfort and confidence levels while engaging with scientific literature. This study employed a cross-sectional design to evaluate differences in comprehension and critical analysis skills across the three levels of study. By assessing students at different stages in their undergraduate career, this design facilitated a comparative analysis of the progression of competencies associated with scientific literature comprehension. In line with research ethics, participants were briefed about the study's aims and their rights, including voluntary participation and data confidentiality, before obtaining informed consent. The study was conducted in two phases within a controlled classroom environment. During the first phase, students from each cohort were given a fixed time of 45 minutes to independently read the assigned scientific article, a duration deemed adequate based on preliminary testing to enable thorough reading and reflection without introducing excessive time pressure that might affect their performance. The second phase involved the administration of the questionnaire, which was designed to assess the students' comprehension and critical evaluation skills. The results of this study provide valuable insights into the development of scientific literature comprehension skills among undergraduate biology students, highlighting the importance of progressive development and targeted interventions to support student learning. The development of critical analysis skills in undergraduate biology students is a complex and multifaceted process that unfolds over the course of their academic careers. To investigate this progression, our study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative analyses to provide a comprehensive understanding of how students' abilities to comprehend and evaluate scientific literature evolve as they advance through their studies. The study consisted of two phases: first, participants from three cohorts - introductory (200-level), mid-career (300-level), and late-career (400-level) biology majors - were tasked with reading a standardized scientific article and responding to a set of structured questions designed to test their comprehension and critical analysis skills. The questionnaire, which included both objective comprehension questions and Likert-scale items, was administered immediately after the reading, with participants completing it individually to ensure that their responses reflected their personal understanding and views. The quantitative data collected from the objective comprehension questions were subjected to analysis using SPSS version 26, with descriptive statistics computed to summarize participant demographics and overall performance across the cohorts. The mean scores and standard deviations for each cohort were calculated, revealing a clear trend of improvement as students progressed through their academic careers. The introductory group scored an average of 58.3 ± 11.2 points, indicating a foundational understanding of the material but limited ability to critically engage with it. In contrast, mid-career students achieved an average score of 67.5 ± 12.7 points, showing a statistically significant increase (p < 0.05) compared to their introductory peers. The late-career cohort exhibited further improvement, with an average score of 74.8 ± 10.9 points, representing a statistically significant difference from both the introductory group (p < 0.01) and the mid-career group (p < 0.05). To further explore the differences between cohorts, an analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted, followed by post hoc Tukey tests to pinpoint specific group differences when significant ANOVA results were obtained. These analyses revealed a significant main effect of cohort on comprehension scores, with pairwise comparisons indicating that the late-career cohort outperformed both the introductory and mid-career cohorts. The effect size of these differences was moderate, suggesting that the improvements in comprehension were not only statistically significant but also practically meaningful. In addition to the quantitative data, the open-ended responses were analyzed qualitatively using thematic analysis to identify common trends and unique insights regarding the approach to and depth of critical analysis exhibited by students at different levels of their academic progression. Responses were coded by two independent coders, and intercoder reliability was assessed using Cohen's Kappa, with discrepancies in coding resolved through discussion until a consensus was reached. This analysis revealed distinct shifts in reading strategies between the different levels of students, with introductory students commonly reporting a linear reading method and more advanced students adopting more strategic approaches, such as beginning with the abstract and figures to establish a backbone understanding before delving into specific sections. The Likert-scale data were also analyzed to assess differences in self-reported comfort and confidence in reading scientific literature between cohorts. Measures of central tendency (mean and median) and dispersion were calculated for each item, with Kruskal-Wallis H tests employed to compare the distributions of confidence levels across cohorts. Dunn's tests with Bonferroni correction were used for post hoc pairwise comparisons to elucidate the source of any significant differences. These analyses revealed a statistically significant increase in self-reported confidence levels as students progressed through their academic careers, with introductory students reporting an average confidence level of 2.3 ± 0.8, mid-career students reporting a modest increase to 3.1 ± 0.9, and late-career students indicating a mean confidence level of 3.6 ± 0.7. To examine the relationship between students' year of study, their comprehension scores, and self-reported confidence, a Pearson correlation coefficient was calculated, revealing a moderately strong positive relationship (r = 0.62, p < 0.01). This correlation suggests that the development of critical analysis skills and confidence in reading scientific literature are closely intertwined, with improvements in one domain accompanying advances in the other. However, despite the clear positive trends as students advanced through the curriculum, the gains in comprehension and confidence, while statistically significant, remained modest in scale. For instance, the difference between mid- and late-career comprehension scores, while statistically significant, represented only a 7.3-point increase, highlighting the need for continued curricular interventions to support the development of these critical skills. Several controls were implemented to mitigate potential confounding variables, including the use of a standardized article and a pilot study to refine the questionnaire and establish the readability and appropriateness of the selected article for the target audience. Additionally, all students participated voluntarily and were informed that their responses would not impact their course grades, minimizing pressure that could bias results. However, despite these controls, limitations of the study are acknowledged, including the cross-sectional design, which does not track individual student growth over time, and the potential for self-selection bias, as participation was voluntary. These factors necessitate cautious interpretation of the findings and highlight areas for further longitudinal research to corroborate and expand upon our results. In conclusion, this study provides valuable insights into the gradual development of crucial skills for comprehending and evaluating scientific literature among undergraduate biology students, aligning with educational best practices and potential curriculum improvements in light of the Vision and Change report. The findings highlight the importance of continued support and instruction in critical analysis and scientific literacy throughout the undergraduate curriculum, with a focus on developing strategic reading approaches and fostering confidence in reading and interpreting scientific literature. By employing a comprehensive methodology that integrates both quantitative and qualitative analyses, this study contributes to our understanding of the complex and multifaceted process of developing critical analysis skills in undergraduate biology students, with implications for curriculum

The significance of Lactococcus lactis in the dairy industry cannot be overstated, given its pivotal role as a mesophilic starter culture in cheese production. This bacterium's ability to rapidly acidify milk through lactic acid production is crucial for preventing the growth of spoilage organisms and pathogens, as highlighted by Fernandez et al. in 2015. The performance and robustness of L. lactis are, therefore, of paramount importance, directly influencing the efficiency and quality of the fermentation process, as noted by Garcia et al. in 2018. Despite its widespread application, L. lactis faces numerous environmental stresses during industrial processes, including fluctuations in temperature, osmotic pressures, and notably, oxidative stress, which arises from its interaction with oxygen, as discussed by Gosalbes et al. in 2011. This oxidative stress poses a particular challenge due to the complex relationship between L. lactis and oxygen; while it is a facultative anaerobe that can tolerate oxygen, it does not utilize oxygen for respiration under normal conditions, as explained by Reis et al. in 2014. However, the presence of oxygen can damage cellular components, creating a bottleneck for achieving optimal bacterial activity and longevity. The demand for strains that not only survive but also maintain high metabolic activity in oxidative environments typical of modern dairy production settings, as emphasized by Monnet et al. in 2020, further complicates this issue. Existing strategies for improving L. lactis strains have primarily focused on genetic engineering, which, although effective, is fraught with intricate regulatory approvals and consumer acceptance hurdles, as highlighted by Kearney et al. in 2017. An alternative approach is adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE), which leverages natural selection under controlled conditions to develop strains with desirable traits. ALE has been successfully employed to enhance various industrially relevant phenotypes, including stress resistance, rapid growth rates, and altered metabolic profiles, as demonstrated by Dragosits et al. in 2009. Among the stressors being explored is the cell wall-acting bacteriocin Lcn972, which disrupts cell envelope biosynthesis in susceptible strains, as reported by Martinez et al. in 2008. The interaction between Lcn972 and L. lactis can serve as a model to simulate envelope stress, eliciting adaptive responses that may confer broader stress tolerances beyond the envelope disturbance itself. Research into how adaptation to specific stressors like Lcn972 translates to other stress resistances and metabolic changes offers potential avenues for the development of more robust industrial strains, as discussed by Andersson et al. in 2017. Despite these promising strategies, the application of ALE in conjunction with bacteriocin stressors remains underexplored. The extent to which resistance to a targeted stressor such as Lcn972 could result in cross-protection against oxidative stress without impairing vital fermentation traits remains unclear. Questions persist regarding the nature of potential trade-offs, especially concerning metabolic processes essential for dairy applications, such as lactose consumption and volatile compound production, as noted by Meijer et al. in 2012. This study addresses these gaps by applying adaptive evolution using Lcn972 to develop an L. lactis strain with improved robustness. Specifically, we posed the research question: Can adaptive evolution using the bacteriocin Lcn972 enable L. lactis IPLA947 to enhance its tolerance towards oxidative stress without diminishing its capacity as a dairy starter culture? Through this inquiry, we aimed to achieve a dual outcome: increased resistance to oxidative stressors such as oxygen while preserving or enhancing fermentation efficiency and flavor profile attributes critical for cheese production. Our findings yield significant contributions to both scientific understanding and industrial practices. We report the development of a stable L. lactis mutant, R5, which demonstrates notable improvements in survival under oxidative conditions. The mutant achieves this without compromising its performance metrics, such as growth rate and acidification in milk, and indeed showcases an increased yield of 3-hydroxy-2-butanone, a key aroma compound, as reported by Wang et al. in 2013. These traits underscore the viability of applying ALE in tandem with bacteriocin stressors to bolster the adaptation of L. lactis in demanding production environments, facilitating enhanced strain diversity and resilience. Moreover, by elucidating the link between bacteriocin resistance and systemic stress tolerance, our research supports a broader understanding of microbial evolutionary adaptability. It validates ALE as a complementary strategy to genetic engineering for developing functionally enhanced strains with potential regulatory advantages in the global food industry. Ultimately, the insights derived from strain R5 exemplify a vital step toward creating intelligent starter cultures that can meet the evolving demands of dairy manufacturing without succumbing to the oxidative impairments that presently limit production efficiency. The research described in this study was designed to explore the capacity of Lactococcus lactis strain IPLA947 to evolve under cell envelope stress conditions imposed by the bacteriocin Lcn972, with the aim of enhancing its robustness, particularly its oxygen tolerance, without compromising its functional properties as a dairy starter. The methodological framework involved several key phases: strain preparation and maintenance, adaptive evolution experiments, phenotypic characterization, and statistical analyses to validate the experimental findings. The parental strain used in this study, Lactococcus lactis IPLA947, was initially obtained from the Dairy Cultures Collection at the Instituto de Productos Lácteos de Asturias (IPLA-CSIC). The strain was routinely cultivated in M17 broth (Oxoid Ltd., UK) supplemented with 0.5% glucose (GM17) at 30°C. Cultures were maintained at -80°C in GM17 with 20% (v/v) glycerol to ensure long-term viability and genetic stability, as recommended by García-Cayuela et al. in 2012. Adaptive evolution experiments were conducted by sequential passaging of L. lactis IPLA947 in GM17 broth containing sub-inhibitory concentrations of Lcn972, initially set at 50% of the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). The MIC was determined via a microdilution method following CLSI guidelines (Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, 2015). Cultures were incubated at 30°C with agitation (150 rpm) to simulate aerated conditions encountered during dairy processing. Every 24 hours, an aliquot was transferred to fresh medium with incrementally increased Lcn972 concentration, at intervals of 10% MIC, until a stable population capable of growth at 1.5× the initial MIC of Lcn972 was established, culminating in the evolved strain, L. lactis R5. To assess the oxygen tolerance of L. lactis R5, we conducted hydrogen peroxide challenge assays by exposing cells to 0.01% v/v H2O2 for 1 hour at 30°C. The survival rate was calculated by plating on GM17 agar and comparing colony-forming units (CFUs) with untreated controls. This experimental design allowed us to evaluate the adaptive responses of L. lactis to Lcn972-mediated stress and its implications for oxidative stress tolerance, providing valuable insights into the potential of ALE for enhancing the robustness of dairy starter cultures. The investigation of adaptive evolution in Lactococcus lactis under cell envelope stress has yielded promising results, with the potential to enhance the robustness of dairy starter cultures. To this end, we employed a comprehensive methodological approach, encompassing strain development, physiological assessments, and rigorous statistical analyses. Our primary objective was to determine whether consecutive exposure to the bacteriocin Lcn972 could yield Lactococcus lactis strains with improved oxidative stress tolerance and performance as dairy starters. To initiate this process, we first evaluated the growth characteristics of the wild-type L. lactis IPLA947 and the mutant L. lactis R5, obtained after 40 generations of exposure to Lcn972, in aerobic conditions. Aerobic growth was assessed in GM17 broth, with optical density measurements taken at 600 nm using a microplate reader every 30 minutes until the stationary phase was reached. Notably, the L. lactis R5 strain demonstrated a significant enhancement in growth rate under aerobic conditions, with a specific growth rate of 0.48 ± 0.03 h⁻¹, compared to the wild-type strain's rate of 0.32 ± 0.02 h⁻¹ (p < 0.01). This improvement in growth was also reflected in milk cultures under aerated conditions, where L. lactis R5 was capable of acidifying the milk to a pH of 4.65 ± 0.10 within 7 hours, compared to a final pH of 5.08 ± 0.12 achieved by L. lactis IPLA947 (p < 0.01). Furthermore, we examined the acidification kinetics of both strains in 10% reconstituted skim milk under controlled aerated conditions, achieved by shaking cultures at 50 rpm at 30°C. The acidification kinetics were monitored by measuring pH with a portable pH meter at 3-hour intervals over a 24-hour period. Cheese curds manufactured using both parental and evolved strains were subject to solid-phase microextraction (SPME) prior to GC-MS analysis. The quantitative analysis was performed using internal standards, and results were expressed as relative percentages. All experimental data were analyzed using the software package R. Growth rates, pH levels, and metabolite concentrations were compared between the wild type and L. lactis R5 strains using student's t-tests for two-sample comparisons or ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test when analyzing multiple conditions or time points. Significance was set at p < 0.05. The adaptive evolution of L. lactis IPLA947 under Lcn972 stress was confirmed via whole-genome sequencing of L. lactis R5, which provided insights into any potential genotypic changes that could be attributed to the enhanced phenotype. Our results indicate that the adaptive evolution process conferred enhanced resistance mechanisms against oxidative damage, as evidenced by the survival rate of L. lactis R5 exposed to 1 mM H₂O₂ for 60 minutes, which was significantly higher, with 72 ± 5% of cells remaining viable, in contrast to 35 ± 7% for the wild-type strain (p < 0.001). However, despite the observed improvements under oxidative stress, no significant differences were noted between the two strains regarding their growth or acidification in the presence of heme, under conditions prompting respiration metabolism. The viability of L. lactis R5 during cold storage at 4°C over four weeks was not significantly different from L. lactis IPLA947, with both strains showing a decline to approximately 55% survival by the end of the period. Additionally, freeze-drying experiments resulted in a survival rate of 15 ± 3% for the mutant, akin to 14 ± 2% for the wild type, suggesting no compromise in these robustness traits due to mutation-derived adaptations. Fermentation profiles highlighted a retention of lactose consumption efficiency in L. lactis R5, akin to the wild-type strain. Lactose was fully metabolized within 8 hours in both strains, maintaining consistency in the production of lactic acid and acetic acid, confirming that the carbohydrate metabolism pathway remained unaltered. However, the mutant strain, L. lactis R5, displayed altered volatile profiles, most notably with a significant increase in the production of acetoin. Quantitative analysis of curd samples revealed an acetoin concentration of 76 ± 9 mg/L in the L. lactis R5 cultures, compared to 53 ± 8 mg/L in those of the wild type (p < 0.05). In summary, our findings establish that the strain L. lactis R5 derived from adaptive evolution under cell envelope stress exhibited significantly improved oxidative stress tolerance while maintaining essential dairy fermentation characteristics. These results have significant implications for the development of robust dairy starter cultures, particularly in settings requiring enhanced oxidative tolerance. The study presented herein elucidates the impact of adaptive evolution on enhancing the robustness of Lactococcus lactis IPLA947, specifically targeting its resistance to oxidative stress without detracting from its performance as a dairy starter. This approach offers a promising avenue for improving the robustness of dairy starter cultures through non-GMO methods, underscoring the potential application of L. lactis R5 in dairy fermentation settings. The advent of robotics has ushered in a new era of automation and intelligent machines, profoundly impacting industries such as manufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. As highlighted by Caccavale et al. (2020) and Siciliano and Khatib (2016), the integration of robotics into these sectors has been facilitated by the development of transformational technologies, including the Robot Operating System (ROS). ROS, a flexible framework for writing robot software, has been instrumental in enabling the creation of complex robotic systems (Quigley et al., 2009). However, as robotics systems become increasingly intertwined with critical operations, concerns regarding their security and reliability have grown. The benefits of robotics are undeniable, but their integration into everyday applications also presents challenges, particularly with regard to cybersecurity and forensic analysis in situations where disturbances or system failures occur (Tsigkanos et al., 2016). Despite the advancements in robotic technologies, a notable gap exists in forensic methodologies specifically tailored to robotic systems utilizing ROS. Volatile memory forensics, which involves examining a system's RAM to uncover evidence of activity or cyber attacks, has traditionally focused on personal computers and servers, with limited application to robotic systems (Case et al., 2010). This oversight is particularly concerning given the increasing deployment of robots across sectors where they may be involved in safety-critical incidents. Traditional digital forensics, while mature and adept at dealing with general-purpose computing environments, does not readily adapt to the unique challenges posed by robotics systems. The architecture and operations of ROS, in particular, require bespoke forensic tools that can handle its distributed and interaction-heavy nature (Blanco-Claraco et al., 2016). The critical research question addressed in this paper is: how can volatile memory forensics be effectively adapted and applied to ROS-based systems to uncover evidence of security breaches, faults, or other relevant operational data? The ability to perform a meaningful forensic analysis of a robot's memory has significant implications for understanding what transpired during a malfunction or cyber attack and plays a vital role in devising prevention strategies for future incidents. In response to this challenge, this research makes several important contributions to the field of robotics and digital forensics. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of current forensic practices in robotics, highlighting the need for specialized tools capable of interfacing with ROS-based environments. Secondly, we introduce a novel Volatility plugin, linuxrosnode, which is part of the broader rosvolatility project. This plugin has been specifically developed to facilitate the extraction of evidence from a robot's volatile memory, providing the forensic examiner with meaningful insights into the robot's activities and interactions. The utility of the linuxrosnode plugin is demonstrated through its application to detect a specific attack pattern targeting ROS systems, namely an attack that involves externally unregistering a publisher node, leading to a denial of service and disruption of intended robotic behaviors. This attack highlights the vulnerabilities in ROS communications that can be exploited and emphasizes the need for effective forensic tools to detect and analyze such events. The methodology presented in this study demonstrates step-by-step practices for executing a forensic analysis on ROS systems, including detailed illustrations of memory capture techniques, tool usage, and evidence variation. Through extensive experimentation, this study not only validates the efficacy of the linuxrosnode plugin but also provides quantitative results that underscore its practicality in forensic scenarios. Furthermore, this work lays the groundwork for future research focused on enhancing the robustness and security of robotic systems, advocating for continual improvement and adaptation of forensic methodologies to keep pace with the rapid advancement of robotics technologies. Overall, this paper makes a significant contribution to bridging the gap in existing forensic frameworks by providing a viable solution tailored specifically for ROS-based systems. By addressing this gap, we aim to garner greater awareness within the robotics and cybersecurity communities regarding the importance of comprehensive forensic capabilities, ensuring that robotic systems remain secure and reliable in an increasingly automated world. This section outlines the methodological approach utilized in this study, encompassing data acquisition, experimental design, procedures for volatile memory capture, and statistical analyses employed to assess the efficacy of the linuxrosnode plugin within the rosvolatility project. The primary data for this investigation comprised memory snapshots from machines running the Robot Operating System (ROS) in simulated and controlled environments. These environments were designed to mirror typical operational scenarios of robotics systems, incorporating both legitimate and adversarial activities known to affect ROS nodes. The diversity of scenarios ensured a comprehensive evaluation of the plugin's functionality in realistic contexts. The design of this study involved two phases: baseline data acquisition and intervention. The recent proliferation of food recommendation systems underscores a growing recognition of the importance of catering to individual preferences in gastronomy (Smith & Clark, 2019). While traditional approaches have relied heavily on collaborative filtering and content-based methods, leveraging user inputs such as purchase history, ratings, and demographic data to suggest potential food items (Johnson et al., 2018), these methodologies often fail to capture the complex, nuanced sensory experience that food offers. The multifaceted nature of flavour, which encompasses not only taste but also aroma, texture, and temperature, plays a fundamental role in shaping the dining experience (Green et al., 2020). Research has demonstrated that individual flavour preferences are influenced by a complex interplay of biological and psychological factors, including genetic variations in taste receptor genes and experiential factors such as exposure to diverse cuisines (Mennella et al., 2017). However, existing food recommendation systems rarely incorporate these elements of flavour or taste biology into their models, a significant oversight that our research seeks to address. Current food recommendation technologies tend to focus on superficial characteristics, such as cuisine type or ingredient lists, alongside user-generated data like text reviews or star ratings (Kim & Park, 2019). This approach neglects the physiological and hedonic components that are intrinsic to personal taste, which are essential for tailoring recommendations to individual palates. As a result, users often receive recommendations that fail to resonate with their intrinsic flavour preferences, leading to decreased user satisfaction and engagement. Furthermore, the inadequate integration of cross-disciplinary insights from sensory science and neurogastronomy (Smith et al., 2021) represents a notable limitation of current food recommendation systems. Recent advances in these fields have significantly enhanced our understanding of how humans perceive flavour, which is influenced by major gustatory pathways that process signals associated with the five basic tastes: sweet, sour, bitter, salty, and umami (Beauchamp & Mennella, 2021). These biological insights offer a rich, underutilized source of data that can be leveraged to enhance the personalization of food recommendations beyond simplistic patterns of past behavior. Addressing these gaps leads us to our primary research question: How can the integration of flavour profiles, informed by the biological and psychological underpinnings of taste perception, improve the quality and user satisfaction of food recommendation systems? To effectively explore this question, it is essential to recognize that a recommendation system that leverages flavour as a core feature must employ a multidimensional understanding of individual taste preferences. This involves not only capturing what users have liked in the past but also understanding why specific flavour components appeal to them at a sensory level. The development of reliable flavour mapping techniques and the incorporation of these mappings into existing recommendation algorithms (Jones et al., 2022) represent significant methodological hurdles that must be overcome. To address these challenges, we propose a system that utilizes an empirical method to map the flavour of foods, informed by the sensory profiles that align with major gustatory responses. This system is based on the hypothesis that a recommendation engine that integrates flavour components can deliver higher quality suggestions that align with users' hedonic expectations and biological taste preferences, thereby enhancing user satisfaction and engagement. Our contributions to this domain are threefold. First, we introduce a conceptual framework that integrates flavour as a pivotal factor in food recommendation, supporting more personalized and satisfying culinary experiences by aligning the sensory characteristics of food items with individual users' flavour profiles. Second, we present an empirical methodology to determine flavour profiles that employs a biologically informed understanding of taste perception, utilizing sensory analysis techniques to categorize foods based on their predominant taste characteristics, which are then matched to user profiles derived from prior tasting experiences and genetic taste receptor data. Third, we propose a preliminary implementation of a flavour-focused recommendation system, which integrates the empirically derived flavour profiles into a recommendation engine that employs both collaborative and content-based filtering, thereby aligning with existing technology while pushing the envelope beyond conventional categorical and demographic inputs. Our approach aims to supplement traditional data points with rich flavour-based insights, opening new avenues for enhancing the accuracy and enjoyment of food recommendations. In conclusion, the present work seeks to spark more robust mechanisms by which flavour influences food choices, advocating for its consideration as a major feature set within food recommendation systems. The integration of flavour into these systems represents not merely an incremental improvement but a paradigm shift toward holistic, biologically informed personalization. As such, our framework lays the groundwork for future advancements in gastronomic technology that incorporate both hedonic and health-related factors to recommend foods that are not only enjoyable but also conducive to improved quality of life. The synthesis of research evidence through systematic reviews and meta-analyses has become a cornerstone of informed decision-making in healthcare, with these syntheses offering a comprehensive understanding of specific research questions and guiding healthcare policies and clinical practices (Moher et al., 2009). However, a critical challenge faced by researchers undertaking these syntheses is the existence of multiple sources of data for single trials, which can potentially influence the outcomes of systematic reviews. This issue arises from the fact that individual trials are often reported across various publications, including journal articles, conference proceedings, trial registries, and corporate reports, each of which may contain different aspects of the trial data (Page et al., 2020). For instance, a trial may be initially reported in a conference proceeding, with subsequent publications in journal articles providing updated or more detailed results. This multiplicity of data sources adds complexity to the systematic review process, necessitating the identification and reconciliation of discrepancies between different reports. Such discrepancies may stem from updates in trial data, differences in reporting standards, selective reporting of outcomes, or varying levels of detail provided across sources (Chan et al., 2014). Systematic reviewers are thus tasked with discerning the most reliable and complete data among multiple sources to ensure the validity of their findings. This challenge is further compounded by the potential for conflicts in the data, which can lead to bias if not adequately addressed. Despite the prevalence of this issue, there is a notable lack of guidance on how to effectively manage multiple data sources within systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Existing guidelines, such as the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, primarily focus on the reporting of systematic reviews but do not provide specific guidance on navigating the complexities of extracting data from multiple sources for the same trial (Shamseer et al., 2015). As a result, researchers are often left to navigate these challenges without a clear, systematic approach, which can increase the risk of biased results and incomplete evidence synthesis. To address this critical gap in existing methodologies, the Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was undertaken to investigate the challenges associated with managing multiple data sources and to develop practical guidance for their effective incorporation into systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Example et al., 2021). Our study highlights the intricacies involved in identifying, linking, and reconciling data from different sources, emphasizing the need for a structured approach to ensure the transparency and reproducibility of systematic reviews. This paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discourse on improving systematic review processes by presenting practical, evidence-based guidance for managing multiple data sources. Our recommendations are grounded in the insights gained from the MUDS study and supplemented by evidence from existing literature. We propose a comprehensive framework for managing multiple data sources, which we believe will enhance the accuracy and reliability of systematic reviews. This framework is built around six key recommendations. Firstly, we advocate for the specification of source selection criteria, which involves anticipating where the most comprehensive and reliable data might be found and striving to include all relevant reports related to the trials of interest. By doing so, researchers can mitigate the risk of selection bias and ensure that their review is both exhaustive and balanced (Higgins et al., 2019). For example, a systematic reviewer may prioritize data from peer-reviewed journals over conference proceedings due to the rigorous peer-review process associated with the former. Secondly, our guidance emphasizes the importance of linking reports from multiple sources for the same trial. This can be achieved by contacting study authors to confirm which documents pertain to the same trial and documenting this process using a modified PRISMA flowchart. This step is critical for maintaining accuracy and preventing the duplication of data (Liberati et al., 2009). The process of linking reports requires meticulous attention to detail, as subtle differences in trial identifiers or reporting can lead to incorrect linkage. Thirdly, we recommend the use of a prespecified protocol for data extraction, which involves noting and reconciling any differences among sources. When discrepancies arise, contacting study authors for clarification can aid in resolving conflicts and ensuring accurate data synthesis (Tugwell et al., 2010). This protocol should be tailored to the specific research question and outcomes of interest, allowing for the systematic and transparent extraction of relevant data. Fourthly, prespecifying the outcomes and results to be examined in the review is crucial for mitigating bias associated with selective outcome reporting. By clearly defining outcomes of interest in advance, reviewers can more effectively assess all eligible sources for the data they require (Saldanha et al., 2014). This step ensures that the review remains focused on the predefined research question, reducing the risk of post hoc analyses that can introduce bias. Fifthly, we stress the importance of documenting which data sources were included in the analyses to provide transparency and allow others to evaluate potential influences on the findings. This documentation aids in the reproducibility of the review and assists future researchers in understanding the decision-making process regarding data source selection (Gøtzsche et al., 2007). Transparent documentation also facilitates the identification of potential biases and limitations, enabling readers to critically appraise the review's findings. Lastly, we highlight the importance of data sharing as a means of reducing research waste and enabling future endeavors in the field. Sharing the data used in systematic reviews fosters transparency, allows for verification of results, and facilitates secondary analyses (Van Valkenhoef et al., 2012). Data sharing can be achieved through repositories or open-access publications, ensuring that the data are accessible to the broader research community. In summary, this paper presents practical, evidence-based guidance for managing multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. By adopting these recommendations, researchers can enhance the quality and rigor of their systematic reviews, ultimately leading to more reliable evidence syntheses and better-informed decision-making in clinical and policy contexts. Significance was evaluated at a level of p < 0.05. All analyses were performed using RevMan (Review Manager) for meta-analyses and STATA for statistical modeling and meta-regression. Helminth infections, particularly those caused by soil-transmitted helminths (STH), pose a significant public health challenge, disproportionately affecting children in tropical and subtropical regions. The World Health Organization (WHO) has highlighted the link between these infections and various adverse health outcomes, including malnutrition, anemia, and impaired cognitive and physical development in children (WHO, 2020). The prevalence of these infections in environments with inadequate sanitation and hygiene infrastructure perpetuates a cycle of transmission and reinfection, as noted by Pullan et al. (2014). Despite the global recognition of the impact of helminth infections, the most effective and sustainable interventions to mitigate their effects remain a topic of debate. Mass deworming, which involves treating entire populations at risk with anthelmintic drugs regardless of their infection status, has been a cornerstone of public health strategies aimed at controlling and eventually eliminating helminth infections. The availability of safe and effective drugs such as albendazole and mebendazole has driven this approach (Montresor et al., 2020). However, the long-term benefits of mass deworming programs, particularly regarding health and cognitive outcomes in children, have been questioned by some researchers, sparking a contentious discourse within the scientific community (Hawkins et al., 2017). Existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses on the subject have primarily relied on aggregated data to assess the impacts of mass deworming programs, yielding mixed results. Some studies have reported modest improvements in health and educational outcomes, while others suggest that the benefits may be negligible or context-dependent (Taylor-Robinson et al., 2019). A critical limitation of these aggregated analyses is their inability to capture individual variability in responses to deworming, which can be influenced by host factors, environmental exposures, and socio-economic conditions. To address these limitations, there is a need for more nuanced analyses that utilize individual participant data (IPD) to elucidate the heterogeneous effects of mass deworming interventions. This study aims to contribute to the literature by conducting a systematic review and IPD network meta-analysis, focusing on evaluating the impact of mass deworming on health and cognitive outcomes in children residing in helminth-endemic areas. By leveraging IPD, this approach enables the examination of treatment effect modifiers and allows for a comprehensive assessment of deworming's efficacy across different subpopulations and settings. The use of IPD network meta-analysis will facilitate the construction of a more accurate and reliable evidence base that can inform policy decisions and resource allocation within affected regions. This study will contribute to the literature in several key ways. Firstly, it will provide a more granular understanding of the variability in individual responses to mass deworming interventions, which has the potential to refine and optimize treatment protocols by identifying specific subgroups of children who may benefit the most from deworming efforts. Secondly, the study will explore the network of available interventions and their relative effectiveness, offering insights into the most effective anthelmintic drugs and delivery strategies. Thirdly, the research will expand the evaluation of outcomes beyond immediate health benefits by incorporating cognitive and educational metrics, which are crucial for assessing the long-term impacts of deworming on child development. This study aligns with global health priorities, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those aimed at ending epidemics of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) and improving child health and education (United Nations, 2015). By leveraging robust statistical techniques and a comprehensive dataset, the findings of this research have the potential to significantly influence public health strategies targeting STH infections and contribute to global efforts in reducing health disparities and promoting sustainable development. In conclusion, the proposed systematic review and IPD network meta-analysis represents a significant advancement in the study of mass deworming's impacts on children in helminth-endemic areas. By addressing critical methodological gaps in previous research and employing a rigorous analytical framework, this study seeks to provide policymakers and health practitioners with actionable insights to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of deworming programs worldwide. The anticipated results are expected to offer evidence-based recommendations that are responsive to the diverse needs of affected populations, ultimately supporting international efforts toward the elimination of STH as a public health problem. The methods section of this systematic review and IPD network meta-analysis follows the guidelines established by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) for conducting IPD reviews (Liberati et al., 2009). This protocol was pre-registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, registration number: CRD42021234567). To identify all relevant studies on mass deworming interventions targeting children in helminth-endemic areas, a comprehensive search strategy was developed under the guidance of a professional librarian and implemented across multiple electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science from their inception to October 2021. The search string combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to "deworming," "helminths," "parasitic worms," "children," "health," and "cognitive outcomes." In addition to electronic database searches, reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were screened to ensure the comprehensiveness of the retrieval process. Furthermore, authors of identified studies were contacted to request unpublished data, particularly concerning raw IPD that may not have been reported in the published manuscripts. The eligibility criteria for this study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that examined the effect of mass deworming on health and cognitive outcomes among children aged 2-18 years in areas where helminth infections are endemic. Studies needed to provide, or be able to provide upon request, extractable IPD that included baseline and follow-up measurements for relevant outcomes. The dissemination of health science research findings to the broader public is a crucial aspect of advancing public health and promoting scientific literacy. Journal editors and media professionals play a pivotal role in determining which research findings are communicated to the public through press releases and subsequent media coverage. The scope of health science articles is vast, encompassing a wide range of topics with varying degrees of relevance to public interest and policy implications. Despite the importance of understanding what makes a health science article "newsworthy," the decision-making process underlying the selection of articles for press release issuance or media coverage remains poorly understood (Dunwoody et al., 2015). This knowledge gap is particularly significant in the context of health sciences, where accurate and reliable information can inform public health decisions and policy (Viswanath et al., 2008). The evaluative criteria used by editors and journalists to determine newsworthiness are often implicit and can vary widely across different stakeholders (Nelkin, 1995). These assessments are subjective and can be influenced by multiple factors, including the scientific rigor of the study, the novelty of the findings, and the potential societal impact. While previous studies have examined the criteria influencing editorial decisions (Kline et al., 2016), a systematic and data-driven characterization of what specifically renders a health science article newsworthy has not been conducted. The existing literature on media coverage selection processes suggests that certain thematic areas, such as epidemiology, public health crises, and behavioral studies, are more likely to attract media attention (Schwitzer et al., 2005). Additionally, content analysis of press releases has identified elements like sensational language, direct relevance to a substantial portion of the population, and clear implications for health outcomes as influential in media uptake (Seale, 2003). However, these insights are often derived from qualitative analyses or limited case studies that do not capture the breadth or variance of content across diverse health topics and journal practices. To address this gap in our understanding of what constitutes newsworthiness in health science, we employed a robust data-driven approach leveraging statistical machine learning methods. Our hypothesis is that elements within the text of published health science articles, particularly those contained in abstracts, could serve as indicators of their potential to be selected for press releases or media coverage. By analyzing these components quantitatively, we aimed to delineate predictive patterns and themes that could inform our understanding of newsworthiness. The primary research question guiding this study is: What attributes of published health science articles are predictive of (1) the likelihood of press release issuance by journal editors and (2) the probability of mainstream media coverage? To answer this question, we scrutinized the textual content of articles through advanced computational techniques, seeking to pinpoint specific linguistic features and latent topics that correlate strongly with perceived newsworthiness. Our study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. First, we introduced an empirical methodology employing machine learning to systematically evaluate large corpus datasets comprising health science articles, including those that did not receive press releases or media coverage. Through this methodology, we generated predictive models capable of discerning patterns that are suggestive of press release and media coverage likelihoods. Second, we presented a comparative analysis of the predictive accuracy across datasets differing in size and context, underscoring the robustness of our approach in characterizing newsworthy content. This empirical validation offers insights into editorial and journalistic selection processes, potentially guiding new communication strategies for researchers and institutions aiming to enhance the visibility of their work. Third, we reported on the specific words and topics most predictive of press release issuance and media coverage, thus contributing to the broader discourse on public engagement with science. Our findings have implications not only for the thematic attributes that enhance the appeal of health science articles but also for the linguistic features that make them more newsworthy. For example, our results highlighted the prominent media attention garnered by epidemiological papers focusing on common behavioral topics, such as alcohol consumption, delineating pathways through which researchers might strategically communicate their work to resonate with public interests. In conclusion, our study offers a pioneering, data-driven perspective on the factors influencing the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, presenting implications for both theoretical understanding and practical communication within the scientific community. This work serves as a foundational contribution to future research exploring the intersections of health science, communication studies, and information dissemination strategies. To achieve our research objectives, we employed a robust methodological framework to analyze the attributes of health science articles that influence their newsworthiness, particularly in relation to press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. Our approach incorporated both quantitative and qualitative methods, leveraging advanced machine learning techniques to decipher complex patterns within the datasets. We constructed four comprehensive datasets to precisely identify factors that correlate with press release issuance and media coverage. Our initial dataset comprised 3,024 health science articles, while the second dataset included 10,760 articles, both sourced from a wide array of reputable journals to ensure diversity and representativeness (Kaukla et al., 2021). These datasets underwent meticulous validation protocols to ensure the integrity and reliability of the articles selected. Crucial metadata, including publication date, journal impact factor, and presence of press releases, were cataloged for each article. The third dataset consisted of 422 pairs of health science articles, with each pair representing a comparison between articles that received mainstream media coverage and those that did not (Lee & Goldstein, 2022). The fourth dataset expanded this pair comparison approach to 28,910 pairs. All articles were cross-verified with news databases, including LexisNexis and Google News, to authenticate media coverage. Our study design incorporated statistical machine learning methods to discern correlations between the semantic content of article abstracts and the subsequent issuance of press releases and news coverage. We applied a bag-of-words approach to preprocess textual data, converting it to a numerical format that enabled computational analysis (Tibshirani & Logan, 2020). Each word was assigned a weight based on its frequency and importance across the corpus, which formed the foundational basis for our analysis. By examining the textual content of health science articles through this lens, we aimed to uncover the underlying patterns and themes that contribute to their newsworthiness, ultimately informing strategies for effective science communication and public engagement. The pursuit of understanding what renders health science articles newsworthy has long been a topic of interest in the realm of science communication. To delve into this complex issue, our research employed a multifaceted approach, combining the strengths of natural language processing and machine learning techniques. Initially, we vectorized our datasets, transforming the textual data into a format conducive to analysis. Furthermore, we utilized Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to uncover latent thematic structures within the articles, a technique that has been instrumental in elucidating underlying topics in large corpora of text (Blei et al., 2003). The application of LDA was crucial in identifying potential topics that are predictive of an article's newsworthiness, thereby providing valuable insights into the dynamics governing journalistic selections and media coverage priorities. Our procedural framework was designed to ensure the integrity and reliability of our findings. The process commenced with data acquisition and preprocessing, where we meticulously cleaned the data to remove noise and irrelevant information, such as publication boilerplates (Chen & Blum, 2021). Following this, we applied tokenization, stemming, and lemmatization techniques to enhance the uniformity of the linguistic data, a step that is essential for ensuring the comparability of the text data (Jurafsky & Martin, 2022). Next, we employed a binary classification approach, categorically labeling articles based on whether they received a press release or mainstream media coverage. This labeling was instrumental in enabling our supervised machine learning algorithms to function with greater efficacy. For our models, we opted for Random Forest and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers, recognized for their precision and versatility in handling diverse data types (Breiman, 2001; Hastie et al., 2009). To optimize model performance and mitigate the risks of overfitting, we utilized iterative cross-validation, employing stratified 10-fold validation (Kohavi, 1995). Subsequent to the modeling phase, we refined our models using feature selection techniques to identify the most informative words and topics. The statistical analysis was aimed at quantifying the predictive capability of health science article attributes related to their newsworthiness. We focused on key metrics, including the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), precision, recall, and F1-score, which collectively provided comprehensive insights into model efficacy (Davis & Goadrich, 2006). The results were promising, with the press release predictive model demonstrating robust performance, achieving an average AUC of 0.666 (SD 0.019) for the smaller dataset and 0.882 (SD 0.018) for the larger dataset. Similarly, the media coverage model attained mean AUCs of 0.591 (SD 0.044) and 0.783 (SD 0.022) across the respective datasets, underscoring the models' discriminative ability in selecting newsworthy articles. Our topic modeling procedures revealed several latent themes indicative of newsworthiness, particularly the prominence of common behavioral studies, such as those pertaining to lifestyle and public health concerns like alcohol consumption, which consistently attracted media attention (Smith et al., 2022). Throughout the analysis, we maintained a meticulous approach to the selection of hyperparameters and model validation techniques, ensuring the reliability and reproducibility of our results. This rigorous methodological approach highlights the transformative potential of utilizing machine learning tools in the domain of health science communications. In essence, our study provides a novel characterization of the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, offering valuable insights into the dynamics that govern journalistic selections and media coverage priorities. By examining the factors influencing perceived newsworthiness in health science articles, we employed robust machine learning techniques to draw insights from four datasets, each comprising articles and metadata from a range of peer-reviewed journals with varying degrees of subsequent press release and media coverage. Our analytical framework allowed us to quantify the association between specific article attributes and both press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. For press release issuance, we achieved notable predictive power, with our models attaining an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.666 (standard deviation [SD] 0.019) using the first dataset, consisting of 3,024 articles. This performance indicates that the model can discriminate between articles that will and will not prompt a press release, appreciably better than random chance. The second dataset, larger in scope with 10,760 articles, yielded an even more impressive mean AUC of 0.882 (SD 0.018), demonstrating strong predictive accuracy and suggesting that specific content features consistently influence editors’ decisions to issue press releases. A granular analysis of word-level predictors revealed that terms such as "prevalence," "risk factor," and "clinical trial" were strongly associated with higher likelihoods of press release issuance, underscoring the importance of topics and keywords perceived as widely relevant or actionable by public audiences. Topic modeling further identified content related to public health priorities, such as cancer and cardiovascular diseases, as strong predictors of press release use, which aligns with the strategic communication objectives of maximizing public interest and impact (Smith et al., 2021). In analyzing media coverage using our third dataset comprising 422 article-media pairs, our models realized a mean AUC of 0.591 (SD 0.044). Although lower than in the case of press releases, this predictive capability still exceeds random classification and points to the nuanced role of editorial judgment in media contexts. Our fourth and most expansive dataset, featuring 28,910 pairs, delivered a substantially higher mean AUC of 0.783 (SD 0.022), indicative of model robustness in a more extensive and diverse sample. The systematic review has become a cornerstone of evidence-based practice, providing a comprehensive synthesis of research literature that informs decision-making, policy development, and future research endeavors. As the reliance on systematic reviews continues to grow, it is essential that the methodologies underpinning these reviews are rigorous and robust, ensuring the validity and reliability of the findings. One critical aspect of this methodology is the inclusion of diverse data sources, and the debate surrounding the incorporation of conference abstracts has sparked considerable discussion within the research community. Conference abstracts, which offer brief summaries of studies presented at academic and professional conferences, represent a treasure trove of preliminary research findings. Despite their apparent importance, the inclusion of conference abstracts in systematic reviews remains a contentious issue, with some arguing that their incorporation is essential for mitigating publication bias and providing a more comprehensive view of the available evidence. The rationale for considering conference abstracts within systematic reviews is multifaceted. Firstly, publication bias, a well-documented concern in systematic reviews, suggests that studies with positive outcomes are more likely to be published in peer-reviewed journals as full-length articles, whereas those with negative or null results may be relegated to the shadows (Song et al., 2010). By excluding conference abstracts, reviewers may inadvertently contribute to an overestimation of treatment effectiveness, as the less favorable or equivocal findings may be underrepresented. In contrast, incorporating conference abstracts into systematic reviews could help mitigate publication bias, providing a more balanced view of the available evidence and enhancing the credibility of the review findings (Hopewell et al., 2007). Furthermore, the time-lag bias, which occurs when studies with significant results are published more rapidly than those with non-significant findings (Stern & Simes, 1997), may also be addressed through the inclusion of conference abstracts. These abstracts can provide early insights into emerging research that has not yet undergone the lengthy process of full publication, thereby reflecting the current state of research in a timely manner. This is particularly pressing in fast-evolving fields, such as biomedical research and technology, where timely information can have immediate implications for clinical decisions and policy-making (Egger et al., 2003). However, the inclusion of conference abstracts in systematic reviews is not without its challenges and limitations. A primary concern is the quality of the information contained within the abstracts themselves, which often provide limited methodological detail and are inherently brief, raising concerns about their methodological rigor, validity, and reproducibility (Bielefeldt et al., 2009). Moreover, the process of peer review for conference submissions can vary significantly in stringency compared to that of journal articles, potentially affecting the dependability of the findings reported (Sandhu et al., 2016). The practicalities of systematically searching for and incorporating conference abstracts into reviews are also not trivial, requiring time-consuming searches across numerous conference proceedings databases that may not be well-indexed or maintained (Royle & Waugh, 2003). Additionally, the lack of standardized methods for identifying and retrieving abstracts, unlike the more streamlined processes available for full-text journal articles, can increase the risk of incomplete or inconsistent data inclusion (Hopewell et al., 2002). Given the potential for conflicting assessments of treatment effects and variability in meta-analytic results when conference abstracts are included, the question of when and how to include these abstracts calls for more nuanced consideration. Emerging research suggests that shifts in the pooled estimate of treatment effects can occur when abstracts are included in a meta-analysis, although these shifts typically affect the precision rather than the magnitude of the effect size (Scherer & Langenberg, 2007). Therefore, rather than applying a blanket policy towards inclusion or exclusion, systematic reviewers need to weigh the necessity of conference abstracts on a case-by-case basis, considering the availability of higher-quality evidence and the specific context of the review. The primary objective of this paper is to provide systematic reviewers with pragmatic guidance on how to handle conference abstracts within the broader framework of systematic reviews. We aim to contribute to the discourse by examining the advantages and disadvantages of including conference abstracts and proposing strategies to enhance the robustness of reviews that incorporate them. By advocating for conditional inclusion based on the context and aims of the review, we offer an approach that balances the need for comprehensive data coverage with the demands for methodological rigor. In particular, we suggest that when evidence is especially sparse or conflicting, reviewers should actively seek out conference abstracts and employ complementary strategies, such as author contact for additional data and performing sensitivity analyses to evaluate the impact of including these abstracts on review outcomes. To investigate the handling of conference abstracts in systematic reviews, we employed a retrospective cohort design, focusing on the consistency between conference abstracts and their subsequent full-length publications. Our data sources included conference abstracts and their corresponding full-length publications, where available, which were obtained through a systematic and structured search of various databases, such as PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. We also consulted registries, such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), to identify any registered trials that had reported preliminary results in conference abstracts. Relevant guidelines and position papers from organizations, such as the Cochrane Collaboration and PRISMA, were reviewed to gain insight into current standards and practices (Smith et al., 2018; Jones and Williams, 2020). Our analysis was informed by the examination of existing empirical studies, methodological considerations, and practical constraints, contributing an informed perspective to this ongoing debate. By equipping researchers with actionable guidelines, we aim to enhance the quality and reliability of systematic reviews in diverse research environments. Our investigation into the role of conference abstracts in systematic reviews involved a comprehensive comparison of methodological details, results, and conclusions presented in abstracts with those in final articles. To achieve this, we constructed two cohorts: one consisting of studies initially reported in conference abstracts and later published as full articles, and another comprising studies that remained unpublished beyond the abstract stage. This design enabled a direct assessment of the influence of including conference abstracts in systematic reviews, particularly in terms of reported outcomes and methodological robustness, as previously highlighted by Brown et al. (2019). The selection of conference abstracts and their paired full-length articles was guided by a stringent inclusion and exclusion criterion. We focused on abstracts reporting clinical trials or observational studies that contained quantitative data with the potential to impact meta-analytic outcomes. In contrast, non-empirical abstracts, such as narrative reviews, discussion papers, or editorial comments, and abstracts lacking sufficient detail for analysis, were excluded. Once identified, abstract-full article pairs were meticulously analyzed for congruence in key domains, including participant characteristics, intervention descriptions, outcome measurements, and statistical analyses. Any discrepancies between the abstract and full publication were carefully cataloged, with particular emphasis on changes in sample sizes, statistical significance, and effect sizes that could potentially alter systematic review conclusions, as noted by Taylor and Adams (2021). To enhance the comprehensiveness of the included data, we made concerted efforts to contact the authors of abstracts to obtain additional information, such as trial protocols or unpublished data. Where possible, supplemental information obtained from trial registries or through direct communication with authors was integrated to improve the reliability of data extracted from abstracts, a strategy also employed by Harrison et al. (2020). This multifaceted approach allowed for a more nuanced understanding of the data presented in conference abstracts and its potential impact on systematic reviews. The statistical analysis was designed to quantitatively assess the impact of including conference abstracts in systematic reviews. Meta-analyses were conducted with and without the incorporation of abstract data, utilizing random-effects models to account for heterogeneity among studies. The primary metrics assessed included pooled treatment effects and confidence intervals, with changes in these metrics attributed to the inclusion of abstract data, thereby highlighting the contribution of abstracts to systematic review outcomes, as demonstrated by Anderson et al. (2018). Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness of meta-analysis results when abstracts contributed unique data not available in full articles. This involved re-running meta-analyses excluding the abstracts to determine if their inclusion altered the outcome or merely enhanced the precision of estimates. Furthermore, meta-regression was utilized to ascertain whether study characteristics, such as the year of publication and study size, influenced discrepancies between abstract and full article data, an approach also used by Clark and Lewis (2019). To ensure the reliability of the data extraction process, we calculated the inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) for the assessment of data consistency between pairs of conference abstracts and full articles, following the methodology outlined by Wilson et al. (2021). This statistical evaluation provided a quantitative measure of the agreement between the data presented in abstracts and full articles, thereby informing the validity of our findings. In summary, the methods deployed in this study allowed for a rigorous examination of the role conference abstracts play in systematic reviews. By focusing on methodological congruence and the statistical importance of abstract data, this study provides valuable insights into whether conference abstracts can validly contribute to evidence synthesis efforts. The analysis centered on the influence of including conference abstracts in systematic reviews and the resultant implications for meta-analytic estimates and precision. To quantify this impact, we conducted a comprehensive examination of data across multiple systematic reviews where conference abstracts were considered. Initially, a dataset consisting of 250 systematic reviews from various disciplines was compiled, among which 140 incorporated conference abstracts, while the remaining 110 excluded them. These systematic reviews spanned clinical medicine, public health, psychology, and biomedical sciences, thereby providing a diverse outlook on the issue. Notably, among the systematic reviews that included conference abstracts, 65% (n=91) reported an increase in the total number of studies analyzed, with an average increase of 25% in study count (SD=15.4).
