The utility of soft biometric traits, such as sex, age, ethnicity, and eye color, lies in their ability to provide a coarse yet useful description of an individual. While these traits are not distinctive enough to identify a person on their own, they can significantly narrow down a search space, complement primary biometric modalities, and support applications where explicit identification is unnecessary or undesirable. As Jain, Dass, and Nandakumar (2004) and Dantcheva, Elia, and Ross (2016) have noted, soft biometric traits can be particularly useful in various contexts. Among these traits, sex is one of the most widely studied, with applications in indexing large biometric databases, demographic analysis, human-computer interaction, and forensic investigation. Predicting sex from a person's appearance is commonly referred to as "gender classification" in the literature; however, we use the term "sex-prediction" to emphasize that the quantity inferred from biometric data is a biological attribute rather than a social identity, as highlighted by Bobeldyk and Ross (2016). The face is the most intuitive source for sex-prediction, and deep learning has made face-based sex classification highly accurate under favorable conditions. Nevertheless, in many real-world scenarios, the full face is not available due to occlusions such as surgical masks, scarves, helmets, or extreme poses and viewing angles. In such cases, the periocular region, which encompasses the eye, eyelids, eyelashes, eyebrows, and surrounding skin, emerges as an attractive alternative. This region remains visible even when the rest of the face is occluded, can be captured by a wide range of sensors, and combines shape, texture, and color information that is useful for recognition, as demonstrated by Park, Ross, and Jain (2009) and Alonso-Fernandez and Bigun (2016). Periocular images also arise naturally from iris acquisition in the near-infrared (NIR) spectrum and from visible wavelength (VW) imaging with smartphones and other consumer devices. Early research showed that the periocular region contains information about sex, with Merkow, Jou, and Savvides (2010) reporting accuracies of roughly 85% from periocular crops of web-collected face images using hand-crafted features. Dong and Woodard (2011) further demonstrated that eyebrow shape alone carries a discriminative signal. For NIR iris and ocular images, Thomas et al. (2007) and Lagree and Bowyer (2011) predicted sex from texture descriptors, achieving accuracies typically between 60% and 80%. More recent studies have applied convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and obtained better results, with Tapia and Aravena (2018) obtaining high accuracy from NIR iris images, and Bobeldyk and Ross (2016, 2018) examining which ocular regions contribute most to sex-prediction and how covariates influence it. Rattani, Reddy, and Derakhshani (2018) extended the problem to smartphone-based VW ocular images and reported competitive accuracies with deep architectures. These studies collectively suggest that sex can be inferred from the periocular region with a reasonable degree of reliability. However, the reported figures must be interpreted with caution. Most studies train and test on a single database, often using a single sensor, which can lead to inflated performance due to the exploitation of sensor-specific or session-specific cues rather than sex-related structure. This concern is more than theoretical, as Kuehlkamp, Becker, and Bowyer (2017) have shown that apparent sex-related information in iris images can be partly attributed to cosmetics such as mascara, resulting in a substantial drop in accuracy once this confound is removed. Furthermore, it is well documented that biometric algorithms trained on one sensor often degrade when evaluated on another, which is the cross-sensor problem studied extensively in iris and periocular recognition, as noted by Alonso-Fernandez, Raja, Busch, and Bigun (2019). If sex-prediction is to be deployed on periocular images of unknown origin, accuracy estimated under same-sensor conditions is an optimistic upper bound. Another limitation of prior studies is that NIR and VW periocular images are almost always treated separately, despite the fact that the two spectra differ in the visual information they offer. NIR imaging suppresses melanin-related pigmentation and emphasizes structural texture, whereas VW images contain color, pigmentation, and cosmetic cues. The question of whether sex-related patterns learned in one spectrum transfer to the other, and whether a single model can handle both, remains largely unexplored. This question is crucial for heterogeneous deployments, such as when a model trained on NIR iris-capture databases is applied to selfie-type VW images, or vice versa. The methodological details of prior studies also make results difficult to compare, as they differ in image size, periocular region cropping, architecture, partitioning protocol, and whether subjects are disjoint across training and test sets. Few studies have tested the generalization of a single model across many databases with a consistent protocol, and the effect of fusing heterogeneous sources into one training set has received little attention. These gaps lead to the central research question of this paper: How accurately can the sex of a subject be predicted from periocular images when the sensor and the spectrum of the test images are unknown at training time? We split this question into three subquestions: (i) What accuracy can be expected when training and testing are performed on disjoint sensors within the same spectrum (NIR-NIR and VW-VW)? (ii) How well does a model generalize across spectra, that is, when trained on NIR data and tested on VW data, and vice versa? (iii) Can a single model trained on a multi-spectral collection perform comparably to spectrum-specific models? To answer these questions, we train CNNs on fused sets composed of several NIR and VW periocular databases acquired with different sensors and evaluate them under protocols that keep the test sensor out of training. This design reflects a more realistic setting in which the origin of an image is not known beforehand and discourages the network from using sensor-specific artifacts as shortcuts. The contributions of this work are threefold: (1) a cross-sensor evaluation within each spectrum, using leave-one-database-out protocols to estimate sex-prediction accuracy for unseen sensors in NIR and VW imagery; (2) a cross-spectral evaluation, quantifying the transferability of learned sex-related features between NIR and VW; and (3) an examination of the effectiveness of a single model trained on a multi-spectral collection in performing comparably to spectrum-specific models. Our approach involves training CNNs on a heterogeneous mixture of NIR and VW periocular databases, which prevents the network from relying on any single sensor's signature. By doing so, we aim to provide a more realistic estimate of sex-prediction accuracy and to investigate the generalizability of our model across different sensors and spectra. The results of our study will provide valuable insights into the feasibility of sex-prediction from periocular images in various scenarios, including those where the sensor and spectrum of the test images are unknown at training time. Ultimately, our work seeks to contribute to the development of more robust and reliable sex-prediction systems that can be deployed in a wide range of applications, from biometric identification to demographic analysis and human-computer interaction. The periocular region has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential as a soft biometric trait, with applications in various fields, including security and surveillance. A crucial aspect of this research is the ability to predict a subject's sex from periocular images, which has been explored in several studies. However, a comprehensive understanding of the feasibility of sex prediction from periocular images, particularly in unconstrained environments, remains elusive. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an extensive study using a large collection of periocular images from publicly available databases, covering two spectra (near-infrared and visible-wavelength) and several acquisition sensors. Our experiments were designed to evaluate the performance of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in predicting sex from periocular images, with a focus on the impact of spectrum and sensor variability. We used a consistent and reproducible protocol across all databases, applying the same preprocessing, periocular cropping, network configurations, and partitioning rules. This allowed us to attribute any differences in performance to the acquisition scenario rather than to differences in experimental design. The results of our study provide a more realistic estimate of the feasibility of sex prediction from periocular images and highlight the challenges associated with applying current approaches to unconstrained data. The databases used in our study comprised a total of seven datasets, including BioSec, CASIA-Iris-Thousand, IITD-Iris, ND-CrossSensor, UBIPr, MICHE-I, and CSIP. These datasets were divided into two sets: near-infrared (NIR) and visible-wavelength (VW). The NIR set contained approximately 41,000 images from 1,650 subjects, while the VW set contained around 22,000 images from 940 subjects. The proportion of female subjects ranged from 29% to 47% across databases. To ensure reliable sex labels, we excluded subjects without verified labels, resulting in a binary classification task (male or female). Preprocessing of the images involved localizing the eye regions using a landmark detector for VW images and a Hough-transform-based segmentation for NIR images. A periocular region of interest was then cropped around the eye center, including the eyebrow, eyelids, and surrounding skin, while avoiding hair and facial context. The cropped images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels using bicubic interpolation and normalized using the ImageNet channel statistics. Images with failed landmark detection or segmentation were discarded, resulting in a loss of 3.1% of the total samples. We used two feature extractors, ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121, which were initialized with ImageNet weights and fine-tuned end-to-end. The original classification layer was replaced with a global average pooling layer, a dropout layer, and a two-unit softmax layer. The models were optimized using stochastic gradient descent with momentum, with an initial learning rate of 10⁻³ and a weight decay of 5 × 10⁻⁴. Training was performed for a maximum of 60 epochs with early stopping, and the loss was measured using cross-entropy. To reduce the effect of class imbalance, we used class-balanced mini-batches drawn by oversampling the minority class. Data augmentation consisted of random rotations, scaling, translations, brightness and contrast jitter, and Gaussian blur, applied on the fly. Our experimental protocols were designed to evaluate the performance of the models in various scenarios. We defined three scenarios: cross-sensor within spectrum, cross-spectrum, and multi-spectral. In the cross-sensor within spectrum scenario, we applied a leave-one-database-out protocol, where a model was trained on the union of all other databases of the same spectrum and tested on the held-out database. This resulted in seven train-test configurations. In the cross-spectrum scenario, models were trained on the union of all NIR databases and tested on each VW database, and vice versa. In the multi-spectral scenario, models were trained on the union of NIR and VW databases, excluding one database that served as the test set. This was repeated for all seven databases. The results of our study show that a single CNN trained on combined NIR and VW data can attain an average accuracy of 83%, which is only a few points below the within-spectrum case. This suggests that a substantial portion of the discriminative information is spectrum-independent. The average classification accuracy across all scenarios was around 82%, indicating that sex prediction from periocular images is feasible, even in unconstrained environments. However, the performance of the models varied significantly across databases and scenarios, highlighting the challenges associated with applying current approaches to real-world data. The findings of our study have implications for both the design of soft-biometric systems and the discussion of privacy. The ease with which sex can be inferred from periocular images captured without a subject's explicit intent has significant implications for how such data are stored and shared. Our results suggest that current approaches to sex prediction from periocular images may not be robust enough to handle the variability present in unconstrained data. Therefore, further research is needed to develop more robust and generalizable models that can handle the challenges associated with real-world data. In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the feasibility of sex prediction from periocular images, highlighting the challenges associated with applying current approaches to unconstrained data. The results of our study have significant implications for both the design of soft-biometric systems and the discussion of privacy, and highlight the need for further research in this area. By developing more robust and generalizable models, we can improve the accuracy and reliability of sex prediction

The advent of deep learning has revolutionized the field of machine learning, and a key driver of this progress has been the concept of transfer learning. At its core, transfer learning involves training a model on one task, typically with an abundance of data, and then leveraging the knowledge it has acquired to improve performance on other tasks where labeled data is scarce. In the realm of natural language processing, one of the most prominent forms of transfer learning is the use of pretrained word embeddings, such as those introduced by Mikolov et al. (2013) and Pennington et al. (2014). More recently, researchers have explored the use of contextualized representations obtained from language models or other pretraining objectives, as seen in the work of Peters et al. (2018) and McCann et al. (2017). Similarly, in computer vision, convolutional features pretrained on ImageNet have become a standard starting point for a wide range of downstream problems, as demonstrated by Donahue et al. (2014), Yosinski et al. (2014), and He et al. (2016). Despite the differences between these approaches, they share a common thread: the transfer of unary features, which are essentially vectors associated with individual data units, such as words, tokens, or image regions. However, unary features only capture a portion of the information that a model needs to understand the structure of its input. Many of the most critical regularities in data concern the relationships between pairs of units. For instance, in language, a word's meaning is often dependent on its syntactic head, coreferent mentions, or semantically related phrases. Similarly, in images, the interpretation of a pixel is influenced by its neighboring pixels, which may belong to the same edge or object. Modern architectures have developed various ways to encode this structural information, such as recurrent networks, which propagate information along a fixed sequential order, convolutional networks, which impose a fixed local connectivity, and self-attention models, like those introduced by Vaswani et al. (2017), which learn input-dependent weights to determine how strongly each unit attends to every other. In particular, attention can be viewed as a latent relational graph over the input units, with edge weights computed on the fly. Nevertheless, in nearly all existing transfer learning pipelines, this relational structure is learned from scratch for each task, using limited labeled data. Meanwhile, structured representations, such as syntactic parses or knowledge graphs, have been shown to be beneficial for many tasks, as demonstrated by Tai et al. (2015), Marcheggiani and Titov (2017), and Kipf and Welling (2017). However, these representations often require expensive human annotation or an external parser that is itself trained with supervision and is only available for certain languages and domains. This observation motivates the central question of this work: can we learn generic latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data, and can such graphs be transferred to improve downstream tasks? A positive answer would offer a complementary route to transfer learning, where a pretrained model provides not only better initial feature vectors but also a structure describing how the units of a new input relate to one another, which a downstream model can use to organize its own computation. Such graphs have several potential advantages. They are separable from the features that produced them, making them reusable with different embeddings. They are potentially modality-agnostic, as the notion of pairwise dependency applies equally to words and pixels. Furthermore, they can be learned without labels, allowing them to exploit the vast, virtually unlimited text corpora that have driven recent advances in language representation. However, realizing this idea poses several challenges. First, we need an unsupervised objective that encourages a network to produce graphs that are useful and not merely arbitrary. Second, the graphs must be decoupled from the features, so they can be applied to a downstream model with different embeddings or architecture. Third, the graphs should be input-dependent, as the relevant dependencies differ from sentence to sentence and image to image, yet they must be computable for new inputs at transfer time without access to the original task's labels or features. To address these challenges, we propose GLoMo (Graphs from LOw-level MOdules), a framework that trains a network on an unsupervised predictive task in which two components are explicitly separated. A graph predictor takes the raw input and produces, at several layers, a set of affinity matrices whose entries give the strength of the dependency between each pair of units. A separate feature predictor then uses these matrices to aggregate information from layer-wise features and make predictions about held-out parts of the input. In the language setting, the objective is to predict the next word (and previous word, in the backward direction) given context, with the graph restricted to depend only on the input tokens and not on the feature pathway that consumes it. By forcing the graph predictor to provide all the information about how units should be combined, while the feature pathway processes only the content, the graphs are compelled to encode reusable relational structure. At transfer time, the graph predictor is frozen and applied to the downstream input, and the resulting graphs are plugged into the downstream network as additional, fixed-weight routing structures that mix the downstream model's own features across units, alongside its usual computation. We evaluate GLoMo on a diverse set of problems, including question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. In language tasks, adding transferred graphs yields consistent improvements over strong baselines, including models that already use pretrained GloVe or ELMo embeddings, indicating that the graphs provide information complementary to unary features. We further demonstrate that the learned graphs are transferable across representation spaces, as they can be applied on top of embeddings on which they were not trained, including GloVe, ELMo, and task-specific RNN hidden states. Finally, we show that the idea extends beyond language, as graphs learned over image pixels improve classification accuracy, demonstrating that the framework does not rely on word embeddings or any modality-specific components. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce the problem of transferring learned relational graphs, as opposed to unary features, from unlabeled data. Second, we propose GLoMo, an unsupervised framework that decouples graph prediction from feature prediction, making graphs transferable. Third, we provide empirical evidence that the learned graphs can be successfully transferred to improve downstream tasks, offering a new and complementary route to transfer learning. By exploring the potential of latent relational graphs, we hope to further advance the state-of-the-art in machine learning and natural language processing, enabling models to better capture the complex structural relationships present in data. The emergence of learned graphs has been shown to enhance performance across a range of language tasks, as well as image classification, with the added benefit of transferability across various embedding types and even to embedding-free units. To delve deeper into this phenomenon, we propose a two-stage framework, dubbed GLoMo (Graph from Learned Moments), which leverages the strengths of graph-based representations to capture complex patterns in data. At its core, GLoMo consists of a graph predictor that, in the absence of labels, generates latent relational graphs over input units, be they words or image positions. Concurrently, a feature predictor utilizes these graphs to solve an unsupervised objective, thereby learning to represent the input data in a meaningful way. The graph predictor, denoted as g, is a neural network that maps an input sequence x = (x1, ..., xT) to a set of K affinity matrices, 𝒢 = {G^(k)}, where each G^(k) is a T×T matrix. The computation of each entry Gij in these matrices follows the form of attention mechanisms, where the compatibility between a "query" projection of unit i and a "key" projection of unit j is normalized and asymmetric. This process is facilitated by a stack of L layers, each capable of producing its own graph, allowing for layer-specific and multi-headed graphs. The hidden states h, which are used to compute these graphs, are derived solely from the raw input and are kept separate from the downstream features, ensuring that the graphs encode relational information rather than content. In the context of language, the graph predictor g is instantiated as a stack of 1D convolutions with gated linear units, operating over word-level inputs. For images, g takes the form of a stack of 2D convolutions, with units corresponding to spatial positions in a feature map. The feature predictor f, on the other hand, takes the input units and the graphs as input and produces representations through graph-based propagation. This process involves the application of a gated nonlinearity with a residual connection, as well as a learned matrix U, to propagate information along the graph. To prevent the predictor from resorting to trivial solutions, it is tasked with solving a self-supervised objective, such as masked-context language modeling for language or predicting the pixel values of the lower half of an image from the upper half for images. The pretraining of GLoMo is carried out on large-scale datasets, including the One Billion Word benchmark for language and the unlabeled training split of CIFAR-10 for images. The text data is tokenized, lowercased, and truncated to a 100K-word vocabulary, with sentences batched by length and a maximum sequence length of 50 tokens. For images, the models are pretrained on the CIFAR-10 dataset with labels discarded, as well as on ImageNet-sized data at reduced resolution. The optimization of the models is performed using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-3, gradient clipping, and dropout. Upon completion of the pretraining phase, the graph predictor g is frozen, and the learned graphs are transferred to downstream tasks. For a given input, the graphs are computed from the raw tokens or pixels and combined with task-specific features through a lightweight transfer module. The downstream model, which remains unchanged, is then trained on labeled data to fine-tune the task-specific features. The transfer of graphs across different embeddings is achieved without requiring retraining of g, as demonstrated by switching the downstream base features between GloVe, ELMo, and RNN states. The evaluation of GLoMo is conducted on six benchmarks, encompassing question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. The results show that the incorporation of learned graphs leads to significant improvements in performance, often surpassing state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, the ablation of the number of layers and graphs reveals the importance of these components in capturing complex patterns in data. Overall, the proposed GLoMo framework demonstrates the efficacy of learned graphs in enhancing performance across a range of tasks, while also providing insights into the underlying mechanisms that enable such improvements. In the question answering task, GLoMo is evaluated on the SQuAD v1.1 dataset, using both a BiDAF-style and a self-attentive reader as base models. The results show that the incorporation of learned graphs leads to significant improvements in exact match and F1 scores. Similarly, in the natural language inference task, GLoMo is evaluated on the MultiNLI dataset, with matched and mismatched dev sets, using ESIM-like baselines. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of GLoMo in capturing complex semantic relationships between sentences. The sentiment analysis task is evaluated on the IMDB and Stanford Sentiment Treebank datasets, with GLoMo achieving state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks. In the image classification task, GLoMo is evaluated on the CIFAR-10 dataset, using a standard residual network, with the graphs acting on the spatial positions of intermediate feature maps. The results show that GLoMo achieves significant improvements in performance, even in low-resource settings where only a fraction of the labeled training data is available. The baselines used in the evaluation include the base model alone, the base model with ELMo or GloVe, the base model with a trained-from-scratch self-attention layer, and the base model augmented with graphs from a randomly initialized, untrained g. The results demonstrate that the improvements achieved by GLoMo are not simply due to the addition of parameters or computation, but rather the result of the learned graphs capturing meaningful patterns in the data. In conclusion, the proposed GLoMo framework demonstrates the effectiveness of learned graphs in enhancing performance across

The study of complex networks has become increasingly important in recent years, with many real-world systems being represented as large graphs. Social networks, such as Facebook, boast billions of users, while bibliographic databases like DBLP index millions of authors and publications. A fundamental task in these networks is community detection, which involves identifying groups of densely connected vertices that share common characteristics. Traditional community detection methods partition an entire graph, which can be costly and time-consuming, especially for large networks. Furthermore, these methods often produce communities that are not tailored to specific users. Community search, on the other hand, addresses these limitations by finding cohesive subgraphs containing a given query vertex, usually online and without examining the entire graph. Community search has numerous applications, including product advertisement, social event recommendation, and the discovery of functional modules in protein interaction networks. The cohesiveness of a community is typically measured using minimum-degree constraints, such as the k-core model, which requires every vertex in the community to have at least k neighbors inside it. Other models, such as the k-truss, k-clique, and k-edge-connected component, also use topology to define community cohesiveness. However, these approaches can return communities that are internally dense yet semantically incoherent, as they only consider the network's structure and ignore the attributes of the vertices. Recent studies have incorporated vertex attributes into community search, returning subgraphs whose members share a set of keywords or other attributes. However, these models often treat attributes as a flat set of independent labels, which can be limiting in many real-world networks where labels are organized hierarchically. For example, in bibliographic networks, an author's research interests can be mapped onto the ACM Computing Classification System, where "Machine learning" is a specialization of "Computing methodologies." Similarly, in biomedical networks, genes and proteins are annotated with Gene Ontology terms, and publications are indexed with Medical Subject Headings. Online retailers and social platforms also organize items and user interests into category trees. We refer to a graph whose vertices carry such hierarchical labels as a profiled graph, and the label hierarchy attached to a vertex as its P-tree. A P-tree is a rooted subtree of a global taxonomy, which contains a label together with its ancestors that generalize it. This allows two vertices to share a meaningful theme even if they have no identical leaf-level labels. For instance, one author may work on "deep learning" and another on "support vector machines," yet both are connected through the shared ancestor "machine learning." This observation highlights a gap in existing work, as structure-only community search ignores semantics entirely, while keyword-based community search can only match identical labels and misses communities whose members are related at different granularities. In this paper, we study the profiled community search (PCS) problem, which aims to find subgraphs that are both structurally cohesive and semantically cohesive. Given a profiled graph G, a query vertex q, and an integer k, PCS returns subgraphs that satisfy two conditions: each vertex has degree at least k within a connected subgraph containing q, and the vertices share a common subtree of P-trees that is maximal and contains the P-tree structure rooted at the taxonomy's root. Each answer is thus a profiled community paired with its shared theme, represented as a maximal common subtree. We investigate three research questions. First, can hierarchical profiles yield communities that are more cohesive and more interpretable than those from structure-only and keyword-based community search? Second, can PCS be solved exactly at the scale of real networks? Third, can it be answered online, at interactive latencies? PCS poses several challenges, including the exponential growth of candidate subtrees with the size of the P-tree, making enumeration and testing infeasible. Moreover, the subtree space has a structure that flat-set approaches cannot exploit directly, requiring adapted pruning rules. To address these challenges, we make several contributions. First, we introduce the PCS problem and formalize profiled graphs, P-trees, and profiled communities. We show that the maximal common subtree semantics yield themed communities at a granularity that adapts to the data and analyze their basic properties, including anti-monotonicity of the k-core with respect to subtree inclusion. This property underlies our pruning strategies. Second, we design the CP-tree, a compact index that organizes the vertices of G by their labels over the taxonomy and stores, for each node, the core numbers needed to retrieve candidate vertex sets. We develop a basic query algorithm that traverses candidate subtrees level by level, as well as advanced algorithms that use anti-monotonicity and vertex-set intersection to avoid verifying most candidates. Finally, we evaluate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on real-world networks, demonstrating the benefits of profiled community search in terms of community cohesiveness and interpretability. Our experiments on a DBLP-derived graph with ACM-CCS profiles show that k-core communities containing a given author have, on average, only 1.3 common labels at depth two or deeper in the taxonomy. This suggests that structurally cohesive communities are often thematically loose, highlighting the need for semantic considerations in community search. By incorporating hierarchical profiles into community search, we can discover more meaningful and cohesive communities that adapt to the data, enabling applications such as personalized recommendation, community-based advertising, and functional module discovery. Overall, our work addresses the gap in existing community search methods by providing a framework for profiled community search that balances structural and semantic cohesiveness, paving the way for more effective and interpretable community discovery in complex networks. The evaluation of Profiled Community Search (PCS) on real-world graphs, including DBLP and a PubMed-based biomedical network, reveals its effectiveness in identifying high-quality communities. To assess community quality, we employ a combination of structural measures, such as density and clustering coefficient, and semantic measures, including label-based similarity and the depth of shared themes. Our results show that PCS communities consistently outperform those obtained from k-core, k-truss, and keyword-based community search (CS) approaches. For instance, on the DBLP graph, PCS communities have, on average, 2.1 times the number of shared labels as structure-only communities, and their shared themes are 1.8 levels deeper in the taxonomy. A case study of well-known researchers demonstrates that PCS successfully separates an author's distinct research areas into different, interpretable communities, whereas other approaches tend to merge them. In terms of efficiency, our index-based algorithms demonstrate a significant improvement over the naive approach, with a speedup of two to three orders of magnitude. This enables online queries on large graphs, with over one million vertices, in under a second on average. The construction of the CP-tree index, which is essential for efficient query processing, can be completed in minutes, and its space overhead is proportional to the total size of the vertex P-trees. This makes it a practical solution for large profiled graphs. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of related work, while Section 3 formally defines the PCS problem. Section 4 presents the CP-tree index and the query algorithms, and Section 5 reports the experimental results. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. To formulate the PCS problem, we model a profiled graph as an undirected graph G(V, E), where each vertex v ∈ V is associated with a profile P(v), a rooted subtree of a global concept hierarchy T. The profile is closed under ancestors, meaning that if a label belongs to P(v), all its ancestors up to the root are also included. This property allows us to treat the set of labels of a vertex as a rooted subtree, which we refer to as a P-tree. The common P-tree of a vertex set S is the intersection of the P-trees of its members, resulting in a well-defined rooted subtree. Cohesiveness is measured using the minimum-degree criterion, which underlies the k-core concept and has been widely adopted in community search. Given a query vertex q and an integer k, a profiled community is a connected subgraph Gq ⊆ G that contains q, has a minimum degree of at least k, and has a maximal common P-tree. The maximality condition ensures that no connected k-core containing q shares a strictly larger common P-tree. The PCS problem returns all pairs (Gq, M), where M is the maximal common P-tree of Gq. It is possible for multiple incomparable maximal subtrees to exist, resulting in a query returning several communities, each characterized by a different theme. We evaluated PCS on four real profiled graphs, including Flickr, DBLP, PubMed, and DBpedia, which vary in size, structure, and profile characteristics. The graphs range from 0.9 million to 8.2 million vertices and from 5.4 million to 51 million edges. Average profile sizes range from 7.3 to 18.6 labels, and the hierarchies have depths of 4 to 11 levels. We preprocessed the graphs by removing self-loops and duplicate edges, retaining only the largest connected component, and discarding vertices with empty profiles. Each profile was then completed with all ancestor labels to ensure the subtree property. Additionally, we generated synthetic profiled graphs by attaching random subtrees of a fixed hierarchy to the vertices of Barabási–Albert graphs, allowing us to vary graph size and profile size independently in the scalability experiments. For each dataset, we sampled 200 query vertices uniformly at random from those with a core number of at least 6, ensuring that nontrivial communities exist for the default parameter k = 6. We also varied k from 4 to 8 in the sensitivity analysis. All reported figures are means over the workload unless stated otherwise. Our baseline algorithm is based on a level-wise search, similar to Apriori, which motivates the use of a hierarchical search strategy. The algorithm starts with the single-node tree consisting of the root and expands every feasible tree by one leaf label, taken from a child of an existing node that also appears in P(q). The process terminates when no candidate survives, and the feasible trees from the last non-empty level are the maximal common P-trees. Although this approach is correct, it has high computational costs due to repeated graph traversals and subtree-containment tests. To address this issue, we developed the compressed profile tree (CP-tree) index, which supports online queries efficiently. The CP-tree index is constructed by merging the label hierarchy with the k-core decomposition of G. For each label x in T, we define Vx as the set of vertices whose profiles contain x, and G[Vx] as the induced subgraph. The induced subgraphs are nested along every root-to-leaf path, allowing the core decomposition of G[Vx] to be stored incrementally. Each CP-tree node stores the label x and a compressed list of vertices with their core numbers in G[Vx], and a vertex is stored only at the deepest node on each path where its core number changes. This enables efficient query processing, as a query for (q, k, T′) can retrieve the connected k-core of q in G[V{T′}] from the index without scanning the entire graph. The construction of the core decomposition of a graph proceeds in a top-down manner, starting from the root node. Specifically, the linear-time peeling algorithm (Batagelj & Zaversnik, 2003) is used to compute the core decomposition of each child's induced subgraph, and connected components are labeled using a union-find structure. This approach yields a time complexity of O(Σx (|Ex| + |Vx|)), which is bounded by O(|P̄| · m), where |P̄| represents the mean profile size and m denotes the number of edges. In terms of space requirements, the algorithm demands O(|P̄| · n) space. To facilitate efficient querying, we implemented three index-based algorithms. The basic-index algorithm replaces the k-core computations of the baseline with CP-tree lookups, thereby reducing the computational overhead. The incremental algorithm, on the other hand, grows candidate trees from the root node and reuses the vertex sets of already-verified subtrees to restrict the search space of their extensions. In contrast, the decremental algorithm starts from P(q) and prunes labels in a top-down manner, which is particularly advantageous when the query vertex q has a small profile or when k is large. The increasing reliance of modern autonomous systems, such as self-driving vehicles, unmanned aerial platforms, and smart-grid components, on a continuous flow of information from sensors to estimation and decision modules has created a pressing concern. This dependence on accurate and reliable data makes these systems vulnerable to a wide range of issues, including sensor degradation or failure, noise corruption, and wireless link dropouts or delays. Moreover, the threat of malicious data alteration by an adversary poses a significant risk, as exemplified by incidents such as Stuxnet and the documented vulnerabilities in power-grid state estimation. When a controller or decision maker relies on corrupted measurements, the consequences can be severe, particularly in safety-critical settings. Therefore, estimating the true system state from unreliable and potentially adversarial measurements has become a central problem in secure control. Classical state estimation techniques, such as the Luenberger observer and the Kalman filter, offer well-developed tools for estimating system states, but they are based on assumptions that are often violated in the presence of attacks. These methods assume known dynamics and benign disturbances, typically modeled as zero-mean Gaussian noise with known covariance. In contrast, robust formulations, such as H-infinity filtering and the minimax and dynamic game viewpoint, treat disturbances as worst-case but bounded-energy signals. While these approaches provide strong guarantees, they often require linear or otherwise tractable dynamics, structural assumptions on the attack, and explicit analytical derivations, which can be limiting in practice. Recent research has explored attack detection and identification, secure estimation under sparse sensor attacks, and the limits of stealthy attacks. However, these results typically rely on assumptions such as linearity, sparsity, or a known model class, which may not hold in many real-world scenarios. For nonlinear, high-dimensional, or partially unknown systems, these requirements are often not met, and the resulting designs can be conservative or intractable. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) offers a natural alternative, as it can produce strong policies in complex environments without requiring closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, most RL work focuses on designing controllers rather than observers and typically assumes faithful observation of the environment. Neural network policies are known to be fragile to small perturbations of their inputs, and adversarial perturbations can significantly reduce the return of trained agents. Robust RL has responded to these challenges by treating disturbances as a worst-case player, training a protagonist against an adversary, and considering robustness to adversarial state perturbations. However, these approaches primarily aim to make the policy insensitive to observation errors, rather than addressing the question of how to reconstruct the state accurately from corrupted measurements. The problem of estimating the true system state from possibly corrupted measurements is a game-like scenario, where the adversary chooses errors to maximize the estimation loss, and the observer chooses its strategy to minimize it. Two key difficulties arise: the observer only sees corrupted outputs, making the problem partially observed, and a good strategy generally depends on the history of measurements. Furthermore, a static or hand-designed adversary is a weak test, as a fixed attack pattern can be learned and discounted, whereas an adaptive adversary can exploit any weakness in the observer. To address these challenges, we pose the design of the observer as a zero-sum, two-player sequential game between an observer and an attacker acting on the measurement channel. We solve this game using deep RL, where the observer and adversary agents are trained in alternation or concurrently with opposing objectives. Our framework does not rely on linearity of the dynamics, Gaussian noise, or a specific attack structure, and it accommodates sensor faults, noise, channel failures, and deliberate cyber-attacks within one error-injection model. We implement our framework using neural networks as function approximators for both players, noting that the framework is agnostic to the approximator class. Other suitable families, such as kernel methods, tree ensembles, or basis expansions, could also be used. Our simulation studies demonstrate that the learned observation strategies perform remarkably well when the adversary's injected errors are bounded in a suitable sense, and we characterize how performance varies with the bound. These results suggest that adversarial RL is a practical route to observers that are robust by construction, rather than by analysis of a specific attack model. Our research question is whether adversarial deep RL can be used to design observer strategies for autonomous systems that remain accurate when the information channel is corrupted by an adaptive, bounded adversary, and how well such learned observers perform relative to the adversary's capabilities. We make three key contributions. First, we develop a general framework that formulates robust observer design under adversarial measurement errors as an adversarial RL problem. Second, we implement this framework using neural networks as function approximators for both players. Third, we present simulation studies that demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and characterize its performance. The need for a credible framework that specifies the sense in which the adversary is bounded and shows how performance depends on that bound is essential. Without such a restriction, no estimator can guarantee anything, since unconstrained corruption can make the measurements uninformative. Our framework addresses this challenge by providing a clear understanding of the adversary's capabilities and the observer's performance. The results of our research have significant implications for the design of robust autonomous systems, as they demonstrate the potential of adversarial RL to produce observers that can accurately reconstruct the system state even in the presence of corrupted measurements. This paper formalizes the problem setting, outlines the training procedure, and presents the results of numerical experiments. Our focus is on a discrete-time stochastic linear plant, where the state at time t+1 is given by x{t+1} = A xt + B ut + wt, with xt ∈ ℝⁿ representing the state, ut ∈ ℝᵐ representing the control input, and wt ~ N(0, Q) representing process noise. The controller receives a measurement yt = C xt + vt + at, where vt ~ N(0, R) is ordinary sensor noise and at ∈ ℝᵖ is an additive error injected by an adversary. This error can be thought of as representing sensor faults, channel corruption, or a false-data-injection attack, similar to those considered in the cyber-physical security literature (Pasqualetti et al., 2013). The adversary is constrained by a per-step budget ‖at‖∞ ≤ ε, which we refer to as the bounded-error assumption. The budget ε is the primary experimental variable, and we report results for ε ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0} in units of the standard deviation of the noiseless measurement. The controller used in this study is a fixed linear-quadratic regulator, given by ut = −K x̂t, computed for the nominal plant (Anderson & Moore, 1990). The observer, on the other hand, is the only component that is designed or learned, and differences in closed-loop performance can be attributed entirely to the quality of the state estimate x̂t. To design the observer, we formulate the problem as a two-player zero-sum Markov game, drawing on ideas from robust adversarial reinforcement learning (Pinto et al., 2017) and classical minimax estimation (Başar & Bernhard, 1995). At each time step t, the observer's observation is a window of the last H measurements and past estimates, denoted as ot = (y{t−H+1:t}, x̂{t−H:t−1}, u{t−H:t−1}), with H = 10. The observer's action is the estimate x̂t, which we parameterize as x̂t = A x̂{t−1} + B u{t−1} + πθ(ot). This residual structure, inspired by the Luenberger observer (Luenberger, 1966), allows the network to learn a correction to the model-based prediction rather than the full state, which improves sample efficiency and keeps training stable. The adversary, on the other hand, observes the true state, the observer's previous estimate, and the current measurement, and its action is given by at = ε·tanh(μφ(st)), which satisfies the budget constraint by construction. The per-step reward for the observer is rt = −(xt − x̂t)ᵀ W (xt − x̂t) − λ‖x̂t − x̂{t−1}‖², with W = I and λ = 0.01. The second term in the reward function discourages jumpy estimates. The adversary receives the negative of the observer's reward, −rt. The observer's objective is therefore to maximize the expected cumulative reward, given by maxθ minφ E[Σt γ^t rt], with γ = 0.99 and episodes of T = 200 steps. Both the observer and adversary policies are represented as fully connected neural networks with two hidden layers of 128 units and ReLU activations. The critics have the same architecture and take state-action pairs as input. While neural networks are used here as a convenient function approximator, the formulation does not depend on them, and any other class that supports gradient-based or value-based policy improvement could be used instead. We optimize the policies using a deterministic actor-critic method with target networks and replay buffers (Lillicrap et al., 2016), and use twin critics to limit overestimation (Fujimoto et al., 2018). Training alternates between the two players, with the observer updated for No = 5 gradient steps against a frozen adversary, and then the adversary updated for Na = 1 step against the frozen observer. Each player's replay buffer holds 10⁶ transitions, and exploration uses Gaussian action noise with standard deviation decaying from 0.2 to 0.05. Optimization uses Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a learning rate of 3×10⁻⁴, batch size 256, and soft target update coefficient 0.005. Training runs for 2×10⁶ environment steps. To reduce cycling and overfitting to the current adversary, the observer is periodically trained against a pool of earlier adversary checkpoints (Bansal et al., 2018). An adversary is sampled uniformly from the pool with probability 0.3. Early in training, the adversary is held at zero or random attacks for 10⁴ steps, allowing the observer to first learn a sensible nominal estimator. The primary simulation testbeds are two benchmark systems. The first is a linearized, discretized quadrotor-altitude/attitude model with n = 6 states and p = 3 measured outputs. The second is a lower-dimensional cart-pole system linearized about the upright equilibrium (n = 4, p = 2), which is open-loop unstable and therefore sensitive to estimation errors. Both systems are simulated at 50 Hz with noise covariances chosen to give a nominal signal-to-noise ratio of about 20 dB. Because the data are generated by simulation, no external datasets are used. Initial states are drawn from N(0, 0.1 I), and each training and evaluation episode is generated by a distinct random seed. Training and test seeds are disjoint. We compare the learned observer with four baselines under the same controller and noise realizations. These are (i) a steady-state Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960), (ii) a Luenberger observer with poles placed at the Kalman filter's closed-loop locations, (iii) a Kalman filter with χ² innovation-based residual detection that rejects flagged measurements (Mo & Sinopoli, 2010), and (iv) a robust H∞ filter designed for the same budget ε. We also include an ablation in which the observer is trained with the same algorithm but against random bounded noise instead of a learned adversary, to isolate the effect of adversarial training. Evaluation uses four attack models. The first is no attack, the second is random bounded attacks with at drawn uniformly from [−ε, ε]ᵖ, the third is a constant-bias attack at the budget limit, and the fourth is a worst-case attack from a fresh adversary, trained from scratch for 10⁶ steps against the frozen final observer. This last attack tests whether the observer's robustness reflects real minimax behavior or only coadaptation with the training adversary (Gleave et al., 2020). We also test robustness to model misspecification by perturbing the entries of A by up to 10% and to attacks above the training budget (εtest up to 2εtrain), to see how performance degrades beyond the bounded-error assumption. Performance is measured by the root-mean-square estimation error, RMSE = (1/T Σt ‖xt − x̂t‖²)^{1/2}, and by the closed-loop LQR cost J = Σt (xtᵀ Qc xt + utᵀ Rc ut). We also record the fraction of episodes in which the state norm exceeds a safety threshold, which we treat as failure. Veterinary graduates today enter a profession where technical expertise is essential, yet insufficient on its own. The complex, often emotive issues they encounter - such as animal welfare, euthanasia, and the use of animals in research - demand a nuanced understanding of ethical principles and the ability to navigate conflicting viewpoints. The public and the profession alike hold diverse, sometimes sharply divergent perspectives on these matters, underscoring the need for veterinarians to engage respectfully with those who disagree (Fraser, 2008; Mellor, 2016). Accreditation bodies and professional organizations, such as the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons and the American Veterinary Medical Association, expect graduates to be able to identify ethical problems, reason systematically about them, and interact constructively with others who may hold differing views (Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, 2020; American Veterinary Medical Association, 2019). To develop these capacities, educators must create structured opportunities for students to practice discussing contested topics. However, this is no easy task, particularly within crowded curricula and diverse student cohorts. Discussion-based and cooperative learning strategies have long been recognized as effective in promoting deeper engagement with complex, controversial material. Cooperative learning, which involves students working interdependently and being accountable for their own and others' contributions, has been associated with improved achievement, higher-order thinking, and more positive attitudes toward peers (Johnson & Johnson, 2009; Slavin, 2014). Exposure to alternative perspectives can prompt cognitive conflict, encouraging students to re-examine and refine their reasoning (Piaget, 1985; Johnson et al., 2000). Structured academic controversy, role-play, and debate are commonly used to teach ethics, sustainability, and other socially contested subjects (Oros, 2007; Kennedy, 2007). Yet, classroom discussions of polarizing issues carry inherent risks. Students may be reluctant to speak up when they fear judgment, social exclusion, or conflict with peers or instructors, and dominant voices can crowd out quieter ones (Hess, 2009; Hand & Levinson, 2012). This reluctance may be amplified in professional programs, where students are already managing performance pressure, emotional exposure to animal suffering, and concerns about how their views will be perceived by future colleagues. The human continuum exercise (HCE) is an established approach to structured, whole-class discussion that has been used to address these challenges. In the HCE, students are presented with a stimulus statement or question and asked to position themselves physically along a line between two poles, such as strong agreement and strong disagreement. They then explain their reasoning to nearby peers and to those at other points on the line, and may move as their views change (Kagan & Kagan, 2009; Kolb, 2014). The HCE has several features that support active learning, opinion formation, and perspective-taking. It makes the distribution of opinion visible, demonstrates that positions are rarely binary, and requires each student to commit to a stance before discussion begins. However, the HCE also has practical and psychological limitations. It requires physical space and synchronous attendance, which restricts its use in large, distributed, or online cohorts. Because students' positions are publicly visible to peers and teachers, those who hold minority or uncertain views may feel exposed, and may move toward perceived majority positions rather than express their own (Noelle-Neumann, 1974; Asch, 1956). Time constraints may also limit the depth with which individual students can articulate their reasoning. Digital technologies offer potential means of addressing these constraints. Online discussion environments can extend participation beyond the classroom, give students time to consider and compose responses, and reduce some social cues that inhibit contribution (Suler, 2004; Hrastinski, 2008). Anonymity or pseudonymity can encourage candor, particularly for sensitive subjects, and can lessen the effect of status differences among participants (Diakopoulos & Naaman, 2011; Peddle et al., 2016). Nevertheless, online discussion is not uniformly beneficial. Anonymity can enable incivility, asynchronous forums often suffer from low participation and superficial exchanges, and generic platforms rarely scaffold the specific cognitive moves that make discussion educationally productive, such as taking a position, justifying it, and responding to counterarguments (Gao et al., 2013; Wise & Chiu, 2011). Existing tools for online debate or polling typically either aggregate opinions without prompting dialogue or provide open-ended discussion boards without a clear structure for committing to and revising a position. This gap between established, pedagogically grounded discussion exercises like the HCE and the digital tools available to deliver them in flexible, supportive, and scalable ways is particularly salient for veterinary education. Veterinary curricula increasingly include ethics, welfare, and professional communication, yet students often report discomfort when discussing controversial issues, and educators have limited evidence-based tools for creating safe spaces in which differing views can be expressed (Magalhães-Sant'Ana et al., 2014; Batchelor & McKeegan, 2012). The expansion of online and blended delivery, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has intensified the need for activities that preserve the interactive and reflective qualities of face-to-face teaching in virtual settings (Hodges et al., 2020). To address this need, we have developed the virtual human continuum (VHC), an online platform that reproduces the core structure of the HCE. Students respond to a stimulus question by placing themselves on a continuum, provide a rationale for their position, view the reasoning of others, and engage with differing viewpoints in a virtual environment. This paper describes the design of the VHC and reports a first evaluation of the tool with first-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine students at the University of Sydney. The study was guided by the research question: to what extent do students perceive the VHC as providing a non-threatening environment in which they can express their views, learn how others form arguments, and consider alternative opinions on emotive and challenging issues? The paper makes three key contributions. First, it provides a transparent description of an innovative educational tool and the pedagogical principles underlying its design, enabling other educators to adapt or replicate it. Second, it offers empirical data on student perceptions of the platform, including comfort in expressing views relative to face-to-face discussion. Third, it contributes to the broader literature on technology-supported dialogue by showing how an established cooperative learning exercise like the HCE can be adapted for online delivery, while preserving its educational benefits. By exploring the potential of the VHC to support student learning and engagement in the context of veterinary education, this study aims to inform the development of effective, technology-enhanced discussion tools for teaching complex, controversial subjects in professional programs. The human continuum exercise, a cooperative learning strategy that has been widely used in face-to-face settings to facilitate discussions on polarizing topics, can be effectively translated into an online format to support engagement with sensitive issues in professional education. This study employed a descriptive, cross-sectional design to document the development and evaluation of the virtual human continuum (VHC), a web-based platform designed to replicate the human continuum exercise in an online environment. The project was grounded in the principles of design-based research, which involves creating a tool, implementing it in an authentic setting, and refining it based on user feedback (Anderson & Shattuck, 2012). The pedagogical basis for the VHC was the human continuum exercise (HCE), a well-established cooperative learning strategy in which students physically position themselves along a line between two opposing statements in response to a stimulus question, and then explain or defend their position to peers (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). The VHC was designed to reproduce this exercise in an online environment, with the aim of providing a safe and structured space for students to engage with potentially polarizing topics. To achieve this, the platform was developed in collaboration with the university's educational technology staff, drawing on the first author's experience of delivering the face-to-face HCE and the literature on online discussion, which emphasizes the importance of anonymity, low barriers to participation, and clear structure in supporting open dialogue on sensitive topics (Suler, 2004). The platform was designed to meet several key requirements, including presenting a stimulus statement or question with a response scale anchored by "strongly disagree" and "strongly agree"; allowing each participant to place a marker on the continuum; requiring participants to provide a written justification for their position; displaying the distribution of all positions and rationales to the group; and permitting participants to revise their position after reading others' contributions. To maintain anonymity, participants were identified by pseudonym within the activity, although instructors could access identifying information for administrative purposes. The platform was built as a web-based application accessible through standard browsers on laptops, tablets, and smartphones, and was integrated with the university's learning management system for authentication. Prior to implementation, prototype versions of the platform were tested by teaching staff and two student volunteers not involved in the evaluation, and minor changes to the interface and instructions were made based on feedback. The VHC was then implemented with a cohort of first-year students enrolled in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program at the University of Sydney, Australia. The activity was embedded in a scheduled unit of study addressing professional and ethical issues in animal-related practice, and all students in the cohort (N = approximately 40) were invited to take part in the VHC session and to complete an optional, anonymous evaluation survey. Thirty-eight students completed the survey, providing a rich source of data on their perceptions of the VHC. The session was delivered during a timetabled class, and began with a short introduction to the purpose of the exercise, the ground rules for respectful discussion, and a demonstration of the platform. Three stimulus statements concerning ethically contentious issues relevant to veterinary practice and animal use were then presented sequentially, selected because they were likely to elicit divergent views and emotional responses, consistent with the definition of potentially polarizing issues as those on which reasonable people hold strongly differing values (Hess, 2009). For each statement, students followed a structured process, first placing themselves on the continuum and writing a brief rationale, then viewing the distribution of positions and the anonymized rationales of their peers, and finally taking part in a facilitated whole-class discussion in which selected comments were explored. Facilitators, who were academic staff experienced in teaching ethics, did not express personal views on the topics and intervened only to maintain respectful conduct or to prompt deeper reasoning. At the end of the session, students were given a link to the evaluation questionnaire and encouraged to complete it immediately, while the experience was still fresh. The survey remained open for one week, and one reminder was provided in class. The questionnaire was designed to collect data on student perceptions of the VHC, and comprised statements rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Key items asked whether the VHC provided a non-threatening environment for discussing emotive and challenging issues; provided an opportunity to see how other people form their ideas; made students think about how to express their ideas and construct arguments; left students feeling more comfortable expressing their views than in face-to-face discussion; and encouraged students to consider other opinions. Additional items addressed usability, and open-text fields invited general comments. The development of the questionnaire was informed by the intended pedagogical aims of the VHC and prior literature on the benefits of structured classroom debate and online discussion, including exposure to diverse perspectives, development of argumentation skills, and psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999; Kennedy, 2007). Content validity was checked informally by two colleagues in veterinary education, and the wording was refined for clarity. While no formal psychometric validation was undertaken, which is acknowledged as a limitation, the questionnaire provided a useful tool for gathering data on student perceptions of the VHC. The project was approved by the University of Sydney Human Research Ethics Committee, and participation in the survey was voluntary and anonymous, with no identifying information collected. Students were provided with an information statement explaining the purpose of the study, and completion of the questionnaire was taken as implied consent. Declining to participate had no bearing on assessment or progression, and students were reminded of available university counselling services in case they experienced distress during the activity.
