The 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola virus disease outbreak was a pivotal moment in the history of filovirus epidemics, marked by unprecedented complexity and scale. With over 28,000 reported cases and 11,000 deaths, primarily in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, it highlighted the limitations of traditional response strategies in the face of rapidly evolving outbreaks (WHO Ebola Response Team, 2016). In contrast to earlier Central African outbreaks, which were typically confined to remote rural areas and contained through rapid case detection, isolation, and community engagement (Chowell & Nishiura, 2014), the 2014-2015 outbreak spread swiftly into densely populated urban centers and across porous borders, overwhelming already weakened health systems. The consequences of this rapid spread were far-reaching, with health workers being infected at disproportionately high rates and the supply of trained staff, laboratories, vehicles, and basic communication infrastructure being severely strained (Kieny et al., 2014; Gostin & Friedman, 2015). Under these circumstances, the speed and quality of information flow from the village to the district, national command center, and international partners became a critical factor in the response. However, the reliance on paper-based reporting in most affected areas introduced significant delays, transcription errors, and difficulties in reconciling data from different sources (Fäh et al., 2015; Tom-Aba et al., 2015). The incomplete contact lists and poor linkage between laboratory results and clinical records that resulted from these challenges hindered timely control and decision-making, as epidemiological pictures were often outdated or inconsistent (Frieden et al., 2014). In this context, mobile health (mHealth) technologies, defined by the World Health Organization as medical and public health practices supported by mobile devices (WHO, 2011), emerged as a potential solution to address these gaps. With mobile phone penetration in sub-Saharan Africa having grown rapidly over the preceding decade, often outpacing access to electricity, roads, and fixed-line networks (GSMA, 2014), mHealth tools had already demonstrated promise in disease surveillance, community health worker support, and data collection in low-resource settings (Braa et al., 2012; Aranda-Jan et al., 2014). Previous outbreaks, including cholera in Haiti and Zimbabwe, H1N1 influenza, and Marburg and Ebola in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, had also seen the deployment of mobile or electronic systems, albeit often at a small scale and with limited evaluation (Freifeld et al., 2010; Black et al., 2013). The 2014-2015 outbreak presented both an urgent need and an unprecedented opportunity to apply mHealth technologies at scale. In response, a diverse array of mHealth initiatives emerged, with governments, ministries of health, international agencies, non-governmental organizations, academic groups, technology companies, and volunteer developers building or adapting tools for various purposes, including electronic case reporting, contact tracing, laboratory result transmission, and health worker training (Sacks et al., 2015; Tom-Aba et al., 2015; Oluwafemi et al., 2015). While some of these tools were adaptations of existing platforms, such as DHIS2, Open Data Kit, CommCare, and Magpi, others were developed specifically for the outbreak. Many reports describe rapid deployment, often within weeks, and suggest that mobile data collection improved the timeliness of contact follow-up and shortened the delay between data capture and analysis (Tom-Aba et al., 2015; Fäh et al., 2015). The contribution of digital tools to improved control of EVD in the later phases of the epidemic has been widely acknowledged (Kamadjeu et al., 2015). However, despite this enthusiasm, the evidence base on what was actually developed and used remains fragmented, with information scattered across peer-reviewed articles, conference abstracts, technical reports, press releases, and project websites. Existing overviews have generally been narrative or focused on single projects, countries, or functionalities, such as contact tracing (Sacks et al., 2015; Danquah et al., 2019). Moreover, the rapid, parallel development of mHealth tools by multiple actors raised concerns about duplication of effort, lack of interoperability, limited alignment with national information systems, unclear data governance, and low sustainability beyond the emergency period (Heeks, 2006; Kamadjeu et al., 2015). The lack of a structured overview of mHealth tools used during the 2014-2015 outbreak hampers the ability of public health agencies and developers to build on earlier experience and risks repeating fragmented development in future outbreaks. Outbreak control relies on a chain of linked activities, including surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management, which are not independent. A tool that addresses only one step may speed up that step but leave bottlenecks elsewhere, and data silos can prevent the integrated view needed for decision-making. Systems that cover several of these functions within a single platform may reduce duplicate data entry and facilitate real-time linkage of cases, contacts, and test results (Tom-Aba et al., 2015). However, whether such integrated tools were common during the 2014-2015 outbreak has not been systematically assessed. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a systematic review of mHealth tools developed or used in the context of the 2014-2015 West Africa EVD outbreak. Our research question was: what mobile tools were reported for EVD management in 2014 and 2015, and which core functionalities (surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management) did they support? Our objectives were to identify and describe the available tools, characterize their functionalities and the extent to which they were integrated, and highlight the most promising approaches to guide future mHealth development for infectious disease control. By examining the range of mHealth tools used during the 2014-2015 outbreak, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the role of digital technologies in outbreak response and inform the development of more effective and sustainable mHealth solutions for future epidemics. This study makes three significant contributions to the field of mHealth tools in outbreak response. Firstly, it presents the first comprehensive and systematic inventory of mHealth tools developed or deployed during the 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola virus disease outbreak, utilizing a rigorous search strategy across multiple databases and a dual-review process adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. This systematic approach ensures the reproducibility and reliability of the findings, offering a foundation for future research and development in the area. Secondly, the study introduces a functionality-based classification system for mHealth tools, enabling comparisons based on the core activities central to outbreak response, rather than solely on technical architecture. This perspective is crucial for understanding the practical applications and potential of mHealth tools in real-world scenarios. Thirdly, it identifies tools that integrate multiple core functions, highlighting them as priority candidates for further development, evaluation, and inclusion in preparedness planning efforts. These contributions collectively enhance our understanding of the mHealth landscape during the Ebola outbreak and provide valuable insights for improving future outbreak responses. The study's design and reporting framework were carefully structured to ensure clarity and adherence to established standards. We conducted a systematic review of mHealth tools, following the PRISMA statement guidelines (Moher et al., 2009; Liberati et al., 2009), which is the gold standard for systematic reviews. Given the focus on describing and comparing tool functionalities rather than estimating intervention effects, no meta-analysis was planned, and thus, the review was not registered in a prospective protocol registry. The definition of mHealth was aligned with the World Health Organization's (WHO) description of medical and public health practice supported by mobile devices, including mobile phones, smartphones, tablets, and patient-monitoring devices (WHO, 2011). A "tool" was defined as a distinct software application, platform, or system with a named identity or a clearly described set of functions, whether developed de novo or adapted from an existing platform. Our search strategy was comprehensive and systematic, aiming to capture all relevant reports published between January 1, 2014, and December 31, 2015. We utilized Google Scholar, MEDLINE (via PubMed), CAB Abstracts (Global Health), POPLINE, and Web of Science, applying a tailored search string to each database: ("outbreak" OR "epidemic") AND ("mobile phone" OR "smartphone" OR "smart phone" OR "tablet" OR "mHealth") AND ("Ebola" OR "EVD" OR "VHF" OR "Ebola virus disease" OR "viral hemorrhagic fever") AND ("2014" OR "2015"). Searches were conducted on titles, abstracts, and keywords where possible, and for Google Scholar, the full-text option was used, screening the first 200 records sorted by relevance. This pragmatic approach is commonly applied for Google Scholar searches (Haddaway et al., 2015). Additionally, we screened reference lists of included records and relevant narrative reviews, examined grey literature such as reports from the WHO, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Médecins Sans Frontières, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, and technology developers' websites. Records in languages other than English or French were translated using machine translation and verified by a fluent colleague when available. To ensure the relevance and quality of the included records, we established clear eligibility criteria. Records were eligible if they (1) described one or more specific mHealth tools; (2) explicitly stated that the tool was developed, adapted, or used in the context of the 2014-2015 West Africa EVD outbreak; and (3) provided sufficient information to characterize at least one functionality. We included a range of publication types, such as original research articles, implementation reports, conference abstracts, technical reports, and descriptive commentaries, provided they contained primary information on a tool. Conversely, we excluded records that referred to mHealth in general terms without specifying a tool, addressed other outbreaks or diseases without reference to the 2014-2015 EVD epidemic, were purely opinion pieces or news items, concerned non-mobile information technology solutions, or were duplicates. For tools described in multiple records, we grouped these under a single tool entry, using the most informative record as the primary source and supplementing with additional records as necessary. The study selection process was meticulous and transparent. All retrieved records were exported to a reference manager, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, followed by the assessment of full texts of potentially relevant records. Disagreements at any stage were resolved through discussion, and when necessary, a third reviewer was consulted. The inter-rater agreement at the title-and-abstract stage was quantified using Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960), with values above 0.60 indicating substantial agreement (Landis & Koch, 1977). The selection process was fully documented in a PRISMA flow diagram, detailing the number of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons), and included. Data extraction was standardized and rigorous. A data extraction form was developed in Microsoft Excel, pilot-tested on a random sample of included records, and refined to address any ambiguities. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and discrepancies were reconciled through consensus. For each tool, we recorded a range of characteristics, including name, developer, type of developer, country of deployment, publication type and year, development stage, platform and hardware, connectivity requirements, open-source status, and target users. The primary focus of our data collection was on the functionalities of each tool, categorized into four core areas based on the epidemiological workflow of EVD response (WHO, 2014) and previous typologies of mHealth functions (Labrique et al., 2013). These functionalities included: (1) Surveillance, encompassing the collection, transmission, or analysis of data on suspected, probable, or confirmed cases and deaths; (2) Case management, supporting the clinical care of patients; (3) Contact tracing, involving the identification, listing, and follow-up of contacts of confirmed cases; and (4) a fourth category that was critical for the comprehensive management of the outbreak. By examining these functionalities, we aimed to provide a detailed understanding of the capabilities and potential applications of mHealth tools in outbreak response scenarios. The identification of tools that combine several core functions is particularly noteworthy, as these tools may offer enhanced utility and efficiency in real-world outbreak response scenarios. By highlighting these multifunctional tools, our study provides valuable insights for further development, evaluation, and preparedness planning efforts. The systematic approach and comprehensive analysis presented in this study contribute significantly to the field, offering a foundation for improving the use of mHealth tools in future outbreak responses and enhancing global health security. The persistence of high reoffending rates across various jurisdictions has significant implications for victims, communities, and individuals, as well as correctional budgets. A comprehensive synthesis of recidivism studies conducted by Fazel and Wolf (2015) highlights the challenges of cross-jurisdictional comparisons due to the variability in follow-up periods and definitions. Moreover, the financial burden and collateral consequences of incarceration have prompted policymakers to seek alternative community-based sanctions that balance accountability with public protection. The existing evidence suggests that custodial sentences may not be an effective deterrent, and may even modestly increase reoffending rates compared to non-custodial alternatives (Gendreau et al., 1999; Nagin et al., 2009; Villettaz et al., 2006). In response to these concerns, day reporting centres (DRCs) have emerged as a potential solution. These non-residential facilities provide structured supervision, monitoring, and services to individuals under criminal justice supervision, who are required to attend regularly. The concept of DRCs originated in the United States, adapting from British day training and probation day centres, and has since expanded rapidly as an intermediate sanction. DRCs are utilized at various decision points, including as a condition of probation, diversion from jail or prison, sanction for supervision violations, and step-down for individuals released on parole or post-release supervision. The typical components of DRCs include drug testing, curfew checks, electronic monitoring, cognitive-behavioural programming, substance-use treatment, education and employment assistance, and referrals to housing and health services. The theoretical rationale underlying DRCs is complex, combining elements of incapacitation, deterrence, and rehabilitation. On one hand, the close monitoring and certainty of detection associated with DRCs may serve as a deterrent. On the other hand, the provision of criminogenic-need-focused services, as emphasized by the Risk-Need-Responsivity framework (Andrews et al., 1990; Lowenkamp et al., 2006), may contribute to rehabilitation. The effectiveness of DRCs in reducing recidivism, however, remains uncertain. While some evaluations suggest that DRCs may be beneficial, particularly when targeting higher-risk individuals, others have found no reduction in recidivism or even increased technical violations and revocations (Petersilia & Turner, 1993). The mixed findings in the existing literature may be attributed to the heterogeneity of DRC programmes, populations, and comparison conditions. Primary studies have yielded inconsistent results, with some reporting lower rearrest or reconviction rates among participants, while others have found no significant differences. For instance, Marciniak (2000) compared probationers receiving day reporting with those on intensive supervision alone, while Ostermann (2013) examined the effectiveness of New Jersey's DRC and halfway-back programmes for individuals on parole. Boyle et al. (2013) evaluated a statewide parole DRC programme in New Jersey, using a design intended to address differences between participants and comparison cases. Despite the accumulating evidence, the single-site and heterogeneous character of the literature makes it challenging for decision-makers to determine the effectiveness of DRCs. The absence of a systematic review that comprehensively identifies, appraises, and synthesizes the evidence on DRCs has left practitioners and policymakers relying on individual evaluations of uncertain quality. This knowledge gap has significant implications for researchers, who lack a clear understanding of the strengths and limitations of the existing evidence. To address this gap, this systematic review aims to investigate the effect of DRCs on subsequent offending among individuals involved in the criminal justice system. The review will explore the impact of DRCs compared to alternative sanctions or supervision arrangements, as well as the potential moderating factors, such as the stage at which DRCs are used, participant characteristics, programme features, and recidivism outcomes. Where possible, the review will also examine the effects on intermediate outcomes, including employment, substance use, and programme completion. This protocol outlines the methods for a systematic review prepared in accordance with Campbell Collaboration standards and reported with reference to PRISMA guidance (Page et al., 2021). The review will contribute to the existing literature in four key ways. Firstly, it will provide the first systematic, transparent estimate of the effects of DRCs on recidivism, using explicit eligibility criteria, comprehensive searches, and structured risk-of-bias assessment. Secondly, through meta-analysis and structured narrative synthesis, it will explore the sources of heterogeneity across programmes, populations, and comparison conditions. By synthesizing the existing evidence on DRCs, this review aims to provide policymakers, practitioners, and researchers with a comprehensive understanding of the effectiveness of DRCs in reducing recidivism. The findings of this review will have significant implications for the development of evidence-based correctional policies and practices, ultimately contributing to the reduction of reoffending rates and the improvement of community safety. Aphasia, a debilitating consequence of left-hemisphere stroke, affects approximately one-third of stroke survivors, with a substantial proportion experiencing persistent symptoms in the chronic phase (Engelter et al., 2006; Flowers et al., 2016). The disorder is notably heterogeneous, with patients exhibiting varying degrees of impairment in different language components, such as phonology, semantics, syntax, and fluency, as well as domain-general cognitive abilities like short-term memory and executive function (Butler et al., 2014; Fridriksson et al., 2018; Lacey et al., 2017). Traditional taxonomies, including Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction, and anomic aphasia, attempt to capture this heterogeneity but are limited in their ability to account for the complex, multidimensional profiles characteristic of real patients. Many individuals do not fit neatly into these categories or may shift between them over time (Kertesz & Poole, 1974; Wilson et al., 2018). To better understand the underlying structure of aphasia, researchers have employed data-driven approaches, using principal component analysis (PCA) and related methods to derive latent factors from patients' performance on extensive behavioral batteries. These studies have consistently identified a small set of factors, typically reflecting phonological, semantic, fluency/speech production, and cognitive-executive abilities, which collectively explain a significant proportion of the variance in aphasic performance (Butler et al., 2014; Halai et al., 2017; Mirman et al., 2015; Ingram et al., 2020). Furthermore, these factors have been linked to lesion location and white-matter damage, providing a more nuanced and mechanistically interpretable account of brain-behavior relationships than traditional aphasia syndromes (Halai et al., 2017; Kümmerer et al., 2013; Schumacher et al., 2019). In addition to these impairment scores, the paraphasias produced by patients are a crucial aspect of the clinical description of aphasia. Errors in picture naming, in particular, are used to characterize the nature of the underlying disorder. For instance, semantic paraphasias (e.g., "dog" instead of "cat") are often taken to indicate disrupted semantic representation or lexical selection, while phonological paraphasias and neologisms (e.g., "cap" or "tat" instead of "cat") suggest disrupted phonological retrieval or encoding. Other errors, such as omissions, circumlocutions, and dysfluent attempts, are thought to reflect various failures of retrieval or articulation (Dell et al., 1997; Schwartz et al., 2006; Kohn & Goodglass, 1985). These error types are explicitly included in the diagnostic criteria and classification of aphasia, forming the basis of influential computational models like the interactive two-step model, which estimates the integrity of semantic-lexical and lexical-phonological mappings based on the relative proportions of semantic and phonological errors (Dell et al., 1997; Foygel & Dell, 2000; Schwartz et al., 2006). Lesion-symptom mapping studies have reported that semantic errors are associated with damage to anterior temporal and middle temporal regions, whereas phonological errors are linked to damage in the posterior superior temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, and the underlying arcuate fasciculus (Schwartz et al., 2009; Walker et al., 2011; Mirman et al., 2015; Halai et al., 2017; Pillay et al., 2017). Despite this, the field has largely treated language impairments and paraphasias as separate topics, with most studies focusing on either scores summarizing deficits or error analyses in isolation, without reference to the patients' broader language-cognitive profile. This separation is problematic, as the relationship between impairments and errors is unlikely to be one-to-one. For example, semantic errors may arise from degraded semantic knowledge, impaired phonological retrieval, reduced executive control, or limited speech output (Mirman et al., 2015; Schwartz et al., 2006; Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006). Similarly, omissions may reflect failures at multiple processing stages and are often excluded from analyses or considered uninformative. Moreover, previous studies of errors have typically examined a restricted subset of error categories or collapsed errors into composite scores or ratios, presupposing a particular theoretical account and ignoring the co-occurrence structure of the full range of errors patients produce. This approach may obscure the relationship between less-studied categories, such as circumlocutions, mixed errors, and dysfluent responses, and underlying deficits. Furthermore, because errors and impairment scores are rarely modeled together, the lesion correlates reported for each are difficult to relate, and it remains unclear whether error-based and deficit-based analyses converge on the same neural substrates or capture partially distinct aspects of the aphasic syndrome. To address these issues, an integrated, data-driven framework is needed. Such a framework should derive the structure of paraphasias empirically, from the pattern of co-occurrence across a broad set of error types, rather than imposing a theory-driven selection or combination. It should also align this error structure with the patients' multidimensional language and cognitive profile within a single model and relate the resulting fused dimensions to lesion data, allowing for the simultaneous consideration of errors, deficits, and neural correlates. Dimension-reduction techniques, such as PCA, are well-suited to this purpose, as they identify orthogonal latent factors, permit the examination of cross-loadings, and produce continuous factor scores that can be used in lesion-symptom mapping without the need for arbitrary categorization (Butler et al., 2014; Halai et al., 2017; Mirman et al., 2015). In the present study, we applied this approach to a cohort of individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia who completed an extensive language and cognitive battery and a picture-naming task in which responses were coded into fifteen error types. Our analysis consisted of three steps. First, we used PCA to establish the pattern of co-occurrence among these error types. Second, we entered the resulting error components, together with the patients' scores from the neuropsychological battery, into an omnibus PCA to generate fused impairment-paraphasia factors. Third, we mapped these factors onto the patients' structural lesion profiles to identify their neural correlates. Our primary research questions were: (1) what are the latent dimensions underlying naming errors when all error types are considered together; (2) how do these dimensions map onto language and cognitive impairments, and which relationships are one-to-one versus distributed across multiple factors; and (3) which lesion correlates are associated with the fused factors, and do they converge with those reported in previous studies or reveal novel aspects of the neural basis of aphasia? This study seeks to contribute to the existing literature on post-stroke aphasia in three key ways. First, from a methodological standpoint, it presents a unified, theory-agnostic model that eschews the selective focus on specific errors or experimenter-derived composites that has characterized much of the previous research in this area. By adopting a more comprehensive approach, we aim to provide a richer understanding of the complex relationships between different error types and the underlying cognitive deficits that give rise to them. Second, on an empirical level, our study sheds new light on the intricate relationships between specific error types, such as omissions and circumlocutions, which have hitherto received relatively scant attention. Third, from a neural perspective, we investigate whether the lesion correlates of these combined factors align with established brain regions implicated in phonology, semantics, and speech production, thereby furnishing a more complete characterization of post-stroke aphasia. Our study drew on a cohort of patients with chronic post-stroke aphasia, recruited from community stroke groups and clinical services, who met a set of predetermined inclusion criteria. These criteria included a left-hemisphere middle cerebral artery infarct at least one year prior to testing, premorbid right-handedness, native English fluency, and the absence of any other neurological or psychiatric disorder. Patients were also required to have a clinical diagnosis of aphasia, as confirmed by the Western Aphasia Battery-Revised (WAB-R), and to have completed both a picture-naming task and an extended language-cognitive battery. All patients provided written informed consent, with supported-consent procedures in place for those with comprehension difficulties, and the study was approved by the local National Health Service research ethics committee. Our sample consisted of 70 patients, whose age and demographic details are provided in the Results section. Each patient underwent a detailed neuropsychological assessment, following the approach used in earlier data-driven studies of aphasia. This assessment spanned both language and cognition, and included a range of tasks designed to tap into phonological processing, such as auditory discrimination, word and nonword repetition, and phoneme segmentation and blending. Semantic processing was assessed using the 64-item Cambridge Semantic Battery, which included spoken word-to-picture matching, picture-based and written-word-based semantic association tests, and category fluency. We also evaluated phonological working memory, using digit span and word and nonword span tasks, as well as executive-cognitive function, using Raven's Coloured Progressive Matrices and a test of nonverbal reasoning. Speech production and fluency were quantified from the WAB-R spoken-output subscales and from connected speech elicited by the Cinderella story-telling task, from which we derived a range of metrics, including the number of words, number of utterances, and speech rate per minute. Although reading and writing tasks were also administered, these are not analyzed in the present study. The picture-naming task was assessed using the 60-item Object and Action Naming Battery, with items presented one at a time on a computer screen and patients allowed ample time to respond. Responses were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim, with the first complete response (or, where explicitly self-corrected, the final response) coded by trained raters who were blind to lesion data. Each response was classified into one of fifteen mutually exclusive categories, adapted from existing taxonomies, including correct, omission, semantic paraphasia, circumlocution, and a range of other error types. Two raters independently coded 25% of responses, with disagreements resolved by consensus before one rater coded the remainder. For each patient, the number of responses in each category was expressed as a proportion of total trials, giving fifteen error-rate variables. The correct category was excluded from the error analysis, as it is the complement of the total error set. Neuroimaging data were acquired using a 3.0T Philips Achieva scanner, with structural T1-weighted MRI scans obtained for each patient. Lesions were identified using an automated, patient-specific approach, which involved normalizing images to MNI space and thresholding fuzzy-clustering outliers relative to a healthy control sample. The resulting binary lesion maps were checked and, where necessary, manually corrected by an expert neurologist. Lesion volume was calculated for each patient and used as a covariate in lesion analyses. Our statistical analysis proceeded in two stages. First, we conducted a principal component analysis (PCA) of the fifteen error-rate variables, using varimax rotation to characterize the co-occurrence of errors without selecting a subset of error types or imposing experimenter-defined groupings. Because error proportions are often skewed and zero-inflated, we examined the distributional properties of each variable and transformed them as necessary prior to analysis. We assessed sampling adequacy using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure and Bartlett's test of sphericity, and determined the number of components to retain using the Kaiser criterion in conjunction with inspection of the scree plot and parallel analysis. The resulting component scores for each patient were saved for subsequent analysis. In the second stage of our analysis, we combined the five paraphasia component scores with the patients' scores from the neuropsychological battery in a second PCA, which we term the "omnibus PCA". Before entry, all variables were z-scored, so that the error components and test scores contributed on a comparable scale, and missing data (<5%) were imputed using the expectation-maximisation algorithm. We extracted and retained components using the same criteria as before, with the aim of aligning error patterns with underlying deficits. By adopting this two-stage approach, we sought to provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between error types, cognitive deficits, and neural correlates in post-stroke aphasia. In our analysis, we employed a combination of statistical techniques to uncover the underlying structure of naming errors in post-stroke aphasia. The decision to use varimax rotation was motivated by the desire to enhance interpretability and yield factors that load on a restricted set of variables. We set a threshold of ≥ 0.4 for factor loadings, which allowed us to identify the most salient loadings for each factor. The alarming prevalence of insufficient physical activity worldwide has significant implications for public health, as it is a leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, various cancers, and premature mortality. According to estimates, physical inactivity is responsible for 6% to 10% of the global burden of major noncommunicable diseases and approximately 9% of premature deaths (Lee et al., 2012). Despite the well-established benefits of regular physical activity, a mere 25% of U.S. adults meet the national guidelines for both aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities (Blackwell & Clarke, 2018; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018). This disparity is not evenly distributed, with adults in rural areas engaging in less leisure-time physical activity and exhibiting higher obesity rates compared to their urban counterparts. National estimates suggest that approximately 40% of rural residents are obese, compared to 33% in urban settings (Befort et al., 2012). The challenges faced by rural residents are further compounded by structural barriers, including limited access to recreational infrastructure, fewer programs, and constrained public health resources (Frost et al., 2010; Bauman et al., 2012). Fortunately, a substantial evidence base has been established on strategies to promote physical activity at the population level. The Community Guide for Preventive Services, developed by the Community Preventive Services Task Force, recommends a multifaceted approach that encompasses informational, behavioral, and environmental strategies (Kahn et al., 2002; Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2016). Socioecological models also emphasize the importance of sustained behavior change, which is most likely to occur when individual-level support is combined with changes in the social, physical, and policy contexts in which people live (Sallis et al., 2006; Sallis et al., 2012). Community-wide multicomponent interventions, grounded in these principles, offer a promising means of shifting population activity levels. However, the evidence for such interventions is largely derived from urban and suburban settings, with a notable dearth of studies conducted in rural communities, particularly those with diverse and rapidly changing demographics. The term "rural" is often used as a monolithic category, but it encompasses a wide range of communities with distinct characteristics. Micropolitan communities, defined as having an urban core of 10,000 to 49,999 residents, occupy an intermediate position between rural towns and metropolitan areas. These communities often lack the resources and infrastructure of larger urban areas, making it challenging to adapt evidence-based recommendations to their unique contexts. The situation is further complicated in micropolitan communities that have become new immigrant destinations, such as those in the rural Midwest and South. The influx of immigrants from Latin America and other regions has led to rapid demographic change, with linguistically and culturally diverse newcomers settling alongside long-term residents (Massey, 2008; Lichter, 2012). Immigrant and Latino adults in the United States often report lower rates of leisure-time physical activity, and their activity patterns tend to decline with acculturation and time in the United States (Crespo et al., 1996; Marquez & Bryan, 2011). Newcomers in these communities face numerous challenges, including language barriers, physically demanding work schedules, limited transportation, and unfamiliarity with local resources (Lichter, 2012). Interventions developed in other contexts cannot be assumed to translate directly to these settings, and the literature offers few examples of community-wide physical activity interventions designed for communities that are simultaneously rural and rapidly diversifying. One potential approach to bridging this gap is the use of lay health advisor models, which have been shown to improve health behaviors and outcomes in underserved and minority populations (Balcázar et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2014). Evidence from Latino and rural communities suggests that peer-led walking groups and other group-based activities can increase physical activity while building social capital and local capacity for sustaining programs (Ayala et al., 2011; Cleland et al., 2012). However, few studies have integrated a lay health advisor approach with the full range of Community Guide recommendations in a single community-wide effort, and fewer still have done so in a micropolitan new destination. To address this gap, it is essential to consider how evidence-based interventions are adapted and evaluated. Adaptation frameworks emphasize the systematic modification of intervention content, delivery, and context to improve fit while preserving core functions (Escoffery et al., 2018). Community-based participatory research principles stress shared decision-making between researchers and community partners throughout this process (Israel et al., 1998). Evaluation frameworks, such as RE-AIM, encourage assessment not only of effectiveness but also of reach, adoption, implementation, and maintenance, which are dimensions of particular relevance to resource-constrained settings (Glasgow et al., 1999). In this context, community-wide interventions are often challenging to evaluate using a single design. A more comprehensive approach involves combining population-level surveillance with longitudinal cohort data, observational measures of the environment, and qualitative and process data. This can provide a more complete understanding of what changes, for whom, and why. The Active Ottumwa project, a community-wide intervention aimed at increasing physical activity in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents, offers a unique opportunity to address these gaps. Ottumwa has experienced significant demographic change linked to employment in meatpacking and related industries, with a growing Latino population. As part of a community-academic partnership, local organizations and researchers are working together to design and implement an intervention that integrates a lay health advisor approach with the full range of Community Guide recommendations. The early implementation of Active Ottumwa is described in this paper, with a focus on the challenges and opportunities associated with adapting evidence-based interventions to a micropolitan new destination. The development of the Active Ottumwa intervention was a collaborative effort, with residents and community partners playing a crucial role in shaping the initiative. By adapting strategies recommended by the Community Guide, our goal was to increase physical activity among residents of a micropolitan new destination community. The Community Guide's recommendations were tailored to fit the specific needs of Ottumwa, a mid-size rural community undergoing significant demographic changes due to immigration. The initiative's core component was the use of trained lay health advisors, or physical activity leaders, who were responsible for delivering group-based activities such as walking groups, tai chi, and yoga. The overarching research question guiding this study was whether a multicomponent, lay health advisor-based intervention could effectively increase physical activity among residents of Ottumwa. To address this question, we also explored several secondary research questions, including the reach of the intervention across different population subgroups, the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted strategies, and the contextual factors that facilitated or constrained implementation. This report aims to contribute to the existing literature in three key ways. Firstly, it extends the evidence base on physical activity promotion to a setting that is underrepresented in the literature: a mid-size rural community undergoing immigration-driven demographic change. Secondly, it provides a transparent account of the process of adapting and integrating evidence-based, multilevel strategies through a community-academic partnership. This includes the training and deployment of 45 physical activity leaders and the execution of a five-channel communication campaign. Thirdly, it presents a multi-method evaluation design that combines a cross-sectional community survey, a longitudinal cohort, observational data, key informant interviews, and project records, which may serve as a model for evaluating community-wide interventions in similar settings. The Active Ottumwa intervention was developed within a community-academic partnership in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents located in the southeastern part of the state. Ottumwa is a new immigrant destination, with a growing Latino and Pacific Islander population drawn to the area by the meatpacking and related industries. As a result, the city is more ethnically and linguistically diverse than most rural Iowa communities. The partnership brought together university researchers, local public health and healthcare organizations, city and parks officials, schools, faith-based organizations, and residents. Throughout the project, partners played an active role in prioritizing physical activity as a health concern, reviewing intervention materials for cultural and linguistic appropriateness, and interpreting early findings. This collaborative approach was guided by the principles of community-based participatory research, as outlined by Israel et al. (1998). We employed a single-community, pre-post design with multiple data sources to evaluate the intervention. A convergent mixed-methods framework guided the evaluation, with quantitative and qualitative data collected in parallel and integrated at the interpretation stage (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). The study protocol was approved by the University of Iowa Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent in English or Spanish. To develop the intervention, we selected strategies from the Community Guide for Preventive Services recommendations for physical activity (Task Force on Community Preventive Services, 2002; Kahn et al., 2002) and adapted them through a review of local assets, barriers, and resources with our community partners. The intervention comprised three categories of approaches: behavioral and social, campaign and informational, and environmental and policy. The central strategy used a lay health advisor model, where physical activity leaders were recruited through partner organizations, workplaces, churches, and neighborhood networks, with a focus on reaching residents who were bilingual or trusted in immigrant communities. Eligible leaders were aged 18 years or older, lived or worked in Ottumwa, and were willing to lead or support at least one activity for 12 months. Leaders completed a structured training program of approximately 8 hours, covering physical activity guidelines (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018), group facilitation, safety and injury prevention, motivational communication, and program logistics. The training content was informed by social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986), emphasizing self-efficacy, modeling, and social support. Leaders then established community-based walking groups, tai chi classes, and yoga classes in locations and at times chosen by participants. In addition to the behavioral and social approaches, we developed a community-wide communication campaign delivered over five channels: local print media, radio, social media, community events with printed materials, and signage or flyers placed at partner sites. Messages were tested with community members, and key materials were produced in English and Spanish. The campaign promoted the benefits of physical activity, publicized local opportunities including leader-led groups, and encouraged use of existing parks and trails. We also worked with city and parks partners to identify and promote low-cost changes that support activity, such as wayfinding and trail signage, publicized walking routes, and improved access to existing facilities. Furthermore, we documented policy discussions and actions relevant to active living, including shared-use arrangements and municipal planning efforts. The evaluation of the Active Ottumwa intervention followed the RE-AIM framework (Glasgow et al., 1999), assessing reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance. Our evaluation methods comprised a cross-sectional community survey, a longitudinal cohort, systematic observation, key informant interviews, and project records. To assess population-level change, we conducted repeated cross-sectional surveys of adult Ottumwa residents at baseline and at the end of the intervention period. Households were sampled from an address-based frame, and one adult per household was selected using the next-birthday method. Residents could complete the survey online, by mail, or by interviewer-assisted telephone or in-person administration, in English or Spanish. The survey instrument assessed leisure-time and transportation-related physical activity using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire short form (Craig et al., 2003), along with perceived neighborhood environment, social support for activity, self-efficacy, awareness of Active Ottumwa messages and programs, and sociodemographic characteristics. In addition to the cross-sectional survey, we recruited a cohort of adult residents through community events, partner organizations, leader networks, and direct outreach, including both people who participated in leader-led programs and those who did not. Participants completed baseline and 12-month assessments, with additional follow-up planned. Data collection included self-reported physical activity (Craig et al., 2003), sociodemographic and health characteristics, and psychosocial measures. A subsample of participants wore hip-mounted accelerometers for 7 days, with valid wear defined as at least 10 hours per day on at least 4 days (Troiano et al., 2008). By providing a detailed account of the intervention's development, implementation, and evaluation, we aim to inform practitioners and researchers seeking to translate evidence-based recommendations into the diverse rural communities where they are most needed. Cerebral palsy (CP) is a complex and multifaceted condition, characterized by a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture that ultimately lead to significant activity limitations. The etiology of CP is attributed to non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain, and it is often accompanied by a range of comorbidities, including disturbances of sensation, cognition, communication, perception, behavior, and epilepsy. As the most common cause of physical disability in childhood, CP poses a substantial and sustained burden on affected individuals, their caregivers, and the healthcare system as a whole. This burden is multifaceted, encompassing not only the physical manifestations of the condition, such as pain, contractures, hip displacement, and scoliosis, but also the significant psychosocial and economic implications, including reduced participation and substantial lifetime costs. Spasticity is a dominant feature of CP, affecting the majority of children with the condition. It is characterized by a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes, resulting from the hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex. Over time, spasticity combines with weakness, impaired selective motor control, and altered muscle growth, leading to a range of secondary musculoskeletal problems, including shortened muscle-tendon units, fibrotic change in muscle, and fixed contractures. The management of CP is inherently multidisciplinary, incorporating a range of interventions, including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, orthoses, oral antispastic drugs, intramuscular botulinum toxin A, intrathecal baclofen, selective dorsal rhizotomy, and orthopedic surgery. While evidence supports the efficacy of several of these interventions, particularly botulinum toxin, casting, and goal-directed training, their effects are often modest or transient, and they are not without limitations. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of complementary and alternative therapies, including traditional medicine approaches, which are widely used alongside conventional rehabilitation in East Asia. One such approach is acupotomy, also known as needle-knife therapy, which was developed in China in the 1970s. This technique integrates the principles of traditional acupuncture with those of modern minimally invasive surgery, utilizing a stainless-steel needle with a flat blade at its tip to puncture the skin, cut, release, or dissect fibrotic or adherent soft tissue. The proposed mechanisms of action are multifaceted, including the release of local tension and adhesions, improved local microcirculation, modulation of inflammatory mediators, and reduced abnormal mechanical stress on connective tissue. In the context of CP, the rationale for using acupotomy is that releasing shortened or fibrotic muscle-tendon units and myofascial restrictions may reduce passive resistance to stretch, improve joint range of motion, and facilitate motor training. Clinicians in China and Korea have also proposed that acupotomy at selected sites could alter afferent input and reduce excitability of the spinal stretch reflex arc, although direct evidence is limited. Acupotomy is typically applied to the muscles and tendons most affected, such as the adductors, hamstrings, gastrocnemius-soleus, and cervical or paraspinal structures, and is usually delivered as a short course in combination with rehabilitation training. While clinical research on acupotomy has grown in recent years, primarily in China, the evidence base is not without its limitations. Randomized and non-randomized studies have reported improvements in muscle tone, joint mobility, gross motor function, and activities of daily living when acupotomy is added to rehabilitation in children with spastic CP. However, systematic reviews have noted important methodological limitations, including small samples, heterogeneous protocols, and a high or unclear risk of bias. Furthermore, acupotomy involves cutting soft tissue, which distinguishes it from filiform needling in terms of technique, tissue effect, and risk profile, and therefore, evidence on acupuncture cannot be assumed to apply to acupotomy. The reported adverse events associated with acupotomy, including bleeding, infection, nerve injury, and procedural pain, are particularly relevant in children, and safety must therefore be assessed together with efficacy. Despite the growing use of acupotomy for CP, several gaps remain in our understanding of its efficacy and safety. To date, no comprehensive systematic review has quantitatively evaluated randomized evidence for acupotomy in CP across outcomes, and the primary studies vary widely in terms of participant age, CP subtype and severity, Gross Motor Function Classification System level, acupotomy technique, treatment frequency, comparators, and co-interventions. This heterogeneity makes it challenging for clinicians to interpret the findings, and the methodological quality of these trials, including randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome reporting, has not been systematically appraised. The present study aimed to address these gaps by systematically evaluating the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for CP. Specifically, we sought to determine whether, in children and adults with CP, acupotomy alone or combined with conventional rehabilitation is more effective than rehabilitation alone, sham treatment, or other active comparators in improving spasticity, gross motor function, joint range of motion, and activities of daily living, and whether it is acceptably safe. We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance to ensure the rigor and transparency of our review. This study makes three key contributions to the existing literature. Firstly, it provides the first structured synthesis of randomized evidence for acupotomy in CP, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of its efficacy and safety. Secondly, it assesses the methodological quality of the included trials, providing a critical appraisal of the evidence base. Finally, it evaluates the certainty of the evidence using a structured approach, such as GRADE, enabling guideline developers and clinicians to make informed decisions about the use of acupotomy in multidisciplinary CP care. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to provide a comprehensive assessment of the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for cerebral palsy (CP), while also evaluating the risk of bias and certainty of evidence for each outcome. To achieve this, we conducted a thorough search of multiple databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, among others, using a combination of controlled vocabulary and free text terms related to the condition and intervention. Our search strategy was designed to capture all relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of acupotomy in children and adolescents with CP, with no language restrictions. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO prior to the commencement of the search, and the study was reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement. We adhered to the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, which provided a framework for the design, conduct, and reporting of our review. As our analysis relied solely on published data, ethical approval was not required. Our eligibility criteria were defined using the PICOS framework, which enabled us to clearly specify the participants, interventions, comparators, outcomes, and study design that were relevant to our review. In terms of participants, we included children and adolescents aged 0-18 years with a diagnosis of CP, regardless of subtype or Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) level. We excluded studies that focused on motor impairment from other causes, as our primary interest lay in the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for CP. The experimental intervention was acupotomy, also known as needle-knife or miniscalpel-acupuncture, which combines acupuncture with soft-tissue release. We excluded studies that combined acupotomy with other traditional Chinese medicine modalities, unless these modalities were also applied to the control group. Our primary outcome of interest was gross motor function, as measured by the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM-88 or GMFM-66). Secondary outcomes included muscle tone or spasticity, activities of daily living, range of motion, quality of life, and total effective rate, as defined by the original trials. We also evaluated safety outcomes, such as adverse events, including infection, bleeding, nerve injury, needle breakage, and treatment discontinuation. Only parallel-group RCTs were eligible for inclusion, while quasi-randomized trials, non-randomized studies, case reports, animal experiments, and reviews were excluded. To identify relevant studies, we employed a comprehensive search strategy that combined controlled vocabulary and free text terms related to the condition and intervention. We applied a filter for randomized trials to ensure that only relevant studies were captured. The full search strings for each database are provided in the Supplemental Digital Content. After removing duplicates, two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by a full-text assessment against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or, if necessary, by a third reviewer. The selection process is illustrated in a PRISMA flow diagram. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using a standardized, piloted form. The form captured information on study characteristics, including first author, year, country, sample size, age, CP subtype, GMFCS level, acupotomy technique, co-interventions, comparator, treatment length, follow-up, outcomes, and adverse events. For each outcome, we extracted the post-treatment mean and standard deviation (SD), or the change from baseline when only that was reported. When data were missing or unclear, we contacted the corresponding authors to request additional information. If means and SDs were not reported, we estimated them from medians and ranges or interquartile ranges using established methods. To evaluate the risk of bias, we used the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, which assesses the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. Each domain was rated as low risk, some concerns, or high risk. Given the procedural nature of acupotomy, blinding of participants and therapists is challenging; therefore, we paid particular attention to the blinding of outcome assessors and the potential influence of knowledge of allocation on parent-reported outcomes. The certainty of evidence for each primary and key secondary outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach, which considers risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. We rated the certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. Statistical significance was set at a two-sided P <.05. For continuous outcomes measured on the same scale, we calculated the mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence interval (CI). When trials used different scales for the same construct, we employed the standardized mean difference (SMD) as Hedges' g. Dichotomous outcomes, including total effective rate and adverse events, were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI. For rare adverse events, we used the Mantel–Haenszel method without continuity correction or the Peto odds ratio when events were very sparse. Due to the expected clinical heterogeneity in acupotomy protocols, co-interventions, and CP phenotypes, we pooled effect sizes under a random-effects model with inverse-variance weights. Our analysis aimed to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for CP, while also identifying methodological shortcomings in the existing literature and offering recommendations for the design, conduct, and reporting of future trials. Additionally, we calculated 95% prediction intervals to provide insight into the expected range of effects in future settings, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of the treatment's potential impact. To assess the heterogeneity among the trials, we employed Cochran's Q test, with a significance level set at P < 0.10, and quantified it using the I² statistic. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental component of natural language processing pipelines, providing crucial input for downstream tasks such as entity linking, relation and event extraction, question answering, and knowledge base population. The progress made in NER to date has been largely driven by a handful of shared benchmarks, including the CoNLL-2003 shared task data and OntoNotes. These benchmarks have enabled the development of highly effective neural sequence labelling architectures, from BiLSTM-CRFs to contextualised pretrained representations, which have achieved impressive performance gains. However, this success is closely tied to the way these benchmarks represent the task, with each token belonging to at most one entity mention and a small label inventory, typically ranging from four to eighteen types. This coarse-grained view of NER, while effective for certain applications, discards much of the semantic content of natural language, where entity mentions often contain other entity mentions. Consider, for example, the mention "University of California, Berkeley", where the organisation contains a state and a city, or "the Bank of China", where a financial institution contains a country. Such nested structure is pervasive in various domains, including news and biomedical text, and the inner mentions often play a crucial role in downstream tasks. A relation extractor that only sees the outer organisation, for instance, cannot recover the fact that the organisation is located in, or named for, a particular country. Moreover, nested mentions provide valuable insights into how names are compositionally constructed, which can aid in disambiguation and linking. Unfortunately, the flat annotation guidelines used in most benchmarks force annotators to choose a single span, usually the outermost or the one that best fits a narrow set of types, resulting in models that are blind to the more nuanced structure of natural language. The research community has long recognised this limitation, and early work on nested NER explored various approaches, including cascaded or layered tagging, discontinuous or parse-based methods, and mention hypergraphs. More recent methods have built on these foundations, incorporating techniques such as layered and stacked neural taggers, transition-based systems, and span-enumeration models. However, the evaluation of these methods has been limited to a narrow set of resources, primarily the ACE 2004 and 2005 corpora and GENIA. While these corpora provide some insights into nested NER, they are limited in their coverage, with ACE containing a small number of coarse entity types and shallow nesting, and GENIA restricted to the biomedical domain with a specialised ontology. As a result, models for nested NER are often tested on data that does not fully exercise their capabilities, and conclusions about their effectiveness may be specific to the idiosyncrasies of these corpora. In parallel, fine-grained entity typing has developed as a separate line of research, with work on larger type inventories demonstrating the benefits of richer types for downstream inference. However, fine-grained resources are often built using distant supervision, which introduces noise, or are focused on typing already-identified mentions rather than detecting them. Moreover, these resources typically do not annotate nested structure, with some notable exceptions, such as BBN's pronoun coreference and entity type corpus, which provides a hierarchical inventory of 64 types over the Wall Street Journal. Despite these efforts, no existing dataset combines broad coverage of entity types, genuinely nested annotation, and a widely studied and linguistically well-understood text source. This paper addresses this gap by presenting NNE, a manually annotated dataset of fine-grained, nested named entity mentions over the full Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB). Our annotation comprises 279,795 mentions of 114 entity types, with up to six layers of nesting, and builds on the BBN type hierarchy, extending it to capture additional distinctions. By choosing the PTB as the base text, we leverage the existing syntactic and semantic annotations, including PropBank and the CoNLL-2003 NER annotation, enabling comparison and joint modelling with these resources. The alignment of nested entity boundaries with constituent boundaries also allows for the study of how syntax can inform nested NER and how entity structure can inform parsing. The creation of NNE is motivated by the need for a dataset that satisfies three key requirements. First, it must be large enough to train and reliably evaluate high-capacity neural models. Second, it must have a sufficiently rich type inventory to make nesting semantically meaningful, rather than an artefact of a few coarse classes. Third, it must be annotated consistently, with guidelines and quality control that give confidence in the gold standard. To achieve this, we describe not only the resulting data but also the annotation scheme, the process by which annotators were trained and guided, and measures of inter-annotator agreement. We also provide a quantitative analysis of the data, characterising the distribution of types, the depth and structure of nesting, and the relationship between entity structure and the PTB's syntax. Our contributions are threefold. First, we release NNE, the largest manually annotated nested NER dataset for English, covering the entire WSJ portion of the PTB with 279,795 mentions across 114 fine-grained types and up to six layers of nesting. Second, we provide a detailed description of the annotation scheme and process, including type definitions, handling of ambiguous cases, and agreement statistics, to facilitate understanding, extension, and replication of the resource. Third, we offer a quantitative analysis of the data, providing insights into the characteristics of nested NER in newswire text and the potential applications of NNE in future research. The study of nested and fine-grained entity recognition has been hindered by the lack of a comprehensive dataset that captures the complex relationships between entities and their underlying syntactic structure. To address this gap, we have developed the Nested Named Entity (NNE) corpus, which provides a detailed annotation of entity structure and type distributions, as well as an examination of how annotation relates to the underlying syntactic structure. Our goal is to provide a benchmark for evaluating the performance of existing nested NER approaches and to encourage the development of new techniques that can effectively handle the challenges of nested and fine-grained entity recognition. To create the NNE corpus, we annotated the complete Wall Street Journal (WSJ) portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB), which spans sections 00-24. The PTB is a widely used resource that provides a rich annotation of part-of-speech tags, constituency structure, and semantic role and coreference layers. By annotating the WSJ portion of the PTB, we can study nested entity structure in conjunction with existing syntactic and semantic information. We retained the original tokenization of the PTB to ensure that mention boundaries align with the treebank, and annotators were able to see neighboring sentences to resolve ambiguous types. Our annotation scheme began with the BBN Pronoun Coreference and Entity Type Corpus, which was already annotated over the same WSJ text. We extended this scheme by incorporating ideas from the Extended Named Entity Hierarchy, the ACE guidelines, and the GENIA ontology. Through several rounds of pilot annotation on held-out documents, we refined our type inventory, adding, merging, or splitting types as necessary to ensure that frequent phenomena had suitable labels. The final scheme consists of 114 types organized in a three-level hierarchy, with top-level categories including person, organization, geopolitical entity, location, facility, event, product, work of art, law, language, and several numeric and temporal families. Annotators were instructed to choose the most specific applicable type for each mention, allowing the hierarchy to be collapsed to coarser labels when needed. Guidelines defined a mention as a contiguous token span that refers to an entity of one of the scheme's types, and names, numeric expressions, and temporal expressions were annotated, while pronouns and generic common-noun phrases were not. Nesting was permitted to arbitrary depth, subject to the constraint that any two mentions must be either disjoint or strictly nested, with no partially overlapping spans allowed. Identical spans with different types were permitted only in documented cases of genuine type ambiguity, such as metonymic uses. To ensure consistency and accuracy, the annotation procedure involved a team of trained annotators with linguistics backgrounds, who received a guideline document and supervised practice before working on the main corpus. We developed a browser-based interface for efficient span selection and hierarchical type assignment, which supported keyboard shortcuts, type search over the hierarchy, and visual display of nested mentions. The tool pre-populated candidate annotations from the existing BBN labels where compatible, and annotators then corrected, extended, and re-typed them. Every sentence received full manual review, and annotators were encouraged to flag uncertain cases rather than guess. To evaluate the quality of the annotations, we measured inter-annotator agreement on a subset of documents that were annotated independently by multiple annotators from scratch. Since chance-corrected coefficients such as Cohen's kappa are poorly defined for this task, we followed Hripcsak and Rothschild (2005) in treating one annotator's labels as the reference and computing precision, recall, and F1 for the other. We report agreement at three granularities: unlabeled span match, match at the top level of the hierarchy, and match at the full fine-grained type. This allows us to separate disagreements about where mentions are from disagreements about what they are. We also compared agreement at different nesting depths to determine whether inner mentions are harder to annotate than outermost ones and examined confusion between types to identify systematically ambiguous distinctions. Finally, we computed descriptive statistics over the final corpus, including the number of mentions, the frequency of each type, the distribution of mention lengths in tokens, and the distribution of nesting depths. These statistics provide a detailed understanding of the characteristics of the NNE corpus and can inform the development of new models and techniques for nested and fine-grained entity recognition. In addition to the NNE corpus, we provide standard training, development, and test splits, as well as an evaluation of existing nested NER approaches as baselines. This will enable researchers to assess the performance of their models on the NNE corpus and to compare their results to those of other approaches. We hope that the public release of the NNE corpus will encourage the development of new techniques for nested and fine-grained entity recognition and will support research on how entity structure interacts with syntax, linking, and other downstream applications. By providing a comprehensive and carefully annotated dataset, we aim to advance the state of the art in entity recognition and to facilitate further research in this important area. Furthermore, the NNE corpus offers a unique opportunity to study the relationships between entity structure and syntactic structure, which can inform the development of more effective models for entity recognition. The corpus can also be used to investigate the impact of nesting depth and type granularity on the performance of entity recognition models, and to explore the use of syntactic and semantic features to improve entity recognition. By making the NNE corpus available to the research community, we hope to stimulate further research in these areas and to contribute to the development of more accurate and effective entity recognition systems. In conclusion, the NNE corpus is a valuable resource for the research community, providing a comprehensive and carefully annotated dataset for the study of nested and fine-grained entity recognition. The corpus offers a unique opportunity to investigate the relationships between entity structure and syntactic structure, and to develop more effective models for entity recognition. We believe that the NNE corpus will be an important tool for advancing the state of the art in entity recognition, and we look forward to seeing the new insights and innovations that it will enable. We also plan to continue updating and expanding the NNE corpus, incorporating new annotations and features as they become available. This will ensure that the corpus remains a relevant and useful resource for the research community, and will provide a foundation for further research in entity recognition and related areas. By working together to develop and refine the NNE corpus, we can advance our understanding of entity recognition and develop more effective systems for extracting and representing entities in text.
