The prevalence of code clones, which are fragments of source code that are identical or similar to one another, is a well-documented phenomenon in modern software systems. Studies have shown that between 5% and 20% of the code in typical large systems is cloned, with developers creating clones for a variety of reasons, including copy-and-paste reuse, language limitations, and deliberate performance or stability trade-offs. The debate over whether clones are harmful has been ongoing for over a decade, with some research associating them with inconsistent updates, propagated defects, and increased maintenance effort, while others have found that clones can be short-lived, stable, or even beneficial in specific contexts. One of the practical consequences of clone detection is that it can leave developers with a triage problem. Clone detectors can report thousands of clone groups for a mature project, and not all clones are equally important. Developers with limited time must therefore decide which clones are worth refactoring, a process that can be time-consuming and requires a deep understanding of the context of each clone instance. Refactoring is not without its costs, however, as it can introduce regressions or entangle components that were intentionally kept separate. As a result, refactoring every detected clone is neither feasible nor desirable, which motivates the need for clone recommendation, the task of identifying the clones that developers are likely to find worth removing. Prior research has approached clone recommendation from two complementary angles. The first approach focuses on the present state of the code, assessing whether a clone group is a good refactoring candidate based on its structural and syntactic properties, such as cohesion, coupling, size, and location within the class hierarchy or package structure. The second approach uses the past history of the project, mining version histories to determine how clone peers evolved, for example, whether they changed together, how often they were modified, and whether they were modified inconsistently. Clones that repeatedly co-change are plausible candidates for refactoring because the duplication imposes a recurring maintenance burden. While there has been progress in clone recommendation, existing approaches face several limitations. Each tool considers only a restricted set of factors, chosen mostly on the basis of the authors' intuitions about what makes a clone worth refactoring. It remains unclear whether the factors used so far are sufficient, whether they overlap, or whether other properties of clones carry additional predictive signal. For example, features describing the evolution of an individual clone, such as how long it has existed, how often it has been edited, and who edited it, have received much less attention than co-change relations between clone peers. Furthermore, syntactic differences between peers are seldom combined with spatial relations such as same-file or same-package placement. Another limitation of existing approaches is that much of the earlier evaluation relied on small data sets, manually labeled ground truth, or a single project, which makes generalization hard to assess. In particular, it is rarely examined whether a model learned on one project can recommend clones in another project, a cross-project setting that matters in practice because new projects lack the history required for training. Additionally, the literature offers little systematic comparison of which categories of factors contribute most to recommendation accuracy, or of which learning algorithms are best suited to the task. Without such comparisons, tool builders cannot make informed decisions about which information is worth the cost of collecting. The existence of several tools that use different yet individually useful signals suggested to us that a more accurate recommender could be obtained by considering as many factors as possible within a single framework and letting a learning algorithm determine how they should be weighed. This leads to the central question of this paper: to what extent can combining a broad set of present and past features of clones, characterizing both individual clones and the relations among clone peers, improve the recommendation of clones for refactoring, in both within-project and cross-project settings? We further ask which categories of features are most informative and how sensitive the results are to the choice of learning algorithm. To answer these questions, we present CREC, a learning-based approach to clone recommendation. CREC takes a set of software repositories as input and automatically mines their histories to identify clone groups that developers actually refactored (R-clones) and clone groups that persisted without being refactored (NR-clones). This automatic labeling removes the need for manual annotation and yields a training set that reflects real developer decisions at a scale unattainable by hand. For each clone group, CREC extracts 34 features in five categories: the content of individual clones, the evolution behaviors of individual clones, and the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers. A classifier trained on these features then predicts whether a new clone group should be recommended for refactoring. We evaluated CREC on six large open-source projects. In the within-project setting, where the classifier is trained and tested on data from the same project, CREC achieved an F-score of 83%. In the cross-project setting, where the classifier is trained on other projects and applied to an unseen one, it achieved an F-score of 76%. We compared CREC against the state-of-the-art approach of Wang and Godfrey (2014) on the same data set. Our results show that CREC outperforms the existing approach, demonstrating the benefits of combining a broad set of present and past features of clones. We also examined the importance of different categories of features and the sensitivity of the results to the choice of learning algorithm, providing insights into the factors that contribute most to recommendation accuracy. Overall, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of CREC in recommending clones for refactoring and highlights the importance of considering a broad set of features in clone recommendation. Our findings have implications for the development of clone detection and recommendation tools, suggesting that a more comprehensive approach to clone analysis can lead to more accurate and effective recommendations. By providing a framework for evaluating the importance of different features and learning algorithms, our study contributes to the ongoing effort to improve the accuracy and usefulness of clone recommendation tools. The development of effective clone management tools is crucial for maintaining the quality and integrity of software systems. To address this challenge, we have designed and evaluated a novel approach, CREC, which leverages machine learning to recommend clones for refactoring. Our approach has achieved significant improvements over a state-of-the-art baseline, with F-scores of 83% and 76% in within-project and cross-project settings, respectively. This substantial enhancement is particularly noteworthy when historical data from the target project is unavailable. To gain a deeper understanding of the factors that contribute to these results, we conducted a thorough analysis of the contribution of each feature category and compared the performance of several widely used learning algorithms. This paper presents the following key contributions: (1) an automated approach to building ground truth, which enables the construction of large training and evaluation sets without manual labeling; (2) the largest feature set to date for clone recommendation, comprising 34 features that integrate present and past information; (3) a learning-based recommender, CREC, which accurately recommends clones for refactoring; and (4) an empirical analysis of factors and algorithms, providing insights to guide the design of future clone-management tools. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by providing background and motivating examples in Section 2. Section 3 describes the design of CREC, including the extraction of refactored and non-refactored clone groups, the feature set, and the classifier training. The experimental setup and results are presented in Section 4, while Section 5 discusses threats to validity. A review of related work is provided in Section 6, and we conclude with a summary of our findings and implications in Section 7. Our study was guided by three research questions. First, we sought to determine the accuracy with which CREC recommends clone groups for refactoring in within-project and cross-project settings, compared to a state-of-the-art baseline. Second, we aimed to quantify the contribution of each feature category to the overall performance of CREC. Third, we investigated the impact of the choice of learning algorithm on the effectiveness of CREC. To address these questions, we designed CREC as a three-stage approach: (1) automatic construction of a labeled data set of refactored clone groups and non-refactored clone groups from version histories; (2) extraction of 34 features capturing the present and past of each clone group; and (3) training and applying a classifier that predicts whether a clone group deserves refactoring. We selected six open-source Java projects with long, well-maintained Git histories as the subject projects for our study. These projects, namely Ant, Cassandra, jEdit, JGit, Lucene, and Tomcat, were chosen based on three criteria: more than 5,000 commits, at least eight years of development, and varied application domains and sizes. To keep the analysis tractable, we sampled snapshots at release tags and at every 100th commit between releases, yielding a total of 1,412 snapshots. This sampling approach is common in clone-genealogy research, where the unit of analysis is the evolution of clones across versions rather than individual commits. For each snapshot, we detected Type-2 and Type-3 clones using NiCad, with a minimum size of 10 lines, a maximum dissimilarity threshold of 30% after pretty-printing and identifier normalization, and blind renaming. Clone fragments were grouped into clone groups, where each member is similar to the others in the group. We then mapped clone groups across consecutive snapshots using a location- and similarity-based mapping, resulting in a set of clone genealogies that describe how each group was created, changed, and removed. To automatically label refactored and non-refactored clone groups, we detected refactorings between successive snapshots using RefactoringMiner, which reports Extract Method, Pull Up Method, Move Method, Extract Superclass, and related operations with high precision. A clone group was labeled as refactored if its genealogy ended due to the disappearance or dissimilarity of at least two fragments, and a clone-removal refactoring was detected involving at least two fragments of the group in the same commit interval. Clone groups that survived at least five consecutive snapshots or at least one year without any clone-removal refactoring were labeled as non-refactored. Groups with ambiguous histories were discarded, and two authors manually validated a random sample of 300 labeled groups, achieving a high level of agreement with the automatic labels. The final data set consisted of 1,028 refactored clone groups and 4,876 non-refactored clone groups. CREC computes 34 features at the snapshot immediately preceding the labeling event, which are organized into five categories: code features, evolution-history features, spatial features, syntactic-relation features, and co-change features. These features capture various aspects of the present and past of each clone group, including its content, evolution, spatial relations, and syntactic differences. Code features, which describe the present content of a clone group, include metrics such as average lines of code, number of tokens, number of peers, cyclomatic complexity, and cohesion. Evolution-history features, which describe the past of each clone, include metrics such as age, number of commits touching it, number of distinct authors, time since last change, and change frequency. Spatial features characterize the location of clone peers, including same method, same file, same package, or different modules, as well as file-path distance and inheritance relation between enclosing classes. Syntactic-relation features capture the differences between clone peers, including token-level and AST-level similarity, number of differing statements, and gap lines in Type-3 clones. In the next section, we present the results of our experimental evaluation, which demonstrate the effectiveness of CREC in recommending clones for refactoring. We also discuss the implications of our findings and provide insights into the design of future clone-management tools. Malaria remains a paramount parasitic disease globally, with the World Health Organization estimating approximately 219 million cases and 435,000 deaths in 2017, predominantly in the African Region, which accounted for about 93% of cases and 94% of deaths (World Health Organization, 2018). The significant progress achieved in the early 2000s, through scaled-up vector control, the introduction of artemisinin-based combination therapy, and improved diagnostics, which collectively reduced the global burden by around 40% (Bhatt et al., 2015), has stalled in several high-burden countries. A critical challenge in malaria control is its heterogeneity; transmission intensity varies not only over small geographical distances but also across different seasons and years, influenced by a complex interplay of factors including climate, land use, vector ecology, human movement, socioeconomic conditions, and the coverage of interventions (Gething et al., 2011; Kabaria et al., 2017). This heterogeneity complicates the interpretation of national averages, as they mask the specific foci and periods of risk that are crucial for effective control and elimination strategies. The issue is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where resources are limited, making targeted interventions essential. To address this challenge, spatio-temporal modelling has emerged as a central tool for characterizing the heterogeneity of malaria transmission. By elucidating how disease risk varies jointly over space and time, these models support a range of critical applications, including the mapping of disease burden, early warning systems for epidemics, the identification of hotspots and high-risk periods, and the evaluation of interventions (Hay et al., 2009; Pigott et al., 2015). The rapid expansion of this field can be attributed to several factors. The increasing availability of georeferenced data, such as national household surveys with GPS coordinates (e.g., Demographic and Health Surveys and Malaria Indicator Surveys), health facility records from routine information systems like DHIS2, and parasite rate databases compiled by the Malaria Atlas Project (Guerra et al., 2007; Gething et al., 2011), has been pivotal. Additionally, advancements in satellite remote sensing now provide high-resolution environmental data, including rainfall, temperature, vegetation indices, and other relevant measures (Hay et al., 2006). Computational advances, particularly in hierarchical Bayesian geostatistical inference, have made it feasible to apply complex models to large datasets, with techniques such as Markov chain Monte Carlo and the integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) with the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) approach allowing for flexible modelling (Rue et al., 2009; Lindgren et al., 2011). The methodologies employed in spatio-temporal modelling of malaria are diverse and depend on the nature of the data and the objectives of the analysis. For area-level data, models often involve Poisson or negative binomial likelihoods to account for the count of cases in each area over time, incorporating expected counts or population at risk, covariates, spatially structured and unstructured random effects, temporal terms, and space-time interactions (Besag et al., 1991; Knorr-Held, 2000). For point-referenced survey data, geostatistical binomial models are common, which include Gaussian processes with Matérn covariance to capture spatial and temporal dependencies (Diggle et al., 1998; Gething et al., 2012). Other approaches include spatial scan statistics for cluster detection (Kulldorff, 1997), generalized additive models, spatio-temporal autoregressive and distributed-lag models for climate-driven forecasting, machine learning techniques such as random forests and boosted regression trees, and mechanistic or hybrid models that combine transmission dynamics with spatial structure (Smith et al., 2012; Reiner et al., 2015). Each of these approaches is based on distinct assumptions regarding stationarity, dependence structure, interaction between space and time, and the relationship between covariates and risk, and the choice of approach is further influenced by the scale of analysis and the quality and completeness of the underlying data. The covariates included in these models are equally diverse, reflecting the multifactorial nature of malaria transmission. Environmental and climatic variables, such as temperature, rainfall, humidity, vegetation indices, elevation, and hydrology, are frequently used due to their biological relevance to vector and parasite development (Craig et al., 1999; Mordecai et al., 2013). Socioeconomic indicators, housing quality, urbanization, population density, access to healthcare, intervention coverage (including insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, and treatment), and human mobility are also considered, although their inclusion is less standardized and they are often less consistently available and measured. Decisions regarding lagged effects, spatial resolution matching, collinearity, variable selection, and handling covariates that are themselves modelled or interpolated are made inconsistently and often without clear justification. Similarly, the practices used to validate models vary, ranging from simple in-sample fit statistics (such as deviance information criterion, R²) to out-of-sample cross-validation, spatial block validation, and prospective forecast evaluation using proper scoring rules (Roberts et al., 2017; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007), with the neglect of residual spatial and temporal autocorrelation potentially leading to overestimation of predictive performance. While existing reviews have addressed various aspects of this landscape, a comprehensive overview that synthesizes the full range of spatio-temporal approaches, covariates, and validation strategies across different settings is lacking. Earlier syntheses have focused on specific topics, such as the use of geographic information systems and remote sensing in malaria epidemiology (Hay et al., 2006; Eisele et al., 2012), early warning systems and climate-based forecasting (Thomson et al., 2006; Zinszer et al., 2012), mapping of parasite prevalence (Hay et al., 2009), or particular techniques. The absence of a systematic comparison of the diverse methodologies, covariates, and validation strategies employed in spatio-temporal modelling of malaria hinders researchers and national malaria control programs aiming to develop models for burden estimation, forecasting, or intervention targeting, as they lack consolidated guidance on the applicability and effectiveness of different methods under various data conditions. This knowledge gap is particularly significant in LMICs, where data are often sparse, noisy, and reported at aggregated administrative scales, and methodological choices can directly influence resource allocation. Given the heterogeneity in aims, designs, and outcomes across the literature, a scoping review is more appropriate than a conventional systematic review with meta-analysis. A scoping approach enables the mapping of the extent, range, and nature of the evidence, the identification of key concepts and gaps, and the establishment of a foundation for best-practice recommendations (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010; Tricco et al., 2018). The overarching goal of such a review is to provide a comprehensive framework that can guide the development and application of spatio-temporal models for malaria control, ultimately contributing to more effective and targeted interventions against this persistent and heterogeneous disease. The question at the heart of this review is a pressing one: what approaches have been employed to model the spatio-temporal dynamics of malaria in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and what covariates and validation techniques have been used to inform these models? To address this question, we have identified five key objectives. Firstly, we aim to provide a detailed description of the aims and settings of existing spatio-temporal malaria modelling studies, including the spatial and temporal scales employed and the data sources utilized. Secondly, we seek to catalogue and classify the various statistical and mathematical modelling frameworks that have been applied to this problem. Thirdly, we will summarize the covariates that have been included in these models and how they have been processed. Fourthly, we will document the procedures used to validate and assess the performance of these models. Finally, we hope to identify methodological gaps and derive recommendations to guide future modelling decisions. This review makes three significant contributions to the field. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive and structured synthesis of spatio-temporal malaria modelling efforts over the past five decades, incorporating not only peer-reviewed literature but also grey literature that may have been overlooked by conventional searches. Secondly, it explicitly links modelling choices to data characteristics, spatial scale, and purpose, thereby enabling a more transparent and informed approach to method selection. Thirdly, it highlights underutilized methods, weaknesses in validation and reporting, and priority areas for research, ultimately supporting the development of more rigorous and reproducible modelling approaches in the settings where they are most needed. Our review follows the PRISMA-P reporting guidance (Moher et al., 2015) and is registered in PROSPERO (CRD42017076427). The methodological framework for this scoping review is based on the work of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), as refined by Levac et al. (2010) and the Joanna Briggs Institute (Peters et al., 2015). The protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement (Moher et al., 2015; Shamseer et al., 2015) and was registered with PROSPERO before the screening process began. The final review will be reported using PRISMA guidance, including a flow diagram of study selection. We opted for a scoping design because our primary aim is to map the range of spatio-temporal approaches, covariates, and validation practices employed in malaria modelling, rather than to pool effect estimates. The review process proceeds through five stages: (1) identifying the research question, (2) identifying relevant studies, (3) selecting studies, (4) charting the data, and (5) collating, summarizing, and reporting the results. Our research question is focused on the spatio-temporal modelling approaches, covariates, and validation techniques used to assess the burden of malaria in LMICs within the limits of malaria transmission. Eligibility criteria were structured using the Population–Concept–Context framework. The population of interest comprises human malaria cases, infection prevalence, incidence, or mortality, at any spatial scale from household to continental. The concept of interest is the application of statistical, mathematical, or geostatistical models that explicitly incorporate both spatial and temporal dimensions, such as Bayesian hierarchical models, spatio-temporal geostatistical models, space–time scan statistics, generalized additive or autoregressive models with spatial structure, and mechanistic models with spatial components. The context is any LMIC, as defined by the World Bank income classification, lying within the spatial limits of malaria transmission (Gething et al., 2011; Guerra et al., 2008). Studies were included if they were published between January 1968 and April 2018, in any language for which translation was feasible, and as primary research, methodological papers, theses, or technical reports. We excluded studies that were purely spatial or purely temporal with no joint modelling, those conducted in high-income or non-endemic settings, those that considered only vector distribution or entomological outcomes without human burden, and commentaries, editorials, or narrative reviews without original modelling. Reference lists of excluded reviews were hand-searched for eligible primary studies. To identify relevant studies, we will conduct a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, JSTOR, Cochrane CENTRAL via Wiley, Academic Search Complete, MasterFILE Premier, CINAHL, and MEDLINE via EBSCOhost, as well as Google Scholar. The search strategy was developed in collaboration with an information specialist and combines controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH) with free-text terms in three concept blocks joined by the Boolean operator AND: (i) malaria ("malaria" OR "Plasmodium" OR "falciparum" OR "vivax"); (ii) spatio-temporal methods ("spatio-temporal" OR "spatiotemporal" OR "space-time" OR "geostatistic" OR "Bayesian hierarchical" OR "disease mapping" OR "geographic information system" OR "remote sensing" OR "kriging" OR "CAR model" OR "INLA"); and (iii) burden or outcome terms ("prevalence" OR "incidence" OR "burden" OR "transmission" OR "mortality" OR "risk"). Terms within each block are joined by OR. A country-level filter listing LMICs, adapted from the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care group filter (Cochrane EPOC, 2017), will be used to improve specificity. The search will be piloted in PubMed, peer-reviewed using the PRESS checklist (McGowan et al., 2016), and adapted to the syntax of each database. Due to the large number of records returned by Google Scholar, the first 200 hits for each search string will be screened (Haddaway et al., 2015). In addition to searching databases, we will also seek out grey literature through various channels, including OpenGrey, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, the World Health Organization Global Malaria Programme repository, the Malaria Atlas Project, the MEASURE DHS and Malaria Indicator Survey publications, conference proceedings of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene and the Multilateral Initiative on Malaria, and institutional repositories of African universities. Furthermore, we will contact experts in malaria spatial epidemiology to identify unpublished work. The persistence of homogeneous leadership in organizations, despite decades of diversity initiatives and a growing commitment to equal opportunity, is a striking phenomenon. In many professions, women, racial and ethnic minorities, and other nondominant group members enter in substantial numbers, only to see their representation dwindle at each successive step of the career ladder. This pattern is particularly evident in what can be termed upward mobility career systems, where careers unfold as a series of evaluations and promotions that progressively narrow the pool of candidates. For instance, in academia, women earn roughly half of doctoral degrees in many fields, yet they remain underrepresented among full professors and in senior leadership positions. The "leaky pipeline" metaphor, often used to describe this phenomenon, is somewhat misleading, as it implies a passive loss of talent rather than the outcome of repeated decisions made by identifiable individuals at specific points in the system. The fact that this pattern persists in organizations that explicitly espouse meritocratic values is particularly puzzling. As Castilla and Benard (2010) have noted, a paradox of meritocracy can arise, where organizations that emphasize meritocratic values can actually exhibit greater bias in favor of dominant group members. This is because the belief in one's own objectivity can lead decision makers to relax their vigilance, making them more susceptible to moral licensing and less likely to monitor their own behavior. Furthermore, the criteria used to evaluate merit are often constructed or reweighted to favor certain candidates, as merit is rarely defined in a way that is independent of who displays it. Decades of research have shown that stereotypes can shape the evaluation of competence, the attribution of success, and the interpretation of ambiguous performance information, particularly when evaluation criteria are ambiguous, accountability is low, and time is short. Gatekeepers, who control access to valued resources and positions, occupy a pivotal position in this process. They are often members of the dominant group, having been successful under existing rules, and are therefore prone to reproduce homophilous patterns of selection. However, the majority of diversity interventions are directed elsewhere, focusing on fixing the nondominant group member through mentoring, networking, or leadership training, or changing attitudes broadly through diversity training for all employees. While these approaches may have some benefits, the evidence suggests that they have modest and often short-lived effects, and that mandatory training can even provoke resistance. In contrast, programs that target the people and procedures at decision points, such as accountability, transparency, and task forces responsible for diversity outcomes, have been shown to be more effective. However, these types of interventions have been relatively understudied, and the available evidence is limited. Two further limitations characterize the literature on diversity interventions. First, much of the evidence on bias comes from laboratory or vignette experiments, which, while valuable for demonstrating mechanisms, say little about how bias operates in the collective, repeated, and politically embedded decision processes of real organizations. Second, systemic approaches, which view inequality as an emergent property of interacting parts of an organization, have been advocated for some time, yet they are rarely translated into concrete guidance for practitioners. As a result, change agents, including diversity officers and consultants, are left with broad principles but few specifics on what an intervention should contain and why it should work. The empirical base for "what works" in systemic interventions is thin, and rigorous evaluations in naturally occurring organizational settings remain scarce. This article seeks to address these gaps by asking: What design specifications should systemic diversity interventions meet if they are to engage gatekeepers, improve the quality of decision making, and mitigate bias in upward mobility career systems? I use the term design specifications in the sense of design science, referring to general, evidence-informed prescriptions that state the properties an intervention should have to produce a desired outcome in a class of contexts, while leaving room for local adaptation. To derive these specifications, I draw on research on the paradox of meritocracy, bias in evaluation, and group decision processes to identify the mechanisms through which gatekeepers reproduce inequality and the leverage points at which they might be disrupted. I also ground the specifications in the limited empirical evidence on systemic interventions, examining three illustrative examples from academic settings: a bias literacy program, participatory modeling of organizational dynamics, and participant observation of decision making in committees. Universities offer a particularly informative context because their career systems are archetypal examples of upward mobility, their gatekeeping processes are formalized and visible, and their commitment to meritocratic ideals is especially strong. The contribution of this article is threefold. First, I extend the diversity literature by shifting the unit of intervention from the disadvantaged individual or the undifferentiated workforce to the gatekeepers and the decision-making processes they control. Second, I provide a set of design specifications for systemic diversity interventions that can be applied in a variety of contexts, while leaving room for local adaptation. Finally, I demonstrate the value of a design science approach to developing and evaluating diversity interventions, which can help to build a more robust and evidence-based field of practice. By focusing on the mechanisms and leverage points that shape the behavior of gatekeepers, we can develop more effective interventions that address the root causes of inequality in upward mobility career systems. This research endeavors to bridge the gap between the study of bias and organizational change by examining the decision-making processes that underlie systemic diversity interventions. To achieve this, I have developed a set of design specifications that synthesize the existing evidence on effective interventions, with a focus on features such as engagement, self-generated insight, and attention to the decision process. Each specification is accompanied by a concrete example of a successful intervention, providing a foundation for future evaluation research and inspiration for diversity officers and consultants. By combining these contributions, I aim to make systemic change in the composition of the upper echelons of career pyramids a more tractable and evidence-based pursuit. The research approach employed in this study follows a design science methodology, which seeks to generate prescriptive knowledge in the form of design specifications. These specifications take the form of general statements that outline the conditions under which a particular outcome can be achieved, and are judged on their utility and the plausibility of their underlying mechanisms. Given the scarcity of rigorous evaluations of systemic diversity interventions, I drew on three sources of input in an iterative, abductive process. Firstly, I conducted a theoretical analysis of the paradox of meritocracy in upward mobility career systems. Secondly, I undertook a purposive review of the existing evidence on interventions. Thirdly, I developed a formal sketch of how bias in gatekeeping decisions accumulates across a career pyramid. By moving back and forth between these sources, I refined the design specifications until each was tied to an identified mechanism, at least one empirical example, and a plausible implementation route. The scope of this research is focused on upward mobility career systems, which are organizations in which individuals progress through hierarchical stages, with advancement decided by gatekeepers who evaluate candidates against criteria of merit. Examples of such systems include academia, professional service firms, and large public bureaucracies. A systemic diversity intervention is defined as one that targets the decision-making processes, structures, or routines through which advancement occurs, rather than solely focusing on the attitudes or skills of individuals from nondominant groups. Nondominant group members are those whose social category is underrepresented at higher organizational levels and who are subject to negative stereotyping or reduced status in the evaluative context. To identify and select intervention evidence, I conducted a comprehensive search of major databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and Google Scholar, for English-language publications from 2000 to 2022. The search strings combined terms related to the intervention level, target, topic, and setting. I supplemented the database search with backward and forward citation tracking from key works, as well as reports from funded programs such as the U.S. National Science Foundation ADVANCE initiative and the European structural change projects. Studies were included if they described an intervention aimed at influencing gatekeepers' evaluations, selections, or promotions, or altering the structures or routines within which they operate, and reported some form of outcome evidence. Interventions aimed solely at individual development of nondominant group members, or one-off awareness sessions without follow-up, were excluded. Given the limited evidence base, I employed a purposive, criterion-based selection approach to identify exemplary cases that maximized variation in the mechanism of change. Three interventions in academic settings were chosen, each engaging gatekeepers through a different route. The first was a bias literacy program, which equips gatekeepers with the knowledge and strategies to recognize and counter biases in their evaluations. The second was participatory modeling, which involves gatekeepers and other stakeholders in the construction of a formal or semiformal model of the career system, allowing them to see how local decisions aggregate into pyramid-level representation. The third was participant observation, in which a researcher-practitioner observes actual decision meetings and provides feedback to gatekeepers on the discursive and procedural patterns that shape their evaluations. For each intervention, I extracted the target group of gatekeepers, core activities, theory of change, implementation conditions, outcome measures, and reported effects and limitations. I then coded the material using a mechanism-oriented template adapted from realist evaluation, seeking to understand what it was about the intervention that produced change, for whom, and under what conditions. The coding process involved three passes: firstly, open descriptive categories were coded; secondly, these categories were clustered into higher-order mechanisms drawing on the literatures on stereotyping, accountability, and structured decision making; and thirdly, each cluster was translated into a design specification and checked against disconfirming cases to identify boundary conditions. Specifications were retained when they were supported by at least two independent sources, or by one empirical source and a well-established theoretical mechanism, and were flagged as provisional otherwise. To clarify why modest gatekeeper bias yields large representation gaps at the top, and to provide a transparent basis for the participatory modeling example, I developed a formal model of bias accumulation. This model illustrates how biases in gatekeeping decisions can accumulate across a career pyramid, resulting in significant representation gaps at the top. By providing a clear understanding of the mechanisms underlying bias accumulation, this model can inform the development of more effective interventions aimed at promoting diversity and inclusion in upward mobility career systems. The career advancement process can be conceptualized as a multistage pipeline, where individuals progress through a series of promotion stages (Martell et al., 1996; Nielsen & Börjesson, 2022). To better understand the dynamics of this process, consider a system with K promotion stages, where pk represents the promotion probability for dominant group members at stage k. The nondominant group's promotion probability, on the other hand, is pk(1 − δk), with δk ∈ [0,1) denoting the proportional reduction in promotion probability due to biased evaluation. At each stage, the share of nondominant group members can be calculated using the formula fK = f0 ∏{k=1}^{K}(1 − δk) / [ f0 ∏{k=1}^{K}(1 − δk) + (1 − f0) ]. This formula highlights the cumulative effect of biased evaluation across multiple stages. For instance, if the nondominant group's share at entry is f0 = 0.50, and the proportional reduction in promotion probability is constant at δ = 0.10, then after K = 5 stages, the nondominant group's share at the top would be approximately 0.37. This disparity arises despite the fact that no single stage exhibits a dramatic gap, underscoring the insidious nature of cumulative disadvantage. The meritocratic belief that selection is unbiased can lead to the attribution of these gaps to individual differences, which, in turn, can increase bias (Castilla & Benard, 2010). To illustrate the potential impact of interventions, the model can be used heuristically to demonstrate how reducing δk at selected stages or increasing the number of transparent, structured stages can shift fK. The demographic landscape of the US school-age population is undergoing a significant shift, with English Language Learners (ELLs) emerging as one of the fastest-growing segments. According to the most recent national data, ELLs comprise approximately one in ten public school students, totaling over five million children (National Center for Education Statistics, 2022). Notably, the majority of these students are enrolled in elementary grades, a critical period during which foundational knowledge and attitudes toward science are formed. However, despite their growing numbers, ELLs have not achieved the same level of academic success as their English-proficient peers. The National Assessment of Educational Progress has consistently revealed substantial gaps in science achievement between ELLs and non-ELLs, with these disparities persisting across grade levels and student cohorts. Such inequities can have far-reaching consequences, limiting ELLs' access to advanced coursework and STEM pathways, and ultimately restricting their participation in a society increasingly shaped by science and technology (Lee, 2005; Lee, Quinn, & Valdés, 2013). In response to these concerns, science educators and policy documents have advocated for the adoption of inquiry-based approaches to instruction. This approach engages students in a range of activities, including posing questions, planning investigations, collecting and interpreting evidence, and constructing explanations, rather than simply receiving information passively (National Research Council [NRC], 2000). Contemporary standards, such as A Framework for K–12 Science Education and the Next Generation Science Standards, place these practices at the forefront of science learning (NGSS Lead States, 2013; NRC, 2012). Proponents of inquiry-based instruction argue that it is particularly well-suited to ELLs, as hands-on investigations provide concrete, multimodal experiences that can make abstract ideas more comprehensible. Moreover, collaborative discourse creates authentic opportunities for language use, and open-ended tasks can draw on the cultural and linguistic resources that students bring to the classroom (Rosebery, Ogonowski, DiSchino, & Warren, 2010; Stoddart, Pinal, Latzke, & Canaday, 2002). From this perspective, science and language are learned together, with scientific practice serving as a context for language development (Lemke, 1990; Hakuta, Santos, & Fang, 2013). While the evidence suggests that inquiry-based instruction can be effective in improving science achievement for students in general, the picture is more nuanced. Syntheses of the literature have shown that inquiry-based instruction can yield positive effects on science achievement, particularly when students are actively engaged in investigation and when teachers provide guidance (Furtak, Seidel, Iverson, & Briggs, 2012; Minner, Levy, & Century, 2010). However, meta-analytic work on discovery-based learning has also highlighted the importance of scaffolding, feedback, or worked examples in supporting student learning, while unguided instruction can be less effective (Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich, & Tenenbaum, 2011). The broader debate over minimally guided instruction has raised concerns that inquiry may place heavy demands on working memory and potentially disadvantage novice learners (Kirschner, Sweller, & Clark, 2006). Others have countered that well-scaffolded inquiry can support learners in managing complexity (Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, & Chinn, 2007). However, these syntheses have largely been based on samples of students who are proficient in the language of instruction, and rarely have results been disaggregated by language status. For ELLs, the question of whether inquiry-based instruction is effective is more complicated. While the features that make inquiry attractive, such as hands-on investigation and collaborative discourse, may also create obstacles for ELLs. Inquiry lessons often rely on extended oral discussion, interpretation of ambiguous data, and the production of written explanations and arguments, all of which require command of the academic language of science (Cummins, 2000; Janzen, 2008). Where language support is weak, ELLs may participate less in group work, struggle to follow investigative procedures, and ultimately gain less from inquiry than their English-proficient classmates (Lee, 2005). In contrast, when teachers integrate language scaffolds, such as visuals, sentence frames, native-language support, and explicit vocabulary instruction, inquiry may help to narrow the gaps between ELLs and non-ELLs (Cuevas, Lee, Hart, & Deaktor, 2005; Lee, Maerten-Rivera, Penfield, LeRoy, & Secada, 2008; Settlage, Madsen, & Rustad, 2005). Ultimately, whether inquiry is effective for ELLs, and under what conditions, is an empirical question that cannot be resolved through theory alone. Despite a growing body of intervention studies, systematic evidence on the effectiveness of inquiry-based instruction for ELLs is limited. Existing reviews of science education for ELLs have been largely narrative, emphasizing conceptual frameworks, research agendas, and promising practices over quantification of effects (Janzen, 2008; Lee, 2005). Individual studies have varied widely in design, duration, outcome measures, and the degree of language support embedded in instruction, and many have involved small samples within a single school or district. As a result, it remains unclear whether the reported benefits of inquiry are consistent across studies, whether they are comparable in magnitude to those found for non-ELLs, and which features of instruction or context account for variation. Without such evidence, calls to implement inquiry with ELLs rest on theoretical appeal and the extrapolation of findings from other populations, rather than on a cumulative empirical base. The present study addresses this gap through a meta-analytic review of research on inquiry instruction and the science achievement of ELLs in elementary school. We focus on the elementary grades for two reasons. First, early schooling is a critical period during which science identities and foundational concepts develop, and when language support is most readily integrated into instruction. Second, the elementary literature offers a sufficiently large set of studies with comparable outcomes for quantitative synthesis. Specifically, we ask three questions: (1) What is the overall effect of inquiry instruction, relative to direct or traditional instruction, on the science achievement of ELLs? (2) Does the effect of inquiry differ for ELLs and non-ELLs when both groups are studied under comparable conditions? (3) Which contextual, instructional, and methodological factors moderate these effects? This review aims to make three contributions. First, it provides the first quantitative estimate of the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for elementary ELLs, converting a scattered set of studies into a cumulative evidence base. Second, by comparing ELLs and non-ELLs, it tests whether inquiry is equally beneficial across language backgrounds or whether it may unintentionally widen existing gaps, a distinction with direct implications for equity-oriented reform. Third, by examining moderators such as language support, intervention characteristics, and study design, it identifies the conditions under which inquiry is most likely to benefit ELLs. In doing so, the review aims to inform teachers, curriculum developers, and policymakers who are implementing inquiry-oriented standards, and to guide researchers toward the questions that remain unresolved. Our literature search followed the reporting guidelines of the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009) and the procedures for research synthesis. We conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including ERIC, PsycINFO, and Web of Science, using a range of keywords related to inquiry-based instruction, science education, and English language learners. We also searched the reference lists of relevant articles and contacted experts in the field to identify additional studies. Our search yielded a total of [X] studies, which were then screened for inclusion based on the following criteria: (1) the study involved ELLs in elementary school, (2) the study compared inquiry-based instruction to traditional or direct instruction, and (3) the study reported quantitative data on science achievement. A total of [X] studies met these criteria and were included in the meta-analysis. We then extracted data from each study, including sample size, grade level, language support, and outcome measures, and coded these data using a standardized protocol. Our analysis used a random-effects model to estimate the overall effect of inquiry instruction on science achievement, as well as to examine the moderators of this effect. We also conducted sensitivity analyses to test the robustness of our findings to different assumptions and methodological choices. The results of our analysis are presented below. Our systematic review was guided by the synthesis framework outlined by Cooper (2010), with the aim of investigating the effectiveness of inquiry-based science instruction for English language learners (ELLs) in kindergarten through Grade 6. To achieve this, we conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including ERIC, PsycINFO, Education Source, Web of Science, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, for reports published between January 2000 and December 2019. This timeframe was chosen to reflect the period following the publication of Inquiry and the National Science Education Standards (National Research Council, 2000), which marked a significant shift towards inquiry-based reform in U.S. classrooms. Our search strategy employed Boolean operators to combine three concept clusters: the population (e.g., "English language learner," "English learner," "limited English proficient," "emergent bilingual," "bilingual," "ESL," "ESOL"), the intervention (e.g., "inquiry," "hands-on," "discovery learning," "problem-based," "project-based," "investigation," "5E"), and the outcome (e.g., "science achievement," "science learning," "science content knowledge," "science performance"). To minimize publication bias, we supplemented our database search with a hand search of key journals (e.g., Journal of Research in Science Teaching, Science Education, TESOL Quarterly), examined reference lists of relevant reviews, and screened conference proceedings and technical reports. Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met six criteria: (a) enrolled students in kindergarten through Grade 6; (b) identified a sample or subsample of ELLs, whether through state classification, home-language surveys, or English proficiency assessments; (c) compared an inquiry-based science intervention with a comparison condition characterized as direct, traditional, or teacher-centered instruction; (d) used an experimental or quasi-experimental design with a comparison group, including pretest–posttest control group designs; (e) reported a quantitative measure of science achievement (e.g., content knowledge tests, standardized science assessments, or performance tasks); and (f) provided data sufficient to compute an effect size. We defined inquiry instruction, following the National Research Council (2000) and Minner et al. (2010), as instruction in which students engage with scientific questions, give priority to evidence, formulate explanations from evidence, connect explanations to scientific knowledge, and communicate and justify their findings. In contrast, studies of activity-based instruction that lacked these features, such as cookbook laboratory exercises with predetermined outcomes, were excluded. Additionally, studies were excluded if ELL results were aggregated with those of other subgroups, if outcomes were limited to attitudes or language proficiency, or if the report was a duplicate of data published elsewhere. After applying these criteria, our final sample comprised 26 articles. The screening and coding procedures involved two reviewers who independently screened titles and abstracts, and then full texts, against the inclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached. Using a structured coding protocol, the same reviewers independently coded each eligible study for a range of characteristics, including publication characteristics (year, publication type), sample characteristics (grade level, ELL sample size, home language, English proficiency level), intervention characteristics (inquiry level, duration in weeks, teacher professional development, and the presence of explicit language supports), design characteristics (random assignment versus quasi-experimental, unit of assignment, and attrition), and outcome characteristics (researcher-developed versus standardized measures, and science domain). Interrater agreement was calculated as Cohen's kappa for categorical codes and as intraclass correlations for continuous codes, with discrepancies resolved through consensus and, where necessary, by consulting the original reports. To evaluate the methodological quality of the included studies, we used criteria adapted from the What Works Clearinghouse standards (WWC, 2020), including baseline equivalence, differential attrition, and the reliability of outcome measures. Studies were coded as high or lower quality, with quality examined as a moderator and used in sensitivity analyses rather than as an exclusion criterion, allowing us to characterize the evidence base broadly. The primary effect size metric used was the standardized mean difference, with Hedges' g computed for each comparison, applying a small-sample correction to Cohen's d (Hedges, 1981; Hedges & Olkin, 1985). Two types of effects were computed: the main effect of inquiry versus direct instruction for ELLs, and the differential effect for studies that reported outcomes for both ELLs and non-ELLs. The statistical analysis accounted for the fact that many studies contributed multiple effect sizes, violating the assumption of independence. The adaptive immune system's ability to recognize pathogens, allergens, tumors, and self-antigens is mediated by the specific interaction of antibodies, B cell receptors, and T cell receptors with discrete molecular features known as epitopes. Understanding which regions of an antigen are recognized by which receptors, in which host species, and in which disease context is crucial for vaccine design, diagnostic development, and the characterization of autoimmune and allergic diseases, as well as for the development of cancer immunotherapies. Over the past three decades, a range of experimental approaches, including peptide-MHC binding assays, T cell functional assays, X-ray crystallography of antibody-antigen complexes, and high-throughput screening of peptide libraries, have generated a vast amount of epitope-level knowledge. However, this knowledge is scattered across a large and heterogeneous literature, making it challenging to access and utilize. The Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) was established in 2003 to address this issue by curating published epitope data into a structured, searchable, and freely accessible resource. Initially, the IEDB focused on epitopes from NIAID category A-C priority pathogens and emerging infectious agents, but its scope has since expanded to include epitope data from all species studied, including humans, non-human primates, rodents, and other model organisms, as well as across infectious, allergic, autoimmune, and transplant-related contexts. The IEDB's curation process involves manually extracting data from the primary literature using a defined ontology-based schema that captures information on epitope structure, antigen and source organism, host, assay type and outcome, immune receptor or MHC restriction, and disease or immunization context. In addition to the curated epitope data, the IEDB hosts a suite of analysis resources that provide prediction and analysis tools for MHC class I and class II binding, proteasomal processing, B cell epitope likelihood, and epitope population coverage. These tools have been extensively benchmarked and used by the community, demonstrating their value in supporting epitope-focused research. Since its inception, the IEDB has undergone significant growth and development, with the number of curated references, distinct epitopes, and assay records increasing steadily. This growth has been driven by the expansion of the literature, systematic curation of entire fields, and the inclusion of data from large-scale studies and research consortia. The nature of the data has also become more complex, with contemporary studies reporting T cell receptor sequences, peptide-MHC complexes characterized by mass spectrometry, epitope-specific responses measured with multimer staining and single-cell approaches, and neoantigens identified through tumor sequencing. As the IEDB continues to evolve, it faces a clear challenge in terms of user accessibility. The database serves a diverse community of immunologists, vaccinologists, computational biologists, clinicians, and regulatory scientists, who require efficient and effective tools to retrieve and analyze the data. Simple keyword-based or single-field queries are no longer sufficient, and users need to combine multiple criteria, such as epitope source, host, assay type, MHC allele, and disease state, to define the relevant subset of data. Furthermore, the increasing reuse of IEDB data in downstream resources and in the benchmarking of prediction algorithms highlights the need for stable, well-documented, and reproducible data access, including bulk downloads and programmatic interfaces. The IEDB's development is also guided by the broader movement toward findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) data principles. To achieve this, the database must be integrated with other resources, such as protein sequences, structures, pathogen taxonomy, and immune receptor repertoires, using consistent community ontologies and identifiers. This requires continued coordination with related resources, including the Immunogenetics/HLA database, the Immune Receptor Repertoire community, and the Immunology Database and Analysis Portal. In this context, the principal gap addressed in this work is the need for query, reporting, and data-organization tools that can scale with the increasing volume and complexity of curated epitope data while remaining accessible to non-expert users. Existing interfaces, designed when the database was smaller and less complex, did not fully support iterative refinement of searches, transparent presentation of result composition, or rapid generation of summaries suitable for publication or downstream computational use. To address this, we have developed an updated version of the IEDB, which includes redesigned search and reporting functionality, extensions to curation and data representation, and improved analytical resources. In this article, we provide an update on the IEDB, summarizing the current status of its data holdings and describing recent developments in curation, user interface design, and analytical resources. Specifically, we report on the current quantity and composition of curated data, including distribution across epitope types, host species, and disease categories. We also describe the redesigned search and reporting functionality, which allows users to build complex, multi-parameter queries and visualize and export summaries of the results. Additionally, we highlight extensions to curation and data representation, including the accommodation of emerging data types and the integration of T cell receptor information and epitopes relevant to allergy, autoimmunity, and cancer. The social and economic factors that shape population health and health inequalities are well-established, with income, housing, employment, education, social connectedness, and the physical environment all playing a significant role (Dahlgren & Whitehead 1991; Marmot 2010). In primary care, where most people first seek help for health concerns, many patients present with problems that are rooted in social, emotional, or practical difficulties rather than clinical disease. General practitioners in the UK, for instance, report that a substantial proportion of their consultations are driven by non-clinical needs, such as loneliness, debt, housing difficulties, or unemployment (Torjesen 2016; Polley et al. 2017). These consultations can be time-consuming and often result in prescribing or onward referral that fails to address the underlying issue. As health systems grapple with the challenges posed by ageing populations and rising numbers of people with long-term conditions, there is a growing interest in approaches that connect patients with sources of support outside the healthcare system (Naylor et al. 2016). One such approach is social prescribing (SP), which enables health professionals in primary care to refer patients with non-clinical needs to local, non-clinical services and activities, typically provided by community, voluntary, and social enterprise organisations (Friedli & Watson 2004; Brandling & House 2009; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). Examples of these services include befriending schemes, arts and exercise programmes, volunteering opportunities, gardening groups, and welfare, debt, and employment advice. In many models, patients are not referred directly to the activity, but rather to a "navigator," "link worker," or "community connector," who assesses their needs, helps them identify goals, and supports them in accessing appropriate community resources (Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015; Polley et al. 2017). SP is not just a referral pathway, but an attempt to build partnerships between the health and social sectors to address the wider determinants of health in a more coordinated way. As a result, policy interest in SP has grown, with national strategy documents in England, Scotland, and Wales promoting its use, and a rapid expansion of link worker roles planned within primary care networks (NHS England 2016). Despite this momentum, the evidence base for SP remains limited, with several systematic and scoping reviews highlighting methodological weaknesses in primary studies, including the absence of control groups, small samples, high attrition, short follow-up, and inconsistent outcome measurement (Bickerdike et al. 2017; Mossabir et al. 2015; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). Some evaluations have reported improvements in psychological well-being, self-reported health, social connectedness, and reductions in healthcare utilisation (Dayson & Bashir 2014; Cawston 2011), but the reliability of these findings is uncertain, and reviews have generally concluded that evidence is insufficient to determine whether SP is effective or cost-effective (Bickerdike et al. 2017). A further challenge is the heterogeneity of SP services, which differ in their aims, target populations, referral routes, the presence and role of a navigator, and the range and quality of community activities available (Husk et al. 2016; Bickerdike et al. 2017). This heterogeneity complicates the interpretation of outcomes and the transfer of lessons across settings. Moreover, whether an SP service achieves its intended effects depends not only on what the intervention is, but also on how it is implemented and delivered. Complex interventions that cut across organisational boundaries are shaped by contextual factors, such as leadership, funding arrangements, workforce stability, inter-organisational relationships, and the readiness of the settings in which they are introduced (Greenhalgh et al. 2004; Damschroder et al. 2009). Partnerships between general practices and small third-sector organisations may be particularly vulnerable to these influences, given the differences in culture, governance, resources, and professional language, as well as the often-precarious funding arrangements of voluntary organisations. Weak implementation can undermine an otherwise promising intervention, and null findings in effectiveness studies may reflect implementation failure rather than inherent ineffectiveness. Conversely, understanding the conditions under which SP services are successfully established and sustained could help explain variation in reported outcomes and inform the design of future services and evaluations. Existing syntheses have paid limited attention to these questions, with most reviews focusing on outcomes and implementation issues treated as secondary findings or described only in relation to individual evaluations (Bickerdike et al. 2017; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). A realist review protocol has set out to explore what works, for whom, and in what circumstances (Husk et al. 2016), but to our knowledge, no systematic review has specifically collated and synthesised evidence on the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services. This review aims to address this gap by identifying and synthesising the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services based in general practice and involving a navigator. We restricted the scope to this model for two reasons: first, the presence of a navigator is a defining feature of many contemporary SP services and represents the model most prominent in current policy; second, restricting the scope to a more clearly specified service model allowed a more coherent synthesis than would have been possible across the full range of loosely related referral schemes. By focusing on implementation and delivery, we aimed to identify the modifiable factors that decision-makers can influence, rather than outcomes that may not be directly actionable without an understanding of the mechanisms and contexts that produce them. This review makes three key contributions. First, it provides the first systematic synthesis of barriers and facilitators to implementing and delivering navigator-based SP services in general practice, drawing on a broad search of published and grey literature. Second, it offers a nuanced understanding of the complex factors that shape the implementation and delivery of SP services, highlighting the importance of contextual factors, such as leadership, funding arrangements, and inter-organisational relationships. Third, it provides guidance for commissioners, service managers, and providers who are currently making decisions about how to establish and scale up SP services, with little consolidated guidance on likely challenges and enabling conditions. By shedding light on the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services, this review aims to inform the development of more effective and sustainable SP services that can improve the health and well-being of patients and communities. This systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the implementation and delivery of Social Prescribing (SP) services, with a focus on identifying the key factors that influence their success. To achieve this, we employed a three-pronged approach. Firstly, we conducted a thorough search of the literature to identify all relevant studies, regardless of their design or methodology. This involved searching multiple electronic databases, as well as scouring the grey literature and consulting with experts in the field. Secondly, we appraised the methodological quality of the included studies using a tool specifically designed for assessing the quality of mixed-methods research. This enabled us to transparently evaluate the strength of the conclusions that can be drawn from the available evidence and highlight any shortcomings in the reporting of SP evaluations. Thirdly, we translated the findings into practical considerations that can inform the planning and delivery of future SP services, while also identifying priorities for further research on the implementation of SP. In terms of design and reporting, our review followed the principles outlined by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD) for undertaking systematic reviews in healthcare, and we reported our findings in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. Our review protocol was developed a priori and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), ensuring that our approach was systematic and transparent. Given the complexity of SP services and the diversity of study designs and outcomes, we opted for a narrative synthesis using thematic analysis rather than statistical pooling. This approach allowed us to integrate the findings from a wide range of studies and identify key themes and patterns that can inform the implementation and delivery of SP services. For the purposes of this review, we defined Social Prescribing (SP) as a service based in or linked to general practice, through which patients with predominantly non-clinical needs are referred to a navigator or link worker. The navigator assesses the patient's needs and connects them to local non-clinical services and activities, typically provided by the third sector. We excluded studies that did not involve a navigator or link worker, such as direct referral by a clinician to a single activity without a navigation or assessment step. Our eligibility criteria were structured around the population, intervention, context, and outcomes of interest. We included studies of any design (qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods) that reported factors, experiences, or perceptions relating to the implementation or delivery of SP services. Relevant participants included commissioners, managers, general practitioners, and other practice staff, navigators, third-sector providers, and patients. We were interested in identifying barriers and facilitators to implementation, as well as the organisational and contextual determinants of SP services. As such, studies were not required to report clinical effectiveness outcomes, and we included peer-reviewed articles and grey literature, provided they contained primary data and a sufficiently described methodology. Our search strategy involved searching eleven electronic databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, using a combination of free-text terms and controlled vocabulary related to social prescribing and primary care. We deliberately did not apply filters for study design to maximise sensitivity and ensure that we captured all relevant studies, regardless of their methodology. In addition to searching electronic databases, we also searched the grey literature using OpenGrey and consulted the websites of relevant organisations, such as the King's Fund and the Health Foundation. We contacted experts in the field and examined the reference lists of all included studies and relevant systematic reviews to identify any additional studies that may have been missed. Once we had identified all relevant studies, we imported the records into reference management software and removed duplicates. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, and full texts of potentially relevant records were obtained and assessed independently by two reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted when consensus could not be reached. We recorded the reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage and assessed inter-rater agreement at the title and abstract screening stage using Cohen's kappa. To extract data from the included studies, we developed a standardised data extraction form, which was piloted on two studies and refined before use. One reviewer extracted data from each included study, and a second reviewer checked the extracted data for accuracy and completeness. We collected information on the author, year, and country of the study, as well as the study aims, design, setting, and funding. We also extracted information on the description of the SP service, participant characteristics, sample size, data collection and analysis methods, and reported barriers and facilitators to implementation and delivery. To appraise the methodological quality of the included studies, we used the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), Version 2011. This tool permits the appraisal of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods designs within a single framework, making it well-suited to our review. Two reviewers independently rated the relevant criteria for each study, and scores were expressed as the percentage of criteria met. For mixed-methods studies, the overall score was taken as the lowest score across the qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods components. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion, and we used the quality assessment to describe the strengths and limitations of the available evidence, rather than as a criterion for exclusion. Overall, our review provides a comprehensive overview of the implementation and delivery of SP services, highlighting the key factors that influence their success and identifying priorities for further research. By synthesising the findings from a wide range of studies, we aim to inform the planning and delivery of future SP services, ultimately improving the health and wellbeing of patients with non-clinical needs. Our approach to data analysis was iterative and reflexive, with the process of exclusion informing our interpretation of the findings and our confidence in each emerging theme.
