The notion that the loss of one sense can be offset by the enhancement of others has a long history, dating back to philosophical and early psychological thought. This idea is deeply ingrained in popular culture, where blind individuals are often perceived as having a more acute sense of smell, touch, or hearing, which enables them to navigate a world primarily designed for the sighted. In the context of olfaction, this notion is reinforced by anecdotal reports from blind individuals themselves, who frequently rely on their sense of smell to recognize people, locate places, and evaluate food and objects (Wakefield, Homewood, & Taylor, 2004). Olfaction is a particularly intriguing case, as it is a chemical sense that has a relatively weak link to the visual system in everyday behavior, yet is closely tied to cognition, emotion, and memory (Herz & Engen, 1996). The theoretical foundation for expecting compensatory adaptations in olfaction lies in the neuroplasticity literature, which has shown that in congenitally and early blind individuals, the occipital cortex is not simply silent, but is instead recruited for a range of non-visual functions, including Braille reading, auditory localization, speech comprehension, and verbal memory (Sadato et al., 1996; Röder et al., 2002; Amedi et al., 2003; Bedny, 2017). Behavioral studies have often reported superior performance in blind individuals on tasks such as pitch discrimination, sound localization, and tactile acuity, although these findings are not uniform and depend on task demands and the age at which vision was lost (Collignon, Voss, Lassonde, & Lepore, 2009; Wan, Wood, Reutens, & Wilson, 2010). Moreover, neuroimaging studies have suggested that olfactory stimulation may engage regions beyond the classical olfactory network in blind individuals, such as the occipital areas, which are typically associated with visual processing (Kupers et al., 2011; Araneda et al., 2016). These results indicate that cross-modal reorganization could, in principle, have consequences for olfactory perception. However, the behavioral evidence for enhanced olfactory abilities in blind individuals is far less consistent. Olfactory function is a complex and multifaceted construct, comprising several partly separable components, including lower-level, sensory-driven abilities such as detection threshold and odor discrimination, as well as higher-order abilities that involve cognitive and linguistic processes, such as cued and free odor identification (Hummel, Sekinger, Wolf, Pauli, & Kobal, 1997). Performance on these tasks depends on a range of factors, including semantic memory, verbal ability, and attention, in addition to sensory sensitivity (Cain, 1979; Larsson, 1997). It is possible that blindness could selectively affect some of these components, for example, by improving higher-order processing through increased attention to olfactory cues, without altering peripheral sensitivity. Empirical findings, however, do not clearly support either a general or a selective enhancement of olfactory abilities in blind individuals. Several studies have reported lower olfactory thresholds in blind compared to sighted participants (Cuevas, Plaza, Rombaux, De Volder, & Renier, 2009; Beaulieu-Lefebvre, Schneider, Kupers, & Ptito, 2011), while others have found no difference (Smith, Doty, Burlingame, & McKeown, 1993; Rosenbluth, Grossman, & Kaitz, 2000) or even poorer performance in blind individuals (Wakefield et al., 2004). Similarly, studies of odor discrimination have yielded mixed results, with some reporting an advantage for blind participants (Cuevas et al., 2009) and others reporting equivalent performance (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska, Sorokowski, & Karwowski, 2013). The picture for odor identification is also mixed, with some investigations showing superior free or cued identification in blind participants (Murphy & Cain, 1986; Rosenbluth et al., 2000; Cuevas et al., 2009), while others have found no group differences (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska et al., 2013). The heterogeneity in methods used across studies may partly explain these discrepancies. Studies differ in the psychophysical procedure used, the odorants tested, the criteria for sample selection, and the way blindness is characterized. Moreover, many studies have small samples, which limits statistical power and increases the probability that observed effects, whether positive or null, are unreliable (Button et al., 2013). Participant characteristics, such as age and sex, are also a source of uncertainty, as olfactory function declines with age and differs between women and men, with women often outperforming men on several olfactory measures (Doty & Cameron, 2009; Sorokowska et al., 2017). If the age or sex composition of blind and sighted samples differs, or if these factors moderate the effects of sensory deprivation, estimates of group differences could be distorted. Most importantly, the timing of vision loss may be critical, as plasticity is thought to be greatest during sensitive periods of development, so early or congenitally blind individuals might show larger compensatory effects than those who lose their sight later in life (Voss, Lepore, Gougoux, & Zatorre, 2010; Collignon et al., 2009). Yet, studies of olfaction have often combined early and late blind participants, or have not reported onset in sufficient detail, making it difficult to determine whether the timing of blindness matters. Narrative reviews have summarized parts of this literature (Sorokowska, 2016; Kupers & Ptito, 2014), and they generally conclude that evidence of superior olfaction in blindness is equivocal. However, narrative approaches are vulnerable to selective citation and cannot quantify the magnitude or consistency of effects, nor assess whether the published record is distorted by selective reporting. Publication bias is a particular concern in this field, as an intriguing and intuitively appealing finding of superior performance in blind people may be more likely to be published than a null result, which would inflate the apparent evidence for compensation (Rothstein, Sutton, & Borenstein, 2005). Meta-analytic methods, on the other hand, allow the combination of effect sizes across studies, the examination of heterogeneity, the testing of moderators, and the application of procedures that detect and adjust for small-study effects (Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009; Duval & Tweedie, 2000). To our knowledge, no previous study has quantitatively synthesized the evidence on olfactory abilities in blind individuals across the full range of olfactory functions. The present work therefore provides a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing blind and sighted individuals on four outcomes: odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification. By using meta-analytic methods, we aim to provide a more comprehensive and quantitative understanding of the relationship between blindness and olfactory abilities, and to shed light on the mechanisms underlying any potential compensatory effects. Our investigation into the relationship between blindness and olfactory performance was motivated by a fundamental question: does blindness confer an advantage in olfactory abilities, and if so, does this advantage vary between sensory-driven tasks, such as threshold and discrimination, and higher-order tasks, such as identification? To address this question, we conducted a comprehensive meta-analysis, taking care to assess and correct for publication bias, which can significantly influence estimates of effect sizes. Additionally, we performed exploratory moderator analyses to examine whether factors such as participants' age, the proportion of women in the samples, and the onset of blindness (early vs. late) contribute to variability in effect sizes across studies. This research contributes to the field in three key ways. Firstly, it provides the first comprehensive quantitative estimate of olfactory performance in individuals with blindness, replacing anecdotal summaries with precise effect sizes and confidence intervals. Secondly, it examines whether the published literature supports the notion of compensatory plasticity in olfaction, once publication bias is taken into account. Thirdly, it identifies methodological gaps, such as small sample sizes and inconsistent reporting, that can inform the design of future research on sensory compensation. Our review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009) and followed recommendations for meta-analysis in the behavioral sciences (Borenstein et al., 2009; Cooper et al., 2009). The inclusion criteria, outcomes, and analytic strategy for the primary analyses were predefined prior to data extraction. The analyses of moderators were exploratory in nature. To identify relevant articles, we conducted a comprehensive computerized search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and PsycINFO, supplemented by Google Scholar. The search terms combined keywords related to blindness (e.g., blind, visual impairment, visual deprivation) with terms related to olfaction (e.g., olfact, smell, odor, odour, chemosens). We imposed no restrictions on publication year and covered records from database inception until the date of the final search. We also screened the reference lists of all eligible articles and relevant narrative reviews, and searched for conference abstracts and unpublished dissertations to minimize the risk of missing unpublished data. When essential statistics were missing, we contacted corresponding authors via email. Studies were included in our analysis if they met the following criteria: (a) compared a group of blind participants with a group of sighted controls, (b) assessed at least one of four olfactory outcomes (odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, or free odor identification), (c) used human participants, and (d) reported data sufficient to calculate an effect size. Blindness was defined as congenital or acquired total blindness or severe visual impairment, as described by the original authors. Studies were excluded if they lacked a sighted control group, if participants had additional conditions known to affect olfaction (e.g., neurodegenerative disease, Kallmann syndrome, head trauma, or chronic rhinosinusitis), or if the data were reported only for subjective ratings of odor properties or for olfactory-related tasks that did not map onto the four outcomes. We defined the four olfactory outcomes as follows: odor threshold tasks estimated the lowest concentration at which an odorant could be detected, typically using a staircase or forced-choice procedure (e.g., Sniffin' Sticks). Discrimination tasks required participants to identify the odd item among three odorants presented in a triangle test. Cued identification required selection of the correct label from a list of alternatives, whereas free identification required participants to name the odor without any response options. Because threshold is generally considered a sensory-driven function and identification a higher-order function dependent on semantic and mnemonic processes (Hummel et al., 1997), we analyzed the four outcomes separately. When studies reported more than one measure within an outcome (e.g., several odorants or subtests), we averaged them to obtain one effect size per study and comparison. When separate early-blind and late-blind groups were compared with the same sighted group, we handled the shared control group as described below. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers, who screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third author. Data were extracted using a standardized form, which recorded authors and year, country, sample size per group, mean age, proportion of women, onset of blindness (early/congenital vs. late), olfactory test used, and the statistics necessary to compute effect sizes. Inter-coder agreement was high (Cohen's κ >.90 for categorical variables), and discrepancies were resolved through consensus. We classified studies as early blind when blindness was congenital or began in early childhood (typically before the age of 5 years, or as defined by the authors), and as late blind otherwise. The effect size was computed as the standardized mean difference, Hedges' g, with positive values indicating better performance in blind than in sighted participants. For threshold tasks, in which lower scores reflect higher sensitivity (in studies reporting concentration), the sign was reversed accordingly. The systematic recording of patents provides a unique window into technological activity, offering a detailed account of inventions, property rights, and the lineage of knowledge that underlies new innovations. As Jaffe and Trajtenberg (2002) have noted, patents disclose not only the technical details of an invention but also the broader context in which it was developed. This information is invaluable to corporate managers, investors, and policymakers, who rely on patent data to inform decisions about research and development allocation, mergers and acquisitions, licensing, and technology forecasting. However, the sheer volume of patent filings - now exceeding several million per year worldwide, according to the World Intellectual Property Organization (2022) - has rendered manual inspection impractical, prompting the development of automated methods for evaluating patent importance. One of the most established indicators of patent importance is derived from citation counts, which have been shown to correlate with both the private and social value of an invention (Hall, Jaffe, & Trajtenberg, 2005; Harhoff, Narin, Scherer, & Vopel, 1999). By analyzing the structure of the citation graph, researchers have developed more sophisticated measures of patent importance, such as PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998) and related eigenvector-type centralities, which assign higher scores to patents cited by other highly ranked patents. These approaches have been used to identify key patents and pivotal technologies (Lukach, Lukach, & Kuperman, 2007; Yan & Ding, 2010), and have been further refined through the use of main path analysis (Hummon & Doreian, 1989; Verspagen, 2007) and measures of disruptiveness (Funk & Owen-Smith, 2017; Wu, Wang, & Evans, 2019). Despite their utility, however, these approaches share a significant limitation: they are fundamentally static, providing a snapshot of a patent's influence at a given point in time, but offering little insight into the dynamic evolution of the technological domain in which it resides. A patent may receive a high PageRank score because it was central to a field that has since been superseded, while a patent with a modest score may sit at the origin of a rapidly emerging cluster. The problem is compounded by the fact that citations accrue with a time lag and are strongly influenced by the life cycle of the technology (Abernathy & Utterback, 1978; Adamson & others, 2012), making it difficult to distinguish between historical importance and prospective value. For investors and managers, who must make decisions about where to commit resources, the latter is typically the more relevant quantity. What is needed, therefore, is a framework that can partition the citation network into coherent technology clusters and forecast the future citation activity of each cluster, thereby characterizing its scale and life-cycle stage. The first requirement - community detection - has been addressed through a range of approaches, including modularity maximization (Newman, 2006; Blondel, Guillaume, Lambiotte, & Lefebvre, 2008), the Infomap algorithm (Rosvall & Bergstrom, 2008), and text-based topic modeling. However, modularity-based approaches suffer from a resolution limit (Fortunato & Barthélemy, 2007), lack an explicit generative model, and offer no principled way to select the number of clusters or compare competing partitions. The stochastic block model (SBM) addresses these concerns by representing the network as a probabilistic mixture of groups with block-specific connection probabilities (Holland, Laskey, & Leinhardt, 1983; Karrer & Newman, 2011). In its Bayesian, nonparametric formulation, model selection can be performed through minimum description length, which avoids overfitting and infers the number of groups from the data (Peixoto, 2014). The hierarchical or nested SBM further organizes groups into a multilevel structure (Peixoto, 2014, 2017), which is attractive for patents because technologies are naturally organized hierarchically, from broad sectors to narrow subfields, as reflected in classification systems such as the International Patent Classification. While SBMs have been applied extensively to social, biological, and information networks, their use for patent citation networks, and in particular the comparison of flat, degree-corrected, and nested variants on such data, remains limited. The second requirement - prediction - has attracted growing attention, with models ranging from preferential-attachment and aging mechanisms (Wang, Song, & Barabási, 2013) to machine-learning predictors of future impact (Abrahams, Fan, Wang, Zhang, & Jiang, 2019; Yan, Tang, Liu, Shan, & Li, 2011). Most of this work targets individual documents, for which citation trajectories are sparse, heavy-tailed, and noisy. Aggregating at the level of technology clusters yields smoother and more interpretable time series that reflect the collective evolution of a field. Recurrent neural networks, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks in particular (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), are well suited to learning nonlinear temporal dependencies and have shown strong performance in sequence forecasting in economics, energy, and bibliometrics (Fischer & Krauss, 2018). Yet, to our knowledge, no study has coupled generative network clustering with deep sequence models to forecast the growth potential of patent clusters, and the extent to which such forecasts are accurate in magnitude and direction has not been established. Against this background, this study addresses two key research questions. First, which variant of the SBM provides the most appropriate description of patent citation networks, as judged by description length and the interpretability of the inferred partitions? Second, can the growth potential of the resulting technology clusters, defined as the future number of citations received, be predicted by an LSTM network with accuracy sufficient to support managerial and investment decisions? We evaluate prediction quality using both the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), which measures errors in magnitude, and directional accuracy, which measures whether an increase or decrease in citation activity is correctly anticipated and is arguably more relevant for strategic decisions than point accuracy. This paper makes three contributions. First, it proposes an integrated framework that moves patent evaluation from static scoring to dynamic, cluster-level assessment by combining Bayesian community detection with deep sequence learning. Second, it provides empirical evidence that the nested SBM is the most suitable model for clustering patent citation networks, as it captures the multilevel organization of technologies and permits analysis at several scales. Third, it demonstrates that LSTM-based forecasts of cluster growth, although yielding high MAPE values that reflect the volatility of citation counts, attain a directional accuracy that is sufficient to support informed decision-making. The ability to anticipate the expansion or contraction of technology clusters is a crucial aspect of strategic decision-making for corporate managers and investors. Our research demonstrates a modest but practically relevant predictive accuracy, exceeding 50%, which offers a quantitative means of evaluating the scale and life cycle of technologies. By constructing a patent citation network from the PatentsView database, which provides disambiguated bibliographic records and citation links for utility patents granted from 1976 onwards, we were able to identify avenues for improving the forecasting of technological change. The patent citation network was constructed by retaining patents granted between 1976 and 2019 for a single technology domain, selected through Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) subclass codes. Each patent was represented as a node, and a directed edge was drawn from a citing patent to each earlier patent it cited, with citations to patents outside the sampled set discarded. To analyze the network, we employed the stochastic block model (SBM), a generative model that assumes a single connected structure. However, since the SBM assumes a single connected structure, we restricted our analysis to the largest weakly connected component of the network. We removed self-loops and duplicate edges, and treated citations as unweighted, as multiple citations between the same pair of patents do not occur in the source data. Furthermore, we pooled examiner-added and applicant-added citations, although we acknowledge that these represent different citing behaviors. Community detection was performed using the SBM, which depends on the groups to which nodes belong. We considered three variants of the SBM: the flat, non-degree-corrected SBM, the degree-corrected SBM (DC-SBM), and the nested (hierarchical) SBM. The DC-SBM adds node-specific propensity parameters to accommodate the heavy-tailed degree distributions typical of citation data, while the nested SBM treats the groups of one level as nodes of a coarser block model at the next level, giving a multiscale partition. We used the microcanonical formulation of each model with noninformative priors, which supports inference without fixing the number of groups in advance. Inference was performed using posterior maximization with the agglomerative multilevel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm implemented in the graph-tool library. For each model, we ran 20 independent initializations and retained the partition with the smallest description length. We then ran an equilibration phase of 1,000 sweeps to refine it. Model selection was based on the minimum description length (MDL) principle, which penalizes overly complex partitions and thus protects against overfitting without requiring a separate hold-out set. We compared the description lengths of the three variants directly and also computed the description length of a configuration-model baseline with a single group, allowing us to quantify compression. For the nested SBM, we examined the hierarchy and selected the level of analysis whose clusters were large enough to yield stable annual time series. We required a median cluster size of at least 100 patents and at least 30 clusters. The stability of the partition was assessed by the normalized mutual information (NMI) between partitions from independent runs, and the final partition was the minimum-description-length solution. In addition to the SBM, we also computed PageRank scores for every patent, with edges oriented so that score accrues to cited patents. Cluster-level mean PageRank was compared with the growth trajectories to illustrate the limitations of static ranking. The prediction target was the growth potential of each cluster, defined as the number of forward citations received in year t by patents assigned to that cluster and granted up to t − 1. We aggregated this quantity annually from 1985 to 2019, yielding 35 observations per cluster. To remove scale differences between clusters while preserving within-cluster dynamics, each series was transformed by log(1 + x) and then standardized by min–max scaling, with scaling parameters estimated on the training period only. Forecasting was performed using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, a recurrent architecture whose gated memory cells mitigate vanishing gradients and capture long-range temporal dependencies. The model received a sliding window of the preceding five annual values and predicted the value one year ahead. The window length was chosen from {3, 5, 7} by validation error. The network comprised a single LSTM layer of 32 hidden units, a dropout layer (rate 0.2), and a fully connected output layer with one unit. Parameters were estimated by minimizing mean squared error with the Adam optimizer, a batch size of 16, and a maximum of 300 epochs. Training stopped early if validation loss did not improve for 20 consecutive epochs. A single model was trained across all clusters, with cluster series pooled as training samples, since individual series were too short to estimate a recurrent network reliably. The data were split chronologically: 1985–2010 for training, 2011–2014 for validation and hyperparameter selection, and 2015–2019 for testing. Random shuffling across time was never applied. Forecasts were generated by one-step-ahead prediction with the true history supplied at each test origin, equivalent to a rolling-origin evaluation. To account for stochastic weight initialization, we repeated the whole procedure with 10 random seeds and report averages. Forecast accuracy was evaluated on the original citation-count scale after inverting the transformations. We used three metrics: mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), root mean squared error (RMSE), and directional accuracy (DA). Because MAPE is unstable when actual values are near zero, clusters with fewer than 10 observations were excluded from the analysis. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in predicting the growth potential of technology clusters. The use of the SBM and LSTM network allows for the identification of complex patterns and relationships in the data, which can inform strategic decision-making for corporate managers and investors. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be applied to other domains, such as predicting the growth potential of industries or companies, and can be used to identify areas of potential innovation and growth. Overall, our research contributes to the development of a quantitative framework for evaluating the scale and life cycle of technologies, and provides a valuable tool for predicting

The proliferation of online reviews has transformed the way consumers, merchants, and platform operators interact, driving a surge of research in sentiment analysis, recommendation systems, and text generation. While most studies have focused on full-length reviews, many platforms also allow users to leave brief, informal remarks known as tips, which capture the essence of a visit or purchase in a concise and readily digestible format. Tips, typically consisting of a single sentence with fewer than ten words, are often the first piece of user-generated content that prospective customers encounter. Despite their practical value, tips have received relatively little attention compared to reviews, and the task of generating them automatically remains largely underexplored. However, generating tips is a worthwhile endeavor for two primary reasons. Firstly, it can reduce the effort required for users to contribute content, as a system that proposes a draft tip tailored to a user and an item can encourage participation, thereby improving the coverage of items with few reviews. Secondly, a tip generator can provide concise explanations for recommendations, which can enhance user trust and decision-making efficiency. To achieve this, the generated text must read as if it were written by the particular user about the particular item, rather than being a generic sentence that, although fluent and sentiment-consistent, lacks informativeness and personal touch. Prior work on review-related generation has emphasized the importance of personalization, with attribute-to-sequence models conditioning a recurrent decoder on user, item, and rating identifiers to produce reviews. Explainable recommendation methods have also been developed to generate justifications from aspects or features. Furthermore, studies on review summarization and tip generation have utilized multi-task learning to share representations between rating prediction and text generation. These methods typically treat users and items as learned lookup embeddings trained end-to-end with the generation loss. However, this design has several limitations. For instance, a deterministic embedding trained for next-word prediction tends to capture the most frequent patterns, neglecting the distinctive language habits that define an individual. Moreover, the same embedding must encode both the user's sentiment preference and writing style, which are only loosely related. Additionally, rare words specific to a user or an item, such as dish names or local idioms, are rarely reproduced due to the low probability assigned to them by the softmax function. We argue that these limitations can be addressed by explicitly modeling persona, which we define as the latent characteristics reflected in the historical text associated with an entity. For a user, persona captures their intrinsic language style, including preferred vocabulary, level of formality, verbosity, and favored aspects. For an item, persona captures its distinguishing characteristics, such as cuisine, atmosphere, and typical complaints. Persona is more stable than the content of any single review and differs from sentiment, as two users may share a rating of an item yet describe it in distinct ways. Therefore, persona-aware generation requires representations that summarize the full history of tips and reviews for each user and item, remaining useful even when the history is noisy and sparse. To obtain such representations, we propose a framework built on adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE). A variational auto-encoder learns a probabilistic latent space in which similar inputs map to nearby regions, and the stochasticity regularizes the representation, reducing overfitting for entities with limited data. However, a known weakness of VAEs is that the aggregate posterior can diverge from the prior, resulting in poor samples and weakly informative codes. To address this, we incorporate a discriminator that pushes the aggregate posterior toward the prior, improving the regularity of the latent space. We train separate aVAE encoders on the historical documents of users and items, treating the latent variables as persona embeddings. While latent embeddings are compact, they lose lexical detail. To mitigate this, we introduce a persona memory that stores words associated with each user and item, drawn from their histories. During decoding, a Pointer Network learns when to copy a word from the memory and when to generate one from the vocabulary, allowing the model to produce entity-specific terms without requiring high softmax probability. This complements the continuous persona embedding with direct access to the surface forms that characterize each entity. Furthermore, persona needs to interact with sentiment, as the persona embeddings of a user and an item serve as latent factors in a rating prediction component, estimating the user's sentiment toward the item. The predicted sentiment, together with the persona embeddings, conditions a recurrent neural network decoder that generates the tip. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we formulate persona-aware tips generation as a new task, requiring generated tips to reflect both the language style of the user and the characteristics of the item, in addition to being fluent and sentiment-consistent. Secondly, we introduce an aVAE-based persona modeling approach that learns latent user and item embeddings from historical tips and reviews, demonstrating that adversarial regularization of the latent space yields more informative persona representations than a standard VAE or deterministic embeddings. Thirdly, we design a persona memory with a Pointer Network that retrieves user- and item-specific words during generation, integrating it with a rating prediction component and an RNN-based decoder to produce high-quality, persona-aware tips. By addressing the limitations of existing methods and incorporating persona into the generation process, our approach has the potential to create more informative, personalized, and engaging tips that enhance the user experience and improve the effectiveness of online review platforms. Our approach integrates a decoder into a single framework, which is trained jointly with the other components. To evaluate the effectiveness of this framework, we conducted extensive experiments on real-world datasets, assessing its performance using automatic metrics for overlap and diversity, rating prediction error, and human judgments. We also analyzed each component through ablation studies and case studies to gain a deeper understanding of their contributions. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. First, we review related work on review and tip generation, personalized text generation, and latent-variable models, highlighting the key challenges and opportunities in these areas. We then describe our proposed framework in detail, including its components and training procedure. Next, we present the experimental setup and results, discussing the datasets, preprocessing, and evaluation metrics used. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the limitations of our approach and directions for future work. We evaluated our framework on two public review corpora: the Yelp Dataset Challenge data, which includes reviews of restaurants and services, and the Amazon Product Data for the Books category. Each instance in these datasets is a tuple of user, item, star rating (1-5), review text, and tip text. Following prior work on tips and review summarization, we removed instances with empty tips, tips shorter than three or longer than 30 tokens, and reviews longer than 300 tokens. To obtain reliable persona signals, we kept only users and items with at least five interactions. After filtering, the Yelp subset contained 213,402 instances, representing 14,871 users and 11,206 items, while the Books subset contained 287,915 instances, representing 18,342 users and 15,630 items. The mean tip length was 11.4 tokens on Yelp and 13.1 on Books. To preprocess the text data, we lowercased and tokenized the text using the NLTK tokenizer. We then constructed a vocabulary comprising the 20,000 most frequent tokens in each corpus, mapping other tokens to an unknown symbol. Each dataset was split chronologically per user into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, ensuring that a user's earliest interactions were used for training and persona construction. Persona information for a user or item was built exclusively from training-set reviews and tips, preventing leakage of test-time text into the persona representations. Users and items without training history were excluded from the test sets. Our framework consists of four components: (i) a persona modeling component based on adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE), (ii) a persona memory with a pointer-based retrieval mechanism, (iii) a rating prediction component, and (iv) a recurrent tips generator. All components were trained jointly to optimize the overall performance of the framework. The persona modeling component uses aVAE to learn compact and informative persona embeddings for users and items. For each user u and item i, we concatenated the historical reviews and tips (up to 500 tokens, most recent first) into a document d. We then embedded the words using 300-dimensional GloVe vectors, which were fine-tuned during training. A bidirectional GRU encoder mapped d to the parameters of a diagonal Gaussian posterior q(z|d), and a latent persona vector z of dimension 64 was sampled using the reparameterization trick. A GRU decoder reconstructed the document from z. To mitigate the issue of posterior collapse in text models, we replaced the Kullback-Leibler (KL) term of a standard VAE with an adversarial regularizer, following the approach of adversarial auto-encoders. A discriminator, implemented as a two-layer perceptron with 128 hidden units, was trained to distinguish samples from the prior N(0, I) from encoded posterior samples, while the encoder was trained to fool it. The resulting aVAE objective was the sum of the reconstruction loss and the adversarial loss. Separate encoders were used for users and items, yielding user persona embeddings zᵤ and item persona embeddings zᵢ. To preserve lexical features that a compact latent code may lose, we constructed a persona memory for every user and item. For each entity, we ranked the words in its history by TF-IDF weight, removed stop words, and stored the 50 highest-scoring words as memory slots. Each slot held the word's embedding. At each decoding step t, the decoder state attended over the concatenated user and item memories, using the attention distribution as a pointer distribution over memory words. The final output distribution was a mixture of the vocabulary softmax and the pointer distribution, weighted by a learned gate pgen. This design allows the model to copy persona-specific wording, such as characteristic expressions of a user or distinctive attributes of an item. The rating prediction component uses the persona embeddings as latent factors in a rating predictor, following the approach of latent factor models. The predicted rating was r̂ = MLP([zᵤ; zᵢ; zᵤ⊙zᵢ]) + bᵤ + bᵢ + μ, where μ is the global mean and bᵤ and bᵢ are learned biases. The hidden layer of the MLP is 64-dimensional with ReLU activation. The penultimate layer of this predictor yields a sentiment vector s that summarizes the expected polarity of the user toward the item. The rating loss was the mean squared error against the observed rating. The tips generator was a single-layer GRU with 512 hidden units. Its initial state was a linear projection of [zᵤ; zᵢ; s]. At each step, the input was the concatenation of the previous word embedding and the same persona-sentiment vector, which helps keep the generated text consistent with the persona and the predicted sentiment. Generation was trained with teacher forcing and token-level cross-entropy over the mixed vocabulary and pointer distribution. The total loss was L = Lgen + λ₁Lrating + λ₂LaVAE, where λ₁ = 0.5 and λ₂ = 0.1 were set based on validation performance. At inference time, we used beam search with width 4 and a length penalty, and forbade repeated trigrams. We implemented our models in PyTorch and optimized them using Adam at a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁴, a batch size of 128, and gradient clipping at 5.0. Dropout of 0.3 was applied to embeddings and recurrent outputs. The discriminator was updated once per generator update. To mitigate instability, we annealed the weight of the adversarial term linearly over the first 10,000 iterations. We trained our models on a single NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU with 16 GB of memory. The training process took approximately 3-4 days to complete, depending on the specific dataset and model configuration. Our experiments were designed to investigate the effectiveness of the proposed persona-aware tips generation framework, which we refer to as PATG. To train our model, we employed a strategy that involved running the training process for a maximum of 30 epochs, with early stopping triggered by the validation perplexity, using a patience of 3 epochs. The past fifteen years have seen a significant shift in the landscape of data-processing systems, with the emergence of a family of systems built around the map-shuffle-reduce paradigm. This paradigm, first introduced by Dean and Ghemawat in 2004, allows for a wide range of computations to be expressed as a pair of user-supplied functions, with the runtime responsible for managing tasks such as partitioning, scheduling, fault tolerance, and data movement. The subsequent development of open-source implementations, most notably Hadoop, has made this abstraction accessible to organizations that lack the resources to build such infrastructure themselves. Later systems, such as Spark, have built upon this foundation, relaxing the rigid two-stage structure and introducing features like in-memory caching. Despite these advancements, the core premise of these systems remains unchanged: data are gathered into large, bounded collections, partitioned across a cluster, and processed in coarse passes. The success of this paradigm can be attributed to several factors. For one, it provides a scalable and fault-tolerant framework for processing large datasets, making it an attractive solution for organizations dealing with massive amounts of data. Additionally, the simplicity of the programming interface and the ability to hide distributed-systems complexity behind a small API have contributed to its widespread adoption. However, the popularity of the map-reduce paradigm has also been driven by less technical factors, such as the value associated with the term "Big Data" and the desire to be seen as organizationally modern. As a result, the paradigm has often been adopted without a thorough analysis of the actual requirements of the problem at hand. Surveys of production workloads have revealed that, in many cases, the problems being solved are significantly smaller than the infrastructure applied to them. For instance, Appuswamy et al. observed that the median job size in several large analytics deployments fits comfortably in the memory of a single server, while McSherry et al. demonstrated that a carefully written single-threaded program can outperform a cluster of machines on common graph benchmarks. These findings do not diminish the capabilities of map-reduce systems on truly massive and unstructured datasets, but rather highlight the need for a more nuanced approach to problem-solving. The default choice of a batch-oriented cluster framework deserves scrutiny, particularly for a category of problems that we refer to as time-dependent and boundable. Time-dependent and boundable problems are characterized by the need to process data arriving continuously, with the relevance of any datum decaying or limited to a window, and the result of a computation can be bounded, approximated, or cached without loss of practical value. Examples of such problems include monitoring and alerting, fraud scoring, recommendation freshness, sensor aggregation, and operational dashboards. For these problems, the batch model introduces structural inefficiencies, such as the need to accumulate data before processing, which leads to latency that is bounded below by the batch interval. The shuffle phase also moves intermediate data across the network, even when the result of earlier computations could be reused, and each run recomputes over a mostly unchanged history, due to the lack of a natural notion of persistent, incrementally updated state. Practitioners have responded to these limitations with workarounds, such as shorter batch intervals, micro-batching, and the lambda architecture, which maintains parallel batch and speed layers. While these approaches reduce latency, they come at the cost of duplicated logic, operational complexity, and consistency problems between layers. A parallel line of work has approached the problem from the stream-processing side, with early data stream management systems and later systems like Storm, Flink, and MillWheel treating data as unbounded sequences and supporting windowing, event-time semantics, and managed state. The dataflow model of Akidau et al. unified batch and streaming under one formalism, but these contributions tend to retain much of the architecture of the systems they replace, including a cluster runtime, a partitioned and often shuffled keyed state, and checkpointing machinery designed for very large state. For workloads in which state is small or can be bounded, this machinery may be disproportionate. Moreover, the programming abstractions typically remain tied to operators over distributed collections rather than to simple, composable functions over flows. The gap we address lies between these two bodies of work. Batch frameworks are simple but ill-suited to time-dependent problems, while general streaming engines are expressive but heavy, and neither exploits systematically the fact that many practical computations are bounded and cacheable. What is lacking is a processing model that treats statelessness as the default, confines state to explicit, bounded, and cacheable locations, and expresses computation as flows of data through functions, thereby avoiding the global redistribution step that defines the shuffle. Such a model would also have to retain the properties that made map-reduce attractive: a small programming interface, predictable scaling, and straightforward recovery from failure. This paper asks the following research question: can a partly stateless, flow-oriented function and data model replace the map-shuffle-reduce model for time-dependent, boundable problems, delivering lower latency and lower resource consumption without sacrificing scalability or ease of programming? We break this into three subquestions. First, under what formal conditions on time dependence and boundedness does a computation admit a flow-oriented decomposition that needs no shuffle? Second, how should state and caching be represented so that functions remain composable and recoverable? Third, how does the resulting model compare empirically with batch and streaming baselines? Our contributions are fourfold. First, we characterize the class of time-dependent, boundable problems and argue, with reference to published workload analyses, that it covers a substantial share of practical analytics tasks currently handled by batch systems. Second, we present a flow-oriented model in which computations are partly stateless functions composed along data flows, with explicitly scoped caches that replace the shuffle and the recomputation of history. Third, we show how this model supports incremental updates and failure recovery by means of replayable inputs and bounded state. Fourth, we evaluate an implementation against map-reduce and streaming baselines on representative workloads, reporting latency, throughput, and resource cost. We also discuss the limits of the approach, including the problem classes for which map-reduce remains the more appropriate choice. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in more detail, Section 3 presents the model, Section 4 describes the implementation and evaluation, and Section 5 discusses implications and concludes. Our approach, referred to as Fast Data Flow (FDF), is designed to address the limitations of existing batch and streaming systems for time-dependent, boundable problems. By treating statelessness as the default and confining state to explicit, bounded, and cacheable locations, FDF aims to provide a more efficient and scalable solution for these types of problems. The design of our system is grounded in three fundamental premises. Firstly, many time-dependent workloads exhibit solutions that are either bounded, meaning the relevant state at time t is dependent on a finite window of recent events, or cacheable, where previously computed results can be reused when inputs recur, as noted by Akidau et al. (2015). This characteristic is particularly significant, as it allows for the optimization of computational resources. Secondly, traditional batch-oriented map-shuffle-reduce approaches, such as those described by Dean and Ghemawat (2008), incur fixed costs associated with materializing intermediate data and redistributing keys across the network. However, these costs can be mitigated when state can be maintained locally and partial results combined incrementally. This is a crucial consideration, as it has a direct impact on the efficiency and scalability of the system. Thirdly, functions that are stateless with respect to the global dataset, yet retain small, bounded local state, can be executed in a pipelined manner and scaled horizontally with relative ease, as demonstrated by Carbone et al. (2015). Our study was structured as a controlled comparison of architectures on identical workloads, hardware, and input streams. The Model Specification FDF represents a computation as a directed acyclic graph of operators, where each operator is a function f: (e, s) → (E', s'), with e denoting an input event, s representing a bounded local state, E' signifying a set of output events, and s' denoting the updated state. The state is limited to one of three forms: a sliding or tumbling time window of fixed duration W, a fixed-capacity least-recently-used cache of size C keyed by a deterministic function of the event, or a constant-size accumulator for associative and commutative aggregates. Operators are partitioned by a stable hash of the event key, and events are routed directly to the owning partition, thereby eliminating the global shuffle barrier. Partial results from partitions are merged using commutative monoid operations, as described by Boykin et al. (2014), allowing late or out-of-order events within an allowed lateness bound L to be incorporated without recomputation. Events beyond L are diverted to a side output for optional offline reconciliation. Backpressure is propagated through bounded queues between operators, and fault tolerance is provided by periodic asynchronous snapshots of local state using a barrier-based algorithm, as outlined by Chandy and Lamport (1985) and further developed by Carbone et al. (2017). For the purposes of our study, we utilized two baseline systems: an Apache Hadoop MapReduce implementation and an Apache Spark batch implementation, as described by Zaharia et al. (2012), of each workload, with micro-batch intervals of 1, 5, and 30 seconds for the Spark Streaming variant. A Flink-based implementation of FDF operators served as the runtime for the proposed model, ensuring that differences reflect model semantics rather than language runtimes. All implementations were written in Java 11 and used the same serialization format (Apache Avro) and identical business logic classes wherever possible. We selected three workloads to represent time-dependent problems with bounded or cacheable solutions. The first workload, W1, involved a sliding-window aggregation (per-key mean, 95th percentile via a t-digest sketch, as described by Dunning and Ertl (2019), and count) over sensor telemetry. The second workload, W2, was a session and recurrence-detection task, where repeated inputs allow cache hits, modeled on clickstream enrichment. The third workload, W3, was a streaming join between an event stream and a slowly changing reference table. To test the limits of applicability, we added a fourth workload, W4, a global computation (full-corpus inverted index construction) for which bounded state is not sufficient, expected to favor map-reduce. The input data combined a public dataset and synthetic streams. Real data comprised the NYC Taxi trip records for 2019 (approximately 84 million events) and a public web clickstream sample. Synthetic generators produced events with key cardinalities of 10^3, 10^5, and 10^7, with Zipfian key skew (exponent s = 0.8 and 1.2) to emulate realistic hot keys, as described by Breslau et al. (1999). Arrival rates ranged from 10,000 to 1,000,000 events per second. For W2, the repetition rate (the proportion of events whose result had been computed within the cache horizon) was varied from 0% to 90% in increments of 10%. Out-of-order arrival was injected by delaying a random 5% of events by up to 60 seconds. Experiments were conducted on a cluster of 12 identical nodes (16 vCPUs, 64 GB RAM, NVMe storage, 10 Gbit/s network). One node ran coordination services and the load generator, while ten nodes were workers. Scaling experiments used 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 workers. JVM settings, garbage collector (G1), and operating system parameters were fixed across systems, and caches were cleared between runs. Each configuration was run for 30 minutes after a 5-minute warm-up and repeated 10 times with different random seeds. Primary metrics included end-to-end latency (event time to result emission; median, 95th, and 99th percentiles), sustained throughput (maximum rate with bounded queue growth), and resource efficiency (CPU-seconds and bytes shuffled per million events). Secondary metrics included result accuracy and recovery time. The burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, and cancer, is a pressing global health concern, accounting for approximately 70% of deaths worldwide, with a disproportionate impact on low- and middle-income countries (World Health Organization, 2018). The importance of primary care in addressing this burden cannot be overstated, as it is widely regarded as the optimal setting for delivering the continuous, coordinated, and person-centred care that chronic conditions require (Starfield et al., 2005; Kruk et al., 2018). As a result, a plethora of interventions have been developed to improve the detection, management, and long-term support of individuals with NCDs in primary care, encompassing strategies such as structured self-management education, decision support for clinicians, task-shifting to nurses and community health workers, audit and feedback, and multicomponent models of integrated care (Wagner et al., 2001; Coleman et al., 2009). While many of these interventions have been evaluated in randomised controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews of such trials have revealed that their effects are often modest and heterogeneous, with similar interventions yielding markedly different results in different settings (Smith et al., 2016; Tricco et al., 2012). This heterogeneity is not surprising, given the complex nature of interventions in primary care, which typically involve multiple interacting components, target multiple levels (patients, providers, practices, and organisations), require tailoring to local circumstances, and depend on the behaviour of numerous actors (Craig et al., 2008; Hawe et al., 2004). The effects of these interventions are shaped by the context in which they are delivered, including the structure and financing of the health system, workforce availability, and local social and cultural norms (Pfadenhauer et al., 2017). Conventional trials, which report only whether an intervention "worked" on average, are limited in their ability to explain why an effect was or was not observed, whether the intervention was delivered as intended, which components were responsible for any change, or how the findings might transfer to other settings. Null results are particularly challenging to interpret without this information, as they may reflect a flawed intervention theory, poor implementation, or an unsuitable context (Oakley et al., 2006). To address these limitations, process evaluations (PEs) have been advocated, with the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions defining their purpose as examining implementation (what is delivered, and how), mechanisms of impact (how delivered activities produce change), and contextual factors that shape both (Moore et al., 2015). By answering questions of for whom, how, and why interventions have an impact, PEs help distinguish implementation failure from theory failure, identify unintended consequences, and provide the information needed to refine interventions and support scale-up. Earlier frameworks for describing implementation, including those of Steckler and Linnan (2002), Baranowski and Stables (2000), and Grant et al. (2013), and widely used theory-based approaches such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (Damschroder et al., 2009), normalisation process theory (May and Finch, 2009), and RE-AIM (Glasgow et al., 1999), have similarly emphasised the need to examine reach, fidelity, dose, and adaptation alongside outcomes. The MRC guidance further stresses that PEs should be underpinned by a clearly articulated intervention theory or logic model, so that data collection and analysis are directed at the hypothesised causal pathway rather than being purely descriptive (Moore et al., 2015; De Silva et al., 2014). Despite this guidance, there is concern that PEs are inconsistently conducted and reported. Reviews in other fields, such as school-based health promotion and public health, have found that PEs often lack explicit theoretical grounding, apply inconsistent definitions of constructs such as fidelity and context, and rely on convenience samples or purely descriptive data (Oakley et al., 2006; Bonell et al., 2012; Grant et al., 2013). Where theory is absent, it is difficult to judge whether the right processes were examined, and findings from one PE are hard to compare with, or build upon, those of another. Improvements in reporting have been proposed, including the Standards for Reporting Implementation Studies (StaRI) and the TIDieR checklist for describing interventions (Pinnock et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2014), but it is unclear how far these have influenced practice in primary care. Several existing syntheses bear on this topic, but leave important gaps. Systematic reviews of barriers and facilitators to implementing chronic disease interventions have mostly drawn on qualitative studies or focused on single conditions, such as diabetes self-management or hypertension control, and have not examined how the underlying evaluations were designed (Gagliardi et al., 2011; Jeet et al., 2017). Reviews of PEs, in contrast, have concentrated on public health, school, or community settings, where the organisational features of primary care, such as gatekeeping, multidisciplinary teams, continuity of care, and payment systems, are less salient. To our knowledge, no review has systematically described the methods used in PEs conducted alongside RCTs of primary care interventions for NCDs, assessed the extent to which they follow recognised guidance, and synthesised their findings on implementation barriers and facilitators across conditions and health systems. This omission is significant, as primary care interventions are increasingly being adapted for and tested in diverse settings, including low-resource health systems, where many of the assumptions underpinning interventions developed in high-income countries may not hold (Kruk et al., 2018; Legido-Quigley et al., 2013). We therefore conducted a systematic review of PEs alongside RCTs of primary care interventions aimed at improving outcomes for individuals with NCDs, using the MRC guidance for process evaluation as an organising framework. Our review had two primary aims: first, to describe and appraise the methods used in these PEs, including the use of intervention theory and theoretical frameworks, the choice of data collection and analytic approaches, sampling, and the integration of qualitative and quantitative data; and second, to synthesise the principal findings of these evaluations regarding barriers and facilitators to implementation, with attention to the context in which interventions were delivered. This review makes three key contributions. Firstly, it provides the first comprehensive overview of how PEs in primary care chronic disease research are being designed and reported, identifying strengths and weaknesses that can inform methodological practice and the application of the MRC guidance. Secondly, it offers a cross-condition synthesis of recurring implementation challenges, which may be more useful to intervention developers and health system decision-makers. Finally, by examining the extent to which PEs follow recognised guidance and the factors that influence their quality, this review aims to contribute to the development of more effective and sustainable primary care interventions for NCDs, which can be adapted and implemented in diverse settings. The development of effective interventions for non-communicable diseases in primary care settings is a complex and multifaceted challenge. Despite the growing body of research in this area, there remains a need for a more nuanced understanding of the factors that influence the implementation and sustainability of these interventions. Our systematic review of process evaluations conducted alongside randomized controlled trials of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases aims to address this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive overview of the current state of the field. To achieve this, we conducted a systematic review of process evaluations that were conducted in conjunction with randomized controlled trials of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases. Our protocol was registered in PROSPERO prior to the commencement of screening, and our review is reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. We utilized the UK Medical Research Council's guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions as a framework for both data extraction and appraisal, which emphasizes the importance of describing the intervention and its causal assumptions, examining implementation, exploring mechanisms of impact, and considering contextual influences on delivery and outcomes. Our eligibility criteria were defined using the Population, Intervention, Context, and Study design elements. We included studies that reported a process evaluation, which we defined as a study that assessed implementation, mechanisms of impact, or context, alongside a randomized controlled trial. The trial intervention had to be delivered in primary care or community-based primary health care settings and aim to improve outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, cancer, mental health conditions, and musculoskeletal disorders. Interventions could be targeted at patients, providers, practices, or the wider health system. We excluded studies of infectious diseases, those conducted solely in hospital or specialist settings, trials with no process evaluation component, and process evaluations reported only as protocols without results. Our search strategy combined three concept blocks: process evaluation terms, primary care terms, and non-communicable disease terms, together with a trial filter to identify randomized designs. We searched multiple databases, including MEDLINE, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, CINAHL, EMBASE, and Global Health, from 1998 to June 2018. Our search terms were developed in collaboration with an information specialist and piloted against a set of known process evaluations. We also supplemented our electronic searches by hand-searching the reference lists of included studies and relevant methodological reviews, and by checking trial registries and linked publications to identify companion papers reporting process evaluation findings. Study selection was conducted independently by two reviewers, who screened titles and abstracts against our eligibility criteria, followed by independent full-text assessment. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating where consensus could not be reached. We calculated agreement between reviewers at the full-text stage using Cohen's kappa. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded. Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form, structured around the UK Medical Research Council's framework, which was piloted on five studies. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and a third reviewer checked a random sample of extractions for accuracy and consistency as quality assurance. We extracted a range of information, including bibliographic details, country and income setting, clinical condition, description of the intervention using the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) items, level of intervention, trial design, and the timing of the process evaluation relative to the trial. We also extracted information on the process evaluation methods, including whether the authors stated an explicit intervention theory or logic model, whether an existing theoretical or implementation framework was used, the process evaluation research questions, the components assessed, data collection methods, sampling strategy and sample size, the respondents included, analytic approach, and whether qualitative and quantitative data were triangulated or integrated. Furthermore, we recorded whether the process evaluation findings were used to interpret trial outcomes. For findings, we extracted all reported barriers and facilitators to implementation, together with the authors' interpretations and illustrative data, where available. Rather than excluding studies on quality grounds, we appraised the methodological characteristics of process evaluations against the UK Medical Research Council's guidance to describe the field and to identify strengths and weaknesses. Our appraisal criteria included clarity of intervention theory, a priori specification of process evaluation questions, appropriateness of sampling, use of multiple data sources, transparent analysis, and consideration of context. Qualitative components were additionally assessed with reference to the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) qualitative checklist, with the aim of contextualizing the weight placed on individual findings rather than determining inclusion. Our data synthesis was conducted in two parts. First, we summarized the methodological data descriptively using frequencies and proportions, stratified by country income group, intervention level, and whether a theoretical framework had been used. We cross-tabulated the presence of an explicit intervention theory against these characteristics and used Fisher's exact test to explore associations. Our findings provide valuable insights into the current state of process evaluations in primary care settings, highlighting areas of strength and weakness, and informing the development of future interventions that are tailored to the specific needs and contexts of different settings. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of more effective and sustainable interventions that can be implemented and maintained at scale, thereby improving outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases in primary care settings. In addition to the methodological data, we also conducted a thematic analysis of the process evaluation findings, which revealed a range of barriers and facilitators to implementation.
