Lactococcus lactis is a crucial component of mesophilic starter cultures used globally in the production of cheese and other fermented dairy products. The role of starter bacteria in these processes is multifaceted, as they rapidly convert lactose into lactic acid, thereby controlling spoilage and pathogenic microbiota, driving curd formation and syneresis, and contributing to the development of texture and flavor (Smid and Kleerebezem, 2014). Beyond acidification, L. lactis also plays a significant role in flavor development through its proteolytic and peptidolytic activities, amino acid catabolism, and the production of volatile compounds such as diacetyl, acetoin, and others derived from citrate and pyruvate metabolism (Smit et al., 2005; Cocaign-Bousquet et al., 2002). The success of dairy fermentation processes hinges on the viability and metabolic activity of the starter culture, which must withstand a series of stresses. These stresses occur in two phases: first, during starter production, concentration, and storage, where freezing, freeze-drying, and cold storage can be detrimental; and later, during cheese manufacture, where heat, osmotic, acid, and oxidative stress can impact the starter's performance (van de Guchte et al., 2002; Papadimitriou et al., 2016). Among these challenges, oxidative stress is often underappreciated but pervasive. Although L. lactis is aerotolerant, it lacks a complete respiratory chain unless exogenous heme is provided, and its defenses against reactive oxygen species (ROS) are limited (Duwat et al., 2001). In the presence of oxygen, enzymes such as NADH oxidase and pyruvate oxidase generate hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, which can damage DNA, proteins, and membrane lipids, leading to growth arrest and loss of viability (Rochat et al., 2006). The introduction of oxygen during various stages of dairy processing, including handling, pumping, stirring, and vat filling, as well as the large-scale propagation of starters under non-anaerobic conditions, further exacerbates oxidative stress. Moreover, oxygen influences the metabolic fate of pyruvate, diverting flux from lactate towards acetate, acetoin, and diacetyl, which has implications for flavor development (Lan et al., 2006). Consequently, strains with improved oxygen tolerance are of practical interest, as they could exhibit more consistent performance in industrial environments and provide an additional route to modulate aroma formation. Cultivating L. lactis under respiratory conditions, i.e., in the presence of heme and oxygen, can improve biomass yield and robustness (Duwat et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2012). However, this approach requires specific process modifications and is not universally applicable to all dairy applications. Furthermore, strain improvement in food microorganisms is constrained by regulatory and consumer perceptions, and genetically modified organisms are not widely accepted in the dairy sector. As a result, non-recombinant approaches such as spontaneous mutant selection and adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) have become attractive alternatives (Bachmann et al., 2012). ALE leverages the capacity of bacteria to acquire beneficial mutations under sustained selective pressure and has been used to enhance various industrially relevant traits in lactic acid bacteria, including acid and thermal tolerance, osmotolerance, growth in specific substrates, and bacteriophage resistance (Derkx et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2020). A notable feature of this approach is that selection under one stress often results in cross-protection against other stresses, due to the overlap in cellular responses and global regulatory changes (Mols and Abee, 2011). Selecting for a trait that depends on a global physiological response, such as the integrity and remodeling of the cell envelope, could therefore yield strains with generally more robust phenotypes. The cell envelope is the primary barrier against environmental insults, and its stress response is well characterized in L. lactis. Envelope-targeting agents trigger the CesSR and other two-component systems, which induce a regulon that includes genes involved in cell wall biosynthesis, modification of the envelope, and protein quality control (Martínez et al., 2007; Roces et al., 2012). Lcn972, a non-lantibiotic bacteriocin produced by L. lactis IPLA972, inhibits cell wall biosynthesis in sensitive lactococci by binding to lipid II, the cell wall precursor, at the septum, thereby impairing septum formation and cell division (Martínez et al., 1996; Martínez et al., 2008; Roces et al., 2009). Its narrow spectrum, restricted to L. lactis, and its mode of action make it a suitable agent to impose controlled cell envelope stress on lactococcal starters. Previous studies have demonstrated that the response to Lcn972 involves the CesSR system, the overexpression of the stress-inducible protein encoded by the lcn972 resistance-associated locus, and the activation of genes of unknown function (Roces et al., 2012; Kramer et al., 2008; Tymoszewska et al., 2017). Notably, resistance to Lcn972 in mutants of the laboratory strain L. lactis IPLA947 or its derivatives has been linked to altered growth, cell wall properties, and metabolic regulation, which may influence how cells handle other stresses (Roces et al., 2012). However, whether resistance to cell wall-active bacteriocins can be harnessed to improve the technological robustness of an industrial starter remains unexplored. L. lactis IPLA947 is a well-characterized, phage-resistant dairy starter used in the manufacture of artisanal and industrial cheeses, with good acidifying properties and a sequenced and annotated genome (Rodríguez-Alonso et al., 2009; Flórez et al., 2016). Given its industrial relevance, it is an appropriate model to test whether cell envelope stress-driven adaptive evolution can generate variants with enhanced technological traits. Any improvement in stress tolerance must not compromise the core functions of the starter, namely rapid acidification, stable lactose-to-lactate conversion, and an adequate contribution to flavor. Trade-offs between stress resistance and growth, which are well described for mutants affected in global regulators or carbon catabolite control (Ferenci, 2016), can render stress-tolerant variants useless for dairy applications. In this study, we applied adaptive evolution under cell envelope stress by consecutively exposing L. lactis IPLA947 to increasing doses of Lcn972 and screened the resulting derivatives for cross-protection against oxidative stress. We hypothesized that resistance to this envelope-active bacteriocin would select for variants with modified envelope physiology and/or metabolic regulation, conferring a more robust phenotype in the presence of oxygen. We characterized the selected mutant, L. lactis R5, regarding its technological traits and stress tolerance, with a focus on understanding the underlying mechanisms driving its improved performance. Our findings provide insights into the potential of adaptive evolution as a tool for strain improvement in the dairy industry, highlighting the importance of considering the complex interplay between cell envelope stress, metabolic regulation, and stress tolerance in the development of more robust starter cultures. The quest for robust and efficient dairy starters has driven research into the development of strains that can thrive in a variety of environments and withstand the stresses inherent to starter production and storage. Our investigation focused on the adaptation of Lactococcus lactis subsp. lactis IPLA947, a well-characterized dairy starter strain, to the bacteriocin Lcn972, with the goal of obtaining a stable, oxygen-tolerant derivative that retains the desirable technological properties of the parental strain. To achieve this, we employed a strategy of adaptive evolution, where the strain was consecutively exposed to increasing concentrations of Lcn972, allowing it to develop resistance while maintaining its growth and metabolic capabilities. The parental strain, Lactococcus lactis subsp. lactis IPLA947, was grown in M17 broth supplemented with 0.5% glucose (GM17) or in reconstituted skim milk (RSM) at 30 °C, with stocks stored at −80 °C in 20% glycerol. Lcn972 was produced and partially purified from L. lactis IPLA972 supernatants using cation-exchange chromatography, as previously described (Martínez et al. 1996), and its activity was quantified by agar well diffusion assay against L. lactis subsp. cremoris MG1363. To promote respiratory metabolism, hemin (5 µg/ml) was added to GM17 where indicated (Duwat et al. 2001). The adaptive evolution process involved diluting an overnight culture of IPLA947 1:100 in GM17 containing a sub-inhibitory concentration of Lcn972, initially set at 0.5× the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), and incubating for 24 h. The culture was then transferred daily into fresh medium with the Lcn972 concentration raised stepwise whenever growth was visible (OD600 > 0.5). After approximately 30 transfers, equivalent to around 200 generations, the final population was plated on GM17 agar, and isolated colonies were tested for Lcn972 MIC. Clones with the highest MIC were selected and passaged ten times (about 70 generations) in GM17 without bacteriocin to assess phenotypic stability. One stable clone, designated R5, was chosen for further characterization. The identity of R5 relative to the parent strain was confirmed through RAPD-PCR fingerprinting with primer OPA-3 (Ward and Roberts 1994) and by verifying the absence of bacteriophage-induced changes via plaque assays. To evaluate the stress tolerance of R5, we conducted a series of experiments. First, we assessed its survival after a hydrogen peroxide challenge. Exponential-phase cultures of both IPLA947 and R5 were harvested, washed, and resuspended to approximately 10^8 CFU/ml. Hydrogen peroxide was added to final concentrations of 5–20 mM, and cells were incubated at 30 °C for 30 min. After neutralizing the residual H2O2 with catalase, viable counts were determined by plating serial dilutions on GM17 agar. Survival was calculated as a percentage, and log reductions were also determined. Next, we examined the growth of R5 under aerobic and anaerobic conditions. Cultures were grown in GM17 at 30 °C with orbital shaking at 200 rpm (aerobic) or statically in sealed tubes filled to the top (limited oxygen). Specific growth rates were calculated from the slope of ln(OD600) versus time during the exponential phase. To assess respiratory metabolism, growth experiments were performed in GM17 with and without hemin, and growth, final OD600, and biomass were compared. Dissolved oxygen levels were measured using a fiber-optic oxygen sensor in selected experiments. The performance of R5 as a dairy starter was evaluated in milk acidification experiments. Reconstituted skim milk was inoculated with 1% (v/v) of overnight cultures of IPLA947 or R5, washed in sterile saline, and incubated at 30 °C. Aerated cultures were shaken at 200 rpm, while static incubation in filled bottles served as the low-oxygen control. pH was recorded continuously using a data logger or measured at defined intervals. The maximum acidification rate, time to reach pH 5.3, and final pH after 24 h were calculated from the pH curves. We also investigated the survival of R5 during cold storage and freeze-drying. For cold storage, cells from stationary-phase cultures were harvested, resuspended in RSM or in 0.9% NaCl, and stored at 4 °C for 28 days, with viable counts determined weekly. Freeze-drying was performed on cells harvested in late exponential phase, washed, and resuspended in 10% (w/v) skim milk supplemented with 5% sucrose. Aliquots were frozen at −80 °C for 2 h and lyophilized for 24 h. Survival was calculated as the ratio of CFU/ml after versus before freeze-drying, and viability was monitored after 1 and 3 months of storage at 4 °C. Finally, we manufactured experimental miniature cheeses using pasteurized whole cow’s milk inoculated with IPLA947 or R5 as the starter culture. The cheese-making process involved warming the milk to 32 °C, adding starter, CaCl2, and commercial chymosin, followed by coagulation, cutting, stirring, scalding, draining, molding, and pressing. Cheeses were ripened at 12 °C for 30 days, during which counts of lactococci, pH, and the profile of sugars and organic acids were determined. Lactose, galactose, lactic acid, acetic acid, citric acid, and other organic acids were quantified by HPLC from milk fermentations and cheeses. Our results indicate that the R5 derivative, obtained through adaptive evolution under Lcn972 stress, exhibits enhanced resistance to hydrogen peroxide and improved growth under aerobic conditions, while retaining the desirable technological properties of the parental strain. Notably, R5 displays an increased capacity to produce acetoin, a compound of interest in dairy fermentations. These findings support the use of cell envelope stress as a driver of intra-strain diversification in industrial lactococci, offering a promising approach for the development of robust and efficient dairy starters. The analysis of presence-absence data, which records the occurrence of species at different sites in a binary matrix, is a fundamental aspect of community ecology and biogeography. A key question in this field is whether such matrices exhibit patterns that cannot be attributed to chance. Several types of patterns have been identified, including nestedness, where species found at species-poor sites tend to form subsets of those found at richer sites, as well as checkerboard patterns and co-occurrence more generally. To quantify these patterns, researchers often use matrix summaries, such as the NODF or temperature metrics, which are then compared to a null distribution obtained by randomizing the data. The validity of the conclusions drawn from these comparisons depends on how well the null model represents the "no pattern" hypothesis. Null models for presence-absence matrices differ primarily in the features of the observed data that they preserve. Unconstrained models, which treat all cells as exchangeable, are known to produce inflated type I error rates due to the heterogeneous species prevalences and site richnesses that induce nestedness-like structure. In response, the dominant approach has been to preserve the row and column sums of the observed matrix, resulting in the fixed-fixed model. This model has become a default choice, as it is implemented in widely used software, recommended in methodological comparisons for its ability to keep type I error low in simulation studies, and has been applied in numerous studies of nestedness and co-occurrence. However, the computational challenges of sampling uniformly from the set of binary matrices with given margins have led to the development of various algorithms, including the Curveball, swap, and sequential importance sampling algorithms. Despite the attention paid to these computational aspects, less consideration has been given to the statistical implications of conditioning on both margins. In a fixed-fixed model, the row and column sums are treated as known constants, rather than as quantities subject to random variation. This assumption is problematic, as species richness at a site and prevalence of a species are themselves outcomes of the ecological and sampling processes being studied. Moreover, nestedness is directly related to the distribution of the margins, and a perfectly nested matrix is fully determined by its margins. As a result, for many empirical matrices, the set of matrices sharing the observed margins may be small, or even trivially small, in which case no randomization is possible. This phenomenon, which we refer to as limited randomizability, can lead to artificially narrow reference distributions, making it difficult to interpret the results of statistical tests. Related concerns have been raised in the ecological literature, where it has been noted that fixed-fixed models may remove part of the signal of interest, resulting in reduced power. However, the converse risk, that conclusions of significance become overly optimistic, has received little systematic study. A natural alternative to fixed-fixed models is to relax the margin constraints and allow row and column sums to vary around their observed values, preserving them only in expectation. Several such models exist, including the fixed-equiprobable and equiprobable-equiprobable models, which use only a subset of margin information, and proportional models, which sample cells with probabilities that depend on observed margins. However, many of these models are ad hoc, and it is unclear in what statistical sense they reproduce the margins or what probabilistic model of the data they represent. In contrast, the psychometric and ecological literatures offer principled parametric models, such as the Rasch model, which treats each cell as an independent Bernoulli variable whose probability depends on a row effect and a column effect. The Rasch model has been used to describe species-site data and is closely related to the maximum-entropy distribution on binary matrices with margins fixed in expectation. This model offers sound statistical properties, including well-understood estimation by conditional or marginal maximum likelihood, diagnostics for goodness of fit, and the fact that fixed-fixed randomization is exactly the conditional distribution of the Rasch model given its sufficient statistics, the margins. Despite these connections, the practical consequences of choosing between strictly constrained and relaxed null models have not been systematically compared on empirical presence-absence data, with attention to the reliability of the resulting significance statements. Existing comparisons have focused largely on type I error and power in synthetic matrices generated from specific mechanisms, rather than on the behavior of the null models themselves when applied to real data sets with diverse margin characteristics. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing the properties of fixed-fixed models and exploring the potential of Rasch models as a statistically principled alternative with relaxed constraints for assessing nestedness and related statistics. Our research questions are threefold. First, we aim to determine how severely the margin constraints of fixed-fixed models limit the randomizability of real presence-absence matrices. Second, we investigate whether Rasch models can serve as a viable alternative with relaxed constraints for assessing nestedness and related statistics. Third, we compare the significance measures obtained from the two families of models in practice, with a focus on the reliability of the resulting conclusions. By addressing these questions, we hope to contribute to a deeper understanding of the statistical properties of null models for presence-absence data and to provide guidance for researchers seeking to analyze and interpret these data. The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we analyze the properties of fixed-fixed models, showing how the size and structure of the set of matrices with given margins constrain the null distribution. We then explore the potential of Rasch models as a statistically principled alternative with relaxed constraints for assessing nestedness and related statistics. Finally, we compare the significance measures obtained from the two families of models in practice, with a focus on the reliability of the resulting conclusions. By examining the behavior of these models on empirical presence-absence data with diverse margin characteristics, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of each approach and to inform the choice of null models in future studies. The concept of limited randomizability is crucial in the analysis of presence-absence data, as it can significantly impact the results of statistical tests. To quantify this phenomenon, we examined a collection of empirical data sets and compared the performance of different null models. Our study consisted of three main components. First, we evaluated the degree of randomizability in our data sets using various diagnostics. Second, we presented the Rasch model as a null model for presence-absence data and discussed its estimation and sampling. We also explored the relationship between the Rasch model and fixed-fixed models, which are commonly used in ecological studies. Third, we compared the performance of these models empirically and found that fixed-fixed models can yield overly optimistic measures of statistical significance, leading to extremely small p-values for observed structures that appear unremarkable under more relaxed models. To begin, let's define the notation used in our study. We represented the presence-absence data as a binary matrix X = (xij) with n rows (sites) and m columns (species), where xij = 1 if species j is present at site i. The row sums, denoted by ri, were calculated as the sum of the elements in each row, while the column sums, denoted by cj, were calculated as the sum of the elements in each column. We removed rows and columns with sum 0 or m (respectively n) from the analysis, as they carry no information under the models used. Our empirical matrices consisted of published island, habitat-fragment, and mountain-top community datasets commonly used in nestedness studies, including the mammal data of Patterson and Atmar (1986), the Darwin's finch data used by Gotelli and Graves (1996), and further matrices from the compilation of Atmar and Patterson (1993). These matrices varied in size, ranging from approximately 10 × 10 to 100 × 150, and had fills (proportions of ones) between 0.15and 0.60. All analyses were performed in R, utilizing functions from the vegan package (Oksanen et al. 2022) where available and custom code otherwise. To quantify nestedness, we employed three different metrics: NODF (Almeida-Neto et al. 2008), the nestedness temperature (Atmar and Patterson 1993), and the matrix discrepancy measure (Brualdi and Sanderson 1999). NODF, which is the mean of the pairwise paired-overlap values over all row pairs and column pairs, was used as the primary metric, while the other two statistics were used to verify that our conclusions were not dependent on the choice of metric. Because NODF is strongly influenced by the margins, each observed value Tobs was compared to the distribution of T under each null model. Significance was expressed as a one-sided Monte Carlo p-value, calculated as p = (1 + #{Tk ≥ Tobs}) / (N + 1), where T1, …, TN are values from N = 5,000 null matrices, and as a standardized effect size, z = (Tobs − mean(Tk)) / sd(Tk). We used fixed-fixed null models, which sample from the set 𝒰(r, c) of binary matrices with the observed row and column sums (Connor and Simberloff 1979; Gotelli 2000). Three different samplers were employed: the sequential swap, the quasiswap algorithm, and the curveball algorithm. The sequential swap involves repeatedly picking a random 2 × 2 submatrix of the checkerboard form (1 0 / 0 1) and flipping it (Gotelli and Entsminger 2003). The quasiswap algorithm first moves to a random matrix with the correct margins and then applies swaps (Miklós and Podani 2004). The curveball algorithm selects two rows at random and exchanges a random portion of the species that occur in only one of them, preserving both margins (Strona et al. 2014). The curveball algorithm is known to sample uniformly over 𝒰(r, c) in the limit (Carstens 2013; Verhelst 2008). To ensure convergence, we used a burn-in of 100,000 swaps, or 5 × n curveball trades per output matrix, with a thinning interval of the same size. Convergence was checked by comparing the distribution of T across independent chains started from different matrices and by monitoring autocorrelation of T along the chain. To characterize the degree of limited randomizability, we computed three diagnostics. First, for each cell, we estimated the empirical frequency fij = P(xij = 1) from the N fixed-fixed samples. We then recorded the proportion of cells with fij ∈ {0, 1} (cells that are effectively frozen) and calculated the mean entropy of the cell distribution, H = −(1/nm) Σij [fij log fij + (1 − fij) log(1 − fij)]. The Arabic language, with its rich history spanning over 1,400 years, has been a cornerstone of human civilization, serving as the liturgical language of nearly two billion Muslims and boasting a written record that few languages can match (Versteegh, 2014). The earliest extended attestations of Arabic, namely the Qur'anic text and pre-Islamic poetry, date back to the sixth and seventh centuries CE, marking the beginning of a linguistic journey that would be shaped by various factors, including conquest, migration, and contact with other languages such as Persian, Turkish, Aramaic, and European languages (Owens, 2006; Holes, 2004). As the language evolved, it was influenced by the codification efforts of medieval grammarians and the modernization of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, resulting in a complex and multifaceted linguistic landscape. Despite the vast and varied written record of Arabic, its history is often described in broad qualitative terms, with the standard account distinguishing between Classical Arabic, the codified literary language of the early Islamic centuries, and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), the written and formal register that emerged with the Nahḍa (the Arabic cultural revival) and the rise of the modern press (Badawi, 1973; Versteegh, 2014). Intermediate stages, such as Post-Classical or Middle Arabic, are often invoked, but their boundaries and linguistic content are contested, and the picture is further complicated by diglossia, the coexistence of a prestigious written standard with unwritten colloquial varieties (Ferguson, 1959). Moreover, the fact that many writers deviated from the standard, either unintentionally or by choice, means that texts often mix registers in ways that resist simple classification. Most of our current understanding of the history of written Arabic is based on close reading of selected manuscripts, authors, or genres, which, although valuable, are limited in scale and may not generalize across the full range of the written record. Furthermore, such analyses often depend on the analyst's prior assumptions about where period boundaries lie, which can be problematic. In contrast, computational methods offer a promising approach to testing such claims at scale, as has been demonstrated in the study of English, German, French, and other languages, where large-scale analyses of lexical change, semantic shift, and periodization have transformed our understanding of language evolution (Michel et al., 2011; Hamilton et al., 2016; Kutuzov et al., 2018; Gries & Hilpert, 2008; Tahmasebi et al., 2021). The Arabic NLP community has made significant strides in recent years, building a substantial infrastructure of morphological analyzers, disambiguators, open toolkits, pretrained language models, and dialectal resources (Habash, 2010; Pasha et al., 2014; Obeid et al., 2020; Antoun et al., 2020; Inoue et al., 2021; Bouamor et al., 2018). However, this effort has focused primarily on contemporary written Arabic, namely news and web text in MSA, and on the spoken dialects, with historical text often being treated as a single "Classical" block, usually to evaluate the transfer of tools built for MSA (Belinkov et al., 2016). To our knowledge, no existing resource or study treats the Arabic written record as a continuous diachronic object spanning the full 1400 years of its history. The raw material for such a study exists, with large-scale digitization projects, volunteer initiatives, and OCR pipelines having produced collections of premodern Arabic texts, such as the OpenITI corpus and the Shamela digital library, as well as contemporary archives (Nigst et al., 2020). However, these collections pose several challenges for a quantitative history of the language, including inconsistent metadata, approximate or uncertain dates of authorship, OCR and transcription errors, editorial apparatus, and modern commentary interleaved with the historical text. Moreover, the fact that Arabic scholarly culture relied heavily on quotation, paraphrase, compilation, and commentary means that a large share of the text in any collection is reused from earlier works, which, if left unaddressed, would bias frequency-based analyses and make the apparent linguistic character of a period depend on how much its authors copied from earlier ones (Romanov, 2017). This paper addresses these gaps by pursuing a central research question: whether the large-scale statistical structure of the written Arabic record, observed without imposing a prior chronology, matches the periodizations proposed by traditional scholarship, and whether it points to further divisions that manual analysis has not identified. We tackle this question in three steps: building a corpus suitable for diachronic analysis, processing it with existing Arabic NLP tools while accounting for their limitations, and applying quantitative methods that infer period structure from the data themselves. Our contributions include the assembly and release of a large-scale historical corpus of written Arabic, comprising approximately 1.2 billion words from roughly 9,000 works, spanning the seventh to the twenty-first century. We harmonize and verify metadata, assign each work to a date or date range, and document the corpus's composition by century and genre, including its uneven coverage, which is dense for the ninth to eleventh centuries and the twentieth century and sparser elsewhere. We also discuss how such unevenness affects inference. Furthermore, we describe a pipeline that removes non-textual and editorial material, normalizes orthographic variation, applies morphological analysis and lemmatization with existing Arabic NLP tools, and evaluates their performance on historical text. We present a method for detecting reused passages at scale and find that a substantial minority of the corpus, roughly one fifth of all tokens, consists of text that also appears in earlier works. Removing or down-weighting this material changes the estimated temporal profiles of many linguistic features, so we treat reuse as a first-order confound in diachronic studies of Arabic. Finally, we introduce a novel automatic periodization algorithm that segments the timeline into contiguous periods by maximizing a specific criterion. This approach allows us to identify period boundaries and linguistic features that distinguish one period from another, without relying on prior assumptions about the chronology of the language. By applying this method to our corpus, we aim to shed new light on the evolution of written Arabic and provide a more nuanced understanding of its complex and multifaceted history. The study of linguistic evolution over time is a complex task, particularly when dealing with languages like Arabic, which boasts a rich and extensive textual tradition spanning over 1,400 years. To address this challenge, our research employs a novel approach that not only accounts for the internal homogeneity of linguistic features within each segment but also considers corpus size and reuse. Unlike earlier methods that rely on pre-specified boundaries, our approach recovers boundaries from the data itself and quantifies the stability of each boundary under resampling. This empirical account of the history of written Arabic offers a nuanced understanding of the language's development, recovering the established division between Classical Arabic and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), and placing the transition in the nineteenth century, consistent with the traditional association with the Nahḍa. Our analyses also reproduce several finer divisions proposed in the literature, suggesting that the Classical period itself may be divisible into several stages of development, characterized through lexical, morphological, and syntactic features. These findings provide both a resource and a methodology for the quantitative study of Arabic historical linguistics, serving as a template for similar work on other languages with long textual traditions. The remainder of this paper describes the compilation and processing of our corpus, presents the periodization method, reports our findings, and discusses their implications and limitations. To assemble our corpus, we drew from three primary sources, chosen to cover the 1,400 years of written Arabic with the fewest gaps. For the pre-modern period, spanning the 7th to 19th centuries CE, we utilized the OpenITI release, a collection of digitized Arabic-script books in a lightly annotated markup format, supplemented by texts from the Shamela and Shia Online Library repositories. For the modern period, we employed news and periodical text from the Arabic Gigaword and the OSIAN corpus, together with a 2022 Arabic Wikipedia dump. Additionally, we incorporated early materials, including the Qur'an and a set of pre-Islamic and early Islamic poetry collections, from the Quranic Arabic Corpus and OpenITI. The resulting collection comprised 11,742 documents and approximately 3.4 billion raw tokens, each assigned a date based on the author's death year in the Hijri calendar for pre-modern books, converted to the Gregorian calendar, and the publication year for modern sources. However, dates based on author death years are imperfect proxies for composition dates, as authors may have written decades earlier. To account for this uncertainty, we treated all dates as having an uncertainty of roughly ±25 years and performed analyses on bins of at least 50 years. For modern sources, we used the publication year, and documents with undeterminable dates were excluded. Given the vast disparity in size between the modern and pre-modern portions of the corpus, we divided the corpus into 50-year bins up to 1900 and 10-year bins thereafter, subsampling each bin to a maximum of 20 million tokens for comparative analyses to prevent frequency-based measures from being driven by differences in size. Cleaning and normalization of the digitized texts were crucial steps, as they contain OCR errors, editorial apparatus, and markup that can distort linguistic analysis. We removed OpenITI markup, page and volume headers, editorial footnotes, tables of contents, and isnād-annotation tags using regular expressions and OpenITI's structural tags. Subsequent normalization steps included Unicode NFKC normalization, removal of tatweel (kashida), removal of diacritics (except in experiments that explicitly used them), conversion of Persian and Urdu character variants to Arabic equivalents, and replacement of Arabic-Indic digits with ASCII digits. Non-Arabic passages were detected by script and removed when a paragraph contained over 50% non-Arabic characters, and paragraphs shorter than 5 tokens were discarded. To estimate residual noise, we manually annotated a random sample of 2,000 paragraphs, stratified by period, and marked any paragraph containing OCR corruption or non-linguistic material. The estimated proportion of problematic paragraphs decreased from 9.8% before cleaning to 2.1% after. Tokens were then flagged as out-of-vocabulary if they were not analyzable by the CAMeL Tools morphological analyzer. Documents with more than 30% unanalyzable tokens were removed, as were exact duplicates identified by hashing normalized text. The final corpus contained 10,411 documents and 2.9 billion tokens. Linguistic processing involved sentence segmentation using punctuation and, for largely unpunctuated pre-modern texts, a length-based fallback that breaks at conjunctions after 60 tokens. Tokenization, lemmatization, and part-of-speech tagging were carried out with CAMeL Tools, using the MSA disambiguator for all periods and the Classical Arabic model for pre-1800 texts. We compared the two models on a gold-standard sample of 3,000 tokens per period and found that lemma accuracy for the Classical model remained above 93% for texts up to 1500 CE but declined to 88% for texts from 1500 to 1800, a bias we considered when interpreting later results. Additionally, we ran Farasa for segmentation as a robustness check. The detection of reused text is a critical aspect of our analysis, as Arabic literature is characterized by extensive quotation, copying, and paraphrase, which could inflate similarities between periods or authors. We identified reuse using the passim algorithm, which indexes word n-grams, clusters candidate document pairs, and aligns them using Smith–Waterman local alignment. Following established guidelines, we used 25-token n-grams, a minimum alignment length of 50 tokens, and a minimum match proportion of 0.5 in an alignment window, ignoring pairs of documents with the same author. The quality of the detection was assessed on 500 randomly selected alignments, each checked by two annotators, yielding a precision of 0.96 (Cohen's κ = 0.88 between annotators). Aligned passages were marked, and unless otherwise stated, all downstream analyses were run on both the full corpus and a version in which reused passages were removed from the later text in each alignment, ensuring that every shared passage was kept only in its earliest occurrence. The importance of strong primary care in achieving an equitable and efficient health system has been a longstanding theme in international health policy, dating back to the Declaration of Alma-Ata in 1978. The notion that first-contact, comprehensive, continuous, and coordinated care leads to better population health outcomes at a lower cost has been repeatedly reaffirmed, with family medicine emerging as the discipline that embodies these attributes at the level of the individual practitioner. In high-income countries, family medicine has matured into a recognized specialty with well-defined training pathways, scopes of practice, and roles within the health system. However, in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa, family medicine is still in its infancy, with postgraduate training programs only established in the last two decades in countries such as South Africa, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, Ethiopia, and Botswana. The definition, scope, and optimal deployment of family physicians (FPs) in these settings remain contested, with debates ongoing about whether they should function primarily as district hospital generalists, clinical trainers and mentors of primary care teams, or first-contact clinicians in community-based practices. Botswana, for example, has made significant strides in achieving near-universal access to public primary care facilities, implementing a large antiretroviral treatment program, and recording steady gains in several health indicators since independence. Nevertheless, the country faces a dual burden of persistent communicable diseases, such as HIV and tuberculosis, and rapidly rising noncommunicable diseases, all while struggling with a small and overstretched health workforce that has historically relied on expatriate doctors. In this context, inefficiencies in the use of scarce resources, such as doctors performing tasks that could be undertaken by others, fragmented records, duplicated investigations, hierarchical relationships between providers and patients, and unclear referral pathways, have direct consequences for the quality of care. The introduction of a new cadre of specialist generalists into such a system raises fundamental questions about their role and how they should be supported. Debates about the future of African family medicine have largely drawn on models from the United Kingdom, North America, Australia, and other middle-income countries, with less attention paid to smaller European systems that have achieved high performance on equity and efficiency indicators. Denmark, for instance, offers a notable example of a health system with a long-established, gatekeeping-based family practice that has yielded impressive results. Danish general practitioners are primarily self-employed contractors working within a tax-financed national health service, serving as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care for a registered list of patients and remunerated through a combination of capitation and fee-for-service payments. Specialist training in general practice is structured and lengthy, with practices employing nurses, medical secretaries, and laboratory staff who undertake a significant proportion of routine clinical and administrative work. The Danish health system is also distinguished by its early and near-universal adoption of electronic communication in primary care, including shared electronic records, electronic prescribing and referrals, and patient access to their own health data through national portals. Despite the potential relevance of the Danish model to African family medicine, there is a surprising lack of literature that interprets the Danish experience in a way that speaks to the needs of African health systems. Most published accounts of the Danish system are written by Danish authors for European or North American audiences, focusing on organization, financing, or quality indicators, rather than the day-to-day experience of practice from the perspective of a clinician working in a resource-limited setting. The few African contributions to the literature on family medicine have concentrated on training curricula, competencies, and the relationship between FPs and district health systems, leaving a gap in knowledge about how a mature family practice system functions in practice and which elements are transferable to African contexts. One area where the Danish experience may offer valuable insights is in the realm of task shifting, which has been advocated by the World Health Organization as a response to workforce shortages. While the discussion in Africa has focused largely on shifting tasks from doctors to nurses, clinical officers, and community health workers in HIV care, the Danish arrangement represents a different kind of task shifting, one that is institutionalized, remunerated, and supported by information systems. This paper seeks to address the gap in knowledge through a reflective, observational account of a visit by an African family physician to family practices in Denmark, with a central question: what can the organization, training, and practice of Danish family medicine teach Botswana, and by extension other African countries, about the future role of family medicine in resource-constrained health systems? Through this account, we explore four related themes that emerged during the visit: the training and role of the FP, the division of labor between FPs and support staff, the relationship between providers and patients, and the infrastructure of information technology and financing within which practice occurs. This paper makes three key contributions. First, it provides a practitioner's comparative description of Danish family practice from the viewpoint of a physician trained and working in Botswana, highlighting features that are routine in Denmark but would be unfamiliar or even unimaginable in many African settings. Second, it links these observations to wider debates on task shifting, workforce design, and health system financing, moving the discussion of African family medicine beyond the usual suspects of the UK, North America, and Australia. Finally, it offers a grounded, comparative reflection on how a mature family practice system functions in practice, which elements are transferable, and which depend on conditions that African countries do not currently share. As we consider the development of family medicine in Africa, it is essential to look beyond curricula and examine the conditions that enable specialist generalists to be effective. This involves not only understanding the intricacies of healthcare systems but also acknowledging the complexities of implementing change in resource-constrained environments. Our study, which focused on the Danish healthcare system, offers a unique perspective on the features that contribute to the success of family medicine in a country with a strong tradition of primary care. We highlight several key considerations for countries like Botswana, including the formalization of task shifting, revisions to health worker training and roles, the development of reliable information technology, and the fostering of more egalitarian relationships between patients and healthcare workers. Our study employed a descriptive, qualitative, observational design, which allowed us to gather rich, contextual data on the organization and delivery of family medicine in Denmark. This approach, akin to focused ethnography, enabled us to examine how healthcare professionals organize their work and relationships within a specific setting. By immersing ourselves in the daily routines of family practices, we gained a deeper understanding of the intricacies of Danish general practice, from the division of labor among healthcare professionals to the use of electronic records and national health networks. The Danish healthcare system, with its tax-financed, predominantly public structure, provides an interesting contrast to the mixed public and private systems found in many African countries. In Denmark, general practitioners serve as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care, and most practice as independent contractors reimbursed through a combination of capitation and fee-for-service. This setup has contributed to Denmark's strong population health indicators and high degree of digitization in primary care. Our study aimed to identify features of the Danish system that could inform discussions on the future of family medicine in Botswana and other African countries, where family medicine is still being defined and is often characterized by a lack of resources and infrastructure. To achieve this goal, we selected sites for our study purposively, seeking variation in practice size, location, and organization. Our visit program included solo and group practices in urban and semi-rural areas, as well as a university department of general practice. We observed family physicians, practice nurses, medical secretaries, and receptionists, and engaged in informal, semi-structured conversations with these individuals to gather insights into their training, clinical practice, and perceptions of the system. Patients were present in waiting rooms and consultations, but they were not recruited as study participants. Instead, we focused on the healthcare professionals and the systems they work within. Our data collection methods were designed to be flexible and adaptive, allowing us to respond to the complexities of the healthcare environment. We employed direct non-participant observation, sitting in on consultations and following the flow of patients through the practice. We also collected documents and artifacts, such as appointment systems, sample electronic record screens, and training curricula, to corroborate and clarify our observations. Field notes were written daily and expanded into structured reflective accounts each evening, which helped us to identify discrepancies and note impressions that differed from our expectations based on African practice. The analysis of our data involved thematic analysis, which allowed us to identify and refine themes related to the training and role of family physicians, the organization of practices, task shifting and delegation, information technology, patient-healthcare worker relationships, and financing and health system context. We examined these themes against the Botswana and wider African context, comparing each Danish feature with known arrangements in African primary care and identifying those that appeared potentially transferable, those that depended on context, and those that were not feasible under current conditions. Throughout our study, we were mindful of the importance of trustworthiness and reflexivity. We recognized that our own backgrounds and biases could influence our observations and interpretations, and we took steps to mitigate these effects. Our prolonged engagement during the visit, combined with our observational approach and the use of multiple data sources, helped to support the credibility of our findings. By acknowledging the complexities and challenges of implementing change in resource-constrained environments, we hope to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the factors that shape the development of family medicine in Africa. The implications of our study are far-reaching, and we believe that our findings can inform discussions on the future of family medicine in Botswana and other African countries. By examining the features that contribute to the success of family medicine in Denmark, we can identify potential strategies for improving healthcare outcomes in Africa. These may include the formalization of task shifting, revisions to health worker training and roles, and the development of reliable information technology. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of more effective and sustainable healthcare systems in Africa, and we hope that our study will serve as a starting point for further discussion and research. In conclusion, our study highlights the importance of looking beyond curricula and examining the conditions that enable specialist generalists to be effective. By understanding the complexities of healthcare systems and the challenges of implementing change in resource-constrained environments, we can work towards developing more effective and sustainable healthcare systems in Africa. Our findings have significant implications for policymakers, educators, and clinicians who are shaping family medicine in Africa, and we hope that our study will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the factors that shape the development of family medicine in this region. Furthermore, we recognize that the development of family medicine in Africa is a complex and ongoing process, and that our study is just one contribution to this effort. We hope that our findings will be used to inform further research and discussion, and that they will help to shape the development of family medicine in Africa in the years to come. By working together and sharing our knowledge and expertise, we can build stronger, more effective healthcare systems that meet the needs of patients and communities across Africa. The ubiquity of graph-structured data in various domains, including social networks, the web, bioinformatics, and knowledge bases, has led to an explosion in the size of these graphs. The web graph, for instance, comprises tens of billions of pages, while social networks like Facebook and Twitter boast billions of vertices and hundreds of billions of edges. As a result, querying these massive graphs has become a crucial requirement for analysis and decision-making. However, much of the existing work on graph querying relies on the assumption that the graph, or at least its index, can fit in main memory. This assumption is often unrealistic, as graph growth frequently outpaces memory growth, leading to performance degradation or even rendering in-memory algorithms inoperable. Several approaches have been proposed to address this challenge. Disk-based graph stores and indexes can reduce memory demands but often require expensive index structures and suffer from performance degradation when access patterns are not localized. Distributed graph systems, such as Pregel, GraphLab, and Trinity, distribute the graph across a cluster's memory, while Map/Reduce-based approaches have been employed for graph processing and subgraph matching. Nevertheless, these solutions typically presuppose a large cluster and focus on whole-graph analytics rather than ad hoc queries that return a user-specified number of answers. Moreover, such resources are not always available, and many users need to query large graphs on a single commodity machine or a small, fixed set of machines. In this paper, we adopt a divide-and-conquer strategy to tackle this problem. By partitioning the graph into smaller pieces that can fit in memory, we can evaluate queries over these partitions and combine the results to obtain the final answer. This approach allows us to query graphs of any size with a fixed amount of memory, as scalability is bounded by the size of a partition rather than the size of the graph. However, this strategy raises several nontrivial problems. For instance, a query answer may span multiple partitions, requiring the combination of partial results from different partitions. Furthermore, an answer may require the same partition multiple times, necessitating careful bookkeeping of intermediate results to avoid losing or duplicating answers. To address these challenges, we consider three query evaluation approaches given a set of partitions: One Partition At a Time (OPAT), a traditional multi-processor approach, and a Map/Reduce approach. OPAT provides scalability through independent processing of partitions and is the primary focus of this paper. The latter two approaches address response time in addition to scalability, and we present and analyze them to contextualize OPAT. Our research questions are fourfold: (1) What is the minimal information required to maintain across partition loads to ensure that a query over a partitioned graph yields the same answers as over the unpartitioned graph? (2) How do partitioning schemes influence the number of partition loads and the volume of intermediate results for different query types? (3) Can quantitative partition and query metrics be used to select a loading order that reduces response time, particularly when only a specified number of answers is required? (4) How do the three evaluation approaches compare in scalability and response time under varying resource constraints? Our work differs from earlier research on partitioned or distributed graph querying in several respects. Many systems partition a graph for load balancing, assuming that all partitions are concurrently available. In contrast, we treat query answering as the central problem, establishing correctness conditions for cross-partition and repeated-partition answers and exploiting query selectivity and partition characteristics to determine how many partitions need to be loaded and in which sequence. The contributions of this paper are twofold: (1) We present an OPAT query evaluation framework for partitioned graphs that identifies the necessary minimal bookkeeping and proves that it computes complete and duplicate-free answers. (2) We analyze the interaction between partitioning schemes and query processing, correlating query characteristics with partition loads and intermediate result volumes. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first discuss the background and related work on graph querying and partitioning. Then, we present the OPAT query evaluation framework and analyze its correctness and scalability. Next, we examine the interaction between partitioning schemes and query processing, exploring how different partitioning schemes influence query performance. Finally, we conclude by summarizing our contributions and outlining directions for future research. In the context of graph querying, several partitioning schemes have been proposed, including balanced edge-cut minimization, hash or range assignment, and locality-preserving methods. Each scheme has its strengths and weaknesses, and the choice of scheme depends on the specific use case and query characteristics. For instance, balanced edge-cut minimization can reduce the number of partition loads but may lead to increased intermediate result volumes. In contrast, hash or range assignment can provide faster query performance but may result in poorer partitioning quality. To address these trade-offs, we propose a quantitative framework for evaluating partitioning schemes and query metrics. Our framework allows us to correlate query characteristics with partition loads and intermediate result volumes, enabling us to select a loading order that reduces response time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through a series of experiments, showcasing its ability to improve query performance and reduce response time. In conclusion, our work presents a novel approach to querying large graphs on a single commodity machine or a small, fixed set of machines. By partitioning the graph into smaller pieces and evaluating queries over these partitions, we can achieve scalability and reduce response time. Our OPAT query evaluation framework provides a foundation for further research in this area, and our analysis of partitioning schemes and query processing highlights the importance of careful partitioning and query optimization. As graph-structured data continues to grow in size and complexity, our work provides a crucial step towards enabling efficient and effective querying of these massive graphs. The evaluation of graph queries on large, distributed datasets is a complex task that requires careful consideration of several key factors, including the structure and size of the graph, the selectivity of the query, and the number of answers requested. To address these challenges, we have developed a framework for estimating the number of loads and resources needed to evaluate a query on a partitioned graph. This framework is based on a set of quantitative metrics that capture the characteristics of the partitions and intermediate results, which are then used to formulate heuristics for ordering partition loads. The goal of these heuristics is to minimize response time, both for retrieving all answers and for retrieving a specified number of answers. Our approach involves extending an existing graph querying system to evaluate queries on partitioned graphs, and we have conducted experiments on large synthetic and real-world graphs using several partitioning schemes and a variety of query types. These experiments have allowed us to evaluate the effectiveness of our heuristics and to compare the performance of different evaluation strategies, including a multi-processor approach and a Map/Reduce formulation. We have also developed a cost model to analyze the behavior of these strategies and to provide guidance on when each is most appropriate. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we describe our query model and the partitioned-graph evaluation framework, including a correctness argument. Section 3 presents our partitioning analysis, metrics, and heuristics, while Section 4 describes the multi-processor and Map/Reduce approaches. Our experimental evaluation is reported in Section 5, and we discuss our findings and conclude in Section 6. To begin, we model a graph as a directed, labeled multigraph G = (V, E, λ), where λ assigns labels to vertices and edges. A query Q is a connected pattern of k edges with optional label and value predicates, and it is evaluated under subgraph-isomorphism semantics with a result limit r, which can be either all answers or a user-specified number. The graph G is divided into n partitions {P₁,…,Pₙ}, where each vertex belongs to exactly one partition, and edges whose endpoints lie in different partitions are cut edges. Each partition is stored as a self-contained unit that holds its internal edges, its outgoing cut edges, and a catalogue of its boundary vertices. A key aspect of our approach is the use of a minimal bookkeeping mechanism to keep track of suspended partial matches. When a partial match reaches a boundary vertex v whose continuation edge lies in another partition Pj, it is suspended, and a record is kept of the vertex-to-query-node binding, the next query edge to be matched, and the set of (partition, query-edge) expansions that have already been consumed. This allows us to prevent the loss of answers that span partitions and to avoid duplicating answers that need the same partition more than once. We study three evaluation strategies: (i) One Partition At a Time (OPAT), (ii) a traditional multiprocessor approach with shared or message-passing workers, and (iii) a Map/Reduce formulation. OPAT is our primary experimental subject, and we have developed a set of heuristics for ordering partition loads that are designed to minimize response time. The other two strategies are specified and analyzed using a cost model, and their behavior is compared to OPAT on the same workloads. In our OPAT evaluation, we load one partition at a time into memory and evaluate the query against it using an in-memory engine. We keep a minimal record for each suspended partial match, and we use this information to extend the pending partial matches and to start new matches of the query from the internal edges of the current partition. We emit completed answers and re-queue any match that again reaches a boundary into another partition, stopping when the desired number of answers has been found or when all pending queues are empty. We have verified the correctness of our approach through a combination of theoretical argument and empirical evaluation. Our correctness argument is based on soundness and completeness, and we have empirically verified that our approach produces the same results as an unpartitioned in-memory engine on all graphs that fit in memory. In terms of partitioning schemes, we compare four schemes of increasing structural awareness: (a) hash partitioning of vertex identifiers, (b) random balanced assignment, (c) a streaming heuristic, Linear Deterministic Greedy, and (d) multilevel k-way partitioning with METIS, which minimizes edge cut under a balance constraint. We compute several metrics for each partitioning, including the edge-cut ratio, the number of boundary vertices, and the size skew, and we use these metrics to develop quantitative metrics and ordering heuristics that relate query properties to partition characteristics. For each partition Pi and query Q, we compute the estimated seed count, the number of boundary vertices whose labels are compatible with a query edge, and the current pending-queue length. We use these metrics to define a normalized yield score, which captures the potential of each partition to produce answers. We believe that our work has important implications for the development of scalable and efficient graph querying systems, and we hope that it will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in the field. The profession of dental hygiene has undergone significant transformations over the past few decades, with its scope of practice expanding to encompass a wide range of preventive, educational, and therapeutic services. Today, dental hygienists work in diverse settings, including private practices, schools, long-term care facilities, and public health programs, often with greater autonomy or under direct access arrangements. This growth has been accompanied by a concerted effort to establish a distinct body of knowledge, with professional organizations and accrediting bodies emphasizing the importance of evidence-based practice, research grounded in the profession's theoretical frameworks, and the development of graduates who can critically evaluate and apply scientific evidence. A fundamental aspect of this endeavor is the existence of a robust and accessible literature. The dental hygiene profession relies on a sizable and well-organized body of research, which is disseminated through various channels, including journals, books, and online resources. Information professionals play a crucial role in navigating this literature, understanding its organization, publication venues, and indexing. Bibliometric mapping offers a systematic approach to characterizing the literature of a field, and the Medical Library Association's "Nursing and Allied Health Literature Mapping Project" has been a pioneer in this area since the 1990s. The project's methodology involves collecting references from a sample of core journals, categorizing them by format and age, and ranking the cited journals according to Bradford's Law of Scattering. This law posits that the journals contributing to a subject can be divided into zones, each yielding roughly equal numbers of relevant citations, with a small nucleus of core titles producing as many citations as a much larger number of peripheral titles. By applying this methodology, mapping studies can identify the most important journals in a discipline, assess the dispersion of its literature across other fields, and evaluate the coverage of major bibliographic databases. Haaland's 1999 study was the first to apply this methodology to the dental hygiene literature, analyzing citations from a sample of dental hygiene journals. The study identified a small core of titles, demonstrated a heavy reliance on journal articles, with books as the next most frequent format, and documented a significant dependence on literature from dentistry and other health-related fields. These findings were consistent with the profile of a relatively young, applied discipline, with a literature concentrated in a few profession-specific journals, supplemented by sources from dentistry, medicine, and education. However, the landscape of dental hygiene literature has changed profoundly since Haaland's study. The shift from print to electronic publishing has altered the formats researchers cite and the speed with which they can access them. Online journal platforms, open access publishing, institutional repositories, and freely accessible websites of professional and governmental organizations have expanded the range of sources available to authors. Studies in other health professions have documented a corresponding rise in Internet sources in reference lists and, in some cases, a decline in citations to books and other monographic literature. Furthermore, the volume of health sciences literature has grown dramatically, and the number of indexed journals has expanded accordingly. Databases that once offered limited coverage of allied health fields have broadened their holdings, with CINAHL, for example, now offering a "Complete" edition with full-text content, while MEDLINE and EMBASE have also increased the number of dental and related journals they index. The dental hygiene profession itself has developed its own research infrastructure, including the establishment of doctoral and master's programs, the creation of new peer-reviewed journals, and more explicit research priorities set by professional associations. Despite these developments, the structure of the discipline's literature remains poorly understood. Whether the number of core journals, the reliance on literature from other fields, or the age of cited material has changed since Haaland's original study has not been systematically examined. This knowledge gap has significant implications for collection development decisions, database selection, and instruction on searching strategies. Without current estimates of database coverage, librarians cannot provide reliable guidance on the best resources for capturing the dental hygiene literature, nor can they determine whether supplementary searching in additional databases is warranted. The present study aims to update Haaland's analysis and address three research questions. First, how have the formats and ages of sources cited in dental hygiene journals changed between the original study and the present sample, particularly with respect to journal articles, books, government publications, and Internet sources? Second, which journals constitute the core of the dental hygiene literature when ranked according to Bradford's Law of Scattering, and how does their disciplinary focus compare with that of the earlier core? Third, to what extent are the cited journals indexed in CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, and how does this coverage inform database selection? This study makes three significant contributions. Empirically, it provides a current map of the dental hygiene literature based on cited references from a three-year sample of core journals, quantifying changes relative to 1999 in the number of cited titles, the size of the core zone, format distribution, and citation age. Methodologically, it extends the standard mapping protocol by adding an Internet source category, reflecting the changed citation landscape, and pairing the Bradford analysis with a multi-database coverage survey. By exploring the evolution of the dental hygiene literature over time, this study offers insights into the dynamics of a discipline's knowledge base and the implications for information professionals, researchers, and practitioners. This study provides librarians, educators, and researchers with valuable evidence to inform collection development, user education, and search strategy design in the field of dental hygiene. Moreover, it establishes a baseline for measuring future developments in dental hygiene scholarship. To achieve this, we adopted the protocol established by the Medical Library Association's Mapping the Literature of Nursing and Allied Health project, which utilizes citation analysis to identify the most frequently cited journals in a discipline's literature. Our study replicates and extends Haaland's (1999) original dental hygiene mapping study, allowing for direct comparison across approximately two decades. The conceptual framework of our study is grounded in Bradford's Law of Scattering, which posits that journals contributing to a subject can be divided into a core zone and successive peripheral zones, each yielding approximately one-third of the relevant citations while requiring progressively more journals. We chose citation analysis as our primary approach because cited references reflect the sources that authors actually rely on, providing a more direct indicator of use than subscription or circulation data. This approach is particularly useful in understanding the information-seeking behaviors of researchers and practitioners in the field. To identify the source journals for our study, we drew on the original study and current subject listings to select core dental hygiene titles. These included the Journal of Dental Hygiene, the International Journal of Dental Hygiene, and the Journal of Clinical Periodontology, among others. We confirmed the eligibility of these journals against the National Library of Medicine catalog and CINAHL subject headings, applying the following criteria: the journal had to be published in English, peer-reviewed, focused on dental hygiene practice, education, or research, and have published research or review articles during the period 2015-2017. Newsletters and trade publications consisting solely of news items were excluded from our analysis. We selected a three-year window for our study to balance representativeness against feasibility, minimizing the influence of anomalous issues or themed supplements on the citation distribution. Our sampling and data collection process involved screening all articles published in the selected journals from January 2015 through December 2017 for eligibility. We retained original research articles, systematic and narrative reviews, case reports, and position papers containing reference lists, while excluding editorials, letters, book reviews, abstracts of conference proceedings, and items without bibliographies. For each eligible article, we extracted the complete reference list from the publisher's website, PubMed Central, or the full-text PDF when necessary. We transferred the reference lists to a spreadsheet, with each row representing a single citation, and recorded fields including source journal, source article identifier, publication year of the source article, cited item title, cited journal or publisher, cited publication year, and cited format. Citations were collected in 2018, and to minimize transcription errors, a second reviewer independently verified a random 10% sample of articles against the original reference lists. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus, and where systematic errors were found, the affected batch was rechecked in full. We categorized each citation into one of five mutually exclusive format categories: journal articles, books, government publications, Internet sources, and other. Haaland's (1999) scheme employed categories for journals, books, government documents, and miscellaneous items; we added an "Internet sources" category to reflect the increasing presence of web-based material in the field. Internet sources were defined as web pages, online reports, and online resources lacking a traditional publication frame, such as organizational websites, clinical guidelines hosted solely online, and data repositories. Items that could not be reliably classified, such as personal communications, theses, conference presentations, and software, were assigned to the "other" category. Two reviewers independently coded a pilot set of 200 citations, and we assessed interrater agreement using Cohen's kappa. Disagreements were resolved through discussion before coding the full dataset. Our analysis involved calculating citation counts and proportions for each format and comparing them descriptively with Haaland's (1999) published values. We also computed the age of cited material as the difference between the publication year of the citing article and the publication year of the cited item, grouping citations into age categories of 0-5, 6-10, 11-15, 16-20, and more than 20 years. The cumulative proportion of citations aged 10 years or younger was used as a summary indicator of the currency of the literature, consistent with the earlier study. Because proportions from the two studies derive from different samples, we interpreted differences descriptively, calculating 95% confidence intervals for proportions using the Wilson method and conducting chi-square tests of independence to compare the distribution of formats between 1999 and the present sample, with a two-sided significance level of 0.05. Our Bradford analysis of journal citations involved aggregating citations to journal articles by cited journal title, normalizing journal titles by resolving abbreviations, title changes, and variant spellings against the NLM Catalog and ISSN Portal. We ranked journals in descending order of citation frequency, dividing the ranked list into three zones, each containing as close as possible to one-third of the total journal citations. Zone 1 was designated the core, Zone 2 the first peripheral group, and Zone 3 the remaining titles. Each Zone 1 and Zone 2 title was categorized by subject focus using the title's scope statement and NLM subject headings. Our analysis provides a detailed understanding of the citation patterns in dental hygiene literature, highlighting the core journals, authors, and topics that shape the field. By examining the age and format of cited materials, we can gain insights into the information-seeking behaviors of researchers and practitioners, informing the development of more effective search strategies and collection development policies. Ultimately, this study aims to contribute to the ongoing development of dental hygiene scholarship, providing a foundation for future research and informing evidence-based practice in the field. To better understand the discipline-specific nature of the core literature, we conducted an assessment of database coverage. Our analysis focused on the journals in Zones 1 and 2, which we searched in CINAHL Complete (EBSCOhost), MEDLINE (via PubMed and the NLM journal selection list), and Embase (Elsevier). We verified coverage using each vendor's current title list during 2018 and, when necessary, by searching for recent articles from the journal by ISSN. A title was considered indexed if it was covered selectively or comprehensively in the database, and we recorded the type of coverage (cover-to-cover or selective) as well as whether the database offered full text. We calculated coverage as both the percentage of titles and the percentage of citations accounted for by indexed titles in each zone. Our examination of overlap among databases revealed journals indexed in one, two, or all three resources, as well as those not indexed in any.
