Ovarian cancer is a devastating disease, ranking as the eighth most common cancer in women worldwide and one of the most lethal gynaecological malignancies. The statistics are stark: approximately 295,000 new cases and 185,000 deaths occur annually, with the majority of women being diagnosed at an advanced stage due to the asymptomatic nature of early disease and the lack of effective population screening (Bray et al., 2018; Torre et al., 2018; Reid et al., 2017). The standard treatment approach, which combines cytoreductive surgery with platinum- and taxane-based chemotherapy, can lead to initial clinical responses, but the majority of women with advanced disease will relapse, resulting in a five-year survival rate of less than 50% (Torre et al., 2018). As a result, ovarian cancer is increasingly being viewed as a chronic, relapsing condition, characterized by alternating periods of intensive treatment, surveillance, and uncertainty about recurrence. This trajectory, marked by the physical burden of surgery, treatment toxicity, symptoms such as ascites and bowel obstruction, and threats to fertility and body image, places women with ovarian cancer at significant risk of psychological morbidity. Depression and anxiety are the most common psychiatric complications in oncology, with a meta-analysis of interview-based studies estimating the prevalence of major depression at around 14% in oncological settings and 16% in palliative-care settings (Mitchell et al., 2011). Furthermore, anxiety and adjustment disorders contribute a substantial burden, highlighting the need for comprehensive psychological care. The consequences of psychological distress in cancer extend far beyond subjective suffering, with links to poorer adherence to treatment, reduced quality of life, greater healthcare utilization, impaired functioning, and increased suicide risk (Pitman et al., 2018; Fann et al., 2008). Moreover, meta-analytic evidence suggests that depression is associated with higher cancer-specific and all-cause mortality (Satin et al., 2009). In ovarian cancer specifically, experimental and clinical work has suggested that behavioral and neuroendocrine pathways, including adrenergic signaling, may influence tumor progression, providing a biological rationale for the clinical relevance of affective symptoms in this disease (Lutgendorf et al., 2008, 2012). Despite the importance of detecting and managing depression and anxiety, these conditions remain underrecognized and undertreated in cancer care. Clinicians often attribute low mood, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and loss of appetite to the disease or its treatment rather than to a treatable affective disorder, and consultations are frequently dominated by oncological and physical concerns (Mitchell et al., 2011; Pitman et al., 2018). In gynaecological oncology, where patients are often managed within time-limited clinic appointments and with limited access to psycho-oncology services, there is a particular risk that distress goes unidentified. To address this issue, it is essential to have robust data on the prevalence of depression and anxiety in ovarian cancer, as well as the points in the illness trajectory where the risk is greatest. However, the existing literature on this topic is fragmented and inconsistent, with reported prevalence estimates ranging widely from under 10% to more than 40% for depressive symptoms and similarly for anxiety (Norton et al., 2004; Hipkins et al., 2004). Several factors contribute to this heterogeneity, including variations in sampling frames and sample sizes, disease stage and treatment modality, and the instruments used to define caseness. The timing of assessment relative to treatment also differs between studies, which can significantly impact the results. Women assessed shortly after diagnosis may experience a different psychological profile than those undergoing chemotherapy or those in remission, who must contend with fear of recurrence and the late effects of treatment. Previous reviews of psychological outcomes in gynaecological or ovarian cancer have generally pooled findings across the care pathway or focused on quality of life and broader constructs of distress rather than on clinically meaningful depression and anxiety. As a result, it remains unclear whether prevalence differs systematically across the stages of treatment and how it compares with that in the general female population, where the 12-month prevalence of major depression and anxiety disorders is estimated at roughly 6% to 8% and 10% to 15%, respectively (Kessler et al., 2005; Baxter et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2013). This knowledge gap has practical as well as scientific importance, as it can inform the timing and resourcing of screening schedules, referral pathways, and supportive interventions. If depression and anxiety peak at particular junctures, such as around diagnosis, during chemotherapy, or after treatment completion, then targeted interventions can be developed to address these specific needs. Conversely, if prevalence is uniformly elevated across the illness course, continuous surveillance of psychological well-being should be embedded within routine follow-up. Contemporary survivorship frameworks and the growing emphasis on patient-reported outcomes in oncology make this evidence timely. Quantitative synthesis can quantify the extent to which observed prevalence exceeds population norms, informing health-service planning and the design of future trials of psychological and pharmacological interventions in this population. The present study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze the published literature on the prevalence of depression and anxiety in women with ovarian cancer, stratified by stage of treatment. Specifically, we sought to estimate pooled prevalence rates of depression and anxiety separately before treatment, during active treatment, and after treatment completion, and to compare these with prevalence in the healthy female population. We hypothesized that the prevalence of both conditions would be elevated relative to the general population at every stage and that it would vary with the phase of the treatment pathway. This work makes several contributions to the field. First, it provides the first meta-analytic estimates of depression and anxiety prevalence in ovarian cancer that are explicitly differentiated by treatment stage, rather than aggregated across heterogeneous clinical contexts. Second, by applying systematic search procedures and explicit inclusion criteria to primary research, and by pooling data from several thousand patients, it offers more precise estimates than any individual study can provide, together with an appraisal of the sources of between-study variability. Third, it benchmarks these estimates against population-level data, thereby clarifying the extent to which ovarian cancer patients experience elevated levels of depression and anxiety compared to the general female population. By addressing these knowledge gaps, this study aims to inform the development of targeted interventions and improve the psychological care of women with ovarian cancer. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantify the magnitude of excess psychological morbidity in women with ovarian cancer, a critical issue that has garnered significant attention in recent years. The review's primary objective was to estimate the pooled prevalence of depression and anxiety in this patient group, stratified by treatment stage. By synthesizing the existing evidence, we sought to provide a comprehensive understanding of the psychological distress experienced by women with ovarian cancer, which is essential for informing clinical practice and guiding future research. Furthermore, by identifying areas where evidence is sparse or methodologically limited, this review highlights priorities for future studies and contributes to ongoing efforts to ensure that psychological distress in ovarian cancer is recognised and adequately treated. The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement and the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidelines. The protocol was developed a priori by all authors, and any deviations from it were resolved through consensus. To ensure transparency and rigour, the review protocol was carefully designed to minimise bias and ensure that all relevant studies were included. The eligibility criteria for this review were carefully defined to ensure that only studies that met specific criteria were included. Studies were eligible if they were full-length, peer-reviewed journal articles published in English, enrolled adult women with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of ovarian cancer, and assessed depression, anxiety, or both using a validated self-report instrument or a structured or semi-structured clinical interview. Additionally, studies were required to report, or allow calculation of, the number of patients meeting a defined threshold for depression or anxiety, together with the total sample size. Cohort, cross-sectional, and baseline data from randomised or non-randomised trials were considered, while case reports, qualitative studies, reviews, conference abstracts, and dissertations were excluded. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search strategy was developed, combining controlled vocabulary and free-text terms relating to ovarian neoplasms, depression, and anxiety. The search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, from inception to the date of the final search. No restrictions were placed on publication date, and the reference lists of all included articles and relevant previous reviews were hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies. Forward citation tracking was also performed for key papers to ensure that all relevant studies were captured. Study selection was a rigorous process, with two reviewers independently screening titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. The full texts of potentially relevant records were then retrieved and assessed independently by the same reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or, where necessary, adjudication by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the full-text stage was quantified using Cohen's kappa, providing a measure of the consistency between reviewers. Data extraction was conducted independently by two reviewers using a standardised, piloted form, with extracted variables including study design, sample size, mean or median age, cancer stage and histology, and the instrument used to assess depression and anxiety. Treatment stage at the time of assessment was also recorded and classified into three categories: pretreatment, on-treatment, and post-treatment. Where a study reported data at multiple time points, each time point was extracted and assigned to the relevant category, with a single study contributing no more than one estimate to any given treatment-stage pooled analysis. To assess the risk of bias, the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data was used, evaluating the appropriateness of the sampling frame and sampling method, adequacy of sample size, description of participants and setting, coverage of the sample in data analysis, validity and reliability of the measurement of the condition, appropriateness of statistical analysis, and adequacy of the response rate. Each item was rated as yes, no, unclear, or not applicable, with studies classified as being at low, moderate, or high risk of bias. Quality ratings were used to inform sensitivity analyses, rather than as grounds for exclusion. The primary outcomes of this review were the pooled prevalence of depression and the pooled prevalence of anxiety in women with ovarian cancer, each stratified by treatment stage. Prevalence was defined as the proportion of participants scoring at or above the validated cut-off of the instrument used in the primary study, or meeting diagnostic criteria on clinical interview. Because instruments differ in their operating characteristics, the instrument type was recorded and examined as a potential source of heterogeneity. Statistical analysis was conducted using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian-Laird estimator, given the anticipated clinical and methodological diversity among studies. Separate meta-analyses were conducted for depression and anxiety at each treatment stage, with prevalence estimates and their standard errors computed for each study from the number of cases and sample size. The Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation was used to stabilise study-level proportions prior to pooling, and pooled estimates were back-transformed for presentation as percentages with 95% confidence intervals. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and quantified using the I² statistic, with values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% interpreted as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. Between-study variance was estimated as τ², providing a measure of the variability in prevalence estimates across studies. Where sufficient studies were available, subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, including instrument type and treatment stage. In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis provides a comprehensive overview of the prevalence of depression and anxiety in women with ovarian cancer, highlighting the need for increased awareness and support for this patient group. By identifying areas where evidence is sparse or methodologically limited, this review informs priorities for future research and contributes to ongoing efforts to ensure that psychological distress in ovarian cancer is recognised and adequately treated. The findings of this review have important implications for clinical practice, highlighting the need for routine screening and assessment of psychological distress in women

Panic disorder is a prevalent and debilitating anxiety disorder, marked by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks, persistent concerns about future attacks or their consequences, and often maladaptive behavioral changes, such as avoidance of situations that may trigger feared bodily sensations (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). The lifetime prevalence of panic disorder is estimated to be around 2-5%, with 12-month prevalence rates ranging from 2-3%, depending on the diagnostic criteria and region (Kessler et al., 2005; Wittchen et al., 2011). Typically, panic disorder begins in early adulthood and, if left untreated, tends to follow a chronic or relapsing course, resulting in significant functional impairment, reduced quality of life, and high rates of comorbid depression and agoraphobia (Roy-Byrne et al., 2006; Wittchen et al., 2011). Furthermore, individuals with panic disorder often require substantial healthcare services, particularly in primary and emergency care settings, making effective and accessible treatment a pressing public health concern. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely recognized as the most established psychological treatment for panic disorder, with its core components including psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring of catastrophic misinterpretations of bodily sensations, interoceptive exposure, and in vivo exposure to avoided situations. Numerous meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have consistently demonstrated large effects of CBT relative to waitlist and other inactive controls, as well as durable gains at follow-up (Mitte, 2005; Otte, 2011). A network meta-analysis of psychological therapies for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia also found CBT-based approaches, particularly those incorporating exposure, to be superior to many comparators (Pompoli et al., 2016). As a result, clinical guidelines in several countries recommend CBT as a first-line treatment, alongside pharmacotherapy with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Despite the strong evidence base for CBT, a significant treatment gap persists, with most individuals with panic disorder never receiving adequate care. Epidemiological data from the World Mental Health Surveys indicate that only a minority of individuals with anxiety disorders receive minimally adequate treatment, with this shortfall being most pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (Kohn et al., 2004; Alonso et al., 2018). Even in high-income health systems, access to therapists trained in evidence-based CBT is constrained by workforce shortages, long waiting times, and geographic disparities. At the individual level, stigma, cost, time constraints, limited mental health literacy, and reluctance to engage in face-to-face exposure exercises further hinder help-seeking (Andrade et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2004). To address this treatment gap, there is a need for delivery models that are scalable, flexible, and retain the active ingredients of CBT. Internet-delivered psychological treatments have been proposed as one potential solution, offering structured therapeutic content in modular form via web-based platforms or mobile applications, often combining text, audio, video, and interactive exercises with homework assignments and self-monitoring. These interventions can be accessed at any time and place, may reduce therapist time per patient, and may lower the threshold for seeking help due to their anonymity and convenience (Andersson & Titov, 2014). Meta-analytic evidence suggests that Internet-delivered CBT can produce clinically meaningful improvements across anxiety disorders, with some trials demonstrating outcomes comparable to those of face-to-face treatment (Andrews et al., 2010; Olthuis et al., 2016). For panic disorder specifically, early trials showed that therapist-supported Internet-based CBT could achieve effects similar to those of live therapy (Carlbring et al., 2005), and subsequent studies have examined a growing range of formats. Several features distinguish current internet-delivered treatments and may influence both their effectiveness and feasibility in routine care. The degree and type of human support vary substantially, ranging from regular individualized therapist feedback to minimal or on-demand contact, to fully self-guided programs with no personal contact. Reviews across mental disorders suggest that guided interventions generally yield larger effects and better adherence than unguided formats, although the differences are smaller when support is brief or administrative in nature (Baumeister et al., 2014; Johansson & Andersson, 2012). Because therapist time is the main cost driver of guided programs, the question of how much guidance is necessary is central to implementation. Treatment approaches also differ in scope, with disorder-specific programs targeting the maintaining mechanisms of panic disorder directly, whereas transdiagnostic programs address common processes across anxiety and mood disorders, potentially suiting patients with comorbidity or diagnostic uncertainty, as well as services seeking to offer a single flexible program (Newby et al., 2015). Theoretical orientation is no longer confined to CBT, as alternative frameworks such as psychodynamic or acceptance-based approaches are being adapted for online delivery. However, efficacy under trial conditions does not guarantee real-world benefit, and the potential of internet-delivered treatments depends equally on their acceptability to users and providers, commonly operationalized through attrition, adherence to treatment modules, and treatment satisfaction. Dropout and nonusage are persistent problems in digital health, a phenomenon described as the "law of attrition" (Eysenbach, 2005). Attrition and adherence rates vary widely across trials and are influenced by program design, support, and participant characteristics (Christensen et al., 2009; Kelders et al., 2012). Moreover, uptake outside research settings is limited by skepticism among both the public and health professionals, concerns about the therapeutic relationship, data security, and suitability for severe or complex presentations (Apolinário-Hagen et al., 2018; Andersson & Titov, 2014). Given the complexity of these issues, clinicians need a clear and current overview of which internet-delivered formats work, for whom, and with what level of user engagement. However, existing evidence syntheses only partly meet this need, as many reviews pool findings across anxiety disorders or across mental disorders in general, which can obscure differences between diagnostic groups (Andrews et al., 2010; Olthuis et al., 2016). Panic disorder has distinctive treatment components, particularly interoceptive exposure, whose translation into unsupervised digital formats may pose particular challenges. Furthermore, the field has developed rapidly, with newer trials testing self-guided and transdiagnostic programs, comparing different support intensities, and examining alternatives to CBT. These developments have not been summarized with a dual focus on clinical effectiveness and acceptability indicators specific to panic disorder. Consequently, little is known about the relative usefulness of different support formats and treatment approaches in this population. To address this gap, the present narrative review aims to synthesize recent RCT evidence on internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder, with a focus on both clinical effectiveness and acceptability indicators. By examining the existing literature, we hope to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of internet-delivered treatments for panic disorder, highlighting the key features that influence their effectiveness and feasibility in routine care. Ultimately, this review aims to inform the development of scalable, flexible, and effective delivery models that can help bridge the treatment gap for individuals with panic disorder. This review seeks to address two fundamental questions regarding the efficacy and acceptability of internet-delivered treatments for panic disorder. Firstly, how effective are these interventions compared to control conditions, and do outcomes vary depending on the format of support, such as guided versus self-guided, or the treatment approach, such as disorder-specific versus transdiagnostic? Secondly, what is the level of acceptability of these interventions, as reflected in attrition rates, adherence, and participant satisfaction? To capture the current state of the field, we limited our review to trials published within the past five years, thereby reflecting recent technological and methodological advancements. This review contributes to the existing literature in three key ways. It provides a much-needed update on the efficacy of internet-delivered treatments specifically for panic disorder, complementing broader syntheses focused on anxiety disorders. By systematically comparing support formats and treatment approaches, this review informs decisions about implementation in routine and stepped care. Furthermore, it integrates efficacy data with indicators of acceptability, identifying areas where the evidence is strong, limited, or warrants further research, such as improving uptake and identifying moderators of outcome. Our design involved conducting a narrative review of recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder. Given the heterogeneity of interventions, support formats, comparison conditions, and outcome measures, a narrative synthesis was deemed more suitable than a quantitative meta-analysis (Popay et al., 2006). We adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) where applicable, although the review was not prospectively registered. To be eligible for inclusion, studies had to meet specific criteria. They had to be RCTs published in English-language peer-reviewed journals between December 2012 and December 2017, involving adult participants (aged 18 or older) with a primary diagnosis of panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia, established according to DSM-IV, DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), or ICD-10 criteria. Ideally, diagnoses were made using structured or semi-structured clinical interviews. The interventions had to be psychological treatments delivered predominantly via the internet, with or without therapist guidance. Studies were required to report at least one symptom-related outcome for panic disorder, such as panic frequency or severity, agoraphobic avoidance, or general anxiety symptoms. No restrictions were placed on the theoretical orientation of the intervention, the type of support, or the comparison condition. Eligible comparators included waitlist, attention or placebo controls, treatment as usual, face-to-face therapy, and alternative internet-delivered programs. Both transdiagnostic and disorder-specific programs were considered, provided that outcome data were reported for participants with panic disorder. We excluded study protocols, uncontrolled or non-randomized trials, secondary or follow-up analyses that did not report new data, conference abstracts, dissertations, and studies conducted exclusively with children or adolescents. Interventions that used the internet only as an adjunct to face-to-face treatment or delivered solely by telephone or videoconference without a structured online program were also excluded, as were trials of pharmacological interventions or purely psychoeducational websites without a therapeutic component. Our systematic search was conducted in PubMed/Medline and PSYNDEX, covering biomedical and psychological literature in German and English. The search spanned the period from December 2012 to December 2017, reflecting the most recent five years of research in this rapidly evolving field. The search string combined terms related to the condition (e.g., "panic disorder," "panic attack," "agoraphobia"), the mode of delivery (e.g., "internet," "online," "web-based"), and the study design (e.g., "randomized controlled trial," "RCT"). We used controlled vocabulary (Medical Subject Headings in PubMed/Medline) in conjunction with free-text terms in titles and abstracts, adapting the strategy to the syntax of each database. To supplement our database search, we conducted a hand search by screening the reference lists of included articles and recent reviews and meta-analyses on internet-delivered treatments for anxiety disorders (e.g., Andersson et al., 2014; Olthuis et al., 2016). This helped identify trials that may not have been captured by our database search. Records were exported to a reference management program, and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria, and the full texts of potentially relevant articles were retrieved and assessed in detail. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were documented, and disagreements or uncertainties regarding eligibility were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached. For each included study, we extracted data using a standardized form. This included information on the authors, year of publication, country, sample size, participant characteristics (mean age, proportion of women, diagnostic procedure, and comorbidity criteria), intervention characteristics (theoretical approach, content specificity, program duration, number of modules, and type and amount of human support), comparison condition, primary and secondary outcome measures, timing of assessments, and analytic approach. Efficacy was defined as the superiority of an internet-delivered intervention over a control condition or differences between active treatment formats on measures of panic symptoms, such as the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (Shear et al., 1997), the Body Sensations Questionnaire, the Agoraphobic Cognitions Questionnaire, and the Mobility Inventory (Chambless et al., 1984, 1985). Where available, we extracted between-group effect sizes (Cohen's d or Hedges' g) as reported by the authors, interpreting values of approximately 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 as small, moderate, and large, respectively (Cohen, 1988). When effect sizes were not reported, we noted the statistical significance of between-group differences at the post-treatment and follow-up assessments. By synthesizing this information, we aimed to provide a comprehensive overview of the efficacy and acceptability of internet-delivered treatments for panic disorder, highlighting areas of strength and limitation in the current evidence base and informing priorities for future research.

The growing disconnect between humans and the natural world has become a pressing concern in environmental scholarship, education, and public health. The notion of "nature-deficit disorder," popularized by Louv (2005), has sparked a wave of research into the psychological, physical, and civic benefits of interacting with nature. Studies have consistently shown that exposure to green spaces can have a positive impact on mental health, reducing stress and improving attention (Kaplan 1995; Ulrich et al. 1991; Bratman et al. 2019). Moreover, childhood experiences in nature have been linked to the development of environmental concern and pro-environmental behavior in adulthood (Wells and Lekies 2006; Chawla 2020). To capture these relationships, scholars have developed various constructs, including connectedness to nature (Mayer and Frantz 2004), nature relatedness (Nisbet, Zelenski, and Murphy 2009), and biophilia (Wilson 1984; Kellert and Wilson 1993). While this research has shed light on the importance of human-nature connections, it often relies on structured scales that limit our understanding of the complex and nuanced ways people think about nature. Most studies, for instance, ask respondents to agree or disagree with pre-defined statements, which can obscure the richness and diversity of human experiences. A low score on a connectedness scale might indicate boredom, fear, or indifference, while a high score might reflect thoughts of serene landscapes, recreational activities, or ecological interdependence. The meanings attached to nature are socially constructed and historically contingent (Cronon 1995; Williams 1980), suggesting that the associations people make with nature will vary depending on their social positions and experiences. However, few scholars have investigated the fundamental question of what people think about when they contemplate nature, and even fewer have examined how these thoughts differ across social groups. This oversight is significant, as the dominant "positive" framing of nature in the literature may mask a more complex reality. Nature has long been a source of both inspiration and fear, with Tuan (1979) documenting the landscapes of fear that shape human settlement and imagination. Ulrich (1993) and Öhman and Mineka (2001) have argued that humans are predisposed to learn fear of certain natural stimuli, such as snakes, heights, and darkness. In the American imagination, wilderness has been depicted as both sublime and menacing, a site of spiritual renewal and mortal danger (Nash 2001; Cronon 1995). Environmental psychologists have noted that fear of crime, getting lost, or encountering dangerous animals can deter people from engaging in outdoor activities (Jorgensen and Anthopoulou 2007; Bixler and Floyd 1997). For example, Bixler and Floyd (1997) found that adolescents who preferred indoor activities often reported feelings of disgust, fear, and discomfort in wildland settings. These fears are not merely individual quirks but may be patterned by social experience, with historical exclusion, segregation, and racial violence in rural and wild places shaping the relationships many Black, Indigenous, Latino, and Asian American communities have with parks and wilderness (Finney 2014; Taylor 2016; Mock 2018). Research on outdoor recreation has highlighted the role of marginality, discrimination, cultural preferences, and unequal access in shaping differential participation (Floyd 1999; Washburne 1978; Flores, Falco, and Morales 2018). The legacy of lynching and plantation landscapes, for instance, can complicate assumptions about the universality of rural nature as a safe or restorative space (Finney 2014; Kimmerer 2013 offers a contrasting Indigenous perspective emphasizing reciprocity rather than fear). At the same time, scholars caution against essentializing minority communities, which have deep traditions of farming, fishing, gardening, and environmental stewardship (Taylor 2016; Mohai, Pellow, and Roberts 2009). Survey evidence often shows that racial and ethnic minorities express equal or greater environmental concern than whites (Pearson, Schuldt, and Romero-Canyas 2016), highlighting the need for nuanced and contextualized understandings of human-nature relationships. The complexity of these relationships is further underscored by the intersection of multiple social factors, including gender, social class, and parental education. Gender, for example, has been linked to differences in fear of crime and natural hazards in outdoor settings (Pain 2001; Valentine 1989), as well as differing environmental attitudes more broadly (Zelezny, Chua, and Aldrich 2000). Social class and parental education shape access to leisure time, travel, camps, and parks (Stodolska and Shinew 2010), while first-generation college students may bring distinctive experiences and constraints to higher education (Stephens et al. 2012). Age and life stage also influence both exposure and attitude, with academic interest or major emerging as another plausible influence on what people associate with nature (Hungerford and Volk 1990). However, these factors are rarely analyzed together, and when they are not, apparent racial differences may reflect confounding with class, gender, or educational background. An intersectional and multivariate approach is necessary to disentangle these influences (Crenshaw 1991; Finney 2014). College and university students offer a useful population for investigating these questions, as they are at a formative stage in which environmental identities and career orientations are consolidating. They are also the future leaders, professionals, and voters whose decisions will shape environmental policy. Campuses are increasingly diverse in terms of race, class, and generational status, allowing for comparisons across groups that share a common institutional context. Educators seeking to foster environmental literacy and outdoor engagement need to understand the associations students bring with them, including fear, danger, and loathing, if programs are to be welcoming and effective (Chawla 2020; Rickinson et al. 2004). This study addresses two research questions: How do college and university students think about nature, particularly in terms of concepts like fear, danger, disconnection, and loathing? Which social and academic factors, including race and ethnicity, gender, age, social class, parental education, first-generation status, and academic interest, shape these thoughts? By analyzing open-ended responses from 287 American students, this research aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex and multifaceted ways people think about nature. This study makes three significant contributions to our understanding of how students think about nature. Firstly, it redirects attention from the strength of the human-nature connection to the actual content of students' thoughts about nature, shedding light on the nuances of their relationships with the natural world. Secondly, it highlights the negative and ambivalent associations that students have with nature, which tend to be overlooked in the existing literature. Thirdly, it demonstrates that while race is a significant factor in shaping students' perceptions of nature, it intersects with other variables such as academic interest, gender, age, and family educational background, cautioning against simplistic narratives about minority disconnection from nature. Our research design employed a cross-sectional survey with a mixed-methods approach, combining the strengths of both qualitative and quantitative methods. We used open-ended responses to allow students to express their thoughts about nature spontaneously, without being constrained by pre-defined categories or scales. These responses were then systematically coded into thematic categories using a rigorous coding procedure, and the resulting binary indicators were analyzed using descriptive and multivariate statistics. This approach was well-suited to our research question, as it enabled us to capture the complexity and diversity of students' thoughts about nature. In contrast to closed-ended instruments such as the Connectedness to Nature Scale or the New Ecological Paradigm, which measure attitudes towards pre-defined constructs, our open-ended prompt allowed respondents to name their own ideas and associations with nature. This approach was deliberate, as we sought to understand what students think about when they contemplate nature, without imposing our own definitions or categories on their responses. Data were collected from undergraduate students at two public universities in the United States during one academic term, using an anonymous online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform. The survey was distributed by instructors in a range of general education and discipline-specific courses, including environmental science, biology, sociology, business, education, and the humanities, to reach students with diverse academic interests. Participation was voluntary, and some instructors offered a small amount of extra credit, with an alternative assignment of equal effort available. The institutional review board at the lead author's university approved the protocol and classified it as exempt, and informed consent was obtained electronically before respondents could begin the survey. A total of 301 students opened the survey, and after excluding 14 respondents who did not complete the open-ended prompt or demographic items, our analytic sample consisted of 287 students (95.3% of those who started). While our sample is non-probability and drawn from a limited number of courses, we treat the analysis as exploratory, focusing on the direction, magnitude, and consistency of associations rather than population estimates. The questionnaire consisted of an open-ended prompt followed by demographic and background items. The prompt was deliberately neutral, asking respondents to list or describe as many thoughts, ideas, images, or feelings as they wished when they thought of nature. This neutrality allowed us to capture the full range of students' associations with nature, without priming or influencing their responses. Responses ranged from single words to multi-sentence paragraphs, and were coded for eight concepts that prior scholarship has linked to negative or ambivalent relationships with nature, including disconnection from nature, predators or dangerous animals, getting lost, loathsome or hateful places, fear, danger, natural hazards, and human-made hazards. These categories build on research on fear and avoidance of natural settings, racialized experiences of outdoor spaces, and the notion of "nature-deficit." Each concept was coded as 1 if the respondent mentioned it at least once, and 0 otherwise, and we analyzed presence rather than frequency of mention, as the responses were brief and counts would have conflated verbosity with salience. Independent variables included race/ethnicity, gender, age, class standing, parental education, first-generation status, and academic interest. Race/ethnicity was collapsed into a binary variable, and gender was coded as woman or man, with seven non-binary respondents retained in descriptive tables but excluded from multivariate models due to lack of power. Age was measured in years, and class standing was entered as an ordinal variable treated as continuous after sensitivity tests with dummy coding produced substantively identical results. Parental education was the highest level attained by either parent, and first-generation status was coded as 1 if neither parent had completed a four-year degree. Because parental education and first-generation status are conceptually and empirically related, they were never entered in the same model. Academic interest was operationalized as whether a student's major or intended major was in a natural resource, environmental, or life science field, using major as a proxy for interest follows prior work on how disciplinary socialization shapes environmental orientations. Coding followed a hybrid deductive-inductive strategy, with a preliminary codebook derived from the literature, and two coders independently reading a random 20% subsample and proposing additional categories and clarifying decision rules. Definitions and exemplar quotations were revised in two rounds, and both coders then independently coded the full dataset, blind to respondent demographics. Intercoder agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa, with values ranging from 0.78 to 0.91, indicating substantial to almost perfect agreement. Disagreements were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached, and the consensus codes were used in all analyses. Statistical analysis proceeded in three stages. Firstly, we calculated frequencies and percentages for each concept for the full sample and by race/ethnicity, gender, and academic interest. Bivariate associations between the binary outcomes and categorical predictors were tested with Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test when any expected cell count was below five. Effect sizes were reported as phi or Cramér's V. For continuous and ordinal predictors, we used linear regression and logistic regression models to examine the relationships between the independent variables and the presence of negative or ambivalent associations with nature. By examining the intersections between these variables, we aimed to provide a nuanced understanding of how students think about nature, and how their relationships with the natural world are shaped by a complex array of factors. Our analysis employed a multi-faceted approach to examine the relationships between racial/ethnic identity and associations with nature. To begin with, we utilized point-biserial correlations and Mann-Whitney U tests to explore the bivariate relationships between these variables. Given that we examined eight distinct outcomes, we opted to report exact p-values and exercise caution when interpreting results that approached conventional thresholds of significance, rather than relying on a single

Spoken language identification (SLD) is a fundamental component of multilingual speech processing systems, including automatic speech recognition, spoken-document retrieval, speech translation, and call-center routing. The task involves determining the language of a speech utterance without prior knowledge of its content or speaker, and it has become increasingly important in various applications, such as intelligent vehicles, where voice interfaces need to serve drivers and passengers who speak different languages. In such settings, utterances are often brief, typically ranging from one to three seconds, and the acoustic environment is noisy, making accurate and low-latency SLD both practically valuable and technically demanding. Early SLD systems relied heavily on phonotactic information, using techniques such as parallel phone recognition followed by language modeling (PPRLM). This approach decodes speech into phone sequences using one or more phone recognizers and scores the sequences with language-specific n-gram models. While effective for long utterances, these systems require phonetically transcribed data and degrade significantly when dealing with short utterances, as the limited speech available yields too few phone tokens for reliable statistics. In contrast, acoustic approaches model the spectral distribution of each language directly, and Gaussian mixture models trained on shifted delta cepstral (SDC) features and total variability i-vector modeling became the dominant paradigm in the 2000s and early 2010s. However, i-vector estimation is itself unreliable for short segments, as the posterior of the latent variable has high variance when few frames are observed. The introduction of deep neural networks (DNNs) has substantially changed the field, with studies showing that DNNs can outperform i-vector baselines, particularly on short test segments. For instance, Lopez-Moreno et al. (2014) demonstrated that a DNN taking SDC-like inputs and trained directly for language classification achieved superior results. Subsequent studies have used DNN-derived posteriors or bottleneck activations as replacements for, or complements to, conventional cepstral features in the i-vector pipeline. Bottleneck features, which are taken from a narrow hidden layer of a network trained on an auxiliary classification task, compress phonetically discriminative information into a low-dimensional representation. This approach enables the transfer of linguistic knowledge into settings where language-labeled data are scarce, as the auxiliary task can be trained with abundant transcribed speech from a single resource-rich language. Recurrent architectures, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have also been applied to SLD, modeling temporal dependencies and producing an utterance-level decision in an end-to-end fashion. These networks have been reported to be particularly effective for short utterances. Despite the progress made in SLD, several issues remain unresolved. One of the primary challenges is that the performance of nearly all SLD systems declines markedly as the test duration shrinks from 10 seconds or 30 seconds to 3 seconds or 1 second. The AP16 and AP17 Oriental Language Recognition (OLR) challenges, which focus on closely related and acoustically confusable Asian languages, illustrate this issue clearly, with error rates on 1-second utterances being several times those on 3-second or longer utterances. Furthermore, most work on improving short-utterance performance has concentrated on the model side, with relatively little attention paid to manipulating the test utterance itself to provide the classifier with more diverse evidence from the same limited signal. Another area that has received limited attention is the combination of bottleneck features trained on phonetic targets with LSTM-based end-to-end classifiers, particularly when the phonetic training language is itself one of the target languages or is closely related to them. Speech rate offers a possible route to addressing the issue of short-utterance performance, as speaking rate varies naturally across speakers, languages, and situations, altering the temporal structure of phonetic realizations while leaving much of the spectral identity intact. Time-scale modification (TSM) algorithms, such as the phase vocoder, can alter the duration of a signal without changing its pitch, and we hypothesize that presenting a classifier with the original utterance together with slowed and accelerated versions of it can effectively lengthen the observed sequence and expose the network to several plausible temporal realizations of the same content. The research question addressed in this paper is twofold: whether LSTM networks fed with deep bottleneck features learned from a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classifier provide an effective end-to-end SLD solution for short utterances, and whether phase-vocoder-based TSM of the test utterance, combined with splicing of the original, slowed, and accelerated versions, can further reduce errors when only one to three seconds of speech are available. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we propose an end-to-end SLD framework in which an LSTM classifier is trained on bottleneck features extracted from a DNN trained for Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification, thereby transferring phonetic knowledge into the language identification task while keeping the model compact enough for in-vehicle deployment. Second, we introduce a test-time augmentation strategy that applies phase-vocoder TSM to produce speech-rate-reduced and speech-rate-increased versions of an utterance and splices them with the original to extend its effective length. This approach enables the classifier to leverage the temporal structure of the speech signal, which is often discarded in traditional SLD systems. Third, we evaluate the approach on the AP17-OLR database and show that it improves identification performance relative to baseline systems, with the largest gains for 1-second utterances. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining deep bottleneck features with LSTM-based end-to-end classifiers and the benefits of using TSM to manipulate the test utterance and provide more diverse evidence to the classifier. This paper presents a comprehensive examination of language identification in the context of intelligent vehicle interaction, with a particular focus on short test durations of 1 s and 3 s. The proposed system, experimental configuration, and results are described in detail, followed by a discussion of the findings and their implications. The experiments were conducted using the AP17-OLR database, which is an extension of the AP16-OLR database and contains telephone-quality and close-talking recordings of ten languages, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Indonesian, Japanese, Russian, Korean, Vietnamese, Kazakh, Tibetan, and Uyghur. All audio data were resampled to 16 kHz with 16-bit quantization, and the training partition provided approximately 10 hours of speech per language from multiple speakers of both genders. The test partition was evaluated at nominal durations of 1 s, 3 s, and a longer full-length condition, with the 1 s and 3 s conditions being the primary focus due to their relevance to in-vehicle voice interfaces. To develop and evaluate the language identification system, a controlled, ablation-style design was employed, with three key factors: the input representation, the back-end classifier, and the test-time utterance extension strategy. Each factor was varied while the others were held fixed, allowing for the isolation of the contribution of each component. The input representation was either conventional filterbank features or deep bottleneck features (DBF), which were obtained through transfer learning from a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification task. The back-end classifier was either a frame-level DNN or an LSTM, and the test-time utterance extension strategy involved either using the original utterance only or splicing it with time-scale-modified versions. The DBF extraction process involved training a feed-forward DNN to classify each frame into context-dependent tied-state targets derived from a Mandarin corpus with forced alignments. The input to the DNN consisted of 40-dimensional log Mel-filterbank coefficients with cepstral mean normalization, computed over 25 ms windows with a 10 ms shift. The network had five hidden layers of 1024 sigmoid units, with a 64-unit linear bottleneck layer placed before the final hidden layer. The learning rate was halved when the development-set frame accuracy improved by less than 0.5% absolute, and the layers above the bottleneck were discarded after training. The 64-dimensional bottleneck activations of each frame were used as the language-independent but phonetically informed representation for all ten OLR languages. The LSTM-based language identification system used the DBF sequence of an utterance as input and consisted of two stacked unidirectional LSTM layers of 512 cells each, followed by a fully connected layer with a 10-way softmax. Unidirectional recurrence was chosen to allow for low-latency operation in embedded settings. The system was trained using truncated backpropagation through time over segments of 100 frames, and the label was applied to every frame. At test time, the utterance-level posterior was computed as the mean of the frame-level log posteriors over the last 80% of frames. To evaluate the system, two baselines were used: an LSTM on 40-dimensional filterbank features and a frame-averaging DNN on DBF. The performance of the system was reported using the average cost Cavg and the identification accuracy, with the equal error rate (EER) also being reported. Each condition was evaluated separately for 1 s, 3 s, and full-length test sets to analyze the effect of duration. In addition to the baseline systems, a phase-vocoder-based time-scale modification (TSM) algorithm was used to lengthen short test utterances without requiring additional speech. The algorithm modified the speaking rate of each test signal by a factor of either 1.25 (slower speech) or 0.80 (faster speech), which were selected on the development set from a candidate set of factors. The modified signals preserved language-specific spectral cues while changing the temporal realization of phonemes. For each test utterance, three versions (original, slowed, accelerated) were passed through the same DBF extractor, and the three DBF sequences were concatenated in time to give a single sequence. A single LSTM forward pass over the spliced sequence yielded the decision, and the splicing order was fixed as original, slowed, accelerated. The results of the experiments showed that the proposed system achieved state-of-the-art performance on the AP17-OLR database, with significant improvements in identification accuracy and average cost Cavg compared to the baseline systems. The use of DBF as the input representation and the LSTM as the back-end classifier was found to be effective in improving the performance of the system. The phase-vocoder-based TSM algorithm was also found to be effective in lengthening short test utterances, with the spliced sequence approach yielding significant improvements in identification accuracy. The findings of this study have important implications for the development of language identification systems for intelligent vehicle interaction. The use of DBF and LSTM can improve the performance of the system, and the phase-vocoder-based TSM algorithm can be used to lengthen short test utterances. The results of this study can be used to inform the design of language identification systems for a variety of applications, including intelligent vehicle interaction, speech recognition, and language translation. In conclusion, this paper presents a comprehensive examination of language identification in the context of intelligent vehicle interaction, with a particular focus on short test durations of 1 s and 3 s. The proposed system, which uses DBF and LSTM, was found to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the AP17-OLR database, with significant improvements in identification accuracy and average cost Cavg compared to the baseline systems. The phase-vocoder-based TSM algorithm was also found to be effective in lengthening short test utterances, with the spliced sequence approach yielding significant improvements in identification accuracy. The prevalence of relational tables as the primary format for structured data on the web, in enterprise databases, and in open data portals has made understanding the meaning of column headers a crucial task in data management. Knowing the semantic type of a column, such as whether it contains person names, birth places, or monetary amounts, is essential for various data management tasks, including data cleaning and validation, schema matching and data integration, data discovery, and semantic search over tables. These semantic types, which go beyond the basic atomic types used by database systems, are often linked to concepts in knowledge bases like DBpedia and Freebase or to the properties of schema.org. However, in practice, the semantic types of columns are rarely explicitly stated, and column headers are often missing, ambiguous, abbreviated, or inconsistent across sources. As a result, automatic semantic type detection has become a significant area of research. Existing approaches to semantic type detection can be broadly categorized into four families. Dictionary and regular-expression approaches, commonly used in commercial data preparation tools, match column values against curated lists or patterns. While these methods are precise for types with regular surface forms, such as email addresses or postal codes, they struggle with dirty or incomplete values and are limited to a small set of manually maintained types. Knowledge-base matching approaches, on the other hand, link cell values to entities and infer a column type based on the linked entities' classes. However, these approaches are dependent on the coverage and quality of the knowledge base and often perform poorly for numeric columns and domain-specific values. Probabilistic and graphical-model approaches jointly infer types, entities, and relations in a table but typically require expensive inference and large knowledge resources. Machine learning approaches, which treat type detection as a classification problem over columns, have also been explored. Early work used hand-crafted features of column values with traditional classifiers, while more recent approaches, such as Sherlock, have utilized deep learning models trained on large datasets like the VizNet corpus. Despite the progress made in semantic type detection, existing approaches share a fundamental limitation: they predict the type of each column in isolation, ignoring the context provided by the other columns in the table. However, values alone are often insufficient to determine a type, and human annotators typically resolve such ambiguity by considering the rest of the table. For instance, a column of short strings could be a city, a birth place, or a company location, depending on the context provided by neighboring columns. The semantic types in a table are not independent; they co-occur in systematic patterns reflecting the table's subject and exhibit dependencies among adjacent or related columns. Single-column models fail to exploit these regularities, leading to confusion between types with similar value distributions, poor performance on types with uninformative values, and degradation when columns are noisy. Incorporating table context into semantic type detection raises several challenges. First, context must be represented in a way that generalizes across tables of different widths and compositions without presupposing the identity of the other columns' types. Second, the model must capture both global, table-level context and local context, which reflects how the type of one column constrains the types of others. Third, the approach should remain scalable and trainable on a realistic corpus of web tables, where type frequencies are highly skewed. Finally, evaluation metrics should go beyond support-weighted measures, which are dominated by frequent types, and also consider macro-averaged measures that reflect performance across the whole type inventory. This paper investigates whether jointly modeling column values and table context can improve the accuracy of semantic type detection. We also explore which types of context are useful, how much each contributes, and for which types the gains are concentrated. To address these questions, we introduce Sato, a hybrid model for contextual semantic type detection. Sato builds on a single-column deep learning predictor with value-based features and augments it with two complementary sources of context. To capture table-level semantics, Sato derives a table intent vector using a topic model trained on the values of entire tables and supplies this vector as additional input to the column-wise predictor. To capture dependencies among column types, Sato employs structured prediction in the form of a linear-chain conditional random field that sits on top of the column-wise scores and decodes a jointly consistent type assignment for all columns. The combination allows the model to use value evidence, global table theme, and inter-column type co-occurrence in a single framework while remaining efficient at inference time. The contributions of this paper are multifaceted. Firstly, we demonstrate the importance of incorporating table context into semantic type detection and show that our hybrid model, Sato, can effectively capture both global and local context. Secondly, we evaluate the performance of Sato on a large corpus of web tables and demonstrate its ability to improve accuracy, particularly for rare and domain-specific types. Finally, we provide insights into the types of context that are most useful for semantic type detection and the types of tables that benefit most from our approach. By addressing the limitations of existing approaches and providing a more comprehensive understanding of the role of context in semantic type detection, this paper contributes to the development of more accurate and robust methods for automatic semantic type detection. The task of semantic type detection in relational tables is a complex one, and previous approaches have often relied on single-column models that fail to account for the rich contextual information present in these tables. In this work, we reformulate semantic type detection as a table-level, context-dependent prediction problem, and demonstrate through a large-scale analysis of a table corpus that column types exhibit a strong co-occurrence structure that is ignored by single-column models. Our proposed approach, Sato, integrates a deep column-wise model with LDA-based table topic features and a conditional random field for structured output prediction, allowing us to capture both table-level semantics and the types of neighboring columns. To evaluate the effectiveness of Sato, we conducted a comprehensive analysis on a large-scale corpus of web tables, comprising 78 semantic types. Our results show that Sato achieves state-of-the-art performance, with support-weighted and macro-average F1 scores of 0.925 and 0.735, respectively. Notably, Sato exhibits the largest gains for types that are ambiguous from values alone and for types with few training examples, highlighting the importance of contextual information in semantic type detection. At the heart of our approach is the recognition that semantic type detection is a fundamentally multi-column problem. We consider a relational table T with n columns, each comprising a sequence of string-valued cells, and aim to assign each column ci a type ti from a fixed vocabulary of 78 DBpedia-derived semantic types. Unlike single-column approaches, which model the probability of a type given a column independently, P(ti | ci), we model the joint distribution of types given the whole table, P(t1, ..., tn | T). This allows two kinds of context to inform each prediction: table-level semantics, which capture the overall "theme" of the table, and the types of neighboring columns. Our analysis is based on the VizNet corpus, specifically the WebTables-derived collection, which we matched to the 78 types by header normalization to DBpedia properties. We retained tables with at least two columns having a valid type label, yielding approximately 80,000 tables and 120,000 labeled columns. Columns whose headers did not map to a type were retained as unlabeled context for feature extraction but excluded from the loss and evaluation. To prevent models from relying on column headers, we removed them from the input, forcing models to rely solely on values and context. The type distribution in our corpus is highly imbalanced, with the most frequent types accounting for several thousand times more columns than the rarest. This motivated our use of macro-averaged metrics, which provide a more nuanced understanding of performance across types. We created five random splits of the tables into training and test sets, splitting by table rather than by column to prevent leakage between columns of the same table. A validation set of 10% of the training tables was held out for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. For single-column feature extraction, we adopted 1,588 features from Sherlock, which fall into four categories: global statistics, character-level distributions, word embeddings, and paragraph embeddings. These features provide a rich representation of each column, capturing aspects such as the number of values, the fraction of numeric cells, and the entropy of the value distribution. We standardized these features using training-set statistics to prevent feature dominance. To capture table-level semantics, we employed a Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model, treating each table as a document and its cell values as tokens. We trained the LDA model on the training tables only, with K topics, and computed the posterior mean topic vector θT for each table at inference time. This topic vector serves as a table-level feature vector, injecting global context into our model without requiring explicit column interactions. We set K = 400, selected on the validation set from a range of values. Our single-column prediction network is a feed-forward network that takes as input the concatenation of the four Sherlock feature groups and, in the context-augmented variant, the topic vector θT. Each feature group is processed by its own subnetwork, and the group embeddings are concatenated and passed through a primary network. For the topic-aware variant, θT has its own subnetwork, and its output is concatenated with the others. The network outputs a score vector for each column, from which unary potentials are derived. We trained the model using the Adam optimizer, with a learning rate of 1e-4, weight decay of 1e-4, batch size of 100, and up to 100 epochs with early stopping on validation loss. To model dependencies among column types within a table, we employed a linear-chain conditional random field (CRF) over the columns in their original left-to-right order. The CRF captures type co-occurrence and adjacency, allowing us to model the joint probability of a type sequence t = (t1, ..., tn) given a table T.
