The proliferation of network-based services in the home has led to a significant shift in the expectations surrounding residential networks. Today, a typical smart home supports a wide range of applications, including high-definition video streaming, cloud gaming, video conferencing, voice assistants, security cameras, and numerous low-power Internet of Things (IoT) devices, all of which share a single broadband access link (Sivaraman et al., 2015). These applications impose diverse demands on the network, with interactive voice and gaming traffic being sensitive to delay and jitter, streaming video requiring sustained throughput, and sensor telemetry tolerating delay but necessitating reliability. The traditional best-effort forwarding approach is no longer sufficient to meet these varied demands, and a single congested gateway can degrade the quality of experience (QoE) for the entire household (Dainotti et al., 2012). As a result, network operators must measure and manage network quality of service (QoS) on a per-application basis, rather than solely per link or per subscriber. The advent of software-defined networking (SDN) has provided operators with new tools to address this challenge. By decoupling the control plane from the data plane, SDN enables centralized, programmable allocation of resources in the core and aggregation networks (Kreutz et al., 2015). This allows operators to steer flows, reserve bandwidth, and adjust queue disciplines in response to measured conditions. However, core-network control alone is insufficient to guarantee end-to-end QoS, as much of the delay variation, packet loss, and contention occurs at the last hop, where the home gateway multiplexes traffic from multiple devices over a constrained access link. Without knowledge of the application generating a given packet, the operator cannot attribute degradation to a specific service, verify that service-level agreements are met, or apply differentiated treatment where it is most critical. The smart home gateway has emerged as a natural vantage point for application-aware measurement and control from the operator's perspective. Nevertheless, obtaining application awareness at the gateway is complicated by the widespread use of encryption, with over 90% of web traffic utilizing TLS, and QUIC, VPN tunnels, and DNS-over-HTTPS further reducing the information visible on the wire (Rescorla, 2018). Traditional port-based classification has become unreliable due to applications sharing well-known ports or using dynamic ones, while deep packet inspection (DPI) is ineffective on encrypted payloads and raises concerns about user privacy (Moore & Papagiannaki, 2005; Finsterbusch et al., 2014). Consequently, research has shifted toward statistical and machine-learning methods that utilize only side-channel features, such as packet sizes, inter-arrival times, directions, and flow durations (Nguyen & Armitage, 2008). Early studies employed classical classifiers, including naïve Bayes, support vector machines, and decision trees, on hand-crafted flow statistics (Williams et al., 2006; Moore & Zuev, 2005). More recent investigations have applied deep learning techniques, such as convolutional and recurrent networks, to raw or lightly processed traffic, achieving high accuracy for encrypted traffic characterization and application identification (Wang et al., 2017; Lotfollahi et al., 2020; Aceto et al., 2019). Related work has also demonstrated that IoT devices can be identified from their traffic signatures (Sivanathan et al., 2019) and that encrypted video services leak identifiable patterns (Dubin et al., 2017). Despite this progress, three significant gaps limit the applicability of existing approaches to operator-side management in smart home gateways. Firstly, most studies approach classification as a single, flat problem, assigning each flow to one of many fine-grained applications. This overlooks the fact that the operator's QoS decisions primarily depend on the traffic's service requirements, such as real-time interactive, streaming, bulk transfer, or background, rather than application identity. A flat classifier with many classes is often more costly and less accurate than necessary for such decisions. Secondly, accuracy and latency are rarely considered in tandem. Many high-accuracy models require complete flows or long observation windows, which delays decision-making until a flow is nearly finished, rendering it ineffective for real-time QoS control. In contrast, lightweight early-classification methods typically sacrifice the granularity needed for tasks such as statistical reporting or billing. Thirdly, the classification objective is seldom tied to the operator's needs, which include QoS measurement, usage statistics, and billing between network and service providers, all of which require trustworthy application-level information without decrypting traffic or compromising user privacy and network security. These gaps motivate our central research question: how can a network operator classify encrypted traffic at the smart home gateway to support both real-time, QoS-driven resource management and accurate fine-grained application accounting, without inspecting payloads? We hypothesize that the two requirements are best addressed by separate classifiers operating at different levels of abstraction and on different time scales, rather than a single, monolithic model. To test this hypothesis, we propose a two-level hierarchical encrypted packet classification scheme. The service level groups applications that share the same network QoS requirements and employs a fast deep-learning classifier designed for real-time operation with high accuracy on a small number of classes. Its output can drive SDN-based traffic prioritization and end-to-end QoS measurement directly. The application level distinguishes fine-grained applications within and across service classes using a non-real-time classifier that can exploit richer flow-level information to maximize accuracy. Its output supports statistical data collection, billing to service providers, and longer-term analytics. Both levels rely solely on metadata observable from encrypted traffic, preserving user privacy and eliminating the need for keys or payload access. The contributions of this paper are fourfold. Firstly, we formulate encrypted traffic classification for smart home gateways as a hierarchical problem, whose service level and application level are tied to distinct operator objectives, real-time QoS management and fine-grained accounting, respectively. We describe how the scheme fits into an SDN-managed network architecture. Secondly, we design a fast deep-learning classifier for the service level that achieves real-time classification from limited per-flow information while maintaining high accuracy. Thirdly, we develop a non-real-time application-level classifier that attains high accuracy for fine-grained applications and demonstrate how it complements the service-level classifier. Finally, we evaluate both classifiers experimentally, comparing accuracy, classification latency, and computational efficiency against representative baselines, and discuss the trade-offs that justify the hierarchical design. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the system architecture, the data, and the design of the two classifiers. Section 3 presents the evaluation results. Section 4 delves into the implications, limitations, and future directions of our research. At the heart of our proposed classifier lies a hierarchical framework, which operates at the smart home gateway and relies solely on metadata extracted from encrypted traffic, thereby ensuring that payloads remain uninspected. This framework consists of two distinct levels of classification: the service level and the application level. The service level is responsible for mapping each flow to one of K classes that share common network Quality of Service (QoS) requirements, such as real-time conferencing, streaming video, interactive/IoT control, bulk transfer, and background traffic. This classification must be performed within a short observation window, enabling the gateway to mark or queue packets in real-time. In contrast, the application level assigns a flow to a specific, fine-grained application, such as a particular video-conferencing or streaming service. This level is typically run on completed or long-observed flows, either offline or near-line, for purposes such as billing, statistics, and QoS auditing. Notably, these two levels are decoupled, with the service-level decision not conditioned on the application label, which helps to avoid error propagation. However, the application-level classifier can utilize the service-level output as a prior to restrict its candidate set, thereby enhancing its performance. Our data collection and labeling process involved two primary sources. The first source was the public ISCX VPN–nonVPN dataset, which was introduced by Draper-Gil et al. in 2016 and contains labeled encrypted and tunneled traffic from common applications. This dataset has been widely used as a benchmark for encrypted traffic classification, as seen in the works of Wang et al. in 2017 and Lotfollahi et al. in 2020. The second source consisted of traffic captured in a smart home testbed that was specifically built for this study. This testbed comprised a residential-grade gateway running Open vSwitch on a Linux single-board computer, along with a diverse range of devices, including smartphones, laptops, a smart television, IP cameras, voice assistants, and smart plugs. Traffic traces were captured at the LAN-facing interface using tcpdump over several weeks, under both Wi-Fi and wired access, and at different times of day, in order to capture variations in congestion and background load. To obtain ground-truth application labels, we ran one application at a time in controlled sessions and employed host-side process-to-socket attribution for concurrent sessions, following the approach outlined by Taylor et al. in 2016. Each application label was then mapped to one of the K service classes according to published QoS requirements for delay, jitter, loss, and throughput, as specified in ITU-T G.1010 and 3GPP TS 23.203. This mapping was independently checked by two annotators, with any disagreements resolved through discussion, and the agreement was quantified using Cohen's κ. In terms of preprocessing and flow definition, packets were grouped into bidirectional flows based on the 5-tuple, consisting of source and destination IP, source and destination port, and transport protocol, with a 120-second inactivity timeout for flow termination. We removed non-informative traffic, such as DNS, mDNS, and DHCP, as well as any flows with fewer than 10 packets. To avoid label leakage, IP addresses, ports, and TLS handshake fields, including SNI, were masked and not used as inputs. However, retransmitted and zero-payload ACK packets were retained, as they carry valuable information about transport behavior. For the service-level classifier, each flow was represented by its first N = 30 packets, which were selected based on experiments described below, as a matrix X ∈ ℝ^{N×3}. Each row in this matrix contains the signed packet size, with positive values indicating uplink and negative values indicating downlink, the inter-arrival time, and the transport-layer window size. Flows with fewer than 30 packets were zero-padded. Packet sizes were scaled by the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU), and inter-arrival times were log-transformed and standardized using the formula x̃t = (log(1 + Δtt) − μ) / σ, where μ and σ were estimated solely from the training set. In contrast, the application-level classifier used a set of 96 statistical features computed over the full flow, including the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, skewness, and kurtosis of packet length and inter-arrival time per direction, flow duration, byte and packet counts, uplink/downlink ratios, burst length and burst interval statistics, and the number of active/idle periods, as outlined in the works of Draper-Gil et al. in 2016 and Moore and Zuev in 2005. These features were ranked according to their mutual information with the label, and those with pairwise correlation above 0.95 were pruned to avoid redundancy. The service-level classifier is based on a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN), which was chosen for its low inference latency on gateway-class hardware. This CNN consists of three convolutional blocks, each with a kernel size of 3 and 32, 64, and 64 channels, respectively, followed by batch normalization, ReLU activation, and max-pooling. The output of these blocks is then passed through a global average pooling layer and a 64-unit fully connected layer with dropout, where the dropout probability is set to 0.3. Finally, a softmax layer generates the class probabilities, given by the formula p(k | X) = exp(zk) / Σj exp(zj). The parameters θ of this model were learned by minimizing the class-weighted cross-entropy loss, L(θ) = −(1/B) Σ{i=1}^{B} Σ{k=1}^{K} wk y{ik} log p(k | Xi; θ) + λ‖θ‖², where wk is inversely proportional to the class frequency, which helps to counter class imbalance, and λ is the weight decay. The window length N was varied over the set {5, 10, 20, 30, 50} to characterize the trade-off between classification delay and accuracy. Microsurgical free tissue transfer has become a cornerstone of reconstructive surgery, offering a reliable means of restoring form and function in the aftermath of tumor resection, trauma, burns, and chronic wounds, particularly in the head and neck, breast, and extremities. The success rates of this procedure have improved dramatically over the years, with many high-volume centers now reporting success rates exceeding 95% (Khouri et al., 1998; Pohlenz et al., 2012). However, despite these advances, vascular compromise at the anastomosis remains a significant concern, and is still the leading cause of flap loss. The incidence of arterial inflow obstruction or venous outflow obstruction, often due to thrombosis, kinking, compression, or vasospasm, can range from 5% to 25% of cases, depending on the series and the type of flap (Chen et al., 2007; Kroll et al., 1996). Notably, most of these events occur within the first 48 to 72 hours after surgery (Kroll et al., 1996), underscoring the need for close monitoring during this critical period. The prognosis of a compromised flap is heavily dependent on the prompt recognition of the problem. Muscle and other metabolically active tissues are particularly vulnerable to warm ischemia, and the no-reflow phenomenon can limit reperfusion after prolonged ischemia (Wang et al., 2015). As a result, salvage rates are significantly higher when re-exploration takes place within a few hours of vascular compromise, whereas delayed diagnosis can lead to salvage rates of 30% or lower (Yii et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2007). Therefore, reliable early detection is crucial to flap survival, and is arguably as important as the original operation itself. To date, numerous monitoring methods have been proposed, each with its own strengths and limitations. Clinical observation of skin color, capillary refill, temperature, turgor, and bleeding on pinprick remains the most widely used approach, and serves as the standard against which other techniques are compared (Smit et al., 2010). This method is straightforward, inexpensive, and requires no specialized equipment. However, it is inherently subjective, and its accuracy depends on the experience of the examiner. Moreover, intermittent assessment can miss events that develop between rounds, and nighttime examination under poor lighting can be unreliable. Furthermore, clinical signs often appear late, when ischemia is already established, and buried flaps or those without a skin paddle, such as free jejunum or muscle flaps used in pharyngeal and intraoral reconstruction, cannot be assessed by skin appearance at all. In response to these limitations, several adjunctive technologies have been developed. Handheld Doppler ultrasonography, for example, can detect flow in the pedicle or in perforators, but is operator-dependent and intermittent, and can provide false reassurance when the signal comes from adjacent vessels (Smit et al., 2010). Implantable Doppler probes allow continuous monitoring of anastomotic flow, but require a second invasive procedure to place and remove, may dislodge, and have been reported to produce false-positive results (Rozen et al., 2008). Other techniques, such as laser Doppler flowmetry and photoplethysmography, provide continuous measures of microcirculatory perfusion, but are sensitive to motion, probe position, and ambient light, and yield relative rather than absolute values (Hölzle et al., 2006). Tissue oxygen tension, pH, and temperature probes, microdialysis, and fluorescence angiography with indocyanine green offer physiological information, but are invasive, expensive, and require specialized personnel, and do not provide true continuous bedside measurement (Udesen et al., 2000; Smit et al., 2010). In recent years, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) has emerged as a promising optical technique that may meet the need for a noninvasive, continuous, objective, and simple-to-use monitor. NIRS exploits the fact that biological tissue is relatively transparent to light in the near-infrared range of about 700 to 900 nm, where oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin have distinct absorption spectra. By measuring light attenuation at several wavelengths, the relative concentrations of each chromophore can be estimated, and a regional tissue oxygen saturation can be calculated (Jöbsis, 1977). Because the signal comes mainly from small vessels (arterioles, capillaries, and venules), NIRS reflects the balance between oxygen delivery and consumption in the microvascular bed, and does not require pulsatile flow. NIRS has been used for years to monitor cerebral oxygenation during cardiac and carotid surgery and in neonatal intensive care, as well as in muscle physiology and the evaluation of peripheral vascular disease (Murkin and Arango, 2009). Its use in reconstructive surgery has been explored more recently, with early clinical studies in breast reconstruction and in head and neck and extremity flaps suggesting that falling tissue oxygen saturation accompanies both arterial and venous compromise, and may precede visible clinical changes (Keller, 2009; Repez et al., 2008; Steele et al., 2011). However, the published experience is still heterogeneous, with different devices, probe designs, and algorithms being used, and many reports focusing on breast flaps or small series. Furthermore, descriptions of the temporal relationship between the fall in regional oxygen saturation and the onset of visible color change are limited, which is crucial in determining the practical value of the technique for earlier intervention and salvage. The current study addresses this knowledge gap by investigating the use of NIRS in a mixed series of free flaps. We asked whether postoperative monitoring of regional oxygen saturation with the INVOS system, which uses a disposable adhesive sensor with a continuous bedside display, can detect vascular compromise in free flaps early enough to allow successful salvage. To answer this question, we prospectively monitored 57 patients undergoing free tissue transfer, recording regional oxygen saturation continuously after surgery and comparing the trends with clinical findings and with the outcomes of re-exploration. Our study makes three key contributions: first, it describes the use of the INVOS system as a continuous, noninvasive flap monitor in a consecutive clinical series; second, it documents the temporal behavior of regional oxygen saturation in cases of arterial and venous insufficiency, particularly its decline before pallor or congestion became visible; and third, it reports that all patients in whom insufficiency was detected were salvaged by re-exploration, which supports the potential of NIRS as a valuable tool in reconstructive surgery. In the context of postoperative flap monitoring, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) offers a promising adjunct to traditional clinical assessment. To investigate its potential, we conducted a prospective, single-center observational study of consecutive patients undergoing microsurgical free tissue transfer in our department of plastic and reconstructive surgery. Over the course of the study, 57 patients were enrolled, all of whom were adults with free flap reconstruction featuring a cutaneous or musculocutaneous component of sufficient size to accommodate an optical sensor. The reconstructive indications for these patients were diverse, encompassing head and neck cancer defects, breast reconstruction, and traumatic or oncologic defects of the extremities. To ensure the reliability and generalizability of our findings, we established clear eligibility criteria. Patients with flaps lacking a skin paddle, such as those with buried flaps, were excluded, as were individuals with severe skin pigmentation disorders or extensive scarring at the planned sensor site. Additionally, patients who could not be monitored for at least 72 hours postoperatively were not included in the study. The institutional review board approved our protocol, and all patients provided written informed consent prior to participation. Our study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, ensuring the ethical treatment of all participants. As part of our data collection, we recorded a range of demographic and clinical variables, including age, sex, comorbidities (such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and smoking history), flap type, recipient site, ischemia time, and anastomotic details. These factors are known to influence outcomes in free flap reconstruction and were therefore considered essential to our analysis. The surgical procedures were performed by experienced microsurgeons under general anesthesia, with anastomoses conducted under an operating microscope using 9-0 or 10-0 monofilament nylon. The choice between end-to-end and end-to-side arterial anastomoses was determined by the conditions of the recipient vessels. Venous anastomoses were performed using either a hand-sewn technique or a coupling device, with venous outflow reconstructed using one or two veins, depending on the specific flap type. To verify intraoperative vessel patency, we employed the milking test and inspected flap bleeding following reperfusion. In terms of postoperative care, our standard protocol included low-dose aspirin and adequate hydration, with unfractionated heparin administered at the surgeon's discretion in high-risk cases. Patients were nursed in a warm room (maintained at approximately 25–28 °C) with the flap kept free of external pressure and with controlled head and limb positioning. Clinical monitoring was conducted in parallel with the investigational device, involving hourly assessments of flap color, temperature, turgor, capillary refill, and bleeding on pinprick for the first 24 hours, followed by evaluations every 2–4 hours until postoperative day 3, and every 8 hours thereafter. These clinical criteria have been widely accepted as the reference standard for detecting vascular compromise. The nursing staff and clinicians responsible for making clinical decisions applied the same criteria used for any patient, taking into account both clinical and device data when deciding whether re-exploration was necessary. The clinical team was aware of the oximetry readings, which informed their decisions regarding patient care. To monitor regional tissue oxygen saturation (rSO2), we utilized the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy (INVOS) oximeter, which employs near-infrared spectroscopy to measure tissue oxygenation. This technology exploits the relative transparency of biological tissue to light at 700–1000 nm and the differing absorption spectra of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin. The oximeter uses two wavelengths (approximately 730 and 810 nm) generated by a light-emitting diode in a disposable adhesive sensor. Two silicon photodiode detectors placed at different distances from the emitter record the returning light, allowing for the calculation of rSO2. Sensors were applied in the operating room immediately after completion of the anastomoses and reperfusion, once the flap was stable and bleeding had been controlled. The sensor was placed on the skin paddle, away from the pedicle and from the flap edges and suture lines, and avoiding visible superficial veins. To minimize interference from ambient light, the sensor was covered with an opaque dressing and fixed with minimal pressure to avoid compressing the flap. A second sensor was placed on normal skin at a comparable site near the flap as an internal reference for systemic changes in oxygenation. Baseline rSO2 was defined as the mean value over the first 30 minutes of stable recording after reperfusion. Readings were then recorded continuously through the first 72 hours and afterwards at the time of each clinical assessment until postoperative day 7 or until the patient was discharged. We also recorded systemic variables that might influence tissue oxygenation, including arterial oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry, hemoglobin concentration, blood pressure, body temperature, and use of vasopressors. Given the lack of validated absolute thresholds for rSO2 in free flaps, we established alert criteria in advance, informed by earlier reports of NIRS in flaps. A vascular event was suspected if flap rSO2 fell by 20% or more relative to its own baseline value and the decrease persisted for at least 10 minutes without a corresponding fall in the reference-site value or in arterial saturation. The investigators also recorded whether the pattern suggested arterial insufficiency (a rapid, steep decline to low values) or venous insufficiency (a more gradual decline). If a decrease in rSO2 triggered an alarm, the clinical team conducted an immediate examination of the flap, verified positioning and dressing, and excluded technical artifacts. If clinical examination also suggested compromise, or if rSO2 continued to decline despite correction of reversible causes, the patient was taken back to the operating room for re-exploration. The final diagnosis of arterial or venous insufficiency was made at re-exploration, based on the finding of a thrombosed or kinked vessel at the anastomosis or in the pedicle. We recorded the time of the first rSO2 alarm, the time at which clinical signs (such as pallor or congestion, change in capillary refill) were first noted, and the time of return to the operating room. Salvage was defined as survival of the flap without partial or total necrosis at the conclusion of the study period. The concept of local features has been a cornerstone of computer vision for decades, with applications spanning a wide range of areas, including panorama stitching, structure-from-motion, multi-view stereo, visual localization, and image retrieval. At its core, the idea of local features involves extracting distinctive, repeatable, and locally invariant structures from images, which can then be matched across different views to establish correspondences. This process typically involves a nearest-neighbor search in descriptor space, followed by geometric verification using robust estimators such as RANSAC. The first generation of local features was entirely handcrafted, with corner detectors and their scale-covariant extensions providing the foundation for the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT). Introduced by Lowe in 2004, SIFT combines a difference-of-Gaussians detector with a 128-dimensional gradient-orientation histogram descriptor, and its effectiveness has endured, with it remaining the default reference in many pipelines to this day. However, subsequent work has focused on improving efficiency and invariance, with approaches such as SURF, BRIEF, ORB, BRISK, and FREAK replacing floating-point vectors with bit strings compared via Hamming distance, and fast corner detectors like FAST reducing descriptor size and matching cost by one to two orders of magnitude. In addition to these efforts, researchers have also explored affine-covariant region detectors, which can handle viewpoint changes that exceed the capacity of similarity-invariant detectors. The work of Mikolajczyk et al. in 2005 provides a systematic comparison of these detectors, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses. More recently, the advent of deep convolutional networks has led to a shift towards learned features, with patch descriptors being learned end-to-end using siamese and triplet architectures. This has resulted in compact and highly discriminative descriptors such as L2-Net and HardNet, which have been shown to outperform traditional handcrafted features in many cases. However, the rapid development of learned features has also led to a large and heterogeneous literature, with methods differing in what they learn, the supervision they require, and the data on which they are trained and evaluated. This has created a challenge for newcomers and experts alike, as it is often unclear why a particular design decision was made, which limitations of earlier approaches it addresses, and which of the many claimed improvements transfer to practical settings. Existing surveys have either predated the deep-learning era or focused on one component, such as patch descriptors, and therefore rarely provide a comprehensive understanding of how the principles of handcrafted design have been reinterpreted in learned models. The evaluation of local features raises a related difficulty, as early benchmarks measured detector repeatability and descriptor precision-recall on small sets of planar scenes with known homographies, while large-scale patch-level benchmarks have enabled deep descriptors to be trained and compared. However, improvements measured on patch verification, retrieval, and matching tasks have not always carried over to downstream applications, with learned descriptors that outperform SIFT on patch-level metrics not consistently yielding more complete or more accurate reconstructions in structure-from-motion pipelines. Similar observations have been made for visual localization and wide-baseline stereo, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of the requirements of different tasks and the interplay between feature type, matcher, and robust geometric estimator. Our perspective is motivated by 3D reconstruction, where the precise localization of features is critical, and correspondences provide the measurements entering triangulation and bundle adjustment. Keypoint localization errors of even a fraction of a pixel can propagate directly into pose and structure estimates, emphasizing the importance of properties such as sub-pixel accuracy, repeatability under viewpoint and illumination change, and the spatial distribution of features. Many modern learned detectors operate on downsampled feature maps or optimize a coarse notion of matchability, which can compromise localization precision relative to scale-space detectors. Understanding where and why this happens requires a return to the design principles of handcrafted methods, and a careful consideration of the trade-offs involved in different design choices. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of local features, tracing the evolution of handcrafted detectors and descriptors through to modern learned approaches. We will examine the key design principles and innovations that have shaped the development of local features, and provide a critical evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of different methods. Our goal is to provide a nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between feature type, matcher, and application, and to highlight the importance of careful evaluation and consideration of the requirements of different tasks. By doing so, we hope to provide a foundation for the development of more effective and efficient local features, and to shed light on the ongoing quest for improved performance in computer vision applications. This includes a consideration of the trade-offs involved in different design choices, such as the balance between efficiency and invariance, and the importance of properties such as sub-pixel accuracy and repeatability under viewpoint and illumination change. By examining the evolution of local features in a chronological and systematic way, we can gain a deeper understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different methods, and shed light on the ongoing quest for improved performance in computer vision applications. The evaluation of local features is a critical component of this process, as it provides a way to compare and contrast different methods, and to identify areas for improvement. However, the evaluation of local features raises a number of challenges, from the choice of benchmark datasets to the selection of evaluation metrics. Early benchmarks measured detector repeatability and descriptor precision-recall on small sets of planar scenes with known homographies, while large-scale patch-level benchmarks have enabled deep descriptors to be trained and compared. However, improvements measured on patch verification, retrieval, and matching tasks have not always carried over to downstream applications, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of the requirements of different tasks and the interplay between feature type, matcher, and robust geometric estimator. Our perspective is motivated by 3D reconstruction, where the precise localization of features is critical, and correspondences provide the measurements entering triangulation and bundle adjustment. Keypoint localization errors of even a fraction of a pixel can propagate directly into pose and structure estimates, emphasizing the importance of properties such as sub-pixel accuracy, repeatability under viewpoint and illumination change, and the spatial distribution of features. Many modern learned detectors operate on downsampled feature maps or optimize a coarse notion of matchability, which can compromise localization precision relative to scale-space detectors. Understanding where and why this happens requires a return to the design principles of handcrafted methods, and a careful consideration of the trade-offs involved in different design choices. This paper makes three contributions. First, we provide a largely chronological overview of local features, moving from handcrafted detectors and descriptors, through methods that employ machine learning to optimize individual components of an otherwise handcrafted pipeline, to modern learned approaches that integrate detection and description. Second, we examine the key design principles and innovations that have shaped the development of local features, and provide a critical evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of different methods. Finally, we highlight the importance of careful evaluation and consideration of the requirements of different tasks, and provide a nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between feature type, matcher, and application. As self-driving vehicles transition from research prototypes to commercial deployment, the need for a reliable perception stack that can protect vulnerable road users, particularly pedestrians, becomes increasingly pressing. According to the World Health Organization's global status reports, pedestrians account for approximately one in five road fatalities worldwide, and the ability of automated systems to avoid them will be a critical factor in their evaluation. Two scenarios, in particular, pose significant challenges: imminent-crash situations, where the vehicle must choose between striking an inanimate object or a pedestrian, and road intersections, where pedestrians may be partially occluded by other vehicles or street furniture, requiring the vehicle to stop reliably and promptly. In both cases, the consequences of a missed detection far outweigh those of a false alarm, making the log-average miss rate a more relevant metric than raw average precision in this domain. The evolution of pedestrian detection methods has been marked by several generations of approaches. Early detectors relied on hand-crafted features, such as histograms of oriented gradients combined with linear support vector machines, which were later extended with deformable part models and integral channel features. However, these approaches still struggled to detect small, occluded, or low-contrast pedestrians, as evidenced by the Caltech Pedestrian Benchmark. The advent of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has significantly improved the accuracy of pedestrian detection. Region-based detectors, such as R-CNN, Fast R-CNN, and Faster R-CNN, have been followed by pedestrian-specific adaptations, including CompACT-deep, the region proposal network with boosted forests, and approaches that exploit semantic segmentation or multi-scale feature pyramids. Among these, the Fused Deep Neural Network (F-DNN) currently reports the lowest miss rate on the Caltech benchmark, generating candidate boxes with a Single Shot Multi-Box Detector (SSD), classifying them using an ensemble of deep classifiers, and fusing their outputs with a soft-rejection mechanism and optional semantic-segmentation refinement stage. However, the accuracy of F-DNN comes at a considerable computational cost, making it unsuitable for real-time deployment. Running multiple deep classifiers on a large number of candidate regions, and subsequently performing fusion and segmentation, yields processing rates far below those needed for a vehicle traveling at speed. In contrast, single-stage detectors, such as SSD and YOLO, offer a more favorable accuracy-speed trade-off by predicting class scores and box offsets directly from feature maps in a single forward pass. Nevertheless, SSD was designed and tuned for general-purpose, multi-class benchmarks, and its default-box configurations, matching thresholds, hard-negative-mining ratios, and data-augmentation strategies may not be optimal for pedestrian detection. A second line of research has focused on accelerating CNN inference through hardware acceleration on GPUs, ASICs, and FPGAs. While GPUs provide high throughput, they are often limited by high power consumption and variable latency. ASICs, such as the TPU and Eyeriss, offer efficient but inflexible and expensive solutions. FPGAs, on the other hand, occupy an attractive middle ground, allowing custom datapaths, reduced-precision arithmetic, and deep pipelining, which can provide deterministic latency and strong performance per watt. However, most published FPGA accelerators target image classification networks, and few address full object-detection pipelines with their multi-scale prediction heads, default-box decoding, and non-maximum suppression. The Altera (Intel) Arria 10 family, with its hardened floating-point DSP blocks, large on-chip memory, and support for OpenCL-based design flows, is a promising yet underexplored target for such workloads. This leaves a clear gap in the current state of research: the most accurate pedestrian detector, F-DNN, is too slow for real-time deployment, while faster detectors have not been systematically adapted to pedestrians nor mapped to an efficient, automotive-suitable hardware platform. The research question we address is therefore: can a pedestrian-optimized SSD, accelerated on an FPGA, approach the accuracy of F-DNN while meeting real-time throughput and latency requirements within an embedded power budget? To answer this question, this paper makes two contributions. First, we train SSD for pedestrian detection and systematically tune its hyperparameters, including default-box scales and aspect ratios, matching thresholds, negative-to-positive sampling ratios, input resolution, and augmentation, to improve miss rate on the Caltech benchmark. Preliminary results show that the tuned SSD is within 3% of the miss rate of F-DNN while running four times faster in software. Second, we propose a new FPGA design for accelerating the tuned model on the Altera Arria 10 platform, exploiting parallelism across convolution channels and feature-map tiles, on-chip data reuse, and pipelined execution of the detection heads. We expect this design to yield a further speedup that substantially reduces the gap between the accuracy and efficiency of pedestrian detection systems. The significance of this research lies in its potential to enable the development of reliable and efficient pedestrian detection systems for self-driving vehicles. By optimizing SSD for pedestrian detection and accelerating it on an FPGA, we can achieve a balance between accuracy and speed that meets the stringent requirements of real-time deployment. This, in turn, can help reduce the number of pedestrian fatalities and injuries, making our roads safer for all users. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be extended to other object detection tasks, making it a valuable contribution to the field of computer vision and autonomous systems. In conclusion, the development of pedestrian detection systems for self-driving vehicles is a complex task that requires careful consideration of both accuracy and efficiency. By leveraging the strengths of CNNs and FPGAs, we can create systems that are not only reliable but also efficient and scalable. The proposed approach, which combines a pedestrian-optimized SSD with an FPGA-based acceleration platform, offers a promising solution to this challenge. As the field of autonomous systems continues to evolve, research in this area will play a critical role in enabling the widespread adoption of self-driving vehicles and improving road safety for all users. The ability to detect pedestrians in real-time is a crucial aspect of autonomous vehicles, and our proposed system achieves this goal by leveraging a Single Shot Multi-Box Detector (SSD) and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) accelerator. While the resulting system incurs a small loss in accuracy, this is more than offset by the significant gain in speed, enabling real-time pedestrian detection in self-driving vehicles. This paper provides an overview of our approach, detailing the SSD adaptation and training procedure, the accelerator architecture, and the accuracy and performance results. We also discuss the implications and limitations of our system. Our proposed system consists of two primary components: a SSD network, whose training procedure and hyperparameters were tuned specifically for pedestrian detection, and an FPGA accelerator designed to optimize the performance of the trained network. The software and hardware components were developed sequentially, with the tuned network defining the computational workload and the accelerator designed around its layer shapes, numerical precision, and memory footprint. Throughout this paper, we use the F-DNN of Du et al. (2017) as a reference for accuracy and latency. To train and evaluate our system, we utilized the Caltech Pedestrian Detection Benchmark (Dollár et al., 2012), which comprises approximately 10 hours of 640×480 video recorded at 30 Hz from a vehicle in urban traffic. Following the standard protocol, we used sets 00–05 for training and sets 06–10 for testing. To reduce redundancy between consecutive frames, we sampled training frames every third frame, using the commonly employed "10x" setting. We also used the annotations from Zhang et al. (2016) for training, as they correct many labeling errors in the original ground truth. For test results, we reported on the original annotations to ensure comparability with published results. The evaluation protocol followed the Caltech "Reasonable" setting, which considers pedestrians at least 50 pixels tall and at least 65% visible. Detections were matched to ground truth at an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5, and the performance metric used was the log-average miss rate (MR), computed from the miss rate against false positives per image (FPPI) curve. The MR is calculated as MR = exp((1/9) Σ{i=1}^{9} ln(mr(fi))), where the fi are nine FPPI values evenly spaced in log space over [10⁻², 10⁰] and mr(fi) is the miss rate at the largest FPPI not exceeding fi. A lower MR indicates better performance. We held out a validation split from the training sets (set 05) for hyperparameter selection and used the test sets only for final reporting. The SSD architecture used in this study was based on the SSD300 model with a VGG-16 backbone pre-trained on ImageNet (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015). We converted the fully connected layers to convolutions and appended extra feature layers to provide six detection scales. At each location of each feature map, the network predicts class confidences and four box offsets relative to a set of default boxes. The training objective is a weighted sum of a localization loss and a confidence loss, given by L(x, c, l, g) = (1/N) [Lconf(x, c) + α Lloc(x, l, g)], where N is the number of matched default boxes, Lconf is the softmax loss, Lloc is a smooth-L1 loss between the predicted box l and the ground-truth box g, and α weights the two terms. Since pedestrians are a single class with a narrow aspect-ratio distribution, we reduced the model to two classes (pedestrian and background). We restricted the default-box aspect ratios to {1:2.4, 1:2} around the typical pedestrian ratio of about 0.41 (width/height) found in Caltech, replacing the generic {1, 2, 3, 1/2, 1/3} set. We also re-estimated the minimum and maximum default-box scales from the distribution of annotated pedestrian heights to ensure that small pedestrians are covered by the finest feature maps. Input images were upsampled to 640×480 prior to feature extraction to prevent the loss of small pedestrians after repeated downsampling. The training process employed stochastic gradient descent with momentum 0.9 and weight decay 5×10⁻⁴. Data augmentation followed Liu et al. (2016), including photometric distortion, random expansion, random cropping constrained by minimum IoU with ground-truth boxes, and horizontal flipping. Hard negative mining maintained a ratio of negatives to positives at 3:1. The hyperparameters tuned were the base learning rate, learning-rate schedule, batch size, matching IoU threshold for default boxes, negative-to-positive mining ratio, the localization weight α, default-box scales and aspect ratios, and input resolution. We used a staged search approach rather than a full grid search. First, we scanned the learning rate (10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³, log-spaced) and batch size (8, 16, 32) with other parameters at their default values. Then, with these fixed, we varied the matching threshold (0.4–0.6), mining ratio (2:1–5:1), and α (0.5–2) one at a time. Finally, we tuned the default-box configuration and input resolution jointly, as they interact strongly. Each configuration was trained for a shortened schedule and scored by log-average MR on the validation set; the best configurations were then retrained for the full schedule. Non-maximum suppression used an IoU threshold of 0.45, which was also tuned on validation data. Training was performed using the Caffe framework on a single GPU. We compared the final SSD with F-DNN (Du et al., 2017), which fuses several detectors and refines their outputs with a bank of classification networks, using published F-DNN miss rates and, for speed, inference runs on the same GPU and image size. Latency was measured as the mean per-frame time over the test sequences after warm-up, excluding image I/O, and throughput is reported in frames per second (fps). The speedup is the ratio of F-DNN to SSD per-frame time. Because training is stochastic, the final SSD configuration was trained with five random seeds, and the mean and standard deviation of MR are reported. The difference from F-DNN is expressed in absolute percentage points of MR. The FPGA accelerator design began with a workload analysis, where we computed per-layer multiply-accumulate (MAC) counts, parameter sizes, and activation sizes of the tuned SSD analytically. For a convolutional layer with Cin input channels, Cout output channels, K×K kernels, and an H×W output map, the MAC count is MACs = H · W · Cout · Cin · K². These values determine the compute-to-memory ratio of each layer and identify which layers are compute-bound or bandwidth-bound. The increasing reliance on reused data from patients and research participants has become a cornerstone of biomedical research and healthcare. The sheer volume and granularity of data generated from electronic health records, biobanks, consumer devices, and high-throughput sequencing have reached unprecedented levels, making it possible to conduct more powerful studies of disease, accelerate clinical trial recruitment, and foster a learning health system where care and discovery inform each other. In response, funders, journals, and policymakers have established expectations for data sharing, emphasizing the need for data to be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, as outlined in the FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016). Initiatives such as the National Institutes of Health Genomic Data Sharing Policy (NIH 2014) and the growing use of repositories and data discovery indexes (Ohno-Machado et al. 2017) have been implemented to facilitate data sharing. However, the same data that hold such promise for advancing biomedical research are often highly sensitive, revealing intimate details about individuals, including diagnoses, treatments, and behaviors, as well as information about biological relatives that persists over a lifetime. A substantial body of research has demonstrated that de-identification, or the removal of explicit identifiers, is not a reliable means of protecting privacy. Demographic combinations can be used to single out individuals in supposedly de-identified releases (Sweeney 2002), and patients can be linked to hospital discharge records and other secondary sources (Malin and Sweeney 2004; El Emam et al. 2011). Genomic data, in particular, have proven to be vulnerable to re-identification, with aggregate allele frequencies able to reveal whether an individual participated in a study (Homer et al. 2008), surnames inferable from Y-chromosome markers and public genealogy databases (Gymrek et al. 2013), and even simple "beacon" services capable of leaking membership in a dataset through repeated queries (Shringarpure and Bustamante 2015). These findings have led to a reevaluation of the assumption that a dataset can be labeled "anonymous" or "public" without ongoing assessment of risk. The tension between access and privacy is a complex, multifaceted issue that is both technical and social in nature. On one hand, overly permissive sharing can expose participants to discrimination, stigma, or loss of trust, potentially jeopardizing the research enterprise as a whole. On the other hand, overly restrictive practices can impede reproducibility, delay discovery, and waste the contributions of participants who volunteered their data in the expectation that it would be used to advance biomedical research. Legal and ethical frameworks, such as the HIPAA Privacy Rule in the United States and the General Data Protection Regulation in the European Union (European Parliament and Council 2016), have been established to manage this tension, emphasizing consent, purpose limitation, de-identification, and governance. However, these frameworks were largely designed for settings in which data were collected for a specific purpose and held by a single organization, and they may not be well-suited to contemporary research, where data are frequently repurposed, linked across institutions, and analyzed by parties that the original participants never met. Consent models are also evolving, shifting from study-specific agreements to broader, more dynamic approaches that provide participants with greater ongoing involvement (Kaye et al. 2015; Grady et al. 2015). However, it remains unclear how such models should operate in emerging environments, such as mobile health studies and large precision medicine cohorts. A second set of challenges concerns infrastructure, as data are distributed across hospitals, consortia, and repositories with different policies, formats, and risk tolerances. Researchers need ways to discover whether suitable data exist before requesting access, and federated query tools, such as i2b2 and SHRINE, have been developed to enable investigators to estimate cohort sizes across institutions without centralizing patient-level records (Weber et al. 2009; Murphy et al. 2010). Nevertheless, even aggregate counts can leak information, particularly for small or distinctive populations, which has motivated research into cryptographic protocols, such as homomorphic encryption and secure multiparty computation, as well as statistical protections, like differential privacy (Dwork and Roth 2014). These techniques offer formal guarantees, but their costs in terms of computation, communication, and loss of data utility are still being characterized for clinical and genomic applications. A third challenge is that privacy risk is not static, but rather depends on the data type, the auxiliary information available to an adversary, the incentives to attack, and the countermeasures in place. Recent work has therefore shifted from asking whether a dataset is "safe" to modeling how risk varies with context and how data holders can make principled tradeoffs. Quantitative risk assessment, decision-theoretic and game-theoretic models of data recipients and adversaries, and calibrated release of summary statistics are examples of this approach (Wan et al. 2017). By treating privacy protection as an optimization problem, balancing the utility of shared information against the likelihood and cost of misuse, rather than as a binary property, researchers can develop more effective strategies for managing privacy risk. Despite this progress, the literature on biomedical data sharing and privacy remains fragmented, with different communities and vocabularies often addressing distinct aspects of the issue, such as consent, data discovery, risk measurement, secure computation, and data publication. This fragmentation can make it difficult for informaticians and data stewards to see how advances fit together across the data lifecycle. Each year brings a large volume of publications, and it is not always clear which contributions are most significant for practice or for shaping future research. This paper aims to address this gap by surveying notable contributions from 2017 on biomedical data sharing, with a focus on data access and privacy. The guiding question is: what advances published in 2017 most meaningfully expand the ability to share and use biomedical data while managing the privacy risks to the individuals who provide it? To answer this question, we conducted a comprehensive search of PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and the AAAI Digital Library. We selected candidate papers based on their relevance to biomedical data sharing and privacy, and had international experts review them against six predefined criteria. The editorial board of the IMIA Yearbook then made the final selection of best papers. This paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured, reproducible account of how the leading 2017 literature on data sharing and privacy was identified and evaluated. Second, it synthesizes five selected papers along the lifecycle of biomedical data, covering topics such as consenting strategies for emerging environments, software for searching and retrieving datasets across organizations, measurement of privacy risks for newer data types like genomic data, cryptographic techniques for cohort discovery over clinical data, and game-theoretic strategies for publishing summary information from genome-phenome studies. Third, it draws cross-cutting lessons, primarily that no single solution to privacy fits all biomedical data and settings, but that emerging technologies create opportunities to enable data use while reducing risk. Ultimately, our goal is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of biomedical data sharing and privacy, highlighting the key challenges, opportunities, and advances in this critical area of research. By doing so, we hope to facilitate the development of more effective strategies for managing privacy risk, enabling the responsible sharing and use of biomedical data, and accelerating the discovery of new treatments and therapies. The importance of this endeavor cannot be overstated, as the ability to share and use biomedical data while protecting individual privacy is essential for advancing our understanding of human health and disease, and for improving the care and treatment of patients around the world. The perspective outlined in this study provides a framework for researchers, data stewards, and policymakers to navigate the complex landscape of biomedical data sharing, identifying areas where further research is needed and evaluating the trade-offs between data access and privacy. To achieve this, we conducted a structured, multi-stage review of the 2017 literature on biomedical data sharing, focusing on the tension between data access and privacy. Our approach was modeled on the selection procedure used for the International Medical Informatics Association (IMIA) Yearbook, which involves a rigorous, multi-step process. The review process began with a broad bibliographic search, followed by a curated selection of candidate papers, expert review, and finally, editorial selection of the best papers. Unlike a systematic review or meta-analysis, which aims to estimate pooled effects, our goal was to identify and summarize notable contributions to the field, highlighting key findings and methodologies. To organize our review, we adopted a lifecycle approach, considering the various stages of biomedical data, from collection and consent to discovery, retrieval, analysis, and dissemination of derived or summary information. This framing allowed us to examine how privacy and access concerns arise at different points in the lifecycle and require distinct technical and policy responses, as highlighted by Sweeney (2002) and Dwork (2006). Our search strategy involved querying five bibliographic resources, including PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and the AAAI Digital Library, to cover both biomedical and computational literatures. We limited our search to papers published in 2017, including articles that appeared electronically ahead of print, and restricted our search to English-language, peer-reviewed publications. Our queries combined controlled vocabulary with free-text terms, addressing two concept groups: data sharing and access, and privacy and confidentiality. We also included queries on specific data types, such as genomic, phenotypic, electronic health record, and mobile or sensor-derived data, which have been the focus of recent privacy research. Within PubMed, we utilized Medical Subject Headings, such as "Confidentiality," "Computer Security," and "Information Dissemination," alongside title and abstract keywords. For the other databases, we adapted our queries to each platform's syntax, searching titles, abstracts, and author keywords. We joined terms within a concept group with OR and the two groups with AND. The topics of the Yearbook section guided our query refinement, and we iteratively adjusted our queries until further modification no longer yielded relevant results. We exported the records to a reference manager, de-duplicated them by title, author, and digital object identifier, and proceeded to the next stage of the review process. The first step in our review process involved the independent screening of titles and abstracts by two section editors. We excluded papers that did not substantially address biomedical or health-related data or that mentioned privacy only in passing. We also excluded editorials, commentaries without original analysis, and purely narrative opinion pieces, although these informed our understanding of the policy context. Papers that passed this screening were read in full or in substantial part and tagged by lifecycle stage, data type, and contribution type. The editors then nominated candidate best papers, emphasizing originality, potential to influence practice or subsequent research, and diversity of perspective across the lifecycle and across technical, empirical, and ethical or legal work. Disagreements about inclusion were settled through discussion until consensus was reached. In the second step of our review process, each candidate paper was sent to a team of international reviewers with expertise in biomedical informatics, privacy and security, ethics, or related fields. Reviewers included section editors and external experts who were not authors of, and had no declared conflicts of interest with, the papers they evaluated. Each candidate paper was assessed by multiple independent reviewers, in line with the Yearbook's standard of several reviews per candidate. Reviewers rated each paper against six predefined criteria: relevance to the section topic, originality and novelty of the contribution, scientific rigor and soundness of the methodology, significance and potential impact, validity and clarity of the results, and quality of presentation and organization. Reviewers provided scores for each criterion, along with free-text comments, particularly about limitations such as unrealistic adversary models, small or synthetic evaluation datasets, or weak generalizability. The section editors compiled the scores and comments into a ranked summary for each paper, which was then forwarded to the Yearbook editorial board. The board made the final selection of best papers, considering not only the aggregate scores but also the balance of the final set, ensuring that the selected papers collectively represented different stages of the data lifecycle and different strategies for reconciling access with privacy, without duplicating one another. The dissemination of scientific findings in health and medicine is a complex process, with peer-reviewed publications serving as the primary conduit for specialist audiences. However, for the broader public, the mass media plays a crucial role in mediating knowledge of new health research. Surveys have consistently shown that television, newspapers, and online news outlets are among the primary sources through which lay audiences learn about science and medicine. The significance of media coverage extends beyond mere information dissemination, as it can shape public understanding, influence health behaviors, inform policy debates, and affect clinical practice. Moreover, research has demonstrated that media coverage can have a downstream impact on scholarly citation patterns, with articles covered by the press tend to be cited more frequently than those that are not. The pathway from journal article to news story is far from direct, involving multiple stages of selection and filtering. A substantial body of research in communication studies has highlighted the role of "information subsidies" – materials produced by interested parties, such as press releases – in reducing the costs associated with gathering and verifying information. In the context of health science, these subsidies are typically prepared by journal editorial offices or university and institutional press offices, which identify findings deemed likely to interest reporters and package them for distribution through channels like EurekAlert!. Journalists, operating under time pressure and with limited specialist science desks, rely heavily on these materials, often drawing directly on press releases and reproducing their language and exaggerations. This pipeline is characterized by at least two successive selection steps. Firstly, journal editors or press officers decide which published articles merit a press release, and secondly, journalists and news editors determine which articles, with or without a press release, warrant a story. Each step filters the vast volume of published research, reflecting judgments about what is deemed "newsworthy." The concept of newsworthiness has a rich history in journalism scholarship, with foundational work identifying features such as timeliness, proximity, prominence, consequence, conflict, and human interest as determinants of which events are selected for coverage. Subsequent research has adapted these ideas to science reporting, suggesting that journalists favor findings that are novel, relevant to common or personally significant health conditions, carry clear implications for individuals, or can be narrated in a compelling manner. Empirical studies of health news selection have examined various features, including study design, journal prestige, sample size, and industry funding, and have reported that observational studies and findings with striking or surprising results are overrepresented in coverage relative to their prevalence in the literature. In contrast, randomized trials and null results are often neglected. While this work has been invaluable, it has typically relied on manual coding of modest numbers of articles, predefined hypotheses about which attributes matter, and metadata rather than the substantive content of the research itself. The limitations of manual annotation, hypothesis-driven designs, and metadata analysis have constrained our understanding of the factors that influence the selection of health science articles for press release issuance and media coverage. Recent advances in natural language processing and statistical machine learning have made it feasible to analyze text at scale and discover associations without specifying them in advance. Text-based models have been used to predict citation impact, online news popularity, and social media virality, and topic models offer a means of summarizing large corpora in terms of latent themes that can be related to outcomes of interest. However, these approaches have seldom been applied to the specific question of which health science articles are selected for press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. The few computational studies that exist have typically considered a single stage of the pipeline, a single outlet or journal, or small datasets, and have not systematically characterized the lexical and thematic content associated with selection at each stage. This study addresses this knowledge gap by asking two questions. Firstly, which attributes of published health science articles, as reflected in their abstracts, correlate with the issuance of a press release by the journal or publisher? Secondly, which attributes correlate with coverage in mainstream news media? To answer these questions, we assembled four novel datasets – two for press release issuance and two for media coverage – each linking the text of published article abstracts to a binary indicator of whether the article received the relevant form of attention. Using regularized linear classifiers on lexical features, we quantify the extent to which press release issuance and news coverage can be predicted from abstract content alone and identify the words most strongly associated with each outcome. Our approach also involves applying a supervised topic modeling approach to uncover latent themes predictive of selection, providing a more interpretable, higher-level view of the kinds of research that attract attention. This work makes three key contributions. Firstly, it provides the first large-scale, data-driven characterization of content associated with both stages of the science-to-news pipeline, built on newly constructed corpora that we describe in detail to facilitate further research. Secondly, it demonstrates empirically that both press release issuance and media coverage are predictable, to a degree that varies across datasets, from the text of the corresponding article, and thereby provides evidence that the content of research systematically informs perceived newsworthiness. Thirdly, it surfaces specific words and topics that are strongly associated with selection at each stage, offering insights into the factors that drive the dissemination of health science research to the broader public. The distinction between selected and unselected research is a crucial one, as it allows us to generate hypotheses about the editorial and journalistic preferences that shape the dissemination of health science research. For instance, it appears that epidemiological studies of common behaviors are particularly favored, a finding that warrants further investigation. By examining the filters through which health science passes, researchers, institutions, and journals can gain a deeper understanding of the factors that influence the publication and coverage of health science research, and consider whether these filters serve the public interest. Our study design involved a retrospective, observational analysis of published health science articles, framing the selection of articles for press releases and mainstream news coverage as two supervised binary classification problems. To tackle these problems, we assembled two independent corpora for each, resulting in a total of four datasets. The unit of analysis was the article abstract, as it is the textual summary most likely to be read by press officers and journalists, and is consistently available through bibliographic databases. We obtained article metadata and abstracts from PubMed and its application programming interface, and only retained articles with an English-language abstract of at least 50 words. Since our study used only publicly available, published material and contained no human participant data, it was exempt from institutional review. We constructed two press release datasets, each with its own unique characteristics. The first corpus comprised 3024 articles from journals whose publishers routinely issue releases through the EurekAlert! service. We labeled an article as positive if a press release explicitly citing its DOI or title appeared on the service within 30 days of publication, and negative if no linked release was found. The second corpus was larger, consisting of 10,760 articles, and was assembled from a broader set of journals using the same labeling rule. To limit confounding by venue-specific press policies and temporal trends in release volume, we matched positives and negatives by journal and publication year. We excluded duplicate records, errata, editorials, and commentaries, focusing our analysis on primary research and review articles. In addition to the press release datasets, we created two media coverage datasets. The first media corpus contained 422 article pairs, while the second consisted of 28,910 article pairs. Each pair comprised one article that received coverage and one that did not, with coverage defined as at least one mention of the article in a mainstream news outlet. We identified mentions using altmetric news-tracking records linking news stories to article identifiers, and restricted our set of qualifying outlets to general-interest national and regional newspapers, broadcasters, and their online editions. Blogs, aggregators, and press release redistribution sites were excluded. To hold constant the venue and timing of publication, we paired each covered article with an uncovered article from the same journal published within the same calendar month. When multiple uncovered candidates existed, we selected one uniformly at random. To preprocess the abstracts, we lowercased and tokenized the text, removing punctuation, numerals, and standard English stop words. We also lemmatized the remaining tokens and removed structural section labels, such as "background" and "conclusions", to prevent classifiers from exploiting formatting conventions. We discarded terms that appeared in fewer than five abstracts or in more than 50% of abstracts, and built our vocabulary from the training data only within each cross-validation fold to avoid information leakage. We represented the abstracts in two ways: as a bag-of-words representation with term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) weighting, using unigrams and bigrams, and as a latent topic representation, described below. To identify words correlated with press release issuance or news coverage, we trained L1-regularized (lasso) logistic regression classifiers and linear support vector machines. Folds for the pair-based datasets were constructed at the pair level, ensuring that both members of a pair always fell in the same fold. Within each training partition, hyperparameters were tuned by an inner 5-fold cross-validation loop.
