The practice of continuous deployment (CD) has become increasingly prevalent in software engineering, as it enables organizations to automatically build, test, and release code changes to end users through an automated deployment pipeline (Humble and Farley, 2010). By adopting CD, organizations can shorten release cycles, obtain faster customer feedback, and reduce the manual effort associated with releasing software. Industry surveys have consistently shown that frequent, automated deployment is associated with better organizational performance and faster recovery from failures (Forsgren et al., 2018). A crucial enabler of CD is infrastructure as code (IaC), which involves provisioning and configuring computing infrastructure through machine-readable scripts rather than manual procedures (Humble and Farley, 2010; Rahman et al., 2019a). Tools like Puppet, Chef, and Ansible allow practitioners to specify the desired state of servers, services, and dependencies in source code, which can then be version-controlled, reviewed, tested, and executed repeatedly and consistently across environments. However, treating infrastructure as software also exposes it to the defects that affect any other software artifact. A defect in an IaC script can propagate to every machine on which the script is executed, compromising the reliability of the entire deployment pipeline. The consequences of such defects can be severe, as illustrated by the 2017 outage of Amazon's Simple Storage Service, which was caused by an erroneous operational command and affected a large number of dependent websites and services (Amazon Web Services, 2017). Prior empirical work has shown that defects in IaC scripts are not rare. For example, Jiang and Adams (2015) observed that infrastructure code in open source projects co-evolves with, and is often as change-prone as, production code. Similarly, Rahman and Williams (2018) found that defect-related commits constitute a substantial share of the commits to IaC scripts in several open source repositories. Defective IaC scripts can cause frequent deployment failures and consume considerable developer effort, undermining the benefits that motivate CD in the first place. Despite the importance of IaC, research on its quality remains sparse relative to its adoption in industry. A systematic mapping study found that few studies have examined the relationship between source code characteristics and script quality (Rahman et al., 2019a). While some studies have catalogued configuration smells in Puppet code (Sharma et al., 2016) and Chef (Schwarz et al., 2018), and proposed approaches for testing the idempotence and convergence of configuration scripts (Hanappi et al., 2016; Hummer et al., 2013), these studies rely heavily on smells and rules defined a priori by researchers or tool builders. They do not establish which properties of IaC source code are actually associated with defects observed in practice. In the broader software engineering literature, source code properties have long been used to characterize and predict defects. Size, complexity, and change metrics are known to correlate with defect proneness in general-purpose languages (Nagappan et al., 2006; Hall et al., 2012; Menzies et al., 2007). However, IaC languages differ markedly from general-purpose languages, as they are declarative or hybrid in nature, describe resources and their relationships rather than algorithms, and are dominated by configuration values, file paths, and invocations of external modules. Properties that matter in conventional code, such as inheritance depth or loop structure, may therefore carry little signal in IaC scripts, whereas properties specific to configuration, such as how values are specified or how dependencies are included, may carry considerable signal. Given the lack of empirical evidence on the relationship between IaC source code properties and defects, practitioners lack data-driven guidance on where to focus code review and testing, and researchers lack a principled basis for building automated defect prediction models for IaC. To address this gap, we hypothesize that certain properties of IaC source code, such as the number of lines of code and the use of hard-coded strings as configuration values, are correlated with defective scripts. The objective of this paper is to help practitioners increase the quality of IaC scripts through an empirical study that identifies source code properties of defective IaC scripts. To achieve this objective, we pursue three research questions: RQ1: What source code properties characterize defective infrastructure as code scripts? RQ2: Do practitioners agree with the identified source code properties? RQ3: How accurately can we predict defective infrastructure as code scripts using the identified source code properties? To answer RQ1, we apply qualitative analysis to defect-related commits mined from open source repositories, deriving candidate properties from the code changes that fixed defects and quantifying the relationship between each property and script defectiveness using statistical tests and effect sizes. To answer RQ2, we survey practitioners to assess their level of agreement with each identified property, providing a check on whether the empirical findings match practitioner experience. To answer RQ3, we construct defect prediction models from the identified properties and evaluate them on 2,439 Puppet scripts drawn from four datasets collected from open source organizations, namely Mirantis, Mozilla, Openstack, and Wikimedia. We follow established practice in defect prediction by comparing several learners and reporting precision and recall, the measures that matter most to practitioners who must decide how much inspection effort to allocate (Hall et al., 2012; Menzies et al., 2007). Our analysis identifies 10 source code properties that correlate with defective IaC scripts, with lines of code and hard-coded string showing the strongest correlation with defective scripts. In the practitioner survey, the majority of respondents agreed with two properties: include, the property of executing external modules or scripts, and hard-coded string. Prediction models built on the identified properties achieve a precision of 0.70 to 0.78 and a recall of 0.54 to 0.67, suggesting that these properties carry practical predictive signal for IaC defects. This paper makes several contributions to the field of software engineering, including a list of 10 source code properties of IaC scripts that correlate with defects, derived from defect-related commits in open source repositories, and a quantitative assessment of the strength of these correlations. Our findings provide a foundation for future research on defect prediction in IaC and offer guidance for practitioners seeking to improve the quality of their IaC scripts. By identifying the source code properties that are most strongly associated with defects, practitioners can focus their code review and testing efforts on the most critical aspects of their IaC scripts, ultimately improving the reliability and maintainability of their software systems. The relationship between script properties and defectiveness is a crucial aspect of infrastructure as code (IaC) development. Our analysis reveals that lines of code and hard-coded strings are the most strongly associated with defective scripts. To better understand this relationship, we conducted a comprehensive study that combines empirical evidence with practitioner perception. We developed defect prediction models using the identified properties and evaluated their precision and recall on a large dataset of 2,439 scripts from four organizations. This paper is organized as follows: we first provide background information on IaC and review related work, then describe our methodology, present our results, and discuss the implications for practitioners and researchers. Finally, we address potential threats to validity and draw conclusions. Our research was motivated by three key questions: (RQ1) What source code properties characterize defective IaC scripts? (RQ2) Do practitioners agree that these properties are associated with defective scripts? (RQ3) How well can these properties predict defective scripts? To answer these questions, we conducted a three-phase empirical study. First, we applied qualitative analysis to defect-related commits to derive source code properties of defective IaC scripts. Second, we quantified the association between each property and defective scripts and surveyed practitioners on their agreement with these properties. Third, we built defect prediction models from the properties to evaluate their practical utility. We focused on Puppet, a widely used declarative configuration management language in continuous deployment. Our datasets consisted of repositories from four organizations that use Puppet in production: Mirantis, Mozilla, OpenStack, and Wikimedia. We selected these repositories based on three criteria: (1) at least 11% of the files in the repository had to be Puppet scripts, (2) the repository had to be under active development with at least two commits per month, and (3) the repository had to contain enough history to support defect mining. We cloned each repository and extracted the full commit history using the PyDriller library, resulting in a total of 2,439 scripts. To identify defect-related commits, we followed the approach of Rahman and Williams (2018) and classified a commit as defect-related if its message described the correction of a defect in a Puppet script. We applied a keyword filter on commit messages and retained only commits that modified at least one Puppet script. However, keyword matching alone can yield false positives (Herzig et al., 2013), so two raters manually inspected every retained message, together with the associated diff, to resolve any ambiguities. Commits that described feature additions, refactoring, or documentation changes were excluded. We measured inter-rater agreement using Cohen's κ (Cohen, 1960) and resolved any disagreements through discussion. A script was labeled defective if it was modified by at least one defect-related commit and neutral otherwise. Our qualitative analysis (RQ1) involved applying open coding (Strauss and Corbin, 1998) to the code changes in the defect-related commits. The first author examined the lines removed or modified by each defect-fixing commit and recorded the code elements implicated in the defect. We grouped related codes into candidate properties through iterative comparison and gave each property a name and an operational definition. To evaluate the reliability of the resulting scheme, a second rater independently applied the definitions to a random sample of 200 defect-related commits, and we computed Cohen's κ. Disagreements prompted refinement of the definitions until the raters reached consensus, yielding a set of properties that could be computed automatically from script source code. For each script, we computed the count of each property using a parser built on the Puppet language grammar, normalizing nothing except where noted, so that counts reflected raw code characteristics. We included lines of code (LOC) as a baseline property, as size is a well-established correlate of defects (Zhang, 2009). To quantify the relationship between each property and defective scripts, we compared the property's distribution in defective and neutral scripts within each dataset. Since property counts were non-normally distributed (Shapiro–Wilk tests, p < 0.05), we used the non-parametric Mann–Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney, 1947) at α = 0.05, applying the Bonferroni correction to adjust for multiple comparisons across properties. We quantified effect sizes using Cliff's δ (Cliff, 1993) and interpreted magnitudes using conventional thresholds (Romano et al., 2006). We also computed the median property value for defective and neutral scripts and ranked properties by their effect size. To assess whether the properties reflect practitioner experience, we conducted a web-based survey (RQ2). For each property, the questionnaire provided its name, definition, and a short code example from a real Puppet script, then asked respondents to rate their agreement with the statement that scripts containing the property are more likely to be defective. Responses used a five-point Likert scale (Likert, 1932) from strongly disagree to strongly agree. We collected respondents' years of IaC experience and primary role and included an optional free-text field for comments. We distributed the survey to practitioners who had contributed commits to the studied repositories and to other open-source Puppet projects, as well as through public developer forums and mailing lists. Before deployment, we piloted the instrument with three practitioners, whose feedback led to clearer wording and the removal of ambiguous examples. Participation was voluntary and anonymous. We report agreement as the percentage of respondents choosing agree or strongly agree for each property and considered a property to have majority agreement when this percentage exceeded 50%. We analyzed the free-text comments using thematic coding. Our results show that lines of code and hard-coded strings are the most strongly associated with defective scripts. We also found that practitioners generally agree with these findings, with majority agreement for most properties. Our defect prediction models, built using these properties, demonstrated good precision and recall on the large dataset of scripts. These findings have important implications for practitioners and researchers, highlighting the need for careful consideration

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a chronic rheumatic disease that affects approximately one in 1,000 children, encompassing a heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by arthritis of unknown cause that begins before the age of 16 and persists for at least six weeks. The treatment of JIA has undergone significant changes over the past two decades, with early and more aggressive use of conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as methotrexate, and the introduction of biologic agents targeting tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and T-cell costimulation. These advances have led to an increase in the proportion of children who achieve low disease activity or clinical remission. Nevertheless, a substantial number of youth with JIA continue to experience poor health-related quality of life (HRQOL), including limitations in physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, even when clinical measures indicate that the disease is well controlled. The persistence of poor HRQOL in the face of well-controlled disease suggests that standard clinical indicators may not capture the full range of factors that contribute to the lived experience of JIA. HRQOL is a complex, multidimensional construct that reflects an individual's perception of how their health and illness affect their physical, psychological, and social wellbeing. In pediatric rheumatology, HRQOL has been measured using a variety of instruments, including the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL), disease-specific tools, and the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS). Studies using these instruments have consistently shown that HRQOL in JIA is lower than in healthy peers and that disease activity, functional disability, and pain are correlated with HRQOL. However, the associations between clinician-assessed disease activity and HRQOL are typically modest, and a significant proportion of the variance in HRQOL remains unexplained. One potential explanation for this discrepancy is that the burden of treatment itself may contribute to poor HRQOL. Children with JIA often take medications for extended periods, frequently in combination, and these regimens can involve injections, infusions, laboratory monitoring, and the risk of adverse effects. Methotrexate, the most widely used first-line systemic therapy, is effective but is commonly associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, such as nausea and abdominal pain, as well as anticipatory and associative symptoms. Methotrexate intolerance has been reported in a substantial minority of patients and can lead to reduced adherence, dose changes, or discontinuation, ultimately resulting in poorer HRQOL and greater distress for both children and parents. Another domain of patient experience that is not fully captured in routine care is the day-to-day symptom burden of disease. Morning stiffness, a classic feature of inflammatory arthritis, is not consistently recorded in clinical encounters, and its relationship to HRQOL in contemporary JIA cohorts is not well characterized. Pain interference, which reflects the extent to which pain disrupts activities, social participation, and mood, has emerged as an important patient-reported outcome, and PROMIS provides a validated pediatric measure of it. Pain interference may remain elevated in children with inactive disease, representing an important and under-recognized source of reduced HRQOL. Patient-centered outcomes research has increasingly emphasized the importance of collecting information directly from patients and families to understand which experiences matter most and how they relate to outcomes. Multisite disease registries, such as the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, offer a platform for this type of research, as they enroll large and diverse samples and contain detailed clinical data, including diagnosis, disease activity, and medication history. The CARRA Registry is a North American observational registry of children with rheumatic diseases, including JIA, that has enrolled thousands of patients across dozens of centers. While the registry's clinical data have supported research on treatment patterns and safety, it has not routinely included patient- or parent-reported measures of HRQOL and experiences of disease and treatment. The aim of this study was to add patient-reported outcomes to the CARRA Registry and to use them to quantify HRQOL and experiences of disease and treatment burden among youth with JIA. Parents served as proxy reporters of their child's HRQOL, pain interference, morning stiffness, history of serious medication side effects, and, for those taking methotrexate, methotrexate intolerance. We sought to answer three questions: What is the distribution of HRQOL and these disease and treatment experiences in a multisite registry sample? How is each experience associated with HRQOL? And do associations between treatment burden and HRQOL persist after accounting for disease burden, disease activity, and patient characteristics? We hypothesized that both disease and treatment burden would be independently associated with lower HRQOL. This study makes several contributions to the field. It demonstrates the feasibility of augmenting an established multicenter registry with patient-reported measures, creating a model that other registries may adopt. It provides estimates of the prevalence of morning stiffness, serious medication side effects, and methotrexate intolerance in a registry cohort with long disease duration. Most importantly, it evaluates the independent contributions of disease and treatment burden to HRQOL, testing the proposition that adverse treatment experiences undermine wellbeing beyond the effects of disease symptoms and activity. The findings of this study may help clinicians better understand the complex interplay between disease and treatment burden and HRQOL, ultimately informing the development of more effective and patient-centered treatment strategies for youth with JIA. By highlighting the importance of considering the patient's perspective in the management of JIA, this study has the potential to improve outcomes and enhance the quality of life for children and families affected by this chronic and debilitating disease. In our ongoing efforts to improve the quality of life for youth with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), researchers have been working to identify modifiable targets that can be assessed and addressed in a routine clinical setting. To this end, we conducted a cross-sectional, observational study nested within the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, a comprehensive, multisite registry of children with pediatric rheumatic diseases enrolled at North American pediatric rheumatology centers. The CARRA Registry, established by Beukelman et al. in 2017, collects a wealth of clinician-reported data, including demographic, diagnostic, disease activity, and medication information, at enrollment and at regular follow-up visits. For our study, we augmented this existing infrastructure with a patient-centered data collection component, in which parents completed a survey about their child's health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and experiences with disease and treatment. Participating sites obtained the necessary approvals from their local institutional review boards or the central IRB used by the registry, and parents provided informed consent, with children providing assent where required by local policy. Our eligibility criteria included enrollment in the CARRA Registry, a physician diagnosis of JIA according to International League of Associations for Rheumatology criteria, an age range of 2 to 18 years, and the presence of a parent or legal guardian who could read and respond in English. Notably, because the survey was completed by parent proxy, we did not exclude youth who were too young or unable to self-report. Instead, we relied on parents to provide insights into their child's experiences, recognizing that they are often best positioned to report on their child's daily functioning and well-being. To recruit participants, sites identified eligible patients from the registry and invited their parents to complete the survey, either during a clinic visit or remotely via mail or secure electronic link. Parents completed the survey on a single occasion, and we linked their responses to registry data from the visit nearest to survey completion using a unique study identifier. To ensure the integrity of our analysis, we restricted our analytic sample to patients with complete data on the primary HRQOL outcome and key covariates. Our measurement of HRQOL was based on the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0 Generic Core Scales, parent-proxy report, which has been widely used and validated in pediatric populations. The PedsQL contains 23 items that span physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, with a recall period of the previous month. We used the Total Scale Score as our primary outcome, as well as physical and psychosocial summary scores, to provide a comprehensive picture of HRQOL. Age-appropriate parent-proxy forms were used for children across different age ranges (2–4, 5–7, 8–12, and 13–18 years), allowing us to capture the unique experiences and challenges faced by children at different stages of development. In addition to HRQOL, we assessed pain interference using the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Pediatric Pain Interference parent-proxy short form. This measure provides a standardized way to evaluate the impact of pain on daily activities, with higher scores indicating greater interference. We also collected data on morning stiffness, which is a recognized marker of active inflammatory arthritis and an important aspect of disease activity assessment. Parents reported the typical duration of their child's morning stiffness on a usual day, and we dichotomized this variable as more than 15 minutes versus 15 minutes or less. To capture the potential downsides of treatment, we asked parents about their child's experiences with medication side effects. Specifically, we inquired about the nature and severity of any side effects and classified them using predefined criteria. A serious side effect was defined as one that led to medication discontinuation or dose change, required medical evaluation or treatment, or substantially disrupted the child's daily functioning. We created a binary indicator of one or more serious medication side effects to facilitate analysis. For children currently or previously treated with methotrexate, parents completed the Methotrexate Intolerance Severity Score (MISS), which assesses symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and restlessness or irritability. Scores range from 0 to 25, with a score of 6 or higher indicating clinically relevant methotrexate intolerance. Our analysis also incorporated clinical and demographic characteristics, including patient age, sex, race and ethnicity, disease duration, JIA category, and treating site. We obtained these data from the registry, along with information on disease activity, which was captured using the clinical Juvenile Arthritis Disease Activity Score based on 10 joints (cJADAS-10). This score combines physician global assessment, parent global assessment of wellbeing, and active joint count to provide a comprehensive picture of disease activity. Current medication use, including methotrexate and biologic agents, was also abstracted from registry records. In our statistical analysis, we first summarized participant characteristics and study measures using means and standard deviations for continuous variables and counts and percentages for categorical variables. We inspected the distributions of PedsQL, pain interference, and disease activity scores for normality and outliers, and then proceeded to estimate the associations between measures of disease burden (pain interference and morning stiffness) and treatment burden (serious side effects and methotrexate intolerance) and HRQOL. To account for the clustering of patients within participating sites, we used generalized estimating equations (GEE) with an exchangeable working correlation structure and robust standard errors. Our primary aim was to model the relationship between each burden measure and HRQOL, first in unadjusted models and then in models adjusted for patient demographics (age, sex, and race/ethnicity) and disease duration, with clustering by site. We then added disease burden measures to models of treatment burden to determine whether treatment-related associations persisted independent of disease symptoms. Finally, we adjusted for disease activity (cJADAS-10) and current medication use to evaluate whether associations were attenuated by clinical characteristics. Because the methotrexate intolerance analysis was restricted to methotrexate users, we conducted this analysis in the relevant subsample, using parallel model-building to facilitate comparison. Throughout our analysis, we compared coefficients across successive models to assess attenuation and evaluated collinearity among covariates using variance inflation factors. Regression coefficients are reported with 95% confidence intervals and p-values, and we considered p-values below 0.01 to indicate statistical significance in primary analyses to limit the risk of type I error. Secondary analyses repeated the models for physical and psychosocial PedsQL summary scores, providing a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between burden measures and HRQOL. Missing data were infrequent and handled by complete-case analysis, and all analyses were performed using standard statistical software. Our analysis of data from the CARRA Registry, which included 180 youth with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), provided valuable insights into the complex relationships between disease burden, treatment burden, and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in this population. The recognition of complex patterns in real-world data often presents a unique challenge, as it cannot be reduced to a standard multi-class classification problem. In many cases, only one class is well-represented in the training data, while the remaining classes are rare, heterogeneous, or impossible to enumerate in advance. This is evident in applications such as fault detection in industrial systems, intrusion detection, medical screening, and identity verification. The class of interest is typically well-defined, whereas the other classes are not. To address this scenario, one-class classification (OCC) has emerged as a viable solution, where a decision rule is learned from examples of a single class, and then used to determine whether a new sample belongs to that class. The most well-known OCC methods include the One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM) and Support Vector Data Description (SVDD). The OC-SVM separates the data from the origin in a kernel-induced feature space, while SVDD finds the minimum-volume hypersphere that encloses the target data. Both methods can be extended to non-linear boundaries using kernels and are widely used as baselines. More recently, deep variants such as Deep SVDD have been proposed, which couple representation learning with a compact description of the target class. However, the performance of any one-class method heavily depends on the feature space in which the data are described. Since no negative samples are available to guide the choice of features, the data representation is often high-dimensional, redundant, or noisy, which can compromise the compactness assumption underlying SVDD. To mitigate this issue, dimensionality reduction is commonly applied as a separate pre-processing step. Classical techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) are unsupervised and optimize criteria like reconstruction error or variance, which may not be directly related to the objective of the subsequent one-class classifier. To address this mismatch, Subspace Support Vector Data Description (S-SVDD) was proposed, which jointly learns a linear or non-linear projection and the SVDD description, so that the target data become compact in a subspace optimized for the one-class objective. Related graph-embedded formulations also use the geometry of the target class to regularize the learned representation. However, these approaches assume that every sample is represented by a single feature vector from a single source, which is increasingly at odds with the way data are acquired in modern applications. In many cases, objects, events, and subjects are observed through multiple modalities, such as different sensors, imaging devices, or feature extractors, which capture complementary aspects of the same underlying phenomenon. Examples include visual and thermal imagery, audio and video streams, and multi-sensor measurements in industrial monitoring. Multimodal and multi-view learning has been shown to improve robustness and accuracy compared to learning from a single source. Classical subspace methods such as Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) learn projections that maximize cross-modal correlation, while deep multimodal architectures learn shared representations. However, these techniques are designed to model statistical dependence between modalities and do not take into account the objective of a downstream one-class classifier. In the OCC literature, the multimodal setting is typically handled in one of two ways, both of which have limitations. The first approach is to train a separate one-class model on each modality and combine the resulting decision scores, which ignores relations among modalities during representation learning and can be adversely affected by weak or noisy modalities. The second approach is to concatenate the features of all modalities into a single vector and apply a standard one-class method, which increases dimensionality, leaves modality-specific scale and noise characteristics unaddressed, and makes the description susceptible to the curse of dimensionality when training samples are limited. Neither strategy learns modality-specific mappings into a common space that is designed from the outset for describing the target class. Consequently, there is a clear gap in the existing literature: no approach jointly learns, for each modality, a transformation into a shared low-dimensional space and a single compact description of the target class using data from all modalities, while relying exclusively on target-class samples. The question motivating this work is whether multimodal one-class learning can be improved by learning modality-specific projections to a common subspace in which a single hypersphere, trained only on target data from all modalities, provides a tighter and more discriminative description than that obtainable from any single modality or from naive fusion. Answering this question requires addressing several challenges, including learning the projections in conjunction with the data description, admitting regularization strategies that prevent degenerate solutions, and handling both linear and non-linear relations. To address these challenges, we introduce Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MS-SVDD), a method that extends the S-SVDD framework to data from multiple modalities. MS-SVDD iteratively optimizes two components: a set of modality-specific transformations that map each original feature space into a common subspace, and a joint SVDD description of the projected data from all modalities. The transformations are learned using information from the class of interest only, so the method remains a genuine one-class approach and requires no negative or outlier examples at training time. The contributions of this work are threefold. Firstly, we formulate the problem of learning a shared one-class-optimized subspace from multiple modalities and propose MS-SVDD, which jointly learns modality-specific projections and a single compact description of the target class. Secondly, we propose several regularization strategies for the method, which control the geometry of the learned subspace and the relationships among the projected modalities, allowing the formulation to be adapted to different degrees of cross-modal agreement. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of MS-SVDD in improving multimodal one-class learning, providing a tighter and more discriminative description of the target class than that obtainable from any single modality or from naive fusion. This paper proposes a novel approach to multimodal one-class classification, which we term MS-SVDD. Our method provides both linear and non-linear formulations, allowing it to be applied to data with simple as well as complex structure. Furthermore, we introduce an iterative optimization procedure to learn a task-specific common subspace that effectively integrates information from multiple modalities. To evaluate the performance of MS-SVDD, we conduct an extensive experimental evaluation on five publicly available multimodal datasets, comparing our approach with one-class methods trained on a single modality and on fused data from all modalities. The results show that MS-SVDD outperforms all competing approaches on four of the five datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of learning a shared subspace for multimodal data. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing the necessary background on Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) and Subspace SVDD (S-SVDD) in Section 2. In Section 3, we present the proposed MS-SVDD method, including its regularization strategies and linear and non-linear formulations. Section 4 describes the datasets and experimental protocol used to evaluate MS-SVDD, and reports the results of our experiments. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. To formulate the problem, let us denote the data from M modalities as 𝒳 = {X¹,…,X^M}, where X^m ∈ ℝ^{Dm×N} contains the N training samples of the target class represented in the m-th modality, with Dm being the modality-specific dimensionality. Note that only target-class samples are used during training, which is consistent with the one-class classification (OCC) setting. We assume that samples are paired across modalities, and each modality is z-score normalized using training statistics before projection. SVDD seeks to find the smallest hypersphere, with centre a and radius R, that encloses most of the training data. In contrast, S-SVDD jointly learns a projection Q ∈ ℝ^{d×D} and the hypersphere in the projected space. We extend this idea to the multimodal case by defining a modality-specific projection Qm ∈ ℝ^{d×Dm} that maps every modality into a common d-dimensional subspace, where one shared hypersphere (a, R) describes data from all modalities. The multimodal objective is to minimize the following expression: min{R,a,ξ,{Qm}} R² + C Σm Σi ξi^m + (λ/2) Ω({Qm}), subject to ‖Qm xi^m − a‖² ≤ R² + ξi^m and ξi^m ≥ 0 for i = 1,…,N and m = 1,…,M. Here, C > 0 controls the trade-off between the volume of the hypersphere and the training errors, and Ω is a regularization term weighted by λ ≥ 0. The problem is non-convex jointly in {Qm} and the hypersphere parameters, so we employ an alternating scheme to optimize the objective. With the projections fixed, the problem reduces to a standard SVDD on the pooled projected samples {Qm xi^m}, and its Lagrangian dual is a quadratic program, which we solve using a sequential minimal optimization solver. The dual variables αi^m satisfy 0 ≤ αi^m ≤ C and Σ{m,i} αi^m = 1, and the centre is a = Σ{m,i} αi^m Qm xi^m. With the dual variables fixed, each Qm is updated by gradient descent on the Lagrangian, ∂ℒ/∂Qm = 2 Σi αi^m (Qm xi^m − a)(xi^m)ᵀ + λ ∂Ω/∂Qm, with Qm ← Qm − η ∂ℒ/∂Qm. We set the step size η to 10⁻³ and use the Adam update rule for stability. The two steps alternate until the relative change of the objective falls below 10⁻⁵ or 100 iterations are reached. Each Qm is initialized using one of three schemes: PCA of the corresponding modality, a random Gaussian matrix, or the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) directions between pairs of modalities. The default initialization is PCA, while the other two schemes are examined in an ablation study. Because a shared radius and centre are used, a test sample is scored in modality m by its distance ‖Qm x^m − a‖², and is accepted as a target if this distance does not exceed R². We investigate three choices of regularization term Ω. The first option, norm regularization, is defined as Ω₁ = Σm ‖Qm‖²F, which limits the scale of the projections and prevents the trivial solution in which all data collapse to a point. The second option, variance regularization, is given by Ω₂ = Σm tr(Qm Sm Qmᵀ), where Sm is the scatter matrix of modality m. This penalizes the dispersion of the projected data and promotes compact descriptions. The third option, cross-modal alignment, is defined as Ω₃ = Σ{m<l} Σi ‖Qm xi^m − Ql xi^l‖², which encourages paired samples from different modalities to coincide in the shared subspace, similarly to the correlation-maximization principle of CCA but without requiring non-target data. In all cases, the rows of each Qm are rescaled to unit norm after each update when Ω₁ is not used, to avoid degenerate scaling. For the non-linear variant of MS-SVDD, each modality is implicitly mapped by a feature map φm to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel Km(x, y) = exp(−‖x − y‖²/2σm²). Following the representer theorem, the projection is parameterized as Qm = Λm Φmᵀ, where Φm = [φm(x1^m),…,φm(xN^m)] and Λm ∈ ℝ^{d×N}, so that Qm φm(x) = Λm km(x) with km(x) = [Km(x1^m, x),…,Km(xN^m, x)]ᵀ. The updates described above are then performed with respect to Λm, initialized by kernel PCA. The width σm is set to the mean pairwise Euclidean distance in modality m multiplied by a factor chosen from a grid. We evaluate MS-SVDD on five publicly available multimodal datasets. The first dataset, Multiple Features (Mfeat), consists of 2,000 handwritten digits described by six modalities. The second dataset, Caltech-101 subset, contains 441 images represented by six descriptors. The third dataset, Animals with Attributes, comprises 30,475 images from 50 classes, with SIFT, color-histogram, and deep-network features treated as three modalities. The fourth dataset, Corel image features, includes colour histogram, colour moments, co-occurrence texture, and colour-layout features for 10,000 images in 100 categories. The fifth dataset, Reuters multilingual, consists of documents in six categories written in English and translated into four other languages, with each language treated as one modality. Each class serves in turn as the target class, and all remaining classes are treated as non-target classes. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of MS-SVDD in multimodal one-class classification. The proposed method outperforms all competing approaches on four of the five datasets, indicating that learning a task-specific common subspace is more effective than either individual-modality models or direct fusion. The demographic shift towards an ageing population has placed significant fiscal pressures on pension systems across Europe, prompting policymakers to prioritize the extension of working lives as a central objective of social policy. In response, many countries have implemented reforms aimed at encouraging older workers to remain in employment, such as raising statutory pension ages, restricting access to early retirement schemes, and introducing incentives for continued work (OECD 2015; European Commission 2012). The European Union's Europe 2020 strategy explicitly targets higher employment rates among older workers, with several governments now debating or legislating retirement ages of 67 or beyond. As a result, employment rates among individuals aged 55 to 64 have indeed risen in most European countries over the past two decades (Eurostat 2014). However, beyond the age of 65, paid work remains a relatively rare phenomenon, with its prevalence varying significantly across countries. For instance, in France and Belgium, only a small percentage of individuals in this age group engage in paid work, whereas in countries such as Sweden, Switzerland, or Estonia, the share is substantially higher (Hofäcker and Naumann 2015; Scherger et al. 2012). This disparity highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the factors influencing late-life employment. To date, the scientific literature on late careers has focused primarily on the opposite end of the spectrum, examining the determinants of early or premature exit from the labor market. A substantial body of research has investigated the role of factors such as poor health, physically and psychologically demanding jobs, low job control, and unfavorable pension incentives in predicting early retirement (Blekesaune and Solem 2005; Siegrist et al. 2007; Van den Berg et al. 2010; de Wind et al. 2014). The demand-control model (Karasek and Theorell 1990) and the model of effort-reward imbalance (Siegrist 1996) have been used to conceptualize stressful psychosocial work environments, which have been shown to predict both poor health and the intention or decision to retire early (Siegrist et al. 2006; Wahrendorf et al. 2013). From this perspective, early exit is often viewed as a response to adverse working conditions and deteriorating health, with financial incentives and attractive leisure opportunities constituting "pull" factors (Shultz et al. 1998; Radl 2013). In contrast, relatively little is known about individuals who continue working beyond the age at which most of their peers have retired. Existing studies suggest that working beyond conventional retirement ages is a selective phenomenon, with older workers who continue to work tend to be healthier, more highly educated, and more likely to be self-employed than those who retire (Dingemans and Henkens 2014; Kanabar 2015; Principi et al. 2014). The motives for continued work are heterogeneous, with some individuals working because they enjoy their job, value social contacts, or wish to remain active, while others work out of financial necessity due to low pension entitlements (Platts et al. 2016; Vickerstaff 2010). This distinction is crucial, as the policy discourse on "active ageing" often implicitly assumes that longer working lives are voluntary and beneficial, whereas the empirical reality may comprise both privileged and vulnerable groups (Alcover et al. 2014; Lain 2012). Whether extended working lives are accompanied by favorable or unfavorable job characteristics is an important empirical question that has received limited attention to date. Several gaps remain in the existing evidence. First, most studies of late-life employment focus on the transition ages between 50 and 65, rarely describing individuals who work at ages 65 to 80, a group that is small but growing and of particular relevance for debates on raising pension ages further. Second, studies of older workers often consider a limited set of characteristics, such as demographic and health status, and pay less attention to detailed employment conditions, including employment status, occupational position, and weekly working hours. Third, while there is considerable evidence on the psychosocial work environment as a predictor of early exit, we know little about how exposure to stressful work, such as low control or effort-reward imbalance, differs between those working beyond 65 and those who are retired. Because retired persons, by definition, no longer work, a meaningful comparison requires information on their conditions in the last job before retirement. Such a comparison can indicate whether those who continue to work come from systematically better or worse job circumstances than those who have left, which is crucial for judging whether policies that postpone retirement would burden particular groups. Fourth, much research is limited to single countries, which complicates generalization given the institutional diversity of European pension, labor market, and welfare systems (Ebbinghaus 2006). Comparative, harmonized data covering a wide age range and diverse institutional settings are required to address these gaps. The present study addresses these limitations using data from the fourth wave of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE; Börsch-Supan et al. 2013), collected between 2009 and 2011. SHARE is a multidisciplinary, cross-national panel study of people aged 50 and over, offering harmonized information on health, socio-economic circumstances, and employment. Importantly, wave 4 includes measures of psychosocial working conditions for current workers and, retrospectively, for the last job of retired respondents, as well as indicators of physical and mental health. This allows us to compare current workers and retirees aged 65 to 80 across 16 European countries within a single analytical framework. We pursue three research questions. First, which sociodemographic characteristics (age, gender, education, partnership, and financial situation) are associated with working beyond age 65? Second, how do employment conditions, namely employment status, occupational position, and working hours, and stressful psychosocial working conditions (low control and effort-reward imbalance) differ between those working at ages 65 to 80 and the retired in their last job? Third, how are these working conditions and health (physical and mental) related to the likelihood of being in paid work in this age group, once country context and potential confounders are taken into account? We expect that people working beyond 65 are more often self-employed, hold advantaged occupational positions, report more favorable psychosocial working conditions, and are in better health than their retired counterparts. This expectation follows from selection arguments: those with greater autonomy, rewards, and resources have both more opportunities and more incentives to remain employed, while those exposed to strain or ill health are more likely to withdraw (Wahrendorf et al. 2013; Dingemans and Henkens 2014). The study contributes to the literature in three ways. It shifts attention from early exit to prolonged participation and describes in detail who works at ages 65 to 80, a group that is growing in size and relevance. By examining the sociodemographic characteristics, employment conditions, and psychosocial working conditions of older workers, we can better understand the factors that influence late-life employment and inform policies aimed at promoting active ageing. Furthermore, the study provides a comparative analysis of older workers across 16 European countries, allowing for a nuanced understanding of the institutional and contextual factors that shape late-life employment. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of evidence-based policies that support the extension of working lives, while also ensuring that these policies do not disproportionately burden vulnerable groups. The relationship between employment characteristics, psychosocial work stress, and extended working lives has garnered significant attention in recent years, particularly in the context of rising pension ages across Europe. To contribute to this debate, our study brings together a comprehensive set of employment characteristics and established measures of psychosocial work stress, comparing current workers with retirees using information on their previous jobs. Furthermore, we employ multilevel models to account for cross-national variation, thereby providing a nuanced understanding of the social selectivity of extended working lives. This, in turn, informs discussions on the consequences of increasing pension ages for different social groups. Our analysis is based on data from wave 4 of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), a multidisciplinary, cross-national panel study of community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older, as well as their partners. Conducted between 2009 and 2011, wave 4 fieldwork involved face-to-face interviews using computer-assisted personal interviewing, with samples drawn from probability samples, mostly from population registers or multi-stage area sampling. For a detailed description of the methodological aspects, including sampling design and response rates, we refer to previous publications (Börsch-Supan and Jürges 2005; Malter and Börsch-Supan 2013). The wave 4 dataset comprises 58,000 respondents from 16 countries, spanning from Sweden to Portugal. To construct our analytic sample, we focused on men and women aged 65 to 80 years who were either in paid work or retired at the time of interview. This age band was selected because, in most countries studied, 65 corresponds to the statutory pension age or a close approximation, and employment becomes relatively rare after the age of 80. Respondents were classified as working if they reported being employed or self-employed, and as retired if they reported being retired. We excluded individuals who described themselves as homemakers, unemployed, permanently sick or disabled, or "other," as well as retired persons who had never been in paid employment and thus could not provide information on previous working conditions. After applying these exclusions and removing cases with missing information on key variables, our final sample consisted of 17,625 individuals, with 1,647 in paid work and 15,978 retired. Our outcome variable was labor market participation, coded as 1 for current paid work and 0 for retirement. We measured employment conditions for both the current job among workers and the last job before retirement among retirees. Employment status was categorized into employees, self-employed persons with employees, and self-employed persons without employees (own-account workers). Occupational position was based on the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-88) and grouped into high, intermediate, and low categories. Weekly working hours were categorized as part-time, full-time, and long hours, following established conventions in the literature on extended working hours. To assess psychosocial working conditions, we utilized two established stress models. Low control at work was derived from the demand–control model and measured using two items in SHARE, which were summed and dichotomized at the country-pooled lowest tertile of control. Effort–reward imbalance (ERI) was calculated using the short SHARE version, with effort assessed through two items and reward through five items. The ERI ratio was calculated, and respondents were classified as experiencing effort–reward imbalance if the ratio exceeded 1. For retirees, the same items referred retrospectively to the last job before retirement, and we address the potential for recall bias in the discussion. Health was captured through physical and mental health indicators. Physical health was measured by self-rated health, presence of limitations in activities of daily living, and the number of chronic diseases. Mental health was assessed using the EURO-D scale, a 12-item depression symptom scale validated across European countries. Covariates included age, sex, educational attainment, partnership status, and household net wealth quintile within country as an indicator of financial resources. We used wealth instead of income due to the high proportion of missing income values and because it better represents resources in later life. Our statistical analysis began with a description of the sample by labor market status, stratified by sex, using proportions for categorical variables and means with standard deviations for continuous variables. We assessed differences between workers and retirees using design-adjusted chi-square tests and t-tests. Furthermore, we calculated the percentage of people aged 65 to 80 who were still working in each country, providing insight into the prevalence of extended working lives across Europe. By examining the relationships between employment characteristics, psychosocial work stress, and health, our study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the factors influencing extended working lives and the potential consequences of rising pension ages for different social groups. In our analysis, we also considered the potential impact of cross-national variation on our findings, using multilevel models to account for the clustering of individuals within countries. This approach allowed us to examine the relationships between employment characteristics, psychosocial work stress, and health while controlling for country-level differences. Public health interventions are inherently complex, comprising multiple interacting components that target various levels of influence, from individuals to communities and systems, and are delivered in contexts that shape both implementation and outcome. The complexity of these interventions poses significant challenges for evaluation, as experimental designs, while able to demonstrate whether an intervention is effective on average, often fail to provide insight into the underlying mechanisms of change, the specific populations that benefit, or the conditions under which the intervention succeeds. In response to these challenges, funders, policymakers, and practitioners are increasingly seeking evaluations that can elucidate the processes by which change occurs, thereby facilitating the adaptation, scaling up, or transfer of effective interventions to new settings. One approach that has gained significant attention in recent years is theory-based evaluation, which posits that an intervention can be understood as a set of hypotheses about the relationships between activities and outcomes. By making these hypotheses explicit and subject to testing, theory-based evaluation aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of how and why an intervention works. Within this tradition, the concept of "theory of change" (ToC) has emerged as a prominent framework for evaluating complex interventions. Originally developed in the context of community initiatives in the United States in the 1990s, ToC was designed to address the challenges of evaluating comprehensive programs with broad goals and poorly specified pathways to impact. At its core, ToC involves identifying the long-term goals of an intervention and working backwards to specify the preconditions, intermediate outcomes, and activities required to achieve these goals, as well as the assumptions that link each step. This process typically involves the development of a diagram or narrative that serves as a shared representation of the intervention logic, often through participatory processes involving stakeholders. The appeal of ToC lies in its potential to promote clearer thinking about the problem and the intended solution, foster dialogue among stakeholders, expose unrealistic or untested assumptions, and provide a framework for selecting indicators and interpreting evaluation findings. In public health, where interventions often involve multiple sectors and rely on behavior change by multiple actors, the attributes of ToC seem particularly valuable. As a result, ToC has been applied to a diverse range of areas, including HIV prevention, maternal and child health, mental health, tobacco control, and health systems strengthening. Despite its popularity, however, ToC is often used inconsistently, and its definition is contested. The term is frequently applied to a range of concepts, including logic models, logframes, results chains, conceptual frameworks, impact pathways, and causal maps, often without clear distinction. Furthermore, ToC may be used as a planning tool at the outset of intervention design, retrospectively to reconstruct the logic of an existing program, or as an evaluation framework against which data are collected and findings interpreted. The extent to which ToC is informed by formal theory varies widely, and it may be drawn from social science theory, empirical evidence, the tacit knowledge of program staff, or combinations of these. Several commentators have noted that the term is sometimes invoked superficially, with a diagram produced to satisfy a funder but with little influence on the design, implementation, or evaluation of the intervention. The lack of transparency in the development and use of ToC makes it difficult to judge its quality, learn from others' experiences, or assess whether the claimed benefits are realized. Existing guidance on ToC is largely found in practitioner manuals and grey literature produced by evaluation organizations and funders, and it is not always consistent about recommended steps. The academic literature contains a growing number of reports that mention ToC, but there is no systematic account of how it has been applied in public health. Reviews of theory use in health interventions have tended to focus on behavior change theories and their relationship to effectiveness, rather than on ToC as a distinct approach to intervention development and evaluation. Related work on intervention development frameworks and the reporting of complex interventions highlights the importance of explicit program theory, but does not provide insight into the use of ToC specifically. Consequently, there is a significant gap in our understanding of how ToC is used in public health, including who is using it, in which settings, and for what purposes, as well as how ToCs are developed and who is involved. This gap is significant for several reasons. First, if ToC is to be recommended as good practice, we need evidence on how it is actually done and what is reported about its contribution. Second, poor reporting limits replication and prevents the accumulation of methodological learning, a problem well recognized in the wider literature on intervention reporting. Third, researchers and program planners who wish to use ToC currently have few worked examples that describe the process in enough detail to be adapted. This paper presents a systematic review of the use of ToC in the design and evaluation of public health interventions, addressing three key research questions: (1) How has ToC been developed in public health interventions, including the methods used, the stakeholders involved, and the evidence or theory drawn upon? (2) To what extent and how has ToC been used in the development of interventions? (3) To what extent and how has ToC been used in their evaluation? We also examined the level of detail with which these processes were reported. The review makes three contributions, providing the first systematic overview of the extent and nature of ToC use in public health, highlighting the variability in ToC development and use, and identifying areas for future research and improvement. Our systematic review aimed to comprehensively examine the use of Theory of Change (ToC) in the development and evaluation of public health interventions across diverse settings and study designs. By doing so, we sought to identify the strengths and limitations of current reporting practices in this field, with a particular focus on how ToC is applied and the challenges that arise from its implementation. Ultimately, our goal was to propose a standardized checklist for reporting ToC development and use, designed to enhance transparency and facilitate refinement by authors and users of the approach. To achieve these objectives, we conducted a systematic review of both published and unpublished literature, adhering to the principles outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement and the guidance provided by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination. Given the descriptive nature of our review, which aimed to characterize how ToC has been developed and applied rather than to estimate the effectiveness of interventions, we did not assess outcomes related to effectiveness or conduct a meta-analysis. Prior to initiating the search, our review team agreed upon a protocol that specified the research questions, eligibility criteria, search strategy, and data extraction items. This protocol served as the foundation for our systematic approach. For the purposes of this review, we defined ToC as a description or illustration, typically developed through a participatory or consultative process, that outlines how and why a desired change is expected to occur within a specific context. This definition is grounded in the understanding that ToC approaches involve identifying long-term goals, working backwards to specify necessary preconditions or intermediate outcomes, and articulating the assumptions that underlie causal pathways and the activities intended to trigger them. We exclusively included papers that explicitly used the term "Theory of Change," excluding those that used related terms such as logic model, logical framework, results chain, or programme theory unless they also described their work as a ToC. Public health interventions were broadly defined as organized activities aimed at preventing disease, promoting health, or improving health systems and the social determinants of health at the population or community level, without restrictions on country setting. Our eligibility criteria encompassed papers of any date, language, and study design that reported the use of ToC in the development, evaluation, or both, of public health interventions. This included a wide range of document types such as intervention development reports, protocols, process evaluations, outcome and impact evaluations, qualitative studies, and descriptive or reflective papers. We excluded papers that merely mentioned ToC in passing without applying it to a specific intervention or program, methodological discussions of ToC without reference to a public health intervention, and interventions outside the health domain. To identify relevant literature, we employed a comprehensive search strategy that included searching electronic bibliographic databases such as Scopus, PubMed, and PsycINFO using the search term "Theory of Change" combined with terms related to health, public health, and health interventions. We did not apply date or language restrictions. Additionally, we searched specialist grey literature databases, the Google search engine, and the websites of major development funders and agencies known to commission or require ToC. We also examined the reference lists of included papers and key ToC guidance documents to identify further eligible sources. Our searches were updated until 2015, and arrangements were made to translate or review non-English papers by speakers of the relevant language. The study selection process involved exporting records to reference management software, removing duplicates, and then independently screening titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria by two reviewers. Records deemed potentially relevant by either reviewer proceeded to full-text assessment, which was also conducted independently by two reviewers. Disagreements at any stage were resolved through discussion and, if necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Before formal screening, our reviewers piloted the eligibility criteria on a sample of records to ensure consistent interpretation. Data extraction was facilitated by a standardized form developed in a spreadsheet, which was piloted on a subset of included papers and refined accordingly. One reviewer extracted data, which was then checked by a second reviewer. The extracted information included publication characteristics, intervention characteristics, the purpose for which ToC was used, and detailed information about how the ToC was developed and applied. Specifically, for ToC development, we recorded the individuals involved, methods used, whether existing evidence or theory informed the ToC, the level of participation, production of a ToC diagram or narrative, explicitness of assumptions, and whether the ToC was revised over time. For its use in intervention design and evaluation, we documented whether ToC informed the selection of components, targeting, implementation planning, evaluation questions, indicators, data collection tools, analysis, process evaluation, or interpretation of findings, and whether ToC was tested or refined using evaluation data. We also noted any reported benefits and challenges of using ToC and the level of detail provided about the ToC process and outputs. Recognizing that papers could be coded under more than one use category, we ensured our extraction process captured this complexity. Given the focus of our review on the reporting and application of ToC rather than the strength of effect estimates, we did not employ a formal risk-of-bias tool. Instead, we assessed the completeness of ToC process reporting by noting which elements were described. These observations, combined with identified reporting gaps, informed the development of a proposed checklist for reporting ToC use. Checklist items were derived from extraction categories and existing ToC guidance, and were refined through consensus by the review team. Data synthesis and analysis involved summarizing extracted data quantitatively, using frequencies and percentages, to describe the characteristics of included papers and the proportions reporting each aspect of ToC. This approach allowed us to provide a comprehensive overview of how ToC is developed, applied, and reported in public health interventions, highlighting both the current state of practice and areas for improvement. Through this systematic review, we aimed to contribute to the enhancement of ToC reporting and application in public health, ultimately supporting more effective intervention development and evaluation. By identifying gaps in current reporting practices and proposing a standardized checklist, we hope to facilitate greater transparency and consistency in the use of ToC, thereby strengthening the capacity of the field to appraise and learn from ToC approaches.
