Spontaneous spoken dialogue is inherently imperfect, with speakers frequently pausing, hesitating, restarting, and repairing their own utterances as they navigate the complexities of speech production. This phenomenon is particularly evident in conversational corpora, where disfluencies are a ubiquitous feature: approximately 5-6% of words in the Switchboard corpus are part of a disfluency. Rather than viewing disfluencies as mere noise, research has shown that they convey valuable information about a speaker's intended meaning and cognitive state. For instance, a typical self-repair can be broken down into a reparandum (the material to be abandoned or corrected), an optional interregnum (e.g., an editing term such as "uh" or "I mean"), and a repair (the material that replaces the reparandum). Listeners effortlessly process this structure, using it to infer the speaker's intended meaning and cognitive state. In contrast, a dialogue system that fails to account for disfluencies will likely misinterpret users, fail to track their actual intentions, and respond in ways that feel unnatural. To develop effective disfluency processing in dialogue systems, two key requirements must be addressed. The first is incrementality: human conversation is highly interactive, with participants frequently completing each other's utterances, interrupting, backchanneling, and beginning to respond before the other has finished. To exhibit such behavior, a system must interpret input word by word, deciding, as each word arrives, whether it belongs to a reparandum, an interregnum, or a repair. Many successful disfluency detectors operate on complete utterances, leveraging bidirectional context, parsing-based features, or reranking over entire sentences. While these approaches are useful for cleaning transcripts, they are ill-suited for the low-latency processing required in live interaction. Incremental approaches have been proposed, but their accuracy on standard benchmarks has lagged behind that of non-incremental ones. Recent neural sequence-tagging methods have achieved strong results, but they often rely on bidirectional encoders or features that are not available online. The second requirement concerns data efficiency and robustness. From a developer's perspective, it is highly desirable to build a dialogue system from "clean" examples of the target task, as collecting and annotating large amounts of disfluent, domain-specific speech can be prohibitively expensive. However, disfluencies are diverse, and the same intended content can be realized with an unbounded variety of hesitations, restarts, and substitutions. A model trained on one domain's disfluent data may not transfer to another, and a model trained only on fluent data will typically break when faced with repairs. Ideally, a disfluency detection component would be domain-general, trained once on a general-purpose resource and then used in new domains, passing on fluent-equivalent input or structural annotations to downstream components trained only on clean data. This paper addresses these two requirements jointly, asking whether a simple, strictly word-by-word incremental neural model can detect disfluency structure accurately enough to compete with existing incremental systems, and whether what it learns from a large general corpus of human conversation can transfer to a different domain without any additional training. To answer the first part, we train and evaluate on the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus, which provides disfluency annotations over transcribed telephone conversations. To answer the second, we test the same trained model on bAbI+, an extension of the bAbI goal-oriented dialogue task in which clean dialogues are systematically augmented with disfluencies generated by controlled templates. This allows for a fine-grained analysis of generalization that is impossible with naturally occurring data alone. Our approach is a multi-task LSTM model that processes the utterance left to right and, at each word, predicts the disfluency tag. Training with multiple related objectives is known to improve representations and generalization in sequence labeling. Here, the auxiliary task is to predict the next word, a language-modeling objective that encourages the shared recurrent layer to capture local lexical and syntactic regularities, including the repetitions and mismatches that signal a repair. Alongside the main tagging objective, we also predict utterance-level and word-level labels that capture the structure of the disfluency. The resulting architecture is considerably simpler than previous neural incremental systems, requires no hand-crafted features or external parsers, and can be attached to any incremental consumer of text, such as an incremental semantic parser, or used on its own to produce a continuously updated "cleaned" version of the utterance. The paper makes several key contributions. First, we present a simple multi-task LSTM architecture for strictly incremental disfluency detection and show that it outperforms previous neural incremental approaches on SWDA by around 10 percentage points. Second, we demonstrate through experiments on bAbI+, without any retraining or adaptation, that the model transfers to a domain with very different vocabulary and dialogue structure, supporting the claim that disfluency detection can be treated as a domain-general capability. Third, exploiting the controlled nature of bAbI+, we analyze performance by disfluency type, identifying which phenomena (e.g., hesitations versus self-corrections of different kinds) are readily handled in a domain-general way and which remain challenging. This analysis sheds light on where future work, whether in modeling or in data collection, should concentrate. We used two datasets in our experiments. The first is the Switchboard Dialogue Acts corpus (SWDA), a subset of the Switchboard telephone conversations annotated with disfluency structure. We used the standard split, with the training portion comprising conversations with identifiers beginning sw2–sw3, the held-out set sw4[5-9], and the test set sw4[0-1]. Transcripts were preprocessed to remove disfluency annotations and converted to a format suitable for our model. The second dataset is bAbI+, which provides a controlled environment for evaluating the generalization of our model to new domains. By analyzing performance on bAbI+, we can identify areas where our model excels and where it requires further improvement, ultimately informing the development of more effective disfluency processing systems. The preprocessing of the Switchboard Dialog Act Corpus (SWDA) involved lowercasing all text and removing punctuation and partial-word markers, in line with the methodology outlined by Hough and Schlangen (2017). This preprocessing step is crucial for ensuring that the results obtained are comparable with those from earlier incremental work. Each token in the corpus was then annotated with a tag from the disfluency scheme described below. In addition to SWDA, we utilized the bAbI+ dataset (Shalyt et al., 2017; Eshghi et al., 2017), an extension of the bAbI Dialog Task 1 (Bordes et al., 2017) restaurant-booking dialogues. The bAbI+ dataset introduces disfluencies into the otherwise clean utterances through template-based transformations, resulting in three primary types of disfluencies: hesitations, restarts or false starts, and corrections of previously mentioned content. For instance, hesitations are exemplified by phrases such as "we will be uh eight," while restarts or false starts are illustrated by phrases like "can you make a restaurant uh sorry a reservation." Corrections, on the other hand, involve revising previously mentioned content, as in "with Italian uh sorry Spanish food." The probabilities of disfluency insertion are controlled, allowing for a known distribution of disfluency types, and gold annotations are available for every token. It is worth noting that the bAbI+ dataset was exclusively used for evaluation purposes, with no training or tuning of the model on this dataset. This approach enables the assessment of zero-shot, domain-general transfer from SWDA. Our disfluency annotation scheme adheres to the standard reparandum–interregnum–repair structure (Shriberg, 1994; Meteer et al., 1995). The reparandum refers to the material that is to be repaired or abandoned, while the interregnum contains editing terms such as "uh" or "I mean." The repair, on the other hand, constitutes the material that replaces the reparandum. Following the methodology outlined by Hough and Schlangen (2017), we converted the bracketed annotation into word-level tags. Specifically, <e/> denotes edit terms, including interregnum and filled pauses, <rmn/> indicates a reparandum word, where n specifies the number of tokens back in the utterance at which the reparandum begins, <rpn/> represents a repair word, and <f/> signifies fluent words. This encoding scheme is strictly incremental, as each tag can be assigned based solely on left context, thereby allowing the system to recover the extent of the reparandum rather than merely detecting its presence. Furthermore, repairs are distinguished as substitution (<rpSub/>), repetition (<rpRep/>) or deletion (<rpDel/>), in accordance with Hough and Schlangen (2017). The model architecture employed in this study is a unidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) sequence tagger, which processes an utterance one word at a time. Consequently, each tag prediction depends exclusively on the words seen thus far. The input words are mapped to 50-dimensional embeddings, and the vocabulary is restricted to the training data, with singletons replaced by an unknown token. Part-of-speech (POS) tags, produced for SWDA using the tags available in the corpus, are concatenated with the word embedding as input in the POS-enriched conditions. The model consists of a single LSTM layer with 50 hidden units, which feeds a softmax output layer. A key design element of our model is the incorporation of multi-task learning (Caruana, 1997; Søgaard & Goldberg, 2016). Two output layers share the same LSTM representation, with the primary task being disfluency tagging and the auxiliary task being prediction of the next word in the sequence, i.e., incremental language modelling. An additional auxiliary task, evaluated in separate ablations, involves prediction of the utterance's POS tag sequence. The auxiliary tasks provide a training signal that does not depend on disfluency annotation, thereby encouraging the shared layer to represent syntactic and lexical context. The total loss is a weighted sum of the cross-entropy losses of the tasks, L = Ltag + λLaux, with λ selected on the held-out set from {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}. For comparison, we also trained a single-task baseline with the same architecture but no auxiliary output. During the training procedure, models were implemented in Keras with a TensorFlow backend and trained using the Adam optimiser (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a batch size of 32. To prevent overfitting, dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) of 0.2 was applied to the embedding and LSTM outputs. Early stopping was based on tagging loss on the held-out set, with a patience of 5 epochs. Hyperparameters were selected on the held-out set only. Given that LSTM training is stochastic, each configuration was trained with ten random initialisations, and we report the mean and standard deviation across runs. Evaluation of our model on SWDA employed three families of measures. Firstly, token-level F1 was computed for the reparandum tags (<rm>) and for edit terms (<e>), following common practice in disfluency detection (Ferguson et al., 2015; Zayats et al., 2016). Secondly, given that the system is designed to be incremental, we evaluated it as it processes the utterance. Specifically, we report the time-to-detection, the number of words after the onset of a reparandum or edit at which the correct tag is first output, and edit overhead, the proportion of unnecessary tag revisions made as the utterance unfolds (Hough & Schlangen, 2017; Zwarts et al., 2010). Thirdly, we report the utterance-level exact match of the predicted tag sequence against gold. For the bAbI+ dataset, the trained SWDA model was applied without any retraining or fine-tuning, and word embeddings for out-of-vocabulary tokens were mapped to the unknown token. As POS tags were not available in this dataset, we used the model variants that take only words as input. We report F1 for each tag type, split by disfluency category (hesitation, restart, correction), to examine which phenomena transfer across domains. Additionally, we compute the proportion of utterances whose "cleaned" output, after removing tokens tagged as reparandum or edit, exactly matches the original clean bAbI utterance. This measure assesses the practical goal of ensuring that a downstream interpreter, trained only on fluent dialogues, receives the intended input. Statistical analysis involved assessing differences between model variants over the ten runs per configuration. We employed paired comparisons on matched random seeds with a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the significance threshold set at α = 0.05, and applied Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons across variants. For comparison with previously published systems, we cite their reported scores on the same test split. As the per-run variance of these systems is unavailable, no significance tests were applied to those comparisons, and we report absolute differences in F1. For bAbI+,

Named entity recognition (NER) is a crucial step in biomedical text mining, as it enables the identification of key concepts such as genes, proteins, cell lines, chemicals, diseases, and organisms in the literature. This, in turn, underlies various downstream tasks, including relation extraction, database curation, and literature-based discovery (Krallinger et al., 2017; Huang and Lu, 2015). The sheer volume of biomedical publications, with over one million new entries added to PubMed each year, renders manual annotation impractical, making accurate automated NER a central focus of community evaluations like BioCreative, BioNLP, and JNLPBA (Kim et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2008; Arighi et al., 2017). In the traditional approach to NER, a document is segmented into sentences and tokens, with each token receiving a label indicating whether it begins, continues, or lies outside an entity, typically using a BIO or BIOES scheme (Ramshaw and Marcus, 1995). Early biomedical systems, such as BANNER (Leaman and Gonzalez, 2008) and ABNER (Settles, 2005), relied on feature-based models like conditional random fields (Lafferty et al., 2001). However, with the advent of neural architectures, hand-engineered features have given way to more sophisticated approaches. Bidirectional LSTMs with CRF output layers, combined with word and character embeddings, have become the standard approach (Huang et al., 2015; Lample et al., 2016; Ma and Hovy, 2016), and have been successfully adapted to biomedical corpora (Habibi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Crichton et al., 2017). The introduction of pretrained contextual representations like ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), and domain-specific variants such as BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020), SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019), and PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2021) has further improved performance on benchmark datasets. Despite this progress, nearly all existing systems share a common limitation: they assume that the input has already been split into tokens, and that entity boundaries coincide with token boundaries. While this assumption is relatively benign in general-domain newswire text, it frequently fails in biomedical text, where entity mentions are often embedded within hyphenated compounds, slash-separated expressions, or alphanumeric strings. For instance, entity mentions like "IL-2-dependent," "p53/MDM2," "GFP-tagged," "TNF-alpha–induced," or "Ras-GAP" occupy only part of what a conventional tokenizer treats as a single word. Annotation guidelines for corpora like GENETAG (Tanabe et al., 2005) and BioCreative Bio-ID (Arighi et al., 2017) explicitly permit sub-word entity spans, and the JNLPBA corpus (Kim et al., 2004) contains many mentions whose boundaries fall inside whitespace-delimited strings. However, a model that predicts labels only at the word level cannot recover such spans exactly, and under strict-match evaluation, each of these errors counts as both a false positive and a false negative. The standard remedy for this limitation is to rely on specialized tokenization. Biomedical tokenizers apply hand-crafted rules or learned heuristics to split text at hyphens, slashes, digit–letter transitions, and case changes, so that entity boundaries are more likely to coincide with token boundaries (He and Kayaalp, 2006; Jiang and Zhai, 2007; Neumann et al., 2019). While such tokenizers can improve NER performance, they have several drawbacks. They require domain expertise to design and maintain, are often tuned to a particular corpus or entity class, and introduce a pipeline dependency in which tokenization errors propagate irrecoverably to the tagger. Over-segmentation can fragment entities and inflate sequence lengths, while under-segmentation leaves boundary mismatches unresolved. Moreover, a tokenizer optimized for one annotation scheme may not transfer to another, forcing practitioners to redesign rules for each new dataset. Subword representations offer a natural way to relax the dependence on word-level tokenization. Byte-pair encoding (BPE), originally a data compression technique (Gage, 1994), was adapted for neural machine translation to handle rare and unseen words by decomposing them into frequent character sequences (Sennrich et al., 2016). Related approaches include WordPiece (Wu et al., 2016), the unigram language model (Kudo, 2018), and SentencePiece, which operates on raw text without pre-tokenization (Kudo and Richardson, 2018). These methods are widely used in transformer-based language models, including BERT and its biomedical descendants. However, in NER, they are typically used only to build input representations, with labels still assigned at the level of whole words, usually by taking the prediction of the first subword piece (Devlin et al., 2019). As a result, subword units improve the handling of out-of-vocabulary terms but do not allow the model to predict entity boundaries within a word. Character-level models (Kim et al., 2016; Gillick et al., 2016) can, in principle, label at arbitrary positions, but they produce long sequences, lack a learned inventory of meaningful units such as morphemes and common biomedical affixes (e.g., "-ase," "anti-," or "-mab"), and are often harder to train and scale. This leaves an unaddressed gap in existing biomedical NER methods, which either operate at the word level and depend on carefully engineered tokenization to align with entity boundaries or use subword units merely as inputs while still predicting at the word level. What is missing is an approach in which the units of prediction themselves are learned, subword-sized, and independent of domain-specific tokenization rules, allowing entity spans to start and end wherever the data indicate. To address this gap, we ask the following research question: can a model that assigns entity labels directly to BPE units, learned from raw text, recover biomedical entity spans, including those that fall within words, with accuracy competitive with systems that depend on specialized tokenizers? To answer this question, we introduce a subword-level approach to NER that combines BPE segmentation with convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Our approach segments text using a BPE vocabulary learned from the training data, with minimal pre-processing. Convolutional layers capture local orthographic and morphological patterns within and across adjacent units, and recurrent layers model longer-range context across the sentence. The network produces a tag for every BPE unit, and these byte-level tags are mapped back to character offsets to yield entity spans that need not align with whitespace-delimited words. Our contributions are as follows. First, we propose a tokenization-agnostic NER architecture that predicts labels at the BPE level, allowing entity boundaries to be learned from the data rather than being predetermined by a tokenizer. This approach has the potential to improve the accuracy of biomedical NER, particularly for entity mentions that do not align with word boundaries. Second, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on benchmark datasets, showing that it can achieve competitive performance with systems that rely on specialized tokenizers. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the strengths and limitations of our approach, highlighting its potential applications and areas for future research. By introducing a subword-level approach to NER, we aim to advance the state of the art in biomedical text mining and provide a new tool for researchers and practitioners in the field. The task of named entity recognition (NER) in biomedical text poses a unique set of challenges, particularly with regards to the accurate identification of entity boundaries. A major hurdle in this context is the fact that these boundaries often fall within words, rather than coinciding with word boundaries. This issue necessitates the development of approaches that can effectively handle such cases without relying on hand-crafted rules for splitting words. In this study, we address this challenge by evaluating an approach that leverages learned subword units, rather than traditional word-level tokens, for biomedical NER. Our evaluation is conducted on three widely used benchmarks in the field: the BioCreative VI Bio-ID, JNLPBA, and GENETAG corpora. These datasets differ significantly in terms of the types of entities annotated, the conventions used for annotation, and the degree to which entity boundaries are misaligned with word boundaries. One of the primary advantages of our approach is its ability to eliminate the need for specialized biomedical tokenization expertise. Traditional methods often require extensive knowledge of biomedical terminology and the development of customized tokenization rules to handle the complexities of entity recognition in this domain. By moving away from word-level tokens and towards learned subword units, we can simplify the process of deploying NER systems across different corpora. Moreover, this shift allows us to quantify the impact of using subword units on the performance of NER systems, particularly in cases where entity boundaries do not align with word boundaries. Our analysis begins with an examination of the datasets used in this study. The BioCreative VI Bio-ID corpus, for instance, consists of figure legends from open-access articles annotated for a variety of entity classes, including genes, proteins, small molecules, cell types, and tissues. The annotations in this corpus are normalized to database identifiers, but for our purposes, we only utilized the mention spans and coarse types. In contrast, the JNLPBA shared-task dataset is derived from the GENIA corpus and contains MEDLINE abstracts annotated with five specific types: protein, DNA, RNA, cell line, and cell type. The GENETAG corpus, used in BioCreative II Gene Mention, annotates a single gene/protein class across 20,000 MEDLINE sentences, with alternative acceptable boundaries provided for some mentions. We adhered to the official training and test partitions for each dataset, using a random 10% of each training set as a development set for hyperparameter selection and early stopping. A crucial aspect of our approach involves the segmentation of raw text into subword units using byte-pair encoding (BPE). Unlike traditional rule-based biomedical tokenizers, BPE allows us to split text at whitespace and learn merges based on frequency, without pre-defined rules for handling punctuation, hyphens, or other special characters. This process begins with a character inventory and iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs until a target vocabulary size is reached. We treated the vocabulary size as a hyperparameter, exploring values of 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, and 8,000. Each BPE unit retains its character start and end offsets, enabling the representation of entity boundaries that fall within whitespace-delimited chunks. For comparison, we also trained a SentencePiece BPE model on the same text and found its segmentations to be comparable to those of our primary BPE model. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we projected gold character-level spans onto the BPE units using a BIO scheme with entity types. This involved labeling each unit as B-t if it started an entity of type t, I-t if it lay inside one, and O otherwise. Predicted spans were then converted back to character offsets by taking the start offset of the first unit and the end offset of the last unit of each decoded entity. This process allowed us to quantify the fraction of gold entities whose start and end offsets both coincide with unit boundaries, which we refer to as the oracle recall. We computed this quantity for each dataset and vocabulary size, alongside development F1, to diagnose the performance of our model and select the optimal vocabulary size. Our model architecture is based on a convolutional-recurrent design, which combines local subword context with recurrent sequence modeling. Each BPE unit is mapped to an embedding, and local context is captured through a one-dimensional convolution over the embedding sequence. The convolutional layer is followed by a bidirectional LSTM, which provides contextualized representations of each unit. These representations are then passed through a linear layer and a softmax to produce a distribution over tags. We used Viterbi decoding restricted to valid BIO transitions to ensure well-formed spans during inference. Dropout was applied to the embeddings and between recurrent layers to prevent overfitting. In comparison to traditional word-level approaches, our subword-level approach offers several advantages. By moving away from word boundaries, we can more accurately capture entity boundaries that fall within words. Moreover, our approach eliminates the need for specialized tokenization rules, making it easier to deploy NER systems across different corpora. Our results demonstrate that this approach achieves competitive performance relative to established systems, while providing a simpler and more effective way to handle the complexities of biomedical NER. Overall, our study highlights the potential of learned subword units for improving the robustness and deployability of NER systems in the biomedical domain. The rapid proliferation of GPS-enabled mobile devices has led to an explosion in the growth of Location-based Social Networks (LBSNs), such as Foursquare, Gowalla, and Yelp, where users share their physical presence at Points-of-Interest (POIs) through check-ins, tips, and reviews. This phenomenon has been extensively studied in recent years, with researchers like Bao et al. (2015) highlighting the potential of LBSNs to support a wide range of services, including urban planning, location-targeted advertising, and personalized travel assistance. Among these services, POI recommendation has emerged as a central task, as it enables users to explore their surroundings and helps businesses reach potential customers (Ye et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017). However, as the numbers of users and venues grow into the millions, effective POI recommender systems are needed to counter information overload and provide users with relevant and personalized recommendations. Early POI recommenders were largely adapted from general-purpose collaborative filtering techniques, which learn latent user and POI representations through matrix factorization (MF) approaches. These approaches, such as those proposed by Koren et al. (2009) and Hu et al. (2008), approximate observed preferences by taking the inner product of the latent representations. However, since check-in data only record positive, implicit feedback, these methods typically treat unobserved entries as weighted negatives or optimize pairwise ranking objectives (Rendle et al., 2009). Nevertheless, researchers soon recognized that POIs differ from items such as movies or books because they are anchored in geographic space, and therefore, geographical context plays a crucial role in POI recommendation. To address this issue, existing work has augmented collaborative filtering with spatial information, for example, by fitting power-law or kernel density models of check-in distances (Ye et al., 2011; Zhang & Chow, 2013), by embedding activity areas into latent factors (Lian et al., 2014), or by combining social, temporal, and categorical signals with geographical influence (Cheng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015). These studies consistently show that geographical context is a decisive signal, consistent with Tobler's (1970) first law of geography, which states that near things are more related than distant ones. Despite this progress, two challenges remain in POI recommendation. The first challenge is modeling non-linear user-POI interactions from implicit feedback. MF and its geographical extensions assume that preference is a linear function of latent factors, which limits their capacity to capture the complex, heterogeneous motivations behind check-in behavior. Deep learning offers a remedy to this challenge. Neural collaborative filtering replaces the inner product with a learned non-linear interaction function (He et al., 2017). Autoencoder-based models, such as AutoRec (Sedhain et al., 2015), the collaborative denoising autoencoder (Wu et al., 2016), and variational autoencoders for collaborative filtering (Liang et al., 2018), reconstruct a user's interaction vector through non-linear mappings and achieve strong top-N performance. However, these autoencoders compress a user's history into a single representation by uniformly aggregating the embeddings of all interacted items. In the POI setting, this is problematic because a user's check-ins are highly diverse, and a single user may frequent a workplace cafeteria, a gym, and a handful of tourist sites, each reflecting a different intention and with different significance for predicting future behavior. The second challenge is incorporating context information, particularly geographical coordinates, into neural architectures. Most neural recommenders operate on identifiers alone, and the few that exploit location typically feed coordinates or discretized grid cells as additional input features (Yang et al., 2017). This design discards the continuous nature of geographic distance and does not express the underlying behavioral principle that a user who visits a POI is likely to visit its nearby and similar neighbors. Moreover, the data are extremely sparse, with typical LBSN check-in matrices having densities well below 1%. Propagating a user's preference to spatially adjacent venues is a natural way to mitigate sparsity and improve generalization. However, the question remains as to how to inject such neighborhood effects into a non-linear model in a principled, end-to-end trainable manner, rather than as a post-hoc re-ranking step. These observations motivate the central research question of this paper: can a non-linear autoencoder framework adaptively weigh the multiple facets of a user's check-in history and explicitly encode geographical neighborhood influence, so as to produce more accurate POI recommendations from sparse implicit feedback? Attention mechanisms provide a promising route to the first goal. They were introduced to align and weigh elements of a sequence in neural machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and have since been generalized to self-attention, which relates elements of a single input to one another (Vaswani et al., 2017). In particular, multi-dimensional structured self-attention produces several attention distributions over the same input, each capable of focusing on a different aspect (Lin et al., 2017). This property suits POI recommendation, where a user's preferences are naturally multi-faceted. For the second goal, kernel functions of spatial distance offer a smooth, differentiable measure of geographic proximity. The radial basis function (RBF) kernel, for instance, assigns high affinity to nearby locations and decays rapidly with distance. Building on these ideas, we propose SAE-NAD, an autoencoder with a Self-Attentive Encoder (SAE) and a Neighbor-Aware Decoder (NAD). The encoder applies multi-dimensional self-attention over the embeddings of a user's checked-in POIs and learns several attention weightings that distinguish the preference degrees of individual POIs along different aspects. These weightings are aggregated into a compact user representation. The decoder reconstructs the user's check-in preferences over all POIs and, crucially, makes a user's reachability to unvisited POIs higher when they are similar to and near the POIs the user has visited. This is realized through the inner product of POI embeddings, which captures similarity, combined with an RBF kernel over pairwise geographical distance, which captures proximity. The model is trained end-to-end on implicit feedback, so the geographical influence is learned jointly with the user-POI relations rather than imposed through separate, hand-tuned components. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose SAE-NAD, a novel autoencoder-based framework for POI recommendation that models non-linear user-POI relations from implicit feedback while jointly leveraging attention-based preference modeling and geographical context. We design a self-attentive encoder that employs multi-dimensional attention to adaptively differentiate the importance of a user's checked-in POIs across multiple aspects, in contrast to prior autoencoders that weigh all interactions equally. We devise a neighbor-aware decoder that integrates POI embedding and geographical distance to capture the complex, heterogeneous motivations behind check-in behavior. Overall, our approach provides a principled, end-to-end trainable framework for POI recommendation that effectively incorporates geographical context and attention mechanisms to produce more accurate recommendations from sparse implicit feedback. In this study, we propose a novel approach to Point of Interest (POI) recommendation, leveraging the strengths of both autoencoder-based collaborative filtering and geographical modeling. Our model, Self-Attentive Encoder-Neighbor Aware Decoder (SAE-NAD), incorporates a self-attentive encoder to capture complex user preferences and a neighbor-aware decoder to account for geographical context. By using a radial basis function (RBF) kernel to model the similarity between POIs based on their geographical distance, we can effectively raise the reachability of nearby and similar POIs, thereby enhancing the overall recommendation performance. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on three real-world Location-Based Social Network (LBSN) datasets, namely Gowalla, Foursquare, and Yelp. Our results demonstrate that SAE-NAD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple ranking metrics. Furthermore, ablation analyses confirm that both the self-attentive encoder and the neighbor-aware decoder contribute to the gains in recommendation performance. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing related work on POI recommendation and autoencoder-based collaborative filtering. We then formulate the problem and present the SAE-NAD model in detail, highlighting its key components and the intuition behind its design. Next, we describe the experimental setup and report the results of our evaluation, including the datasets used, the preprocessing steps taken, and the performance metrics employed. Finally, we conclude the paper by summarizing our findings and outlining directions for future research. Our evaluation datasets consist of three public LBSN check-in datasets: Gowalla, Foursquare, and Yelp. Each check-in record contains a user identifier, a POI identifier, a timestamp, and the POI's geographical coordinates. Following common practice in POI recommendation, we removed users with fewer than 15 check-ins and POIs visited by fewer than 10 users to mitigate extreme sparsity and yield stable estimates. After filtering, the datasets contained 18,737 users, 32,510 POIs, and 1,278,274 check-ins for Gowalla; 24,941 users, 28,593 POIs, and 1,196,248 check-ins for Foursquare; and 30,887 users, 18,995 POIs, and 860,888 check-ins for Yelp. Since the task is based on implicit feedback, each user is represented as a binary vector, where a value of 1 indicates at least one check-in at a particular POI. Repeated visits are collapsed into a single positive observation. For each user, we randomly assigned 70% of check-ins to training, 10% to validation for hyperparameter selection and early stopping, and 20% to testing. The split was repeated with five different random seeds to ensure robustness. The problem formulation involves estimating, for each user, a reachability score for every unvisited POI and returning the top-k ranked POIs. Candidate sets for ranking comprise all POIs absent from a user's training and validation records. Our model architecture consists of an autoencoder that maps the user's binary vector to a latent representation and reconstructs a dense score vector over all POIs. The encoder is a self-attentive encoder, which captures several aspects of user preference using multi-dimensional structured self-attention. Each POI has an input embedding, and the embeddings of the POIs visited by a user are stacked to form a matrix. The self-attention mechanism computes a weighted sum of these embeddings, where the weights are learned based on the user's preferences. The attended representation is then passed through a fully connected layer with a nonlinear activation to produce the user latent vector. The decoder is a neighbor-aware decoder, which incorporates geographical context by adding a neighbor term to the scoring function. For each POI pair, we define the neighbor influence as the product of the inner product of the decoder-side POI embeddings and a radial basis function (RBF) kernel with bandwidth ρ. The final score is computed as the sigmoid of the sum of the user latent vector, the POI embedding, and the neighbor term. The RBF kernel decays smoothly with distance, allowing the model to capture both local and global geographical patterns. We trained our model using a weighted binary cross-entropy loss function, where unobserved entries are treated as weak negatives and downweighted using a hyperparameter α. To avoid computing the loss over all POIs, we sampled five unobserved POIs per positive per epoch. Dropout with rate 0.5 was applied to the latent layer to reduce overfitting. Parameters were initialized using the Xavier scheme and optimized using Adam with a learning rate of 0.001 and mini-batches of 256 users. Training stopped if validation Recall@10 failed to improve for 10 consecutive epochs. We searched the hyperparameter space by varying the embedding dimension, number of attention aspects, attention size, RBF bandwidth, negative weight, and regularization strength. Selection used the validation set, one factor at a time around a default configuration. Unless otherwise stated, the reported results use an embedding dimension of 50, three attention aspects, an attention size of 50, and an RBF bandwidth of 1 km. Our baselines include representative methods from three families: classical implicit-feedback and geographical models, neural network-based models, and graph-based models. We compared SAE-NAD against these baselines using multiple ranking metrics, including Recall@k, Precision@k, and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG@k). Our results demonstrate that SAE-NAD consistently outperforms the competing methods, with significant improvements in recommendation performance. In conclusion, our study proposes a novel approach to POI recommendation, leveraging the strengths of both autoencoder-based collaborative filtering and geographical modeling. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and we outline directions for future research, including exploring other architectures and incorporating additional contextual information. By developing more accurate and personalized POI recommendation systems, we can enhance the user experience and provide more effective recommendations for users in location-based social networks. The loss of an upper limb is a profound and life-altering event that significantly impacts an individual's ability to engage in daily activities, maintain relationships, and participate in leisure pursuits. The hand and arm play a vital role in manipulation, tactile exploration, and non-verbal communication, and their absence can result in a disability that extends far beyond the physical deficit. According to population estimates, over a million people in the United States are living with limb loss, and this number is projected to more than double by mid-century due to the increasing prevalence of vascular disease and diabetes (Ziegler-Graham et al., 2008). Notably, while lower-limb amputation is primarily dysvascular in origin, upper-limb loss is often the result of traumatic injury, affecting younger, working-age individuals who have been involved in industrial accidents, road traffic collisions, or armed conflict (Dillingham et al., 2002; Atkins et al., 1996). As these individuals face decades of life with limb loss, the quality of their care has significant functional, psychological, and socioeconomic implications. Prosthetic fitting is the most well-known intervention for upper-limb amputation, and the range of available devices has expanded to include passive cosmetic restorations, body-powered hooks, myoelectric hands, and advanced multi-articulating and pattern-recognition-controlled systems. Techniques such as targeted muscle reinnervation have increased the number of intuitive control signals available to individuals with high-level amputations (Kuiken et al., 2009). However, despite advances in technological sophistication, sustained use of prosthetic devices has not been reliably achieved. Surveys and reviews spanning 25 years of literature have reported substantial rates of prosthesis rejection and abandonment, often attributed to factors such as discomfort, weight, poor functional return, and inadequate training (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Davidson, 2002). Satisfaction with prosthetic use is influenced by a range of factors, including the timing of fitting, the quality of follow-up services, and the user's preparedness to operate the prosthesis in daily life (Pezzin et al., 2004; McFarland et al., 2010). Furthermore, comparative evidence on myoelectric and body-powered devices suggests that neither is uniformly superior, highlighting the importance of user training and context in determining successful prosthetic use (Carey et al., 2015). This situation underscores the critical role of rehabilitation in the care pathway for individuals with upper-limb amputation. Prosthetic rehabilitation is a structured, multidisciplinary process that begins at or before amputation and continues after definitive fitting. It encompasses a range of activities, including pre-prosthetic care, such as wound healing, edema control, desensitization, and maintenance of range of motion and strength. Subsequent training focuses on muscle control and signal acquisition, donning and doffing, controlled operation of the terminal device, and bimanual functional activities. Additionally, rehabilitation addresses phantom sensation and pain, as well as the psychosocial adjustment necessary for reintegration into work and community roles (Smurr et al., 2008; Resnik et al., 2012). As prosthetic technology becomes increasingly complex, the needs of users become more pronounced, and clinicians have noted that the evidence base for training approaches has not kept pace with engineering developments (Resnik et al., 2012). Several rehabilitation strategies have been proposed or tested, including general conditioning programs, graded motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, mirror therapy, myoelectric training with biofeedback, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual reality or augmented reality environments in which users practice control before or alongside physical device use. Mirror therapy and related visual-feedback methods have been primarily investigated for phantom limb pain (Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, 1996; Chan et al., 2007), while recent work suggests that virtual and augmented reality combined with myoelectric pattern recognition can improve control and alleviate pain (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2016; Powell & Thakor, 2013). These approaches draw on different theoretical bases, including motor learning, cortical reorganization, and task-specific practice, and are applied in various settings and at different times after amputation. However, the resulting literature is characterized by fragmentation, with most studies being small case series or single-center studies with heterogeneous outcome measures, and incomplete descriptions of training content, intensity, and sequencing. This fragmentation limits both clinical practice and research, as clinicians lack a consolidated summary of the components of rehabilitation programs, their delivery, and associated outcomes. Health systems, too, face challenges in deciding how to allocate resources between therapy services and devices, due to a lack of synthesized evidence on the added value of rehabilitation. Previous reviews have primarily focused on prosthesis design, control strategies, or user acceptance and abandonment (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Carey et al., 2015), while others have examined phantom limb pain interventions or lower-limb amputation. To our knowledge, few have systematically examined the content of rehabilitation programs specifically for individuals with upper-extremity amputations or considered the implications of this body of work for the importance of rehabilitation in successful prosthetic use. The present review aims to address this gap by identifying and cataloging the components of upper-limb prosthetic rehabilitation reported in the literature, appraising the methodological quality of available studies, and arguing that rehabilitation should be regarded as an integral part of prosthetic provision. Following the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009), we conducted a systematic search of the literature, applied explicit inclusion criteria, extracted data on intervention components, and assessed methodological quality. This review makes three key contributions. Firstly, it provides clinicians with a consolidated reference of the components of upper-limb prosthetic rehabilitation, including general exercise, motor tasks, phantom exercises, muscle training, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual image and virtual reality exercises. Secondly, it appraises the methodological quality of available studies, highlighting strengths and weaknesses in the evidence and indicating areas where more rigorous trials are needed. Finally, it argues that rehabilitation should be considered an essential component of prosthetic provision, with implications for service planning, clinical guidelines, and future research on upper-limb loss. The design and reporting framework for this systematic review were guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Statement 2009 (Moher et al., 2009). The review question was framed using the PICO structure, with the population comprising individuals of any age with an acquired or congenital upper extremity amputation or limb difference. By examining the content and effectiveness of rehabilitation programs for individuals with upper-limb amputation, this review aims to inform clinical practice, service planning, and future research, ultimately contributing to improved outcomes and quality of life for individuals with upper-limb loss. The rehabilitation of individuals with upper extremity amputations poses a complex challenge, with a wide range of factors influencing the outcome of prosthetic fitting and use. To address this issue, we conducted a systematic review of the literature, focusing on the content and importance of rehabilitation protocols in this context. Our review considered any prosthetic rehabilitation program, including pre-prosthetic and prosthetic training, and compared these interventions to alternative rehabilitation approaches, standard care, or no comparator in the case of single-group designs. The outcomes of interest included functional performance, prosthesis use, muscle control, pain, and related patient-reported measures. Given the aim of describing and appraising the content and importance of rehabilitation protocols, rather than estimating a pooled treatment effect, we opted for a narrative synthesis approach. This decision was made in advance, and a formal protocol was not registered. To identify relevant studies, we performed a systematic literature search across multiple electronic databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, PEDro, and Google Scholar. Our search strategy combined controlled vocabulary, such as MeSH terms, with free-text keywords linked using Boolean operators. The search terms included population-related keywords, such as "upper extremity," "upper limb," "arm," "hand," "amputee," and "amputation," as well as intervention-related terms, including "rehabilitation," "prosthesis," "prosthetic training," "myoelectric," "occupational therapy," "physical therapy," and "virtual reality." For example, our PubMed search strategy used the following syntax: ("upper extremity" OR "upper limb") AND (amputation OR amputee) AND (rehabilitation OR "prosthetic training" OR prosthesis). We adapted the search syntax to conform to the indexing rules of each database. In addition to the electronic search, we hand-searched the reference lists of retrieved articles and relevant reviews to identify any additional eligible studies. We did not impose any restrictions on the year of publication, but only considered articles published in English. To be eligible for inclusion, studies had to meet specific criteria. These included involving participants with upper extremity amputation or limb loss at any level, from partial hand to shoulder disarticulation; examining a rehabilitation intervention directly connected with prosthetic fitting or use; reporting at least one functional, physical, or patient-reported outcome; and being original research published in a peer-reviewed journal. We considered a range of study designs, including randomized controlled trials, non-randomized trials, cohort studies, case series, and case reports. In contrast, studies were excluded if they focused exclusively on lower extremity amputation, addressed only surgical or technological aspects of prosthesis design without a rehabilitation component, or were narrative reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, or animal and laboratory studies. The study selection process involved several stages. Initially, all records retrieved from the electronic search were exported to reference management software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers then independently screened the titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. The full texts of potentially relevant records were obtained and assessed independently by the same reviewers. Any disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted when necessary. The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram, which recorded the number of records identified, screened, excluded with reasons, and included. The initial search yielded 620 records, of which nine studies met the inclusion criteria and were retained for data extraction. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, which was piloted on two studies before being used for the full dataset. Two reviewers independently extracted the data, and any discrepancies were reconciled by consensus. The extracted information included study characteristics, such as first author and year of publication, country, study design, sample size, and participant characteristics. We also extracted details of the rehabilitation protocol, including its components, content, frequency, duration, and setting, as well as the outcome measures and principal findings. Particular attention was given to the specific components of each protocol, which were categorized inductively into general exercise programs, motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, Muscle Training System use, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education exercises, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual image or virtual reality exercises. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed independently by two reviewers. Given the diversity of study designs, we selected an appraisal instrument according to the study type. Randomized and controlled trials were evaluated using the PEDro scale, which scores eleven items related to eligibility, randomization, allocation concealment, baseline comparability, blinding, follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis, between-group comparisons, and point and variability measures. Case series and case reports were appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists. Studies were then classified as being of high, moderate, or low quality according to the proportion of criteria satisfied. Risk of bias judgments was considered when interpreting results, but quality scores were not used as a basis for excluding studies, given the small number of eligible studies. The data synthesis and statistical analysis were tailored to the characteristics of the included studies. Given the substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, a quantitative meta-analysis was deemed inappropriate. Instead, we undertook a structured narrative synthesis, tabulating study characteristics and results, and grouping findings according to the type of rehabilitation component and the outcome domain addressed. Descriptive statistics, including frequencies and percentages, were used to summarize the number of studies by design, quality category, and protocol component. Where original studies reported effect sizes, means, standard deviations, or p values, these were reported as published without reanalysis. The consistency of direction of findings across studies was considered when drawing conclusions regarding the importance of prosthetic rehabilitation. The limitations in the strength of evidence arising from small samples and variable study quality were also taken into account in the interpretation. The role of universities in advancing global health equity cannot be overstated. As major recipients of public funding, these institutions are responsible for conducting a significant proportion of biomedical research in the United Kingdom, which in turn contributes to the development of new medicines, diagnostics, and vaccines. The choices universities make regarding research priorities, intellectual property management, and knowledge dissemination have far-reaching implications, not only for the scientific community but also for the individuals and communities who stand to benefit from their discoveries. Given their commitment to the public good and their charitable purpose, universities have a moral obligation to ensure that their research addresses the needs of those who are most vulnerable, including populations in low-income settings. The disparity between the global disease burden and the allocation of research resources is a long-standing concern. The 10/90 gap, which refers to the fact that only about 10% of global health research spending is devoted to addressing the conditions responsible for 90% of the global disease burden, has been a persistent issue for over two decades. Neglected diseases, including neglected tropical diseases, malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS, disproportionately affect the poorest populations, yet they attract relatively little commercial investment due to the limited market returns they offer. While public and philanthropic funders, as well as product development partnerships, have helped to fill this gap to some extent, the proportion of research addressing the health problems of low- and lower-middle-income countries remains modest compared to the burden of disease in these settings. Universities, as key recipients of public and charitable funding, play a critical role in determining whether this imbalance is corrected or perpetuated. However, there is a dearth of information on the extent to which university research addresses the needs of low-income populations or how this activity is distributed across institutions. To address this knowledge gap, it is essential to examine the research priorities of universities and how they allocate their resources. In addition to research priorities, universities' management of intellectual property is a crucial factor in determining access to health technologies. The licensing of medical discoveries made in universities can have a significant impact on the availability and affordability of essential medicines in low-income countries. Exclusive licensing agreements, which grant a single company the exclusive rights to a particular technology, can lead to high prices and restricted supply, making it difficult for patients and health systems in resource-poor settings to access these medicines. The case of the antiretroviral drug stavudine, developed at Yale University and licensed to Bristol-Myers Squibb, illustrates the potential consequences of such licensing decisions and the importance of advocacy efforts in promoting change. In response to these concerns, there has been a growing movement towards "global access" or "equitable access" licensing, which prioritizes affordability, non-exclusive licensing for use in low-resource settings, and humanitarian carve-outs. The Statement of Principles and Strategies for the Equitable Dissemination of Medical Technologies, endorsed by several North American and European institutions, and the Nine Points to Consider in Licensing University Technology, provide guidance on socially responsible licensing practices. Universities Allied for Essential Medicines (UAEM) has also been a vocal advocate for such policies and has developed a university report card to evaluate the performance of institutions in the United States and Canada. However, the extent to which UK universities have adopted similar policies and the nature of their licensing practices remain unclear. Another critical mechanism for promoting global health equity is the publication of research findings. The traditional subscription-based model of scientific publishing can create significant barriers to access, particularly in resource-poor settings where library budgets are limited. Open access publishing, whether through publication in open access journals or deposit of manuscripts in repositories, aims to remove these barriers and make research findings more widely available. The type of license under which an article is published is also important, with Creative Commons Attribution (CC-BY) licensing allowing for unrestricted reuse, including text and data mining, translation, and redistribution. In the UK, funder mandates from Research Councils UK, the Wellcome Trust, and other charities, as well as the Finch Report and the Higher Education Funding Council for England's open access requirement for the post-2014 Research Excellence Framework, have transformed the publishing landscape. Universities are responsible for implementing these mandates through policies, repositories, and article-processing-charge funds, but their approaches have varied. Despite these efforts, it is unclear whether the resulting proportion of health research that is freely available and published under open licenses is high across institutions. The three domains of research priorities, intellectual property management, and publication practices represent the primary levers through which universities can contribute to global health equity. While previous studies have examined each of these areas in isolation, typically at the level of funders, countries, or individual technologies, or in institutions in North America, there is a need for a comprehensive assessment of UK universities. The UK plays a prominent role as a funder and producer of global health research, and its universities have a critical part to play in addressing the global health equity agenda. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a study to describe the current state of global health equity policies and practices in a sample of 25 UK universities. Our research questions were threefold: (1) What proportion of each university's health research funding from major UK funders is directed to neglected diseases and to health in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and how is this funding distributed across institutions? (2) What policies and practices govern the licensing of university-owned health technologies, and do they promote global access? (3) What are universities' open-access publishing policies, and what proportion of their health research articles is freely available and licensed under CC-BY? This study makes several important contributions to the field. First, it provides the first institution-level quantification of UK university health research funding for neglected diseases and LLMIC health, enabling comparison with the global burden of disease. Second, it sheds light on the licensing practices of UK universities and their potential impact on global access to health technologies. Third, it examines the open-access publishing policies of UK universities and the extent to which they make their research findings freely available and accessible to researchers, clinicians, and policymakers in resource-poor settings. By examining these three domains in a single assessment, this study provides a comprehensive overview of the global health equity policies and practices of UK universities and highlights areas for improvement. The quest for equitable access to healthcare and innovative treatments has become a pressing concern globally, with a growing recognition of the need for universities to align their research, licensing, and publishing practices with the needs of the world's most vulnerable populations. This study aims to document the presence and content of equitable licensing and open-access policies, as well as observed practices, across a sample of United Kingdom universities. Furthermore, it seeks to identify gaps in current policies and practices and propose practical steps that universities can take to better serve the needs of low- and middle-income countries. Our research design involved a cross-sectional landscape analysis of global health equity policies and practices at 25 UK universities, covering three key domains: research funding directed towards neglected diseases and health in low- and lower-middle-income countries, intellectual property (IP) licensing policies and practices, and open-access (OA) publishing policies and outputs. We drew on the framework used by Universities Allied for Essential Medicines (UAEM) for its Global Health University Report Card, which assesses universities on innovation, access, and empowerment. Our sample of 25 universities was selected in two stages: first, we identified the 20 UK universities receiving the largest amounts of health research funding from major public and charitable funders, using publicly available grant records; and second, we added five institutions with known activity in global health or technology transfer for health products, to ensure a diverse range of policies and practices. Institutions were anonymized in the main reporting, where agreed, and are referred to by code in the results. We extracted grant data from the databases of the five largest UK funders of health research, covering the period 2011-2014. For each grant awarded to a study university, we extracted relevant information, including award title, abstract or lay summary, start date, total award value, lead institution, and funder. Grants were included only if they had a clear health research purpose, defined as research intended to improve understanding, prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of disease, or the delivery of healthcare. We excluded grants for training fellowships without a defined research program, infrastructure, and public engagement. Grant values were not adjusted for inflation, given the relatively short period. Each grant was coded independently for two non-exclusive categories: "neglected disease" (ND) research and "health in low- and lower-middle-income countries" (hLLMIC) research. ND research was defined as research on diseases included in the Policy Cures Research G-FINDER survey scope, while hLLMIC research was defined as research conducted in, or explicitly aimed at improving health in, countries classified as low-income or lower-middle-income by the World Bank. A grant could be coded in both categories, one, or neither. Two reviewers independently coded every grant using title and abstract, with a keyword-assisted search used to flag likely candidates. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating unresolved cases. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Cohen's kappa. For each university, we calculated the proportion of total health research funding attributable to each category, as well as the institution's share of total funding to that category across all 25 universities. We also calculated the combined share of the four highest-ranked institutions as a measure of concentration. To contextualize the scale of research effort, we compared the proportions obtained with the share of the global burden of disease in low- and middle-income settings, using Global Burden of Disease estimates of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Regarding IP licensing policies and practices, we obtained information from publicly available documents, including IP policies, technology transfer office (TTO) web pages, annual reports, and statements to UAEM and other surveys. Where information was missing or unclear, we contacted the TTO or research office of each university by email, followed by telephone, with up to three reminders. We asked about the presence of written policies or commitments ensuring that health technologies arising from research are accessible and affordable in low- and middle-income countries, as well as the inclusion of access provisions in licenses, participation in patent pools or open licensing initiatives, and records of licensing health inventions. Two researchers classified each institution's policies against pre-specified criteria, with a policy recorded as present only if it explicitly addressed affordability or access in resource-poor settings. We also collected data on institutional OA policies from university websites, the Registry of Open Access Repository Mandates and Policies (ROARMAP), and the SHERPA/JULIET and SHERPA/FACT services, with confirmation by direct contact with library or research office staff. We recorded whether institutions had OA policies in place, as well as the nature of these policies, including any requirements for OA deposition, embargoes, or restrictions on reuse. By examining these three domains, our study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the policies and practices in place at UK universities and identify areas for improvement to better serve the needs of low- and middle-income countries. The findings of this study have important implications for universities, policymakers, and the broader research community. By highlighting gaps in current policies and practices, we can work towards creating a more equitable and just system for accessing healthcare and innovative treatments. This requires a concerted effort to align research, licensing, and publishing practices with the needs of the world's most vulnerable populations. Our study provides a foundation for this effort, and we hope that it will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the complex issues involved and inform the development of more effective policies and practices in the future. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the need for UK universities to re-examine their research, licensing, and publishing practices to ensure that they are aligned with the needs of low- and middle-income countries.
