Text classification is a cornerstone of natural language processing, with a wide range of applications in areas such as news categorization, sentiment analysis, spam filtering, and information retrieval. However, supervised classifiers, which are often highly effective when trained on large datasets, can struggle when applied to new, unseen data - a common scenario in many real-world applications. The root of the problem lies in the fact that labeling documents is a time-consuming and expensive process, and classifiers trained on one dataset often fail to generalize well to others, due to differences in vocabulary, style, and topical composition. This challenge is particularly pronounced in cross-domain text classification, where the goal is to leverage labeled data from a source domain to build an effective classifier for a target domain. The key obstacle here is the distribution shift between the two domains, which can cause a model fitted to the source domain to perform poorly on the target domain. To address this issue, researchers have developed various methods aimed at reducing the discrepancy between the feature distributions of the two domains. One prominent line of work focuses on identifying pivot features that are shared across domains and learning a projection that relates domain-specific features to these pivot features. Other approaches, such as transfer component analysis and co-clustering, seek to find a latent subspace in which the distance between domain distributions is minimized, or link domain-specific words through shared words. Deep models have also been used to align hidden representations between domains, using techniques such as marginalized denoising or adversarial training. Probabilistic topic models have been adapted to the cross-domain setting, where latent topics play the role of a shared semantic space between domains. Despite their differences, most of these methods rely on the assumption that domain differences can be eliminated by an exact alignment, where features are matched one-to-one or the two domains are forced through a common projection matrix or shared topic-word distribution. However, this exact alignment approach can be overly restrictive, imposing a strong constraint on what the model can learn. When the semantic distributions of the domains are very different, forcing a precise correspondence can compel the model to compromise, resulting in topics that mix domain-specific semantics, blur category boundaries, and ultimately reduce classification accuracy in the target domain. In other words, the stricter the alignment, the less capacity the model has to represent the genuine differences between domains. We argue that alignment should instead be performed at a coarser, more flexible level, which we term group alignment. This approach recognizes that semantic content in a domain is naturally organized into groups, such as sets of related topics that together describe a broader theme. Two domains may describe the same theme using different specific words and different fine-grained topics, yet the themes themselves correspond. Aligning the domains at the level of these semantic groups requires only that each group be shared, leaving the particular topics and words within a group free to vary by domain. Group alignment alone, however, does not guarantee that the learned groups are meaningful or that the topics within them are discriminative. Unsupervised topic models, which are driven by word co-occurrence, may not produce topics that correspond to the categories relevant to classification. Supervised variants, such as supervised LDA and Labeled LDA, tie topics to document labels and can substantially improve discrimination. In the cross-domain setting, labels are available only in the source domain, which suggests a partial supervision approach, where labels guide the learning of semantic groups and of the topics within them in the source domain, whereas the target domain is modeled without labels but is connected to the source via the group structure. This partial supervision helps the model learn better groups and better within-group semantics, resulting in a representation that is both transferable and class-informative. Based on these ideas, we propose Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), a probabilistic topic model that embeds group alignment and partial supervision in a single generative framework. Source-domain labels define semantic groups, each of which is associated with a set of topics that are shared by both domains at the group level. Topics within a group may have domain-specific word distributions, so that the same group is realized differently in the source and the target. Documents in the target domain draw their topics from the same groups without requiring label information. Inference yields topic-based document representations that can be fed to a standard classifier. Our study addresses three key research questions. First, does aligning semantics at the group level yield better target-domain classification than exact alignment, especially when domain semantics diverge? Second, does partial supervision in the source domain improve the quality of the learned groups and of the semantics within them? Third, are the resulting topics interpretable and consistent with the underlying categories? The contributions of this paper are fourfold. We identify the restrictive nature of exact alignment in cross-domain text classification and propose group alignment as a more flexible alternative. We introduce a partial supervision scheme in the source domain that helps the model learn more coherent semantic groups and more discriminative within-group topics. We integrate both mechanisms in CDL-LDA, a cross-domain topic model, and derive an inference procedure for it. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the standard 20Newsgroups and Reuters datasets, including quantitative evaluations of classification accuracy and perplexity and qualitative topic detection analyses, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. In the realm of cross-domain text classification, a crucial challenge arises when dealing with datasets that exhibit significant discrepancies in vocabulary and semantic distribution between the source and target domains. To address this issue, we focused on the development of a novel approach that leverages group alignment and partial supervision. Our evaluation was conducted on two widely-used benchmark corpora: 20Newsgroups and Reuters-21578. For the 20Newsgroups dataset, we adopted the hierarchical protocol initially proposed by Dai et al. (2007) and later expanded upon by Pan et al. (2010). This protocol involves utilizing top-level categories, such as "comp," "rec," "sci," and "talk," as class labels, while sub-categories are divided between domains. Notably, each top-level category contributes distinct sub-categories to both the source and target domains, resulting in the two domains sharing class labels but differing in vocabulary and semantic distribution. We constructed several binary tasks from category pairs, such as "comp" versus "sci" and "rec" versus "talk," following the methodology outlined by Dai et al. (2007). Similarly, for the Reuters-21578 dataset, we defined tasks as "orgs" versus "people," "orgs" versus "places," and "people" versus "places." In each task, sub-categories were partitioned to ensure that source and target documents originated from disjoint sub-topics, and each task was executed in both directions. In our experimental setup, all labeled source documents and all unlabeled target documents were available for training, while target labels were reserved exclusively for evaluation purposes. To preprocess the text data, we lowercased and tokenized the text, removed stop words, numbers, and header fields, and discarded words with a document frequency below three in the pooled corpus. The vocabulary was defined as the union of source and target words. Additionally, documents containing fewer than five remaining tokens were excluded from the analysis. Each target set was randomly split into 80% for training (without labels) and 20% for perplexity evaluation, with splits repeated using ten random seeds. Our proposed model, Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), extends upon the foundations of LDA (Blei et al., 2003) and Labeled LDA (Ramage et al., 2009) by incorporating two key components: partial supervision in the source domain and group alignment across domains. The topic groups in CDL-LDA are organized into C + 1 groups, with one group Gc corresponding to each class label c, and a shared background group G0 that captures class-independent content. Each group contains Kg topics, resulting in a total of K = (C+1)Kg topics, with each topic belonging to exactly one group. The partial supervision aspect of CDL-LDA restricts the document-topic distribution θd for a labeled source document d with label cd to topics within G{cd} ∪ G0, similar to Labeled LDA. However, the supervision is partial, as it only constrains which group of topics may generate a document, without specifying the individual topic or word. This allows topics within a group to remain latent and discover finer-grained semantics, such as sub-categories. In contrast, unlabeled target documents can utilize all K topics, with θd ~ Dirichlet(α) over the full set. Group alignment in CDL-LDA is achieved through the prior, rather than exact alignment, which would force each source topic and its target counterpart to share a single word distribution. This is overly restrictive when the domains' semantics differ. Instead, each domain s ∈ {S, T} has its own word distribution φ^sk for each topic k, and alignment is imposed at the group level. For topic k in group g, φ^sk ~ Dirichlet(β V ωg), where ωg is a group-level word distribution shared by both domains, and V is the vocabulary size. This encourages topics in the same group to concentrate on semantically related words in both domains, while allowing each topic to assign different weights and permitting domain-specific words to appear in one domain only. The generative process of CDL-LDA involves the following steps: (1) estimating the group-level base measure ωg for each group g; (2) drawing φ^sk ~ Dirichlet(βVωg) for each domain s and topic k in group g; (3) drawing θd for each document d in domain s; and (4) drawing a topic z ~ Multinomial(θd) and then a word w ~ Multinomial(φ^sz) for each word position. The base measure ωg is estimated using empirical Bayes, following the hierarchical-prior approach of Wallach et al. (2009). Specifically, ω{g,w} is set to the smoothed relative frequency of word w among tokens assigned to group g across both domains. Inference in CDL-LDA is performed using collapsed Gibbs sampling (Griffiths & Steyvers, 2004). For token i in document d of domain s, the conditional probability of topic k is proportional to (n^{-i}{d,k} + α) · (n^{-i,s}{k,w} + βVω{g(k),w}) / (n^{-i,s}{k} + βV), where k ranges over allowed topics. We ran 1,500 iterations, discarded the first 1,000 as burn-in, and averaged estimates over samples taken every 50 iterations. Hyperparameters were set to α = 50/K and β = 0.01, following common practice. The number of topics per group, Kg, was selected from the set {2, 5, 10, 20} based on perplexity on held-out labeled source documents, ensuring that no target labels were used for tuning. For classification, we computed the group posterior P(g | d) = Σ{k∈Gg} θ{d,k} for a target document d. Since the background group carries no class information, the predicted label was determined as ĉ = argmax{c} P(Gc | d), considering only class groups. As an alternative approach, we utilized the K-dimensional vector θd as features for a linear SVM trained on source documents, allowing us to assess the quality of the learned representation independently of the group-based decision rule. To evaluate the effectiveness of CDL-LDA, we compared its performance against a range of baseline methods, including source-only classifiers (linear SVM and logistic regression on TF-IDF), transductive and co-clustering methods (transductive SVM, CoCC, TPLSA, and Collaborative Dual-PLSA), feature-alignment and projection methods (SFA and TCA), and representation learning methods (mSDA and DANN). Additionally, we conducted ablation studies to isolate the contributions of the two components of CDL-LDA: Labeled LDA trained on pooled source and target data, CDL-LDA without supervision, and CDL-LDA with exact alignment. The performance of CDL-LDA and the baseline methods was evaluated using accuracy and macro-F1 on target test documents. Furthermore, we assessed the quality of the topic models using perplexity and other relevant metrics. By examining the results of these evaluations, we aimed to gain insights into the strengths and limitations of CDL-LDA and its potential applications in cross-domain text classification. Evaluating public health interventions is a complex and resource-intensive endeavor. These interventions often comprise multiple interacting components, target behaviors or organizational structures at various levels, and are highly context-dependent (Craig et al. 2008; Hawe et al. 2004). As a result, the stakes are high, and ineffective, poorly implemented, or harmful interventions can have far-reaching consequences, including the waste of scarce public funds, diversion of attention from more promising approaches, and exacerbation of health inequalities (Rychetnik et al. 2002). Full-scale evaluations, typically in the form of randomized controlled trials or well-designed natural experiments, are costly and time-consuming, and are often compromised by problems that could have been anticipated, such as difficulties with participant recruitment and retention, poorly specified intervention components, inadequate delivery fidelity, and unrealistic assumptions about the likely size of the effect (Bowen et al. 2009; Eldridge et al. 2016a; Moore et al. 2015). When such problems are discovered only after a definitive evaluation is underway, the consequences can be severe, including underpowered or inconclusive findings, protocol amendments, premature termination, and avoidable research waste. To mitigate these risks, exploratory studies, often labeled as pilot or feasibility studies, are widely regarded as a crucial step in the evaluation process (Craig et al. 2008; Thabane et al. 2010). These studies provide an opportunity to identify and address potential problems before committing to a larger, more resource-intensive evaluation. The Medical Research Council guidance on developing and evaluating complex interventions emphasizes the importance of feasibility and piloting as a distinct stage between intervention development and evaluation, with the aim of testing procedures, estimating recruitment and retention, and informing sample size calculations (Craig et al. 2008). A well-conducted exploratory study can provide valuable insights into the acceptability of an intervention to those who deliver and receive it, its potential for implementation as intended, the workability of the proposed evaluation design, and the overall viability of proceeding to a larger study (Bowen et al. 2009; Lancaster et al. 2004). By doing so, exploratory studies can improve the quality of subsequent evaluations, reduce costs, and limit exposure of participants and populations to ineffective or harmful interventions (Kistin and Silverstein 2015). Despite their recognized importance, however, the conceptual and methodological basis of exploratory studies remains contested. The terms "pilot study" and "feasibility study" are used inconsistently, with some authors treating them as synonyms, others regarding feasibility as an overarching concept that encompasses pilot work, and others distinguishing between them based on whether a study replicates the design of the intended main evaluation (Arain et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016a; Thabane et al. 2010). Reviews of published studies have highlighted considerable heterogeneity in stated aims and conduct, with many studies describing themselves as pilots yet reporting hypothesis tests of effectiveness, using small-sample effect estimates to power subsequent trials, or omitting pre-specified criteria for judging success (Arain et al. 2010; Lancaster et al. 2004; Leon et al. 2011). Such practices have been criticized for their potential to produce imprecise and misleading effect estimates, as well as for leaving the decision to proceed vulnerable to post hoc rationalization (Kraemer et al. 2006; Eldridge et al. 2016b). The reporting of exploratory studies is also variable, making it difficult for readers to judge what was learned and how findings influenced the decision to proceed, amend, or abandon an intervention. The CONSORT extension for randomized pilot and feasibility trials was introduced to address this problem (Eldridge et al. 2016c), but its scope is limited to a particular design. These challenges are particularly pertinent to public health, where existing guidance on pilot and feasibility work has been developed largely with clinical trials of individually delivered treatments in mind (Thabane et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016a). Public health interventions, by contrast, are often delivered at the level of groups, organizations, or whole populations, and may be evaluated using cluster randomized, quasi-experimental, or other non-randomized designs (Craig et al. 2012; Hawe et al. 2004). In this context, an exploratory study must address a broader set of questions, including the plausibility of the underlying program theory, the acceptability and scalability of the intervention, and the practicality of evaluation designs that do not conform to the conventional trial template (Moore et al. 2015; Bonell et al. 2012). The balance between standardization and flexibility is also more difficult to strike when intervention components are expected to vary with context (Hawe et al. 2004). It is unclear whether existing recommendations address the unique needs of public health interventions or whether they can be applied coherently by researchers working in this field. The decision of whether, and in what form, to proceed from an exploratory study to a full evaluation is a further source of uncertainty. Progression is often framed in terms of "stop/go" criteria, such as thresholds for recruitment, retention, or fidelity (Eldridge et al. 2016b; Avery et al. 2017), but little is known about how such criteria should be selected, justified, and applied, or how qualitative and contextual evidence should be weighed alongside quantitative indicators. Furthermore, the relationship between exploratory studies and preceding intervention development work, as well as subsequent evaluation, is rarely specified, despite the fact that the value of an exploratory study depends on the strength of the evidence that precedes it (Wight et al. 2016; Bleijenberg et al. 2018). As a result, researchers, funders, and reviewers lack a shared basis for judging when an exploratory study is warranted, what it should seek to answer, and what findings should lead to progression. Previous reviews have examined aspects of this literature, such as the definitions of pilot and feasibility studies, the reporting of pilot trials, and methods for sample size estimation in preparation for randomized trials (Arain et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016a; Lancaster et al. 2004). However, to our knowledge, no systematic review has synthesized the available guidance specifically in relation to exploratory studies of public health interventions, nor considered the full sequence of decisions, from justifying the study through design and conduct to progression and reporting. This knowledge gap highlights the need for a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the role of exploratory studies in the evaluation of public health interventions, and for the development of guidance that is tailored to the unique challenges and complexities of this field. The need for a comprehensive synthesis of existing guidance on exploratory studies is evident, as it will enable us to pinpoint areas of consensus, identify conflicting recommendations, and highlight gaps in current guidance. This systematic review represents the first phase of a broader research program aimed at developing standalone guidance for public health researchers on the design and conduct of exploratory studies. Our primary objectives were to identify, examine, and synthesize existing recommendations regarding the timing and rationale for undertaking exploratory studies, the research questions they should address, suitable methodologies, criteria for progressing to a full-scale effectiveness study, and appropriate reporting practices. To achieve these objectives, we conducted a systematic review of methodological guidance, encompassing both published and unpublished documents that provide recommendations on the design, conduct, analysis, or reporting of exploratory studies preceding a full-scale evaluation of an intervention. Notably, reviews of guidance differ fundamentally from reviews of intervention effects, as the units of analysis are recommendations and their underlying rationales, rather than empirical study findings. Consequently, we adhered to the general principles of systematic review methodology, as outlined by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (2009), and reported our review in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, where applicable (Moher et al., 2009). Our protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD42016047843), ensuring transparency and accountability throughout the review process. In defining the scope of our review, we employed the term "exploratory study" as an umbrella concept, encompassing any preparatory study undertaken prior to a full-scale evaluation to assess feasibility and inform decisions regarding the progression of an intervention. This inclusive definition incorporated studies labeled as pilot, feasibility, proof-of-concept, phase II, or developmental studies, reflecting the heterogeneous terminology prevalent in this field (Arain et al., 2010; Eldridge et al., 2016). We focused on public health interventions, which we regarded as complex interventions, characterized by multiple interacting components, targeting multiple levels or behaviors, or being sensitive to the context of delivery (Craig et al., 2008; Moore et al., 2015). Our review encompassed guidance relevant to population-level, community, organizational, and policy interventions, as well as individually targeted behavioral interventions. To ensure the relevance and applicability of our findings, we established explicit eligibility criteria for documents. We included documents that provided explicit recommendations or guidance on at least one of the following aspects: the timing and rationale for undertaking exploratory studies, the research questions to be addressed, suitable methods, criteria for progressing to an effectiveness evaluation, or reporting practices. Furthermore, documents were required to be relevant to public health or complex interventions, or to be sufficiently generic to apply to these contexts. We considered documents published or made available between January 2000 and November 2016, including peer-reviewed articles, book chapters, reports from funding bodies and research organizations, and other grey literature. Primary empirical studies, protocols, and reports of individual pilot studies were excluded, unless they also presented generalizable methodological recommendations. Editorials and commentaries were included only if they offered substantive guidance, rather than opinion alone. We limited our search to English-language publications, acknowledging the potential for language biases. Our search strategy was developed iteratively, in collaboration with an information specialist and the review team, using a set of key papers known to the team to test sensitivity. We combined search terms relating to exploratory study terminology, study type, and guidance, with subject headings and free-text variants adapted to each database. Searches were conducted in multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, the Applied Social Sciences Index and Abstracts, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Methodology Register. We deliberately avoided applying study design filters to prevent the exclusion of methodological articles that are inconsistently indexed. To identify unpublished and grey literature, we searched the websites of major funding and research organizations, including the UK Medical Research Council, the National Institute for Health Research, and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, among others. We also searched OpenGrey and used targeted Google searches, screening the first 100 hits for each query. Additionally, we screened the reference lists of included documents and undertook forward citation tracking in Google Scholar and Web of Science. Finally, we consulted topic experts, including authors of key guidance and members of relevant trial methodology networks, to identify further sources, including documents in preparation. The final searches were completed in November 2016. Following the completion of the search, records were exported to reference management software, and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria by one reviewer, with a second reviewer independently screening a random 20% sample to ensure consistency. Full texts of potentially eligible records were then retrieved and assessed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or, where necessary, by consulting a third member of the team. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded, providing a transparent audit trail. To extract relevant data from included documents, we developed a standardized extraction form, which was piloted on a subset of documents and refined accordingly. For each document, we extracted bibliographic details, type of document, country and disciplinary origin of the authors, intended audience, type of intervention or setting addressed, terminology used for exploratory studies, and stated definition and purpose of such studies. We then extracted verbatim all text containing recommendations on: when and why to conduct an exploratory study; the research questions to be addressed; recommended designs and methods (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed); sample size considerations; analytical approaches; and criteria for progressing to an effectiveness evaluation. By synthesizing these recommendations, we aimed to clarify the current state of guidance, identify inconsistencies and omissions, and provide an evidence base for subsequent consensus-building and guidance development. The advent of high-throughput sequencing has revolutionized the field of oncology, enabling tumor genomic profiling to become a standard practice. The use of targeted gene panels, whole-exome sequencing, and increasingly whole-genome approaches has transformed our ability to guide diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy selection (Berger and Mardis 2018). A series of landmark studies has demonstrated the clinical value of this approach, including the identification of activating EGFR mutations that predict response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors in lung adenocarcinoma (Lynch et al. 2004), BRAF V600 mutations that predict response to vemurafenib in melanoma (Chapman et al. 2011), and the BCR-ABL1 fusion that predicts response to imatinib in chronic myeloid leukemia (Druker et al. 2001). Large-scale efforts, such as the MSK-IMPACT initiative, have further shown that a substantial proportion of patients harbor alterations that are actionable by approved or investigational agents (Zehir et al. 2017). However, realizing the full potential of precision oncology for the broader patient population requires accurate interpretation of the complex genomic landscape of individual tumors, extending beyond the small set of well-characterized alterations. In practice, interpretation remains the primary bottleneck. A typical tumor sequenced with even a modest panel harbors multiple somatic coding variants, but only a few of these have well-established functional or clinical significance. Pan-cancer studies have suggested that most tumors contain only a handful of true driver events amidst a multitude of passenger alterations (Vogelstein et al. 2013; Bailey et al. 2018). Distinguishing between these two categories is far from trivial, and consequently, many variants reported in clinical and research settings are assigned to the category of variants of unknown significance (VUS). This classification, borrowed from the framework developed for germline variant classification by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (Richards et al. 2015), offers little actionable guidance for clinicians and patients. A VUS cannot be used to justify targeted therapy, nor can it be dismissed as benign, resulting in a growing body of unused information that disproportionately affects patients whose tumors lack canonical hotspot alterations. To mitigate this challenge, several resources and computational strategies have been developed. Curated knowledge bases, such as OncoKB (Chakravarty et al. 2017), CIViC (Griffith et al. 2017), and the Cancer Genome Interpreter (Tamborero et al. 2018), provide annotations on the oncogenic effect and therapeutic implications of specific variants, while ClinVar aggregates clinical assertions for germline and somatic variants (Landrum et al. 2018). In silico predictors, including SIFT (Kumar et al. 2009), PolyPhen-2 (Adzhubei et al. 2010), and CADD (Kircher et al. 2014), estimate the deleteriousness of amino acid substitutions based on sequence conservation and structural features. However, benchmarking against functionally validated cancer mutations has revealed that the accuracy of these tools is limited and varies widely across genes and algorithms (Martelotto et al. 2014). Furthermore, deleteriousness is not equivalent to oncogenicity, as a damaging change in a tumor suppressor and an activating change in an oncogene have distinct implications. Population databases, such as ExAC, provide a complementary filter by removing germline polymorphisms, as variants observed at appreciable frequency in apparently healthy individuals are unlikely to be tumor drivers (Lek et al. 2016). However, this filter does not identify which of the remaining rare variants are significant. A distinct and statistically principled source of evidence is recurrence, where mutations that arise repeatedly at the same position across independent tumors are unlikely to do so by chance and often indicate positive selection. This logic underlies the identification of mutational hotspots in cancer genes (Lawrence et al. 2014; Chang et al. 2016) and its extensions to three-dimensional clusters of residues (Gao et al. 2017). The Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) is the most extensive repository of such observations, compiling variants from the literature and large-scale screens (Forbes et al. 2015). Nevertheless, recurrence analyses depend on the size and composition of the underlying cohorts. COSMIC is dominated by variants from whole-exome and whole-genome studies and from certain well-studied tumor types and genes, so rare variants, variants in less-studied cancers, and variants in genes covered mainly by clinical panels may reach the threshold of recurrence only when data are aggregated across additional sources. Variants that appear only once or twice in COSMIC may be flagged as private or rare, although they are in fact recurrent in newer, larger, and more clinically representative data sets. The American Association for Cancer Research Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (AACR Project GENIE) offers precisely such a data set, providing an international, publicly accessible registry of clinical-grade genomic data from patients treated at participating cancer centers, linking sequencing results to clinical annotation across a wide variety of tumor types (AACR Project GENIE Consortium 2017). Because the data are generated in the course of routine care, they represent the patient population seen in practice, including uncommon histologies and patients who would not typically be enrolled in research cohorts. To date, however, much of the published analysis of GENIE has focused on well-known drivers and previously identified hotspots. A systematic assessment of the large remainder of variants, including those absent from or poorly represented in COSMIC, has not been performed. As a result, it remains unclear how many patients carry variants that are currently labeled VUS but whose recurrence indicates they merit closer attention. In this study, we sought to address this knowledge gap by combining GENIE and COSMIC to identify recurrent variants that would be overlooked when either resource is used alone. We first removed variants that are already well understood, namely known hotspot variants, inactivating variants in tumor suppressor genes, and likely benign variants identified by their frequency in ExAC (Lek et al. 2016). This left a set of variants of uncertain significance, from which we asked three questions. First, how many variants observed in GENIE are novel with respect to COSMIC, and what is the typical per-patient burden of pathogenic, likely pathogenic, and uncertain variants? Second, how many variants recur in GENIE at a frequency that would be notable but are rare or private in COSMIC? Third, what is the clinical and biological significance of these recurrent variants, and how do they inform our understanding of the genomic landscape of cancer? By addressing these questions, we aimed to shed light on the complex and often uncharted territory of VUS and to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the genomic alterations that underlie cancer development and progression. The integration of large-scale genomic datasets has revolutionized our understanding of cancer biology, yet significant gaps remain in our knowledge of the mutational landscape. Three key questions emerge when examining the intersection of the GENIE and COSMIC datasets: what variants are absent in COSMIC, how many additional variants meet a recurrence threshold when the two datasets are combined, and what proportion of patients harbor these variants? Our analysis addresses these questions, yielding three primary contributions. Firstly, we compile a comprehensive catalogue of tens of thousands of variants unique to GENIE, highlighting the vast expanse of unexplored variation in clinical cohorts. Secondly, we identify several hundred variants that recur in GENIE but have limited support in COSMIC, as well as a substantially larger set that achieves recurrence only through the integration of both resources. We propose these variants as high-priority candidates for functional and clinical investigation. Thirdly, we estimate the fraction of patients whose molecular profiles would be impacted by these newly recognized recurrent variants, providing insight into the potential reach of improved variant interpretation. It is essential to note that recurrence alone does not establish pathogenicity, and we do not advocate for treating these variants as drivers without further evidence. Instead, we argue that they should be prioritized above other variants of unknown significance (VUS) for experimental characterization, computational modeling, and incorporation into clinical knowledge bases. This nuanced approach recognizes the complexity of cancer biology and the need for rigorous evaluation of variant pathogenicity. Our analysis drew upon somatic variant data from the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (GENIE) public release. GENIE aggregates clinical-grade targeted sequencing data from multiple international cancer centers, each employing institution-specific gene panels. We utilized the mutation data file, clinical sample and patient files, and gene panel annotation files distributed with the release, focusing on single-nucleotide variants and small insertions and deletions mapped to the GRCh37 reference assembly. Records lacking essential annotations, such as protein-level annotation, genomic coordinate, or valid sample identifier, were excluded. To avoid inflating recurrence through serial or multi-site sampling, variants were counted once per patient at each genomic position when multiple samples from the same patient were present. Cancer type was assigned using the OncoTree classification supplied by the consortium. Reference data on previously observed somatic variants were obtained from the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC). We employed the COSMIC genome-screen and targeted-screen mutation export, which reports the number of independent samples in which each variant was observed. Variants were matched between datasets by gene symbol, HGVS protein-level change, and, where available, genomic coordinates and nucleotide change. Gene symbols were harmonized to HGNC-approved nomenclature, and transcript-specific annotation differences were resolved by preferring the canonical transcript. Population allele frequencies were obtained from the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC), which provides allele counts from over 60,000 exomes. To distinguish mechanisms of pathogenicity, genes were classified as oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, or other, using the cancer gene annotations in COSMIC Cancer Gene Census, supplemented by curated oncogene and tumor suppressor lists. Genes annotated with both roles were treated as context-dependent and retained for both filtering paths. Genes lacking an annotation were treated as unclassified, and no gene-role-based filtering was applied to them. The analytic strategy involved removing variants whose significance is already established or whose pathogenic potential is very low, leaving a pool of VUS for recurrence analysis. Filtering proceeded in three stages. Firstly, known hotspot variants were removed, as they are generally considered to be of high pathogenic potential. A variant was considered a known hotspot if it was reported in COSMIC in at least three independent samples, consistent with common recurrence thresholds used to nominate candidate driver positions. Secondly, inactivating variants in tumor suppressor genes were excluded, as they are typically presumed to be loss-of-function and treated as likely pathogenic under standard interpretive frameworks. Missense and in-frame variants in tumor suppressors were retained, as their pathogenic potential is less clear. Thirdly, likely benign variants were removed using population frequency, as variants with a minor allele frequency greater than 0.1% in any ExAC continental population, or observed in more than one homozygous individual, are likely to be germline polymorphisms. After filtering, a variant was labeled novel if it was observed in GENIE but absent from COSMIC. A variant observed in COSMIC in fewer than three samples was designated a low-recurrence COSMIC variant. Variants were further categorized by predicted consequence, including missense, in-frame insertion or deletion, splice region, synonymous, or other. To estimate the burden of variants per patient, we tallied the total number of coding variants, the number classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic, and the number remaining as VUS for each patient. Variants were designated pathogenic or likely pathogenic if they were known hotspots or inactivating mutations in tumor suppressor genes, and as VUS if they remained after filtering and were not considered benign. Summary statistics, including mean, median, and interquartile range, were calculated across patients and stratified by cancer type and sequencing center, to evaluate the influence of panel size on observed burden. Due to substantial differences in panel size among institutions, comparisons across centers were interpreted with caution, and per-megabase normalization was applied using panel footprints from the gene panel files when comparing burden among institutions. Secondly, we integrated the GENIE and COSMIC datasets to identify variants that achieve recurrence only through the combination of both resources. Ambient air pollution poses a significant threat to global health, accounting for millions of premature deaths annually, primarily due to cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, and lung cancer. The World Health Organization and various studies have underscored the severity of this issue, with short-term exposure to high concentrations of particulate matter, ozone, and nitrogen dioxide linked to increased hospital admissions, asthma exacerbations, and cardiovascular events. While structural reductions in emissions are crucial for mitigating this problem, progress is often slow and incomplete, making it essential for individuals to take protective measures during pollution episodes. To this end, many countries and cities have implemented air quality warning systems, which translate pollutant concentrations into indices or banding schemes, such as the US Air Quality Index or the UK Daily Air Quality Index. These systems provide tiered health advice, typically encouraging sensitive groups and the general population to reduce outdoor activity, avoid busy roads, and follow treatment plans. The underlying assumption of these systems is that informed individuals will modify their behavior, reducing exposure and associated harm. However, this assumption relies on a complex chain of events, where individuals must be aware of the warning, understand its relevance, and be willing and able to act on the advice. Research on health risk communication suggests that awareness does not necessarily translate into behavior change, with factors like risk perception, trust in information sources, and confidence in one's ability to act influencing responses. In the context of air pollution, the invisible nature of the hazard, delayed effects, and potential conflicts with daily routines can further complicate behavior change. Despite the importance of understanding how individuals respond to air quality warnings, evidence on this topic is scattered and inconclusive. Economists have investigated averting behavior in response to smog alerts, using proxies like attendance at outdoor venues or purchases of protective products, but results have been mixed. Public health researchers have conducted surveys and panel studies on awareness, intended behavior, and self-reported behavior among various populations, including those with asthma or cardiovascular disease. However, these studies vary significantly in their populations, warning systems, behaviors considered, and measurement of adherence, making it challenging to draw firm conclusions about the effectiveness of air quality warnings. A critical gap in our understanding concerns the extent to which people adhere to the health advice accompanying air quality warnings and the demographic and psychosocial factors that predict adherence or non-adherence. Several studies have examined correlates of protective behavior, including age, sex, education, income, and health conditions, but findings are inconsistent. Others have explored psychosocial factors like knowledge, risk perception, and self-efficacy, but these are often not organized within a coherent theoretical framework, making it difficult to identify promising targets for intervention. The COM-B model, which proposes that behavior arises from the interaction of capability, opportunity, and motivation, offers a useful framework for understanding behavior change in this context. The production of speech is a complex process that involves a coordinated sequence of movements of the articulators, including the lips, jaw, tongue, velum, and larynx. As these articulators move, they continuously reshape the vocal tract, the airway that extends from the glottis to the lips, thereby modulating airflow and creating different resonant cavities. The time-varying shape of the vocal tract plays a crucial role in determining the acoustic properties of the speech signal, as demonstrated by Fant (1970) and Stevens (1998). Consequently, understanding the mapping between vocal tract geometry and acoustics remains a central problem in speech science, with significant implications for phonetics, speech technology, clinical assessment, and the study of language variation (Narayanan et al., 2014; Lingala et al., 2016). To tackle this problem, researchers have relied on various instrumentation techniques to observe articulation, including electromagnetic articulography, ultrasound, X-ray microbeam, and video of the face. While these methods provide valuable insights, they each capture only a partial view of the articulatory process, focusing on flesh-point trajectories, the tongue surface, or the external lips (Whalen et al., 2005; Stone, 2005). In contrast, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers a non-invasive and radiation-free means of visualizing the entire vocal tract, including regions such as the pharynx and velum that are difficult to access using other modalities. Recent advances in fast acquisition and reconstruction have made real-time MRI (rtMRI) of speech a practical reality, enabling the capture of dynamic articulation in the midsagittal plane during natural, continuous speech (Narayanan et al., 2004; Bresch et al., 2008; Lingala et al., 2016). The availability of large rtMRI corpora, such as the USC-TIMIT database and related multi-speaker collections, has facilitated the quantitative study of articulation across many speakers (Narayanan et al., 2014). However, most computational work on rtMRI speech data has relied on hand-designed or semi-automatic representations of the vocal tract, including air-tissue boundary segmentation, cross-distance functions along the vocal tract midline, and region-of-interest time series that capture constriction formation at the lips, tongue tip, tongue body, and velum (Kim et al., 2014; Bresch & Narayanan, 2009; Proctor et al., 2010). While these representations are interpretable and have supported insights into coarticulation, compensatory articulation, and the composition of articulatory gestures (Browman & Goldstein, 1992), they require segmentation or parameterization pipelines that may be sensitive to image quality and speaker anatomy, and may discard information that is not captured by the chosen parameters. A complementary approach is to learn representations directly from the image sequences, allowing the data to determine which spatial and temporal features are informative about the speech sounds being produced. Deep learning provides a powerful toolkit for this strategy, with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learning hierarchical visual features and achieving strong results in image recognition (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015; He et al., 2016). For video data, the challenge is to also model temporal dynamics, with approaches including 3D convolutions (Ji et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2015), two-stream networks combining appearance and motion (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014), and architectures that couple per-frame CNN features with recurrent networks such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) are a prominent example of the latter, where a CNN extracts deep visual features from each frame, and a recurrent layer integrates them over time, making the model deep in both space and time (Donahue et al., 2015). While LRCN models have been successfully applied to action recognition, video description, and other sequence-learning tasks, and have also been used for visual speech recognition from lip images (Assael et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2017), their application to rtMRI of the full vocal tract has received relatively little systematic attention. This gap in the existing literature is significant, as studies of automatic recognition from articulatory data have mostly used point-tracking measurements or lip-region video, or have used articulatory features as auxiliary inputs to acoustic recognizers (King et al., 2007; Hueber et al., 2010). Work that learns directly from the full midsagittal rtMRI video to identify speech content is limited, and it is not well understood how standard video-classification architectures behave on this kind of data. One of the key challenges in applying LRCN models to rtMRI data is that vocal tract videos differ significantly from the natural-scene videos for which these architectures were designed. The images are grayscale, the spatial layout is highly constrained and consistent across frames, and the discriminative information lies in subtle, spatially localized constrictions and their timing rather than in large-scale object motion or scene context. Moreover, the sequences of interest, such as vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) utterances, are short and the relevant dynamics are brief and coarticulated, so assumptions about the value of long temporal context or of pretrained appearance features may not carry over. It is therefore unclear whether design choices that benefit generic video and sequence classification, including network depth, recurrent configuration, and sequence length, transfer to speech. This paper takes a step towards addressing this question by investigating whether speech content can be identified directly from the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract in rtMRI, using video action recognition techniques. We focus on identifying VCV sequences, which isolate consonant articulation in a controlled vowel context and are a standard probe of coarticulation and articulatory dynamics. Our approach involves formulating speech identification from rtMRI as a video classification problem and applying LRCN models to 2D rtMRI of VCV utterances from 17 speakers. We conduct a comparative evaluation of this class of models under various parameter settings and for several classification tasks, providing an empirical characterization of what matters for this data. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we demonstrate the feasibility of speech identification from rtMRI using LRCN models, which combines deep CNN feature extraction with recurrent sequence modeling. Second, we conduct a systematic evaluation of the performance of LRCN models under various parameter settings, including the CNN and recurrent components, and for several classification tasks. Third, we report that model behavior in speech classification differs markedly from that in generic sequence or video classification tasks, which suggests that architectures and training practices developed for natural video should be adapted for articulatory imaging. Together, these findings inform the design of data-driven models linking vocal tract shape geometry to speech acoustics, and highlight the need for further research into the application of deep learning techniques to rtMRI data. The study of vocal tract dynamics and speech production has long been a topic of interest in the field of linguistics and speech science. Recent advances in real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rtMRI) have provided a unique opportunity to examine the articulatory movements of the vocal tract during speech production. In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of the acoustic mapping from articulation using a database of 2D rtMRI images of the midsagittal vocal tract acquired from 17 native speakers of American English. The database consists of vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences, which provide a rich source of information on the dynamics of speech production. The image acquisition protocol followed established procedures (Narayanan et al., 2004; Narayanan et al., 2014), where participants lay supine in a scanner and a fast spiral gradient-echo sequence was used to image a single midsagittal slice that covered the lips, tongue, velum, larynx, and pharyngeal wall. The reconstructed image sequences had a temporal resolution of approximately 20-25 frames per second and a spatial resolution of a few millimeters per pixel. The images were stored as grayscale video and were accompanied by simultaneous audio recordings, which were used to segment the utterances. The audio signals were denoised using a noise-cancelling optical microphone and a denoising algorithm (Bresch et al., 2006), but were not used as input to any classifier. Each speaker produced a set of VCV tokens with a symmetric vowel context, where the same vowel precedes and follows the consonant. The inventory of consonants spanned stops, nasals, fricatives, and approximants, and was crossed with the corner vowels /a/, /i/, and /u/. Each token was repeated several times in a carrier-free, isolated manner, and individual tokens were cut from the continuous recording using the acoustic signal. The clips were manually checked for visible motion artifacts, incomplete articulations, or acquisition failures, and tokens with such issues were discarded. The remaining clips were labeled with their VCV identity, consonant, and vowel context. Preprocessing of the images involved cropping the frames to a fixed region of interest around the vocal tract, resizing them to 224 × 224 pixels using bilinear interpolation, and replicating them across three channels to facilitate the use of ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks (Deng et al., 2009). The intensities were normalized per speaker by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, which reduced inter-speaker differences in coil sensitivity and overall brightness. To account for variations in speaking rate, each clip was converted to a fixed length of T frames, with longer clips being uniformly subsampled and shorter clips being padded by repeating the last frame. The value of T was treated as a design parameter. The main model used in this study was a Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Network (LRCN; Donahue et al., 2015), which consists of a convolutional network that processes each frame independently and yields a fixed-length feature vector, followed by a recurrent network that maps the sequence of feature vectors to class probabilities. The convolutional network used was VGG-16 (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015), and the recurrent network was a long short-term memory (LSTM) network (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). The final hidden state of the LSTM network was fed to a softmax layer, and dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) was applied before the recurrent and output layers. To place the LRCN results in context, we trained three reference models on the same splits: a frame-wise CNN that ignores temporal order, a late-fusion CNN that concatenates features over time (Karpathy et al., 2014), and a 3D convolutional network that learns joint spatiotemporal filters (Tran et al., 2015). These reference models allowed us to examine whether explicit sequence modeling is necessary to capture the dynamics of speech production. The experimental design involved defining three classification tasks: VCV identification, consonant classification, and vowel classification. In the VCV identification task, the model predicted the full VCV label, requiring the inference of both the consonant and vowel context. In the consonant classification task, clips from all vowel contexts were pooled and labeled only by the consonant, requiring invariance to the surrounding vowel. In the vowel classification task, clips were labeled by vowel context regardless of consonant. For each task, we varied several parameters, including clip length T, the number of LSTM units and layers, the CNN backbone, initialization, and recurrence direction. To estimate generalization to unseen speakers, we used speaker-independent evaluation, where the 17 speakers were partitioned into folds for cross-validation. In each fold, a subset of the remaining speakers was held out as a validation set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection, and no test speaker data influenced model selection. We also ran a speaker-dependent condition, where tokens from every speaker were split across training and test sets by repetition, to quantify the gap caused by inter-speaker variability in vocal tract anatomy. Networks were trained by minimizing categorical cross-entropy with the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015), and the initial learning rate was set to 1e-4 for pretrained layers and 1e-3 for newly initialized layers. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the acoustic mapping from articulation using rtMRI images of the vocal tract. Phylogeography, the study of the processes that shape the geographic distribution of genealogical lineages, has become a crucial tool for understanding the emergence, dispersal, and diversification of pathogens across space and time. In the context of rapidly evolving organisms, such as RNA viruses, where evolutionary and epidemiological timescales overlap, phylogeographic analysis enables researchers to reconstruct the complex dynamics of disease transmission. This is particularly important for infectious diseases like influenza A, rabies, HIV-1, Ebola, and SARS-CoV-2, where the ability to track the movement of pathogens is essential for effective surveillance, control, and prevention. Bayesian phylogeographic frameworks, which treat location as a discrete trait evolving along a phylogeny, have been successfully applied to various viral systems. These approaches rely on the analysis of genetic sequences, often obtained from public databases like GenBank, to infer the origins and spread of pathogens. However, the accuracy of these analyses depends critically on the quality of the geographic information associated with each sampled sequence. Unfortunately, the metadata provided with GenBank records, such as country, isolation source, and geolocation name, are often incomplete, inaccurate, or lacking in sufficient detail. The limitations of GenBank metadata are well-documented. Submitters may omit crucial information, provide only country-level data, or enter free-text values that vary widely in format and granularity. Moreover, country-level resolution is frequently inadequate for modeling the transmission of viruses within a country or between neighboring regions. For instance, understanding the spread of a virus between provinces, cities, or even individual farms requires location data at a much finer scale. Furthermore, the country listed in a GenBank record may reflect the location of the sequencing laboratory rather than the origin of the host, and for viruses sampled from migratory animals or travelers, the place of infection may differ from the place of sampling. Several studies have highlighted the importance of location granularity and accuracy in phylogeographic analyses. The choice of location scale and the precision of assigned locations can substantially alter inferred migration networks and root-location estimates. When metadata are insufficient, researchers often turn to the publications linked to GenBank records, which may provide more detailed information about the sampling campaign. However, extracting this information manually is a time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult-to-reproduce process, particularly for studies involving hundreds or thousands of sequences drawn from many articles. Automating the extraction of geographic locations from text offers a promising solution to this problem. The computational task of recognizing place names in text, known as toponym recognition, is a crucial step in geographic information retrieval. Toponym recognition is conventionally treated as a form of named entity recognition (NER) and addressed using sequence labeling models, such as conditional random fields (CRFs) and neural architectures. However, general-purpose NER systems often perform poorly on biomedical text, where geographic names are intermingled with names of strains, genes, hosts, and institutions that share surface forms with places. The scarcity of annotated data for toponym recognition in virology articles is a significant obstacle. Manual annotation of geographic mentions requires domain expertise and is costly, making it impractical for large-scale analyses. Distant supervision, which generates training labels automatically by aligning an existing knowledge base with unlabelled text, offers an alternative. However, the use of weak labels derived from existing database records, such as GenBank metadata and gazetteers like GeoNames, is inherently noisy and may not provide the same level of accuracy as fully supervised models. Two key gaps remain in the development of methods for extracting fine-grained geographic locations from the literature for virus phylogeography. First, there is no established method tailored to the peculiarities of virus-related articles, such as strain nomenclature, sampling descriptions, and host-related terminology. Second, it is unclear whether weak supervision derived from existing database records can approximate the accuracy of fully supervised models, thereby removing the annotation bottleneck. To address these gaps, we ask two questions: (i) to what extent can a supervised sequence labeling model with features tailored to virology articles detect geographic location mentions, and (ii) can a distant supervision approach, using weak labels derived from existing database records, achieve comparable accuracy to fully supervised models? The dissemination of scientific knowledge has traditionally relied on a limited number of channels, including printed journals, scientific meetings, and, more recently, journal websites and indexing databases. However, over the past decade, social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook have emerged as important tools for disseminating research, with many medical journals now maintaining active accounts and sizable followings. The underlying assumption driving this trend is straightforward: by posting a brief message and link to a new article, journals can increase exposure to readers who might not have encountered the work otherwise, thereby boosting page views, downloads, and ultimately, citations. This assumption is intuitive, and editors, publishers, and professional societies have largely embraced it, with social media activity now a standard component of the publication process for many journals, including those in cardiovascular medicine. Studies have consistently shown that articles mentioned on Twitter or other social platforms tend to accumulate more views, downloads, and citations than those that are not mentioned. For instance, research by Eysenbach, Shuai et al., and Fox et al. has demonstrated a positive association between social media attention and various metrics of article impact. These findings have, in turn, fueled the development of alternative metrics, which aggregate online attention to research outputs and are increasingly displayed alongside traditional bibliometric indicators. However, it is essential to note that these associations are susceptible to confounding, as articles that attract social media attention may differ systematically from those that do not. For example, they may address topics of broad public interest, originate from well-known investigators or institutions with large online followings, or be more novel or clinically important. Furthermore, readers who encounter an article through social media may already be inclined to read it, which can further complicate the interpretation of observational comparisons. To address these limitations, randomization offers a more robust approach, allowing researchers to separate the causal effect of social media promotion from the characteristics of the articles and authors selected for promotion. A previous randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation allocated original research articles to social media exposure or no exposure and compared 30-day page views between the groups. Although the investigators found no significant difference in page views between the arms, this result was somewhat surprising, given the favorable associations observed in observational studies. A subsequent trial in a different setting reported similar findings, suggesting that the null result was not unique to a single journal. However, the Circulation trial left an important question unresolved: whether the lack of effect reflected an intervention that was too weak to produce a measurable change or a true absence of benefit from social media exposure at any level of intensity. This distinction is crucial, both scientifically and practically. If a light-touch approach fails due to inadequate intensity, then journals might reasonably expect that a more concerted effort would succeed, justifying the resources devoted to expanding followings and repeating posts. In contrast, if a more intensive strategy also fails to change readership, the case for social media as a driver of article traffic becomes considerably weaker, and journals may need to reconsider their expectations or goals. The importance of considering a dose-response perspective is well recognized in the evaluation of behavioral and communication interventions, where a negative trial of a low-intensity program is generally not considered sufficient to rule out the value of a more substantial one. Social media campaigns in health are inherently heterogeneous, varying in reach, frequency, and engagement, and the effect of exposure is likely to depend on factors such as audience size and engagement, content delivery frequency, and algorithmic or paid amplification. Several features of platform behavior make intensity a plausible determinant of effect. For instance, on Twitter, the lifespan of an individual post is short, and a message may be seen by only a fraction of followers in the narrow window during which it is visible. On Facebook, organic reach to followers is limited, and paid promotion can substantially extend the audience of a post. Repeating messages at different times of day can increase the likelihood of being seen, and retweets by the journal account can extend visibility further. A larger follower base provides a larger potential audience for each of these actions. In light of these considerations, we conducted a second randomized controlled trial at Circulation to determine whether a more intensive social media strategy increases 30-day page views of original research articles. Building on the design of the earlier trial, we randomized accepted manuscripts to social media exposure or no exposure and implemented a range of strategies to increase intensity, including expanding the journal's follower base through advertising and organic growth, presenting each exposed article in three separate posts, boosting posts on Facebook, and retweeting posts on Twitter. We also prespecified an interim analysis with stopping rules for futility and examined whether the effect of the intervention differed by manuscript type, geographic location of the corresponding author, timing of publication, and the presence of an accompanying editorial. This study makes three key contributions. First, it provides randomized evidence on the effect of a substantially intensified social media intervention, addressing the principal limitation of the earlier trial. Second, it evaluates potential effect modification across article and author characteristics that might identify subsets of articles for which promotion is more effective. Third, it offers practical guidance for journals deciding how to allocate effort and resources to social media, contributing to a broader understanding of the role of social media in disseminating scientific knowledge and informing evidence-based decisions about the use of these platforms. By exploring the impact of social media on article readership and engagement, this research aims to provide valuable insights for researchers, journals, and the broader scientific community. The relationship between online attention and actual readership of scientific work has been a topic of interest in recent years. To explore this further, we conducted a prospective, parallel-group, single-center randomized controlled trial at Circulation, a weekly peer-reviewed cardiovascular journal of the American Heart Association. This trial was designed as a follow-up to an earlier study that investigated the impact of social media exposure on page views, which found no significant increase in 30-day page views with a standard-intensity strategy (Fox et al., 2016). Our study aimed to build upon these findings by implementing a more intensive social media strategy and examining its effect on article readership. The unit of randomization in our study was the individual original research manuscript. We began randomizing articles published in January 2015, and the trial was conducted in accordance with the CONSORT recommendations for reporting randomized trials (Schulz et al., 2010). To ensure the integrity of the study, we obtained exemption from formal institutional review, as the study involved no human participants and only utilized publicly available, aggregate journal web metrics. Eligible articles for our study were original research manuscripts accepted for publication in Circulation and scheduled for release in the weekly print and online issues. We excluded other content types, such as editorials, letters, and case reports, from randomization, although we did record the presence of an accompanying editorial for each randomized article. Manuscripts were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either social media exposure (intervention) or no social media exposure (control). A statistician not involved in the social media activity performed the allocation using a computer-generated random sequence, stratified by article type to promote balance across arms. Given that the intervention was delivered by journal staff, it was not possible to blind them to the randomization assignments. However, page view data were extracted objectively from the journal's web analytics, eliminating the potential for observer bias. Authors were not informed of the randomization assignments to prevent any potential influence on their behavior. Articles assigned to the intervention arm received social media exposure through the journal's official Facebook and Twitter accounts. To increase the intensity of the intervention relative to the earlier trial, we employed several strategies. First, we expanded the follower base of both accounts through paid advertising campaigns and organic growth, such as regular posting of engaging content, cross-promotion across American Heart Association channels, and interaction with followers. We recorded follower counts at the start and end of the study period to document growth. Second, each intervention article was promoted in triplicate, with three distinct posts published on each platform at different times and on different days after publication, using varied wording and images to reduce redundancy and capture different audiences across time zones. Third, on Facebook, we used paid promotion to boost posts and extend their reach beyond existing followers. Fourth, on Twitter, we retweeted the journal's posts from the journal account at later times to extend visibility. Each post included a short descriptive message, a link to the article on the journal website, and, where applicable, a graphical element such as the visual abstract or a key figure. To minimize variation in content between articles, posts were designed using a standardized template by the journal's social media editors. In contrast, control articles received no promotion from the journal's Facebook or Twitter accounts. However, control articles were still subject to all other standard journal dissemination mechanisms, including table of contents e-mail alerts, press releases for selected articles, and the journal's website and print edition. While authors, readers, and outside organizations were not prevented from independently sharing any article on social media, we assumed that such activity would be evenly distributed across arms due to randomization. The primary outcome of our study was the number of page views of the article during the first 30 days after publication, defined as the sum of full-text HTML and abstract views recorded by the journal's website analytics. We counted page views from the day of online publication. Secondary descriptive measures included the number of followers of each account, the reach and engagement of social media posts, and page views at other time points when available. We also recorded baseline covariates for each manuscript, including article type, geographic location of the corresponding author, the presence of an accompanying editorial, and the date of publication, categorized by trimester to account for potential temporal trends in readership and follower growth. Our target enrollment was based on the number of original research articles expected to be published in Circulation across the calendar year, anticipating roughly 300 manuscripts. Given the practical limit on the available sample, our study was designed to detect a moderate difference in 30-day page views between arms. We prespecified an interim analysis once 50% of the anticipated manuscripts had been randomized and had completed 30 days of follow-up. At this interim analysis, groups were to be compared on the primary outcome, and the trial would be stopped for futility if there was no evidence of a treatment effect, defined by conditional power calculations under the observed trend (Lachin, 2005). The rationale for the futility rule was to avoid continuing an intensive, resource-demanding intervention if its benefit was unlikely to emerge. We did not plan to stop the trial for efficacy, as our focus was on determining whether increased intensity would produce a benefit that the previous trial failed to demonstrate. All analyses in our study followed the intention-to-treat principle, with articles analyzed according to their randomized assignment. We summarized baseline characteristics by arm using counts and percentages for categorical variables and medians with interquartile ranges for continuous variables. To assess balance between arms, we used chi-square or Fisher exact tests for article type, corresponding author location, and editorial status. Given that page view counts are right-skewed, we summarized the primary outcome using medians and interquartile ranges and compared arms using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. We also fit models adjusted for the stratification factor and baseline covariates to assess the robustness of the unadjusted comparison.
