Empirical software engineering, a field that relies heavily on observable artifacts like source code, version histories, and defect reports, often derives claims about software development and maintenance that extend far beyond the data from which they were drawn. For instance, a technique that proves effective in a set of open-source projects is frequently presented as a universal solution, and results observed during one period are implicitly assumed to hold true in subsequent periods. However, this assumption is rarely tested, despite the fact that software projects are in a constant state of flux due to the introduction of new features, changes in team composition, refactoring, and evolving development practices. A critical question arises: will a researcher's conclusions remain valid a year from now for the same software projects? There are compelling reasons to doubt this. Previous research by Menzies and Shepperd (2012) has highlighted the instability of many findings in software analytics, citing "conclusion instability" as a major obstacle to building a cumulative body of knowledge. Subsequent studies have reinforced this notion, demonstrating that conclusions often vary significantly across different data sets, learners, and experimental configurations (Menzies et al., 2013; Shepperd et al., 2014; Tantithamthavorn et al., 2016). Findings that appear robust in one context may weaken or even reverse in another. Notably, most of this research has focused on variation across space, i.e., across projects, data sets, or methods, with relatively little attention paid to variation across time. This is a significant oversight, given that software evolves over time and the practical application of prediction models is inherently temporal. Defect prediction, an active research area for over two decades, provides a particularly informative setting in which to investigate this problem. The primary goal of defect prediction is to identify files, modules, or changes that are likely to contain defects, enabling limited quality-assurance resources to be allocated effectively (Zimmermann et al., 2009; Hall et al., 2012). A substantial body of work has proposed new learners, features, and transfer strategies, reporting improvements over prior approaches. Cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), which involves training a model on one or more source projects to predict defects in a different target project, has received significant attention due to its potential to address the common scenario where a project lacks sufficient historical data to train its own model (Turhan et al., 2009; Zimmermann et al., 2009; Nam et al., 2013). Comparative studies have identified approaches that appear to outperform others (Herbold et al., 2018; Hosseini et al., 2019), and these rankings are frequently taken as guidance for both researchers and practitioners. However, the conventional evaluation protocols used in defect prediction can obscure temporal instability. Standard methods, including k-fold cross-validation and random train/test splits, ignore the chronological order of the data, allowing models to be trained on instances from the future of the instances being predicted – a form of information leakage that no practitioner could replicate in deployment (Tan et al., 2015; Jimenez et al., 2019). Furthermore, defect labels are often derived with delay, as a defect may be discovered long after the code that introduced it was written. Evaluations that disregard this lag can overstate performance. Even when time is respected, evaluations typically report a single aggregate figure computed over the entire history, masking how performance fluctuates between releases or periods. A method that appears superior on average may only be superior in certain intervals. This aggregation, therefore, conceals exactly the temporal behavior on which a practitioner's decision to adopt a model depends. This gap is significant for several reasons. Firstly, a defect predictor is deployed on future releases, so the relevant evidence is its performance on data that postdate its training. Secondly, if the ranking of techniques changes from one release to the next, a study that selects the "best" approach from one evaluation window cannot support a claim that this approach will remain the best. Thirdly, the metrics used to quantify performance may themselves behave differently over time. Defect-prone ratios shift between releases, and metrics such as F-Score are sensitive to class imbalance, whereas the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) is more robust to it (Yao and Shepperd, 2020; Chicco and Jurman, 2020). Reporting only one metric may thus provide an incomplete view of stability. In this article, we empirically investigate the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models. To do this, we adopt a time-aware evaluation approach where models are trained only on data available in the past and evaluated only on data from the future. Instead of presenting a single aggregate result, we examine performance as a function of the evaluation period and compare how conclusions drawn in one period compare with those drawn in subsequent periods. We measure performance using three complementary indicators: F-Score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and MCC. Our study is guided by three research questions: RQ1: How does the performance of cross-project defect prediction models vary across time periods? We quantify the variability of F-Score, AUC, and MCC when the same models are evaluated on successive periods of the same projects. RQ2: Are conclusions about the relative performance of defect prediction approaches stable over time? We examine whether the ranking of approaches, and the statistical significance of differences between them, persist across evaluation periods or change from one period to the next. RQ3: How sensitive is conclusion stability to the choice of performance metric? We compare the three metrics to determine whether instability is an artifact of a particular measure or a more general phenomenon. This work makes several contributions. Firstly, to our knowledge, it presents one of the first systematic investigations of time-based conclusion stability in cross-project defect prediction, shifting the focus from stability across data sets to stability across time for the same projects. Secondly, it provides a time-aware evaluation procedure where training uses only past data and testing uses only future data, avoiding the leakage inherent in conventional cross-validation and allowing performance to be tracked period by period. Thirdly, it shows empirically that the performance of defect predictors, in terms of F-Score, AUC, and MCC, can vary significantly over time, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of conclusion stability in software engineering research. By exploring the temporal stability of defect prediction models, this study aims to provide insights into the dynamic nature of software development and the challenges of building reliable prediction models that can withstand the test of time. The findings of this research have significant implications for both researchers and practitioners, as they underscore the importance of considering time in the evaluation and deployment of defect prediction models. Ultimately, this work seeks to contribute to the development of more robust and reliable software engineering practices, ones that can adapt to the evolving nature of software projects and provide lasting benefits to the software development community. The remainder of this article is organized as follows. We first provide a detailed overview of the related work in defect prediction and conclusion stability, highlighting the key challenges and limitations of existing research. We then describe our research methodology, including the data sets used, the experimental design, and the performance metrics employed. Next, we present the results of our empirical study, discussing the variability of defect prediction performance across time periods and the stability of conclusions about the relative performance of different approaches. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the implications of our findings, the limitations of our study, and directions for future research. In conclusion, this article highlights the critical importance of considering time in software engineering research, particularly in the context of defect prediction. By examining the temporal stability of defect prediction models, we can gain a deeper understanding of the complex and dynamic nature of software development, ultimately leading to the development of more reliable and effective software engineering practices. The findings of this study have significant implications for both researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the need for a more nuanced and time-aware approach to software engineering research. Overall, our research contributes to the growing body of literature on conclusion stability in software engineering, providing new insights into the temporal dynamics of defect prediction and the challenges of building reliable prediction models. Complex systems, whether in nature, society, or technology, are inherently composed of numerous interacting units, whose collective behavior cannot be fully understood by examining these units in isolation. The language of network science has been instrumental in describing such systems, with nodes representing individual units and links representing the interactions among them (Newman 2003; Boccaletti et al. 2006). However, the traditional formulation of network science has often relied on the assumption that a system can be represented by a single graph, implying a single type of interaction. This assumption has become increasingly recognized as overly restrictive, as real-world systems often involve multiple types of interactions. For instance, individuals in a society interact through various means, including face-to-face contact, online social platforms, and professional ties, while a transportation system may comprise airline, rail, and road connections among the same set of cities. Similarly, a cell relies on genetic, protein, and metabolic interactions among overlapping sets of molecular components. In each of these cases, a common set of nodes participates in multiple distinct layers of connectivity, and its role may differ significantly from one layer to another. The multilayer or multiplex framework was developed to capture this complex structure (Kivelä et al. 2014; Boccaletti et al. 2014; De Domenico et al. 2013). This framework has revealed a range of phenomena that have no counterpart in isolated networks, including abrupt, cascading failures in interdependent systems (Buldyrev et al. 2010), altered percolation and robustness properties (Gao et al. 2012), modified synchronization and controllability, and rich interplay between coupled spreading processes, such as the spread of an epidemic and the diffusion of awareness about it (Granell et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2019). However, almost all of these advances presuppose that the multiplex topology is known. In practice, the connection structure of real systems is often only partially observable or entirely hidden, whereas time series of the nodal states are relatively easy to record. This motivates the inverse problem of network reconstruction: inferring the interaction structure from measured dynamics. For single-layer networks, a substantial literature now exists, with approaches including driving-response and perturbation schemes (Timme 2007), methods based on correlation and information-theoretic measures (Bullmore and Sporns 2009; Schreiber 2000), and compressive sensing, which exploits the sparsity of real networks to recover topology from short data records (Wang et al. 2011; Han et al. 2015; Shen et al. 2014). Compressive sensing has been applied to various systems, including evolutionary games, epidemic spreading, and oscillator networks, and variants have been developed for hidden nodes and for identifying network structure from binary-state dynamics (Su et al. 2014; Shen et al. 2016). Related statistical strategies, including maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, have been proposed for diffusion and cascade networks (Gomez-Rodriguez et al. 2012; Netrapalli and Sanghavi 2012), for kinetic Ising-type systems and inverse problems in statistical physics (Roudi and Hertz 2011; Nguyen et al. 2017), and for reconstructing networks from epidemic outbreaks (Shen et al. 2014; Hoffmann et al. 2019). These studies have shown that, with appropriate dynamical models and sparsity-aware algorithms, accurate reconstruction can be achieved from limited data. However, extending these ideas to multiplex networks is far from straightforward, and the problem remains largely open. One of the primary difficulties is that the observed data are a superposition of effects from several layers, making it challenging to disentangle the contributions of each layer. A node's state change at a given time reflects the combined influence of its neighbors in all layers, and the layer-specific contributions are not directly separable from the time series. Applying a single-layer method to such data would either produce an aggregated network in which layer identity is lost or yield spurious links through mixing of the layers. Another difficulty is dimensionality: the number of unknown parameters grows with the number of layers, making the inference problem harder precisely when each layer is only weakly constrained by the data. Furthermore, the layers can host dynamical processes of different kinds, with different transmission mechanisms and rates, so that a reconstruction framework must be able to attribute observed transitions to the appropriate process. Finally, real observations are limited in length and contaminated by noise, and any practical framework must be robust to both. Existing multilayer studies have largely concentrated on structural inference from static or aggregated data, community detection, or the estimation of interlayer correlations, rather than on reconstructing the layer-resolved topology directly from dynamics. The present work addresses this gap by posing the following question: given only binary time series of the states of a set of shared nodes, subject to the coupled action of distinct dynamical processes propagating on different layers, can the full layer-resolved connectivity be recovered, and under what structural and dynamical conditions is the recovery accurate and robust? We focus on duplex networks, the simplest multiplex systems, which host two different types of spreading dynamics, as a prototypical setting that retains the essential difficulties described above while remaining analytically and numerically tractable. Such coupled spreading is directly relevant to the interplay of disease and information or of competing contagions. To tackle this problem, we develop a mean-field-based maximum likelihood estimation framework. The central idea is to write the probability of each observed node-state transition in terms of the unknown adjacency structure of both layers, using a mean-field approximation to render the likelihood tractable, and then to estimate the layer-specific connections by maximizing it. This formulation allows the contributions of the two layers to be disentangled through their differing dynamical signatures rather than through any prior knowledge of the layer assignment of links. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate the multiplex reconstruction problem for coupled spreading dynamics and provide a principled, likelihood-based solution that separates layer-specific structure from superposed binary observations. Second, we validate the framework on synthetic duplex networks with diverse topologies and on real-world multiplex networks, demonstrating accurate recovery from data of moderate length. Third, we carry out a systematic analysis of how reconstruction accuracy depends on structural parameters such as network size, mean degree, and interlayer correlation; on dynamical parameters such as spreading rates; and on the amount of data and the level of observational noise, thereby clarifying the regimes in which reconstruction is reliable. Together, these results extend data-driven network inference from single-layer to multiplex systems and provide a foundation for uncovering the hidden structure of complex systems. The architecture of complex systems, characterized by multiple interaction types, is a rich and dynamic field of study. To better understand these systems, we employed multiplex network models, which consist of multiple layers of interactions between nodes. Specifically, we focused on duplex networks, comprising two layers, denoted as α ∈ {1, 2}, with binary symmetric adjacency matrices A^α describing the connections between nodes. The widespread collection of personal data by online services, healthcare providers, retailers, and social platforms has led to the creation of detailed databases that describe individual behavior. These databases are often shared or released, with the justification that identifiers have been removed or replaced with pseudonyms. However, a growing body of research suggests that this form of anonymization provides weak protection against privacy breaches. One of the earliest and most influential studies in this area was conducted by Sweeney in 2002, who demonstrated that a small number of quasi-identifiers, such as ZIP code, birth date, and sex, can be used to single out most individuals in a population. This work motivated the development of formal notions of anonymity, including k-anonymity. Subsequent studies have further highlighted the limitations of anonymization. For example, Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) showed that an anonymized release of movie ratings could be linked to public profiles on a separate platform using only a handful of approximate observations per user. They later applied the same principle to social-network graphs (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2009). These studies demonstrate that privacy leakage is often not a property of a single dataset, but rather arises from the statistical dependence between the released data and auxiliary information available to an adversary. Differential privacy (Dwork, 2006; Dwork & Roth, 2014) provides a framework for understanding and mitigating privacy risks, but it is not widely used in practical data-sharing settings. As a result, there is a need for a principled understanding of when de-anonymization is feasible, in order to assess the risk of sharing data. Two broad lines of work address this question. The first is algorithmic and empirical, focusing on the design of heuristics that exploit similarity between records or neighborhoods in graphs, and evaluating their performance on real data (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008, 2009; Ji et al., 2016). The second is information-theoretic, seeking to understand the fundamental limits of correlation between two databases, and how much information is required to align them. In graph settings, information-theoretic approaches have produced sharp thresholds for matching correlated Erdős–Rényi graphs (Pedarsani & Grossglauser, 2011; Cullina & Kiyavash, 2016; Korula & Lattanzi, 2014). For databases with feature vectors, Cullina, Mittal, and Kiyavash (2018) characterized the fundamental limits of alignment under a permutation model, and Dai et al. (2019) obtained analogous results for jointly Gaussian features. These results suggest that the mutual information between corresponding records is the key quantity that governs matching, and that matching becomes possible once the number of attributes per record is large enough relative to the logarithm of the number of records. However, existing analyses often rely on specific distributional assumptions, such as Gaussian features, Bernoulli or Erdős–Rényi structure, or independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) entries. These assumptions are convenient, but often unrealistic. Real-world attributes, such as time-stamped ratings, location traces, or sequential medical measurements, are heterogeneous and temporally correlated, requiring models that permit richer dependence. This paper addresses this gap by studying the matching of two high-dimensional databases in which each row corresponds to a user and each column corresponds to an attribute. One database is released with its rows permuted by an unknown permutation, and the other serves as the adversary's auxiliary information. The relation between corresponding entries is described by an arbitrary joint distribution, and the dependence across the attributes of a given user is allowed to be non-i.i.d. Our central question is: under what conditions on the joint distribution and on the relative sizes of the database dimensions can an adversary recover the unknown permutation with vanishing probability of error, and when is this provably impossible? Answering this question for general distributions, rather than for isolated families, would yield a unified criterion for the privacy risk of correlated releases. To address this question, we develop a typicality-based approach, which rests on concentration of measure (Ledoux, 2001; Boucheron et al., 2013). When the number of attributes grows, empirical statistics of a pair of rows concentrate sharply around their expectations. This is the mechanism behind the asymptotic equipartition property and the notion of typicality used in the proofs of channel coding theorems (Cover & Thomas, 2006). We exploit this concentration phenomenon to develop a matching scheme that declares a pair of rows to be a match when they are jointly typical, and then selects the permutation consistent with these declarations. A union bound over the competing permutations, combined with laws of large numbers for the relevant empirical averages, yields explicit conditions under which the scheme succeeds. This typicality-based strategy was introduced for pairs of correlated graphs by Shirani et al. (2019), and we extend it here to databases with general entry distributions. The contributions of this work are fourfold. First, we propose a general matching scheme and achievability result, showing that if the number of users grows at most exponentially in the number of attributes, with a growth rate strictly below a limiting information quantity of the source, then the scheme recovers the permutation with probability tending to one. For i.i.d. entries, this quantity is the mutual information between a pair of corresponding entries. Second, we prove a matching converse, identifying a class of joint distributions for which, when the database growth rate exceeds the same information quantity, the probability of correct matching vanishes for any matching scheme. Together with the achievability result, this yields a sharp phase transition between the regimes where de-anonymization is feasible and infeasible. Third, we evaluate the conditions for i.i.d. databases, recovering known thresholds as special cases and thereby validating the general framework. We then treat Markovian database models, in which entries within a row are temporally correlated. The relevant threshold is an information rate expressed through the stationary distribution and transition kernel of the underlying chain. The analysis shows how memory in the data changes the number of attributes needed for reliable matching relative to an i.i.d. model with the same marginals. Finally, our proof technique extends beyond the cases treated, using only typicality and concentration of measure, and can be applied to other models and settings. Overall, this work provides a unified framework for understanding the privacy risks of correlated data releases, and sheds light on the fundamental limits of correlation between two databases. The results have important implications for the design of data-sharing protocols and the assessment of privacy risks in a variety of applications, from healthcare and social media to finance and marketing. By providing a principled understanding of when de-anonymization is feasible, this work can help to inform the development of more effective privacy protections and data-sharing strategies. The theoretical framework presented in this paper is grounded in fundamental principles of probability theory, including the laws of large numbers. A key advantage of this approach is that it does not rely on closed-form likelihood computations or specific parametric families, making it broadly applicable whenever empirical averages concentrate. This flexibility opens up new avenues for exploring various dependence structures. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a rigorous formulation of the database model and the concept of matching reliability. Section 3 introduces the matching scheme and presents an achievability theorem, while Section 4 focuses on proving the converse. Section 5 delves into the specialization of these results to independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) models and Markov models, and Section 6 discusses the implications and outstanding problems. To initiate this exploration, we consider a database model comprising two databases, D⁽¹⁾ and D⁽²⁾, each with m rows (representing users) and n columns (denoting attributes). Specifically, row i of D⁽¹⁾ is denoted by Xi = (X{i1}, …, X{in}) ∈ 𝒳ⁿ, where 𝒳 is a finite alphabet. The corresponding row in the second database, Yi = (Y{i1}, …, Y{in}) ∈ 𝒴ⁿ, is drawn from another finite alphabet 𝒴. The rows of the pair (Xi, Yi) are independent across users, but within a row, the joint law is defined by a distribution p{X^nY^n}. This setup encompasses both the i.i.d. model, where p{XY}ⁿ applies when entries are independent across columns, and the stationary Markov model, where the column index can be interpreted as time. This construction aligns with stochastic database models previously utilized to study de-anonymization of correlated data (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008; Cullina, Mittal, & Kiyavash, 2018; Dai, Cullina, Kiyavash, & Grossglauser, 2019). The released database D⁽²⁾ is anonymized, with its rows permuted by an unknown permutation Θ drawn uniformly from the symmetric group Sm, independently of all data. Consequently, the released rows are represented as Ỹ{Θ(i)} = Yi. An adversary, with access to both D⁽¹⁾ (for instance, a public auxiliary dataset) and D⁽²⁾, aims to recover Θ, knowing the joint distribution of the entries. A matching scheme is defined as a map Θ̂(D⁽¹⁾, D⁽²⁾) ∈ Sm. We term the matching reliable if the per-user error probability Pe = maxi P(Θ̂(i) ≠ Θ(i)) tends to zero as n → ∞. Notably, the number of users grows exponentially with the number of attributes, following m = mn = 2^{nR+o(n)}, where R > 0 is the database growth rate. The primary objective of this study is to characterize the set of pairs (R, p{XY}) for which reliable matching is achievable. The proposed matching scheme operates as a typicality-based decoder, drawing inspiration from joint-typicality decoding in channel coding (Cover & Thomas, 2006; Csiszár & Körner, 2011). For a pair of sequences (xⁿ, yⁿ), the joint empirical distribution π{xⁿ,yⁿ}(a,b) = n⁻¹ Σk 1{xk = a, yk = b} is a crucial metric. By fixing εn > 0, we define the pair as εn-typical with respect to p{XY} if |π{xⁿ,yⁿ}(a,b) − p{XY}(a,b)| ≤ εn p{XY}(a,b) for all (a,b) ∈ 𝒳×𝒴. The choice of εn is such that it tends to zero slowly enough to ensure that n εn² / log m → ∞, thereby aligning the typicality threshold with the exponential scaling of m. For Markov models, typicality is defined on the empirical distribution of consecutive pairs ((xk, yk), (x{k+1}, y{k+1})), consistent with the method of types for Markov sources (Csiszár & Körner, 2011). The decoding process unfolds in three steps: (i) computing the joint empirical distribution of (Xi, Ỹj) for every row i of D⁽¹⁾ and every row j of D⁽²⁾, and testing for typicality; (ii) setting Θ̂(i) = j if exactly one row j of D⁽²⁾ is jointly typical with row i; and (iii) declaring an error for row i if no such row or more than one exists, which in practice is resolved by an arbitrary guess. The computational cost of this scheme is O(m² n), primarily due to the m² pairwise comparisons involved. Analyzing error events is crucial. For a given row i, an error occurs if one of two events happens: E₁, where the true pair (Xi, Yi) is not εn-typical, or E₂, where some incorrect row j ≠ Θ(i) is jointly typical with Xi. Concentration inequalities for the empirical distribution are used to bound P(E₁). In the i.i.d. model, each count π(a,b) is an average of n independent bounded variables, allowing Hoeffding's inequality (Hoeffding, 1963) to be applied, together with a union bound over |𝒳||𝒴| symbols, yielding P(E₁) ≤ 2|𝒳||𝒴| exp(−2nεn² pmin²), where pmin is the smallest positive entry of p{XY}. This inequality quantitatively reflects the weak law of large numbers. For Markov models, concentration bounds for functions of ergodic finite-state chains and their mixing properties (Boucheron, Lugosi, & Massart, 2013) are utilized, with rate constants dependent on the spectral gap of the chain. The probability of E₂, where an incorrect row Ỹj is independent of Xi and has the marginal law of Y, can be bounded using standard properties of typical sets (Cover & Thomas, 2006). Specifically, the probability that independent sequences are jointly εn-typical is at most 2^{−n(I(X;Y) − δ(εn))}, where δ(εn) → 0 as εn → 0. Applying a union bound over the m − 1 incorrect rows gives P(E₂) ≤ m · 2^{−n(I(X;Y) − δ(εn))}. Substituting m = 2^{nR+o(n)} reveals that P(E₂) → 0 whenever R < I(X;Y), establishing the achievability condition through the mutual information I(X;Y) in the i.i.d. case. Array-intensive programs are a cornerstone of various compute-heavy domains, including scientific simulation, signal and image processing, linear algebra, machine learning, and more. These programs are characterized by their control flow, which is dominated by nested loops, and their data, which is typically stored in multidimensional arrays accessed through affine index expressions. This regular structure makes them well-suited for parallel execution, both within a single machine and across a cluster of nodes. As a result, array-intensive programs have been extensively studied in the context of high-performance computing (HPC) and compiler research, with seminal works by Feautrier (1992) and Kennedy and Allen (2001) laying the foundation for this field. To achieve good performance, array-intensive programs often undergo a series of transformations, which can be broadly categorized into loop transformations, arithmetic transformations, and parallelizing transformations. Loop transformations, such as interchange, skewing, tiling, fusion, fission, unrolling, and peeling, aim to restructure the iteration space to improve locality and expose parallelism (Wolf & Lam, 1991; Kelly & Pugh, 1995). Arithmetic transformations, including algebraic simplification, common sub-expression elimination, strength reduction, and the exploitation of associativity and commutativity, seek to reduce the computational cost or reshape the computation for vectorization. Finally, parallelizing transformations map the restructured computation onto threads, vector units, accelerators, or distributed processes, often using frameworks like OpenMP, MPI, or CUDA. The development of polyhedral compilers (Bondhugula et al., 2008; Grosser et al., 2012) and domain-specific systems like Halide and TVM (Ragan-Kelley et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018) has automated many of these transformation steps. However, despite this progress, automatic parallelizing compilers remain limited in practice. Dependence analysis can be overly conservative in the presence of irregular accesses, pointer aliasing, or non-affine subscripts, while profitable transformation sequences can be difficult to identify using static cost models. Moreover, performance-critical code is often tuned for a specific architecture, memory hierarchy, or interconnect, which can further complicate the optimization process. As a result, experienced programmers continue to apply hand-optimized transformations, often in combination with compiler-generated ones, and then iteratively tune the result through profiling and experimentation. This process can lead to significant changes in the program's structure, including the reorganization of loop nests, the introduction or elimination of temporary arrays, and the rewriting of expressions. While this flexibility is essential for achieving high performance, it also increases the risk of introducing errors, such as off-by-one errors in tiled loop bounds, dependence violations after fusion, or data races in parallel regions. These errors can be notoriously difficult to detect, and testing alone is often insufficient due to the huge input space and the potential for failures to appear only under specific problem sizes or thread interleavings. The need to establish the functional equivalence of the optimized program to the original sequential specification is therefore paramount. Two broad approaches address this challenge: verifying the transformation engine and translation validation or equivalence checking. The former involves proving that a compiler pass preserves semantics, as demonstrated in the CompCert project (Leroy, 2009). While powerful, this approach can be expensive and may not cover transformations applied by hand or external tools. The latter approach, on the other hand, treats the transformation as a black box and checks the equivalence of each (original, transformed) program pair separately (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000). This method is well-suited to the mixed human-compiler workflows common in HPC. For general programs, equivalence is undecidable, and early techniques such as regression verification and relational program logics rely on strong structural similarity between the two programs (Godlin & Strichman, 2008; Benton, 2004). However, array-intensive programs have a restricted structure, characterized by static control flow, bounded loops, and affine index expressions, which enables more specialized and complete methods. Over the past two decades, a significant body of work has emerged on the functional verification of array-intensive programs. One line of research models programs as systems of affine recurrence equations and decides their equivalence using polyhedral techniques (Barthou et al., 2002). Another represents programs as array data dependence graphs (ADDGs) and checks equivalence through synchronized traversal and reasoning over the iteration domains and dependence mappings, handling loop and algebraic transformations (Shashidhar et al., 2005; Karfa et al., 2013). Subsequent work has extended these ideas to recurrences using widening (Verdoolaege et al., 2012), to code-motion transformations through value propagation (Banerjee et al., 2014), and to the verification of loop-parallelizing transformations and parallel program models (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2015). Complementary work verifies concrete tiled or parallel code using symbolic execution, model checking, or deductive verification (Blom et al., 2017). Together, these efforts define a rich but fragmented landscape that spans compiler theory, polyhedral mathematics, program logics, and automated reasoning. For newcomers to this field, the relevant literature can be daunting, with papers scattered across venues in electronic design automation, programming languages, formal verification, and HPC. Different program representations and assumptions, such as affine versus non-affine subscripts, sequential versus parallel targets, and static versus recurrent dependences, can make it challenging to navigate this landscape. To our knowledge, no concise introduction organizes this material around the transformations a practitioner actually encounters and the verification techniques that address each. This paper aims to address this gap by providing a narrative survey of the techniques for verifying the functional equivalence of optimized array-intensive programs. Our guiding question is: which techniques exist for verifying that an optimized array-intensive program, produced through loop, arithmetic, and parallelizing transformations, is functionally equivalent to its sequential original, and what are their scope and limitations? We make three contributions. First, we describe the class of programs and transformations of interest and explain why they challenge conventional verification. Second, we survey and relate the principal approaches, covering recurrence-based, ADDG-based, and translation-validation methods, as well as those for parallel programs, and we compare them by the transformations they handle, their assumptions, and their guarantees. Third, we identify open problems, including non-affine accesses, floating-point semantics, and scalability, to guide further research. We intend this survey to serve as a quick but rigorous starting point for readers entering the field, providing a foundation for understanding the complexities of verifying array-intensive programs. To provide a newcomer with a comprehensive introduction to the literature on functional verification of array-intensive programs, our methodology encompasses four key aspects: scoping the field, identifying and selecting relevant literature, organizing the selected works into a classification framework, and conducting a qualitative comparison of techniques. Notably, we did not perform any statistical analysis, as the surveyed works report heterogeneous benchmarks, tool chains, and hardware, which cannot be meaningfully pooled. To define the scope and problem, we consider an array-intensive program to be one whose computation is dominated by loop nests that read and write multi-dimensional arrays, where the array subscripts and loop bounds are typically affine functions of the enclosing iterators and symbolic parameters. This class of programs is commonly studied under the polyhedral model, which includes dense numerical kernels, stencils, and signal- and image-processing pipelines frequently encountered in high-performance computing and embedded systems. The verification problem, in this context, involves determining whether an original sequential program and a transformed program compute the same input-output relation, a problem we approach as equivalence checking. We exclude the verification of properties of a single program, such as assertions, absence of out-of-bounds accesses, or termination, except where these properties support an equivalence argument. The transformations of interest can be categorized into three groups: loop transformations, including interchange, fusion, fission, skewing, tiling, unrolling, and bumping; arithmetic and data-flow transformations, such as algebraic simplification, expression propagation, and operator reassociation or commutation; and parallelizing transformations, which include those that produce multithreaded, vectorized, or GPU code. We consider translation validation, where the verifier checks each compilation instance, and verification of hand-optimized code as two settings of the same problem, noting that in the latter setting, no compiler provides hints about the applied transformations. To identify the relevant literature, we conducted a thorough search of the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and DBLP, and utilized Google Scholar for forward and backward citation tracking. Our search queries combined terms related to the object of verification, such as "array-intensive," "affine programs," "data-dominated," "loop nest," and "static control programs," with terms related to the task, including "equivalence checking," "translation validation," "regression verification," "program equivalence," "verification of loop transformations," and "verification of parallelizing transformations." We also included transformation-specific terms, such as "code motion," "tiling validation," and "recurrence." Our search began with a small seed set of foundational papers on equivalence checking of data-dominated programs and followed citations in both directions until no new relevant work appeared. Additionally, we reviewed the principal venues for compiler verification, program analysis, electronic design automation, and formal methods, including PLDI, POPL, CAV, TACAS, CC, DATE, DAC, and IEEE TCAD, for the period from the early 1990s to the present. Our inclusion and exclusion criteria were as follows: a paper was included if it addressed equivalence or refinement between two programs, or between a program and a specification in program form, where arrays are first-class data; handled at least one of the three transformation groups in a way that goes beyond scalar-only programs; and presented a technique with enough detail to assess its soundness conditions and limits. We excluded work whose main contribution was a transformation or optimization framework without a correctness-checking component, as well as purely testing-based or fuzzing-based validation without a formal argument, bounded model checking limited to tiny fixed array sizes, and domain-specific hardware verification that does not operate on program-level array semantics. Several adjacent areas, such as data-race and deadlock detection for parallel programs and general relational verification and product-program constructions, were handled selectively, with inclusion only where they clarified how equivalence of array programs differs from, or reuses, their ideas. When an extended journal version superseded a conference paper, we cited the journal version and mentioned the earlier paper only when it introduced a distinct idea. To develop our classification framework, we read each selected paper against a fixed set of dimensions and then grouped the papers by their main modeling formalism. We recorded the program representation, such as array data dependence graphs, finite state machines with datapath, systems of affine recurrence equations, or polyhedral and integer-set representations. We also recorded the equivalence-checking strategy, distinguishing between synchronized traversal of dependence graphs with slice-based comparison, cut-point or bisimulation-style correspondence between control states, and direct comparison of closed-form or recurrence-based input-output mappings. Furthermore, we recorded the decision machinery, such as Presburger arithmetic and integer-set libraries, SMT solvers, and normalization of arithmetic expressions. Additionally, we recorded the transformation coverage across the three groups, including whether recurrences and data-dependent control flow are supported, as well as the guarantees, namely soundness, completeness for stated program classes, and the way each method fails. We also recorded the assumptions about the input pair, including whether the loops are statically controlled, whether single-assignment form is required, and whether the transformations must be known in advance. In our comparative analysis, we assessed three properties qualitatively for each group: expressiveness, meaning the range of transformations and program features handled; scalability, meaning whether the method depends on loop bounds or array sizes or is parametric in them; and automation, meaning the degree of user guidance, annotations, or proof effort required. Where papers reported empirical results, we extracted the benchmark families, typically PolyBench-style kernels and multimedia or signal-processing codes, together with the reported verification times and the instances on which a method failed or returned an inconclusive answer. We did not rerun tools or normalize these numbers across papers, citing them only as indications of practicality. Throughout, we separated claims established by proof in the original papers from claims supported only by experiments. Our methodology has limitations, primarily due to its selective nature and reliance on keyword and citation searches, which may have missed relevant works. Despite these limitations, our survey provides a comprehensive introduction to the literature on functional verification of array-intensive programs, highlighting the key techniques, their strengths, and their limitations. The use of citations as a metric for evaluating scientific output has become a ubiquitous practice, underpinning journal rankings, institutional assessments, funding decisions, and even individual career progression in many countries (Garfield, 2006; Hicks et al., 2015). However, the distribution of citations is notoriously skewed, with a small proportion of articles garnering the majority of citations, while a significant share receives few or none (Seglen, 1992; Price, 1976). This skewness is a major concern, as it renders the mean-based journal impact factor a poor descriptor of the typical article, and its use for evaluating individual papers has been subject to repeated criticism (Seglen, 1997; Larivière et al., 2016). At the lower end of the citation distribution lie uncited articles, which are those that, within a defined observation window, have not been cited by any other indexed document. The study of non-citation has a long history in bibliometrics, with early estimates suggesting that a substantial fraction of the scientific literature remained uncited for years (de Solla Price, 1965; Garfield, 1973). Some provocative claims even proposed that most papers were never cited (Hamilton, 1990, 1991), although these claims were later shown to be exaggerated due to methodological limitations, such as the failure to separate research articles from other document types and the neglect of differences across fields and citation windows (Pendlebury, 1991; Garfield, 1998). Subsequent analyses, based on more careful designs, have demonstrated that the proportion of uncited papers is strongly dependent on discipline, document type, publication year, and database coverage (Egghe et al., 2011; Wallace et al., 2009; Van Noorden, 2017). Notably, uncitedness tends to be lower in biomedical and life sciences, where reference lists are lengthy and citation practices are intense, and higher in the humanities and certain social sciences, where books, local audiences, and slower citation dynamics prevail (Nederhof, 2006; Hyland and Jiang, 2018). However, it is essential to recognize that non-citation does not necessarily imply a lack of value, as articles may be read, used in teaching, incorporated into clinical or public policy practice, or discussed in the media without generating formal citations (Bornmann, 2014; Thelwall et al., 2013). Furthermore, citations are influenced by social and structural factors, such as the visibility of the journal, language, author reputation, collaboration networks, international coauthorship, and the degree of indexing in major databases (Bornmann and Daniel, 2008; Tahamtan et al., 2016). Despite these limitations, in evaluation systems that rely on citation counts, an uncited article is effectively invisible, and a journal with a high proportion of uncited articles may face reputational and financial consequences. Therefore, examining the percentage of non-citation offers a complementary perspective to average-based metrics, as it describes the lower tail of the distribution and signals how effectively a journal integrates its content into the scholarly conversation. Public health is a fascinating area for investigating this phenomenon, as it is an inherently multidisciplinary field that brings together epidemiology, biostatistics, health policy and management, and the social and human sciences (Almeida Filho, 2000; Nunes, 2005). In Brazil, this field is known as "saúde coletiva" and has its own distinct intellectual identity, shaped by the sanitary reform movement and a strong articulation with the national health system (Paim and Almeida Filho, 1998; Luz, 2009). The Brazilian public health community has established a large postgraduate network and a set of national journals that publish mostly in Portuguese, but also increasingly in English and Spanish. Many of these journals are open access, indexed in regional repositories such as SciELO, and several are also indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science (Packer, 2009; Meneghini et al., 2008). Their dual mission—communicating with local practitioners and policymakers while reaching international readers—makes the citation profile of these periodicals particularly relevant. While citation patterns in Brazilian journals have been explored in some areas, mainly focusing on impact factors, language effects, and the international visibility of Latin American science (Rios-Gonzalez, 2014; Packer and Meneghini, 2006; Meneghini and Packer, 2007), these analyses often rely on aggregated indicators that conceal within-journal heterogeneity. Moreover, the proportion of articles that never receive any citation, and whether journals within a single national field differ in this respect, have received relatively little attention. To our knowledge, no study has examined non-citation in public health journals, either nationally or internationally. Existing analyses of uncited papers in health sciences have focused on clinical specialties, nursing, or general medicine (Weale et al., 2004; Wallace et al., 2009), leaving a significant gap for a multidisciplinary field with strong local roots. This gap is important for several reasons. First, Brazilian science policy agencies, such as CAPES and CNPq, use citation-based indicators and journal classification systems (Qualis) in the evaluation of graduate programs and researchers, so that differences among journals have practical consequences for authors' strategies (Barata, 2016). Second, editors need descriptive evidence on how often their articles go uncited and how fast this proportion declines in the years following publication, in order to assess editorial policies, internationalization efforts, and the effects of language choices. Third, from a theoretical perspective, comparing journals of a single national field enables an assessment of whether disciplinary orientation, for instance epidemiological versus social-science-oriented content, is associated with differential citation behavior, as suggested by studies of cognitive and structural determinants of citation (Didegah and Thelwall, 2013; Onodera and Yoshikane, 2015). In this study, we aim to address the following questions: What proportion of articles published in Brazilian public health journals remains uncited, and how does this proportion differ among journals? Do journals form distinct groups in terms of non-citation? How does the percentage of non-citation evolve during the first three years after publication, and are there journals in which it declines consistently? We focus on eight journals indexed in Scopus and on articles published between 2008 and 2012, a period that allows an adequate citation window. By examining these questions, we seek to provide a comprehensive understanding of non-citation in Brazilian public health journals and to shed light on the dynamics of citation patterns in this field. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we provide the first systematic description of non-citation in a national public health literature, establishing a benchmark for future comparisons. Second, our analysis offers insights into the factors that influence citation behavior in public health journals, which can inform editorial policies and internationalization strategies. Third, our study contributes to the ongoing debate about the role of citations in evaluating scientific output, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complexities of citation patterns and the limitations of citation-based metrics. The dynamics of citation patterns in applied, multidisciplinary fields, such as public health, are complex and multifaceted. To better understand these dynamics, we conducted a retrospective, descriptive bibliometric study of articles published in Brazilian public health journals, leveraging the capabilities of Scopus, a comprehensive database that indexes a larger number of Latin American and Brazilian titles than the Web of Science. The choice of Scopus was motivated by its reliable article-level citation counts and export functions, which have been widely recognized in the literature (Falagas et al., 2008; Mongeon & Paul-Hus, 2016). Our study design involved identifying journals through the Scopus source list, using the subject area "Medicine" and the subcategory "Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health," filtered by country of publication (Brazil). We applied a set of inclusion criteria to ensure that only journals that were active and indexed in Scopus throughout 2008-2012, published predominantly in the public health/collective health field, and published at least 100 citable documents over the study period were included in our analysis. This resulted in a sample of eight journals: Cadernos de Saúde Pública, Ciência & Saúde Coletiva, Revista de Saúde Pública, Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia, Physis: Revista de Saúde Coletiva, Interface – Comunicação, Saúde, Educação, Saúde e Sociedade, and História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos. Notably, the last four journals are considered more closely aligned with the social sciences and humanities, whereas the first four have a stronger biomedical and epidemiological orientation, a distinction that we used only for interpretation and not for selecting articles. We retrieved all documents published between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2012, a five-year window that allowed every article at least a minimum of several years of exposure to citation. To analyze non-citation within a fixed three-year citation window after publication, we only considered document types that are typically cited, such as original articles, review articles, and short communications/research notes. Editorials, letters, errata, book reviews, interviews, obituaries, and news items were excluded, as they are generally cited rarely and can inflate non-citation rates (Moed & van Leeuwen, 1995; Van Noorden, 2017). We also removed duplicate records, identified by DOI, title, and volume/page, to ensure data integrity. Our data extraction process involved exporting records in CSV format in a single session, which allowed us to freeze citation counts at a common date, referred to as the census date. We extracted fields such as authors, title, source title, year, volume, issue, pages, DOI, document type, language, affiliations, and total number of citations received. The data were then processed in a relational database, enabling us to obtain year-by-year citation counts for each article through the Scopus "citation overview" function. This function provides citations per calendar year, allowing us to reconstruct the citation history in the first three years after publication. We did not remove self-citations, as our aim was to describe the actual citation visibility of the articles in the database, and because the proportion of self-citations among low-cited articles is generally small in absolute terms (Aksnes, 2003). To analyze the data, we defined non-citation as an article with zero citations recorded in Scopus at the census date. For each journal j, we calculated the overall percentage of non-citation as Pj = (Uj / Nj) × 100, where Uj is the number of uncited articles and Nj is the total number of citable articles published by journal j between 2008 and 2012. To describe temporal patterns, we also computed the percentage of articles of publication year t that remained uncited within a fixed window of three years after publication: P{j,t}^{(3)} = (U{j,t}^{(3)} / N{j,t}) × 100, with t = 2008, …, 2012. Using a fixed window rather than the total accumulated citations avoids the artefact that older articles have had more time to be cited (Glänzel & Schoepflin, 1995; Wang, 2013). Because the three-year window for the 2012 cohort extends beyond the census date for part of the sample, the census was set after the end of 2015, ensuring that all cohorts had a complete window. In addition to the main outcome variable, we also computed secondary descriptive variables, including the number of articles per journal and year, language of publication, document type, and the mean and median number of citations per article. Given that citation distributions are highly skewed (Seglen, 1992; Price, 1976), we preferred medians and interquartile ranges to means for summarizing central tendency. Our statistical analysis involved describing absolute and relative frequencies of articles and uncited articles by journal and by publication year, as well as computing 95% confidence intervals for proportions using the Wilson score method, which performs better than the Wald interval for small samples and extreme proportions (Newcombe, 1998). To test for differences in the overall percentage of non-citation among journals, we used a chi-square test of homogeneity of proportions across the eight journals. Where the global test was significant, we carried out all pairwise comparisons (28 comparisons) using two-sample tests of proportions, with p-values adjusted by the Bonferroni–Holm procedure to control the family-wise error rate at α = 0.05 (Holm, 1979). Journals that did not differ significantly from one another after adjustment were grouped, allowing us to identify clusters of journals with similar non-citation patterns. Our results provide insights into the dynamics of recognition of articles in Brazilian public health journals, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive model of citation determinants in applied, multidisciplinary fields. The role of universities in driving innovation and economic growth has become increasingly prominent, with the "entrepreneurial university" concept suggesting that institutions have undergone a significant transformation, prioritizing the capitalization of knowledge alongside traditional research and teaching missions (Etzkowitz, 2003; Etzkowitz et al., 2000). This shift has been accompanied by a growing trend towards "academic capitalism," where declining public funding and intensifying competition have led institutions and individual scholars to adopt more market-oriented behaviors in pursuit of resources (Slaughter & Leslie, 1997). While the commercialization of research has received considerable attention, with studies focusing on patenting, licensing, and spin-off formation (Shane, 2004; Perkmann et al., 2013), a more fundamental question remains understudied: to what extent do academics themselves exhibit an entrepreneurial disposition, and does this disposition contribute to increased research productivity? Research productivity is a crucial aspect of an academic's career, as well as a key factor in determining the competitiveness of universities and national systems. Various individual and organizational factors, including gender, career stage, collaboration networks, institutional resources, and workload, have been linked to productivity (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005; Hesli & Lee, 2011). However, the dispositional and behavioral characteristics of researchers have received relatively little systematic attention. The concept of entrepreneurial orientation (EO) has been extensively studied in the management literature, where it is used to capture an actor's strategic posture through innovativeness, proactiveness, and risk-taking (Miller, 1983; Covin & Slevin, 1989; Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Meta-analytic evidence has shown a positive association between EO and performance in firms (Rauch et al., 2009), and this construct has been extended to the individual level, where it describes a person's propensity to pursue opportunities, act ahead of events, and tolerate uncertainty (Bolton & Lane, 2012). Yet, it remains unclear whether EO is also a significant predictor of scholarly output among academics. There are compelling reasons to expect both a positive and a more nuanced relationship between EO and research productivity. On one hand, academic research involves identifying opportunities, mobilizing resources, and accepting uncertain returns, all of which are characteristic of entrepreneurial behavior. Academics who proactively seek out funding, collaborators, and publication outlets, and who are willing to take risks, may indeed accumulate more output over time. On the other hand, certain philosophical and sociological perspectives on science suggest that research is often conducted within established "paradigms," or circumscribed areas of study with shared assumptions, methods, and problem sets (Kuhn, 1962). Within these boundaries, "normal science" may involve incremental puzzle-solving, and journals and peer reviewers may reward conformity as much as novelty (Azoulay et al., 2011). If this is the case, the innovativeness dimension of EO may not be a reliable predictor of productivity, and some research may not be inherently innovative at all. The question of whether the various dimensions of EO matter equally, or whether only some translate into output, is therefore an empirical one that existing theory does not settle. A related gap in the literature concerns the adoption of novel technological methods in the research process. The rise of digital platforms has created new opportunities for financing and conducting research, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D (Mollick, 2014; Belleflamme et al., 2014; Lakhani et al., 2013; Afuah & Tucci, 2012). These approaches may be particularly relevant in contexts where traditional funding is scarce. However, little is known about academics' willingness to adopt these methods or whether a technological propensity of this kind is associated with higher output. By treating this propensity as a distinct but complementary construct to EO, we can separate a general entrepreneurial posture from the specific readiness to use new tools for resourcing and conducting research. These issues are particularly pertinent in developing-country contexts, where universities often face significant resource constraints. In South Africa, for example, universities operate with limited public funding relative to enrollment growth, heavy teaching loads, and a need to address historical inequities, all while facing strong performance incentives (Cloete et al., 2015). In this environment, academics who can mobilize alternative resources and act proactively may have a distinct advantage. Conversely, if unconventional financing and research methods are underutilized, this may signal untapped opportunities for a sector that cannot rely on increases in conventional funding. Research from such settings is also valuable because the entrepreneurship and higher education literatures have been dominated by evidence from advanced economies with very different funding and incentive structures. Against this background, our study addresses two research questions. First, to what extent are academics entrepreneurial, and is a higher self-reported level of EO, and of each of its constituent dimensions, associated with higher research productivity? Second, is a greater propensity to apply novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, associated with higher productivity, and how prevalent is the use of such methods? To answer these questions, we conducted a survey of academics at a large South African university, using a comprehensive purposive sampling process that yielded 292 usable responses. We estimated the relationships using ordinary least squares regression and assessed the robustness of the findings with bootstrapped standard errors and negative binomial regression, which is suitable for the count-based and over-dispersed nature of publication output (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013). Our study makes three key contributions. First, it extends entrepreneurship theory to a setting in which it has seldom been applied, demonstrating that EO, a construct developed to explain firm behavior, can be meaningfully measured among individual scholars and linked to a core academic outcome. In doing so, it responds to calls for closer synthesis between educational and entrepreneurship theory and for greater attention to the micro-foundations of the entrepreneurial university (Fini et al., 2018). Second, by disaggregating EO into its dimensions, the study contributes to the debate on whether innovativeness, in particular, is rewarded in paradigm-bound academic work. Our findings suggest that, although individuals with higher endowments of EO may be more productive, innovativeness is not significantly related to productivity, which complicates simple narratives about the role of entrepreneurship in academic research. Finally, our study highlights the importance of considering the adoption of novel technological methods in the research process, particularly in contexts where traditional funding is scarce. By exploring the relationship between technological propensity and research productivity, we can better understand the ways in which academics can leverage new tools and approaches to enhance their research output. The notion that scholarly success is inextricably linked to novelty is a pervasive one in academic circles. However, this perspective overlooks the complex interplay of factors that contribute to research productivity. Our study seeks to address this limitation by exploring the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and academic research productivity. Furthermore, by examining the use of crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, we provide insight into the technological propensity of academics, highlighting the potential for these methods to be underutilized. The implications of our findings are particularly relevant for university leaders and policymakers in resource-constrained systems, as they inform the design of research support, training, and incentive structures. Next, we describe the data, measures, and estimation strategy employed in our study. We then present the results and robustness tests, followed by a discussion of the implications, limitations, and directions for future research. Our research design and sampling strategy were guided by the need to estimate associations between individual-level dispositions and self-reported performance outcomes in a defined population. To this end, we employed a cross-sectional, quantitative survey design, which is well-suited for this purpose (Creswell & Creswell, 2018). The survey was administered to academic staff at a large, research-intensive public university in South Africa, a setting that combines formal research-output incentives with the resource constraints typical of developing-country higher education. This context is analytically useful, as it allows us to examine the intersection of research productivity and technological propensity in a resource-constrained environment. A comprehensive purposive sampling procedure was applied to select participants. The sampling frame comprised all permanent and fixed-term academics, from lecturer to full professor, who were affiliated with a faculty or school and held a formal research mandate. Staff in purely administrative, support, or short-term teaching-only contracts were excluded, as were postdoctoral fellows, whose research mandates differ structurally. Purposive selection was preferred to probability sampling because the construct of interest, research productivity, is meaningful only for individuals with an opportunity to conduct research (Etikan et al., 2016). Within this boundary, an effort was made to include every eligible academic across all faculties to maximize disciplinary variation. After deduplication and verification against the institutional staff directory, 1,214 eligible individuals were identified. Each was invited by personalized email to complete an online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform. Two reminders were sent at ten-day intervals, resulting in a total of 317 questionnaires being returned. However, 25 of these were excluded due to substantial missing data or straight-lining, leaving 292 usable responses (an effective response rate of 24.1%). This response rate is comparable to those reported in other surveys of academic staff (Baruch & Holtom, 2008). To assess non-response bias, early respondents (first quartile) were compared with late respondents (last quartile) on all focal variables, following Armstrong and Overton (1977). No significant differences were found (all p > 0.10), suggesting that non-response bias is unlikely to be a significant concern. Additionally, the sample was compared with institutional staff records for rank and faculty, and the distributions did not differ materially. A sensitivity analysis showed that a sample of 292 gave over 0.95 power to detect a medium effect (f² = 0.15) in a regression with up to 15 predictors at α = 0.05 (Cohen, 1988), exceeding the minimum of 50 + 8k observations suggested by Green (1991). The measures employed in this study were designed to capture the key constructs of interest. The dependent variable, academic research productivity, was measured as the number of DHET-accredited research output units that respondents reported for the preceding three calendar years. These units include articles in accredited journals, books, book chapters, and peer-reviewed conference proceedings, and are fractionalized by authorship share. A three-year window was used to smooth annual volatility in publication outcomes (Abramo et al., 2011). Self-reports were verified, where respondents consented, against the institutional research-office repository for a random subsample of 40 respondents, and the correlation between the two sources was high (r = 0.93). Entrepreneurial orientation (EO) was measured using the nine-item scale of Covin and Slevin (1989), adapted from the firm level to the individual-academic level in line with Bolton and Lane (2012). The scale operationalizes the three classical dimensions identified by Miller (1983): innovativeness, proactiveness, and risk-taking. Respondents indicated agreement on a seven-point Likert scale, with example items rewritten to reflect research behavior, such as "I favour novel research questions over well-established lines of enquiry" (innovativeness) and "I typically initiate research collaborations rather than respond to others" (proactiveness). Dimension scores were computed as item means, and an overall EO score was computed as the mean of all items (Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Technological propensity, specifically the propensity to apply novel technological methods, was measured using a five-item scale developed for this study, informed by technology-readiness research (Parasuraman, 2000) and the literature on open and crowdsourced innovation (Howe, 2006; Mollick, 2014). Items captured the extent to which respondents had used, or would consider using, crowdfunding to finance research, crowdsourced R&D or citizen-science data collection, online collaborative platforms, and open-data repositories. Responses were captured on a seven-point scale. Control variables were selected for their established associations with research output (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005). Multi-view stereo (MVS) is a fundamental problem in computer vision, aiming to recover the dense three-dimensional geometry of a scene from a set of calibrated images. This technology has far-reaching implications for various applications, including autonomous driving, augmented reality, cultural heritage preservation, and large-scale urban modeling. Despite decades of research, producing accurate and complete depth maps remains a challenging task. Real-world scenes often contain occlusions, illumination changes, non-Lambertian surfaces, and large low-textured regions, where photometric cues are ambiguous. Moreover, MVS methods must be efficient enough to process high-resolution images and large image collections. Traditional MVS methods can be broadly categorized into four groups based on scene representation: voxel-based, point cloud-based, mesh-based, and depth map-based approaches. Depth map-based methods, which process each reference image independently and fuse the resulting depth maps into a final point cloud, have proven to be the most flexible and scalable. Within this family, PatchMatch stereo has become a dominant approach. This method initializes random depth and normal hypotheses at each pixel and iteratively propagates good hypotheses between neighbors, allowing correct hypotheses to spread quickly across the image. Notable extensions of PatchMatch stereo include Gipuma, which introduced a diffusion-like propagation scheme, and COLMAP, which jointly estimates depth, normals, and pixel-wise view selection within a probabilistic framework. In recent years, learning-based MVS has also gained significant attention. Methods such as MVSNet and its successors have achieved strong results on benchmarks by building plane-sweep cost volumes from deep features and regularizing them with 3D convolutions. However, these approaches have limitations, including high memory and runtime requirements, which grow rapidly with image resolution and depth range. Furthermore, their generalization to scenes unlike the training data is not guaranteed. In contrast, traditional PatchMatch methods remain attractive due to their training-free nature, ability to work at full resolution, and modest memory requirements. However, PatchMatch-based MVS faces two significant challenges. The first challenge concerns hypothesis propagation and view selection. Existing checkerboard schemes often rely on a fixed, small neighborhood pattern, which can lead to spatially close and strongly correlated candidate hypotheses. These hypotheses may lie across depth discontinuities or in unreliable areas, resulting in sampled hypotheses that do not accurately reflect the local structure of the scene. Moreover, view selection is typically performed using a single global criterion per image or a per-pixel criterion computed from one hypothesis, which can be noisy and unreliable, particularly early in optimization. The second challenge is the presence of low-textured regions, where photometric consistency measures, such as normalized cross-correlation, are almost uninformative. Enlarging the window size can help, but it also blurs details and increases the computational cost. Planar priors derived from sparse, reliable points and triangulation can be used to improve completeness in low-textured areas, but they depend on the quality of the sparse points and the validity of the piecewise-planar assumption. A natural alternative is a multi-scale strategy, which can help recover reliable estimates in low-textured areas while preserving fine details. In this paper, we investigate how a PatchMatch-based MVS framework can obtain reliable depth in low-textured areas without sacrificing fine details, while maintaining the efficiency and training-free nature of the traditional pipeline. Our approach combines a stronger single-scale base method with geometric consistency guidance across scales. We present a basic MVS method, ACMH, which uses Adaptive Checkerboard sampling and Multi-Hypothesis joint view selection. The adaptive checkerboard sampling selects candidate hypotheses from a wider neighborhood, improving propagation efficiency and robustness near discontinuities. The multi-hypothesis joint view selection uses the whole set of candidate hypotheses to infer the view subset used for cost aggregation at each pixel, resulting in a more stable and informative selection. We also propose ACMM, which embeds ACMH in a multi-scale framework guided by geometric consistency. Depth maps are estimated first on coarse images, where low-textured areas can be matched reliably. Geometric consistency across views is then used to filter the estimates and guide optimization at finer scales, ensuring that reliable coarse estimates are retained and propagated to the finest scale. To correct erroneous estimates propagated from coarser scales, we introduce a novel detail restorer, which identifies regions where the upsampled estimates are inconsistent with finer-scale evidence and restores thin structures and boundaries through hypotheses generated at the finer scale. Our method is evaluated on standard benchmarks, including ETH3D and Tanks and Temples, and achieves state-of-the-art performance among traditional approaches, while being competitive with learning-based methods. The results demonstrate that our approach can recover depth in low-textured areas as well as in fine details, with good computational efficiency. Overall, our work provides a principled way to address the challenges of PatchMatch-based MVS, enabling the recovery of accurate and complete depth maps in a wide range of scenarios. The key to our approach is the combination of a strong single-scale base method with geometric consistency guidance across scales. By using adaptive checkerboard sampling and multi-hypothesis joint view selection, we can improve the efficiency and robustness of hypothesis propagation and view selection. The multi-scale framework guided by geometric consistency ensures that reliable coarse estimates are retained and propagated to the finest scale, while the detail restorer corrects erroneous estimates and restores thin structures and boundaries. In conclusion, our work demonstrates that a PatchMatch-based MVS framework can be designed to obtain reliable depth in low-textured areas without sacrificing fine details, while maintaining the efficiency and training-free nature of the traditional pipeline. The proposed approach has the potential to be widely adopted in various applications, including autonomous driving, augmented reality, and cultural heritage preservation. Future work can focus on further improving the efficiency and accuracy of the approach, as well as exploring its applications in other fields. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in recovering depth in low-textured areas and fine details. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art traditional approaches and is competitive with learning-based methods. The approach is also computationally efficient, making it suitable for large-scale applications. The paper discusses the importance of hypothesis propagation and view selection, as well as the need for a multi-scale strategy to recover reliable estimates in low-textured areas.
