The proliferation of social media and online discussion platforms has revolutionized the way people communicate, but it has also created an environment where abusive content can spread rapidly and at an unprecedented scale. The ubiquity of offensive language, hate speech, sexist and racist remarks, and personal attacks in comment sections, microblogging services, and collaborative platforms is a pressing concern (Waseem and Hovy, 2016; Wulczyn et al., 2017). Research has shown that exposure to such content can have severe psychological consequences for targets, lead to the withdrawal of users from public discussion, and ultimately degrade the communities in which it occurs (Duggan, 2017). As a result, platform operators and policymakers are under increasing pressure to moderate content effectively. However, manual moderation is a time-consuming, expensive, and emotionally taxing process that cannot keep pace with the sheer volume of content generated daily. This has driven a substantial body of research on the automatic detection of abusive language (Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017; Nobata et al., 2016). Early approaches to abuse detection treated it as a supervised text classification problem, relying on hand-engineered features such as bag-of-words and n-gram representations, part-of-speech tags, syntactic dependencies, and lexicons of offensive terms (Yin et al., 2009; Warner and Hirschberg, 2012; Davidson et al., 2017). While these systems are reasonably effective on well-behaved text, they are brittle and require considerable feature engineering. The advent of neural network models has significantly improved the state of the art, with convolutional and recurrent architectures operating on learned word embeddings outperforming feature-based classifiers on several benchmarks (Badjatiya et al., 2017; Park and Fung, 2017; Gambäck and Sikdar, 2017). Recurrent neural networks with gated units, such as LSTMs (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), and models that combine them with attention or additional user-level information (Pavlopoulos et al., 2017; Founta et al., 2019), currently define the state of the art on datasets drawn from Twitter and Wikipedia talk pages. Despite this progress, a fundamental challenge persists in the abusive-language setting: users often obfuscate their words to evade detection. The widespread deployment of keyword filters and automated classifiers has created an incentive for authors of abusive messages to alter offensive terms in ways that preserve readability for humans but defeat automatic matching. Typical strategies include replacing letters with visually similar digits or symbols, inserting or repeating characters, inserting punctuation or whitespace within a word, deliberately misspelling words, and concatenating words. Obfuscation can also arise without any evasive intent, as a consequence of informal writing conventions, typing errors, and the creative orthography typical of social media (Eisenstein, 2013). Whatever the motive, the effect is the same: the surface form of the token falls outside the vocabulary the model has seen during training. Word-level neural models struggle to handle such tokens. A standard pipeline fixes a vocabulary of the most frequent training words and maps every other token to a single shared out-of-vocabulary (OOV) symbol, whose embedding is learned, if at all, from the few training instances in which it occurs. This design has significant consequences for abuse detection. Because one embedding must stand in for every unseen word, the model cannot distinguish an obfuscated slur from a rare proper noun, a misspelled but harmless word, or a genuinely novel term. All of these are collapsed into the same representation, and any evidence carried by the form of the word, such as its resemblance to a known offensive term, is discarded. The problem is not merely one of coverage; in abuse detection, the unseen word is often the most informative token in the message, and replacing it with a generic placeholder removes precisely the signal that the author sought to hide from simple filters but not from a human reader. Pre-trained embeddings only partially mitigate this problem, as obfuscated variants are by their nature sparse and idiosyncratic, and are rarely represented in the corpora from which general-purpose embeddings are trained. Prior work in other areas of natural language processing suggests a potential remedy: building word representations from their characters. Character-level and subword models have been shown to improve language modeling, part-of-speech tagging, and machine translation, especially for morphologically rich languages and noisy text (Ling et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Plank et al., 2016; Bojanowski et al., 2017; Sennrich et al., 2016). Such models can, in principle, produce representations for arbitrary strings and exploit regularities between a word and its variants. However, the application of these ideas to abuse detection has been limited. Some studies employ character n-gram features within linear classifiers (Nobata et al., 2016; Mehdad and Tetreault, 2016), while a few apply character-level networks to entire comments (Park and Fung, 2017). These approaches either discard word boundaries, and with them the word-level structure on which the strongest recurrent models depend, or treat the character information as an additional input channel rather than as a principled means of handling unseen words. To our knowledge, the best-performing recurrent classifiers for abuse detection still fall back on a single OOV embedding and thus do not address the obfuscation problem explicitly. This paper aims to address this gap. Our central research question is whether a recurrent abuse detection model that composes embeddings for unseen words from their characters can recover the information lost by the generic OOV representation, and thereby improve detection performance, particularly in the presence of obfuscated or rare vocabulary. Related questions concern which composition function is most suitable for this purpose and whether any benefit is consistent across domains that differ in style, annotation scheme, and the degree to which obfuscation occurs. We make the following contributions. First, we propose a neural architecture for abuse detection in which in-vocabulary words retain their ordinary word embeddings, while words not found in the vocabulary receive embeddings computed by a character-based composition function. We investigate several such functions, including recurrent and convolutional encoders over character sequences, to determine whether the model can distinguish unseen words from one another according to their orthography rather than relying on a generic OOV symbol. By exploring the potential of character-level models to improve abuse detection, we hope to contribute to the development of more effective and robust content moderation systems. The quest to develop effective abuse detection systems has become increasingly crucial in today's online landscape. A key challenge in this endeavor is handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, which can significantly degrade the performance of automated moderation systems. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that maps each word to a single shared vector, thereby enabling the model to better cope with rare and obfuscated tokens. Our methodology involves evaluating the proposed approach on two diverse datasets: Twitter data annotated for racist and sexist abuse, and comments from Wikipedia talk pages annotated for personal attacks. We demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art systems on both datasets. At the heart of our approach lies the formulation of abuse detection as a supervised text classification task. Given a post comprising a sequence of tokens, the model predicts a label from a dataset-specific label set. We compare a word-level recurrent baseline, which maps all unseen words to a single OOV vector, with models that compose a representation for each unseen word from its characters. Notably, the comparison is controlled, with all models sharing the same recurrent classifier, differing only in how word representations are constructed. We utilize two public corpora from distinct domains. The first dataset, compiled by Waseem and Hovy (2016), consists of roughly 16,900 tweets annotated as racism, sexism, or neither. Due to tweet deletions, we were only able to retrieve a subset of the original collection, which exhibited a skewed class distribution, with the majority of tweets labeled as neither. In accordance with standard practice for this dataset (Badjatiya et al., 2017; Park and Fung, 2017), we report results from 10-fold cross-validation, where 10% of the training portion was held out for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. The second dataset, compiled by Wulczyn et al. (2017), comprises approximately 115,000 comments from Wikipedia talk pages, labeled by crowd workers as personal attacks or not. Attacks constitute a minority class, accounting for around 12% of comments. We employed the provided train, development, and test partitions, enabling direct comparison with earlier work. Both corpora underwent identical preprocessing. Text was lower-cased, URLs and user mentions were replaced with placeholder tokens, and a Twitter-aware tokenizer was used for tokenization. We deliberately refrained from applying spelling normalization or de-obfuscation, as our aim was for the model to learn to cope with noisy tokens itself. For each dataset, the vocabulary V consisted of words in the training partition that also have a pre-trained embedding. All other words, including misspellings, character substitutions (e.g., "b!tch", "fk"), and concatenations, were treated as out-of-vocabulary (OOV). To quantify the OOV rate, we analyzed the validation and test partitions, confirming the extent of the problem. Our baseline architecture represents words in V using pre-trained embeddings e(w) ∈ ℝ^d (d = 300), initialized from GloVe vectors (Pennington et al., 2014) and fine-tuned during training. In the baseline, every OOV word is mapped to one shared trainable vector eUNK: e(w) = E[w] if w ∈ V; eUNK otherwise. The embedded sequence is encoded by a unidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), whose gates are defined as it = σ(Wi [h{t−1}; xt] + bi), ft = σ(Wf [h{t−1}; xt] + bf), ot = σ(Wo [h{t−1}; xt] + bo), ct = ft ⊙ c{t−1} + it ⊙ tanh(Wc [h{t−1}; xt] + bc), ht = ot ⊙ tanh(ct), where xt is the input vector at step t. The final hidden state hn (hidden size 128) is passed through dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) and a softmax layer: p(y | x) = softmax(Wy hn + by). To compose representations for unseen words, each OOV word w is decomposed into its character sequence (c1, …, cm). Each character is mapped to a trainable embedding of dimension 50, initialized randomly. The character sequence is then passed through a composition function fcomp to produce a word vector ecomp(w) ∈ ℝ^d. We explored two such functions: Character LSTM (Char-LSTM) and Character CNN (Char-CNN). The Char-LSTM, following Ling et al. (2015), uses a bidirectional LSTM to read the characters, and the word vector is a linear projection of the concatenated final forward and backward states: ecomp(w) = Wc [→hm ; ←h1] + bc. Non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancers, and chronic respiratory disease, are the primary cause of mortality worldwide, accounting for approximately two-thirds of global deaths, according to the World Health Organization (2011). The economic burden of these diseases is substantial, with Bloom and colleagues (2011) estimating cumulative global output losses of around $30 trillion between 2011 and 2030. Moreover, the costs extend beyond healthcare expenditure to include lost productivity and reduced quality of life for individuals and families. A significant proportion of this burden can be attributed to modifiable risk factors, with poor diet being a major contributor (Lim et al., 2012). Dietary patterns characterized by high consumption of energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods, sugar-sweetened beverages, saturated fat, and sodium, combined with low intakes of fruit, vegetables, and whole grains, are consistently linked to obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and increased all-cause mortality (Lim et al., 2012; World Health Organization, 2003). Modelling studies have shown that population-level dietary changes could yield significant health benefits at relatively low costs (Cecchini et al., 2010). Therefore, the combined economic and social costs of non-communicable diseases provide a compelling rationale for strategies targeting dietary behavior. Overall dietary patterns are constructed from numerous individual, repeated decisions about what to eat, and it is these discrete food choices that interventions must ultimately aim to change. Discrete food choices, such as selecting fruit over a confectionery snack or choosing a sugar-sweetened beverage, are more amenable to precise definition and measurement than global dietary patterns. Moreover, they are the level at which many policy instruments, such as menu labeling, price signals, and school food standards, operate. Effective intervention requires an understanding of the psychological processes that underpin these decisions. Interventions grounded in theory are widely recommended because theory specifies the mechanisms through which behavior is expected to change, allowing these mechanisms to be tested (Craig et al., 2008; Michie & Prestwich, 2010). Among social cognition models, the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB; Ajzen, 1991) is one of the most frequently applied in health research. The TPB proposes that the proximal determinant of behavior is intention, which reflects the motivation to perform the behavior. Intention, in turn, is determined by three constructs: attitude (the overall evaluation of performing the behavior), subjective norm (perceived social pressure to perform or not perform the behavior), and perceived behavioral control (PBC; perceived ease or difficulty of performing the behavior). Because many behaviors are not fully under volitional control, PBC is also proposed to exert a direct effect on behavior to the extent that it reflects actual control (Ajzen, 1991). The TPB's parsimony, clear operational definitions, and generalizability across behaviors have made it attractive to researchers and practitioners alike. Meta-analytic evidence supports the predictive utility of the TPB across health domains. For instance, Armitage and Conner (2001) found that the TPB accounted for 39% of the variance in intention and 27% of the variance in behavior in a review of 185 independent studies. Subsequent syntheses have reported similar findings for physical activity (Hagger et al., 2002) and a range of health behaviors using prospective designs (McEachan et al., 2011). Reviews of the intention-behavior relationship indicate that intentions explain approximately 28% of the variance in behavior (Sheeran, 2002), although experimental evidence suggests that even medium-to-large changes in intention produce only small-to-medium changes in behavior (Webb & Sheeran, 2006). Despite its widespread use, the TPB has been subject to substantial criticism. Critics have questioned whether it omits important determinants, such as habit, affect, and automatic processes, whether its constructs are sufficiently distinct, and whether it has generated interventions that effectively change behavior (Sniehotta et al., 2014). These concerns are particularly pertinent for food choice, which is often habitual, cue-driven, and shaped by hedonic and environmental factors that lie outside conscious deliberation. Nevertheless, the TPB has been widely used to study eating behavior, and the primary literature now spans a diverse array of food choices, including increasing consumption of fruit and vegetables, choosing low-fat or whole-grain foods, limiting sweets, snacks, and fast food, and avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages. Existing reviews of the TPB and diet have been valuable but limited in important respects. Some have examined dietary behavior as a single undifferentiated category or combined food choice with other health behaviors, such as physical activity and substance use (Armitage & Conner, 2001; McEachan et al., 2011). Others have focused on a single food group, most commonly fruit and vegetable intake (Guillaumie et al., 2010), or have encompassed a broad set of social cognitive determinants without focusing on TPB relationships. However, aggregating across heterogeneous food behaviors may mask meaningful differences in the strength of TPB associations. Conceptually, there are good reasons to expect such differences. Choosing to consume a health-promoting food (an approach behavior) may be governed by different processes than refraining from a health-compromising but palatable food (an avoidance behavior), the latter requiring self-regulation against strong hedonic temptations and ready availability. Perceived control may matter more for behaviors that involve resisting temptation than for those that are simply performed. Likewise, the relative influence of attitudes, social norms, and control may vary with the characteristics of those making the choice, including age and gender, because developmental stage and social roles shape both autonomy over food and sensitivity to social influence (Conner & Norman, 2005). Yet these potential moderators have rarely been tested systematically within a single synthesis restricted to discrete food choices. A second limitation concerns the evidential basis of earlier reviews. The rapid growth in the number of TPB food choice studies in recent years means that earlier syntheses omit a considerable body of evidence, and few have systematically sought unpublished work, which may reduce the risk of publication bias. Without a current, comprehensive, and behaviorally specific synthesis, researchers lack the quantitative information needed to judge when the TPB is an appropriate framework for understanding discrete food choices. This limitation underscores the need for a systematic review that can provide a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between TPB constructs and discrete food choices, as well as the potential moderators that may influence these relationships. By examining the existing evidence in a comprehensive and systematic manner, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the psychological processes that underpin food choice and develop more effective interventions to promote healthy eating behaviors. In conclusion, the TPB has been widely used to study eating behavior, and the primary literature now spans a diverse array of food choices. However, existing reviews have been limited in important respects, and there is a need for a systematic review that can provide a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between TPB constructs and discrete food choices. Scene understanding has been a cornerstone of computer vision research for decades, with its definition undergoing significant expansion over the past ten years. Initially, the focus was on recognizing objects and labeling pixels, but more recent endeavors have pushed the boundaries of what we expect from a vision system. Tasks such as dense captioning, scene graph generation, and visual question answering (VQA) require models to establish relationships between visual evidence and language, thereby substantially broadening the scope of scene understanding. The introduction of datasets like VQA, CLEVR, and GQA has driven the development of more sophisticated skills, including counting, attribute comparison, spatial reasoning, and multi-step compositional inference. In principle, question answering is an open-ended format, allowing any aspect of a scene to be queried. However, in practice, the prevailing formulations tend to focus on the present state of the scene. Given an image, questions typically inquire about the presence, quantity, color, or spatial relationships of objects. Even tasks that involve video or commonsense, such as video question answering or visual commonsense reasoning, primarily focus on observed events or plausible explanations of the current scene. The future state of a scene, particularly in relation to an action that has not yet occurred, remains a relatively unexplored territory. Yet, this type of reasoning is essential for intelligent agents, as they need to anticipate the consequences of their actions. For instance, a robot must consider the outcome of pushing a cup, a person must judge the stability of a tower when adding another box, and an assistant must predict the result of a planned action. Humans perform this type of reasoning with ease, drawing on their intuitive understanding of physics to mentally simulate the behavior of objects. This intuitive understanding enables them to anticipate how objects will move and interact with each other. In this paper, we introduce a new task, visual what-if question answering, which aims to study this capability. The system is given an image of the current scene and a question that describes a hypothetical action, such as "What happens to the red cube if the green sphere is pushed to the left?" The answer must describe some aspect of the scene after the action has taken place, such as which objects come into contact, which object ends up in a particular position, or whether an object remains stationary. This task extends VQA along a new axis, as the model must predict the scene as it would become, conditioned on an intervention, rather than simply describing the current state. The problem is challenging for several reasons. Firstly, the answer is not directly observable in the input and must be inferred through a model of how the world evolves. Secondly, the outcome depends on object-object interactions, where an action on one object propagates through collisions to others, and small differences in geometry, position, or motion can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. Thirdly, the question is expressed in natural language, requiring the system to ground the described action in the visual scene, translate it into a physical intervention, and finally map the resulting future state back into a linguistic answer. One possible approach would be to train a monolithic end-to-end network that maps the image and question directly to an answer. While such models have been successful on many VQA benchmarks, they must acquire the dynamics of the physical world implicitly from question-answer pairs, which is a weak and indirect supervisory signal. Related work on learned intuitive physics, including interaction networks, visual predictive models, and neural physics simulators, has shown that data-driven prediction is possible but limited in its ability to generalize to novel configurations, numbers of objects, and long horizons. In contrast, physics engines accurately encode rigid-body dynamics and generalize by construction, but they operate on explicit symbolic scene descriptions rather than pixels and language. Motivated by the complementarity of these approaches, we propose a hybrid model that integrates a physics engine into a question answering architecture. The model first perceives the scene and recovers an object-level representation, including object identities, attributes, and positions. It then parses the question to identify the hypothetical action and its target, instantiates this action in a reconstructed simulated scene, and uses the physics engine to roll the scene forward and anticipate the consequences of object-object interactions. The predicted future scene state is then used, in place of the observed one, to answer the question. By leveraging the strengths of both approaches, our model handles the well-understood aspects of rigid-body dynamics using an explicit simulator, while reserving learning for the more challenging aspects of perception and language understanding. Our contributions are threefold. Firstly, we formulate the problem of answering visual what-if questions, which extends the scope of scene understanding from describing the present to anticipating the consequences of actions. Secondly, we present a hybrid architecture that couples a physics engine with a question answering pipeline, enabling explicit simulation of object-object interactions caused by an action. Thirdly, we provide initial results on this new problem and compare them to fully data-driven end-to-end baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. We hope that this work will encourage further research on action-conditioned, predictive scene understanding and on combining learned and simulated components for reasoning about how the world will change. The visual what-if question answering task is defined as follows. Given an image of a scene containing a set of rigid objects and a question that describes a hypothetical action applied to one object, the system must produce an answer from a fixed answer vocabulary. The answer refers to some aspect of the scene after the action has taken place, such as the position of an object or the outcome of a collision. The task requires the system to integrate visual perception, language understanding, and physical reasoning to anticipate the consequences of the hypothetical action. By developing models that can effectively answer visual what-if questions, we can move closer to creating intelligent agents that can reason about the world and anticipate the outcomes of their actions. The task of predicting the outcome of physical actions on a scene requires a model to reason about the current state of the scene, parse the action, and anticipate the physical consequences of object-object interactions. This involves considering properties such as object displacement, contact, and support surface interactions. To address this challenge, we constructed a synthetic dataset using the Blender rendering pipeline and the Bullet physics engine, following the design principles of CLEVR. Each scene in our dataset consists of three to six objects, randomly sampled from a set of three shapes, two sizes, two materials, and eight colors, placed on a planar surface. The objects' positions and orientations are randomly sampled, with rejection of initial interpenetrations, and the scenes are simulated until they reach a stable state. We rendered images of each scene at a resolution of 480×320 pixels from a fixed camera with small random jitter in position and lighting. For each scene, we sampled actions from a set of four primitives: pushing an object in one of four cardinal directions on the ground plane, with a randomly sampled force magnitude. The action was simulated for a fixed duration of five seconds, and the resulting final state was stored along with the full trajectory. We generated questions from templates with functional programs, similar to CLEVR, but evaluated on the simulated future state rather than the initial state. The question families included movement queries, counting queries, relational queries, and collision queries. To limit language priors, we balanced the answer distributions per template using rejection sampling. Our dataset consists of 12,000 scenes, 48,000 scene-action pairs, and 240,000 questions, split into training, validation, and test sets with no scene overlap. We also stored ground-truth object attributes, 3D positions, and orientations as auxiliary supervision. Our model is a hybrid approach, comprising three components: a perception module, a physics-based simulation module, and a question answering module. The perception module uses a Mask R-CNN to detect objects and predict their attributes, as well as a regression head to estimate the object's 3D position on the ground plane. We refined the estimate using the known camera parameters and the predicted size class, resulting in a structured scene representation. The question parsing module employs an LSTM sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder to translate the question into a functional program, which is then used to parse the action into a tuple consisting of the target object, direction, and force class. We trained the program generation using 5,000 annotated question-program pairs and fine-tuned it with the answer-level reward. The physics simulation module grounds the parsed action to a specific detected object and instantiates the scene in the Bullet engine, using primitive collision shapes and calibrated material properties. We ran the simulation for the same duration as in data generation, yielding the predicted future state. To account for perception uncertainty, we ran multiple simulations with perturbed positions and aggregated the answers by majority vote. The answering module executes the program symbolically on the predicted future state, producing the final answer. Notably, the only learned components in our model are perception and parsing, while the dynamics are provided by the physics engine. We compared our model to fully data-driven, end-to-end models, including a language-only baseline, CNN+LSTM, CNN+LSTM+SA, and FiLM. We also evaluated an oracle variant of our model that receives ground-truth scene states and an ablation that substitutes a learned dynamics network for the physics engine. We trained the baselines using Adam with a learning rate of 1e-4, batch size 64, and early stopping on validation accuracy. We initialized the image encoders from ImageNet pretraining and fine-tuned them. We trained the Mask R-CNN for 40 epochs with standard augmentation, excluding flips, which would change the semantics of directional actions. We tuned the hyperparameters of the baselines on the validation set and trained all neural models with five random seeds. We evaluated the models using answer accuracy on the held-out test set, reported overall and per question family, as well as mean absolute error for counting questions. We assessed the differences between our model and the strongest baseline using a paired bootstrap test and McNemar's test, with a significance threshold of p < 0.01 after Bonferroni correction across question families. We also reported 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. To analyze generalization, we evaluated our model on a separate test set and observed its performance on unseen scenes and actions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our hybrid approach in predicting the outcome of physical actions on a scene, and highlight the importance of combining perception, physics-based simulation, and symbolic reasoning for this task. The evaluation of our model and the baselines was conducted using a comprehensive set of metrics, including answer accuracy, mean absolute error, and confidence intervals. We also performed a detailed analysis of the results, including a breakdown of performance by question family and a comparison of the oracle variant and the ablation. The results of this analysis provide insights into the strengths and limitations of our model and the baselines, and highlight the challenges of predicting the outcome of physical actions on a scene. In addition to the evaluation and analysis, we also discuss the implications of our work and the potential applications of our model. Our hybrid approach has the potential to be used in a variety of applications, including robotics, computer vision, and human-computer interaction. The ability to predict the outcome of physical actions on a scene could be used to improve the performance of robots and other autonomous systems, and to enable more effective human-computer interaction. We also discuss the potential limitations of our approach and the challenges that must be addressed in order to achieve more accurate and robust predictions. Overall, our work demonstrates the effectiveness of a hybrid approach that combines perception, physics-based simulation, and symbolic reasoning for predicting the outcome of physical actions on a scene. Anaemia is a pervasive and debilitating condition that affects a substantial proportion of the global population, with children in low- and middle-income countries shouldering a disproportionate burden. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 40% of preschool children and roughly one quarter of the global population were anaemic in 2011, with the highest prevalence rates observed in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The aetiology of anaemia is complex and multifaceted, but iron deficiency is widely regarded as the single most important cause, accounting for around half of all cases. The clinical presentation of anaemia is characterized by fatigue, lethargy, reduced exercise tolerance, and increased physiological strain on the cardiovascular system, as the body attempts to compensate for diminished oxygen-carrying capacity. However, in children, the consequences of anaemia may extend far beyond haematological symptoms, as iron plays a critical role in neuronal energy metabolism, myelination, neurotransmitter synthesis, and dendritic development. The biological plausibility for an association between iron status and neurodevelopment is substantial, with iron-dependent enzymes participating in dopaminergic, serotonergic, and noradrenergic pathways that underpin attention, motor control, and memory. Animal models and neuroimaging studies have shown that iron deficiency during sensitive periods of brain growth can produce changes in hippocampal structure and basal ganglia function that may persist even after haematological correction. In humans, infants with iron deficiency anaemia have consistently been shown to exhibit poorer cognitive, motor, and socio-emotional outcomes, with some of these deficits persisting into adolescence despite iron repletion. While the evidence for school-aged children is less consistent, cross-sectional studies have linked iron deficiency to lower mathematics scores, and trials have reported improved attention, concentration, and school participation following iron supplementation. A meta-analysis of randomized trials concluded that iron supplementation improved global cognitive scores and attention in school-aged children, particularly among those who were anaemic at baseline. However, earlier reviews have highlighted methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, heterogeneous outcome measures, and inadequate control of confounding variables. Confounding is a particular concern in settings where iron deficiency coexists with other adversities, such as poverty, food insecurity, poor sanitation, limited caregiver education, and chronic infection. These factors can independently impair child development and cluster in the same households, making it challenging to disentangle the contribution of iron status from that of infection and socioeconomic disadvantage. Soil-transmitted helminth infections, such as hookworm, Ascaris, and Trichuris, are an important example of how infection can contribute to anaemia and directly influence growth and cognition. Hookworm causes chronic intestinal blood loss, while Ascaris and Trichuris may impair nutrient absorption and appetite, highlighting the need for concurrent assessment of haematological, parasitological, anthropometric, and contextual variables. Unfortunately, this approach is seldom adopted in school-based studies from low- and middle-income countries. In South Africa, the policy context has been shaped by national food fortification, introduced in 2003, and school feeding programs through the National School Nutrition Programme. While nationally representative surveys have indicated that anaemia remains a public health concern in young children, prevalence estimates differ by survey year, age band, and cut-offs applied. Importantly, national figures can mask marked within-country heterogeneity, with rural and peri-urban communities in provinces such as KwaZulu-Natal experiencing high rates of poverty, household food insecurity, and endemic helminth transmission. These conditions create a plausible setting for elevated rates of iron deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia, yet locally derived estimates for primary school-aged children are scarce. Most South African studies of iron status have focused on infants, pregnant women, or adolescent girls, leaving the early school years, when formal learning begins and cognitive demands escalate, comparatively under-investigated. This evidence gap is significant, as children from disadvantaged communities frequently fail to attain their age-appropriate educational potential, and grade repetition and early school leaving remain persistent problems in South Africa. Iron deficiency is potentially modifiable through low-cost interventions, including dietary diversification, targeted supplementation, and deworming, making even modest effects on learning of considerable public health importance. Furthermore, assessment of whether anaemia and iron deficiency are associated with developmental and educational outcomes in this age group is essential for determining whether school health programs should include haematological screening or iron-focused interventions. In the absence of context-specific data, South African policy must extrapolate from studies conducted in settings that differ in diet, infectious disease ecology, and educational systems. A further limitation of the existing literature is that anaemia and iron deficiency are often conflated, with haemoglobin concentration used as a proxy for iron status. However, haemoglobin is a late and non-specific indicator of iron depletion, whereas ferritin, transferrin saturation, and soluble transferrin receptor provide more nuanced information on iron stores and iron-restricted erythropoiesis. Studies relying solely on haemoglobin may therefore misclassify children and attenuate or obscure true associations. Likewise, studies examining a single outcome, such as an intelligence quotient score, may overlook domain-specific effects on fine motor coordination, memory, attention, or behaviour, which may be more sensitive to iron status and more directly relevant to classroom functioning. Against this background, the present study aimed to investigate anaemia and iron status in children aged 6 to 8 years attending school in a peri-urban, disadvantaged community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The study had three primary objectives: to estimate the point prevalence of anaemia, iron deficiency, iron deficiency anaemia, and helminth infection; to examine whether anaemia and iron status were associated with psychomotor development, including cognitive performance, fine motor skills, memory, attention, and behaviour; and to determine whether these haematological variables, together with helminth infection, predicted school performance as reported by teachers. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between anaemia, iron deficiency, and helminth infection and their impact on growth, development, and educational outcomes in children aged 6 to 8 years in a socioeconomically disadvantaged community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. By conceptualising anaemia and iron deficiency as mediating variables, we sought to understand how environmental and nutritional exposures influence child development and educational attainment. To achieve this, we combined clinical, biochemical, and educational data, allowing us to consider the relative roles of anaemia, iron deficiency, and helminth infection concurrently. Our study makes three significant contributions to the existing literature. Firstly, it provides current and locally grounded prevalence estimates for a population that is under-represented in national surveys. Secondly, it integrates iron biomarkers, parasitological screening, and multi-informant educational assessment within a single design, thereby enabling a comprehensive understanding of the complex relationships between these variables. Finally, it documents the practical and methodological challenges of conducting health and education research in rural South African schools, including consent procedures, sampling, laboratory logistics, and statistical constraints, with the aim of informing the design of adequately powered future studies. The study was conducted in a peri-urban community characterised by high unemployment, reliance on social grants, and limited access to piped water and sanitation, creating conditions conducive to both nutritional anaemia and soil-transmitted helminth transmission. Our conceptual framework posited that anaemia and iron deficiency mediate the relationship between socioeconomic disadvantage, nutritional status, and parasitic infection, influencing physical growth, psychomotor development, and school performance. The study was guided by the STROBE guidelines for observational studies and was designed to capture the complex interplay between these variables. Participants were children aged 6 to 8 years enrolled in no-fee public primary schools and living within the catchment community. Children with known haemoglobinopathy, chronic systemic illness, or neurodevelopmental disorders were excluded, as were those who had received iron supplementation or anthelminthic treatment in the preceding four weeks. Schools were purposively selected based on accessibility and quintile ranking, and children were recruited from Grade 1 and Grade 2 class lists. Information sheets and consent forms were sent home via the schools, and caregivers provided informed consent for their child's participation. The target sample size was calculated to estimate prevalence with a specified precision, using a formula that took into account the expected prevalence of anaemia. Assuming an anaemia prevalence of 20%, a 95% confidence level, and an absolute precision of 6%, the minimum sample size was 171 children. To account for non-response and incomplete data, the sample size was inflated, and a total of 184 children were enrolled. However, it is essential to note that the sample was powered for prevalence estimation rather than for detecting associations between exposure and the less common developmental and educational outcomes. As such, the analyses of associations should be regarded as exploratory. Data collection took place at the schools during school hours, and fieldworkers, comprising a paediatrician, registered nurses, and a trained psychometrist, underwent standardisation training before fieldwork. Clinical data were collected through caregiver interviews using a structured questionnaire, which covered household demographics, caregiver education, household income and assets, food security, water and sanitation facilities, breastfeeding history, birth history, and the child's past medical history. Each child underwent a standardised physical examination, during which weight and height were measured, and height-for-age and body-mass-index-for-age z-scores were computed against the WHO growth reference for school-aged children. Biochemical data were collected through point-of-care haemoglobin measurement using a HemoCue Hb 201+ photometer, which has acceptable agreement with reference laboratory methods. Anaemia was defined according to WHO criteria, and iron deficiency was defined as a serum ferritin concentration below 15 µg/L or transferrin saturation below 16%. Because ferritin is an acute-phase protein, children with CRP above 5 mg/L were considered to have inflammation, and in these children, ferritin below 70 µg/L was interpreted as indicating iron deficiency. Stool specimens were collected and examined using the Kato-Katz thick-smear technique for Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and hookworm. A child was classified as helminth-infected if ova of any species were detected. Psychomotor and cognitive assessment were conducted using Raven's Coloured Progressive Matrices, a non-verbal test of reasoning that minimises linguistic and cultural bias. Fine motor skills were assessed using the motor coordination subtest of the Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration. All children with anaemia, iron deficiency, or helminth infection were referred to the local clinic for treatment according to national guidelines, and children with infection received albendazole. In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex relationships between anaemia, iron deficiency, helminth infection, and child development and educational outcomes in a socioeconomically disadvantaged community in South Africa. The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of interventions aimed at improving child health and education outcomes in similar settings. The introduction of infliximab, a chimeric IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), marked a significant shift in the treatment of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. Randomized trials demonstrated its efficacy in Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and rheumatoid arthritis, leading to its approval for these conditions (Targan et al., 1997; Maini et al., 1999; Rutgeerts et al., 2005). Over time, its use has expanded to include ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis. While biologic agents like infliximab have improved disease control and reduced the need for surgical interventions and hospitalizations, their high cost has placed a substantial burden on healthcare systems, limiting access in many settings. The expiration of patents and exclusivity periods for reference biologics has led to the development of biosimilar versions, aimed at increasing access and reducing costs. In 2013, the European Medicines Agency approved CT-P13, the first biosimilar monoclonal antibody, which was followed by the approval of additional infliximab biosimilars in Europe and the United States. It is essential to note that biosimilars are distinct from generic drugs, as they are large, structurally complex proteins produced in living cell systems, and their characteristics can vary depending on the cell line and manufacturing process. Even reference products exhibit batch-to-batch variability, such as differences in glycosylation, making it impossible for a biosimilar to be an exact copy (Kurki et al., 2017). As a result, regulatory approval of biosimilars relies on a stepwise comparability exercise, combining extensive analytical and functional characterization with non-clinical and pharmacokinetic studies, and typically at least one adequately powered comparative clinical trial. The primary objective of this exercise is to demonstrate that there are no clinically meaningful differences in quality, safety, or efficacy between the biosimilar and the reference product. The pivotal infliximab studies, PLANETAS and PLANETRA, demonstrated pharmacokinetic equivalence and comparable efficacy and safety over the study period (Park et al., 2013; Yoo et al., 2013). However, these trials primarily addressed the initiation of therapy or continued dosing of one product and did not investigate the effects of switching between products. In clinical practice, switching between reference infliximab and biosimilars has become increasingly common, driven by economic considerations. Many patients who have been stable on reference infliximab for years are being switched to a biosimilar, raising concerns about the potential impact on treatment outcomes. Infliximab is known to be immunogenic, and the formation of anti-drug antibodies can accelerate clearance, reduce clinical response, and cause infusion reactions (Baert et al., 2003). Theoretical concerns have been raised that exposing a patient to two similar but non-identical molecules could provoke new antibody formation or loss of response. In vitro studies have shown that antibodies to reference infliximab cross-react with CT-P13, suggesting that the products share dominant epitopes (Ben-Horin et al., 2016). However, these findings do not provide insight into the long-term effects of switching in patients, and the potential risks associated with multiple transitions remain unclear. Furthermore, perception-related effects must be considered when evaluating switching data. Open-label switching can lead to patients reporting subjective worsening or discontinuing treatment due to negative expectations, a nocebo effect that can complicate the interpretation of uncontrolled switching data. Regulatory frameworks differ in their approach to switching and interchangeability. The European Medicines Agency evaluates biosimilarity but leaves decisions on substitution and switching to individual member states and clinicians. In contrast, the US Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act created a separate "interchangeable" designation, which allows pharmacy-level substitution without prescriber intervention under state law. To demonstrate interchangeability, the US Food and Drug Administration recommends that sponsors conduct a switching study with multiple alternations between the reference and proposed product, using a sufficiently sensitive population and pharmacokinetic endpoints, and comparing the results against patients who remain on the reference product (US FDA, 2019). This guidance sets a high evidentiary standard, requiring repeated switches and a control group, which most existing clinical literature on infliximab was not designed to meet. Professional societies in gastroenterology and rheumatology have acknowledged the limitations of the evidence on switching and generally recommend a single, physician-managed switch from reference infliximab to a biosimilar, while advising caution about multiple or non-medically driven switches (Danese et al., 2017). The NOR-SWITCH trial, a randomized, double-blind, non-inferiority study, found that switching from reference infliximab to CT-P13 was not inferior to continued reference treatment in terms of disease worsening across several diagnoses (Jørgensen et al., 2017). Since then, numerous randomized trials, extension studies, registry analyses, and single-center cohorts have reported outcomes after switching in various inflammatory disorders. However, most of these studies are observational, uncontrolled, and short in follow-up, with heterogeneous designs, switching conditions, outcome definitions, and concomitant therapy. Much of the information is available only in congress abstracts, making it challenging to assemble and appraise the literature. This systematic review aims to address the gap in the evidence by investigating whether switching patients between reference infliximab and its biosimilars, in either direction, is associated with changes in efficacy, safety, immunogenicity, or drug exposure in patients with inflammatory disorders. We conducted a comprehensive search of the published literature and relevant congress abstracts for studies that reported switching data across all approved indications of infliximab. Our review provides a detailed description of the study designs and populations, the number and type of switches, and the follow-up, and compares the findings with the evidence standard described in regulatory guidance. This review makes three significant contributions. First, it brings together journal and congress data from gastroenterology, rheumatology, and dermatology, which have typically been considered separately. Second, it distinguishes randomized, controlled evidence from uncontrolled observational findings, providing a clear understanding of the strength of the evidence. Third, it evaluates the findings in the context of the regulatory guidance on interchangeability, highlighting the gaps in the evidence and the need for further research to inform clinical practice and policy decisions. By synthesizing the available evidence and identifying areas for further investigation, this review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the safety and efficacy of switching between reference infliximab and its biosimilars, ultimately informing the development of evidence-based guidelines and policy recommendations. The question of whether patients can safely switch between reference infliximab and its biosimilars has been a topic of considerable interest in recent years. While several studies have investigated this issue, the evidence is not yet comprehensive, and there are still gaps in our understanding of the potential risks and benefits associated with switching. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a systematic review of published evidence on switching between reference infliximab and its biosimilars in patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. Our review was guided by the US Food and Drug Administration's draft guidance on interchangeability, which emphasizes the need to demonstrate that a biosimilar produces the same clinical result as the reference product in any given patient, and that the risk of alternating or switching between the two products is not greater than the risk of continuing the reference product. In designing our review, we took a broad approach, considering studies of patients with a range of conditions, including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis. We included studies that reported outcomes in patients who were switched from reference infliximab to a biosimilar, as well as those that included switches from a biosimilar back to the reference product, or between biosimilars. Our search strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for infliximab and its biosimilar products with terms for switching and related concepts, and we searched multiple databases, including MEDLINE and EMBASE, as well as the abstract archives and proceedings of relevant congresses. To ensure that our review was comprehensive and unbiased, we developed a standardized extraction form, which we piloted on a subset of studies. For each included study, we extracted a range of information, including the study design, population, number of patients switched, and the nature of the switch. We also extracted efficacy, safety, immunogenicity, and pharmacokinetic outcomes, using disease-specific measures where possible. In addition, we recorded the definitions of the outcomes and the time points of assessment, as well as the presence and type of a control group. One of the challenges in conducting this review was the heterogeneity of the available evidence. Many of the studies we identified were observational in nature, and few were randomized controlled trials. To address this limitation, we used a descriptive approach to assess the strength of the evidence, focusing on design features rather than excluding studies on quality grounds. For randomized controlled trials, we appraised the risk of bias using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, while for observational studies, we recorded the presence of a control group and the duration of follow-up. Our search strategy identified a large number of records, which we screened against our eligibility criteria. After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, we assessed the full texts of potentially relevant journal articles and congress records. We documented the primary reason for exclusion for each excluded full-text record and resolved disagreements about eligibility through discussion and consultation with a third reviewer. The results of our search and screening process are summarized in a PRISMA flow diagram. The evidence we identified suggests that switching between reference infliximab and its biosimilars is generally safe and effective, with no significant differences in efficacy or safety outcomes between patients who switch and those who continue on the reference product. However, our review also highlights several limitations in the current evidence, particularly the scarcity of data on multiple or alternating switches. Further research is needed to establish interchangeability in these scenarios, as well as in certain patient populations, such as those with a history of immunogenicity or previous adverse reactions. In conclusion, our systematic review provides reassurance about the safety and efficacy of switching between reference infliximab and its biosimilars in patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. However, it also highlights the need for further research to address the gaps in our current understanding of the potential risks and benefits associated with switching. By continuing to monitor the evidence and conduct rigorous evaluations of the available data, we can work towards establishing interchangeability and improving patient outcomes in this important area of clinical practice. Furthermore, the findings of our review have implications for clinical practice and policy. The ability to switch between reference infliximab and its biosimilars could have significant cost savings for healthcare systems, as well as improved access to treatment for patients who may not have been able to afford the reference product. However, it is essential that any decisions about switching are made on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the individual patient's medical history, disease activity, and other relevant factors. In addition, our review highlights the importance of continued research and monitoring in this area. As the use of biosimilars becomes more widespread, it is essential that we continue to evaluate their safety and efficacy, as well as their potential impact on patient outcomes. This will require ongoing investment in research and development, as well as collaboration between clinicians, researchers, and industry stakeholders. Overall, our systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of the current evidence on switching between reference infliximab and its biosimilars. While the results are generally reassuring, they also highlight the need for further research and ongoing evaluation to establish interchangeability and improve patient outcomes. By working together to address these challenges, we can ensure that patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases have access to safe, effective, and affordable treatment options. The review also underscores the importance of considering the nuances of study design and reporting when evaluating the evidence on biosimilars. The use of standardized extraction forms and rigorous assessment of study quality can help to minimize bias and ensure that the results are reliable and generalizable. Furthermore, the inclusion of a range of study designs, including randomized controlled trials and observational studies, can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the potential risks and benefits associated with switching. The proliferation of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems in various applications, including voice search, dictation, and conversational assistants on mobile and embedded devices, has highlighted the importance of contextual information in speech recognition. The context in which a user speaks plays a significant role in determining the likelihood of a particular utterance, and the same acoustic signal can warrant different transcriptions depending on the context. For instance, a request such as "call Jason" is only recognizable if the system has access to the user's contact list, and "play Anomalisa" is only plausible if that title is present in the user's media library or has been recently queried. This context-dependent nature of speech recognition is particularly crucial for rare words, proper names, and other terms that are scarce or absent in the training data, as errors on these terms can be disproportionately costly. Conventional ASR systems have addressed this challenge by incorporating contextual information into the language model through dynamic biasing, where a set of relevant words or phrases is used to modify the language model during decoding. This is often achieved by compiling the contextual phrases into a weighted finite-state transducer (WFST) or an equivalent n-gram model, which is then combined with the static language model to boost hypotheses that match the contextual entries. The pronunciations of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) context terms can be obtained from a grapheme-to-phoneme system or a learned pronunciation model. While this approach is effective, it has some limitations, as the modules are trained independently with different objectives and are only loosely coordinated at test time through hand-tuned interpolation weights and boosting factors. Recent advances in sequence-to-sequence models have led to the development of end-to-end (E2E) models that integrate the acoustic, pronunciation, and language modeling components into a single neural network trained end-to-end. Examples of such models include connectionist temporal classification (CTC), the recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T), and attention-based encoder-decoder models such as Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS). When trained on sufficient data, E2E models have achieved state-of-the-art performance on large-vocabulary tasks, while also having a smaller footprint due to the elimination of separate lexicons, decision trees, and large decoding graphs. However, the integration of contextual information into E2E models is more challenging due to the lack of an explicit language model or lexicon that can be modified at inference time. To address this limitation, researchers have employed various techniques, including the use of external language models or n-gram models built from contextual phrases, which are combined with the E2E model's output scores during beam search using log-linear interpolation, known as shallow fusion. While this approach is simple and keeps the base model unchanged, it inherits the weaknesses of modular design, where the E2E model is not trained to exploit the contextual information, and the external model has no access to the acoustic evidence or the model's internal state. Moreover, shallow fusion with word-level or phrase-level n-grams requires operating on the sub-word units emitted by the E2E decoder, which can lead to sensitivity to the beam search and early pruning of correct but initially low-scoring hypotheses. This leaves a significant gap in the development of E2E recognizers that can effectively utilize contextual information. Ideally, we would like to have a model that treats contextual information as an input that the network itself learns to use, rather than as an external score added after the fact. Such a model would be trained to condition its acoustic and language modeling behavior on arbitrary, variable-sized sets of phrases supplied at inference time, including phrases containing words never seen in training. This raises several important questions, including whether a single network can learn when and how to use context, so that it improves recognition of contextual phrases without degrading performance when the context is irrelevant or empty. Additionally, can the representation of the context be learned jointly with the recognizer, eliminating the need for a separate pronunciation dictionary or biasing model? And does such joint optimization yield better accuracy than the standard practice of independently trained components combined during decoding? In this paper, we address these questions with Contextual Listen, Attend and Spell (CLAS), an all-neural E2E contextual ASR system. CLAS extends the LAS architecture with a context encoder that embeds each context phrase, represented as a sequence of sub-word units, into a fixed-dimensional vector. An additional attention mechanism allows the decoder to attend over these phrase embeddings at every output step, alongside its attention over the acoustic encoding. The context encoder, attention modules, and standard LAS components are optimized jointly with a single cross-entropy objective. To enable the model to learn to use context, we simulate contextual information during training by sampling phrases from the reference transcripts and adding distractors, requiring the model to determine from the audio which phrases are relevant. We also introduce a mechanism that lets the model adapt to the quality of the contextual information, which can vary significantly in practice. By jointly optimizing the context encoder, attention mechanism, and LAS components, CLAS can learn to effectively utilize contextual information, even when the context is variable-sized or contains OOV words. Our approach eliminates the need for separate pronunciation dictionaries, biasing models, or external language models, making it more efficient and scalable. Moreover, CLAS can be trained on a wide range of tasks, including those with limited contextual information, and can adapt to different types of contextual information, such as user-specific data or domain-specific knowledge. The ability of CLAS to learn to use context in a flexible and adaptive manner makes it an attractive solution for a wide range of applications, from voice assistants to conversational systems, where contextual information plays a critical role in determining the accuracy and effectiveness of speech recognition. The importance of contextual information in speech recognition systems cannot be overstated, yet many models tend to ignore context when it does not provide an obvious benefit. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing CLAS, a unified end-to-end architecture that seamlessly integrates arbitrary lists of context n-grams without relying on a separate language model, lexicon, or pronunciation model. Our contributions are threefold. Firstly, we propose a novel training procedure that exposes the model to randomly sampled contextual phrases and distractors, enabling it to generalize to new phrases, including out-of-vocabulary (OOV) terms, at test time. Secondly, we conduct a thorough comparison of CLAS with a strong baseline that utilizes on-the-fly shallow-fusion biasing with an independently trained Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS) model, following established practices for conventional and end-to-end systems. Finally, we evaluate both models on a range of tasks that cover different types of context, such as contact names, media requests, and location queries, demonstrating the superiority of CLAS in reducing word error rates. At the heart of CLAS lies the LAS framework, an attention-based encoder-decoder that models the posterior of a wordpiece sequence given acoustic features. We build upon this framework by incorporating a bias-encoder and a second attention module, allowing the model to jointly optimize the recognizer and its contextual representation. The input features to the model are 80-dimensional log-Mel filterbank energies, computed over 25 ms windows every 10 ms, and stacked and sub-sampled to a 30 ms frame rate. The encoder consists of a stack of unidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) layers that map the features to a sequence of hidden states. The decoder state is computed by a multi-layer LSTM from the previous embedded wordpiece and attention context, with attention weights obtained using an additive scoring function. The proposed CLAS extends the LAS model by introducing a bias-encoder that generates fixed-dimensional embeddings for each context phrase. These embeddings are produced by a sub-word-level encoder, allowing phrases with OOV words to be embedded without modification. The model also includes a learned no-bias embedding, which enables the model to decline using any phrase when the context is irrelevant to the utterance. The decoder attends over the context phrases using a second additive attention, yielding a context vector that is concatenated with the decoder state and acoustic context vector. This allows the model to compute the posterior of the wordpiece sequence with explicit access to the context. To train CLAS, we utilize a large dataset of approximately 35 million anonymized, hand-transcribed English utterances, totaling around 27,500 hours of audio. We employ multi-style training, corrupting clean utterances with simulated room reverberation and additive background noise, to improve the model's robustness. Since the training transcripts do not come with natural context lists, we simulate them by sampling random n-grams from the reference transcript and padding each list with distractor n-grams from other utterances in the same mini-batch. This design enables the model to learn the general relationship between the biasing list and the audio, rather than memorizing specific phrases, and allows phrases not observed during training to be exploited at inference. In comparison, our baseline model is a LAS model with the same acoustic encoder and decoder configuration as CLAS, but without the bias-encoder. Contextualization is performed at decoding time using shallow fusion with an on-the-fly contextual language model, following the biasing approach used in conventional automatic speech recognition (ASR). The context n-grams are compiled into a weighted finite-state transducer (FST) acceptor over words, composed with a speller FST that maps wordpiece sequences to words. During beam search, the hypothesis score is the sum of the LAS log-probability and the contextual LM log-probability, with the weighting factor tuned on a held-out development set for each task. We evaluate CLAS and the baseline model on several tasks that differ in the type of context, including songs, utterances requesting playback of specific songs, contact names, and location queries. Across these tasks, CLAS consistently outperforms the shallow-fusion baseline, reducing the word error rate (WER) by as much as 68% relative. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of jointly optimizing the recognizer and its contextual representation, rather than combining separately trained components at inference time. The ability of CLAS to generalize to new phrases, including OOV terms, and to adapt to different types of context, makes it a robust and versatile model for a wide range of speech recognition applications. Furthermore, the evaluation results highlight the importance of contextual information in speech recognition. The use of context n-grams, such as song titles or contact names, can significantly improve the accuracy of speech recognition systems. However, the effectiveness of these systems relies on the ability to integrate contextual information in a seamless and efficient manner. CLAS achieves this by jointly optimizing the recognizer and its contextual representation, allowing it to capture the complex relationships between the audio and the context. In addition to its technical contributions, this work also has significant implications for the development of speech recognition systems. The use of end-to-end models, such as CLAS, can simplify the development process and improve the accuracy of speech recognition systems. Moreover, the ability of CLAS to generalize to new phrases and adapt to different types of context makes it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications, from voice assistants to transcription services. In conclusion, this work presents a significant advancement in the field of speech recognition, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly optimizing the recognizer and its contextual representation. The proposed CLAS model achieves state-of-the-art results on a range of tasks, outperforming a strong baseline model that utilizes shallow fusion with an on-the-fly contextual language model. The ability of CLAS to generalize to new phrases and adapt to different types of context makes it a robust and versatile model for a wide range of speech recognition applications. The Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme, launched in England in 2008 and rebranded in 2023 as NHS Talking Therapies, has revolutionized the provision of mental healthcare in the United Kingdom. As a cornerstone of national mental health policy, IAPT has made psychological therapy a routinely available, publicly funded, and statistically monitored component of everyday healthcare, with over a million people being referred to its services each year. This development is all the more striking given the historically patchy and variable delivery of talking therapies within the National Health Service (NHS), which often prioritized pharmacological and custodial approaches over psychological interventions. To understand how IAPT became a central component of the UK's mental healthcare system, it is essential to examine the initiative's founding rationale and how it was assembled, justified, and stabilized over time. While existing scholarship has evaluated the programme's outcomes, questioned its evidence base, and critiqued its narrow therapeutic repertoire, these contributions tend to either take IAPT's rationale as given or situate it within broader neoliberal or managerial trends. In contrast, this article seeks to empirically examine the specific configurations of expertise, evidence, and accountability that have enabled IAPT to become a durable and legitimate component of the UK's mental healthcare landscape. The rise of IAPT can be seen as a significant shift in the trajectory of biomedicine, with some scholars arguing that it represents a partial debiomedicalization – a movement away from drug-based, brain-centred models towards talk, cognition, and behaviour. However, this reading assumes a linear, directional change in health systems, which may oversimplify the complex dynamics at play. Instead, it is essential to consider how psychological therapy has been re-legitimized and on what terms, as well as the resources used to achieve this re-legitimization. By examining the development, accounting, and sustenance of IAPT as a national response to mental ill-health, this article aims to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between psychological, economic, and policy factors. Through an analysis of policy documents, economic reports, clinical guidelines, and published evaluations, this article traces the problematization of common mental disorders as a challenge that is simultaneously clinical, economic, and political. A key aspect of this problematization has been the role of economic expertise, exemplified by the influential work of Layard and colleagues, who articulated a compelling case for expanded therapy based on the costs of unemployment, sickness absence, and welfare dependency associated with depression and anxiety. By rendering these costs commensurable with the costs of therapy, Layard and colleagues presented treatment as self-financing, thereby creating a powerful economic rationale for IAPT. The calculative forms of reasoning used by Layard and colleagues have been shown to be performative, shaping the very realities they purport to describe. In the case of IAPT, these forms of reasoning have been joined to particular accounts of pathology and mechanisms of therapeutic change, as well as to forms of evidence, such as the randomized controlled trial (RCT), that are more familiar within biomedical settings. This article argues that the revival of psychological framings of distress has proceeded through, rather than against, biomedical epistemic and administrative forms, complicating narratives of linear biomedicalization or debiomedicalization. The emergence of IAPT has significant implications for our understanding of the place and role of psychology within contemporary healthcare. By documenting the co-production of economic argument, psychological knowledge, and policy rationale, this article extends analyses of audit and accountability in public services into the domain of psychological therapy. Furthermore, the concept of contextification is introduced to describe the process by which IAPT has shifted from being primarily a content of mental healthcare (a set of interventions delivered within services) to a context for it – an organizing presence in relation to which other services, pathways, and professional identities are increasingly designed, justified, and evaluated.
