Furthermore, the curative resection rate, defined as the proportion of patients with R0 resection and no residual tumor, was 86% (95% CI, 80-90%), suggesting that colorectal ESD is an effective treatment for colorectal tumors, with a high proportion of patients achieving complete removal of the tumor. The rates of immediate and delayed perforation were 4.2% (95% CI, 3.5-5.0%) and 0.22% (95% CI, 0.11-0.46%), respectively, while the rates of immediate and delayed major bleeding were 0.75% (95% CI, 0.31-1.8%) and 2.1% (95% CI, 1.6-2.6%), respectively. These findings indicate that perforation and bleeding are relatively rare complications of colorectal ESD, although they can occur in a small proportion of patients. After an average postoperative follow-up of 19 months, the rate of tumor recurrence was found to be 0.04% (95% CI, 0.01-0.31) among patients with R0 resection, and 3.6% (95% CI, 1.4-8.8%) among those without R0 resection. Similarly, the endoscopic en bloc resection rate and curative resection rate were also higher in Asian studies, suggesting that differences in technique, operator experience, or patient population may contribute to variations in outcomes between continents. Our results also suggest that the duration of the procedure and average tumor size may influence the risk of complications. Specifically, studies with shorter procedure durations were associated with a higher rate of immediate perforation (P = 0.009), while larger average tumor sizes were associated with a higher rate of delayed major bleeding (P = 0.04). These findings highlight the importance of careful dissection and hemostasis during the procedure, as well as the need for adequate patient selection and preoperative planning. In conclusion, our systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrate that colorectal ESD is a safe and effective procedure for the treatment of colorectal tumors, with high R0 resection and curative resection rates, and relatively low rates of complications such as perforation and bleeding. Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the factors contributing to variations in outcomes and to optimize the use of colorectal ESD in clinical practice. The findings of our study are consistent with those reported in previous studies, and suggest that colorectal ESD is a valuable treatment option for patients with colorectal tumors, particularly when performed by experienced operators. Breast cancer is a formidable public health concern, affecting millions of individuals worldwide. With approximately 1.7 million new cases diagnosed annually, it is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in its advanced stages (Ferlay et al., 2015). Metastatic breast cancer (MBC), characterized by the spread of cancer cells to distant organs, is generally considered incurable and is responsible for a significant proportion of breast cancer-related deaths (Cardoso et al., 2017). In the United States alone, MBC accounts for approximately 40,000 deaths each year, resulting in substantial economic burdens, with estimated annual costs exceeding $12 billion (Siegel et al., 2017; Yabroff et al., 2011). The primary treatment options for MBC are chemotherapy and targeted therapy (TT), which aim to improve survival, quality of life, and delay disease progression (Baselga et al., 2012). Chemotherapy involves the use of cytotoxic agents to target rapidly dividing cancer cells, whereas TT employs drugs that specifically target molecular abnormalities in cancer cells (Winer et al., 2014). While both treatments have been shown to improve outcomes in patients with MBC, they are often associated with significant side effects and high costs (Chen et al., 2013). In recent years, there has been a growing emphasis on economic evaluations of cancer treatments, including chemotherapy and TT for MBC, to inform decision-making and optimize resource allocation (Drummond et al., 2015). Economic evaluations involve comparing the costs and outcomes of different treatment options, with the goal of identifying the most cost-effective approaches (Gold et al., 1996). Model-based economic evaluations are a common method used to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of cancer treatments, involving the development of mathematical models to simulate the natural history of the disease and the effects of different treatment options (Weinstein et al., 2003). These models can be used to estimate outcomes such as life years gained, quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) gained, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) (Briggs et al., 2006). Despite the increasing number of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, there is a need for a comprehensive review of the existing literature (Hutton et al., 2014). Previous reviews have focused on specific aspects of MBC treatment, such as the efficacy of individual drugs or the cost-effectiveness of specific treatment regimens (Jacobs et al., 2015). However, there is a lack of studies that have examined the broader methodological and reporting quality of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC. Furthermore, there is a need to examine the association between model characteristics and study quality and outcomes, in order to identify areas for improvement in future economic evaluations. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive overview of the existing literature on economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC. The research question guiding this study is: what are the characteristics, quality, and outcomes of model-based economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC? To answer this question, we conducted a systematic literature search in PubMED and the NHS Economic Evaluation Database (NHS EED) to identify studies that assessed the cost-effectiveness of chemotherapy and TT for MBC (Drummond et al., 2015). The search strategy included a combination of MeSH terms and keywords related to MBC, chemotherapy, TT, and economic evaluation (Eckermann et al., 2010). The inclusion criteria consisted of model-based economic evaluations that reported life years (LY) or quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) as the primary outcome measure (Gold et al., 1996). Studies were screened for eligibility based on title and abstract, and full-text articles were retrieved for studies that met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, which included general study characteristics (e.g., publication year, country, sponsor), model characteristics (e.g., type of model, time horizon, health states), and outcomes (e.g., LY, QALY, costs, ICER) (Princes et al., 2013). The quality of the studies was assessed using a checklist consisting of items related to study design, model characteristics, and reporting quality. The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive review of the existing literature on economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, highlighting key methodological and reporting quality issues. Secondly, it will examine the association between model characteristics and study quality and outcomes, providing insights into the factors that influence the results of economic evaluations. Finally, the study will provide recommendations for improving the quality and transparency of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, with the aim of informing decision-making and optimizing resource allocation in the field of oncology. The assessment of the cost-effectiveness of treatments for metastatic breast cancer (MBC) is a complex task that requires careful consideration of various factors, including study design, data sources, model structure, and reporting quality. To evaluate the quality of studies in this area, we employed a checklist of 26 items, adapted from the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria (CHEERS) statement, which provides a set of guidelines for reporting health economic evaluations. Each item on the checklist was scored as "yes" or "no," and the total score was calculated as the sum of all items, with studies scoring 20 or higher considered to be of high quality and those scoring below 15 considered to be of low quality. Our analysis utilized a combination of descriptive statistics and regression analysis to summarize study characteristics, model characteristics, and outcomes, as well as to examine the association between model characteristics and study quality, and between model characteristics and outcomes, such as the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) gained. We also calculated the incremental net monetary benefit (INMB) as the difference between the incremental health benefit and the incremental cost, using a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000 per QALY gained. A positive INMB indicated that the intervention was cost-effective, while a negative INMB indicated that it was not. To examine the association between model characteristics and study quality, we employed a linear regression model, with the quality score as the dependent variable and the model characteristics, such as type of model and time horizon, as independent variables. Similarly, to examine the association between model characteristics and outcomes, we used a multiple linear regression model, with the ICER or QALYs gained as the dependent variable and the model characteristics as independent variables. Our regression models were adjusted for potential confounding variables, such as publication year and sponsor. We also performed sensitivity analysis to examine the robustness of our results to changes in model assumptions and parameters. This included a threshold analysis, which examined the effect of varying the willingness-to-pay threshold on the INMB and the ICER, as well as a probabilistic sensitivity analysis, which examined the effect of varying the model parameters on the ICER and the QALYs gained. The results of the sensitivity analysis were presented as a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, which showed the probability that the intervention was cost-effective at different willingness-to-pay thresholds. Our systematic search of the literature yielded 562 unique citations, of which 24 studies met the inclusion criteria, considering 50 comparisons. These comparisons comprised 20 concerning chemotherapy and 30 targeted therapy (TT) for MBC. Notably, seven comparisons were represented in multiple studies, reflecting the overlap in the assessment of various treatment strategies for MBC. The majority of the studies (18 out of 24) employed a health state-transition model, which allowed for the estimation of life years and QALYs gained from the interventions, a crucial step in calculating the ICER. The extracted studies reported a range of model characteristics and outcomes, which were subsequently analyzed for quality and association with study outcomes. On average, the included studies fulfilled 14 out of the 26 items of the quality checklist, indicating a lack of transparency in reporting. The most common limitations included insufficient detail on model structure, input data, and sensitivity analyses, which are critical components of model-based economic evaluations. For instance, studies sponsored by the industry reported more favorable cost-effectiveness outcomes compared to non-industry-sponsored studies, with a median ICER of $74,111 per QALY gained versus $124,009 per QALY gained, respectively. In terms of health outcomes, the studies demonstrated that TT led to higher incremental QALYs gained compared to chemotherapy, with a median of 0.85 QALYs (range: 0.21-2.13) versus 0.42 QALYs (range: 0.11-1.44), respectively. Moreover, the INMB was positive in 31% of the comparisons, indicating that the additional health benefits of the interventions were not always offset by the increased costs. However, when considering the cost-effectiveness threshold of $100,000 per QALY gained, only 22% of the comparisons yielded an ICER below this threshold, suggesting that many of the interventions may not be considered cost-effective. A closer examination of the studies revealed that the incremental health benefits increased over time, with more recent studies (published between 2010 and 2014) reporting higher QALYs gained compared to older studies (published between 2000 and 2009). Nevertheless, this trend was accompanied by a corresponding increase in treatment costs, resulting in lower value for money. Specifically, the median cost per QALY gained increased from $93,419 in the earlier period to $143,091 in the later period, underscoring the need for ongoing evaluation of the cost-effectiveness of MBC treatments. Furthermore, our analysis of model characteristics and outcomes showed that studies employing a health state-transition model were more likely to report positive INMB and lower ICERs compared to studies using other modeling approaches. Additionally, studies that accounted for utilities and disutilities associated with treatment side effects reported higher QALYs gained and more favorable cost-effectiveness outcomes compared to studies that did not consider these aspects. Overall, the findings of this review highlight the importance of transparency and quality in model-based economic evaluations of MBC treatments. The development of a disease-specific reference model, incorporating key health states and transition probabilities, could improve the comparability and validity of these evaluations. Moreover, our results suggest that the cost-effectiveness of MBC treatments is highly dependent on the modeling approach used, and that studies that account for utilities and disutilities associated with treatment side effects are more likely to report favorable cost-effectiveness outcomes. As such, it is essential to prioritize transparency and quality in the reporting of model-based economic evaluations, and to consider the use of disease-specific reference models and the inclusion of utilities and disutilities associated with treatment side effects in these evaluations. The concept of family medicine has been gaining significant traction globally, as countries increasingly recognize the importance of providing comprehensive, patient-centered, and cost-effective healthcare services. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been at the forefront of promoting this approach, and many countries have begun to adopt family medicine as a cornerstone of their healthcare systems (WHO, 2019). However, in Africa, family medicine is still a relatively new and evolving specialty, with many countries struggling to define its scope and role within their healthcare systems (Mash et al., 2018). Botswana, like many other African countries, faces significant challenges in establishing a robust family medicine system, including resource constraints, inefficiencies in resource utilization, and a shortage of skilled healthcare workers (Kgosidialwa, 2017). The country's healthcare system is also characterized by inadequate infrastructure and limited access to healthcare services, particularly in rural areas, which exacerbates the challenges of providing quality care to all citizens (Ministry of Health, 2020). In light of these challenges, it is essential to explore the experiences of countries with well-established family medicine systems and good health indicators, such as Denmark, which is often cited as a model of a well-functioning healthcare system (OECD, 2020). The Danish healthcare system is characterized by a strong primary care sector, with family physicians (FPs) playing a central role in providing comprehensive and coordinated care to patients. This approach is underpinned by a robust information technology network, which facilitates efficient communication and data sharing among healthcare providers (Kjeldsen et al., 2017). Furthermore, the Danish healthcare system is known for its egalitarian approach, with patients and healthcare workers enjoying a collaborative and respectful relationship (Hansen et al., 2019). These features are in stark contrast to the healthcare systems in many African countries, where resource constraints, inefficiencies, and hierarchical relationships between patients and healthcare workers are common (Gilson et al., 2014). Despite the significant differences between the Danish and African healthcare systems, there are valuable lessons that can be learned from Denmark's experience. For instance, the Danish system's emphasis on task shifting, where nurses and clerical staff attend to simple or uncomplicated aspects of patient care, whilst FPs attend to more complicated patient problems, could be adapted to African contexts. Similarly, the use of information technology to facilitate communication and data sharing among healthcare providers could help to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of healthcare services in Africa. Moreover, the egalitarian approach to patient care in Denmark, which emphasizes collaboration and respect between patients and healthcare workers, could help to improve patient satisfaction and health outcomes in African countries. However, it is also important to recognize the limitations of simply transferring models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries. The context in which healthcare is delivered is critical, and any attempts to adapt models from other countries must take into account the unique challenges and opportunities in African contexts. For example, the higher taxation and higher health expenditure that underpin the Danish healthcare system may not be feasible in African countries, where resources are often scarce. Nevertheless, there are still valuable lessons that can be learned from Denmark's experience, and these can be adapted and modified to suit the specific needs and contexts of African countries. The research question guiding this study is: What lessons can be learned from Denmark's family medicine system, and how can these lessons be applied to improve the development of family medicine in Botswana and Africa? This question is significant because it seeks to explore the potential for knowledge transfer and adaptation of family medicine models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries. By examining the Danish family medicine system and its key features, this study aims to identify potential solutions to the challenges facing family medicine in Botswana and Africa. The study also seeks to contribute to the existing literature on family medicine in several ways, including providing a unique perspective on the application of family medicine models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries, highlighting the importance of task shifting, information technology, and egalitarian relationships in family medicine, and emphasizing the need for increased health expenditure and investment in healthcare infrastructure. The observations made during a visit to family physicians in Denmark were insightful, and highlighted the significant differences between the Danish and African healthcare systems. The training of FPs, the practice of family medicine, and the role of support staff in a family practice were often different and sometimes unimaginable by African standards. The Danish family practices were friendly and enmeshed in an egalitarian and efficient health system, which is supported by an effective information technology network. There was a lot of task shifting, and nurses and clerical staff attended to simple or uncomplicated aspects of patient care, whilst FPs attended to more complicated patient problems. The higher taxation and higher health expenditure that underpin the Danish healthcare system were also notable, and highlighted the need for increased investment in healthcare infrastructure and services in African countries. In conclusion, the development of family medicine in Botswana and Africa requires a comprehensive approach that takes into account the unique challenges and opportunities in these contexts. The widespread adoption of performance-based research funding (PBRF) models by governments and funding agencies worldwide has been driven by the desire to allocate research funding based on the quality and productivity of research output. As Hicks (2012) and Geuna and Martin (2003) have noted, this approach aims to promote high-quality research and enhance the international competitiveness of universities. In Flanders, Belgium, the PBRF model was introduced in 2003, with the specific goal of fostering excellence in research at Flemish universities (Debackere & Veugelers, 2005). A crucial component of this model is a comprehensive bibliographic database of research output in the social sciences and humanities, which serves as the basis for evaluating research performance and allocating funding (Luwel, 2004). However, the increasing proliferation of predatory and questionable journals has raised significant concerns about the validity and reliability of this bibliographic database, as well as the potential consequences for the PBRF model. As Butler (2013) and Beall (2012) have highlighted, the phenomenon of predatory journals, also known as questionable journals, has been extensively discussed in the literature. These journals often exhibit questionable editorial standards, lack transparency, and engage in deceptive practices to attract authors and generate revenue (Beall, 2012). The rise of open access publishing has created new opportunities for authors to publish their research, but it has also introduced new challenges for maintaining the integrity of the scientific record (DOAJ, 2015). The consequences of publishing in predatory journals can be severe, including damage to an author's reputation, loss of credibility, and potential harm to the public and political legitimacy of the research funding system (Cobey, 2015). Despite the growing concern about predatory journals, there is a notable lack of empirical research on the prevalence and characteristics of publications in questionable journals within the context of PBRF models. Most studies have focused on identifying predatory journals and developing criteria for evaluating journal quality (Beall, 2012; Shen & Björk, 2015). However, little is known about the authors who publish in these journals, their motivations, and the potential consequences for the research funding system. This gap in the literature is particularly significant in the context of PBRF models, where the accuracy and reliability of the bibliographic database are crucial for allocating funding and evaluating research performance (Geuna & Martin, 2003). The research question guiding this study is: What are the characteristics of publications in questionable journals within the context of the PBRF model in Flanders, Belgium, and what are the implications for the research funding system? To address this question, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the bibliographic database of research output in the social sciences and humanities in Flanders, focusing on publications in questionable journals over the period 2003-2016. Our study aims to contribute to the literature on PBRF models, open access publishing, and the phenomenon of predatory journals. Specifically, our contributions are threefold. First, we provide an overview of the procedures followed during the screenings for articles in questionable journals submitted for inclusion in the bibliographic database. Second, we present a bibliographic analysis of the publications identified, including the yearly number of publications in questionable journals, disciplinary classification, and authorship characteristics. Third, we discuss the implications of our findings for the research funding system and provide concrete suggestions for those tasked with maintaining bibliographic databases and screening for publications in questionable journals. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The next section presents the methodology used to identify publications in questionable journals and the characteristics of the bibliographic database. We then present the results of our analysis, including the yearly number of publications in questionable journals, disciplinary classification, and authorship characteristics. The discussion section interprets the results and discusses the implications for the research funding system. Finally, the conclusion section summarizes the main findings and provides recommendations for future research and practice. By exploring the characteristics of publications in questionable journals within the context of the PBRF model in Flanders, Belgium, this study aims to contribute to a better understanding of the risks and challenges associated with open access publishing and the importance of maintaining the integrity of the scientific record. The data used in this study originate from the Flemish performance-based research funding model, which has been in place since 2010 (Debackere & Glanzel, 2004). This model relies on a comprehensive bibliographic database that catalogues research output in the social sciences and humanities (Engels et al., 2012). The database is compiled annually, and research institutions in Flanders submit their research output, including articles published in journals, conference proceedings, and books (Spruyt, 2016). As part of the funding model, a screening process is conducted every five years to identify publications in questionable journals (Beall, 2012). Questionable journals refer to journals that have been identified as predatory or of poor quality (Butler, 2013). The screening process involves a review of the bibliographic database to identify articles published in journals that are included on Beall's list of predatory journals (Beall, 2016) or have been flagged by other reputable sources as being of poor quality (Cobey et al., 2013). The screenings are conducted by a team of experts who review the journal titles and evaluate their legitimacy based on a set of criteria, including the journal's editorial board, peer-review process, and publication history (Krell, 2017). The team also consults with researchers and experts in the relevant fields to verify the legitimacy of the journals (Cunningham, 2017). The data for this study consist of the publications identified during the five yearly screenings from 2003 to 2016. A total of 12,514 publications were identified as being published in questionable journals during this period (Spruyt, 2016). The data were analyzed using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods (Bazeley, 2013). First, the yearly number of publications in questionable journals was calculated and plotted over time to examine trends and patterns (Tukey, 1977). Second, the disciplinary classification of the identified journals was analyzed using a classification system developed by the Flemish Interuniversity Council (VLIR, 2018). In addition to the bibliographic analysis, three authorship characteristics were examined: multi-authorship, seniority of authors, and institutional affiliation. The results of our analysis provide insights into the prevalence and characteristics of publications in questionable journals within the context of the PBRF model in Flanders, Belgium. The findings have significant implications for the research funding system, highlighting the need for more effective measures to prevent the inclusion of publications in predatory journals in the bibliographic database. Furthermore, our study underscores the importance of maintaining the integrity of the scientific record and ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the bibliographic database. The implications of our findings are far-reaching, and we provide concrete suggestions for those tasked with maintaining bibliographic databases and screening for publications in questionable journals. Our study contributes to the literature on PBRF models, open access publishing, and the phenomenon of predatory journals, highlighting the need for ongoing research and vigilance in this area. By examining the characteristics of publications in questionable journals within the context of the PBRF model in Flanders, Belgium, this study aims to inform strategies for promoting high-quality research and maintaining the integrity of the scientific record. Ultimately, our research seeks to contribute to a better understanding of the complex issues surrounding open access publishing and the importance of ensuring the accuracy and reliability of bibliographic databases in the context of PBRF models. The relationship between the disciplinary scope of a journal and the departmental affiliation of its authors is a complex one, and has been the subject of considerable research (Larivière et al., 2016). To investigate this relationship, we measured the seniority of authors by calculating the number of years since their first publication, using data from a comprehensive bibliographic database (Persson et al., 2004). We then employed a cognitive-organizational classification system, developed by the authors (Flemish Interuniversity Council, 2018), to analyze the relationship between the disciplinary scope of the journal and the departmental affiliation of the authors. Our analysis was facilitated by the use of R software (R Core Team, 2020), which enabled us to perform a range of statistical tests. We began by calculating descriptive statistics to summarize the data, and then used inferential statistics to compare the characteristics of publications in questionable journals with those in open access journals (Agresti, 2013). A generalized linear mixed model was used to examine the relationship between the yearly rate of publications in questionable journals and the number of publications in open access journals (Bolker et al., 2009). This was supplemented by a series of logistic regression models, which were fitted to the data to examine the relationship between the seniority of authors, multi-authorship, and the disciplinary scope of the journal, while controlling for other variables such as the departmental affiliation of the authors (Larivière et al., 2016). The results of the logistic regression models were used to estimate the odds ratios and confidence intervals for the relationships between the variables (Chenal, 2017). Finally, the results of the analysis were verified by a team of experts to ensure that they were accurate and reliable (VLIR, 2018). Tuberculosis (TB) remains a pressing global health concern, with an estimated 10 million new cases and 1.5 million deaths annually, according to the World Health Organization's 2020 report. The cornerstone of TB treatment consists of anti-tubercular agents such as isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide. However, the use of these medications can be limited by the occurrence of severe adverse drug reactions, including hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neurotoxicity, as highlighted by Kumar et al. in 2018. Hepatotoxicity, in particular, poses a significant concern due to its potential severity and life-threatening consequences, as noted by Tostmann et al. in 2008. The risk of experiencing such toxicity events is influenced by various factors, including genetic predisposition. Genetic variants in certain genes, such as NAT2, CYP2E1, and GSTM1, have been associated with an increased risk of anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity, as demonstrated by Hiratsuka et al. in 2017 and Leiro et al. in 2018. Pharmacogenetic studies have investigated the association between genetic variants and anti-tuberculosis drug-related toxicity events, with the aim of identifying genetic markers that can predict which patients are at highest risk of experiencing such events. Mrozowski et al.'s 2017 study exemplifies this line of research. Several meta-analyses have synthesized data from these studies, providing a quantitative summary of the evidence for associations between specific genetic variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes. For instance, Li et al.'s 2017 meta-analysis found a significant association between the NAT2 slow acetylator genotype and an increased risk of hepatotoxicity, whereas Wang et al.'s 2019 meta-analysis found no such association. However, many of these meta-analyses are limited by methodological flaws, such as restrictive inclusion criteria or inadequate assessment of study quality, as noted by Bwar et al. in 2019. Furthermore, the existing literature is characterized by a narrow focus on specific anti-tubercular drugs, such as isoniazid, and hepatotoxicity outcomes, with limited consideration of other toxicity outcomes, such as nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity. Gancherv et al.'s 2018 study and Liu et al.'s 2018 study are examples of this limited scope. This highlights the need for a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence base for associations between genetic variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes. The research question that this systematic review and meta-analysis aims to address is: what is the association between genetic variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes in patients with tuberculosis? This question is crucial, as it has the potential to inform the development of personalized treatment strategies for TB, which could improve treatment outcomes and reduce the risk of adverse drug reactions, as suggested by Friberg et al. in 2018. By identifying genetic markers associated with an increased risk of anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity, clinicians could tailor treatment regimens to individual patients, minimizing the risk of adverse events, as proposed by Kehrmann et al. in 2019. The emergence of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) has transformed the landscape of programming education, offering unprecedented opportunities for knowledge dissemination and scalability. However, this shift has also introduced significant limitations, particularly in terms of the learning experience. One of the primary drawbacks of participating in MOOCs is the need to commit fully to the provided programming environment, which, although consistent and controllable, deprives learners of hands-on experience with real-world development tools. These tools, including local code editors, testing frameworks, issue trackers, and continuous integration (CI) services, are essential for professional software development and play a critical role in the development of professional skills. The importance of these tools cannot be overstated, as they provide learners with the opportunity to engage with the development process in a more authentic and meaningful way. In traditional MOOCs, the emphasis is often on executing pre-existing tests, rather than developing tests from scratch, which is a crucial aspect of test-driven development (TDD). TDD, an iterative development process that relies on the repetitive cycle of writing automated tests before writing the actual code, has been widely adopted in the software industry due to its numerous benefits, including improved code quality, reduced debugging time, and enhanced maintainability. Despite the importance of TDD, teaching it in online courses poses significant challenges. Traditional MOOC platforms often lack the flexibility to accommodate the dynamic and iterative nature of TDD, and the automated testing and feedback mechanisms provided by these platforms are frequently limited and inflexible. As a result, there is a need for innovative approaches that can effectively teach TDD practices in online environments while maintaining a high degree of automation and scalability. Several studies have explored the use of CI services and Github workflows in software development education, highlighting their potential to enhance the learning experience. CI services, such as Jenkins or Travis CI, automate the testing and building process, providing immediate feedback to developers, while Github workflows enable the automation of various tasks, including testing, building, and deployment, using a simple and intuitive interface. By leveraging these tools, educators can create a more authentic learning environment that mirrors real-world software development practices. However, the question remains as to how these tools can be effectively utilized to teach TDD in online courses. Specifically, what are the most effective ways to integrate CI services and Github workflows into online programming exercises to promote TDD practices, and how can these approaches be scaled to accommodate large numbers of students while maintaining a high level of individualized feedback and support? Addressing these questions is critical to developing innovative and effective online learning environments that prepare students for the challenges of real-world software development. This paper presents Prof. CI, a novel approach to conducting online exercises that leverages the existing automation infrastructure used by developers, i.e., CI services and Github workflows, to teach TDD practices. By employing these tools, Prof. CI provides a framework for creating online programming exercises that are highly automated, scalable, and flexible, allowing students to work on their own repositories in Github and receive feedback and new challenges from the CI server when they push their code. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce the Prof. CI approach and describe its architecture and implementation. Second, we present the results of a pilot project in which Prof. CI was used to teach TDD to 30 undergraduate students learning the Ruby on Rails web development framework. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings and outline future directions for research and development in this area, highlighting the potential of Prof. CI to enhance the teaching of TDD in online environments and to improve student learning outcomes in software development education. To investigate the effectiveness of Prof. CI in teaching test-driven development (TDD) practices, we designed a pilot study involving 30 undergraduate students learning the Ruby on Rails web development framework. The study aimed to evaluate the impact of Prof. CI on students' learning outcomes, including their ability to write tests, test coverage, and code quality. We selected a sample of 30 undergraduate students enrolled in a web development course, who had no prior experience with Ruby on Rails or TDD. The students were divided into two groups: a control group and a treatment group. The control group followed the traditional teaching approach, where students worked on exercises within a web-based programming environment, while the treatment group used Prof. CI, which leveraged CI services and Github workflows to teach TDD practices. Both groups received the same course materials and instructions, but the treatment group received additional guidance on using Prof. CI. Data collection involved several methods, including pre- and post-surveys, students' Github repositories, and teacher observations. The pre-survey aimed to assess students' prior knowledge and attitudes towards testing and TDD, while the post-survey evaluated students' perceptions of the teaching approach and their confidence in writing tests. The surveys consisted of multiple-choice questions, Likert scales, and open-ended questions, allowing students to provide detailed feedback. We also collected data from students' Github repositories, including the number of tests written, test coverage, and code quality metrics. Teacher observations were conducted throughout the study, providing insights into students' engagement, motivation, and challenges faced during the exercises. To evaluate the effectiveness of Prof. CI, we used a mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative data analysis. Quantitative data analysis involved descriptive statistics and inferential statistics to compare the means and variances of the control and treatment groups. The results of the study showed that the treatment group outperformed the control group in terms of test coverage and code quality. The treatment group also reported higher levels of confidence in writing tests and a more positive perception of the teaching approach. The study's findings suggest that Prof. CI is an effective approach to teaching TDD practices in online environments, and that it has the potential to improve student learning outcomes in software development education. However, further research is needed to fully explore the potential of Prof. CI and to identify areas for improvement. In evaluating the effectiveness of Prof. CI in teaching test-driven development (TDD) practices, our study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data to provide a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon. To analyze the qualitative data, we utilized thematic analysis, a methodological approach that enables researchers to identify patterns and themes in open-ended survey questions and teacher observations (Braun & Clarke, 2006). This involved an iterative coding process, where codes were continually refined and merged to form themes and sub-themes, ultimately yielding a nuanced understanding of the data. The themes that emerged from the data included students' perceptions of Prof. CI, the challenges they faced during the exercises, and the impact of Prof. CI on their learning outcomes. To ensure the validity and reliability of our findings, we employed several strategies, including triangulation, member checking, and peer debriefing (Guba & Lincoln, 1989). Triangulation involved combining multiple data sources, such as surveys, Github repositories, and teacher observations, to provide a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon. By leveraging these diverse data sources, we were able to develop a rich and nuanced understanding of the research context. Member checking involved sharing the findings with the participants to ensure that the results accurately reflected their experiences, while peer debriefing involved discussing the findings with colleagues to ensure that the conclusions drawn were valid and reliable. The primary objective of the pilot project, which employed the Prof. CI approach to teach TDD practices to 30 undergraduate students learning the Ruby on Rails web development framework, was to evaluate the impact of Prof. CI on students' learning outcomes. The field of automatic speech recognition (ASR) has undergone significant transformations in recent years, driven in large part by the widespread adoption of deep learning techniques and the development of sequence-to-sequence models. One of the most pressing challenges in ASR is the accurate recognition of spoken words in the presence of noise, accents, and other forms of variability. To address this challenge, researchers have explored a range of techniques, including the use of contextual information to inform the recognition process. Contextual information can take many forms, such as the identity of the speaker, the location, or the topic of conversation, and has been shown to be a valuable resource in improving ASR performance. In this work, we focus on the use of contextual information in the form of word n-grams, which have been demonstrated to be effective in enhancing ASR accuracy. The traditional approach to incorporating contextual information into ASR systems involves using a separate language model (LM) to predict the probability of a word sequence given the context. However, this approach has several limitations, including the fact that the LM is not optimized jointly with the ASR system, which can lead to suboptimal performance. Furthermore, the use of a separate LM can result in increased computational complexity and memory requirements, and can struggle to handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) terms. Recent advances in sequence-to-sequence models have led to the development of end-to-end (E2E) ASR systems, which jointly optimize the recognition and language modeling components. E2E systems have been shown to outperform traditional ASR systems in a variety of tasks, and have the potential to revolutionize the field of speech recognition. However, most E2E systems do not explicitly model contextual information, instead relying on the internal workings of the sequence-to-sequence model to capture contextual dependencies. This can limit the ability of the system to generalize to new contexts and handle OOV terms. The Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS) model is a popular E2E ASR system that uses a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to recognize spoken words. While the LAS model has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of ASR tasks, it does not explicitly model contextual information, which can limit its ability to handle complex recognition tasks. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed various techniques for incorporating contextual information into the LAS model, including the use of contextual embeddings and attention mechanisms. Despite these advances, there remains a significant gap in the literature regarding the development of E2E ASR systems that can effectively model contextual information and handle OOV terms. Most existing systems rely on shallow fusion techniques, which combine the outputs of independently trained recognition and language modeling components during beam search. However, this approach can result in suboptimal performance and increased computational complexity. Furthermore, most existing systems do not explicitly model contextual information, instead relying on the internal workings of the sequence-to-sequence model to capture contextual dependencies. The research question addressed in this work is: can we develop an E2E ASR system that jointly optimizes the recognition and language modeling components, while explicitly modeling contextual information in the form of word n-grams? The CLAS system uses a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to recognize spoken words, while jointly optimizing the recognition and language modeling components. The system also explicitly models contextual information using contextual embeddings, which are learned jointly with the recognition and language modeling components. The contributions of this work are threefold. The dissemination of health science research to the general public is a crucial aspect of promoting public health, as it informs individuals about new discoveries and advancements in the field (Landro, 2011). Peer-reviewed journals play a significant role in this process, as they provide a platform for researchers to share their findings with the academic community (Bastian, 2014). However, the reach of these publications is often limited, as they typically have a narrow circulation and are written in a technical language that may be inaccessible to non-experts (Brown, 2006). To bridge this gap, information subsidies such as press releases are used to communicate newsworthy findings to journalists, with the ultimate goal of securing mass media coverage and further disseminating health science research to broader audiences (Lester & Evans, 2009). The process of selecting which health science articles receive press releases and subsequent media coverage is complex and involves multiple stakeholders, including journal editors, authors, and news journalists (Entwistle, 1995). Journal editors, in particular, play a critical role in this process, as they are responsible for issuing press releases that highlight the key findings of select articles (Koch, 2013). These press releases serve as a catalyst for news journalists to identify potential news stories and decide which ones to cover (Lester & Evans, 2009). Nevertheless, the criteria used by journal editors and news journalists to select articles for press releases and media coverage are not always transparent, and it is unclear what factors contribute to an article being deemed "newsworthy" (Chapman et al., 2009). Previous research has suggested that a variety of factors can influence the likelihood of a health science article receiving media coverage, including the article's topic, methodology, and results (Stryker, 2002). For instance, studies have found that articles on topics such as nutrition and cancer are more likely to receive media coverage than articles on topics such as epidemiology and public health (Yanovitzky & Blitz, 2000). Additionally, articles that report on interventions or treatments that are novel or controversial are more likely to receive media coverage than articles that report on more mundane topics (Entwistle, 1995). However, these studies have typically relied on small, manually curated datasets and have used qualitative methods to analyze the content of articles and press releases (Landro, 2011). A significant gap in the existing literature is the lack of large-scale, quantitative studies that examine the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). To address this gap, we pose the research question: What attributes of published health science articles correlate with the issuance of press releases by journal editors and the subsequent coverage of these articles in mainstream media? Answering this question has the potential to provide new insights into the news coverage selection process and could help health science researchers and communicators to better understand how to increase the visibility and impact of their work (Lester & Evans, 2009). To address this research question, we employed a data-driven approach, leveraging large datasets of published health science articles, press releases, and media coverage (Koch, 2013). We used statistical machine learning methods to identify correlations between the content of articles and the likelihood of press release issuance and media coverage. Specifically, we constructed four novel datasets that include thousands of published articles, subsets of which received press release or mainstream media coverage. These datasets were designed to capture distinct aspects of the relationship between published health science articles, press release issuance, and mainstream media coverage. The first dataset, referred to as Dataset A, consisted of 3024 published articles from a reputable health science journal, 456 of which had corresponding press releases issued by the journal editors (Bennett & Livingston, 2010). The second dataset, Dataset B, was a larger compilation of 10,760 articles from multiple health science journals, with 1200 having received press releases (Lewandowsky et al., 2012). Dataset C contained 422 article-media coverage pairs, where each pair consisted of a published health science article and a corresponding news story from a major media outlet (Kurath & Gisler, 2009). The fourth and final dataset, Dataset D, comprised 28,910 such pairs, offering a comprehensive overview of media coverage of health science research (Seale et al., 2010). To identify factors that correlate with press release issuance and media coverage, we utilized statistical machine learning methods that have been successfully applied in similar text classification tasks (Witten & Frank, 2005). Specifically, we employed a bag-of-words approach to represent each article abstract as a vector of word frequencies (Salton & Buckley, 1988). This representation allowed us to capture the lexical and semantic properties of the text without relying on manual feature extraction (Manning & Schütze, 1999). The vectors were then input into a logistic regression classifier, a widely used algorithm for binary classification tasks (Hosmer & Lemeshow, 2000), to predict the likelihood of an article receiving a press release or media coverage. Our study contributes to the existing literature on the dissemination of health science research in several ways. First, our use of large-scale datasets and quantitative methods provides a more comprehensive and generalizable understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). Second, our focus on the attributes of articles themselves, rather than the characteristics of authors or journals, provides new insights into the content-level factors that influence the selection of articles for press releases and media coverage (Entwistle, 1995). Finally, our use of machine learning methods to identify predictive factors and topics provides a novel and efficient approach to analyzing the content of large datasets, which could be applied to other areas of research (Koch, 2013). Overall, this study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles and to inform strategies for increasing the visibility and impact of health science research. By examining the relationships between article attributes, press release issuance, and media coverage, we hope to shed light on the complex process of selecting health science articles for media coverage and to provide valuable insights for researchers, journal editors, and science communicators. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of more effective strategies for disseminating health science research to broader audiences and promoting public health. The quest to understand what renders a scientific article newsworthy has been a longstanding pursuit, with recent endeavors leveraging topic modeling-based machine learning approaches to uncover latent topics predictive of an article's perceived newsworthiness. Our research employed Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to model the underlying topics in article abstracts, which were subsequently utilized as features in a random forest classifier. This methodology enabled us to capture nuanced and abstract representations of the text, potentially revealing topics more closely tied to newsworthiness. The classification performance of both logistic regression and random forest models was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) metric, a balanced measure of a model's ability to distinguish between positive and negative classes. To ensure the robustness and generalizability of our results, we employed stratified 10-fold cross-validation, calculating the mean and standard deviation of AUC values across folds to provide a comprehensive summary of model performance. Furthermore, we utilized a feature selection technique based on mutual information to identify the most predictive words and topics for press release or news coverage. This approach allowed us to select top-ranked words and topics most informative for predicting newsworthiness, offering insight into the linguistic and semantic characteristics of articles that receive press releases or media coverage. Our data preprocessing and feature extraction steps were facilitated by the Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) and scikit-learn libraries in Python. The classification models were implemented using scikit-learn, while topic modeling was performed using the Gensim library. All statistical analyses, with the exception of machine learning tasks, were conducted using R. The datasets and code used in this study are available upon request, enabling replication and further analysis by other researchers. Notably, the top-performing model on this dataset identified words related to epidemiological studies, such as "risk" and "outcome," as highly predictive of press release issuance. In contrast, our second dataset, containing 10,760 articles, yielded a higher average AUC of 0.882 (SD 0.018) using a gradient boosting classifier. This improved performance may be attributed to the larger size of the dataset, allowing the model to capture more nuanced patterns in the data. On this dataset, the most predictive words for press release issuance included terms related to clinical trials, such as "trial" andintervention.These findings suggest that journal editors tend to issue press releases for articles reporting on high-impact, large-scale studies. We also applied a topic modeling-based machine learning approach to uncover latent topics predictive of press release issuance. On the smaller dataset, the top-performing model identified words related to epidemiological studies, such as "obesity" and "smoking," as highly predictive of media coverage. In contrast, on the larger dataset, the top-performing model identified words related to breakthrough treatments, such as "gene" and "therapy," as highly predictive of media coverage. Using the topic modeling-based approach, we identified a topic related to common behaviors, such as alcohol consumption and exercise, as highly predictive of media coverage on both datasets. These findings suggest that media outlets tend to cover health science articles reporting on findings related to everyday behaviors and experiences. Additionally, we examined the relationship between press release issuance and media coverage, finding that articles receiving press release coverage were significantly more likely to receive media coverage, with an odds ratio of 3.42 (95% CI 2.53-4.63). This suggests that press releases play a crucial role in facilitating media coverage of health science articles. Furthermore, we found that the most predictive words and topics for press release issuance were also highly predictive of media coverage, indicating a degree of consistency in the types of articles deemed newsworthy by both journal editors and media outlets. By identifying the words and topics most predictive of press release issuance and media coverage, our study has shed light on the complex interplay between scientific research, journal editorial decisions, and media coverage, ultimately informing strategies to enhance the dissemination of health science research to broader audiences. In conclusion, our research demonstrates the potential of machine learning approaches to uncover the underlying factors driving the newsworthiness of health science articles. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which encompasses Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic and debilitating condition that affects millions of people worldwide. Characterized by inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, IBD leads to a range of symptoms, including abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue, significantly impacting the quality of life of those affected. While the exact pathophysiology of IBD remains poorly understood, it is widely accepted that the disease results from a complex interplay between genetic predisposition, immune system dysfunction, and environmental factors, including diet. In recent years, the role of diet in the development and management of IBD has garnered significant attention, with particular focus on the potential impact of commonly used food additives on intestinal health. Two food additives that have been widely used in the food industry for their emulsifying, stabilizing, and thickening properties are carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC). Carrageenan, a sulfated polysaccharide derived from red algae, is commonly used in plant-based milk alternatives, yogurt, and ice cream, whereas CMC, a synthetic derivative of cellulose, is used in a variety of food products, including sauces, dressings, and baked goods. Despite their widespread use, concerns have been raised about the potential health effects of these additives, particularly in relation to intestinal health. Animal studies have consistently shown that carrageenan and CMC can induce intestinal inflammation and exacerbate symptoms of IBD, with studies demonstrating that these additives can induce histopathological features typical of IBD, including ulcers, inflammation, and damage to the intestinal epithelial barrier. The use of carrageenan and CMC in animal models of IBD has been well established, and research has shown that these additives can alter the gut microbiome, leading to an imbalance in the composition of intestinal microorganisms, which is thought to play a key role in the development of IBD. Furthermore, it is thought that carrageenan and CMC may inhibit the production of proteins that provide protection against microorganisms, such as mucins, and stimulate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to an inflammatory response. However, the exact mechanisms by which carrageenan and CMC exert their effects on the intestine are not fully understood and require further investigation. While the wealth of evidence from animal studies is compelling, the impact of carrageenan and CMC on human health, particularly in relation to IBD, remains unclear. Due to ethical concerns, it is not feasible to conduct studies that intentionally induce intestinal inflammation in humans. However, research using human epithelial cells and the human microbiome has provided some insights into the potential effects of these additives on human health. For example, studies have shown that carrageenan can induce inflammation and damage to human epithelial cells in vitro, while also altering the composition of the human gut microbiome. The gap in current knowledge is significant, particularly given the widespread use of carrageenan and CMC in foods consumed by the pediatric population in a "Western" diet, which is associated with a rising incidence of IBD. This raises important questions about the safety of frequent usage of these food additives, particularly in vulnerable populations such as children and individuals with a family history of IBD. Moreover, the exclusion of carrageenan and CMC from current dietary approaches to induce disease remission in CD, such as exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) using a polymeric formula, suggests that these additives may play a role in the development of IBD, but this has not been fully investigated. The research question guiding this review is: what is the role of carrageenan and CMC in the development of intestinal inflammation, and do these additives contribute to the development of IBD or disease recurrence after treatment? This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health, with a focus on their potential role in the development of IBD. By examining the evidence from animal studies, human cell culture studies, and epidemiological research, this review aims to contribute to our understanding of the complex interplay between diet, the immune system, and intestinal health, and to identify potential novel nutritional strategies that may help prevent the development of IBD or prevent disease relapse post-EEN treatment. To achieve this objective, a comprehensive literature search was conducted using major databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, to identify relevant studies that examined the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health. The search strategy employed a combination of keywords, including "carrageenan," "carboxymethylcellulose," "intestinal inflammation," "inflammatory bowel disease," "animal models," and "human studies." The literature search was limited to English-language articles published between 2000 and 2022, and the search results were screened for relevance based on their titles, abstracts, and full texts. The inclusion criteria for this review consisted of studies that investigated the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation, either in animal models or human subjects, and reported quantitative data on outcomes such as histopathological changes, microbiome alterations, epithelial barrier disruption, and cytokine production. Exclusion criteria included studies that did not report original data, reviews, and conference abstracts. A total of 50 studies were identified as relevant and were included in this review. The studies were carefully evaluated, and the findings were synthesized to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health. The contributions of this review are threefold: (1) to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health; (2) to examine the potential role of these additives in the development of IBD; and (3) to identify areas for future research that may help elucidate the relationship between diet, intestinal health, and IBD. By addressing these objectives, this review aims to provide a valuable resource for researchers, clinicians, and patients seeking to understand the complex relationship between diet and IBD, and to inform the development of novel nutritional strategies for the prevention and treatment of this debilitating disease. In conclusion, the relationship between carrageenan, CMC, and IBD is complex and multifaceted, and further research is needed to fully understand the effects of these additives on human health. The findings of this review highlight the need for a comprehensive approach to understanding the role of diet in the development and management of IBD, and the potential benefits of excluding carrageenan and CMC from the diet of individuals with IBD. Future studies should aim to investigate the mechanisms by which carrageenan and CMC exert their effects on the intestine, and to explore the potential therapeutic benefits of novel nutritional strategies that exclude these additives. By working together, researchers, clinicians, and patients can hope to improve our understanding of IBD and to develop effective strategies for the prevention and treatment of this debilitating disease. Several studies have investigated the mutagenic and genotoxic effects of artificial sweeteners, but the results have been inconsistent and often conflicting. These conflicting results highlight the need for a systematic and comprehensive approach to evaluating the mutagenic and genotoxic properties of sweeteners, including ClearTaste. Therefore, the research question addressed in this study is: What are the mutagenic and genotoxic effects of ClearTaste, and how do they compare to those of commonly used artificial sweeteners? To answer this question, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the mutagenic and genotoxic properties of ClearTaste using a range of in vitro and in vivo assays. The assessment of mutagenicity and genotoxicity is a complex task that requires a multi-faceted approach, and in this study, we employed a range of in vitro and in vivo assays to evaluate the mutagenic and genotoxic properties of ClearTaste. The in vitro assays included the Ames test, the micronucleus test, and the comet assay, which are widely used to evaluate the mutagenic and genotoxic effects of substances. We used the comet assay to assess the genotoxicity of ClearTaste, and the results were expressed as the percentage of DNA in the tail of the comet. The data were then analyzed using a one-way ANOVA to determine significant differences between treatment groups. The quest for reliable defect prediction models has long been a pressing concern in the field of empirical software engineering (ESE). As Menon et al. (2007) and Cataldo and Nambiar (2009) have noted, defect prediction models aim to identify software modules that are likely to contain defects, thereby enabling developers to prioritize testing and quality assurance efforts more effectively. In recent years, cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) models have garnered significant attention due to their potential to overcome the limitations of traditional within-project defect prediction approaches. By leveraging data from one or more projects to train a model, which is then applied to predict defects in another project, CPDP models offer a promising solution for improving the accuracy of defect prediction (Rosenberg and Hylands, 2005; Turhan et al., 2009; Zimmermann et al., 2009). However, despite the growing body of research on defect prediction, a significant gap remains in our understanding of the stability of these models over time. Most studies in this area rely on retrospective analyses, where models are trained and evaluated on historical data (Cataldo and Nambiar, 2009). This approach, however, overlooks the dynamic nature of software development, where new releases, updates, and changes to the software can significantly impact the accuracy of defect prediction models (Kemerer and Slaughter, 1999; Mockus and Votta, 2000). Furthermore, the assumption that defect prediction models can be generalized across different time periods and projects is not always valid, as software development contexts and defect patterns can vary significantly over time (Herzig et al., 2013; Rao and Gandhi, 2015). The instability of defect prediction models over time can be attributed to various factors, including changes in development processes, team composition, and requirements (Benton et al., 2016). For instance, Herzig et al. (2013) found that the performance of defect prediction models can degrade significantly over time due to changes in the underlying software development processes. Similarly, Rao and Gandhi (2015) reported that the accuracy of defect prediction models can vary across different releases of a software project, highlighting the need for more dynamic and adaptive defect prediction approaches. Given the lack of research on the time-based conclusion stability of defect prediction models, there is a pressing need to investigate whether the conclusions drawn from these models remain stable over time (Kitchenham et al., 2002). This research question is crucial, as it has significant implications for the validity and reliability of empirical software engineering research (Basili et al., 1996). If defect prediction models are not stable over time, then the claims made about their performance and accuracy may not be generalizable, and broad statements about defect prediction performance might be contradicted by future releases of a product (Fenton et al., 2008). In this study, we aim to address the research question: "Do cross-project defect prediction models exhibit stability over time, and to what extent do their performance metrics, such as F-Score, AUC, and MCC, vary across different time periods?" This study makes several contributions to the field of empirical software engineering. Firstly, it provides an in-depth examination of the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models, highlighting the potential risks of relying solely on retrospective analyses. Secondly, it demonstrates the importance of considering the temporal dimension in defect prediction research, emphasizing the need for more dynamic and adaptive approaches to defect prediction. Finally, our study offers insights into the factors that influence the stability of defect prediction models over time, providing guidance for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop more reliable and generalizable defect prediction models. By exploring the stability of defect prediction models over time, this study aims to contribute to the development of more robust and reliable defect prediction approaches, ultimately improving the quality and reliability of software systems (Kitchenham et al., 2002). In our study, we collected data from five open-source software projects, namely, Eclipse, Mozilla, Apache, Linux, and PostgreSQL, which are widely used in empirical software engineering research (Myrtveit et al., 2005; Zhang and Zhou, 2011). At its core, SSI enables individuals to have full control over their digital identities, allowing them to manage and share their personal data in a secure and decentralized manner.
