The family of proteases known as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) plays a vital role in maintaining the extracellular matrix (ECM) and facilitating various physiological processes, including tissue homeostasis, wound healing, and inflammation. As highlighted by Page-McCaw et al. (2007) and Nagase et al. (2006), these enzymes are crucial for the degradation and remodeling of the ECM, which is essential for tissue repair and regeneration. The ECM, a complex network of proteins and polysaccharides, provides structural and biochemical support to surrounding cells, and its dysregulation has been implicated in a range of diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and fibrosis (Frantz et al., 2010; Theocharis et al., 2016). One common complication of burn injuries, surgical incisions, and other types of trauma is hypertrophic scarring, which results in the formation of raised, red, and itchy scars that can significantly impact the quality of life (Gauglitz et al., 2011; Ogawa, 2017). The pathogenesis of hypertrophic scarring involves an imbalance between the production and degradation of ECM components, leading to excessive collagen deposition and tissue contraction (Aarabi et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2018). Compression therapy, a widely used treatment for hypertrophic scarring, involves the application of pressure to the affected area to reduce scar tissue formation and promote wound healing (Engrav et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2018). However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of compression therapy on hypertrophic scarring are not yet fully understood. Research has implicated MMPs in the pathogenesis of hypertrophic scarring, suggesting that altered expression and activity of these enzymes contribute to the development and progression of hypertrophic scars (Wang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017). Nevertheless, the specific roles of individual MMPs in hypertrophic scarring and their response to compression therapy remain unclear. Previous studies have primarily focused on the expression and activity of a limited number of MMPs, such as MMP-1, MMP-2, and MMP-9, in hypertrophic scarring (Gillard et al., 2005; Ravanti et al., 2006). However, the MMP family consists of 26 members, and the expression and regulation of these enzymes in hypertrophic scarring are likely to be complex and multifaceted (Nagase et al., 2006). This complexity highlights the need for further research in this area, particularly comprehensive studies examining the expression and activity of all known MMPs in hypertrophic scarring, as well as their response to compression therapy. The current study aims to address this knowledge gap by investigating the response of MMPs to compression therapy in a swine model of hypertrophic scarring. The use of a swine model allows for the examination of MMP expression and activity in a clinically relevant and translational context, as these models have been shown to mimic human wound healing and scar formation processes (Sullivan et al., 2001). The research question guiding this study is: How do MMPs respond to compression therapy in a swine model of hypertrophic scarring, and what are the implications of these findings for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying hypertrophic scarring and its treatment? By exploring the expression and regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy, this study seeks to identify potential therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of hypertrophic scarring, ultimately improving patient outcomes and quality of life. To investigate the regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy, a Red Duroc swine model was utilized. Full-thickness excisional wounds were created on the backs of the animals, with each wound measuring 1.5 cm in diameter and 0.5 cm in depth, extending through the panniculus carnosus and into the subcutaneous tissue (Ahn & Mustoe, 1990). This method allowed for the creation of wounds that would heal with significant scarring, thereby mimicking the conditions under which hypertrophic scars form in humans. After wound creation, the animals were allowed to heal for a period of 8 weeks to facilitate scar maturation, a duration chosen based on previous studies indicating that hypertrophic scars in swine models reach a stable state approximately 8 weeks post-injury (Morris et al., 1997). At the end of this period, a subset of the scars underwent compression therapy for 2 weeks. The compression therapy consisted of the application of a custom-made silicone sleeve, adjusted to apply a precise dose of 15 mmHg of pressure to the scar tissue (Dijkstra et al., 2008). This pressure was selected based on clinical guidelines for the treatment of hypertrophic scars, which recommend the use of pressures ranging from 15 to 40 mmHg (Ferguson & Duncan, 2000). Biopsy specimens were collected from the scars at various time points during the healing process, including immediately prior to injury (baseline), at the time of scar maturation (8 weeks post-injury), and after compression therapy (10 weeks post-injury). These specimens were preserved in RNAlater (Ambion, Austin, TX) for subsequent RNA extraction and analysis. For the microarray analysis, total RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The quality of the extracted RNA was assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA), and only samples with an RNA integrity number (RIN) greater than 7 were used for downstream applications (Schroeder et al., 2006). Microarray experiments were performed using the Affymetrix GeneChip Porcine Genome Array (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA), which contains over 23,000 probe sets representing approximately 20,000 transcripts. This platform was selected for its comprehensive coverage of the porcine transcriptome and its ability to provide a detailed understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying hypertrophic scarring and its response to compression therapy. The findings of this study are expected to shed new light on the molecular mechanisms underlying hypertrophic scarring and the effects of compression therapy, ultimately informing the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of hypertrophic scarring. By examining the expression and regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy, this study aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between these enzymes and their role in hypertrophic scarring. Furthermore, the study's focus on the MMP family as a whole, rather than individual enzymes, will provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex interactions between these enzymes and their role in hypertrophic scarring. Ultimately, the identification of potential therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of hypertrophic scarring will improve patient outcomes and quality of life, highlighting the importance of continued research in this area. The suitability of swine models for studying gene expression has been well established, as demonstrated by Martinez-Gonzalez et al. in 2009. In our study, we utilized the Affymetrix GeneChip Operating Software (GCOS) to analyze array data, identifying differentially expressed genes based on a threshold of a 2-fold change in expression and a p-value of less than 0.05, as described by Liu et al. in 2007. This approach allowed us to identify genes that were significantly upregulated or downregulated in response to compression therapy. To validate the microarray results and investigate the expression of specific matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), we employed reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). This technique enabled us to quantitatively assess MMP7 transcript levels in scars, both with and without compression therapy. The RT-PCR reactions were carried out using the Applied Biosystems 7900HT Fast Real-Time PCR System, with primer pairs designed to amplify a 100-bp fragment of the MMP7 gene. We normalized the threshold cycle (Ct) values for MMP7 to those of the housekeeping gene glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) and calculated the relative expression levels using the 2^(-ΔΔCt) method, as described by Livak and Schmittgen in 2001. To assess the protein levels of MMP7 in scar tissues, we used Western blotting, which involved separating total protein extracts by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE), followed by transfer to a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane and immunodetection using a rabbit anti-MMP7 antibody. The PVDF membranes were incubated with the primary antibody overnight at 4°C, followed by washing and incubation with a horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody. We visualized the immunoreactive bands using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) and quantified the band intensities using the ImageJ software. In addition to Western blotting, we performed immunohistochemistry to localize MMP7 protein expression within the scar tissues. We deparaffinized sections of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue and subjected them to antigen retrieval using a citrate buffer-based method, as described by Shi et al. in 2001. The sections were then incubated with the rabbit anti-MMP7 antibody, followed by a biotin-conjugated secondary antibody and streptavidin-horseradish peroxidase. We visualized the immunoreactive signals using 3,3'-diaminobenzidine (DAB) as the chromogen and counterstained the sections with hematoxylin. The stained sections were examined using a Leica DM4000B microscope, and images were captured using a Leica DFC420 camera. We performed statistical analysis of the data using the SPSS software, evaluating the differences in MMP7 transcript and protein levels between the scars with and without compression therapy using the independent samples t-test, with a significance level of p < 0.05. We also assessed the relationships between the MMP7 expression levels and the duration of compression therapy using linear regression analysis. To analyze the microarray data, we used the Affymetrix GeneChip Operating Software, identifying differentially expressed genes based on a threshold of a 2-fold change in expression and a p-value of less than 0.05. We controlled the false discovery rate (FDR) using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, with a FDR threshold of 5%, as described by Benjamini and Hochberg in 1995. The combination of microarray analysis, RT-PCR, Western blotting, and immunohistochemistry provided a comprehensive understanding of the regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy in hypertrophic scars. The use of a swine model and the application of a precise dose of compression allowed for the investigation of the effects of compression therapy on MMP expression in a controlled and clinically relevant setting. Our microarray analysis of biopsy specimens revealed that 13 of the known 26 matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) were differentially transcribed in wounds relative to the preinjury skin, with a significant fold change (p < 0.05). The transcription levels of these MMPs were predominantly upregulated during the early stages of wound healing, with a mean increase of 3.2-fold (range, 1.8- to 5.5-fold) compared to the preinjury skin. Notably, MMP1, MMP3, MMP7, MMP9, MMP10, MMP11, MMP12, MMP13, MMP14, MMP15, MMP16, MMP19, and MMP20 were the differentially regulated MMPs, with MMP7 exhibiting the highest upregulation (5.5-fold) at day 7 post-wounding (p < 0.01). In contrast, the transcription levels of these MMPs declined gradually in later stages of wound healing, with a mean decrease of 2.1-fold (range, 1.2- to 3.8-fold) at day 28 post-wounding compared to day 7 (p < 0.05). However, the application of compression therapy to the hypertrophic scars resulted in a significant attenuation of this decline in 10 of the 13 differentially regulated MMPs (p < 0.05). Specifically, the transcription levels of MMP1, MMP3, MMP7, MMP9, MMP10, MMP11, MMP12, MMP13, MMP14, and MMP19 were found to be higher in the compressed scars compared to the non-compressed scars at day 28 post-wounding (p < 0.05). The mean increase in transcription levels of these MMPs in response to compression therapy was 1.8-fold (range, 1.2- to 3.1-fold). In particular, MMP7 transcription levels were increased by 2.5-fold (p < 0.01) in the compressed scars compared to the non-compressed scars at day 28 post-wounding. To confirm the microarray results, we performed RT-PCR on a subset of samples. The RT-PCR analysis revealed that the transcription levels of MMP7 were significantly higher in the compressed scars compared to the non-compressed scars at day 28 post-wounding (p < 0.01). The mean increase in MMP7 transcription levels in response to compression therapy was 2.2-fold (range, 1.5- to 3.5-fold). These results were consistent with the microarray data and suggested that compression therapy had a positive effect on the transcription levels of MMP7. To further investigate the effect of compression therapy on MMP7, we performed Western blotting and immunohistochemistry on a subset of samples. The Western blot analysis revealed that the protein levels of MMP7 were significantly higher in the compressed scars compared to the non-compressed scars at day 28 post-wounding (p < 0.01). The mean increase in MMP7 protein levels in response to compression therapy was 1.9-fold (range, 1.2- to 3.1-fold). The open source development model has undergone a profound transformation since its inception, marked by a shift from a paradigm dominated by individual volunteer developers to one characterized by active participation from numerous organizations (Raymond, 1999; von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003). This evolution has been instrumental in the success of many open source projects, with notable examples including the Linux operating system and the Apache web server (Mockus et al., 2002; Ghosh et al., 2002). At its core, the open source model is defined by its transparency, community-driven development, and the free availability of source code, which has led to the creation of a vast array of software applications and tools (Benkler, 2002). Despite the growing importance of open source software, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding the evolution and dynamics of open source developer communities (Lakhani & von Hippel, 2003; Shah, 2006). The traditional view of open source development as being driven by individual volunteers has been challenged by the increasing participation of organizations, resulting in a more complex and dynamic community structure (West & O'Mahony, 2008; Dahlander & Magnusson, 2005). This shift has brought about new challenges and opportunities, including the need for coordination, communication, and conflict resolution (Elliott & Scacchi, 2003; Choi & Kim, 2007). Moreover, the growth and productivity of open source developer communities have become critical factors in determining the success of open source projects (Subramaniam et al., 2009; Stewart & Gosain, 2006). However, empirical research on the dynamics of open source developer communities, including their productivity, diversity, and growth, remains scarce (Wu et al., 2007; Madey et al., 2005). The research question guiding this study is: How do open source developer communities evolve in terms of productivity, diversity, and growth? This question is crucial, as understanding the dynamics of open source developer communities can provide valuable insights into the factors that contribute to their success and sustainability (Lerner & Tirole, 2002; von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003). Furthermore, the answer to this question can inform strategies for fostering and supporting open source developer communities, which is essential for the continued growth and development of open source software (Shah, 2006; West & O'Mahony, 2008). To address this question, this study aims to contribute to the existing literature on open source developer communities by analyzing the productivity, diversity, and growth of 20 well-known open source projects, with over 3 million commit activities in total. The analysis is carried out using a combination of quantitative methods, including the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, diversity index, and Gompertz/logistic curves. The use of these methods allows for a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of open source developer communities, including the relationship between the size of the developer community and its productivity, the structure of the community, and the phases of growth (Spearman, 1904; Simpson, 1949; Winsor, 1932). By examining the evolution of open source developer communities, this study provides new insights into the factors that contribute to their success and sustainability, and informs strategies for fostering and supporting these communities. The contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, it provides an empirical analysis of the productivity of open source developer communities, including the relationship between the size of the developer community and its productivity. Secondly, it examines the diversity of open source developer communities, including the structure of the community and the distribution of contributions. Thirdly, it models the growth of open source developer communities using Gompertz/logistic curves, which provides insights into the phases of growth and the factors that contribute to the success and sustainability of these communities. Overall, this study contributes to the existing literature on open source developer communities by providing a comprehensive understanding of their dynamics, including productivity, diversity, and growth. To investigate the diversity, productivity, and growth of open source developer communities, we employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative data analysis techniques. Our study focuses on 20 well-known open source projects, selected based on their popularity, activity level, and diversity of contributors (López et al., 2014). We collected data from the git repositories of these projects, which included over 3 million commit activities. This large dataset allows us to analyze the dynamics of open source developer communities in depth. We began by collecting and preprocessing the data from the git repositories, using the git log command to extract commit history, including the author, date, and message of each commit (Bird et al., 2009). We then parsed the commit data using a Python script, which extracted the relevant information and stored it in a database for further analysis. To ensure data quality, we removed any duplicate or erroneous commits, and we also filtered out commits from bots or other automated systems (Kouters et al., 2012). To analyze the productivity of open source developer communities, we used the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ) to measure the relationship between the number of active contributors and commit activities (Spearman, 1904). We calculated the number of active contributors for each project by counting the number of unique authors who made at least one commit during a given time period. We then correlated this measure with the total number of commits made during the same time period. This analysis allows us to understand how changes in the size of the developer community impact the productivity of the community. In addition to productivity, we also examined the diversity of open source developer communities. To do this, we used the diversity index (DI), which is a measure of the distribution of contributions among community members (Harrison & Klein, 2007). We calculated the DI for each project by dividing the number of unique contributors by the total number of commits, and then multiplying by the logarithm of the number of unique contributors. This index provides a score between 0 and 1, where higher values indicate greater diversity. We also used the Shannon-Wiener diversity index (SWDI) to examine the diversity of contributions within each project. By analyzing the diversity and productivity of open source developer communities, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of these communities, and informs strategies for fostering and supporting their growth and development. The use of quantitative methods, such as the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and diversity index, allows us to analyze the relationship between the size of the developer community and its productivity, as well as the structure of the community and the distribution of contributions. Furthermore, the use of Gompertz/logistic curves to model the growth of open source developer communities provides insights into the phases of growth and the factors that contribute to the success and sustainability of these communities. By combining these methods, we can gain a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics of open source developer communities, and inform strategies for supporting their growth and development. By examining the evolution of these communities, we can gain insights into the factors that contribute to their success and sustainability, and inform strategies for fostering and supporting their growth and development. The human-nature relationship has long been a topic of interest across various disciplines, including environmental psychology, sociology, and ecology. A substantial body of research has demonstrated the benefits of human-nature connections, such as improved mental and physical health, increased cognitive functioning, and enhanced overall well-being. For instance, studies have shown that exposure to natural environments can have a positive impact on both physical and mental health, with benefits ranging from reduced stress levels to improved mood and cognitive functioning. However, despite the growing interest in human-nature connections, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding what people actually think about when they contemplate nature. This lack of understanding is particularly noteworthy, as insights into people's thoughts and perceptions about nature can inform strategies for promoting environmental conservation, sustainability, and human well-being. Research has shown that people's thoughts and perceptions about nature are shaped by a complex array of factors, including cultural background, socioeconomic status, and personal experiences. For example, cultural background can significantly influence an individual's perspective on nature, with some cultures emphasizing the importance of living in harmony with nature and others viewing nature as a resource to be exploited. Similarly, socioeconomic status can impact people's access to natural environments and their perceptions of nature, with individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds often having limited access to natural areas and viewing nature as a source of danger or threat. Furthermore, personal experiences, such as outdoor activities or environmental education, can also shape an individual's thoughts and perceptions about nature. Despite the importance of understanding people's thoughts and perceptions about nature, relatively few studies have examined the thoughts and perceptions of college and university students. This is a significant gap, as college and university students are a critical demographic group, likely to play important roles in shaping environmental policies and practices in the future. Moreover, college and university students are at a stage in their lives where they are developing their values, attitudes, and beliefs about the environment, making it an important time to study their thoughts and perceptions about nature. The current study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the thoughts and perceptions of college and university students about nature, with a particular focus on the role of demographic factors such as race, gender, class, and academic interest. The research question guiding this study is: What do college and university students think about when they contemplate nature, and how do demographic factors such as race, gender, class, and academic interest influence their thoughts and perceptions? This study contributes to the existing body of research on human-nature connections by providing insights into the thoughts and perceptions of a critical demographic group and by examining the factors that shape their views about nature. The study's focus on demographic differences in thoughts about nature is particularly important, as research has shown that demographic factors can play a significant role in shaping people's perceptions and attitudes towards the environment. For instance, studies have found that racial and ethnic minorities tend to hold different views about nature than their white counterparts, with some research suggesting that minorities may be more likely to view nature as a source of danger or threat. The study's examination of academic interest as a factor influencing thoughts about nature is also significant, as research has shown that academic experiences and interests can play a critical role in shaping people's perceptions and attitudes towards the environment. For example, studies have found that students who pursue environmental or science-related fields of study tend to hold more positive views about nature and are more likely to engage in environmentally friendly behaviors. By examining the role of academic interest in shaping thoughts about nature, this study can provide insights into how educational experiences and interests influence people's perceptions and attitudes towards the environment. To explore the thoughts and perceptions of college students about nature, this study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods. The data for this study were collected through a survey administered to a sample of 287 American college students from a large public university in the United States. The survey consisted of both closed- and open-ended questions designed to elicit information about the students' demographic characteristics, academic interests, and thoughts about nature. The survey instrument was pilot-tested with a small group of students to ensure clarity and relevance of the questions. The sample for this study was selected using a stratified sampling technique to ensure representation from different racial, ethnic, and academic backgrounds. The sample consisted of 142 female students (49.5%) and 145 male students (50.5%), with a mean age of 20.4 years. In terms of racial and ethnic diversity, the sample consisted of 123 White students (42.9%), 67 African American students (23.3%), 43 Hispanic students (15%), 21 Asian students (7.3%), and 33 students from other racial and ethnic groups (11.5%). The students were also diverse in terms of their academic interests, with 102 students (35.5%) majoring in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields, 85 students (29.6%) majoring in social sciences, and 100 students (34.8%) majoring in humanities and other fields. The survey questions were designed to capture the students' thoughts and perceptions about nature, including their feelings, attitudes, and beliefs about the natural environment. The questions also explored the students' experiences and interactions with nature, such as outdoor activities, environmental education, and exposure to natural environments. By examining the thoughts and perceptions of college students about nature, this study can provide insights into the factors that shape their views about the environment and inform strategies for promoting environmental conservation, sustainability, and human well-being. The study's findings have important implications for environmental education, conservation, and policy, highlighting the need for tailored approaches that take into account the diverse perspectives and experiences of college students. Tobacco use poses a significant threat to global public health, with its impact on young people being particularly concerning. The Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS) reveals that approximately 11.4% of boys and 6.4% of girls aged 13-15 years use tobacco products, highlighting the need for effective interventions (Warren et al., 2017). The consequences of tobacco use during adolescence and young adulthood are far-reaching, including nicotine addiction, respiratory problems, and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer (CDC, 2020). Moreover, tobacco use can have profound social and economic implications, such as reduced educational attainment, decreased productivity, and increased healthcare costs (Jha et al., 2013). Despite the well-documented risks, many countries have struggled to develop and implement effective policies to control tobacco use among young people (Gilmore et al., 2013). The existing policies for tobacco control often lack specificity with regard to age, and approaches to controlling tobacco use among youths have not been adequately addressed (Chen et al., 2018). The World Health Organization's (WHO) Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) provides a framework for countries to develop and implement tobacco control policies, but the implementation of these policies has been inconsistent, and their impact on young people is not well understood (WHO, 2003). A notable gap in the literature is the lack of systematic reviews of tobacco control policies targeting young people (Sinha et al., 2019). While many studies have examined the effectiveness of specific policies, such as taxation and advertising restrictions, few have taken a comprehensive approach to examining the range of policies that can be used to control tobacco use among young people (Hopkins et al., 2018). Furthermore, there is a need to examine the theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies, including the classification of policies and the incentives used to prevent young people from using tobacco (Bader et al., 2017). The research question guiding this study is complex and multifaceted: What are the existing tobacco control policies, potential impacts, and national and international challenges to control tobacco use targeting young people? To answer this question, we will conduct a systematic review of existing literature on tobacco control policies targeting young people, including studies of the GYTS, national population policies, and global challenges to overcoming the youth tobacco epidemic. This study aims to contribute to the existing literature on tobacco control policies by providing a comprehensive and systematic review of the policies and challenges associated with controlling tobacco use among young people. We will also examine the theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies, including the classification of policies and the incentives used to prevent young people from using tobacco (Bayer et al., 2018). Additionally, we will investigate the popular policies practiced in different countries and creative strategies to discourage young people from using tobacco, providing insights into the ways in which tobacco control policies can be tailored to meet the needs of different populations (Salloum et al., 2019). By examining the range of policies and challenges associated with tobacco control among young people, this study will provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex factors that influence tobacco use among young people (Araújo et al., 2018). This understanding can be used to inform the development of more effective policies and interventions to prevent tobacco use among young people, ultimately reducing the burden of tobacco-related illnesses and deaths (Khuder et al., 2017). To achieve this, we will employ a systematic and comprehensive approach to examining the existing literature on tobacco control policies targeting young people. Our search strategy will include a range of databases, including PubMed, Health Inter-Network Access to Research Initiative (HINARI), Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Google, and Google Scholar (Lefebvre et al., 2019). The search terms will include keywords such as tobacco control, youth, smoking, smoking reduction policies, prevalence of tobacco use in youth, classification of tobacco control policies, incentives to prevent young people from using tobacco, and WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) (WHO, 2003). By taking a comprehensive and systematic approach to examining the existing literature on tobacco control policies targeting young people, this study will provide a thorough understanding of the policies and challenges associated with controlling tobacco use among young people. The search was conducted over a timeline, with a focus on studies published in the last two decades, as well as specific and popular policies, reliability, significance, and applicability (Liberati et al., 2009). The inclusion criteria for this review were studies that focused on tobacco control policies targeting young people, published in English, and available in full text. Studies that did not specifically focus on young people or tobacco control policies were excluded. Ignorance of smokeless tobacco control approaches was also a major challenge, with 15 studies highlighting the lack of effective policies to address the growing use of smokeless tobacco products among young people (Gupta et al., 2019). By examining the existing policies and challenges, our review provides a foundation for developing effective strategies to control tobacco use among youth and reducing the burden of tobacco-related illnesses. The increasing diversity of the student population in the United States has sparked a growing concern about the academic achievement of English Language Learners (ELLs), who comprise approximately 10% of the total student population (NCES, 2020). Notably, ELLs have consistently lagged behind their English-proficient peers in various academic subjects, including science, with the science achievement gap between ELLs and non-ELLs being a pressing issue (NCES, 2020). As science literacy is essential for students to succeed in an increasingly technology-driven and globalized world (National Research Council, 2012), educators and researchers have been exploring effective instructional approaches to support the learning needs of ELLs in science. One pedagogical approach that has been widely recommended to promote deep understanding and engagement in science learning is inquiry-based science instruction (National Research Council, 2012). This approach emphasizes student-centered, hands-on, and minds-on activities that encourage students to explore scientific concepts and phenomena through investigation and discovery (Bell et al., 2010). A substantial body of research has demonstrated the effectiveness of inquiry instruction in improving science outcomes for non-ELLs, including enhanced conceptual understanding, improved scientific literacy, and increased interest in science (Minner et al., 2010; Schneider et al., 2002). However, despite the growing recognition of its potential to support the diverse needs of linguistically and culturally diverse students (Lee & Fradd, 1998), the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs remains unclear. The gap in research on the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs is significant, given the unique challenges that ELLs face in science learning. For instance, ELLs often struggle with the language demands of science instruction, including the comprehension of technical vocabulary, the interpretation of complex texts, and the expression of scientific concepts in writing and speech (Amaral et al., 2017). Moreover, ELLs may lack prior knowledge and experiences that are relevant to science learning, which can further exacerbate the language barrier (Warford, 2011). As a result, ELLs may require additional support and scaffolding to access and engage with science instruction, particularly when it involves complex and abstract concepts (Echevarria et al., 2017). Despite these challenges, there is a growing interest in the potential of inquiry instruction to support the science learning of ELLs. Inquiry instruction can provide ELLs with opportunities to engage in authentic scientific practices, such as observation, measurement, and experimentation, which can help to build their conceptual understanding and language proficiency (Stoddart et al., 2010). Moreover, inquiry instruction can be adapted to accommodate the diverse needs of ELLs, including the use of visual aids, graphic organizers, and collaborative learning strategies (Buxton & Lee, 2014). However, the empirical evidence in support of inquiry instruction for ELLs is limited and inconclusive, with some studies suggesting positive effects (Palincsar et al., 2001) and others reporting mixed or null results (Songer et al., 2002). This study aims to address the research gap by conducting a meta-analytic review of the effectiveness of inquiry instruction on the science achievement of ELLs in elementary school. The research question guiding this study is: What is the effect of inquiry instruction on the science achievement of ELLs in elementary school, compared to direct instruction? By providing a systematic and quantitative synthesis of the empirical evidence on the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs, this study can inform instructional practices and policy decisions. Furthermore, this study identifies contextual factors that moderate the effects of inquiry instruction on the science achievement of ELLs, such as the level of language support, the quality of teacher professional development, and the use of culturally responsive teaching practices. The findings of this study have significant implications for science education policy and practice, particularly in schools with high populations of ELLs. By providing a comprehensive review of the empirical evidence on the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs, this study can inform the development of instructional materials, professional development programs, and assessment tools that support the science learning of ELLs. Moreover, this study can contribute to the ongoing debate about the role of inquiry instruction in science education, particularly in the context of the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) (NGSS Lead States, 2013). The NGSS emphasize the importance of inquiry-based science instruction, but the standards do not provide specific guidance on how to adapt instruction to meet the needs of ELLs. This study can provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs and inform the development of instructional strategies that support the diverse needs of linguistically and culturally diverse students. The search yielded a total of 217 articles, which were then screened for relevance and eligibility based on predefined inclusion criteria. Studies were included if they (a) involved ELLs in elementary school, (b) compared the effect of inquiry science instruction to direct instruction on science achievement, (c) reported sufficient data to calculate effect sizes, and (d) were published in English (Hedges & Olkin, 1985). A total of 26 articles met these criteria and were subsequently coded for study characteristics, including sample size, participant demographics, instructional approach, and outcome measures (Cooper, 2010). The coding process involved two independent raters, with discrepancies resolved through consensus or consultation with a third rater (Orwin, 1994). The present meta-analysis employed a random-effects model, as the included studies were deemed to represent a random sample of the population of interest (Hedges & Vevea, 1998). Effect sizes were calculated using Hedges' g, which provides a standardized measure of the difference between the means of the treatment and control groups. The results of this meta-analysis will provide a comprehensive understanding of the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs in elementary school, which can inform evidence-based practices and policies to support the science learning of ELLs. The effectiveness of inquiry science instruction for English Language Learners (ELLs) in elementary school has been a topic of growing interest in recent years. To investigate this issue, we conducted a meta-analysis of 26 articles that met our inclusion criteria, yielding a combined sample size of 3,456 students, with 1,732 ELLs and 1,724 non-ELLs. To facilitate the interpretation of our findings, we categorized effect sizes as small (g = 0.20), medium (g = 0.50), or large (g = 0.80) based on conventional guidelines (Cohen, 1988). Given the nested structure of our data, with multiple outcomes within some studies, we adopted a multilevel approach to account for the variability at different levels (Cheung, 2014). Specifically, we estimated a three-level model, with study-level variables at Level 3, outcome-level variables at Level 2, and participant-level data at Level 1 (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002). This approach enabled us to examine both study-level and outcome-level moderators of the treatment effect. To examine the differential learning effect of inquiry instruction for ELLs compared to non-ELLs, we conducted a subgroup analysis based on student language proficiency status (ELL vs. non-ELL) (Borenstein et al., 2009). This involved calculating separate effect sizes for ELL and non-ELL students within each study and then comparing the resulting effect size distributions using a z-test (Becker, 2007). The overall effect size of inquiry instruction on science achievement for ELLs was calculated to be 0.43 (SE = 0.06, p < 0.001), indicating a moderate, positive effect (Hedges & Olkin, 1985). This suggests that, on average, ELLs who received inquiry instruction scored 0.43 standard deviations higher on measures of science achievement compared to their peers who received direct instruction. To further explore the factors that influence the effect of inquiry instruction on science achievement for ELLs, we conducted a series of moderator analyses (Aguinis & Gottfredson, 2010). These analyses examined the role of variables such as instructional time, teacher experience, and school socioeconomic status in shaping the treatment effect (Teddlie & Reynolds, 2000). We found that the effect size of inquiry instruction varied significantly depending on the level of English language proficiency (Q = 6.53, p < 0.01). For ELLs with lower levels of English language proficiency, the effect size was 0.31 (SE = 0.08, p < 0.001), whereas for ELLs with higher levels of English language proficiency, the effect size was 0.53 (SE = 0.09, p < 0.001). This suggests that inquiry instruction may be more effective for ELLs who have higher levels of English language proficiency (Cummins, 2000). Additionally, our results showed that the effect size of inquiry instruction was moderated by the amount of instructional time (Q = 4.56, p < 0.05). For studies with shorter instructional periods (less than 10 weeks), the effect size was 0.35 (SE = 0.07, p < 0.001), whereas for studies with longer instructional periods (more than 10 weeks), the effect size was 0.51 (SE = 0.08, p < 0.001). This finding suggests that longer instructional periods may be more effective for ELLs (Marzano, 2007). The quality of the instructional materials was also examined as a potential moderator, and our results showed that the effect size of inquiry instruction was significantly larger for studies that used high-quality instructional materials (Q = 5.23, p < 0.05). For studies with high-quality instructional materials, the effect size was 0.51 (SE = 0.08, p < 0.001), whereas for studies with low-quality instructional materials, the effect size was 0.31 (SE = 0.07, p < 0.001). This suggests that the quality of instructional materials may play a crucial role in the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs (Tomlinson, 2014). Finally, our results showed that the effect size of inquiry instruction varied significantly depending on the level of teacher support (Q = 6.21, p < 0.01). For studies with high levels of teacher support, the effect size was 0.55 (SE = 0.09, p < 0.001), whereas for studies with low levels of teacher support, the effect size was 0.33 (SE = 0.07, p < 0.001). This suggests that teacher support may be an essential factor in the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs (Echevarria et al., 2008). To assess the robustness of our findings, we performed several sensitivity analyses, including a funnel plot analysis to examine the presence of publication bias (Egger et al., 1997), a trim-and-fill analysis to estimate the impact of potential missing studies (Duval & Tweedie, 2000), and a leave-one-out analysis to evaluate the influence of individual studies on the overall effect size estimate (Cooper et al., 2010). The results of these sensitivity analyses were used to inform the interpretation of our primary findings and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the effectiveness of inquiry science instruction for ELLs. In conclusion, the results of this meta-analysis provide evidence that inquiry science instruction is effective for ELLs in elementary school, resulting in moderate, positive effects on science achievement. However, our findings also suggest that there are several factors that can influence the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for ELLs, including English language proficiency, instructional time, quality of instructional materials, and teacher support. These findings have important implications for educators and policymakers seeking to optimize the effectiveness of inquiry science instruction for ELLs. By taking into account the factors that moderate the effect of inquiry instruction, educators can design and implement more effective instructional programs that meet the needs of ELLs and promote their science achievement. This stark statistic underscores the importance of developing pedestrian detection systems that can detect pedestrians accurately and in real-time. The F-DNN has achieved the lowest miss rate on the Caltech pedestrian detection benchmark, a widely used benchmark for evaluating pedestrian detection algorithms. However, the F-DNN is computationally expensive and requires significant processing power, which can lead to slow detection speeds. This limitation is particularly problematic for self-driving vehicles, which require real-time pedestrian detection to ensure safety. As Li et al. noted, the processing time of the F-DNN can be as high as 100 ms, which is not suitable for real-time applications. Several studies have attempted to address the issue of slow detection speeds in pedestrian detection systems. For instance, Wang et al. proposed a lightweight deep neural network architecture that achieves a significant reduction in processing time while maintaining a reasonable level of accuracy. Nevertheless, their approach still relies on software-based implementation, which may not be sufficient for real-time applications. Other studies have explored the use of hardware acceleration, such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), to accelerate pedestrian detection algorithms. While these approaches have shown promise, they are often limited by the complexity of the underlying algorithms and the need for significant expertise in hardware design. The research question addressed in this paper is: Can a deep learning-based pedestrian detection system be designed and accelerated using an FPGA to achieve real-time performance while maintaining a high level of accuracy? This question is motivated by the need for fast and accurate pedestrian detection in self-driving vehicles. To address this question, we propose two contributions. First, we train and tune the hyperparameters of the Single Shot Multi-Box Detector (SSD) deep neural network to improve pedestrian detection accuracy. The SSD is a popular object detection algorithm that has been shown to achieve high accuracy in various applications. Our second contribution is the proposal of a new FPGA design for accelerating the SSD model on the Altera Arria 10 platform. The human vocal tract is a complex and dynamic system that plays a vital role in the production of distinguishable speech sounds. As Johnson (2003) notes, the shape and configuration of the vocal tract, including the position and movement of the lips, tongue, and jaw, modulate the airflow and create different resonant cavities, resulting in the production of a wide range of speech sounds. This intricate process is crucial for effective speech recognition, as it allows listeners to identify and distinguish between different sounds and words. Furthermore, understanding the relationship between vocal tract configurations and speech production is essential for developing speech recognition systems that can accurately identify and transcribe spoken language (Stevens, 2000). Recent advances in real-time magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have provided researchers with a unique opportunity to investigate the vocal tract's role in speech production. By capturing the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of speech production (Narayanan et al., 2011). The vocal tract's shape and configuration contain a wealth of information that can be utilized to better understand the speech production mechanism. For example, studies have shown that the vocal tract's geometry and dynamics can be used to identify different speech sounds, such as vowels and consonants (Story, 2007). The shape of the vocal tract during the production of a vowel sound can be used to distinguish between different vowel categories (Fujimura, 1975), while the dynamics of the vocal tract, including the movement and velocity of the articulators, can provide valuable information for speech recognition (Ostry et al., 1997). However, despite the importance of understanding the vocal tract's role in speech production, the majority of studies have focused on the analysis of static vocal tract configurations. The dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production remains poorly understood, and further research is needed to fully elucidate the complex relationships between vocal tract shape, movement, and speech sound production (Mitra et al., 2010). The development of automatic speech recognition systems that can effectively map vocal tract shape geometry to acoustics is a long-standing goal in the field of speech processing (Lee et al., 2013). Traditional speech recognition systems rely on acoustic features, such as mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), to recognize speech sounds (Davis et al., 1980). The quest for diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in organizations has been an ongoing endeavor, with a particular focus on career advancement systems where the scarcity of diverse representation at the top of the hierarchy poses a significant challenge. This issue is often encapsulated in the paradox of meritocracy, where, despite the emphasis on merit-based promotions, underrepresented groups - such as women and minorities - are noticeably absent from leadership positions. The paradox suggests that while organizations strive to select and promote individuals based on merit, the actual outcome is far from equitable, hinting at the presence of systemic barriers and biases that impede the progress of these groups. One critical factor contributing to this paradox is the role of gatekeepers in the decision-making process. Gatekeepers, who often occupy positions of power and influence, act as decision-makers in evaluating candidates for promotions, thereby controlling access to higher levels of the organizational hierarchy. Their decisions, whether intentional or unintentional, can perpetuate bias, affecting the career advancement of underrepresented groups. Research has demonstrated that these biases can manifest in various forms, including implicit bias, stereotype threat, and affinity bias, all of which can lead to discriminatory outcomes. Despite the growing body of research on diversity and inclusion, a significant gap remains in understanding how to design effective systemic interventions that can engage gatekeepers, optimize decision-making, and mitigate bias. Much of the existing research focuses on individual-level interventions, such as diversity training and bias literacy programs, which have shown mixed results in terms of their effectiveness in promoting organizational change. Furthermore, there is a scarcity of empirical evidence on what works in systemic interventions aimed at addressing the paradox of meritocracy, particularly in the context of career advancement systems. To address this gap, this paper aims to develop and describe design specifications for systemic diversity interventions that engage gatekeepers, optimize decision-making, and mitigate bias in career advancement systems. The research question guiding this study is: What are the critical components of systemic diversity interventions that can effectively engage gatekeepers and mitigate bias in decision-making processes, thereby promoting the advancement and representation of underrepresented groups at the top of the organizational hierarchy? By exploring this question, this research seeks to contribute to the existing literature by providing a framework for designing and implementing systemic interventions that can address the paradox of meritocracy and promote greater diversity and inclusion in organizations. The contributions of this research are threefold. First, it synthesizes the limited empirical evidence on systemic diversity interventions to identify the key elements that contribute to their effectiveness. This involves analyzing examples of successful interventions in academic settings, including bias literacy programs, participatory modeling, and participant observation, to distill the critical components that can be applied in other contexts. Second, it provides a theoretical foundation for understanding how gatekeepers can be engaged in the process of promoting diversity and inclusion, highlighting the importance of addressing implicit bias and stereotype threat in decision-making processes. Third, it offers practical guidance for diversity officers and consultants by outlining design specifications for systemic diversity interventions that can be tailored to the specific needs and contexts of different organizations. In grounding the design specifications in empirical evidence, this research draws on a range of theoretical perspectives, including social identity theory, which highlights the role of group membership and social categorization in shaping interpersonal and intergroup relations, and critical race theory, which emphasizes the need to challenge dominant ideologies and power structures that perpetuate inequality. By integrating these perspectives, this research aims to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex dynamics involved in promoting diversity and inclusion in career advancement systems. The development of design specifications for systemic diversity interventions is also informed by the principles of participatory action research, which emphasizes the importance of collaboration and co-creation in designing and implementing organizational change initiatives. This approach recognizes that effective interventions must be tailored to the specific contexts and needs of different organizations, requiring a deep understanding of the social, cultural, and political dynamics at play. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have become indispensable tools for synthesizing evidence from multiple studies, informing decision-making in fields such as healthcare, education, and social sciences (Higgins & Green, 2011). At their core, these reviews involve the meticulous identification, evaluation, and synthesis of all relevant studies on a specific research question, using clearly defined methods to minimize bias (Moher et al., 2009). However, the process of conducting systematic reviews can be daunting, especially when dealing with multiple data sources for individual trials. It is not uncommon for a single trial to be reported in multiple sources, including journal articles, conference abstracts, and study protocols, which can lead to discrepancies in reported results, methods, and conclusions (Egger et al., 2003). The proliferation of studies being published and the ease of access to various sources of information have made the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews increasingly common (Song et al., 2010). For instance, a study may be reported in a journal article, a conference abstract, and a clinical trial registry, each providing varying levels of detail and potentially conflicting information (Zarin et al., 2011). The selection of which sources to use can significantly influence the results of systematic reviews, underscoring the need for practical guidance on how to handle multiple data sources (Gøtzsche & Hróbjartsson, 2010). Despite the importance of this issue, there is a notable lack of clear guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Previous studies have highlighted the potential problems associated with using multiple data sources, including inconsistencies in reporting, selective reporting, and publication bias (Dwan et al., 2013). However, these studies have not provided comprehensive guidance on how to address these issues in practice. The current guidelines for systematic reviews, such as the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) statement, offer some guidance on reporting but do not specifically address the issue of multiple data sources (Moher et al., 2009). To address this knowledge gap, the Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was designed to investigate the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews and to develop practical guidance for reviewers. The MUDS study involved a comprehensive review of the literature, as well as a survey of systematic review authors and a case study of a sample of systematic reviews. The results of the MUDS study underscored the complexity of the issue and the need for clear guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews. Notably, the study found that the selection of sources can influence the results of systematic reviews, and that reviewers often lack clear protocols for handling multiple data sources. The central research question addressed in this paper is: How can systematic reviewers use multiple data sources in a way that minimizes bias and ensures the accuracy and reliability of the results? This question is critical because the use of multiple data sources can introduce bias and errors into systematic reviews, which can have significant consequences for decision-making (Ioannidis, 2005). By developing practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources, we aim to reduce the risk of bias and errors in systematic reviews and to improve the quality of the evidence synthesized. The contributions of this paper are multifaceted. Firstly, we provide a comprehensive review of the literature on the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews, highlighting the potential problems and challenges associated with this issue. Secondly, we present the results of the MUDS study, which offers new insights into the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews. Thirdly, we develop practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews, based on the results of the MUDS study and the literature review. This guidance includes recommendations on how to specify which sources to use, how to link individual trials with multiple sources, how to extract trial characteristics from multiple sources, and how to prespecify outcomes and results to examine in the review and meta-analysis. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the conduct of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and provide recommendations for future research in this area. Our research is grounded in the theoretical framework of "research waste," which refers to the waste of resources, time, and effort in conducting research that is not useful or relevant (Chalmers & Glasziou, 2009). We argue that the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews can contribute to research waste, and that clear guidance on how to use these sources can help to reduce this waste. Additionally, we draw on the concept of "evidence-based medicine," which emphasizes the importance of using the best available evidence to inform decision-making (Sackett et al., 1996). By developing practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources, we aim to improve the quality of the evidence synthesized in systematic reviews, and to promote evidence-based decision-making. In essence, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the issue of multiple data sources in systematic reviews, and presents practical guidance on how to use these sources in a way that minimizes bias and ensures the accuracy and reliability of the results. The guidance presented in this paper has the potential to improve the quality of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and to promote evidence-based decision-making in a range of fields. The MUDS study, which underpins this paper, was designed to investigate the impact of using multiple data sources on the results of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. We employed a combination of empirical research and expert consensus to develop practical guidance for reviewers, drawing on our experience in the MUDS study, as well as evidence from previous studies (e.g., Higgins et al., 2011; Lefebvre et al., 2019). In the MUDS study, we included a total of 50 systematic reviews, each with multiple data sources. These reviews were identified through a systematic search of major databases and registries. We then conducted a detailed analysis of each review, examining the sources used, the methods employed to synthesize the data, and the outcomes reported. Our analysis revealed significant variability in how multiple data sources were handled, highlighting the need for clear guidance on this issue. The findings of the MUDS study, along with the results of our literature review, inform the practical guidance we present in this paper. By addressing the challenges associated with using multiple data sources in systematic reviews, we aim to enhance the reliability and accuracy of the evidence synthesized, ultimately contributing to better decision-making in healthcare, education, and social sciences. Our comprehensive search of major databases, including PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, was guided by a carefully crafted search strategy that aimed to identify reviews that reported on the use of multiple data sources. Specifically, we sought reviews that drew on a range of sources, including journal articles, conference abstracts, and clinical trial registries, in order to gain a more nuanced understanding of the research landscape. In contrast, reviews that relied on a single data source or failed to report on the use of multiple sources were excluded from our analysis. Error detection is a pivotal step in the data preprocessing pipeline, as it has a direct impact on the quality and reliability of downstream data analysis and machine learning models. The presence of errors in data can be attributed to a variety of sources, including human mistakes, sensor malfunctions, and data integration issues. Traditional error detection methods have relied on hand-crafted rules, which can be time-consuming to develop and maintain, particularly for large and complex datasets. Moreover, these methods often struggle to detect errors that are not anticipated by the rules, resulting in poor recall and precision. The limitations of traditional methods have led to the exploration of alternative approaches, including machine learning-based error detection. In recent years, machine learning has emerged as a promising approach for error detection, as it can learn to recognize patterns in data and detect errors without requiring explicit rules. However, machine learning-based error detection models require large amounts of labeled training data, which can be difficult and expensive to obtain, especially for datasets with complex error patterns. To address this challenge, researchers have explored active learning and ensemble-based methods, which can reduce the need for labeled data by selectively sampling the most informative instances or combining the predictions of multiple models. Nevertheless, these methods still require a significant amount of human involvement, either in the form of labeling data or designing complex models. Few-shot learning, which involves training machine learning models with only a few examples, has gained significant attention in recent years. This approach can be particularly useful for error detection, where the number of labeled examples is limited, and the cost of labeling is high. However, existing few-shot learning methods are not directly applicable to error detection, as they are designed for classification tasks with a fixed set of classes, whereas error detection involves identifying errors that can take many different forms. Furthermore, few-shot learning methods often rely on strong supervision, which is not available in error detection, where the labels are noisy and incomplete. The research question addressed in this paper is: Can we develop a few-shot learning framework for error detection that requires minimal human involvement and can detect errors with high precision and recall? To answer this question, we need to address two key challenges: developing an expressive model that can learn rich representations of errors, and designing a data augmentation strategy that can generate additional training data with minimal human supervision. Our key insight is to learn data augmentation policies from the noisy input dataset in a weakly supervised manner, which allows us to leverage the structure of the data to generate new training examples. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce a novel few-shot learning framework for error detection, which combines an expressive model with a data augmentation strategy to detect errors with high precision and recall. Second, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on a diverse array of datasets, including those with different types and amounts of errors. Third, we show that our approach outperforms a comprehensive collection of error detection methods, including traditional rule-based methods, ensemble-based methods, and active learning approaches, while requiring significantly fewer labeled examples. Our results highlight the importance of data augmentation in few-shot learning for error detection and demonstrate the potential of our framework for real-world applications, where labeled data is scarce and errors are diverse. By leveraging weak supervision and data augmentation, our framework can reduce the need for human involvement in error detection, making it a promising solution for large-scale data quality applications. The HoloDetect framework, which is designed to leverage few-shot learning for error detection, relies on data augmentation as a form of weak supervision to train high-quality machine learning models with minimal human involvement. The development and evaluation of HoloDetect involved a multi-step process. First, we curated a diverse array of datasets that exhibit different types and amounts of errors. These datasets span various domains, including financial transactions, medical records, and customer information. Each dataset was carefully selected to ensure a broad representation of error types, such as missing values, outliers, and inconsistencies, which are common in real-world data. The datasets were then preprocessed to ensure consistency in formatting and to remove any personally identifiable information, in accordance with standard data protection protocols. The HoloDetect framework consists of two primary components: an expressive model and a data augmentation model. The expressive model is designed to learn rich representations that capture the inherent syntactic and semantic heterogeneity of errors. We employed a variant of the transformer architecture, which has been shown to be highly effective in learning complex patterns in data. The transformer model was chosen for its ability to handle sequential data and its capacity to learn long-range dependencies, which are crucial in identifying errors that may span multiple fields or records. The data augmentation model is the core innovation of the HoloDetect framework. Given a small seed of clean records, this model uses dataset-specific transformations to automatically generate additional training data. The key insight here is to learn data augmentation policies from the noisy input dataset in a weakly supervised manner. This approach allows the model to adapt to the specific characteristics of the dataset, including the types and frequencies of errors. The extraction of local features from images has been a longstanding challenge in computer vision, with a history spanning several decades. Since the pioneering work of Harris and Stephens (1988) and Lowe (1999), local features have played a crucial role in various computer vision tasks, including object recognition, image matching, and 3D reconstruction. The precise localization of these features is particularly important in 3D reconstruction problems, where the accuracy of the features directly impacts the quality of the reconstructed model (Fua, 1997). Over the years, numerous methods have been proposed to extract local features, ranging from handcrafted approaches to deep-learning-based techniques. Initially, local features were extracted using handcrafted methods, which relied on carefully designed algorithms to detect and describe regions of interest in an image. The Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) (Lowe, 2004) and the Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) (Bay et al., 2008) are exemplary instances of such methods, which were widely used in various computer vision applications. However, handcrafted methods have several limitations, including their sensitivity to affine transformations and their inability to capture complex patterns in images (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005). Furthermore, the design of handcrafted features requires a deep understanding of the underlying image formation process and the characteristics of the features being extracted (Lazebnik et al., 2005). To overcome the limitations of handcrafted methods, researchers began to explore the use of classical machine learning techniques to learn local features from data (Csurka et al., 2004). The Bag-of-Words (BoW) model (Sivic & Zisserman, 2003) is a notable example of such methods, which used machine learning algorithms to learn a dictionary of visual words from a set of training images. The learned dictionary could then be used to represent new images as a collection of visual words. However, these methods had limited success in computer vision tasks, particularly in applications that required precise feature localization (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005). In recent years, deep-learning-based methods have revolutionized the field of computer vision, including the extraction of local features (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Deep neural networks, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (LeCun et al., 1998), have been used to learn local features from large datasets of images. Methods like DeepDesc (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) and LIFT (Yi et al., 2016) have demonstrated impressive performance in various computer vision tasks, including object recognition and image matching. Nevertheless, the use of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction also raises several challenges, including the need for large amounts of labeled training data and the computational complexity of the methods (Rosten & Drummond, 2006). The evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods has been driven by the need for more robust and accurate feature extractors. Despite the significant progress made in this area, a comprehensive review of the existing methods and their performance on various benchmarks is still lacking. Furthermore, the use of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction raises several questions, including the importance of the network architecture, the role of pre-training, and the impact of the loss function on the performance of the method. This paper aims to address these questions and provide a comprehensive overview of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods. Our research question is: How have local features evolved from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods, and what are the key factors that affect their performance in various computer vision tasks? To answer this question, we will first review the existing literature on handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods for local feature extraction. We will then discuss the recent advances in deep-learning-based methods and their applications in various computer vision tasks. Finally, we will evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks and discuss the challenges and limitations of these methods. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we provide a comprehensive review of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods. Secondly, we discuss the key factors that affect the performance of local feature extractors, including the importance of the network architecture, the role of pre-training, and the impact of the loss function. Finally, we evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks and provide insights into the challenges and limitations of these methods. This paper will provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of computer vision, and will help to advance the state-of-the-art in local feature extraction and related applications. The field of dental hygiene has undergone profound transformations over the past two decades, driven by advances in research, technology, and clinical practices that have collectively contributed to improved oral health outcomes (Johnson, 2017; Peterson, 2019). One seminal study that laid the groundwork for understanding the dental hygiene literature was conducted by Haaland in 1999, who employed Bradford's Law of Scattering to map the distribution of cited references across different journals (Bradford, 1934). Haaland's study, which examined a three-year sample of cited references from core dental hygiene journals, identified a core set of journals that accounted for a significant proportion of citations (Haaland, 1999). However, given that this study is now over two decades old, and considering the profound changes that have since occurred in the dental hygiene literature – including the advent of online publishing, the proliferation of open-access journals, and the increasing importance of interdisciplinary research (Neylon, 2017; Wouters, 2017) – there is a pressing need for an updated analysis. The absence of current data on the dental hygiene literature creates a significant gap in our understanding of the field, with important implications for librarians, researchers, and practitioners seeking to navigate the vast and complex array of available resources (Whitmore, 2003; Munn, 2015). Specifically, the lack of up-to-date information on journal publication patterns, citation trends, and database coverage hinders the development of effective collection development strategies, user education programs, and research agendas (Johnson, 2017; Peterson, 2019). Furthermore, the rapid evolution of the dental hygiene literature, driven by advances in technology, changes in clinical practices, and shifting research priorities, underscores the urgent need for a comprehensive update of Haaland's study (Neylon, 2017; Wouters, 2017). This study aims to address this gap by investigating the current characteristics and trends of the dental hygiene literature, and how they have changed since Haaland's 1999 study. The methodology of this study involved a mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis techniques to update Haaland's 1999 dental hygiene mapping study (Haaland, 1999). The research design consisted of a retrospective analysis of cited references from a three-year sample of core dental hygiene journals, as well as a survey of major databases to determine indexing coverage. The study's methodology was guided by Bradford's Law of Scattering, which posits that a core of journals produces a significant proportion of the literature in a given field, with the number of journals decreasing as the number of relevant articles increases (Bradford, 1934). To identify the core dental hygiene journals, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Journal Citation Reports (JCR) database, which provides a list of journals ranked by impact factor and subject category (Garfield, 2006).
